Six years have passed since we assumed the duties of the Presidency of the Civil Service Board, six years during which we have aspired to perform our duty with honesty, impartiality, and a high sense of responsibility, and here we stand today before the sixth report which we submit to the Office of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers with greater determination and resolve to achieve a just and honest administration, an administration that performs its duties with a high degree of professionalism and transparency, supported by employees devoted to public service and voluntarily willing to give and sacrifice, and this is a goal from which we shall never deviate regardless of the obstacles and however costly the sacrifices may be, and over the past years we have outlined the steps aimed at this, the latest of which was what we set forth in our annual report for the year 2003 under the title "A Plan for Administrative Reform". Six years have passed, and we still raise our voice in the hope that the voice may find an echo, raising our voice to say "that in order to build a modern and contemporary administration, we must observe the virtues of integrity, justice, impartiality, scientific rules, a sense of responsibility, and the sanctity of the public interest, making them prevail throughout the administration in all its utilities and activities. What we aspire to in our keenness to perform our duty, appreciate responsibility, and combat corruption in preparation for building the long-awaited administration, ultimately means adhering to the spirit of the system, voluntary submission to the provisions of the law, rising above private interests, and self-denial. Six years, and we still repeat that corruption has penetrated from every side and direction, interests have ramified, and it has acquired ways and outlets through which it infiltrates, and perhaps one of the most important reasons for its supplies to continue and survive is the political and sectarian "immunity" that embodies the protective umbrella for all corrupt persons. The employee who realizes that no political or sectarian umbrella protects him will inevitably continue tirelessly to sharpen his abilities and develop his competencies for the better. In return for this, the methods of appointment and selection must be improved, as it is no longer permissible after today for a candidate to sit for one examination only, and then assume a high administrative position fortified with all kinds of immunities until he reaches the age of sixty-four. The sectarian system that has extended its threads into the administration, hiding at times and brandishing its interests through domination and extortion at other times, is the protector of its corrupt affiliates, as it places partisan and sectarian affiliation ahead of competence and merit, a matter which has frequently turned the administration into a warehouse for storing cronies, henchmen, and the incompetent. Hence, I saw the necessity to re-present the content of what was stated in the annual report on the Board's work for the year 2003, perhaps as a reminder that may benefit people of understanding and insight. The Civil Service Board, which is a fundamental nucleus in the public administration in Lebanon and a pivotal tributary among its tributaries, has been entrusted with tasks defined by the laws in force, the fulfillment of which is governed by regulatory texts, which are the tasks of supervising the transactions received from various ministries, public administrations, public institutions, and municipalities subject to its supervision, relating to employees' affairs and their various functional statuses. However, through these tasks, the Civil Service Board has - in addition to its supervisory role, a pioneering orientalist role, tending towards laying hands on all the negative aspects that constitute tampering with the administration, which, if left untreated, would prevent its advancement towards better performance, and that role is represented in monitoring points of weakness, feebleness, and defect, which are plagues preventing its progress and development, and devising the necessary and appropriate solutions, means, and methods to avert the dangers and damages resulting from those plagues. Whereas the Civil Service Board, over a span of six years, and through its successive annual reports each year, has kept pace with the conditions of the administration and the level of its performance, in all its contents and details, in a spirit of impartiality and responsibility, analysing and detailing the presentation of its facts and proposing draft solutions, patterns, methods, and means which lead, if adopted, to the right direction aimed at saving the administration and liberating it from the causes of its failure and backwardness, and confronting the penetration of corruption into every corner thereof, so as to ensure meeting the citizen's thirst for better service, optimal performance, and more general and comprehensive production, at the lowest cost and in the shortest possible time, the latest of which was what it included in the text and content of its annual report for the year 2003, by which I mean an integrated administrative reform project that lays down the basic foundations and solid pillars for restoring the administrative structure, which would advance the administration and elevate it in a pioneering manner to the ranks of progress and modernity to face the coming challenges. The administrative reform project which this Board presented with pride and honour, certain that it is not permissible for the administration to linger and refrain from adopting it and following its guidelines and premises, to save this homeland and pull it out of its stumble, and by which it intended to sound the alarm, alerting and warning that the time has come to take our pioneering step, sharpen our resolve, and mobilize energies to rise from our stumbling, especially since it is not too late to catch up with a global procession rushing forward at an indescribable speed, making its way in steady escalation according to a geometric progression and driven by the latest technologies, while we are still marking time at the pace of an arithmetic progression with no initiative, no enterprise, no renaissance, and no life in it. And despite what this Board has presented, the state of the administration remains as it is, having not received the required attention, and no one has heeded the consequences it could reach, as the penetration of corruption has spread throughout all the veins and arteries of the administration, and in every aspect thereof, in administrations, institutions, and municipalities: meagre output and service performance at an unacceptable level, where damages have become general and comprehensive, leading to their spillover with their negative effects onto the private sector after their spread in the public sector. The Civil Service Board considers, in light of the foregoing, having grown weary of calling out, reminding, alerting, and warning, that any talk on its part about the conditions of the administration and its project to reform it has come to fall within the framework of rumination, repetition, and local routine, which gradually loses its content and life, so long as every proposal of its collapses and ends up in the corners of neglect, oblivion, and indifference, in a manner that has rendered it a matter of supererogation. However, out of our concern for a homeland we want to be free, and the foremost of its freedom is manifested in liberating its administration from every shackle in which it is bound, which paralyzes its movement and drives it to a slow death. And in compliance with a hope that guides us, a will still accompanied by determination, and a drive that has never lost its faith in God, shaded by the dreams and visions that we foresaw when we assumed our mission in the presidency of this Board, and which we still hope and yearn to see embodied as living, vibrant realities that save us from the horror of disturbing dreams and their nightmares - by which I mean backwardness and ignorance - and place us on the brink of an aperture of light whose beam breathes into us, heralding the start of a launch towards a better administration that restores right to its rightful place. And whereas the project previously presented constitutes - in our opinion - the successful remedy for our chronic illness, and inevitably contains - at a minimum - what contributes to healing the administration of its ailments, so that it becomes a healthy, sound, recovered, and modern administration, therefore it must be swallowed whatever the circumstances and obstacles may be. Accordingly, we deem it incumbent upon us to recall, briefly, its most important pillars, within the framework of the context set forth below, and in light of the reference to what previous governments proposed in an attempt to address administrative activity, on the basis of distributing it and dividing its types between the public and private sectors, or in partnership between the two sectors (mixed utilities). Since this matter has not been definitively resolved to date, whereas the proper course requires resolving it, taking a final decision regarding it, and subjecting it in light thereof to a reconsideration of the study of the structure of the public sector in a manner that embodies the administrative activity entrusted to it, given its impact on its organization and the issuance of the necessary texts for it, so that the matter is not left unchecked indefinitely, and to avoid further decline. Finally, it must be pointed out in this context that many public utilities managed within the framework of public institutions of an investment nature (electricity - water - telecommunications) were previously proposed on the basis that they would be managed by way of "privatization", and accordingly we consider that it is necessary to hasten to bring this matter out of the circle of stagnation, in a way that paves the way for determining the activities that should be managed through the public sector, which must be governed by conditions belonging to modernity and keeping pace with the spirit of the age, to which we previously referred in our reform project included in the report of this Board for the year 2003, and upon which we see no harm in casting a brief glance, as a reminder thereof, so that the reminder may be of benefit. Perhaps the beginning of the reform process must be initiated by defining the role of administrative institutions, which must focus in the coming stage on reorganizing and studying the various administrative bodies and structures in the light of professionalism and transparency, leading to an effective and rapid performance of the functions of the State, such that the job position is not a place for passing time or amusement and a heavy burden on the public treasury, but rather is necessary for performing a required activity within the framework of an administrative structure commensurate with the size of the purpose for which it was established. And such that the employees therein are characterized by the duty of loyalty and dedication to work and performing work in a proper manner, and possess sufficient skills to perform their work within a framework of credibility and a spirit of responsibility. The way to achieve those goals passes through the following constants: 1 - Modernizing structures and reducing their size. 2 - Modernizing public service regulations. 3 - Activating the principle of reward and punishment. 4 - Applying the texts and regulations in force. 5 - Rationalizing expenditure and stopping waste. 6 - Preventing political interference in the administration.

First: Reconsidering and Modernising the Organisational Structures: The central apparatus of the State organised pursuant to Legislative Decree No. 111 dated 12/6/1959, and after six amendments introduced thereto since the year 1966 up to the last amendment effected in the year 2000 pursuant to Law 247, remains below the aspirations of the modern State and is not commensurate with the financial and economic capabilities of Lebanon, and we consider that it has become necessary to determine the economic and service activities from which the State may withdraw and entrust the administration thereof to local councils (municipalities) or to the private sector wherever that is possible, and in light of the activities that remain for the public administration, the organisational structures must be as concise as possible, and in a manner wherein functions and responsibilities become clear where there is no room for duplication, but rather integrate within a framework of complete cooperation and coordination. The foremost pillars of administrative reform are manifested in reforming and modernising the organisational structure, and an objective and in-depth study of the central administrative apparatus of the State and of the number of public institutions affiliated therewith in comparison with what we envision for the role of the administrations of the State, shall lead to numerous results, the least of which is the conviction of the necessity to abolish certain ministries and institutions or to merge some of them with others, in a manner commensurate with the social and economic circumstances that characterise Lebanon under a central administrative leadership working and coordinating side by side with oversight bodies that bear full responsibility in implementing the general policy of governance and of the State, and thereafter moving - after determining this number and after granting the Government the right to issue legislative decrees that facilitate putting those projects into execution rapidly - towards determining the appropriate organisational structures for each ministry and public institution in accordance with the objectives set out therefor, and here we propose: a - Abolishing numerous administrative public institutions and certain non-productive and ineffective investment public institutions, as well as merging numerous councils, funds, bodies, bureaux and committees or annexing them to the parent ministry within its administrative units and abolishing others thereof, whilst fixing the number of members of the boards of directors in public institutions so as not to exceed four members including the Chairman of the Board of Directors, which leads to rationalisation of expenditure and activation of decision-making centres and the speed of issuance thereof, whilst re-subjecting public institutions to Decree No. 4517/72 as amended and to the oversight of the Central Inspection, the Court of Audit and the Civil Service Board in a manner that guarantees the unity of legislation and good performance. b - Fixing the number of ministries so as not to exceed 14 ministries as a maximum in a manner commensurate with the requirements of the modern State, namely: 1 - The Ministry of Justice 2 - The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Emigrants 3 - The Ministry of Finance 4 - The Ministry of National Defence 5 - The Ministry of Culture, Education and Higher Education 6 - The Ministry of Public Health 7 - The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs

8 - The Ministry of Economy, Industry and Trade 9 - The Ministry of Energy and Water 10 - The Ministry of Telecommunications 11 - The Ministry of Agriculture 12 - The Ministry of Tourism and Environment 13 - The Ministry of Public Works and Transport 14 - The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities We have previously indicated in our preceding report that supporting such orientations would control expenditure, abolish ineffective secondary positions, and adopt flat organisational structures, from and to which the transfer of information is facilitated and consequently the provision of services in a better and faster manner, and this requires dispensing with certain positions such as the position of "clerk", "editor" and "typist" and replacing them with the position of "data entry clerk", as well as ceasing the dispersion and distribution of functions and powers pertaining to directorates across a number of departments and sections without any justification or productive motive other than an increase in expenditure, and sufficing as much as possible with providing for a limited number of specialist employees in those directorates (at the level of the Second and Third Categories) who assist the head of the directorate in performing his functions without the need to establish additional affiliated administrative units (at the level of the Third Category) in a manner that impedes

the exchange of information and the speed of rendering the service, in application of the principle of: "the few and the elite in administration". Reconsidering the administrative organisational structure in the manner proposed must take into consideration the anticipated challenges, particularly at the level of increasing competition, increasing productivity and the quality of service, always in parallel with the possibility of transferring numerous functions: "from the central administration to the local administration" in accordance with the principle that must be promoted. We pause here to emphasise a matter and urge that it be placed at the forefront of the State's concern, namely the final job description in light of what the organisational structures of the administration settle upon, and determining the nature of each position, its competencies, and the academic and practical qualifications appropriate therefor, in other words giving municipalities a greater margin of movement and exercise of functions and assuming certain powers that originally pertain to public administrations (after amending the texts necessary therefor), in a manner that enhances the role of local administrative councils and supports the application of administrative decentralisation more clearly and rapidly, particularly in the field of education and instruction, health, public works, social services, agriculture, tourism and environment, and for this reason it is required that we keep in mind that the central administration and the local administration are on the same level in terms of the need of individuals therefor, and that mutual cooperation between them is a fundamental necessity to achieve a distinguished national administration.

Second: Reconsidering the Public Service Regulations and the Necessity of Updating Them There is no doubt that the traditional form of recruitment is no longer consistent with the spirit of leadership and initiative required of the Administration; therefore, what ought to be adopted is a new recruitment system for a limited period, through which persons possessing special knowledge who may be brought in from outside the Administration by way of competitive examination are attracted and impelled to assume leadership positions as well as promoted to important positions, and on this basis, the Administration is freed from the burden of commitment to incompetent persons until they reach the statutory age (64 years), and finds itself before numerous options in accordance with the skill and achievements of the persons, as it either terminates the contract with them, or renews it, or transfers to the permanent establishment those whose competence and professional leadership qualities are proven, and by this methodology we arrive at a modern administration that keeps pace with the requirements of a society that has become full of rapid developments. In this regard, we consider that the political authority must respond to those variables, and work to restore confidence in its ability to craft solutions and confront upcoming challenges if it wishes to lay the foundation for sustainable economic and social development, and the Civil Service Board considers, within this framework, that selection on the basis of competitive examination should be generalised so as to encompass public administrations, public institutions, and municipalities in implementation of Article /12/ of the Constitution, such that entitlement, competence, and merit alone are the criterion of admission for entry into the public office, as a prelude to closing the outlets of recruitment in all its forms (contracting, wage-earners, employment by invoice) outside the field of legitimate competition, that is, within the ambit of the competitive examination, which must be the sole avenue in this direction towards which the State ought to marshal all its authority, so that administrative conditions may be rectified, the State of law and institutions may prevail under the banner of equality and justice, and the citizen's dream may be realised. This reality also necessitates introducing radical and direct amendments to the Personnel Regulations, and all other regulations relating to the public office, so that this office does not remain, as we have previously indicated, guaranteed until the age of retirement is reached whether the employee performs his full responsibilities or not, for so long as he remains under the protection of the political, sectarian, or confessional umbrella that shelters him, and therefore it is imperative to link remaining in service or the renewal of contracting to the results of performance evaluation and to the approval of the Civil Service Board thereon, and not to renew it automatically through the annual decisions issued in this regard. Here we see no harm in recalling the steps that have been accomplished at this level: 1 - The Civil Service Board referred to the Office of the Minister of State for Administrative Reform, pursuant to its letter No. 52/S 1 dated 28/2/2003, a draft law comprising the introduction of fundamental and substantive amendments to the current Personnel Regulations, whereby administrative employees shall be subject to more flexible provisions and greater incentives in accordance with their skills, achievements, specialisations, and academic degrees in accordance with the required demands of change. These persons shall be recruited from within the public sector and from outside it. In order to ascend to this system smoothly, suitable persons must be enticed to shoulder the burden of these tasks by granting "remuneration commensurate with the hardship", and this necessarily requires introducing a rapid amendment to the current salary scales after the lapse of more than five years since the last amendment introduced thereto which entered into force on 1/1/1999, in order for the reform to be more effective and capable of attracting creative elements. Here one must pause before the salaries, wages, and allowances in certain public institutions fostered by confessional and sectarian conditions and climates which are neither proportionate to nor consistent with the rules when measured against other positions in the public administrations, such that unfairness and maldistribution become clearly and manifestly evident in violation of the simplest requirements of justice and equity (the Council of the South, the Council for Development and Reconstruction, the Casino in comparison with the Central Inspection, the Civil Service Board, the Higher Disciplinary Board). And the question arises: what are the tasks performed by the presidents, members, and boards of directors of the aforementioned institutions, in comparison with the tasks assumed by the Board of each of the Civil Service Board, the Central Inspection, and the Higher Disciplinary Board, noting that the high salaries, wages, and allowances received by the presidents and members of the boards of directors of the aforementioned institutions are in their origin consensual, leading to the benefit of a limited number of persons, and the policies, sects, and confessions that were behind their appointment do not benefit directly therefrom. Accordingly, it is mandatory to reconsider the issue of high salaries, rectify them, and adopt a single criterion under which they fall, so that they settle on a basis of the spirit of equity and justice, and in light of the nature of the tasks and the characteristics of the positions or tasks assigned to each beneficiary. In the context of the preceding paragraph, we consider the following: First: With respect to appointment to the permanent establishment: Raising the passing grades for public service positions to become 12/20 as a general average at least, and amending the methods of selection so that greater focus is placed on the analytical skills of the candidates, while emphasising the necessity of the candidate's proficiency in at least one foreign language, and his ability to use the computer as one of the basic conditions in the selection process. And Second: With respect to contracting: Issuing a law permitting contracting for vacant positions in the permanent establishment of all public administrations on the basis of competitive examination and linking its renewal to the results of performance evaluation and to the approval of the Civil Service Board. As for contracting for tasks: it must be restricted to persons possessing special knowledge and qualifications who hold higher university degrees, both technical and technological exclusively, and ceasing contracting for tasks in positions of Category Four and below or with persons holding specialisations available within the conditions of appointment provided for permanent positions (except in the case of contracting for a position), with the necessity of setting a ceiling for contractors for tasks not exceeding the rate of 20% of the total permanent employees in each administration as a maximum limit, provided that—in all cases—the salary scale applicable to employees of public administrations shall apply to contractors for tasks with respect to their allowances, and in accordance with the same bases in force when determining the salary. For today there are among these contractors those whose monthly allowance exceeds the salary of the President of the Civil Service Board or the salary of the President of the State Council..., indeed their total number has exceeded the number of permanent employees, except where the contracting is conducted for technological and technical tasks requiring high and distinguished scientific competencies, in which case it may be allocated allowances, albeit within the limits of a ceiling proposed by the administration concerned and approved by the Civil Service Board. Third: Giving greater effectiveness and role to the results of performance evaluation, and investing them better by taking measures against employees (and contractors) who obtain a result of "average" and below in the evaluation of their performance, starting from transfer to other positions or demotion of category or grade, and ending with termination of service, in a manner that reinforces the principle of "the few and the elite" within the Administration, and links incentives to distinguished performance. 3 - In order to ensure the soundness of selection for the public office and immunise it against all defects, it is imperative to place the right man in the right place, and this shall be done by adopting the "principle of functional specialisation" for assuming public positions, by determining the academic degrees and additional conditions of appointment for each position of Categories Three and Two, and according to the nature of the tasks pertaining thereto, and this is what has actually begun to be adopted in the competitive examination that took place on 6/3/2004 for appointment to administrative positions of Category Two, and here we propose issuing a unified regulatory text encompassing all analogous positions in the public administrations whereby the additional conditions of appointment for each type of position of Categories One, Two, and Three are determined after dividing them into groups according to the nature of the tasks pertaining to each of them. And this must be accompanied by the repeal of the text of Article Two of the Draft Law promulgated by Decree No. 3169 dated 23/4/1972 which repeals the special and additional conditions imposed for appointment to positions of Category One. Furthermore, the Civil Service Board has prepared a draft law aiming at appointment to public positions on the basis of specific academic degrees commensurate with the tasks of the position required to be filled, and this draft was referred to the Presidency of the Council of Ministers pursuant to Letter No. 217/S 1 dated 5/10/2001, and there is also a necessity to reconsider and scrutinise many of the degrees and specialisations held by many an employee or person performing a public service (...) in administrative, investment, or academic public institutions, with the aim of verifying the soundness of those degrees on the one hand, and examining the extent of their proportionality to the tasks or works entrusted to him on the other hand. 4 - In parallel with amending the Personnel Regulations, including the necessity of amending the regulations pertaining to the oversight bodies, such that the rectification process encompasses all technical and structural aspects of the public administrations, radical reforms have recently been introduced to its structure and organisation pursuant to a draft law prepared by the Civil Service Board, leading to a simplified administration but with conditions and standards capable of attracting persons of high capabilities, so that the Administration does not remain a centre into which incompetent elements lacking the required academic level infiltrate, and pursuant to the aforementioned draft, benefits were linked to productivity under penalty of dismissal or transfer to other positions. And in completion of strengthening the role of the Civil Service Board in monitoring the texts relating to the public service and the employees therein, and in preservation

of the principle of legality, we consider it necessary to grant the Board of the Civil Service Board "standing and interest" before the administrative judiciary to file an action for annulment of texts and decisions that violate the laws in force relevant to the Administration.

Third: Activating the Principle of Reward and Punishment Among the essential points that must also be focused on to activate the State administrations is emphasizing the principle of reward and punishment and adopting it as a primary factor of priority in rectification operations, and this shall only be achieved through the availability of: - Proper selection of leading administrative elites. - The existence of strict, serious and continuous hierarchical supervision. - The existence of fair incentives (advancement - promotion - bonus). 1 - We have previously indicated in the body of our previous report that violations resulting from the public office, particularly the violation of the text of Articles / 14/ and /15/ of the Personnel Regulations, are in one way or another the responsibility of four parties, and in view of the importance of the necessity to address the subject of violations in the context of combating administrative corruption and establishing the rules of the desired administrative reform, we reiterate the reminder of the responsibility of those parties, who are: "the offending employee", his immediate superior, and the higher hierarchical superior, in addition to the inspector responsible for inspection works in the administration to which the concerned employee belongs. For among the foremost duties of the immediate superior is to watch over the proper performance by the employees subordinate to him of the tasks entrusted to them, to inspect the departments subordinate to him, to control daily attendance and to watch over the good relationship of the employees with stakeholders, and consequently he is responsible for the works of the departments and the employees subordinate to him. Accordingly, violations and all forms of laxity in a given administration reflect to a large extent the negligence of the immediate superior in watching over the application of the laws and regulations in force, the failure to enforce order, and hesitation in suppressing violations (Article 14 - Legislative Decree 112/59); for instance, many employees in the First and Second Categories and below have come to openly declare their partisan affiliations and their assumption of leadership positions therein, and to participate publicly and in a documented manner in the basic and leadership activities of those parties, thereby violating the prohibition stipulated in Article /15/ of the Personnel Regulations without accountability or oversight, and this may be attributed to two reasons: - The absence of accountability and hierarchical supervision. - The supporting political umbrella. Thereby, the pillars of the law are undermined and the attributes of neutrality and objectivity of the public employee fade away. Hence the focus on selecting administrative leaders who possess values, integrity and impartiality, so as to guarantee without any regard for political repercussions and for the support sought by no small number of employees affiliated with political references and leaders. From here, it is required to strengthen the role of the Central Inspection as a primary supervisory body in combating administrative laxity and the corruption dominating the administration, to confirm the hypothesis that corruption and inspection are two matters each of which is the antithesis of the other; for it is inconceivable for administrative laxity to continue in light of the existence of an inspection body in a given State, and thus it is inconceivable for there to be room for both together. Neglecting the principle of reward and punishment in the past is what led to discouraging honest employees from working in accordance with their consciences, and encouraged corruptors to persist in corruption. 2 - Although the promotion of an employee or his advancement from one category to another category is among the most important incentives secured for him by the State, automatic advancement supported by recommendations to satisfy the electorate must cease, and it must become part of the mechanism adopted by the administration to activate the principle of reward and punishment, based on the results of performance evaluation or on the promotion and advancement roster provided for in the Personnel Regulations, and we see here the necessity of introducing a fair and impartial performance evaluation system, through which the skills and achievements of individuals are measured correctly and more accurately as a prelude to utilizing it in drawing up a statement of the grades included in the promotion roster to propose their advancement or promotion. The Civil Service Board has in this sense referred on 30/1/2002 to the Presidency of the Council of Ministers a new system for performance evaluation that guarantees the achievement of those principles and works to put them into practical application, in the hope of issuing it as quickly as possible, in addition to the promotion and advancement system prepared by the Office of the Minister of State for Administrative Reform, on which this Board expressed an opinion that led to its reconsideration in accordance with the observations presented by this Board at the time in respect thereof. 3 - Supporting a firm application of the "Code of Conduct for Public Employees", and activating the work of the National Anti-Corruption Committee, the establishment of which the Council of Ministers approved by its Decision No. /51/ dated 4/10/2000, in order to get rid of all forms of nepotism and placing oneself above the law.

Fourth: Application of Texts and Regulations in Force: - The non-application, negligence or disregard of a legal or regulatory text has become one of the prominent phenomena in the work of institutions, and this has appeared in multiple forms, either by neglecting the text in its entirety or by applying part of it and omitting the other part thereof for long periods. Examples of this are numerous, and this reality constitutes one of the most harmful elements to the administration which affect the moral force of the issued laws and regulations; for the Illicit Enrichment Law (Legislative Decree 38) - for example - was issued more than 50 years ago on (18/2/1953) and was followed by the Law issued on 14/4/1954, yet it was not put into effect until after it was replaced by a new text in the year 1999, and today there are many issued texts that remain unimplemented to date, including those relating to reform programs, such as Law No. 221 dated 29/5/2000 relating to the organization of the water sector and the merger of the autonomous offices subordinate to it. From here appears the importance of applying texts within the time limits specified for them and within a reasonable period, so as to strengthen confidence in the administration and guarantee the sound application of the law.

Fifth: Rationalising Expenditure and Halting Waste: 1 - The matter of waste in public funds and futile or arbitrary expenditure - so to speak - is the principal factor in the increase of the budget deficit and the growth of this deficit among several factors, and among these factors is the matter of renting government buildings, and we affirm what we have previously indicated in our previous report, regarding the necessity of finding a radical and swift solution to this dilemma by means of constructing government buildings and unifying and grouping them in accordance with the report prepared by the Committee tasked with preparing the practical study for constructing government complexes chaired by the Head of the Department of Research and Guidance, which was published in the Official Gazette /Issue 33 of the year 2002/ page 4010 - This step is capable of saving hundreds of thousands of dollars for the public treasury, and it suffices in this context to cast a glance at the amounts incurred annually by the State on the matter of renting government buildings, some of which exceed the need of those working therein, for us to realise directly the importance of the matter from the financial aspect first and the administrative aspect second, this being in addition to its importance in terms of forming the specialised and suitable administrative building for each administration according to its need and the nature of its work and the necessity of its presence in a place that makes it easy for citizens to commute thereto, and thereby is formed the most important element among the elements that contribute to simplifying administrative work procedures. 2 - Halting all forms of aid and grants to institutions, associations, and free private schools. - The need appears urgent for exceptional and courageous political decisions in this context, as the matter is not limited to certain ordinary measures in reducing expenditure figures in the budget, but must go beyond it to all other issues that drain our revenues, and this is no easy matter due to its connection to tightly interconnected interests. For just as it is not possible under the current financial situation to continue spending without a ceiling specified by a law, it is likewise not permissible to continue giving aid and subsidies to schools, associations, joint projects, and service centres without effective oversight or objective controls and criteria, otherwise what is the role and utility of the ministries of services, and what is the role of the local administrations (the municipalities) if the matter will ultimately devolve to private associations and institutions that enrich themselves at the expense of public funds and absorb what is collected in fees and taxes. 3 - The necessity of enacting a text prohibiting the purchase of furniture and means of transport (cars) for public administrations and public institutions except pursuant to a study of need prepared by the Department of Research and Guidance and in accordance with specified criteria, coupled with its approval thereof. 4 - Emphasising the collection of State revenues periodically and continuously from the investment institutions that it owns wholly or partially, and working to increase their revenues and audit their accounts more effectively, among which are, by way of enumeration and not limitation (Casino du Liban - the Regie...). And we likewise see giving a greater role to the Court of Audit in financial oversight and in approving transactions for the execution of works and tenders, so that it may have its effective impact in this context. 5 - Reconsidering the high and unusual salaries and allowances received by a non-civil servant in public administrations and public institutions, and requesting the latter to draw up an inventory of the committees, offices, and bodies affiliated therewith and their true cost and the number of employees therein, and the tasks entrusted thereto, and indicating the administrative units in the permanent cadre that perform the same tasks performed by those committees, offices, and bodies, and submitting a report in this regard to the Presidency of the Council of Ministers as a prelude to taking the appropriate decision in this matter by abolishing many of the anomalous situations that have come to be known as "parallel administrations" in a manner that ensures the control of expenditure on the one hand and the non-conflict of powers between public administrations and those committees and offices on the other hand. 6 - Activating the Illicit Enrichment Law in order to halt the draining of public funds; it is necessary in this context to grant the Financial Public Prosecutor (after amending the text of the Law) the power to proceed automatically, and without the need for a complaint from an aggrieved party, to initiate the illicit enrichment action in a manner that activates the investigation operations into the funds owned by persons whose ordinary resources do not enable them to own them, especially if the manifestations of wealth and expenditure on their part are not consistent with those resources.

Sixth: Prevention of political interference in the administration: Political interference in the administration has negatively affected the prestige of the State, its standing, and its image before public opinion, and has greatly contributed to the spread of corruption and the violation of laws and regulations as a result of the political pressures exercised by politicians on the administration and its employees, which prompts the taking of swift measures to curb this deterioration which may undermine all efforts aimed at improving the image of the public service before the general public, and among those measures are: 1 - Activating the role of the Directors General by amending Item «Third» of Article (7) of Legislative Decree No. 111 dated 12/6/1959 (Organisation of Public Administrations) as follows: a - The Director General shall initial draft decrees, decisions, and all transactions submitted to the Minister or to whoever exercises by virtue of the law the powers of the Minister, with the exception of constitutional powers, or shall express his written opinion thereon. This written opinion shall be attached to the transaction and referred with it to the competent authorities. The initialling of the Director General or his written opinion shall be deemed an essential and mandatory formality. b - Every person required by law or regulation to submit a recommendation or a proposal must submit his recommendation or proposal within a time limit of seven days for a recommendation and three days for a proposal from the date the transaction is lodged with him; otherwise, the competent authority may proceed with the transaction and execute it without the need for the recommendation or proposal, and in this case the holder of the relevant competence shall bear full responsibility for this transaction if its execution constitutes a violation of the law. 2 - Emphasising the immediate and firm application of Council of Ministers Decision No. 2 dated 27/12/1989 concerning the request to Ministers not to confirm and insist upon the execution of orders and instructions to which their subordinates draw their attention in writing as being in violation of the laws and regulations in force in an explicit and clear manner pursuant to the provisions of Paragraph (2) of Article (14) of the Staff Regulations, except after submitting the matter to the Council of Ministers. 3 - The necessity that the selection of First Category employees, whether from within the general administrative cadre or from outside it, be in accordance with criteria and principles that serve the nature of the position to be filled and operate in its interest, and as a result of oral examinations, and written ones where necessary, conducted by a special committee formed for this purpose in accordance with a specific mechanism. 4 - Deeming political interference in the administration an offence punishable by law, and therefore, in addition to issuing the necessary legislation to this effect, instructions must be issued prohibiting political officials in the State - pursuant to the principle of ministerial solidarity - and other politicians from contacting administrations not directly subordinate to them by any means whatsoever, in return for halting all forms of employment carried out by Ministers under any title or capacity whatsoever, and linking that directly to the Civil Service Board on the basis of competitive examination, merit, entitlement, and equality of opportunity, as set out above. - And the separation of ministerial office from parliamentary representation may play an effective role in this framework. 5 - Repealing the text of Article /97/ of the Staff Regulations, given that these Regulations were emptied of their substance when they included in Article /97/ thereof the subjection of every dispute arising between the Minister and the Civil Service Board to the will of the Council of Ministers such that the latter adjudicates the dispute, and its opinion is adopted even if it is in explicit violation of the law. The absolute interpretation of the aforementioned Article /97/ was used to circumvent laws and regulations, such that decisions of the Council of Ministers in most cases took on the effect of laws that repeal or amend the application of the law, whereas the dispute arising in this area was ordinarily over nothing other than the Civil Service Board's adherence to the application of the law, and thus the decisions of the Council of Ministers that contradict the resolutions of the Civil Service Board became a pretext invoked by employees to justify their unlawful acts and an incentive for them to do so, which reflected negatively on the requirements of the public interest and administrative performance in particular. Therefore, there is an urgent necessity to repeal the text of Article /97/ of the Staff Regulations in order to enable the Civil Service Board to continue its supervisory work in the desired and required manner, as there is neither importance nor an effective role for this Board in light of the existence of the aforementioned Article /97/, and thereby another step is recorded to be added to the qualitative step formed with the issuance of Law No. 259 dated 6/ 10/1993 which made the decisions of the State Council binding on the administration. 6 - In parallel with the foregoing, the necessity of requesting the Chamber of Deputies to observe the non-inclusion in the General Budget Law, or in special exceptional laws, of provisions that infringe upon the fundamental pillars of the public service, particularly those relating to a competitive examination restricted to a specific category of persons in violation of the text of the Seventh and Twelfth Articles of the Constitution, and also those relating to laws that permit granting benefits to a specific category of employees on the basis of partial solutions and in violation of the principle of comprehensiveness and generality that must characterise the law, and also those relating to legislation that exempts certain persons from the requirement of a competitive examination for entry into the permanent cadre, or from the requirement of holding an academic qualification. Finally, that reform may appear difficult in light of the critical economic circumstances, and it therefore requires swift and firm steps with a direct and tangible impact, and the political authority must promote its corrective policies further so that they become better understood by citizens, and this will only be achieved through halting waste, increasing revenues, and reducing the deficit. Whereas the regression or slowing down of reform steps would harm that process and facilitate an assault upon it by the adversely affected holders of privileges, it is therefore necessary to expedite the submission of the laws and regulations required for the points and headings mentioned above within a framework of transparency, calm, and justice, failing which it will be easy to incite public opinion and consequently waste the opportunity once again. The six axes that we have mentioned above are concomitant and interconnected measures; in other words, they are an indivisible whole, which presupposes, for their success, that they be put forward as a single package, so as to ensure sound planning and effective performance. Thus, we have the honour of submitting an integrated reform plan for the coming five years, capable of achieving the hope to which we all aspire. For this project that we present, were it to be put into scientific application, after the issuance of the necessary texts, and the availability of support

political, clear and explicit for it, would move us from an administration of intertwined regulations to a simplified administration that secures speed in providing information and quality in delivering services on the basis of «better work and less expenditure», a decision-making and more transparent administration based on a few elite clean-handed workers, an administration in the service of all such that the employee's loyalty is solely to the nation and the law, thereby enabling us to win the wager of the coming phase.

First: The Civil Service Board since the beginning of the consideration of its establishment: A- The idea of establishing the Civil Service Board had been seriously maturing in the mind of the legislator since the beginning of the forties, that is, since before Independence; for in February of the year 1942, a "Directorate of the Personnel Department" was established in the Presidency of the Republic, to which were entrusted matters of personal files and the rendering of opinion, in what is called today the personal affairs of employees, particularly cases of appointment, promotion, dismissal, and termination of service. Despite that, this "establishment" remained, as it appears, theoretical because matters continued to lack in these cases a central body to undertake them, regulate them, coordinate among them, and at least prevent these matters from reaching the nadir that they reached in the second term of the era of President Bechara El Khoury and which led to the fuelling of the opposition, that opposition which brought down the aforementioned President in September of the year 1952 and attributed to him, at the head of what it forgot, his silence regarding the administrative corruption that reached its peak at the aforementioned time. B - Pursuant to Legislative Decree No. 12/55 dated 7/1/ 1955, the Government established a Civil Service Board in the Presidency of the Council of Ministers. By referring to that stage at the end of the year 1954, it appears that a dispute had arisen between the Government in its endeavour to establish a Civil Service Board in the manner in which it was established

pursuant to Legislative Decree No. 12/55 and the aforementioned Planning Board, and it expressed its reaction in a report it submitted to the Chamber of Deputies dated 25/1/1955, in which the following paragraph appeared verbatim: "Four days before the expiry of the period for issuing legislative decrees, the Government requested the Planning and Economic Development Board to draft a legislative decree to create this institution, but it was surprised by a legislative decree numbered 12 concerning the public service which was under printing in the Official Gazette, and which provides in one of its final articles that the Government has the right to create, by a decree taken in the Council of Ministers, the Civil Service Board composed of the first and second categories, which eliminated the objective of the draft submitted by the Planning and Development Board, which is that the Civil Service Board be independent and that its members be from outside the employees so that it would not be affected by political considerations". In execution of the provisions of the delegation granted to it pursuant to Legislative Decree No. 12/55, the Government issued in May of the year 1955 a decision whereby it formed the structural organisation of the Civil Service Board from the Head of the Chamber of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers as President and from the rest of the Directors General as members. A matter which proved that the apprehension of the Planning and Economic Development Board of the established Board losing its independence was well-founded. C - In an assessment of this early stage of thinking of establishing a Civil Service Board, it may be said that those in charge of the affairs of reform were seriously entertained by the idea of establishing a Civil Service Board enjoying complete independence and undertaking the care of the affairs of the administration and the affairs of its employees in terms of developing its methods of work, modernising its cadres, properly selecting its employees, and following up on their career during

service, in preparation and training, rights and duties, and following up on the performance of their work and incentivising this performance morally through advancement based on good performance alone, and materially through rewards commensurate with the importance and quality of performance.

Second: The Civil Service Board and 12 June of the year 1959 A - Decree No. /193/ dated 26/12/1958 is considered the basic reference for the reform stage which witnessed the publication of 162 legislative decrees in the various aspects of administration and governance, of which 80 legislative decrees were in the period between 16 December 1958 to 10 June 1959, and 62 legislative decrees were announced on a single day, which is 12 June 1959. Legislative Decree 193 addressed the following central issues: defining the tasks of each post and the responsibilities entrusted to the employee, simplifying administrative transactions, or the mechanisms of the work of the administration, supervising execution, keeping political interferences away from the administration and creating a National Institute of Administration concerned with selecting the best employees and training them, and creating the "Civil Service Board" which constituted an important immunity for employees and the securing of protection for them during the performance of their duties, and making maximum use of the reports of experts to develop the Lebanese administration so that it may be compatible with the requirements of building the modern State along the lines of what the most advanced States do. B - On 12 June of the year 1959, the Government issued Legislative Decree No. 114 in which it established a Civil Service Board on the basis of the parliamentary delegation granted to the Government pursuant to the Law issued on 12/12/1958, and the first serious indication of the determination of the Government to establish the aforementioned Board was its proceeding to form what was called the Central Commission for Administrative Reform pursuant to Legislative Decree No. 193/58 mentioned above and entrusting it, among all that it entrusted it with, with "creating an independent body called the Civil Service Board concerned with all the affairs of employees and with constant acquaintance with the functioning of the administration with a view to proposing what leads to its improvement". The Board established pursuant to Legislative Decree No. 114/59 was formed of a board consisting of a President and two members who are the Head

of the Personnel Administration and the Head of the Preparation and Training Administration, and of two administrations which are the Personnel Administration, and the Preparation and Training Administration in which the National Institute of Administration and Development was established, and the Personnel Administration was formed of two departments: the Department of Supervision and Studies and the Department of Competitive Examinations and Personal Files, and the Preparation and Training Administration was formed in its turn of two departments: the Department of Preparation and Training, and the Secretariat of the National Institute of Administration and Development. Alongside that, the Joint Administrative Department was established and was linked directly to the President of the Board. - This formation of the Civil Service Board in the year 1959 came within a conception upon which hopes were pinned in order for it to lead the administration and the reform therein on a permanent basis and to be a guardian of the law, guaranteeing the liberation of the administration from the various pressures, particularly the sectarian and political ones among them, proceeding from its liberation of itself, its non-subjugation, and its independence, and creating a single central methodology in handling the affairs of employees that guarantees their coordination among all public administrations on the one hand and consequently their non-fragmentation on the other hand, and achieves in the end a single administrative authority combining the supervision of the decision and the supervision of its execution, and in short "achieves, according to what some saw, "a radical change in the affairs of employees and recruitment".

Third: The Tasks and Powers of the Civil Service Board: Through the composition set forth in the preceding paragraph, the powers of the Civil Service Board were defined in two forms: comprehensive and specific. A - As for the comprehensive power, it was defined in two scopes: - The scope of what may be called "civil servants' affairs", where there was vested in the Board all that the laws and regulations define for it in respect of the appointment of civil servants, their advancement, their allowances, their transfer, their disciplining, their dismissal from the service, and the rest of their personal affairs. - And the scope of what may be called "raising the professional standard of civil servants, specifically preparing civil servants for the post and training them during service". Perhaps the comprehensiveness of the powers granted to the Civil Service Board in the manner set forth above is what prompted some scholars of public administration to say of it that it is "the fundamental institution in the field of the public service", and others cite what the Central Body for Administrative Reform saw in it as being "the sole means to improve conditions". B - Whereas the specific powers varied across multiple types: B - 1: In the organisational field, tasks were vested in the Board relating to the organisation of public administrations, public institutions, and municipalities, and the determination of their cadres, including granting it the initiative to submit proposals relating to these subjects directly to the Council of Ministers. In explanation of this task, it may be summarised as entrusting to the Civil Service Board two dual matters: The First Matter: is manifested in expressing an opinion on the organisation of public administrations, that is, on the tasks and powers intended to be assigned to the units formed in the public administrations, as well as on the determination of their numerical cadres, and this matter leads the Board to express an opinion on the determination of the conditions of appointment to the posts created in these cadres and on the salaries determined therefor. The Second Matter: crystallises in taking the initiative to propose what is necessary directly to the Council of Ministers regarding the subjects listed above, and this second matter may be understood within what is called the "reorganisation of departments", a subject to which the Civil Servants Regulations accorded the importance it deserves pursuant to Article (72) thereof and in which the Civil Service Board was given a fundamental role. B - 2: In the field of civil servants' personal affairs, the Board was given powers relating to the appointment of civil servants, and appointment does not mean merely verifying the fulfilment of the conditions of appointment, but rather it may extend beyond that as being the authority that undertakes the conduct of competitive examinations in general, which qualify for the selection of civil servants on the basis of merit and entitlement. The Board was also given the power to attend to advancement and promotion through its keeping of personal files, its being entrusted with the matter of organising them and keeping summaries thereof, and its being given the right to produce the advancement list provided for in Article (33) of the Civil Servants Regulations and to approve the promotion roster provided for in Article (34) of the said Regulations, together with what the drawing up of the said list and roster requires in terms of assigning grades to the civil servants concerned therewith and the justifying and warranting reasons for advancement and promotion.

Fourth: The Civil Service Council Between the Present and the Future: Pursuant to Law No. 222 dated 29/5/2000, a structural amendment was introduced to the composition of the Council, and the main objective behind this amendment was separating the National Institute of Administration and Development and establishing a specialised institute managed in accordance with the regulations to which specialised public utilities are subject, enjoying financial and administrative autonomy and subject to the tutelage of the Civil Service Council and to the law of its establishment and its regulations, and the most prominent matter included in the aforementioned Law is the abolition of the Preparation and Training Administration in the Civil Service Council, in addition to amending the composition of the Board of the Council so that it became composed of:

- The President of the Civil Service Council (President). - The Head of the Personnel Administration (Member). - The Head of the Research and Guidance Administration (Member). And on 27/2/2002, Decree No. 7486 was issued, which included determining the details of the application of the provisions of Law No. 222/2000 with respect to amending the Decree Organizing the Civil Service Council No. 8337 dated 30/12/1961 - And in completion of the amendment introduced by Law 222/2000, and after the lapse of over forty years since its establishment on 12 June 1959, it has become necessary to reconsider the role of the Civil Service Council in a radical and qualitative manner, such that it assumes the leadership of the Lebanese administration in a more effective manner, and works on developing it in the field of personnel management or what has come to be known as human resources (administrative) management, and the regulations pertaining thereto in the light of emerging data and variables, and particularly in the following: * Transitioning from the traditional concept of "personnel affairs management", which was generally prevalent in many countries, and which is limited to applying and supervising the application of a set of different rules and procedures in public service regulations, to the modern concept which encompasses new functions and roles, the most important of which is the "strategic role" which aims at laying down policies and plans aimed at managing positions and skills within the prospective outlook for developing administrative human resources, and determining newly emerging positions, and the diverse and continuous training required therefor, and which also aims at keeping pace with the career paths of employees in the administration, and the early selection of administrative leaders with high capabilities in accordance with the principles of merit, entitlement, and equal opportunities. * Adapting to the major challenges facing public administration in the world which drive it towards modernisation and innovation in response to numerous internal and external pressures, the most prominent of which are: private sector competition, worsening financial crises that push towards reducing the size of the workforce in public administrations and injecting new competencies therein through attracting promising young elements to renew future cadres, and developing the capabilities of employees in the administration, so as to reach the management of the few and the elite in a manner that ensures better work and less expenditure; this is in addition to the increasing demands of the citizen in obtaining State services and prestaciones with the necessary speed and efficiency, where the focus has become more on qualitative satisfaction than on quantitative satisfaction, and consequently keeping pace with the effects of globalisation and integration at the global level. All these phenomena require from civil service bodies a serious endeavour to adopt effective policies for developing administrative human resources and for improving and developing public administration in a manner that ensures transforming it into an arm capable of implementing the State's policies and orientations with high efficiency, and working on elevating the level of services for the citizen. In the light of the foregoing, and in order to enable the Civil Service Council to carry out its new role in administrative development and planning for policies related to public sector employees, it was necessary to prepare a modern legal framework for the Civil Service Council that meets keeping pace with the occurring variables referred to above, and specifically through improving the recent amendment introduced by Law No. 222/2000, and making it more proportionate to the new role required of the Council, in a manner that serves the objectives and principles mentioned above. This is in addition to institutionalising the process of reform and development, which constitutes a response to all studies and theories in administrative science, which call for the continuity and permanence of the reform process and placing it in its proper institutional framework, and this is what prompted the creation of a "Development and Advancement Administration" in the cadre of the Council to replace the Preparation and Training Administration formerly, the Research and Guidance Administration currently, where a Directorate for Administrative Development was included in this Administration, which constitutes the practical model for institutionalising the process of modernisation and development, and through that, securing the independence of the new role of the Council and protecting it from pressures by isolating the reform institution from the influences of political institutions. However, that did not prevent providing for provisions requiring cooperation with the authorities that handle administrative development affairs in a manner that guarantees better work in this field and directs all political efforts towards serving the administration in a positive manner. Accordingly, the most prominent matters included in the draft law proposed to amend the organisation of the Civil Service Council are the following matters: 1 - Giving the Council an effective role in the field of formulating policies and strategies in the management of developing and planning administrative human resources in the public sector, while retaining its supervisory role with respect to verifying the legality of various transactions, procedures, and decisions related to the affairs of civil servants and employees submitted for its approval. 2 - Reconsidering the structure of the Council with respect to providing for specialised units capable of exercising the various roles, functions, and powers vested in it, and the structure provided for the following: * The Presidency of the Civil Service Council * The Personnel Administration * The Development and Advancement Administration The "Presidency of the Civil Service Council" is composed of: - The Joint Administrative Directorate - The Informatics Directorate The "Personnel Administration" is composed of: - The Control Directorate - The Studies Directorate - The Competitive Examinations and Specialisation Directorate The "Development and Advancement Administration" is composed of: - The Administrative Development Directorate - The Position Classification Directorate - The Organisation and Work Methods Directorate 3 - Laying down appropriate appointment conditions for Category Two positions, taking into account the new specialisations that must be available in the various units of the Council, guaranteeing the securing of elements characterised by competence and the ability to carry out the tasks entrusted to them on the basis of functional specialisation, in addition to adopting the principle of contracting as one of the options alongside appointment in the permanent cadre of the Council, and this is what gives more flexibility to the process of attracting persons of high competencies. 4 - Activating the competence of the Council with respect to classifying and describing positions, and laying down salary scales more proportionate to the nature of those positions on the basis of "remuneration commensurate with hardship".

The Personnel Administration currently consists of two departments, namely: - The Department of Supervision and Studies. - The Department of Competitive Examinations and Personal Files. The Civil Service Board has comprehensive powers that it exercises through supervision and studies pursuant to the Law of its establishment No. 114/ 59 and its Organizational Decree No. 8337/61, and these powers cover all public administrations, public institutions and municipalities subject to its competence, with the exception of the Judiciary, the Army, the Internal Security Forces, the General Security, the State Security and the civilian personnel attached to those institutions. Among its primary fundamental missions is the exercise of the powers defined for it by the laws and regulations in force, particularly those relating to the appointment of employees, their promotion, their advancement in grade, their transfer, their discipline, their allowances, their dismissal from service and all that pertains to their personal functional affairs. Public administrations, public institutions and municipalities shall restrict their reliance exclusively to the Civil Service Board in requesting approval, seeking an opinion or consultation in all the affairs of permanent and temporary employees, wage earners, staff members and contracted personnel, and consequently in the interpretation of the texts relating to the public service, to employees and to everyone who works in the service of those administrations subject to its competence. The Personnel Regulations promulgated by Legislative Decree No. 112 dated 12/6/1959, the Wage Earners Regulations promulgated by Decree No. 5883 dated 3/11/1994, the General Regulations for Public Institutions promulgated by Decree No. 4517 dated 13/12/1972, the Staff Regulations in public institutions as well as the regulations of the municipalities subject to the supervision of the Civil Service Board, have granted this Board several powers which it exercises through the Department of Supervision and Studies in the Personnel Administration, which handles all matters relating to supervision, studies, allowances

and related allocations. Alongside supervision and studies, the Personnel Administration handles the affairs of competitive examinations and personal files through the Department of Competitive Examinations and Files

First: The Department of Supervision and Studies A: Missions of the Department of Supervision and Studies: This department handles all general matters relating to the regulations of employees and everyone who works in the service of the public administrations, public institutions and municipalities that are subject to the supervision of the Civil Service Board, with respect to expressing an opinion on the legality of appointments or employment and studying all the personal affairs of employees and supervising their transactions, particularly verifying their professional competence and their conduct within the service and outside it, and studying proposals for confirmation of appointment, advancement in grade, promotion and termination of service for incompetence, unfitness or medical disability, and it also expresses its opinion on draft texts relating to the regulations of employees, wage earners, staff members and contracted personnel, and on the need of the administration for new permanent and temporary employees or for contracted personnel with special qualifications and knowledge or for wage earners and staff members, and on the regulations of the State Employees' Cooperative and the manner of their application, and on draft circulars, instructions and publications relating to the public service, and it also expresses its opinion on the conditions for granting allowances, transport fares, rewards, returns, teaching hour wages, grants, advances and everything related to additional expenditure..., and a new mission has also been added to its missions, which is the mission of establishing a classification dividing public posts according to the nature of their missions into categories and ranks..., and determining an independent salary scale for each category of the categories set forth in the classification after conducting a comparative study of similar posts in the public and private sectors. In order to enable this department to perform its missions, a number of senior controllers and controllers have been attached to it to assist its head in performing these missions, and their number has been fixed since the year 1961 at 18 senior controllers or controllers, and one controller was added to them in the year 1970 following the abolition of the Post Classification Division created in this department and the assignment of the classification missions to the Department of Supervision and Studies, so that the number of controllers became 19 controllers. Through these controllers, the Board carries out the work of studying and auditing the transactions of 21 ministries, more than seventy public institutions and ten municipalities. B: On the concept of supervision exercised by the Civil Service Board through the Department of Supervision and Studies: The supervision of the Civil Service Board aims to achieve the following: - Ensuring the proper application of legal texts in accordance with the will of the legislator. - Ensuring the proper functioning of work in public administrations in order to enable them to perform their missions. - Ensuring the necessary guarantee for employees in order to enable them to perform their role. All of this is for the purpose of providing services to citizens in the best manner, in accordance with what the modern State seeks in caring for the affairs of its citizens. The Civil Service Board derives its competence in the field of supervision over the acts of employees from the legal texts relating to the public service and employees as follows: - Comprehensive supervision: This supervision was entrusted to the Board pursuant to the provisions of Legislative Decree No. 114 dated 12/6/1959 and Organizational Decree No. 8337 dated 30/12/1961; Article One of the aforementioned Legislative Decree No. 114 provided for the establishment of the Civil Service Board in the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, whose powers cover all public administrations and public institutions and their employees, major municipalities and the municipalities that the Government subjects to its supervision by a decree taken in the Council of Ministers, with the exception of the Judiciary, the Army, the civilian personnel attached to the Army, the Internal Security Forces, the General Security, the State Security, and the civilian personnel attached to the Internal Security Forces, the General Security and the State Security. Paragraph (1) of Article Two of the aforementioned Legislative Decree provided that the Civil Service Board shall exercise the powers entrusted to it by the laws and regulations with respect to the appointment of employees, their promotion, their allowances, their transfer, their discipline, their dismissal from service, and all other personal affairs of theirs. The first subparagraph of paragraph (6) of Article Nine thereof also provided that the approval of the Civil Service Board or its decision relating to the transactions of permanent employees and contracted personnel is a necessary fundamental operation, and any transaction not accompanied by this approval or this decision shall be considered null and void and of no effect. Furthermore, Article Five of Organizational Decree No. 8337/61 required all public administrations, public institutions and municipalities subject to the competence of the Civil Service Board to restrict their reliance in requesting approval, opinion, consultation or inquiry exclusively to this Board in all the affairs of permanent and temporary employees, wage earners, staff members and contracted personnel, and consequently in the interpretation of the administrative texts relating to the public service, to employees and to everyone who works in the service of public administrations. - The cases provided for by the Personnel Law: In accordance with the content of the text of paragraph (3) of Article Nine of Legislative Decree No. 114/59, and by referring to the Personnel Regulations, it appears that these cases cover: appointment, confirmation of appointment, allowances, transfer, secondment, placement outside the cadre, placement on availability, discipline, termination of service..... - The cases in which the Civil Service Board was entrusted with the power

to approve them, or to seek an opinion thereon, or to be consulted regarding them, or to express an opinion thereon or on one or more points thereof, and which are provided for in all other legal texts in force relating to the various ministries, public administrations, public institutions and municipalities.
