If the subject-matter of an obligation subject to a condition perishes or becomes defective prior to the fulfilment of such condition, the following rules shall apply:

If the thing perishes in its entirety and its loss does not arise from a mutual contract, the thing perishes at the risk of the debtor, in the sense that he is not entitled to demand from the creditor the performance of the counter-performance; and if the thing becomes defective or its value decreases without any act or fault on the part of the debtor, the creditor must accept it in its condition without any reduction in the price; and if the thing perishes in its entirety through the fault or by an act of the debtor, the creditor shall be entitled to claim damages; and if the thing becomes defective or its value decreases or by an act of the debtor, the creditor may elect either to accept the thing in its condition or to rescind the contract. In both cases, he shall not be deprived of the right to claim damages where appropriate, all of the foregoing unless the two parties stipulate otherwise.

A resolutory condition does not suspend the performance of the obligation, but merely obliges the creditor to restore what he has received upon the fulfilment of the condition, and if he is unable to restore it for a cause for which he is answerable, he shall be liable for damages; however, he shall not be obliged to restore the produce and accretions. Any stipulation requiring him to restore the produce shall be deemed unwritten.

The rule laid down in the second paragraph of the ninety-fifth article shall apply to obligations contracted under a resolutory condition with respect to the acts performed by the person whose rights are annulled by the fulfilment of the condition, save for rights lawfully acquired by a third party in good faith.
If a resolutory condition is fulfilled, the acts performed by the creditor in the interim shall become null and void, save for acts of administration, which shall remain valid in all cases.

Obligations may be qualified by a term, and a term is a future event certain to occur which suspends the exigibility or the extinction of the obligation and has no retroactive effect; and if the time at which such event will occur is known in advance, the obligation is of a certain term, and otherwise it is of an uncertain term.

An obligation of deferred performance or with a suspensive term is one whose performance is suspended until the term matures, and if there is no term stipulated or inferred from the nature of the matter, performance may be demanded immediately.
If the term is established for the benefit of the creditor or for the joint benefit of the two parties, it prevents the debtor from the voluntary execution of the obligation.

A creditor subject to a term may maturity, resort to all conservatory measures to preserve his rights, and demand a suretyship or other forms of security, or proceed with conservatory attachment when he finds valid grounds leading him to fear the insolvency of the debtor, his bankruptcy, or his flight.
The party who alone benefits from the term may waive it by his mere will.

The debtor who benefits from the term forfeits his right to benefit therefrom:

1- If he goes bankrupt or becomes insolvent

2- If he commits an act which diminishes the special securities given to the creditor pursuant to the contract creating the obligation or a subsequent contract, or pursuant to the law. However, if the diminution in those securities results from a cause in which the debtor had no choice, the creditor shall be entitled to demand a supplement of security. If he does not obtain it, he shall be entitled to demand the immediate execution of the obligation.

3- If the debtor does not furnish to the creditor the securities which he promised in the contract.
The death of the debtor renders all the obligations with a term owed by him due for payment, with the exception of debts secured by real securities.

The judge may take into consideration the condition of the debtor if he is in good faith, and grant him, with extreme caution, moderate extensions of time for the performance of the obligation and order the stay of proceedings while keeping all things as they are, unless there is a legal provision to the contrary.
Contrary to the legal term, the term of grace does not prevent set-off from being effected where applicable.
In obligations the object of which is the performance of a continuous act or a series of successive acts, the effect of the term is extinguishment.

Ascendants and guardians are liable for every unlawful act committed by minor children residing with them and subject to their authority, and teachers and master craftsmen are liable for the damage resulting from the unlawful acts committed by students or industrial apprentices while they are under their supervision, provided that the Government bears the liability instead of the members of the public teaching body, and liability attaches to the aforementioned persons unless they prove that it was not within their power to prevent the act from which it arose. Liability remains standing even if the perpetrator of the damage is not responsible for lack of discernment.

The master and the principal are liable for the damage of the unlawful acts committed by the servant or the subordinate during the work, or by reason of the work in which they employed them, even if they were not free in choosing them, provided that they have actual authority over them in supervision and direction, and such liability attaches to legal persons just as it attaches to natural persons.

Even in cases other than those aforementioned, a person may be liable for the act of another person, provided, however, that it is proved against him and the commission of a specific fault, not that he be inevitably liable; in that case he is not liable for the act of another, but for his own fault.

The custodian of an animal is liable for the damage of his animal even if it has strayed or escaped, and the rule of this liability also applies in the absence of a contrary provision, even if the custodian and the injured party are bound by a prior contract, such as a contract of employment for example, and liability is not lifted from the custodian unless proof is established of force majeure or of a fault committed by the injured party.

As for damages resulting from the act of wild animals, the landowner or the farmer shall not be held answerable therefor unless proof is established of a specific fault committed by them by act or negligence.

The custodian of movable and immovable inanimate things shall be liable for the damages caused by those inanimate things even at the time when they are not under his actual direction or supervision, such as a car at the time of driving, or an aeroplane at the time of its flight, or an elevator at the time of its use. Such objective liability does not cease unless the custodian establishes proof of the existence of force majeure or a fault on the part of the injured party. It is not sufficient for the custodian to prove that he did not commit a fault, and the existence of a prior contract between the custodian and the injured party does not prevent the application of the rule of liability arising from things unless there is a provision to the contrary in the law.
If the damage results from several inanimate things, such as the collision of two cars for example, the objective liability ceases and is replaced by the ordinary liability based on the personal act.

An obligation subject to an extinctive term has the effects of a simple obligation so long as that term has not fallen due. Upon its falling due, the obligation ceases with respect to the future only.

Obligations arise:

1- From the law

2- From illicit acts (such as a delict or quasi-delict)

3- From unjust enrichment

4- From juridical acts.

Legal obligations are those which derive directly from the law alone, such as the obligations existing between neighbouring owners or such as maintenance debts imposed by the law upon certain relatives by blood or by marriage. Since these obligations are generated independently of the will of the parties concerned, they do not require the existence of any capacity whatsoever on their part, unless the law provides to the contrary.
A delict is an act which harms the interest of another intentionally and without right, and a quasi-delict is an act which prejudices the interest of another without right, but unintentionally.

Every act of any person from which results unlawful damage to the interest of another obliges its perpetrator, if possessed of discernment, to make compensation. An incapacitated person is liable for the illicit acts which he commits with discernment, and if the damage proceeds from a person lacking discernment and the injured party is unable to obtain compensation from the person entrusted with the supervision of that person, the judge is entitled, having regard to the condition of the two parties, to order the perpetrator of the damage to pay equitable compensation.
A person is liable for the damage resulting from his negligence or his imprudence, just as he is liable for the damage arising from an act which he commits.
Compensation is also due from whoever harms another by exceeding, in the course of exercising his right, the bounds of good faith or the purpose for which this right was granted.
A person is necessarily liable for the damage caused by other persons for whom he is responsible, and their number is limited and exhaustive.

The owner of a building shall be liable for the damage arising from its collapse or the partial demolition thereof where the cause of such incident is a lack of maintenance of the building, a defect in its construction, or its age; and such liability shall attach to the owner of the surface of the land if the ownership of the surface is separate from the ownership of the land; however, if the maintenance of the structure is the duty of a person other than the owner, liability shall remain borne by the owner, provided that he has the right to have recourse against that person and may join him as a party in the liability action; and all these rules must be applied even though the owner and the injured party are bound by a prior obligation, unless there is a statutory provision to the contrary.

The compensation due to the party injured by a delict or quasi-delict must in principle be equivalent to the damage that befell him. Moral damage shall be taken into account just as material damage is taken into account, and the judge may take into consideration the interest of affection where it is justified by a bond of legitimate kinship or a bond of consanguinity; likewise, indirect damages must be taken into consideration provided that they are clearly connected to the delict or quasi-delict; and in principle, present actual damages alone enter into the calculation of compensation; however, the judge may, by way of exception, take into consideration future damages if their occurrence is certain on the one hand, and on the other hand he has the necessary means to assess their true value in advance.

If the injured party has committed a fault such as to mitigate to some extent the liability of his opponent without extinguishing it, liability must be apportioned in a manner that leads to the reduction of the allowance of compensation given to the injured party.

Reparation shall in principle be pecuniary, and shall be allocated as an allowance for damages; however, the judge has the right to give it a form that is more suited to the interest of the injured party, thus making it in kind, and it may in particular be by way of publication in newspapers.

If the damage arises from several persons, passive solidarity shall exist among them:

First- If there was participation in the act

Second- If it is impossible to determine the proportion of that damage caused by each person.

No one may exonerate himself, wholly or partially, from the consequences of his fraud or gross fault by inserting a clause excluding his liability or mitigating its severity, and every clause inserted for this purpose in any contract whatsoever is null and void ab initio.

Clauses excluding liability and assumption-of-risk clauses shall be valid and enforceable insofar as they release the author of the clause from the consequences of his act or his unintentional fault, but such release shall be confined to material damage and not to damage affecting persons, since human life and personal safety are above all agreement.
Whosoever reaps, without lawful cause, an enrichment to the detriment of another shall be bound to make restitution.

The obligation of the enriched party towards the party at whose expense he was enriched shall not arise in this manner and on this basis unless the following conditions are fulfilled:

First- That the alleged enriched party has obtained an enrichment, whether such enrichment is direct or indirect, material or moral

Second- That the party at whose expense the enrichment occurred has suffered a corresponding loss in property or an asset of which he divested himself or a service which he performed

Third- That the realised enrichment and the corresponding loss are devoid of a legal cause upon which they rest

Fourth- That the party at whose expense the enrichment occurred has, in order to obtain his claim, no right of action other than that based on the occurrence of the enrichment, and this right is of a subsidiary nature in relation to other legal remedies.

The enriched party shall not be bound to make restitution except to the extent of the enrichment remaining with him on the day the action is brought, unless the law contains a provision to the contrary, and the case shall be otherwise if the enriched party was in bad faith at the time of the enrichment, in which event he becomes liable for all that he gained regardless of any subsequent events of loss, alienation, or deterioration, and in such case he bears all the risks and is bound to restore all the fruits which he reaped or ought to have reaped, and is only entitled to claim necessary expenses.
Whosoever erroneously believes himself to be a debtor and pays that which he does not owe following an error of law or of fact shall be entitled to claim restitution from the enriched party.

There shall be no ground for recovery:

First- If the obligation is civil and subject to a term that has not fallen due, even though the debtor believed it to be due for performance, and in this case no claim may be made for interest for the period intervening between payment and maturity

Second- If the obligation is natural or purely moral and the payer was at least aware of the true state of affairs at the time of payment

Third- If the enriched party was in good faith at the time of payment and destroyed or cancelled his instrument, or deprived himself of the securities guaranteeing his debt, or allowed prescription to be completed in favour of his true debtor.

Recovery may be had:

First- If the obligation was dependent upon a suspensive condition unknown to the debtor and unfulfilled

Second- If the debtor could have defeated the creditor's action by a peremptory defence of whose existence he was unaware

Third- If he believed himself bound by a civil obligation whereas the obligation incumbent upon him was purely moral or natural.
The rules laid down for unlawful enrichment in general apply to the payment of what is not due.

A juristic act is one performed in order to produce legal effects and, in particular, to create obligations, and the juristic act creating obligations may emanate from a single party (such as the declaration of a party's will) or may be an agreement, in which case it is termed a contract.

A single will, even if declared clearly and in a formal manner, is in principle incapable of creating obligatory relations so long as it is not joined with another will representing independent or conflicting interests; however, it is permissible by way of exception and in limited cases provided for by law that obligations arise from the will of a single party, such as an offer to contract (see Article (179) or contracting in favour of a third party (Article 227) or agency of necessity.

An act constitutes agency of necessity when a person of his own accord undertakes the management of the affairs of another knowingly and without authorisation, with the intention of acting on behalf of that other person, and if it happens that a person manages the interests of another person unknowingly because he believes that he is managing his own property, the matter shall then be subject to the provisions of enrichment without cause and not to the provisions of agency of necessity.
Juristic acts, like material acts, may form the subject of the act of an agent of necessity.

The agent of necessity performs his act in a spirit of disinterestedness or with the intention of deriving benefit, particularly in the course of performing his function or his profession. A person lacking capacity cannot be an agent of necessity. And if he performs an act of agency of necessity, he shall be liable towards the principal only to the extent of his enrichment.
The act of the agent of necessity terminates upon his death, as the obligations of his heirs are subject to the provisions of Article 820 relating to mandate.
If the agent of necessity is mistaken as to the identity of the principal, the rights and obligations arising from his act shall accrue between him and the true principal.

Where the principal ratifies expressly or impliedly the act of the intervener, the rights and obligations between the two parties shall be subject to the provisions governing mandate from the commencement of the act as regards the two parties themselves, and from the ratification as regards third parties; and in the absence of ratification, or until it takes place, those rights and obligations shall be subject to the provisions of Article 161 and the following articles.
The intervener shall be subject to the provisions relating to mandate in respect of acts for which he held a special mandate.

The intervener must bestow upon his act the care of a bonus paterfamilias, and must act in accordance with the known or presumed intention of the principal, and he shall be liable for any fault, however slight; provided that he shall only be bound to exercise such care as he bestows upon his own affairs:

First- Where his intervention is to avert an imminent serious damage that threatened the principal

Second- Where he is an heir completing an act commenced by his decedent.

The intervener must continue the act which he has commenced until the principal becomes able to complete it himself, unless the discontinuance of the intervention does not prejudice the interest of the principal.
And he shall be bound by the obligations by which an agent is bound with respect to rendering his accounts and restoring whatever has come into his hands by means of his management.

An intervener who has intervened in the affairs of another person contrary to the known or presumed intention of the principal, or who has performed acts contrary to his presumed intention, shall be bound to compensate for all damages resulting from his act, even if no fault whatsoever can be attributed to him.

Nevertheless, contrariety to the intention of the principal may not be invoked if urgent necessity has compelled the intervener:

1- To perform an obligation incumbent upon the principal arising from the law which the public interest requires to be performed

2- To perform a legal obligation relating to the provision of maintenance, or funeral expenses, or other necessary obligations.

A principal whose affairs have been usefully managed is bound towards the intervener and towards third parties by the obligations provided for in Article 163 and the following articles, and this provision must be applied even if the principal does not enjoy legal capacity. The management of the affair shall be deemed good if, at the time of its performance, it conformed to the rules of good management.

In all cases in which the principal is not bound to recognize the expenses incurred by the intervener, the latter shall be entitled to remove the improvements he has made provided that no damage results from their removal, and to take delivery of the things which he has purchased and which the principal has not accepted.

In the case provided for in Article 161, the principal must relieve the intervener of the liability of his management and indemnify him for what he has advanced or lost in accordance with the provisions relating to agency.

The principal shall not be bound to refund anything when the intervener has undertaken the business without intending to claim the reimbursement of what he has advanced, and the existence of such intention shall be presumed:

1- If the intervention took place contrary to the will of the principal, except in the cases provided for in Article 60

2- In all other cases from the circumstances of which it clearly appears that the intervener did not intend to claim the reimbursement of what he advanced.
An agreement is every concurrence between one will and another for the production of legal effects, and if it aims at creating obligatory relations it is called a contract.

The law of contracts is subject to the principle of freedom of contract; individuals may arrange their legal relations as they wish, provided that they observe the requirements of public order, public morals, and the legal provisions which have a mandatory character.

Contracts are divided into:

1- Synallagmatic contracts and unilateral contracts

2- Onerous contracts and gratuitous contracts

3- Consensual contracts and formal contracts

4- Contracts of mutual negotiation and contracts of adhesion

5- Individual contracts and collective contracts

6- Contracts of acquisition and contracts of security

7- Nominate contracts and innominate contracts.

A unilateral contract is one which binds one or more parties towards one or more other parties, without there being reciprocity in the obligation, such that some become only creditors and the others only debtors, and a synallagmatic or bilateral contract is one in which each party is reciprocally bound towards the other pursuant to the agreement concluded between them. And if one party is originally bound and the other party is exposed to bearing certain obligations subsequently as a result of special circumstances or upon the performance of the contract, the contract does not lose the character of a unilateral contract (as in deposit, loan for use, and pledge).

An onerous contract is one which is made in the interest of all the contracting parties, whereby they obtain benefits considered to be appreciably equivalent (such as sale, barter, lease, contract of employment, and loan with interest), and a gratuitous contract is one which is made in the interest of one party without the other party having a hope of a benefit appreciably equivalent to the sacrifice to which he has consented (such as gift, loan for use, and lending of money without interest).

The contract retains its gratuitous character even if the benefiting party is bound by certain charges or obligations, even though they accrue to the interest of the party from whom he benefits (such as a gift with charges), since the contract must be considered as a whole and according to the spirit in which it was created; and an onerous contract may be synallagmatic (such as sale and barter) or non-synallagmatic (such as a loan with interest), and likewise a gratuitous contract may bind one party only (such as an ordinary gift) or bind both parties (such as a gift with charges).

The division of commutation is one in which the extent of the obligations is originally determined in a fixed manner so that each of the contracting parties is able to know on the day of contracting the amount of the benefits which he reaps from his contracting, and the sum of the sacrifice to which he has consented; and an aleatory contract is one in which the nature of one or several of the obligations or the existence of the obligations depends upon a contingency, the uncertainty of the occurrence of which prevents making an assessment of this kind (such as an insurance contract or a life annuity contract).

Consensual contracts are those the conclusion of which is not dependent upon a special external condition, it being sufficient therein that the consent of the contracting parties be manifested with complete freedom and in any form whatsoever; whereas if the law requires that this consent be manifested in a special form, such as the drawing up of an authentic instrument, the contract is solemn. In principle, contracts are formed by the mere voluntary consent of the contracting parties, and it is not necessary to produce them in any solemn form except pursuant to a provision of the law requiring the use thereof.

A contract of mutual negotiation is one the terms of which are discussed and bargained over and are freely established between the contracting parties (such as an ordinary sale, lease, barter, and lending); and when one of the parties is restricted to accepting a regulatory draft which is merely presented to him and he is not permitted, either legally or in fact, to discuss what is contained therein, the contract is then called a contract of adhesion (such as contracting for carriage with a railway company or an insurance contract).

An individual contract is one which requires the unanimous acceptance of the contracting parties, even if it concerns a large number of natural or juristic persons.

A collective contract is one which a majority imposes upon a minority so that persons who did not accept it are bound thereby (such as a collective employment contract and a composition in the event of bankruptcy).

Contracts of acquisition are those by which it is intended to introduce a new value into the patrimony of the contracting parties or of one of them. Contracts of conservation are those by which it is intended to preserve the state of that patrimony in its entirety.

Contracts are nominate according to whether the law has or has not assigned to them a specific designation and form, and the rules laid down in the First Part of this Law shall apply to nominate and innominate contracts; whereas the rules mentioned in the Second Part shall apply to innominate contracts only by way of analogy and having regard to the similarity between them and the specified nominate contracts.
The consent of the contracting parties is the essence and pillar of every contract, and indeed of every agreement more generally.

It is indispensable:

First- That consent actually exist

Second- That it extend to one or several objects

Third- That there exist a cause which induces it

Fourth- That it be free from certain defects

Fifth- That it be established, in certain cases, in a specific form.

Consent in contracts is the meeting of two or more wills and their concurrence in creating obligatory relations between the contracting parties, and it consists of two elements:

First- The proposal or offer

Second- The acceptance, which also requires, save in contracts of adhesion, negotiations which may be protracted and multifaceted.

An express or tacit offer does not in principle bind its author, in the sense that he may, if he so wishes, revoke it. His death or his loss of legal capacity renders the offer void; the case is otherwise when it results from the nature of the offer or from the circumstances in which it was made or from the text of the law that the author of the offer intended to bind himself, in which case the offer must remain open during the period fixed by its author or derived from custom or the law, notwithstanding the occurrence of his death or his loss of legal capacity; such is the case in particular:

1- If the offer is expressly accompanied by a time-limit

2- If the offer is in commercial matters

3- If the offer is by correspondence.

4- If it is a promise of a reward.

Acceptance, like an offer, is express or tacit, and the absence of a reply is deemed an acceptance when the proposal relates to dealings which already existed between the two parties, and the silence of the buyer of goods after receiving them is deemed an acceptance of the terms specified in the statement of account (the invoice).

The person to whom the offer is addressed is in principle free to refuse and bears no liability whatsoever by refraining from contracting; however, the matter is otherwise if he himself has created a situation of a nature to invite the offer (such as a merchant towards the public, or a hotel proprietor and a restaurant proprietor, or an employer towards workmen); in such case, his refusal to contract must be based upon acceptable grounds. Otherwise, his refusal is arbitrary and liability may attach to him on this score.

Acceptance shall not effectively conclude the contract unless it is in complete conformity with the offer, inasmuch as it is an answer thereto. An answer made subject to a condition or a restriction shall be deemed a refusal of the offer coupled with the proposal of a new offer.

Between persons present, consent shall be deemed to exist and the contract concluded at the time when acceptance is joined to the offer between the contracting parties while they are agreed upon the terms of retirement, unless they have agreed to conclude the contract in a specific form which they have chosen for it (Article 220, paragraph 3).

Where negotiations are conducted by correspondence or through a messenger between absent persons, the contract shall be deemed concluded at the time and at the place in which acceptance was issued by the person to whom the offer was addressed.

A contract concluded by telephone conversation shall be deemed equivalent to a contract concluded between persons present, and in that case its conclusion shall be determined by the will of the contracting parties, or else by the judge and according to the circumstances of the case.
The true object of every contract is the creation of obligations; however, this purpose is not attained unless the obligations themselves have objects in which certain qualities are present.

The object may be an act (and this is an obligation to do), or a forbearance (and this is an obligation not to do), or the transfer of ownership or the creation of a real right (and this is an obligation to give).

The non-existence of the object entails the non-existence of the contract; nevertheless, the object may be a future thing, save that it is not permissible to renounce an unopened succession, nor to conclude any contract over such succession or over any of the things thereof, even with the consent of the person whose succession is in question, failing which the act shall be radically void.
The subject-matter must be sufficiently determined, possible and lawful.

The determination must cover the nature of the subject-matter and its quantity; provided that it is sufficient to determine the kind of the thing and for the contract to contain that whereby the quantity may subsequently be determined.

Every contract that imposes an impossible thing or act is void if such impossibility is absolute and insurmountable; whereas an impossibility that exists only on the part of the debtor shall not prevent the validity of the contract. The obligation that has not been performed shall then be converted into damages.

Every contract that imposes a matter not permitted by law and not in conformity with morals is void, and a thing that is not considered property among people may not be the subject-matter of an obligation; however, in applying this rule, consideration must be given to the fact that commerce has a relative meaning, as certain property, for example, may not validly be the subject-matter of certain transactions whereas it may with full validity enter into other transactions.
A person may promise the act of another, but such promise binds only the person who made it and its effect does not extend to the third party, who retains his full freedom.
A distinction is made between the cause of the obligation and the cause of the contract.

The cause of the obligation lies in the motive that directly and invariably induces it, and it is deemed an inseparable part of the contract, such as the counterpart obligation in synallagmatic contracts, the performance of delivery in real contracts, and the intention to make a liberal disposition in gratuitous contracts. As for onerous non-synallagmatic contracts, the cause is the pre-existing obligation, whether civil or natural.

An obligation that has no cause, or that has a false or unlawful cause, is deemed never to have existed and leads to the contract to which it relates also being deemed non-existent. What has been paid may be recovered.

Mistake shall not affect the validity of a contract if it was not the determining factor thereof, and in particular if such mistake relates to:

First - The accidental or secondary qualities of the thing or of the person

Second - The value of the thing, save in the case of gross lesion (Article 214)

Third - The mere motives that induced one of the contracting parties to contract

Fourth - Figures or calculation, in which case rectification shall be required by law, provided that the contract remains valid.
A mistake of law shall be taken into account and shall vitiate consent in the same manner as a mistake of fact.

A mistake bearing upon the substantial qualities of the thing shall be destructive of the contract only if it proceeds from both parties and enters into the stipulation, whereas a mistake bearing upon the person shall be taken into account even if it proceeds from one party alone.

Fraud does not entirely negate the existence of consent, but vitiates it and leads to the annulment of the contract if it was the determining factor thereof and that which induced the deceived party to contract. Incidental fraud which led to the alteration of the terms of the contract without being the determining factor in its formation shall entitle the deceived party only to claim damages.

Fraud which induced the formation of the contract shall lead to its annulment only if the party who committed it prejudiced the interest of the other party. Fraud committed by a third party shall also be destructive of the contract; if the party was unaware of it, the deceived party shall only be entitled to sue the deceiver for damages.

Every contract formed under the pressure of fear resulting from physical violence or from a threat directed against the person of the debtor or his property, or against his spouse or one of his ascendants or descendants, is void. There is no need to distinguish whether such pressure proceeds from one of the contracting parties, from a third party, or from circumstances extraneous to the sphere of the contract; provided that, in the latter two cases, the coerced party wishing to be released from the contract may be bound to pay compensation to the other party if that party was in good faith. Such compensation shall be in proportion to what equity requires.

Fear shall vitiate consent only if it was the inducement thereto. In order to ascertain its nature and effect, regard should be had to the personality of the coerced party (such as having regard to his age, to whether that party is a woman or a man, to his degree of education, and to his social standing).

Reverential fear towards the father, the mother, or other ascendants shall not suffice to vitiate the contract, nor shall the use of legal means, so long as such use is lawful, that is to say, its purpose is merely to obtain what is due.

The cause shall be untrue if a party undertakes a matter for an imaginary cause which he erroneously believed to exist. An ostensible cause shall not in principle by itself vitiate the contract, but the contract shall remain valid if the true cause of the obligation is lawful.
An unlawful cause is one that violates public policy, morals, and the mandatory provisions of the law.

Every obligation is deemed to be based on a true and lawful cause, even if it is not stated in the contract. The stated cause is deemed to be true until the contrary is proved, and if proof is established of the untruth or unlawfulness of the cause, the party who claims the existence of another lawful cause shall prove the truth of his assertion.

The cause of the contract lies in the personal motive which induced the contracting party to enter into the contract, and it is not deemed an inseparable part of the contract, but varies in every kind of contract, even if they belong to the same category.
If the cause of the contract is unlawful, the contract shall be null and void ab initio.
Consent shall be defective, or even wholly non-existent in certain cases, if it is given by mistake, obtained by fraud, extorted by duress, or if there is gross lesion or incapacity.

If the mistake bears upon the nature of the contract or the reality of the subject-matter of the obligation, it prevents the formation of the contract itself, and the contract shall be deemed never to have existed.

Consent shall be deemed defective only, and the contract voidable:

First- If the mistake bears upon the essential qualities of the thing

Second- If the mistake bears upon the identity of the person or his essential qualities in contracts entered into in consideration of the person of the contracting party.

Third- If the mistake bears upon the efficacy of the cause of the obligation (such as entering into an undertaking for a prior obligation which was believed to be civil whereas it was only natural).
Contracts lawfully formed bind the contracting parties. They must be understood, interpreted and performed in accordance with good faith, equity and custom.

Contracts extend to those who have acquired by universal title the rights of the contracting parties, and their effects operate in principle in their favour or against them either immediately (such as creditors) or after the death of the contracting parties or one of them (such as heirs and universal legatees or legatees by universal title).

The contracting parties are not necessarily the persons whose names appear in the contracts and who sign them, as these may have acted as agents or unauthorised managers of another's affairs. In such a case, the contract does not produce its effect in the person of the representative, but in the person of the represented party (with a fatha on the tha), so that the latter becomes a creditor or debtor to the exclusion of the agent or the unauthorised manager.

The matter shall be otherwise if the agent acts ostensibly in his own name, acting as a nominee, and does not disclose his agency; those who deal with him in this manner cannot sue anyone other than him, nor may anyone other than him sue them. The rules of agency and representation shall apply only to the relations between the undisclosed agent and the principal.

A contract does not in principle produce its effects in respect of a third party, meaning that it is not possible for this person to acquire rights or be made a debtor thereby, for a contract has a relative effect confined to the contracting parties or those who have acquired the rights of the latter by universal title.

However, this rule admits of no exception from the negative aspect; a promise made on behalf of a third party binds the promisor if he has guaranteed to procure that party's consent and has taken the matter upon himself, while the third party retains complete freedom to ratify or refuse (Article 193). Refusal to ratify therefore does not render that person liable for anything whatsoever, but it renders the said guarantor liable to pay damages for failing to perform the act which he guaranteed expressly or impliedly. As for ratification, its effects between the contracting parties commence from the day of the contract, and it has no effect towards the third party except from the day it takes place.

The relative character of contracts admits of exceptions from the positive aspect; a person may contract in his own name for the benefit of a third party so that this person becomes a creditor of the promisor by virtue of the contract itself. Contracting for the benefit of a third party is valid and enforceable:

First- When it relates to an agreement entered into by the stipulator in his own personal interest, whether pecuniary or moral

Second- When it is a condition or a futility to a gratuitous disposition inter vivos or to a testamentary gratuitous disposition consented to by the stipulator for the benefit of another person (gratuitous disposition subject to a condition).
Lesion is the disparity and lack of equilibrium between the obligations established in favour of one party and the obligations imposed upon the other party in onerous contracts.

Lesion does not in principle vitiate the consent of the aggrieved party. It shall be otherwise, and the contract shall become voidable, in the following cases:

First- If the aggrieved party is a minor

Second- If the aggrieved party is of full age and the lesion has two characteristics:

The first is that it is gross and abnormal according to customary practice,

And the second is that the beneficiary intended to exploit distress, levity, or inexperience in the aggrieved party. Aleatory contracts themselves may, to the extent specified above, be annulled on the ground of lesion.
Every person who has completed the eighteenth year of his age is capable of binding himself, unless he is declared incapable by a statutory provision.

The acts of a person completely devoid of the power of discernment, which are subject to annulment (such as an infant and an insane person), are deemed never to have existed. As for the acts of persons who lack capacity but possess discernment, they are subject to annulment (such as a discerning minor). A person who has contracted with an incapacitated person may not invoke the plea of annulment, as it belongs to the rights of the incapacitated person himself, his representative, or his heirs. If the contract entered into by a discerning minor is not subject to a special form, the minor cannot obtain its annulment unless he furnishes proof that he suffered lesion. However, if a special formality was required to be performed, nullity ensues therefrom, without the claimant being obliged to prove the existence of lesion.

A minor legally authorised to engage in commerce or industry may not avail himself of the preceding provisions, but shall be treated as one who has attained the age of majority within the sphere of his trade and to the extent of its requirements.
Every interested party is entitled to invoke the incapacity of convicted persons placed under legal interdiction.
The burden of proof lies upon him who alleges the defect; the soundness of consent is presumed, and the capacity of the contracting parties as well.

The rules applicable to the forms of contracts are prescribed for each category thereof. Where no prescription of this kind exists, the contract is concluded by the mere agreement of the contracting parties. Nevertheless, it may happen that the agreement does not produce all its effects and is not enforceable against a third party except by taking certain measures of publicity which are of general concern, without which the effect of the contract cannot extend beyond the sphere of the contracting parties or their universal successors in title. On the other hand, if the contracting parties agree to cast the contract in a special form not required by law, such as the written form for instance, the contract is neither concluded nor produces its effects, even between the contracting parties, except when it is cast in that form.

A stipulation in favour of a third party may be for the benefit of future persons or of persons who are currently undetermined, provided that their determination is possible when the agreement produces its effects.

A stipulation in favour of a third party requires only compliance with the rules of form required for the validity of the agreement into which it is incorporated; it is therefore not subject to the forms of a gift inter vivos, even though it constitutes a pure gratuitous benefit for the beneficiary third party.
The third party who benefits from such a stipulation becomes immediately and directly a creditor of the promisor.

A party who stipulates in favour of a third party is entitled to revoke his stipulation so long as the beneficiary third party has not accepted it expressly or tacitly. The revocation may also be express or tacit, and the exercise of this right pertains exclusively to the contracting party himself, and neither to his creditors nor to his heirs.

However, such revocation does not necessarily discharge the debtor; unless there is a provision to the contrary or a legal impossibility, he remains bound towards the contracting party, who by this means has reserved to himself or to his heirs the benefit of an act arranged in favour of a third party (such as a life insurance contract- in favour of a third party).

A contract may be dissolved before the arrival of its term and before its complete execution either by reason of a defect affecting it at the time of its formation or by reason of circumstances subsequent to its formation; in the first case it is annulled, and in the second case it is rescinded or terminated.

The annulment of a contract is always on account of an original defect which attached to it at the time of its formation (such as mistake, fraud, duress, lesion, and incapacity), and none other than the court may pronounce the annulment, which then has retroactive effect; however, the contract remains subsisting and continues to produce its ordinary effects so long as the annulment has not been judicially declared.

The right to bring an action for annulment belongs only to the persons in whose favour or for whose protection the law has established the nullity. Specifically excluded from this provision are those who contracted with such persons, and this right passes to the heirs of the person entitled thereto.

The right to bring this action lapses by prescription after ten years, unless the law has fixed another time-limit for a special case, and the said time-limit does not begin to run from the day of the formation of the defective contract, but from the day on which the defect ceased. Thus, in the cases of mistake and fraud, for instance, the time-limit begins to run from the day on which the injured party discovered them. In the case of duress, it begins to run from the day on which it ceased, and in the case of lack of capacity, from the day on which it wholly ceased; and if the contracting party is insane, the time-limit of ten years does not begin to run until the time when he becomes aware of the contract previously formed; and the said prescription is founded on the presumption of tacit confirmation of the contract on the part of the holder of the action for nullity, who is deemed to have waived bringing it.

Confirmation of a contract may be included in another form, express or tacit, in which case it appears as an actual confirmation, not a presumed one. However, express confirmation shall have no effect unless the instrument of confirmation contains the substance of the contract, the defect which was in it, and the intention to waive the action for nullity; and tacit confirmation is inferred from every circumstance and every conduct from which it is gathered that the holder of that action has waived it.

Confirmation, whatever its form, whether presumed, express or tacit, effaces the defect which was in the contract, so that no one may any longer invoke this defect as a ground for objection by any means whatsoever, whether by way of defence or of claim. Confirmation entails the waiver of all means by which the contract could have been objected to, save for the rights acquired by a third party in good faith.
Dissolution may have a retroactive effect, in which case it is called rescission, just as its effect may be confined to the future, in which case it is called termination.

Rescission of a contract occurs either by reason of a condition of rescission inserted therein, or pursuant to a presumed intention of the contracting parties (such as the tacit resolutory clause), or by reason of the lapse of one or more obligations due to the impossibility of performing them (the rules governing the risk of loss).

The fulfilment of a condition of rescission dissolves the contract retroactively in accordance with the provisions of Article 99, save for acts of administration, which remain valid and subsisting. Subject to this restriction, the situation shall be restored to what it ought to have been had the dissolved contract never been concluded at all, and this dissolution takes place ipso jure independently of the intervention of the judicial authority.

A resolutory condition is presumed to exist in all synallagmatic contracts if one of the contracting parties fails to perform what is incumbent upon him and is unable to plead impossibility of performance, unless there is an exception provided for by law. However, the contract is not rescinded ipso jure in this case. The party whose rights have not been performed shall have the option between compulsory performance in one way or another, and the rescission of the contract with a claim for damages. In principle, such rescission shall only take place by a judgment of the judge, who shall examine, in the case of partial performance, whether the deficiency in such performance is of such consequence and importance as to justify the rescission of the contract. The judge may, even in the case of non-performance, grant the debtor one period of grace after another according to the good faith he perceives in him, and the contracting parties are entitled to agree between themselves that the contract, in the event of non-performance, shall be rescinded ipso jure without the intervention of the courts. This condition does not dispense with a formal notice intended to establish non-performance in an official manner. It may also be agreed that such formality shall not be required, in which case the clause exempting from judicial intervention and from formal notice must be couched in categorical and express terms.
Rescission for non-execution of an obligation produces the effects produced by rescission arising from the fulfilment of an express resolutory condition.

If the performance of one or several obligations becomes impossible without fault on the part of the debtor, that obligation or those obligations shall lapse by the mere fact of impossibility in accordance with the provisions of Article 341; and if the matter relates to obligations arising from a synallagmatic contract, the corresponding obligations shall lapse upon the lapse of their counterparts, and the matter shall be concluded as though the contract were dissolved ipso jure without the intervention of the courts; or, in other words, the risks shall fall upon the debtor of the thing which has become impossible, and he shall bear the loss without being able to have recourse in any way whatsoever against his co-contractor. The matter shall be otherwise if the debtor has already performed his essential obligations. For the contract, notwithstanding the impossibility of performing the secondary obligations, shall remain in force. And the debtor who has been discharged by force majeure may nevertheless demand from the other party the performance of what is incumbent upon him; and in this manner the seller of a specific thing who has transferred the thing sold to the buyer may demand the price from him, so that the risks in this case shall be upon the creditor of the obligation the performance of which has become impossible.
If the contract is dissolved for impossibility of performance, there shall be no ground for compensating the losing party, and the risks of the event shall therefore fall upon him.

In principle, contracts may not be terminated except by the mutual consent of all those who created them, save for contracts that end with the death of one of the contracting parties, setting aside rescission in its true sense, and such mutual consent is brought about expressly or tacitly, or by the arrival of the term appointed for the lapse of the contract.

Termination by one party alone is valid if it is stipulated in the contract or in the law. In this manner, it is valid, on the one hand, for a contract of lease to be created for a fixed term and for both parties or one of them to be vested therein with the right to terminate it before the appointed term, just as it is permissible, on the other hand, for certain contracts, such as agency and a partnership of persons, to be subject to termination by one party alone and by his mere will.

A terminated contract ceases to have effect only from the date of its termination, and such termination does not extend to what preceded it. The effects which it had produced remain definitively vested.

The party who terminates the contract exposes himself to the payment of damages if he abuses his right of termination, that is, if he exercises it contrary to the spirit of the law or of the contract.
Obligations must, as far as possible, be discharged in kind, as the creditor has a vested right to recover the very object of the obligation.

This rule is observed not only in obligations to give, but also in obligations to do and obligations to abstain, and the creditor is entitled to apply to the court for authorisation to perform the obligation to do by himself at the expense of the debtor. He is likewise entitled to apply for the removal of what has been done contrary to the obligation to abstain, at the expense of the debtor.

However, this treatment cannot be applied to obligations whose discharge in kind requires the debtor himself to perform the act. The creditor is then entitled to apply for the debtor to be ordered to pay a fine for every day, every week, or every month in which he is in delay, or for every default he commits, with a view to compelling the recalcitrant debtor and bringing him out of his inaction. After the performance of the obligation in kind, the court is entitled to remit the fine or to retain thereof such part as compensates the creditor for the damage he has suffered by reason of the unlawful abstention exhibited by the debtor.

If the obligation is not performed by delivery of the specific thing wholly and completely, the creditor is entitled to take compensation standing in the stead of performance of the obligation in kind, for lack of obtaining what is best, and if the compensation is set against definitive failure to perform, whether partial or total, it is called compensatory damages, whereas if performance in kind is still possible, since the debtor was merely late in fulfilling his obligations, the compensation given to the creditor is called moratory damages.

For damages to become due, it is required:

First - That it be attributable to the debtor

Second - That the damage have occurred as damage

Third - That the debtor have been put on notice for his delay, save in exceptional cases.

In the case of contracting, the debtor shall be liable for the non-performance of the obligation, unless he proves that performance has become impossible in the cases set forth in Article 341, in which case he is discharged by reason of impossibility of performance.

In certain contracts, and by way of exception, the debtor shall not be liable merely for his non-performance of the contract; rather, the imputation of liability to him is conditional upon his commission of a fault which the creditor must prove, and the law determines the degree of its gravity.
The conditions for the attribution of damage, in the absence of contracting, are determined in Article 122 and the articles following it.

The delay of the debtor, without which he is not exposed to the payment of damages, results in principle from a notice sent to him by the creditor by some means. However, it must be in writing (such as a registered letter, a telegram, a formal notification, or the institution of an action against him before the court even if it lacks jurisdiction), and this notice is mandatory regardless of the nature of the obligation and of its origin or the origin of the damages.

Notice ceases to be mandatory:

1- When performance becomes impossible

2- When the obligation is subject to a matured term established for the benefit of the debtor, even if only partially at least.

3- When the subject-matter of the obligation required to be performed is the restitution of a thing which the debtor knows to be stolen or which the debtor had knowingly acquired in an unlawful manner; in the three cases set forth above, the debtor shall ipso jure be in a state of delay without any intervention on the part of the creditor.
The assessment of the amount of damages takes place in principle through the judge, and it may take place by a statutory provision or by an agreement between the contracting parties.
Damages must be strictly equivalent to the damage incurred or the profit lost.
Indirect damage shall be taken into account in the same manner as direct damage, provided, however, that its connection with the non-performance of the obligation is fully proven.
In the case of contract, compensation shall cover only the damage which could have been foreseen at the time of conclusion of the contract, unless the debtor has committed fraud.
Moral damage shall be taken into account in the same manner as material damage, provided that the assessment of its value in money is reasonably possible.
Future damage may be taken into account under the conditions and to the extent prescribed for compensation relating to delicts in Article 134, sixth paragraph.

Where the object of the obligation is a sum of money, compensation for delay shall consist in the payment of interest on the sum due calculated at the legal rate, unless there is a provision to the contrary in the contract or in the law. However, if the debtor is in bad faith, supplemental compensation may be awarded to the creditor who has been harmed by an unlawful refusal.

The contracting parties may fix in advance, in the contract or in a subsequent instrument, the amount of damages in the event of the debtor's failure to perform the obligation in whole or in part. The penalty clause is instituted to compensate the creditor for the damage which he suffers from the non-performance of the obligation. He shall not be entitled to claim both the principal and the penalty together, unless the penalty clause was stipulated for mere delay or by way of compelling the debtor to perform. The judge shall be entitled to reduce the coercive penalty if he finds it excessive, and the judge may reduce the amount fixed in the penalty clause if part of the principal obligation has been performed.
The penalty clause is valid and enforceable even if it is equivalent in fact to a clause excluding liability. However, the case of fraud committed by the debtor shall be excepted.

The creditor has a general right of pledge over the debtor's patrimony as a whole, and not over the individual items of his property. This right, which confers upon the creditor the capacity of universal successor to the debtor, grants him neither a right to follow nor a right of preference; ordinary creditors are in principle equal, without distinction between them by reason of the dates on which their rights arose, unless there exist lawful causes of preference arising from the law or from agreement.

The creditor's right of general lien has attributes each of which is a measure placed at his disposal to enable him thereby to obtain what he is entitled to. Some of those measures are purely conservatory and some of them aim directly at compulsory execution. And there is a third category of measures intermediate between the two preceding categories instituted to prepare the ways of compulsory execution and make ready its means.

Conservatory measures, such as the affixing of seals, the registration of a mortgage, and the interruption of a running prescription, may be invoked by every creditor even though his right is subject to a term or to a condition.

As for measures of execution, on the contrary, it is not permissible for the creditor to use them unless his right is due for performance. The most particular of those measures is executive attachment, and among them also are the method of astreinte (Article 251) and the right of retention, that is, the right of every person who is both creditor and debtor in a single transaction or situation to abstain from performance so long as the other party has not offered to carry out what is incumbent upon him.

The right of retention is not confined to one who is creditor and debtor under a synallagmatic contract, but exists also in every case in which the debt is connected with its subject-matter, that is, where interdependence exists between the obligation claimed and the debt pertaining to the one who exercises the right of retention on account of the obligation; thus it, that is the right of retention, belongs for instance to the possessor, or to the usufructuary, or the holder of a pledged thing, without there being any distinction between movable and immovable property or between a retainer of good faith and of bad faith, save that the holder of lost or stolen things and the holder of things wrested by violence from their true owner are deprived of the right of retention.

The right of retention ceases upon the cessation of holding because it is founded thereon. However, the creditor is entitled, if the thing is wrested from him clandestinely or by violence, to demand the restoration of the situation to what it was, provided that he submits this demand within thirty days beginning from the date of his knowledge of that wresting.

The right of retention, subject to the special case aforementioned, does not confer upon its holder a right of pursuit nor a right of preference, yet it may be set up against all persons, in the sense that the retainer is entitled to refuse to relinquish the thing whatever may be the identity of the opponent.

The intermediate measures which prepare the way of execution for the creditor's right of general lien without completing that execution are: the oblique action, the Paulian action, and the right of separation of patrimonies.

Creditors shall be entitled to exercise in the name of their debtor all rights and to institute all actions pertaining to him, with the exception of rights and actions exclusively attached to his person, and in particular rights and actions the subject-matter of which falls outside the scope of their pledge. However, they may not invoke this prerogative in order to take his place in the administration of his patrimony, for he retains control of its administration notwithstanding the poor state of his affairs. Creditors may bring proceedings directly on behalf of their debtor without previously carrying out any formality to be subrogated to his rights and actions, even though they do not hold an enforceable title. Nevertheless, they may not initiate such proceedings unless their debt is due for payment. The results of the action shall be shared in common among all the creditors without the creditor who initiated the action acquiring any preference whatever over the others.

The position shall be contrary to the foregoing where the law exceptionally grants creditors the right to institute a direct action, for the results thereof shall accrue to the claimant alone, and he shall not be bound to share the benefit between himself and the other creditors. Provided that this procedure may only be carried out if it is established by an express text which shall be construed strictly.

Creditors whose debt has become due for payment shall be entitled to demand in their own names the rescission of contracts concluded by the debtor in prejudice of their rights and which were the cause of creating his insolvency or aggravating such insolvency. As for contracts whereby the debtor merely neglected to make a gain, they shall not be subject to the action for rescission. This action, termed the "Paulian action", may reach persons with whom the debtor contracted fraudulently. However, it may not validly be brought against persons who acquired their rights for valuable consideration unless their participation in collusion with the debtor is proved. None shall benefit from the results of this action except the person or persons who instituted it, and only to the extent required for the preservation of their rights. As for anything in excess thereof, the contract shall remain standing and shall continue to produce all its effects. This action shall be barred by prescription after ten years.

Obligations are transmitted upon death or inter vivos unless there is an impossibility arising from a statutory provision or from the fact that the obligation is purely personal and established in consideration of the person of the contracting party. Transmission by reason of death shall be governed by the rules of testate or intestate succession. Transmission inter vivos shall be governed by the following rules laid down with the distinction between the transmission of obligations viewed from the active aspect (transfer of the creditor's claim), and the transmission of obligations viewed from the passive aspect (transfer of the debtor's debt).

A creditor may assign a debt due to him to another person unless such assignment is prohibited by virtue of the law, or by virtue of the intention of the contracting parties, or by reason of the obligation being purely personal and established between two specified persons in a manner not admitting of change.

An assignment may be made of rights contingent upon a certain circumstance, even if they are purely future. The assignment of a disputed right in respect of which an action on the merits has been brought is valid, provided that the debtor whose debt the creditor has assigned consents thereto. The effects of such assignment remain subject, as regards jurisdiction, to the provisions of Article 3 of the Law promulgated on 17 February 1928.

However, the assignee cannot be bought out where he has a legitimate cause for acquiring the disputed rights, such as being a co-heir with the assignor, or a co-owner with him in property, or a creditor of his.

An assignment is completed as between the contracting parties from the time the agreement is concluded between them, unless such assignment is gratuitous, in which case the rules as to form governing gifts inter vivos must be observed.

The transfer shall not be deemed to exist with respect to a third party, and in particular with respect to the debtor whose debt the creditor has assigned, except by notification of such assignment to the debtor or by a declaration by the debtor in a document bearing a registered date that he has accepted that assignment. So long as neither of these two formalities has been completed, it is valid for the debtor to discharge his obligation to the assignor.

Where the assignor has effected two successive assignments of one and the same debt, the assignee who was first to act in accordance with the law shall have priority over the other, even if the date of his contract is more recent.

The assignor must deliver the instrument of debt to the assignee and vest him with all the means at his disposal to prove and obtain the assigned right. Save in the case of a gratuitous assignment, he warrants to the assignee the existence of the assigned right at the time the assignment is effected together with the validity of such right, provided that he does not warrant the solvency of the debtor. Where, however, the agreement provides to the contrary with respect to the solvency of the debtor, the provision relating thereto must be restricted to present solvency and the liability must be restricted to the value of the consideration for the assignment, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary.

Assignment transfers to the assignee the debt together with all its accessories, such as suretyship, privilege, pledge and immovable real securities, in accordance with the forms and conditions provided for in the Law of Ownership and Real Rights, just as it transfers to him all the defects attached to the debt and the characteristics inherent therein; the debtor is therefore entitled to raise the grounds of plea and defence which he was entitled to raise against the assignee. The contrary shall apply if the debtor has consented to the transfer unconditionally and without reservation: he is then deemed to have waived the means of defence which he possessed up to that time.

The rules set forth above apply not only to the assignment of a creditor's claim, but also to the assignment of rights in general, unless there is a provision to the contrary in the law or something in the nature of the right that prevents their application.

The transfer of a debtor's debt takes place either by agreement between the creditors and the person who assumes the debt, or by agreement between the latter and the debtor. In the second case, the effect of the transfer remains subject to the ratification of the creditor. The contracting parties may, so long as the ratification has not been given, amend or revoke their agreement, and if the creditor does not ratify the transfer, it becomes void.

If he ratifies it, it shall have retroactive effect as from the day on which the agreement was concluded between the debtor and the person to whom the debt was transferred. Ratification may not be given until after the contracting parties have notified the creditor of the transfer.

It must be given within the time limit fixed in the notification, and if no time limit has been fixed, within the period deemed sufficient for making an election. If the time limit expires, the ratification is deemed to be refused.
Real securities remain in force after the transfer of the debt. Personal securities, however, are extinguished unless the persons liable consent to the agreement concluded.

The grounds of plea and means of defence inherent in the debt pass from the debtor to the person who has assumed the debt. As for the means personal to the former debtor, the new debtor is not entitled to invoke them, though he is entitled to raise the grounds of plea and means of defence personal to himself.

Obligations are extinguished:

First- By their performance, which is the natural mode of their extinction (discharge)

Second- By a measure or an event which secures to the creditor the obtaining of a benefit other than that which he is entitled to claim (such as discharge by performance in lieu, novation of the obligation, set-off, and merger)

Third- By causes which extinguish the obligation or may extinguish it regardless of whether the creditor obtains any benefit (such as impossibility of performance, remission of debt, and prescription).

The extinction of the principal obligation entails the extinction of the accessory obligations and the movable securities which pertained to the debt, and gives rise to the right to cancel the registrations pertaining to the immovable securities.

The debtor must perform the obligation in person when it is inferred from the wording of the contract or from the nature of the debt that it is incumbent upon him to carry out the performance himself. In cases other than these, performance may validly be carried out by any person whomsoever without the knowledge of the debtor and without the creditor being entitled to object to such intervention.

Performance must be made into the hands of the creditor, or of his agent holding a legal authorisation, or of the person whom he has designated for this purpose, provided that performance made to an unauthorised person shall not discharge the debtor except in the following cases:

First - If the creditor has consented

Second - If the creditor has benefited from the irregular performance. And the discharge of the debtor shall be to the extent of the benefit derived by the creditor.

Third - If payment has been made in good faith to a person deemed to possess the capacity of the creditor, such as an apparent heir.

A creditor who refuses, without a legitimate reason, the payment tendered to him under conditions conforming to the rules, shall thereby be deemed to be in a state of default from the time his refusal is established by an official instrument, and from that moment the risk of loss or deterioration of the thing shall be borne by such creditor and interest shall cease to run on the debt. Moreover, the debtor shall then be entitled to deposit the subject-matter of the obligation and to charge the creditor with the burden of the expenses and risks, and he shall in this manner be discharged from the obligation.

If the subject-matter of the obligation is an act, and not the delivery of a thing, the debtor shall be entitled, from the time the creditor is in a state of default, to rescind the contract in accordance with the provisions pertaining to the default of the debtor.

When the thing due is capable of being deposited, such deposit shall be effected at the place and under the conditions designated by the court of the place of payment. However, if the thing is not capable of being deposited, as where, for instance, it is perishable or its preservation would entail exorbitant expenses, the debtor may, after obtaining the permission of the judge, sell it publicly and deposit the price.
The debtor may recover the thing deposited so long as the creditor has not declared his acceptance of the deposit. In this case, the debt shall revive with all its accessories.
The expenses of the deposit shall be borne by the creditor when the deposit is lawful.

The very thing due must be paid, and the creditor may not be compelled to accept another, even if it is of higher value than it. Where the thing is determined only by its kind, the debtor shall not be bound to tender it of the highest quality, though he may not tender it of the lowest quality.

The debtor may not compel the creditor to accept partial payment, even if the obligation is divisible, because payment in this sense is indivisible. Derogation from this rule is permissible through the application of the provisions on set-off or by exercising the benefit of division with respect to sureties, and the judge has the right to grant a debtor in good faith grace periods for payment, thereby making the payment of the debt in instalments over a long or short period as the circumstances may require.

Where the debt is a sum of money, it must be paid in the currency of the country. In ordinary times, when the circulation of paper currency is not compulsory, the contracting parties remain free to stipulate payment in specified metallic coins or in foreign currency.

The debt must be paid at the place designated in the contract. Where no express or implied stipulation has been made in this regard, payment must be made at the place of residence of the debtor. However, where the subject-matter of the obligation is a specific thing, performance must be effected where the thing was at the time the contract was formed.

The creditor may not be compelled to accept payment before the term unless the term was established for the sole benefit of the debtor, and where there is no term designated or impliedly inferred from the nature of the matter, the obligation may be performed and such performance may be demanded without delay. Performance must take place on the day of maturity, subject to the provisions of Article 105.
The expenses of payment shall be borne by the debtor.

Payment is ordinarily proved by a deed of receipt given by the creditor to the debtor. It is proof of its own date as regards the contracting parties themselves. Where there is no deed of receipt, proof may be derived either from entries in the creditor's registers and domestic papers, or from annotations written by the creditor at the foot or in the margin of the instrument of debt.

A debtor who has made payment in full has the right to demand, in addition to the deed of receipt, the surrender of the instrument itself to him or its destruction. Where, however, payment is partial, he may demand, in addition to the deed of receipt, that mention of what he has paid be made upon the instrument of debt retained by the creditor.

Where a single debtor owes several debts to a single creditor, the debtor may declare at the time of performance which debt he intends to discharge; if he fails to make such declaration, the choice rests with the creditor, provided that he exercises it without delay in the receipt itself, unless the debtor objects thereto.

The debtor's choice is subject to certain restrictions: in the absence of an agreement with the creditor, he cannot, upon making partial performance, appropriate such performance to the principal before discharging the interest, nor can he prefer the discharge of a debt that has not fallen due over a debt that is due.

Where there is no express appropriation by either of the contracting parties, performance must be deemed appropriated to the debt that has fallen due rather than to the debt whose term has not matured. Where there are several debts that have fallen due, performance shall be appropriated to the debt which the debtor has an interest in discharging before the others, failing which to the debt that is more onerous than the others. In the absence of any other ground for assessment, performance shall apply to the various debts in proportion to their respective amounts.

Performance extinguishes the debt absolutely and finally with respect to all interested parties. Performance may, however, be limited to transferring the debt if it is accompanied by subrogation; in such case, the debt is deemed discharged in whole or in part by a person who ought not to bear the entire burden finally, and who is thereby subrogated to the rights of the satisfied creditor so as to be able to exercise recourse against the principal debtor or the co-debtors in the obligation.
Subrogation takes place either by operation of law or by the will of the creditor or of the debtor.

Subrogation takes place by operation of law in the following cases:

First- In favour of an unsecured creditor, a pledgee, or a mortgagee who discharges the claims of another creditor having priority over him. However, with respect to rights subject to registration in the Land Register, subrogation shall take effect only after such registration has been completed

Second- In favour of a person bound to perform with others (as in joint and several or indivisible obligations) or bound to perform on behalf of others (such as a surety or a third-party holder of mortgaged immovable property), if he was compelled to perform or had an interest in performing

Third- In favour of an heir who has discharged the debts of the estate out of his own funds.

A creditor who accepts performance from a third party may subrogate him to his rights; in such case, the subrogation must be made expressly at the time of performance at the latest. However, the date of the receipt containing the subrogation shall not be deemed certain with respect to third parties, as regards the subrogation, except from the day on which such date becomes authentic.
