Subrogation shall be valid where the debtor borrows a sum of money to pay what he owes and grants his lender, in order to secure him with respect to his money, all the rights that belonged to his original creditor whose debt has been paid. In such case, it is required:

First - That the instrument of loan and the instrument of receipt bear a certain date.

Second - That it be declared in the instrument of loan that the money has been borrowed for the purpose of payment, and that it be declared in the instrument of receipt that the payment has been made with the borrowed money.

Third - That it be declared that the lender has been subrogated to the rights of the creditor whose debt has been paid. The consent of the creditor shall not be required for the validity of this transaction.

Legal or conventional subrogation places the subrogated creditor in the rights of the creditor whose debt has been paid, yet it does not confer upon him the capacity or status of an assignee. He shall not be entitled to bring an action in warranty against the creditor whose debt has been paid. He shall only be subrogated to him to the extent of and in proportion to the money he has paid. Where he is bound with others, he shall only be entitled to sue his co-debtors in the obligation to the extent of the share and portion of each of them. The subrogated creditor shall be entitled, in addition to the right to bring the actions arising from subrogation, to bring the personal action arising from his intervention in the capacity of an agent or a negotiorum gestor.

In the case of partial payment, the subrogated party shall concur with the creditor in the exercise of the rights appertaining to each of them in proportion to what is due to each one, and their debts shall be paid out of the property of the debtor in proportion to the share of each of them.
Payment by means of a cheque remains subject to the provisions of the Law promulgated on 7 April of the year 1330 (1914), which remains in force.

The debt is extinguished if the creditor accepts, in lieu of performance, the rendering of something other than that which was due to him. If any doubt arises and the creditor does not object or make a reservation upon payment by performance in lieu, the creditor shall be deemed, until proof to the contrary is established, to have accepted such payment and to have acknowledged that it discharges the debtor.

The rules of sale apply in principle to payment by performance in lieu, and in particular the rules relating to warranty and to the capacity of the contracting parties. However, the rules of payment apply by analogy and as far as possible, and in particular with respect to the imputation of payment.
Novation is the substitution of a new obligation for the original obligation. Novation of an obligation is not presumed; rather, it must result expressly from the contract.
The creditor must have the capacity to dispose of his right and the debtor the capacity to bind himself.

Novation is not effected unless both the old and the new obligations actually exist and neither of them is subject to a ground of absolute nullity. However, the mere voidability of the one debt or the other does not prevent novation; rather, its effects remain in existence so long as the annulment has not been adjudged. A voidable debt may be replaced by a valid obligation if the holder of the action for annulment was aware of the situation, in which case he is deemed to have waived the right to bring it. A natural obligation may be replaced by means of novation with a civil obligation.

Novation takes place only by introducing a new element into the obligation. The change relates either to the person of one of the contracting parties, or to the subject-matter of the obligation, or to the legal title from which the obligation is derived.

Novation is not inferred from a change in the form of the obligation or a change in the place of performance, nor from the drawing up of a negotiable instrument, nor from the accession of other persons to the obligors.

Novation extinguishes the obligation both in principal and in accessory as against all persons, and the sureties and other obligors may, with their consent, enter under the provisions of the new obligation. An express stipulation may be made requiring that mortgages, privileges and pledges of movables be attached to the new debt on the same conditions as those securing the extinguished obligation, and this takes place only if the owner of the property encumbered with the right of mortgage or privilege consents to such attachment.

Delegation is a mandate given by a person (called the delegator) to another person (called the delegate) to contract an undertaking towards a third person (called the delegatee). It does not necessarily imply the existence of a prior obligation between the contracting parties, and this transaction is not presumed and does not lead to the novation of a prior obligation that bound the delegator to the delegate or the delegator to the delegatee. In the absence of a special stipulation, the new obligation is joined alongside the prior obligations (and this is what is called imperfect delegation).

If the intention of the contracting parties is to replace the prior obligation or obligations with a new obligation (perfect delegation), the delegator is immediately discharged towards the delegatee, provided that the new undertaking assumed by the delegate is valid, and that the delegate is solvent at the time of the delegation.
Where two persons are each creditor and debtor of the other, each of them is entitled to set off against the other what is owed to him by the latter up to the amount of the lesser of the two debts.
Set-off takes place only between debts whose subject-matter is money or fungible things of the same kind.

Only liquidated debts which are due and payable shall enter into set-off. However, a grace period granted by the judge shall not prevent set-off. Nor is it necessary that the two debts be payable in one place. However, circumstances which prevent payment shall, in principle, prevent set-off.

Set-off shall take place whatever the causes of either of the two debts may be, except in the following cases:

1- Upon a claim for the restitution of a thing wrongfully dispossessed from its owner

2- Upon a claim for the restitution of a deposit or a loan for use

3- Where there is an unattachable debt

4- Where the debtor has waived set-off in advance.

Set-off shall not operate ipso jure, but upon the request of one of the two parties, and it shall extinguish the debt on the day on which the conditions required to enable it to be invoked are fulfilled, regardless of events which may have occurred subsequently, such as the extinction of one of the two obligations by prescription.

In principle, set-off, when invoked, produces the effect of payment, but up to the amount of the lesser debt, and it extinguishes the accessories of the obligation (such as a mortgage of immovable property, a pledge of movable property, suretyship, etc.) in proportion to its extinction of the obligation itself. However, the extinction of rights subject to registration in the Land Register shall only be effected by the cancellation of that registration.

A surety may request set-off of what is owed by the creditor to the principal debtor, but this debtor may not request set-off of what is owed by the creditor to the surety, nor may a joint and several debtor invoke the existence of another debt in favour of one of his co-debtors, owed by the creditor. However, if the surety or the joint and several debtor invokes set-off after having become creditors of the creditor, the set-off shall extinguish the debt in respect of the principal debtor or the other debtors. And the latter shall be entitled to invoke the set-off.
Set-off shall not affect rights previously acquired by a third party.
Where there exist between two persons several debts capable of set-off, the rules laid down for the imputation of payment shall apply.

Where the two conflicting capacities, the capacity of creditor and the capacity of debtor, are united in a single obligation and in a single person, there arises from their union a merger which extinguishes the obligation in proportion to such merger. If the cause of the merger ceases to exist and its cessation has a retroactive effect, the debt shall revive with all its accessories in respect of all persons, and the merger of patrimonies shall be deemed never to have occurred at all.

Remission of debt or the waiver by the creditor of his rights for the benefit of the debtor takes place only by virtue of an agreement, since remission presupposes the agreement of the parties concerned.

Remission is not subject to the rules of form pertaining to gratuitous disposition even if effected by the creditor without any countervailing benefit. However, it is subject in such case to the substantive rules pertaining to gratuitous disposition, and in particular those thereof relating to the capacity of the parties concerned.

A contract of remission may be express or implied; it is inferred from every act or every circumstance from which there clearly appears on the part of the creditor the intention to waive his rights, and on the part of the debtor the intention to avail himself of this waiver. The voluntary surrender of the original instrument which was in the possession of the creditor raises a presumption that remission has taken place until the contrary is proved. The return by the creditor of a thing deposited by way of security is not sufficient to found such a presumption.
An obligation is extinguished if, after its inception, its object has become impossible from a physical aspect or a legal aspect without an act or fault on the part of the debtor.

The debtor must establish proof of the existence of force majeure; nevertheless, it remains open to the creditor to prove that the contingency which occurred independently of the debtor was preceded or accompanied by a fault committed by the debtor, such as a delay in performance which placed him in default. In such a situation the obligation remains subsisting.

The debtor is discharged on account of force majeure only to the extent of the impossibility of performance. Extinguishment of the obligation may therefore be only partial. In all cases, even in the case of Extinguishment of the entire obligation, the debtor is bound to assign to the creditor the rights and actions for compensation relating to the former obligation, just as he is bound to deliver to him whatever remains of the perished thing, if there be any remainder.
Obligations are extinguished by the inaction of the creditor who fails to assert his rights throughout a period of time.

The effect of prescription does not operate ipso jure, but must be pleaded by the person in whose interest it then is. He may plead it at all stages of the proceedings, even on appeal for the first time. A judge may not of his own motion apply the provisions of prescription.

A creditor may not waive in advance the operation of prescription, nor lengthen or shorten its period, but he may waive it after it has been acquired. His waiver may be express or tacit. If his waiver is of a fraudulent nature, it is permissible for his creditors to obtain the annulment of that waiver by bringing the Paulian action.

Every joint and several debtor and the surety shall have the right to plead prescription against the creditor, just as another creditor of the debtor shall have the right to plead it by the indirect way.

The operation of prescription shall not commence except on the day the debt becomes due for performance. The period shall be calculated in days, not in hours, and the day of commencement shall not be counted. The period of prescription shall be deemed complete upon the expiry of the last day thereof.
Prescription is completed in principle after the expiry of ten years.

The period of prescription shall be five years in respect of arrears, interest, dividends on shares of profits, and rents of buildings and agricultural lands, and in general in respect of obligations which fall due for performance every year or less. The period of prescription shall also be five years in actions between partners or between them and other persons on account of obligations arising from the partnership contract. This period shall commence from the day of the publication of the dissolution of the partnership or the publication of the withdrawal of one of the partners.

The following shall be barred by prescription after two years:

1- The right of action of sellers, suppliers of goods, and factory owners in respect of the items which they supply.

2- The right of action of farmers and producers of raw materials in respect of the items which they supply where they are used for the domestic needs of the debtor. The period of prescription shall run from the day on which those items were supplied.

3- The right of action of teachers, professors, and proprietors of public and private boarding educational establishments in respect of the fees due to them from their pupils, and of the supplies provided to those pupils. The period of prescription shall run from the maturity of the term fixed for the fees to fall due.

4- The right of action of servants relating to the wages, advances, and other obligations due to them under the contract of service, as well as the right of action of the master against his servants in respect of money advanced to them in their capacity as servants.

5- The right of action of workmen and apprentices in respect of their wages, supplies, daily pay, and money which they have advanced on account of their service. Likewise, the right of action of the employer (mustakhdim, with a kasra under the dal) or master in respect of money advanced to his workmen in their capacity as workmen.

6- The right of action of hotelkeepers and restaurateurs in respect of providing lodging and food to their clients and of money advanced to them.

7- The right of action of lessors of furniture and movable things on account of the rent thereof.

8- The right of action of private and public establishments devoted to the treatment of diseases or to the care of patients on account of the care which they bestow upon them and the provision of supplies and advances to them. The period of prescription shall run from the day on which the care was bestowed upon them or the supplies were provided to them.

9- The right of action of hired labourers in respect of the compensation which they may claim pursuant to Articles 652 and 656 of the said Law.

The following shall also lapse by prescription after two years:

1- The right of action of physicians, surgeons, obstetricians, dentists, and veterinary surgeons for their consultations, the operations they have performed, and the supplies and advances they have provided. The period of prescription begins from the date of the last consultation or operation.

2- The right of action of pharmacists for the medicines they have provided. The period of prescription begins from the date of providing them.

3- The right of action of lawyers and legal agents for their fees and their advances, and the aforementioned period begins from the issuance of the final judgment or from the date of their dismissal from the mandate.

4- The right of action of building and surveying engineers and all other engineers and experts for the plans they draw, the works they carry out, or the advances they provide. The period begins from the date of delivering the plans, completing the works, or making the advances.

5- The right of action of brokers with respect to the payment of the brokerage fee. The period begins from the date of conclusion of the agreement.
In the cases specified in Articles 351 and 352, prescription shall run even if the provision of supplies, delivery, service, or work continues.

Prescription shall not run, and if it is running it shall be suspended:

1- Between spouses during the period of marriage

2- Between the father and the mother and their children

3- Between an incapacitated person or a juristic person on the one hand, and the guardian, curator, or administrator on the other hand, so long as their function has not ceased and they have not rendered a final account of their administration

4- Between the master and the servant so long as the contract of employment is in force.

Prescription against unemancipated minors and all other incapacitated persons who do not have a guardian, a judicial supervisor, or a tutor shall be suspended until after they attain the age of majority, are emancipated, or have a legal representative appointed for them.
Prescription shall also be suspended in general in favour of a creditor for whom it was impossible to interrupt it for a reason independent of his will.

Prescription shall be interrupted:

1- By any judicial or extrajudicial claim having a certain date which has the effect of placing the debtor in default of performing the obligation, even if it is submitted to a court having no jurisdiction or is adjudged void as to form.

2- By an application for the admission of the creditor's debt in the bankruptcy of the debtor.

3- By a conservatory act affecting the property of the debtor or by a petition aimed at obtaining permission to carry out an act of this kind.
Prescription shall be interrupted by the debtor's acknowledgment of the creditor's right.

Where a clause is susceptible of two meanings, that which is most in conformity with the spirit of the contract and the purpose intended thereby shall be adopted, and in all cases the meaning which gives effect to the clause shall be preferred over the meaning under which the clause remains without effect.
The clauses of a single agreement shall be coordinated and interpreted one by another with regard to the whole of the contract.
In case of doubt, the text shall be interpreted in favour of the debtor against the creditor.

Where there are omissions in the text of the contract, the judge must supply them either by the provisions inserted in the law if the contract is nominate, or otherwise by reference to the rules laid down for the contracts most analogous to the contract to be interpreted.
The judge must also, of his own motion, take into account the clauses observed by custom, even though they are not expressly mentioned in the text of the contract.
A sale is a contract whereby the seller binds himself to transfer the ownership of a thing, and whereby the buyer binds himself to pay the price thereof.

The validity of a sale depends upon the agreement of the contracting parties as to the nature of the contract, the thing sold, the price, and the general conditions for the validity of contractual obligations.

A sale may be:

1= In bulk (lump sum), which is that having for its object an aggregate of things in consideration of a single price regardless of number, weight, and measure, unless these are intended to determine the total price.

2= Or by weight, or by count, or by measure.

3- Or subject to the condition of trial

4- Or subject to the condition of tasting

5- Or a sale with right of redemption.

If the operation of prescription is lawfully interrupted, the time which elapsed prior to the occurrence of the act that interrupted it shall not be included in the calculation of the period required for prescription. This period, remaining unchanged, shall in principle begin to run anew from the time when the act interrupting prescription ceases to produce its effects. If the debt is acknowledged in a deed or established by a judgment, the new time limit for prescription shall remain ten years.
The operation of prescription shall constitute proof of the discharge of the debtor, and the presumption of discharge arising therefrom is irrebuttable and admits of no proof to the contrary.

The operation of prescription is not limited to extinguishing the creditor's right to bring an action, but also extinguishes the obligation itself, so that no benefit may thereafter be derived in any manner whatsoever, neither by bringing an action nor by raising a defence; provided that the debtor who has been civilly discharged by prescription remains bound by a natural obligation which may serve as a cause for performance.

Whoever claims to be a creditor is required to adduce proof of the existence of his right. Once he has adduced such proof, whoever claims the extinction of the obligation must prove the truth of his assertion.

A written contract drawn up at the time of contracting is not written with full probative force unless it is signed by the contracting parties. Where the contract is synallagmatic, it must be drawn up in as many copies as there are contracting parties having conflicting interests. Where the agreement is not synallagmatic, these two words "good for" must be written before the signature, and if these two formalities, namely the multiplicity of copies and the mention of the two words "good the term", are not carried out, the agreement shall remain valid, but the written instrument shall only constitute a commencement of proof which must be completed by testimony and presumptions. However, the multiplicity of copies shall not be necessary if the contracting parties agree to deposit the single original with a third party chosen by them.
If one of the contracting parties does not know how to sign his signature, he may replace the signature with his fingerprint.
The rules of evidence relating to the conclusion of agreements and to the creation, transfer, or extinction of obligations are set forth in the Code of Civil Procedure.

In legal acts, the judge must ascertain the true intention of the obligor (if the undertaking is unilateral) or the intention of all the contracting parties (if there is a contract), rather than stop at the literal meaning of the text.
The costs of the instrument of sale and of what is transferred thereby shall be borne by the buyer.
A sale may be made in writing or orally, subject to the rules laid down for the sale of immovable property.
Both the seller and the buyer must have capacity to bind themselves. And the seller must have capacity to dispose of the thing or to assign the right in respect of which the sale is concluded.

The persons referred to hereinafter may not purchase, either by themselves or through interposed persons, even if the purchase is by auction, unless they hold an authorisation from the judiciary. And if they do so, the contract of purchase shall be null and void:

First- Agents for sale may not purchase the property which they have been entrusted to sell

Second- Public administrators may not purchase the property of the State, nor the property of villages, nor the property of institutions the care of which has been delegated to them

Third- Public officers may not purchase the property which they have been entrusted to sell

Fourth- Neither the father nor the mother, nor the tutor, curator, judicial supervisor, or temporary guardian, may purchase the property of the persons whom they represent or supervise.

Neither brokers nor experts may purchase, by themselves or through others, the property, rights, and debts which they have been entrusted to sell or to appraise, nor may they take them in barter or take them in pledge.

Judges, advocates, judicial clerks, and their assistants may not purchase, either by themselves or through others, litigious rights falling within the jurisdiction of the courts within the circuit of which they perform their functions.
The wives of the aforementioned persons their children, even if they are of full age, shall be deemed interposed persons in the cases provided for in the preceding articles.

A sale shall not be concluded in respect of things which may not be dealt in by way of sale, nor things which have no value capable of being appraised, nor those which cannot be delivered by reason of their nature.
The sale of corporeal and incorporeal property is valid.

The thing sold may be a specific item or an undivided or defined right encumbering it, and the sale may also be of a thing determined by its kind only, provided that the sale in this case shall not be valid unless the designation of the kind applies to fungible things sufficiently known by number, weight, quality, or measure so that both contracting parties have clear knowledge of what they have consented to.

The sale of the property of another is null except in the following cases:

First- If the thing sold is a thing determined by its genus or by its kind only.

Second- If the owner ratifies it.

Third- If the seller subsequently acquires the right of ownership over the thing sold. However, if the owner refuses to ratify the sale, the seller shall be liable for damages to the buyer if he knew that he did not own the thing sold and the buyer was unaware of that. The seller may not claim the nullity of the contract on the plea that the sale was concluded over the property of another.

- All of this is subject to the application of the provisions of Decision No. 188 issued by the High Commissioner on 15 March 1926

The contracting parties must determine the price of the thing sold, and the determination of the price may be delegated to a third person. In this case, if the third person refuses or is unable to estimate the price, no sale is concluded.
If the dates for payment of the price and the conditions of this payment are not mentioned in the contract of sale, the sale shall be deemed to be for cash without condition.
A sale shall not be perfected unless the contracting parties agree on the nature of the contract, the thing sold, and the price.

A sale in bulk shall be deemed perfected from the moment the contracting parties agree on the thing sold and the price, even if no weighing, counting, or measuring, such as is necessary to determine the price where required, has taken place.
If the sale is by weight, by count, or by measure, the thing sold shall remain at the risk of the seller until the weighing, counting, or measuring is completed.
The seller shall bear the risks of the thing sold during the period of its transit until the buyer receives it, unless there is a provision to the contrary.

Where fruit on trees, the produce of an orchard, or a crop the time for harvesting which has not yet arrived is sold, the fruit or vegetables shall remain at the seller's risk until ripeness is complete.

The seller has two principal obligations, which are:

First- Delivery of the thing sold

Second- Warranty of the thing sold
Delivery consists in the seller or his representative placing the thing sold at the disposal of the buyer in such a manner that he is able to take possession of it and to enjoy it without hindrance.

Delivery is effected in the following manners:

First- Where the thing sold is immovable property, by relinquishing it and by handing over its keys where appropriate, provided that the buyer does not then encounter anything that prevents him from taking possession of the thing sold.

Second- Where the thing sold consists of movables, by actual delivery, or by handing over the keys of the buildings or chests containing those movables, or by any other means accepted by custom.

Third- Delivery is effected even by the mere consent of the contracting parties where the production of the thing sold is impossible at the time of the sale or where the thing sold is already in the possession of the buyer for another reason.

Fourth- It is also effected by the endorsement or delivery of the warehouse warrant, bill of lading, or waybill where the thing sold consists of items deposited in public warehouses.

The delivery of incorporeal things sold, such as a right of way for example, is effected by handing over the instruments that establish the existence of the right or by the seller's authorisation to the buyer to exercise it, provided that no obstacle prevents such exercise; and where the subject-matter of the right is incorporeal and its exercise requires taking possession of a certain thing, the seller must then enable the buyer to take possession of that thing without hindrance.

The thing sold must be delivered at the place where it was situated at the time of the formation of the contract, unless the contrary is stipulated. Where the contract of sale designates a place for the situation of the thing sold other than the place where it is actually situated, the seller must transport the thing sold to the designated place if the buyer requests its transport.
Where the thing sold has to be dispatched from one place to another, delivery is not effected until the moment when the thing sold reaches the buyer or his representative.
A sale subject to trial is deemed in all cases to be concluded under a suspensive condition.
A sale subject to tasting is not deemed complete so long as the buyer has not accepted the thing sold.

The sale of immovable property or of real rights encumbering immovable property shall have no effect, even between the contracting parties, except from the date of its registration in the Land Register.

The buyer acquires by operation of law ownership of the thing sold, if it is a specific thing, when the sale becomes complete by agreement of the contracting parties, unless there is a contrary statutory provision such as the provision set forth in the preceding Article. The same applies even in the following two cases:

First- If delivery or payment of the price is subject to a term.

Second- If the thing sold is concluded under a resolutory condition.

The buyer is entitled, from the completion of the contract and even before delivery, to assign the thing sold, unless there is a contrary agreement or statutory provision. The seller is entitled to assign his right to the price before receiving it.

The buyer must, from the time the contract becomes complete - unless there is a contrary provision - bear:

First- The taxes, charges, and all other burdens encumbering the thing sold.

Second- The expenses of preserving the thing sold and the costs of collecting them.

Third- The risks of the specific thing.

If the sale is concluded in respect of a thing determined by its kind only, or is concluded subject to weighing, counting, measuring, trial, or tasting, or is concluded merely by description, the seller remains liable for the risks of the thing sold, even if it has come into the hands of the buyer, until it is individualised, weighed, counted, or measured, or is accepted by the purchaser or his representative.
If the sale is alternative and a time limit has been fixed for the choice, the purchaser does not bear the risks until after the choice has been made, unless there is a contrary provision.

Delivery must take place at the time appointed therefor in the contract, and if no time is appointed, delivery must take place immediately upon the conclusion of the contract, subject to the time limits required by the nature of the thing sold or by custom.

A seller who has not granted the buyer a term for payment shall not be bound to deliver the thing sold so long as the buyer has not paid the price to him. An offer of suretyship or any other form of security shall not take the place of payment of the price.

If several things are sold as a whole, the seller shall be entitled to retain them all in his possession until he receives the total of their prices, even if the price of each of them has been fixed separately.

The seller may not refuse to deliver the thing sold:

First- If he has authorised another person to receive the price or the balance due thereof.

Second- If he has accepted an assignment against another person for the payment of the price or the balance due thereof.

Third- If he has granted the buyer, after the contract, a term for payment.

The seller shall not be bound to deliver the thing sold even if he has granted the buyer a term for payment:

First- If the buyer, after the conclusion of the sale, becomes insolvent.

Second- If he was in a state of bankruptcy or judicial liquidation at the time of the sale while the seller was unaware of his condition.

Third- If he has diminished the securities which he provided as a guarantee for payment to such an extent that the seller has become exposed to the risk of loss of the price.

If the seller exercises the right to retain the thing sold pursuant to the aforementioned articles, he shall be liable for the thing sold under the conditions on which a pledgee is liable for the thing pledged with him.

In the absence of a contrary provision or custom, the seller shall bear -:

First- The expenses of delivery, such as the cost of measuring, weighing, counting, or determining the volume.

Second- The expenses necessary for establishing or transferring the right, if the thing sold is incorporeal.

The expenses of taking and receiving the thing sold (such as packing, transport, and shipping), the expenses of paying the price, exchange, and registration, and the cost of the deeds drawn up by the notary public and the stamps required for the deed of purchase, shall all be paid by the buyer unless there is a contrary provision or custom.

The expenses of receipt shall include transit duties, octroi, and customs duties levied during the transport of the thing sold and upon its arrival.
The thing sold must be delivered in the condition in which it was at the time of the sale, and the seller may not thereafter alter its condition.

If the specific thing which is the subject of the sale perishes or sustains a defect prior to delivery by reason of an act or fault committed by the seller, the buyer shall be entitled to claim the value of such thing or compensation corresponding to the diminution in its value, under the conditions pursuant to which he would be entitled to bring an action against any other person.

If the thing sold consists of fungibles, the seller must deliver the equivalent thereof in quality and quantity, without prejudice to the buyer's right to claim additional damages where appropriate.

If the thing sold perishes or sustains a defect prior to delivery by reason of an act or fault on the part of the buyer, he shall be bound to take delivery thereof in its condition and to pay its price in full.

All produce of the thing sold and all its civil and natural accessions shall become the property of the buyer from the date of completion of the sale. They must be delivered to him together with the thing sold - unless there is a provision to the contrary.
The obligation to deliver a thing includes its accessories.
The delivery of immovable property also includes immovables by destination, as they are necessarily deemed to be accessories of the thing sold.

The sale of an animal includes:

First - Its suckling young

Second - The wool or hair which is ready for shearing.
Valuables and precious objects contained within a movable thing shall not be deemed included in the sale unless the contrary is stipulated.
The seller is bound to deliver the contents of the thing sold as specified in the contract, subject to the modifications set forth hereinafter.

Where immovable property is sold with an indication of its area and the price per unit of measure, the vendor shall be bound to deliver to the purchaser, if the latter insists thereon, the quantity specified in the contract. Where the vendor is unable to do so or where the purchaser does not hold fast thereto, the vendor shall be bound to accept a proportional reduction of the price; whereas if the area is found to exceed that which is specified in the contract and the excess amounts to one-twentieth of the specified area, the purchaser may elect either to pay the supplement of the price or to withdraw from the contract.

Where the contract of purchase, in the cases set forth in the preceding Article, requires reference to the entries of the cadastral survey maps, there shall be no ground for increasing or reducing the price unless the difference ascertained after measurement exceeds the tolerated margin.

Where the sale is concluded in respect of a specific, bounded corporeal thing or in respect of distinct and separate immovable properties, whether it begins by specifying the measure or by specifying the thing sold followed by the measure, the statement of the measure shall neither entitle the vendor to claim an increase in the price if the measure is found to be in excess, nor the purchaser to claim a reduction thereof if it is found to be deficient.

In all cases where the purchaser exercises the right to withdraw from the contract, the vendor shall be bound to restituate to him the price, if he has received it, as well as the expenses of the contract.

An action by the vendor to increase the price and an action by the purchaser to reduce it or to rescind the contract must be brought within one year running from the day of the conclusion of the contract, failing which the right to bring the same shall lapse.

The warranty owed by the vendor to the purchaser has two objects:

The first is the warranty of peaceful possession of the thing sold without opposition, and the second is the warranty against latent defects and flaws in the thing sold.

Even though no stipulation concerning warranty is made at the time of the sale, the vendor is bound by law to warrant the purchaser against eviction by a third party from the whole or part of the thing sold, and against the encumbrances claimed upon the thing sold which were not declared at the time of the sale.

The contracting parties may, by special agreement, increase or diminish the effect of this statutory obligation, and they may likewise agree that the vendor shall not be bound by any warranty whatsoever.
The seller, even if he stipulates that he shall not be bound by any warranty, remains bound to warrant his personal act. Every agreement to the contrary shall be void.

In the event of a stipulation of non-warranty, the seller remains bound, upon the occurrence of eviction, to restitution of the price, unless the buyer concluded the purchase and assumed for himself such harm and risks as might occur.

If the promise of warranty is made in an unqualified manner, or if nothing has been stipulated concerning the warranty, the buyer who has been dispossessed of the whole of the thing sold by virtue of eviction is entitled to claim from the seller:

First- Restitution of the price

Second- The value of the fruits if the buyer was compelled to restore them to the evicting owner

Third- The costs incurred by the buyer for the warranty action and the costs of the original claimant

Fourth- Damages, taking into consideration the value of the improvement of the property where applicable, and the costs and legal fees of the contract, provided that the buyer is not entitled to claim damages if he was aware at the time of the sale of the risk of eviction.

If at the time of eviction the thing sold is found to have suffered a diminution in its value or a substantial defect due to negligence committed by the buyer or to an event arising from force majeure, the seller remains bound to restore the price; however, if the buyer has derived a benefit from the deterioration which he caused to the thing sold, the seller may deduct from the price a sum equivalent to the value of that benefit.
The seller must himself reimburse the buyer, or cause the evicting party to reimburse him, for all the expenses of useful repairs and improvements which the buyer has made to the thing sold.
The seller of the property of another, if he is in bad faith, must pay to the buyer all that he has spent on the thing sold for luxuries and embellishments.

If the buyer is dispossessed of only a part of the thing sold and this part is, in proportion to the whole, of such importance that the buyer would have refrained from purchasing had it not existed, he is entitled to rescind the contract.

If the sale is not rescinded in the event of eviction from a part of the thing sold, the seller shall restore to the buyer the value of the evicted part in proportion to the total price, together with damages where applicable.

The buyer must, without delay, apply by petition for an inspection of the thing sold by an expert appointed by the President of the competent court.

If the inspection is not carried out in accordance with due procedure, the buyer shall have to prove the existence of the defect upon receipt. An inspection shall not be required if the sale was concluded according to a sample the identity of which is not in dispute.

If the goods arrive from another country and the seller has no agent at the place of receipt thereof, the buyer must take precautions to preserve the goods temporarily.

If rapid deterioration is feared, the buyer shall have the right to request the sale of those goods pursuant to an authorisation applied for by petition to the President of the court of the place where the goods are located, after carrying out the aforementioned inspection.

If the interest of the seller requires such sale, it shall be the strict duty of the buyer to carry it out in this manner. He shall be bound to notify the seller without delay of all the foregoing, failing which he shall be liable for damages.
In the case provided for in the preceding Article, the expenses of returning the goods shall be borne by the seller.

Where there is cause for returning the thing sold, either on account of defects therein or because it lacks certain qualities, the buyer shall have the right to apply for the rescission of the sale and the restitution of the price. In addition to the foregoing, he shall be entitled to receive damages in the following cases:

First: Where the seller knew of the defects of the thing sold or of its lack of the qualities promised by him and did not declare that he sold without warranty; the seller shall be presumed to have known thereof if he is a merchant or an artisan selling the products of his manufacture.

Second: Where the seller declared that the thing sold was free from defects, unless there are defects that only appeared after the sale or were among the defects of which the seller could be ignorant in good faith.

Third: Where the existence of the qualities which the thing sold proved to lack was expressly stipulated or required by commercial usage.

Where the sale is concluded for an aggregate of specific things and a part thereof is defective, the buyer shall have the right to avail himself of the right granted to him in the preceding Article. Where the thing sold consists of fungible things, the buyer shall only be entitled to demand the delivery of another quantity of the same kind free from those defects. Nevertheless, he shall retain the right to claim damages where appropriate.

Where the thing sold consists of several different things purchased in bulk for a single price, the buyer shall have the right, even after receipt, to rescind the sale with respect to the defective part of those things and to recover a proportionate part of the price. However, where the things cannot be separated without detriment, such as where they form pairs, he shall only be entitled to rescind the sale as a whole.

If the thing sold is encumbered with non-apparent real rights which have not been declared, and which are of such importance that it may be presumed that the buyer would not have bought had he known of them, he shall be entitled to rescind the contract if he does not prefer to be satisfied with taking compensation.

If the buyer has freed himself from dispossession by paying a sum of money, the seller may free himself from the consequences of the warranty by refunding that sum to the buyer together with interest and all expenses.

If the buyer is summoned to trial at the request of a third party claiming rights over the thing sold, he must summon his seller before the court; if he fails to do so and a judgment having acquired the force of res judicata is rendered against him, he loses his right to the warranty, unless he proves that even if the seller had intervened in the action it would not have been in his power to obtain a judgment dismissing it.

The seller warrants against defects in the thing sold which appreciably diminish its value or render it unfit for the use for which it is intended by its nature or pursuant to the contract of sale. However, defects which only slightly diminish the value of the thing sold or the enjoyment thereof, and defects tolerated by custom, do not give rise to warranty. The seller also warrants the existence of the qualities which he has declared, or the existence of which the buyer has stipulated.

However, if the thing sold consists of things the true condition of which cannot be known without making an alteration therein, such as fruits with a hard shell, the seller does not warrant against their latent defects unless he has expressly warranted them or local custom imposes this warranty upon him.

If the sale is concluded by sample, the seller warrants the existence of the qualities of the sample in the goods sold. If it perishes or is damaged, it shall be incumbent upon the buyer to prove that the goods do not conform to it.

The seller warrants only the defects existing at the time of the sale if the thing sold is an individually determined specific thing, or at the time of delivery if the thing sold is a fungible thing and has been sold by weight, by measure or by description.

If the thing sold consists of movables other than animals, the buyer must examine the condition of the thing sold immediately upon receiving it and notify the seller without delay within the seven days following receipt of any defect which the seller is bound to warrant, failing which the thing sold shall be deemed accepted, unless the defects are such as cannot be recognized by an ordinary examination or there are impediments unrelated to the will of the buyer which prevented the examination of the condition of the thing sold. In such a situation, the defects of the thing sold must be notified to the seller immediately upon their discovery, failing which the thing sold shall be deemed accepted; however, a seller in bad faith shall not be entitled to invoke this last provision.

The action for redhibition shall lapse if the defect ceases to exist before the institution of the action for rescission or the action for reduction of the price, or during the course thereof, provided that such defect is by its nature temporary and not liable to reappear. This provision shall not apply if the defect is by its nature liable to recur.

The seller shall not be liable for apparent defects, nor for defects of which the buyer had prior knowledge or which he could easily have known. He shall, however, be liable even for defects which the buyer could easily have known, if the seller declared that the thing sold was free therefrom.

The seller shall not be answerable for the defects of the thing sold nor for the absence of the required qualities therein:

First- If he has declared them

Second- If he has stipulated that he bears no warranty whatsoever.

The buyer's right to the action for redhibition shall lapse:

First- If he has expressly waived it after becoming aware of the defect in the thing sold.

Second- If, after becoming aware of the defect, he has sold the thing or otherwise disposed of it in the capacity of an owner.

Third- If he has applied the thing sold to his personal use and continued such use after becoming aware of the defect.

This rule shall not apply to houses and other similar roofed premises, which may continue to be inhabited or used during the proceedings for the rescission of the sale.

The action arising from the existence of redhibitory defects in the thing sold or from the absence of the promised qualities therein must be instituted in the following manner, failing which the right to institute it shall lapse:

1- In respect of immovable property, it shall be instituted within 365 days after delivery

2- In respect of movable property and animals, it shall be instituted within thirty days after delivery, provided that the notice prescribed in Article 446 has been sent to the seller; and these two time-limits may be extended or shortened by agreement of the contracting parties.
There shall be no ground for instituting the action for redhibition in sales made by the judicial authority.
The buyer has two principal obligations, the first being to pay the price and the second to take delivery of the thing sold.

The buyer must pay the price on the date and in the manner stipulated in the contract. The sale shall be deemed to be for cash, as stated in Article 387, and the buyer shall be bound to pay the price upon taking delivery, in the absence of a provision to the contrary. The expenses of payment shall be borne by the buyer.

Rescission on account of a defect in the principal thing sold extends also to its accessories, even if the price of the accessories was fixed separately. A defect in the accessory does not rescind the sale of the principal.

Reduction of the price is effected by assessing the value of the thing sold in a sound condition at the time of the contract, on the one hand, and then by assessing its value in its present condition, on the other hand. Where the sale is concluded in respect of several things purchased in a single transaction, the assessment of their value shall be based upon the value of all the things of which the transaction is composed.

In the event of rescission of the sale, the buyer must restore:

First- The thing affected by the defect warranting restitution as he received it, together with its accessories, what is deemed a part thereof, and what has accrued to it after the conclusion of the contract.

Second- The fruits of the thing sold from the date of the rescission of the sale by mutual consent or by judgment, and its fruits prior to that date.

However, if the fruits had not formed at the time of the sale, the buyer shall be entitled to take them if he has gathered them, even before maturity, and he shall also be entitled to take the mature fruits even if he has not gathered them; and the seller, on the other hand, is bound:

First- To pay to the buyer the expenses of sowing, watering and maintenance, and the expenses of the fruits which the buyer has restored to him.

Second- To restore the price which he has received together with the lawful expenses of the contract

Third- To indemnify the buyer for the loss which the thing sold has caused him, if the seller was fraudulent.

The buyer shall not be entitled to recover anything or to a reduction of the price if he is unable to restore the thing sold in the following cases:

First- If the thing sold has perished by force majeure or through the fault of the buyer or of persons for whom he is responsible.

Second- If the thing sold has been stolen or taken away from the buyer.

Third- If the buyer has transformed the thing sold into a form in which it is no longer fit for that for which it was originally intended.

If the thing sold perishes by reason of the defect with which it was affected or by force majeure arising from that defect, its loss shall fall upon the seller and he shall be bound to restore the price. If he was in bad faith, he shall also be bound to pay damages.

There shall be no ground for rescission of the sale, and the buyer shall only be entitled to claim a reduction of the price:

First- If the thing sold has become defective through his fault or that of the persons for whom he is responsible.

Second- If the buyer has used the thing sold in a manner that leads to a considerable diminution in its value. This provision shall apply if he used the thing sold before becoming aware of the defect.

However, if the use took place after becoming aware of the defect, the provisions of Article 462 shall apply.

A reduction of the price obtained by the buyer on account of an admitted defect shall not prevent him from claiming rescission of the sale or a further reduction in the price if another defect appears.
Where any time limit is granted for the payment of the price, it shall run only from the date of the formation of the contract if the parties have not appointed another date.
Where the rescission of the sale for non-payment of the price is stipulated, the contract shall be rescinded ipso jure merely by the failure to pay within the appointed term.

Where the sale is concluded and no time limit is granted for the payment of the price, the seller may, upon non-payment, claim the movable things sold so long as they are in the possession of the buyer, provided that the claim is made within fifteen days commencing from the date of delivery and that those things remain in the same condition as they were at the time of their delivery, and such claim shall in the event of bankruptcy be subject to the provisions relating thereto.

A buyer who is disturbed by a third party or is exposed to an imminent and serious risk of the occurrence of such disturbance by reason of a title prior to the sale shall be entitled to withhold the price so long as the seller has not caused the disturbance against him to cease. However, the seller shall be entitled to compel him to pay by furnishing him with a suretyship or sufficient security for the restitution of the price and the lawful expenses of the contract if he is dispossessed of the thing sold. Where the disturbance is confined to a portion of the thing sold, the buyer shall only be entitled to withhold from the price what is proportionate to that portion, and the suretyship shall be confined to the portion exposed to dispossession. The buyer shall not be entitled to exercise the right of retention if payment was stipulated notwithstanding any disturbance or if the buyer was aware at the time of the sale of the risk of his dispossession.
The provisions of the preceding Article shall apply where the buyer discovers a defect in the thing sold that necessitates its restitution.

The buyer must take delivery of the thing sold at the place and time appointed in the contract. In the absence of a provision to the contrary, he must take delivery of the thing sold without delay, subject to the time limit necessary for taking delivery. Where he fails to appear to take delivery of the thing sold, or appears without offering payment of the price at the same time when the sale is for cash, the rules relating to default of the creditor shall apply.

Where the things sold must be delivered in successive instalments, failure to take delivery of the first instalment thereof shall produce the effects produced by failure to take delivery of the whole. All of the foregoing shall apply unless there is an agreement to the contrary between the parties.

A sale with stipulation of a right of redemption, or a sale subject to redemption, is one whereby the buyer binds himself, after the perfected sale, to restore the thing sold to the seller in return for the restitution of the price, and the object of a sale subject to redemption may be movable or immovable things.

No time limit exceeding three years from the date of the sale may be stipulated for the redemption of the thing sold. Where a time limit exceeding the same is stipulated, it shall be reduced to three years.

A seller who exercises the right of redemption may not resume possession of the thing sold unless he refunds:

First- The price which he received

Second- The useful expenditure to the extent by which it has increased the value of the thing sold; as regards luxurious expenditure, the buyer is only entitled to remove the improvements which he introduced into the thing sold if he is able to remove them without damage. He may not claim recovery of necessary expenses, maintenance expenses or the cost of harvesting the fruits. On the other hand, the buyer must restore:

First- The thing sold and any accretion thereto since the conclusion of the contract of sale

Second- The fruits which he has gathered since the day on which the price was paid or deposited. The buyer may exercise the right of retention if what is due to him is not refunded to him, all without prejudice to the conditions agreed upon between the two parties.

The buyer is liable, on the other hand, for any damage to or loss of the thing sold resulting from his act, his fault, or the fault of the persons for whom he is responsible. He is likewise liable for alterations which have resulted in bringing about a substantial change in the thing sold contrary to the interest of the seller. However, he shall not be answerable for what happens to the thing sold as a result of force majeure or a minor alteration. In such case, the seller is not entitled to claim a reduction of the price.

A seller who recovers his property pursuant to the right of redemption acquires at the same time the right to cancel the registrations of all real rights, encumbrances and mortgages which the buyer has created thereon; however, he is bound to perform the contracts of lease concluded by the buyer without fraud, provided that the term of the lease does not exceed the time-limit prescribed for redemption and that the contract of lease has a certain date.

If the thing sold is an agricultural property and the seller exercises the right of redemption during the agricultural year, the buyer, if he or those to whom he leased it have sown the seeds, is entitled to remain in occupation of the cultivated parts until the end of the agricultural year, provided that he is bound to pay what is required of him by local custom for the remaining period from the day of redemption until the end of the agricultural year.

A forward sale (bay' al-salam) is a contract whereby one of the two parties advances to the other a specified sum of money, and that party is bound in return to deliver to him a specified quantity of foodstuffs or other movable things at a date agreed upon by the two parties. This contract may only be proved in writing.
The entire price must be paid to the seller at the time of the formation of the contract.
If no time-limit is fixed for delivery, the two parties shall be deemed to have agreed to what is required by the custom of the locality.

The said time limit is mandatory; the judge may not order its extension even if he had no choice therein. However, if the failure to exercise this right arises from a fault on the part of the buyer, the expiry of the time limit shall not prevent its exercise.

Property sold subject to a right of redemption becomes, by virtue of the sale, the property of the buyer under the condition of redemption, meaning that the buyer remains the owner thereof if the seller does not fulfil the conditions agreed upon for its redemption. However, if he fulfils these conditions, the property sold shall be deemed never to have left the ownership of the seller. In all cases, the buyer shall enjoy the property sold likewise until the time limit expires or until the seller exercises the right of redemption, subject to the provisions of Articles 482 and 485. He is therefore entitled to collect the fruits of the property sold and to bring every action relating thereto, provided that he does not commit fraud.
The right of redemption is exercised by the seller notifying the buyer of his wish to redeem the property sold, and he must at the same time offer to return the price.
If the seller dies before exercising his right of redemption, this right passes to his heirs, who shall exercise it during the period remaining to their predecessor in title of the time limit.

The heirs may not exercise the right of redemption except jointly, nor may they demand anything other than the return of the property sold in its entirety. This provision also applies where several persons have sold, pursuant to a single contract, a thing held in common between them and have not reserved for each of them his right to redeem his share.

An action for the redemption of the property sold may be brought against the heirs of the buyer jointly. However, if the estate has been distributed and the property sold has fallen into the share of one of the heirs, the action for redemption shall be brought against him alone for the whole of the property sold.
If the insolvency of the seller is declared, the right of redemption shall belong to the creditors.
A seller subject to a right of redemption is entitled to bring the action for redemption against the second buyer.

Foodstuffs or other things which are the subject of the sale must be determined by their quantity, their quality, their weight, or their measure, according as their nature requires, failing which the contract shall be null and void. However, if the things sold are such as are neither counted nor weighed, it shall suffice that their quality be accurately determined.
If the place of delivery has not been designated, it must be at the place of the contract.

If the seller is unable, by reason of force majeure and without fault or delay on his part, to deliver what he promised, the buyer may rescind the contract and recover the price which he has advanced, or wait until the following year. If, in the following year, the seller tenders the thing which is the subject of the sale, the buyer must take delivery of it and may not rescind the contract. This provision shall also apply if the buyer has taken delivery of part of the thing sold. However, if the thing contracted for is non-existent, the provisions of the first paragraph of this Article shall apply.

A promise of sale is a contract whereby a person undertakes to sell a thing to another person who does not immediately undertake to buy it. It is of the nature of this contract that it is not reciprocal. It creates no obligation whatever upon the promisee, but binds the promisor definitively, so that he cannot withdraw his offer, and must await the decision of the promisee.
The effects of the contract pass to the heirs of the contracting parties with whatever obligations they entail in their favour or against them.

If the promisor transfers a movable thing to a third party notwithstanding his undertaking, he vests ownership of that thing in the transferee, but renders himself liable to pay damages to the promisee for failing to perform the obligation which he undertook.

When the promisee declares his intention to buy, the promise is converted into a sale without retroactive effect. The transfer of ownership takes place on the day of acceptance. Nevertheless, for determining the extent of lesion, reference shall be made to the day on which the seller made the promise.
A unilateral promise to buy is likewise permissible and must be understood and construed in the same manner as a promise of sale, mutatis mutandis.
Gifts that take effect inter vivos shall be subject to the general rules governing contracts and obligations, subject to the contrary provisions set forth in this Book.

A gift shall be perfected and ownership of the gifted property, whether movable or immovable, shall be transferred when the donor becomes aware of the donee's acceptance, subject to the application of the following provisions.
The donor shall retain the right to revoke the offer so long as acceptance has not taken place.
A manual gift shall be perfected by the donor delivering the thing to the donee.
A gift of immovable property or of real rights over immovable property shall be perfected only by its registration in the Land Register.

A promise of a gift shall not be valid unless it is in writing, and a promise of a gift of immovable property or of a right over immovable property shall not be valid unless it is registered in the Land Register.
Gifts shall not validly exceed the limit of the disposable portion of which the donor is entitled to dispose.
In no case may a gift include the future property of the donor, namely the property of which he has no right to dispose at the time of the gift.
A promise of sale in respect of immovable property is subject to the real property laws in force.
Exchange is a contract whereby each of the contracting parties undertakes to give a thing in order to obtain another thing.

Exchange is concluded by the mere consent of the two parties. However, where the subject-matter of the exchange is real property or rights in rem over real property, the provisions of Article 393 and the provisions of the real property laws in force shall apply.
Where the exchange is concluded in respect of things of unequal value, the contracting parties may pay the difference in money or in other things.
The costs of the contract and its legal expenses shall by operation of law be divided between the parties to the exchange, unless there is another agreement between them.

The rules of sale shall apply in so far as the nature of this contract permits, particularly those relating to warranty against eviction, latent defects, and the nullity of contracting in respect of the property of another.
A gift is a disposition inter vivos whereby a person transfers to another person all or part of his property without consideration.
Gifts that take effect upon the death of the donor shall be deemed acts of last will and shall be subject to the rules of personal status relating to inheritance.
The donor may donate the bare ownership of the property to one person and the right of usufruct thereof to one or several other persons, just as he may reserve such usufruct for himself.
Every person who is capable of contracting and disposing of his property may make a gift. A legal guardian is not entitled to dispose without consideration of the property which he administers.

Every person whom the law has not expressly declared incapable of accepting a gift may accept it. The following are relatively deprived of the capacity to accept:

First- The guardian with respect to the ward

Second- The physician during the period of terminal illness if he is not a relative of the patient.
Persons who are incapable of contracting cannot accept gifts subject to a condition or a charge, except after the authorisation of those who legally represent them.
Gifts granted to unborn children in the womb may be accepted by the persons who represent them.
Gifts granted to persons whom the law declares incapable of accepting them are deemed null and void, even if made under the guise of another contract or through an intermediary.

The donee must accept the gift in person or through another person holding a special power of attorney or a sufficient general power of attorney (such as the father, the mother, and the guardian), failing which the acceptance shall be null and void.
A gift made to several persons jointly is deemed to be granted in equal shares, unless otherwise provided.

The donee takes the place of the donor in all rights and actions pertaining to him upon dispossession by eviction. However, the donor is not bound to warrant the donated property unless otherwise stipulated or the gift is subject to a charge. In the latter case, the donor shall be liable for eviction to the extent of the value of the charge.
If the gift is subject to a condition of paying the debts of the donor, only the debts contracted prior to the gift shall fall under this condition, unless otherwise stipulated.

Every gift inter vivos granted by a person who has no child or legitimate issue may be revoked:

First- If the donor is blessed with children after the gift, even if after his death.

Second- If the donor had a child whom he believed to be dead at the time of the gift, and it later appeared that he is still alive.

Upon revocation of the gift in the case provided for in the preceding Article, the donated property shall be returned to the donor. If it has been alienated, there shall be returned to him the equivalent of the value of the enrichment realised at that time by the donee. However, if the donated property is mortgaged, the donor may redeem its mortgage by paying the sum for the security of which it was mortgaged, provided that he retains the right of recourse for this sum against the donee.

The right to bring an action for the revocation of a gift due to the subsequent appearance of children lapses by prescription after five years commencing from the date of birth of the last child, or from the date on which the donor learned that his son whom he believed to be dead is still alive. It is not permissible to waive the right to bring that action; it is transmitted upon the death of the donor to his children and his issue.

A gift is annulled at the request of the donor if the donee fails to perform, or ceases to perform, one of the conditions or charges imposed upon him. In returning the property to the donor, the rules provided for in the aforementioned Article 525 shall apply.

A gift is also annulled at the request of the donor:

First- If the donee commits a misdemeanour or a felony against the person of the donor, his honour, or his property.

Second- If he commits a serious breach of the duties imposed upon him by law towards the donor or his family.

Upon the revocation of a gift due to the appearance of children or due to ingratitude, or upon the reduction of a gift for being excessive, the donee shall only return the fruits starting from the day the action is brought. However, if the revocation is due to the non-performance of charges or conditions, the donee must return with the property the fruits that he has collected since he ceased to perform those charges or conditions, or since he became in default for failure to execute them.

An action for revocation of a gift by reason of ingratitude may not be waived in advance. This action shall lapse by prescription after one year running from the day on which the donor became aware of the matter, and the right of the donor to bring that action shall not pass to his heirs if he was capable of bringing it and did not do so.

Likewise, it may not be validly brought against the heir of the donee if it had not been brought against the donee prior to his death.

A gift which exceeds - in accordance with what is provided for in Article 512 - the limit of the disposable portion fixed in relation to the value of the property left by the donor at his death, must be reduced by whatever exceeds that disposable portion. However, such reduction shall not annul the effects of the gift, nor the possession by the donor of the fruits during his lifetime.

If two or several gifts have been granted and it is impossible to perform them in full without exceeding the limit of the disposable portion, the gifts most recent in date shall be annulled or reduced to the extent that they exceed the limit of the disposable portion.

The lease of things is a contract whereby a person undertakes to grant another person the enjoyment of an immovable or movable thing or of a right for a specified term in return for a consideration which that person undertakes to pay to him. A lease in the absolute sense is the lease of immovables which do not yield natural fruits and the lease of corporeal movables or rights. An agricultural lease is the lease of agricultural lands.

A contract of lease may not be concluded over a thing which is consumed by use unless it is intended merely for inspection or display.

However, things which depreciate in value by use may be leased.
The provisions relating to the object of a sale shall apply in principle to the object of a lease of things.

The consideration must be determined and may consist either of money or of produce, foodstuffs, or other movables, provided that they are specified as to description and quantity. It may also consist of a portion or an undivided share of the produce of the leased thing. In the lease of agricultural properties, it may be stipulated that the lessee shall carry out specified works counted as part of the consideration, in addition to a sum of money which he pays or a quantity of produce imposed upon him.

If the contracting parties have not determined the rent, they shall be deemed to have agreed upon the prevailing rent for things of the same kind as the leased property at the place of the contract. If there is a fee or tariff in that place, they shall be deemed to have agreed to act in accordance therewith.
A lease is concluded by the agreement of the two parties on the thing, the rent, and all other terms intended to be included in the contract.
Whoever holds over the thing only a right of personal use, a right of habitation, a right of retention, or a security right may not lease it out.

The legal rules governing the lease of immovable property to which the law refers shall apply by analogy, and to the extent permitted by the nature of the things, to the leases of other immovable property and to movable property, unless there is a stipulation, a statutory provision, or a custom to the contrary.

A lease by a usufructuary of immovable property or of rights pertaining to such property without the consent of the bare owner shall cease to have effect with respect to the bare owner after the lapse of three years from the termination of the usufruct; provided that a lease by a testamentary guardian or a legal guardian of immovable property or of rights pertaining thereto may not be concluded for a term exceeding one year except while the guardianship subsists and with the authorisation of the competent court.

An unwritten contract of lease of real property cannot be proved prior to its performance except by the admission of the person against whom the existence of the lease is alleged or by his taking of an oath. If there has been a commencement of performance, it shall be deemed proof of the existence of the lease, and the rent shall be determined, in the event of disagreement between the contracting parties, by an expert, and its term shall be fixed in accordance with the custom of the locality. If the lessee remains in the leased premises after the expiry of the term of the lease and the person concerned leaves him in possession thereof, in particular if he does not demand eviction from him, the lease shall be deemed tacitly renewed and shall be subject to the provisions of Article 592 et seq.

Contracts of lease of built real property intended for residential and non-residential use shall be subject to the freedom of the contracting party and the will of the contracting parties in all matters not inconsistent with the following mandatory provisions:

First:

The term: If the term specified in the contract is less than three years, the lease shall be deemed concluded for a period of time of three years. However, if the lessee benefiting from the extension wishes to vacate the leased premises, he must notify the lessor two months prior to the end of the extended year by an unsealed registered card with acknowledgement of receipt or by means of a letter served through the notary public.

Second: The following are exempted from the preceding provisions:

A- Seasonal lease contracts relating to summer and winter resorts.

B- Lease contracts for premises provided by employers to their employees free of charge or for rent.

Third: If a contract of lease of real property, whether built or unbuilt, exceeds three years in term, it shall have no effect with respect to a third party unless the contract is registered in the Real Property Register, and the registration of the tacit renewal of a lease contract shall be subject to the same rule.

The warranty owed by the lessor to the lessee has two objects:

First- Quiet enjoyment and disposal of the leased property without opposition

Second- Defects in the leased property, and this warranty is mandatorily owed even if it is not stipulated in the contract, and the good faith of the lessor shall not exempt him from the obligation of warranty.

The obligation of warranty includes the duty of the lessor to refrain from any act calculated to prevent the lessee from taking possession of the leased property or to deprive him of the benefits upon which he was entitled to rely according to the purpose for which the leased property was intended and according to the condition in which it was at the time of the formation of the contract. In this respect, the lessor shall be liable not only for his own act, but shall also be answerable for the acts of his workmen, the other lessees, and the holders of rights derived from him.

However, the lessor shall be entitled to carry out, notwithstanding the opposition of the lessee, all urgent repairs that cannot be postponed until the time of the expiry of the contract. Nevertheless, if the lessee is deprived, by reason of such repairs, of the enjoyment of the whole or part of the leased property for a period exceeding seven days, he may demand the rescission of the contract or a reduction of the rent in proportion to the time during which he was deprived of the use of the leased property. The lessor must attend to the urgent repairs and give notice to the lessee a sufficient time before carrying them out. If he fails to give such notice, he shall be deemed liable, unless there is an impediment of force majeure not arising from his negligence.

The lessor is also bound by operation of law to warrant the lessee against any disturbance and eviction affecting the whole or part of the leased property and arising from an action concerning ownership or a real right over the leased property.

The provisions relating to the dispossession of the buyer by reason of eviction shall apply in principle to the dispossession of the lessee.

If the lessee is summoned before the court in an action in which judgment is sought against him to vacate the whole or part of the leased property or to enforce certain easements, he must notify the lessor without delay, and he must not in the meantime relinquish any part of the leased property. In all cases, the lessee must be dismissed from the action once he names the person through whom he holds possession of the leased property. In such a case, the action may only be prosecuted against the lessor, provided however that the lessee may intervene therein.

The lessor is not bound to warrant the lessee against acts of force and violence committed by a third party disturbing his enjoyment, without such person claiming any right over the leased property and without the lessor having done anything that led to such disturbance. However, the lessee shall be entitled to sue such person in his own name.

However, if that disturbance in fact is of such a nature as to deprive the lessee of the enjoyment of the leased property, he may demand the rescission of the contract or a proportional reduction in the rent. However, in this case, he must prove:

First- The occurrence of the disturbance

Second- That this disturbance prevents the continuation of the enjoyment.

The lessor warrants to the lessee all defects of the leased property which appreciably diminish the enjoyment thereof or render it unfit for the use intended for it according to its nature or according to the contract. He shall also be liable for the absence in the leased property of the qualities which he expressly promised or which are required by the intended purpose of the leased property. As for defects which do not prevent enjoyment or diminish it only slightly, the lessee shall not be entitled to have recourse against the lessor on account thereof, and the same applies to defects tolerated by custom.

If there occurs that which gives rise to warranty, the lessee may demand the rescission of the contract or the reduction of the rent. He also has the right to claim damages in the cases provided for in Article 449, and the provisions of Articles 451, 452, and 453 relating to sale shall then apply.
