The lessor does not warrant the defects of the leased property which could easily be ascertained, unless he declared that they did not exist. Nor is he bound by any warranty:

First- If the defects were declared to the lessee

Second- If the lessee knew at the time of the formation of the contract of the defects of the leased property or of the absence therein of the required qualities.

Third- If the lessor stipulated that he would bear no warranty whatsoever.

If the leased property perishes, is damaged, or is altered, or if the lessee is deprived of the enjoyment of the whole or part thereof so that it becomes unfit for the use for which it is intended, without this being due to the fault of either of the contracting parties, the contract of lease is rescinded without compensation to either of them. The lessee is only bound to pay the rent in proportion to his enjoyment. Any clause contrary to the foregoing is null and void.

Article 1 of Law No. 37 dated 6/12/1975

Contrary to the provisions of Article 562 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts, lease contracts relating to leased property that perished, was damaged, or was altered, or where the lessee was deprived of the enjoyment of the whole or part thereof so that it became unfit for the use for which it is intended as a result of the events that took place on Lebanese territory during the year 1975, shall remain in force.

If only a part of the leased property is ruined or damaged and it does not thereby become unfit for the use for which it was leased, or if only a part thereof becomes unfit, the lessee shall then only be entitled to a reduction of the rent in proportion to the damage.

The lessor is subject to three principal obligations, which are:

First- Delivery of the leased property to the lessee

Second- Maintenance of the leased property

Third- Warranty
The delivery of the leased property is subject to the provisions governing the delivery of the thing sold.

The expenses of delivery lie with the lessor. As for the costs of the instruments, they shall be borne by both parties, meaning that each party pays the expenses of the instrument delivered to him. As for the costs of taking possession and receipt of the leased property, they shall be borne by the lessee, all of the foregoing unless there is a usage or a text to the contrary.

The lessor is bound not merely to deliver the leased property in a condition that enables the lessee to use it for the purpose intended for it according to its nature or according to the allocation agreed upon by the two contracting parties, but he is also bound to maintain the leased property and its appurtenances so as to keep it in the aforesaid condition, save in the following:

First- Where other stipulations exist between the two contracting parties.

Second- Where the leased property is real property and the usage of the locality requires that minor repairs be borne by the lessee. If the lessor delays in carrying out the repairs incumbent upon him, the lessee may compel him to carry them out by judicial means, and if he fails to do so, the lessee may obtain from the court authorisation to carry them out himself, provided that he recovers the cost thereof from the rent.

The lessee of real property must carry out minor repairs and restorations in the leased property unless the contract or usage exempts him therefrom. As for the aforesaid repairs, they are: repairing the floor tiles of rooms if only some of them are broken, repairing the glass of windows unless the cause of their breakage is hail or an extraordinary contingency or force majeure not attributable to a fault on the part of the lessee, and repairing doors, latticed windows, the timber of partitions, shop shutters, hinges, bolts and locks. As for whitewashing the walls of rooms, renewing the paint, replacing the papers and restoring the roofs, the cost thereof shall be borne by the lessor even if limited to simple works of whitewashing or restoration.
The lessee shall not be bound to carry out any of the minor repairs if the cause thereof is old age, force majeure, a defect in the construction, or an act committed by the lessor.
The cost of cleaning wells, latrine pits and water drains shall be borne by the lessor unless there is a text or usage to the contrary.
The lessor must pay the taxes and charges pertaining to the leased property unless there is a text or usage to the contrary.

The provisions of Articles 562 and 563 shall apply when the leased property, in whole or in part, and without any fault committed by either of the contracting parties, is devoid of the quality promised by the lessor or required by the intended purpose of the leased property.
The lessee may not bring actions pursuant to the provisions of Articles 562, 563 and 564 after the expiry of the term of the contract.
The lessee shall be liable for fire unless he proves that it occurred due to force majeure, a defect in the construction, or the spreading of flames from an adjacent house.

Where there are several lessees, each lessee among them shall be liable for the fire in proportion to the value of the part which he occupies, unless they prove that the fire broke out in the dwelling of one of them, in which case he alone shall be liable, or unless some of them prove that the outbreak of the fire could not have occurred on their premises, in which case those lessees shall not be liable.

The lessee shall be bound by two fundamental obligations.

1- To pay the rent.

2- To preserve the leased property and to use it in accordance with the purpose for which it was prepared or the purpose specified in the contract, whilst abstaining from excess and misuse.

The lessee must pay the rent at the term specified in the contract, and if no term is specified therein, then in accordance with local custom. Where there is no custom, payment shall be made at the end of the period of enjoyment. It shall be permissible to stipulate that the rent be paid in advance. In all cases, the expenses of payment shall be borne by the lessee.

The rent of immovable property shall be paid at the place where it is situated, and the rent of movable property at the place where the contract was concluded, in the absence of a provision to the contrary.

The lessor shall have the right to retain the furniture and other movables located in the leased premises, whether they belong to the lessee or to a sublessee or assignee of the lease, and he shall also have the right to retain them even if they belong to a third party, in order to secure the rent fallen due and the rent of the current year. He shall likewise have the right to apply to the competent authority to prevent the removal of those things, and if they are removed without his knowledge or despite his objection, he may claim them back in order to return them to the place where they were or to place them in another repository.

However, he may only exercise the right of retention or recovery up to the value necessary to secure his claim, and he shall have no right to follow what has been removed if the things remaining on the leased premises are sufficient to safeguard his rights.

The original lessee guarantees the person to whom he sublets or assigns the lease and remains bound towards the lessor for all the obligations arising from the contract. This obligation ceases:

First - If the lessor directly collects the rent from the hand of the sublessee or the assignee without expressing any reservation regarding his right against the original lessee.

Second - If the lessor expressly consents to the lessee's subletting to another person or to his assignment of the lease to him without expressing any reservation regarding his right against the original lessee.

The sublessee or the assignee of the lease is directly bound towards the lessor to the extent of the debt owed by him to the original lessee at the time of the formal notice sent to him. He may not invoke payments made by him in advance to the original lessee except in the following two cases:

First - If the payment is in conformity with local custom.

Second - If it is established by an instrument bearing a certain date.

The lessor has the right, in all cases where he is entitled to sue the original lessee, to bring an action directly against the sublessee and against the assignee, while retaining his right to sue the original lessee. The original lessee always has the right to intervene in the action.

The assignment of a lease is subject to the provisions governing the assignment of a creditor's claim, and it entails that the assignee takes the place of the assignor in the rights and obligations arising from the contract, subject to the provisions of Article 586.

The lease of things terminates ipso jure upon the expiration of the term agreed upon between the contracting parties without the need for a notice to vacate, subject to any agreement to the contrary if it exists, and subject to the provisions governing the lease of agricultural lands.

If the term is not specified, the lease is deemed to be concluded for a period of a year, six months, a month, a week, or a day, according to whether the rent is fixed per year, half-year, month, etc.. The contract of lease terminates upon the expiration of one of these terms without the need for a notice to vacate, unless there is a custom to the contrary.

If the contract of lease expires and the lessee remains in possession of the leased premises, the lease is deemed renewed on the very same conditions and for the same period if the lease was concluded for a specified period. If the period is not the specified one, each of the contracting parties has the right to terminate the contract; however, the lessee is entitled to benefit from the time limit fixed in accordance with local custom to vacate the premises.

Continuing to enjoy the leased premises does not imply tacit renewal of the contract if vacation has been requested or if one of the two parties has performed another act of this nature from which his unwillingness to renew the contract is inferred.

The lessee shall not be liable for destruction or deterioration arising:

First- From the ordinary and customary use of the leased property, subject to the preceding provisions concerning minor repairs required of the lessee.

Second- From force majeure, if it is not attributable to his fault.

Third- From the age of the building, a defect therein, or the failure to carry out the repairs required of the lessor.
The leased thing must be returned at the place of the contract, and the expenses of its return shall be borne by the lessee, unless there is an agreement or custom to the contrary.
The lessee is entitled to retain the leased property for the debts owed to him by the lessor and relating to the leased property.

If the lessee has erected buildings, plantings, or other improvements that have increased the value of the leased property, the leased property must refund to him at the end of the lease either the value of the expenses or the value of the improvement, provided that such improvements were made with his knowledge and without his objection. Otherwise, the lessor is entitled, after proving that such improvements are of no benefit whatsoever to him, to require the lessee to remove them and to compensate him, where applicable, for the damage caused to the immovable property by such removal.

However, if the lessor prefers to retain the improvements and pay one of the two aforementioned values, the judge may grant him time limits for the payment thereof.

The lessee is entitled to sublet the whole or part of the leased property and to assign the lease to another person, unless the contract stipulates that he is prohibited from subletting or assigning, or such prohibition is inferred from the nature of the leased thing. The prohibition of assigning the lease does not imply prohibiting the lessee from subletting unless it is expressly stated. However, prohibiting the lessee from subletting implies prohibiting him from assigning to another person, even gratuitously, even if such prohibition is not expressly stated. Prohibiting the lessee from subletting must be understood in its absolute sense; it entails prohibiting him from subletting even if it relates to a part of the leased property or if its purpose is to substitute another person, even gratuitously. Where it is stipulated that the lessee has the right to sublet or assign with the consent of the lessor, the lessor may not refuse the sublease or assignment without a legitimate reason.

In all cases, the lessee may not assign or sublet the thing for a use that differs from the use specified in the contract or inferred from the nature of the thing, or for a use that is more burdensome.
The right to reclaim may not be exercised after the expiration of fifteen days commencing from the day on which the lessor became aware of the removal of the things.

The right of retention or to reclaim may not be exercised:

First- In respect of things which cannot be the subject of execution relating to movables.

Second- In respect of stolen or lost things.

Third- In respect of things owned by a third person if the lessor was aware, at the time of their introduction into the leased premises, that they were his property

The lessor's right of retention extends to that which the sub-lessee introduces into the leased premises to the extent of the rights that the first lessee has against the sub-lessee. He is not entitled to invoke what he paid in advance to the original lessee, provided that the exceptions set forth in Article 587 are observed.

The lessee must notify the owner without delay of all acts requiring his intervention, such as urgent repairs, the discovery of unexpected defects, infringement of rights, or objections relating to ownership or to a real right, or damage caused by a third person, failing which he shall be civilly liable.

The lessee must return the leased premises at the end of the fixed term; if he retains them beyond its end, despite a demand for vacation or any act of this kind indicating the lessor's lack of consent, he shall be bound to pay compensation to him.

The amount of this compensation shall be determined in proportion to the rental value, taking into account the damage suffered by the lessor.
If an inventory or description of the leased premises was drawn up between the lessor and the lessee, the latter must return the leased premises as he received them.
If no inventory or description of the leased premises was drawn up, the lessee shall be presumed to have received the leased premises in good condition. And he must return them in that condition.

The lessee shall be liable for the loss or deterioration of the leased premises if it arises from his act. And the lessee of a hotel or other establishment open to the public shall be liable, and upon the travellers or guests whom he receives in the establishment.

In the case provided for in Article 592, the effect of the guarantees given for the first contract shall not extend to the obligations arising from the tacit renewal of the contract; however, pledges and other forms of security shall remain in force.

The lease shall be rescinded in favour of the lessor, while reserving his right to damages where applicable:

First- If the lessee uses the leased property for a purpose other than that for which it was intended according to its nature or pursuant to the agreement.

Second- If the lessee neglects the leased property in a manner that leads to causing significant damage thereto

Third- If he fails to pay the rent that has fallen due.
The lessor may not rescind the lease on the pretext that he wishes to occupy the leased house himself.

The contract of lease shall not be rescinded by the alienation of the leased property, whether the alienation is voluntary or compulsory. The new owner shall stand in the place of the transferor in respect of all his rights and obligations arising from current leases and contracts whose terms have not expired, provided that they are free from fraud and bear a certified date prior to the time of alienation.

If there is no written contract bearing a certified date, the new owner shall be entitled to evict the lessee from the leased property, provided that he grants him the period of notice established by custom.

If ownership of the leased property is dispossessed by an action for recovery of property, the successful claimant shall have the option either to maintain the current leases or to rescind the contract; however, in the second case, he shall be bound to give the prescribed period of notice if the lessee is in good faith. The lessee shall have no right of recourse against anyone other than the lessor to claim the rents and compensation due to him where applicable.
The contract of lease is not rescinded by the death of the lessee nor does the lessor die.
The rescission of the principal lease shall entail the rescission of the subleases concluded by the lessee, except in the cases provided for in the first and second paragraphs of Article 586.
The lease of agricultural land shall be subject to the general rules set forth above and to the special rules provided for in the following Articles.

A lease of agricultural land may be concluded for a term of forty years at most. If the lease is concluded for a term exceeding this limit, either of the contracting parties may rescind the contract upon the expiry of the forty years.

The contract of lease must specify the nature of the crops or produce which are the object of the exploitation, and if this is not specified, the lessee shall be deemed authorised to cultivate whatever may be cultivated on land similar to the leased property.

If the contract of lease includes agricultural implements, livestock, or provisions such as fodder, straw and manure, each of the contracting parties must deliver to the other an accurate inventory signed by him of those assets, and they must jointly appraise their value.

The lessee must enjoy the leased property in accordance with the conditions specified in the contract. He may not enjoy it in a manner prejudicial to the owner. He shall not be entitled to make any change in the manner of exploiting the leased property which might have a harmful effect even after the termination of the lease, unless he is expressly authorised to do so.
The lessee shall have no right to the offspring of animals nor to the accessions accruing to the leased property during the term of the contract.

All works necessary for the enjoyment of the leased property, such as the digging and maintenance of gullies, the cleaning of canals, the repair of roads, paths and hedges, and the carrying out of minor repairs to rural buildings and silos, shall be borne by the lessee in the absence of a provision to the contrary. He must perform them at his own expense without any compensation whatsoever. He shall be liable towards the lessor for damage resulting from the failure to fulfil these obligations.

Construction works and major repairs to buildings and other dependencies of the farm, however, shall fall upon the lessor, as well as the repair of wells, canals, conduits and basins. In the event of delay by the lessor, the provisions of Article 547 shall apply.

If a contract of lease relating to agricultural land states an extent greater or less than that actually comprised in the leased property, the rent shall be increased or reduced, or the contract rescinded, in the cases provided for in the Book of Sale, in accordance with the rules set forth therein. The right of action in this respect shall lapse upon the expiry of one year from the date of the contract, unless another date has been fixed for the commencement of enjoyment, in which case prescription shall run from that date.

If the lessee remains after the expiry of the agreed term and the lessor leaves him in possession of the leased property, the lease shall be deemed renewed for the same period if there was a fixed period, and otherwise the lease shall be deemed renewed until the time of harvesting the next crop.

The lessee of agricultural land, if his produce has not grown at the end of the lease due to an occurrence not attributable to his fraud or his fault, is entitled to remain in the leased property provided that he pays the lessor a rent equivalent to the rent stipulated in the contract, though he is bound to establish the state of the crops at the end of his lease.
The lessee who vacates the agricultural land may not perform any act likely to diminish or delay the enjoyment of the person who will succeed him.

The lessee who vacates the leased property must leave to his successor, a period of time before the latter commences enjoyment, suitable dwellings with all other facilities necessary for the works of the coming year. Likewise, the new lessee must leave to his predecessor suitable dwellings and all other facilities necessary for the consumption of the fodder and the harvesting of the remaining crops, and in both cases the custom of the locality shall be observed.

The lessee must leave, upon vacating the leased property, of the fodder, straw, and manure from the produce of the current year, a quantity equivalent to what he received upon entering the leased property. He may not evade this obligation by alleging need.

If the lessee did not receive any of those materials, the lessor may retain a sufficient quantity thereof after its valuation according to its current price at that time.

The custom of the locality shall also be followed in this matter.

The lessee must return at the end of the contract the things which he received according to the inventory, and he is liable for them save for cases arising from force majeure and not attributable to a fault on his part, and save for deterioration resulting from the ordinary and customary use of those things; and if during the term of the contract he has replaced what was missing of these things or repaired what had deteriorated, he is entitled to recover the money which he expended to this end unless there is a fault attributable to him.

If the lessee has supplemented at his own expense the equipment for the exploitation of the leased property and added to it tools that were not mentioned in the inventory, the owner has the option at the end of the lease between paying him their value after valuation and returning them to him in their existing state.

All other agricultural contracts, such as sharecropping (muzara'a), tending of trees for a share of the fruit (musaqat), and planting of trees for a share of the land and trees (mugharasa), shall remain subject to the provisions of the texts in force and to local custom.

If the lessee is prevented from tilling his land or cultivating it due to force majeure, he shall be entitled to claim the remission of the rent from him or the recovery of what he has paid in advance.

The lessee is entitled to claim the remission of the rent from him or its recovery if his crop perishes completely after sowing due to force majeure not attributable to a fault on his part; and if a part of the crop perishes, there shall be no ground for a reduction of the rent or for its restitution in proportion to such part, unless it exceeds one half.

There shall be no way for the remission of the rent or its reduction if the lessee has received from the person who caused the damage or from an insurance company, compensation for the damage that befell him.

The lessee of the land cannot obtain the remission of the rent if the loss of the fruits occurred after their separation from the land, unless the contract of lease stipulates giving the owner a specific share in kind of the produce. In such case, the owner must bear his share of the loss, provided that the lessee is neither at fault nor in delay in delivering the owner's share of the fruits; and the lessee may also not request the remission of the rent if the cause of the damage existed and was known at the time of the formation of the contract.

It is permissible, pursuant to a special stipulation, to place upon the lessee such contingencies as may occur, provided that such stipulation is made only for ordinary contingencies such as the falling of hail or thunderbolts or the occurrence of frost. However, if such stipulation is made for extraordinary contingencies, such as destruction resulting from wars in regions not targeted thereby, it shall be deemed void.

The contract is rescinded in favour of the lessor of agricultural land:

First- If the lessee abandons the ploughing of the land or does not care for its ploughing with the care of a good father of a family

Second- If he does not place the crop in the places prepared for it pursuant to the contract

Third- If he uses the leased property for a benefit other than that for which it was prepared according to its nature or pursuant to the contract of lease, and in general if he does not fulfill the conditions of the lease and damage to the lessor results from his failure to fulfill them; and all the aforementioned rules shall be observed while reserving the right of the lessor to claim damages where applicable.

The lease of agricultural land terminates automatically upon the expiration of the term fixed for it. If the term has not been fixed, the lease shall be deemed concluded for the term necessary for the lessee to gather all the fruits of the leased land. The notice to vacate must be served at least six months before the end of the current year; arable lands, if divided according to seasons and periods, shall have their lease terminate at the end of the last season.
Where no agreement is concluded to determine the wage or remuneration for the work, it shall be determined in accordance with custom. Where there is a tariff or fee, they must be applied.

The master or principal is bound to pay the wage or remuneration in accordance with the terms of the contract or the custom of the locality. Where there is neither agreement nor custom, payment of the remuneration shall fall due only after the performance of the service or the completion of the work.

Whosoever undertakes to perform a work or a service and is unable to complete it for a cause attributable to his hirer shall be entitled to receive the whole wage promised to him if he has continually remained at the disposal of the hirer and has not let his service to another person- provided that the court may reduce the stipulated wage according to the circumstances of the case.

Whosoever lets his work or his service may not entrust the execution to another person if it is inferred from the nature of the work or from the intention of the contracting parties that it is in the interest of the hirer that the lessor himself should perform the work.

The lessor of work or of service shall not be liable for his fault only, but shall also be answerable for his negligence, his imprudence and his incompetence, and any agreement to the contrary shall be of no effect.

The lessor shall also be liable for the damage resulting from his failure to carry out the instructions which he received if they were express and he had no sufficient reason not to observe them. If, however, he had such a reason and there was no peril in delay, he is bound to notify the principal and await new instructions from him.

The lessor shall be liable for the act of the person whom he substitutes for himself, or employs, or engages to assist him, just as he is answerable for his own act. However, if he is compelled by reason of the nature of the work to seek the assistance of other persons, he shall bear no liability whatsoever, provided that he furnishes proof:

First- that he exercised all necessary care in selecting his workmen and in supervising them.

Second- that he exhausted all within his power to prevent failure to perform the obligation and to avert its harmful consequences.

The lessor who supplies only his work is bound to watch over the preservation of the things delivered to him for the performance of the work or manufacture. He must return them after the performance, and he shall be liable for their loss or deterioration if it did not result from force majeure and he was not in default. The existence of a defect in the thing or its extreme fragility to an extent leading to its destruction shall be deemed to partake of the nature of force majeure. The burden of proof to establish force majeure shall rest upon the lessor. Where the things were not necessary for the execution of the work, he shall only be answerable for them as a depositary is answerable for the deposit.

Where things that must be returned to the master or principal are misappropriated, destroyed, or damaged by fire, what has befallen them shall not be deemed a contingency of force majeure relieving the lessor of liability, unless he proves that he exercised all care to avert the contingencies.

Proprietors of hotels and inns are liable for any damage, destruction, or theft befalling the effects of travellers staying with them, unless they prove that the loss is attributable to the traveller himself, or to persons visiting, accompanying, or serving him, or that it results from force majeure or from the nature of the thing deposited.
Proprietors of hotels and inns are not liable for documents, instruments, securities, or valuables that have not been delivered into their hands or into the hands of their employees.

The hire of services or of industry terminates:

First- Upon the expiry of the agreed term or the completion of the work.

Second- By the pronouncement of a judgment by the judge rescinding the contract in specific cases provided for by law.

Third- By the impossibility of performing the work by reason of force majeure or by the death of the employee or contractor. In this latter case, the exceptional provisions prescribed by law shall be observed. The hire of services or of industry does not terminate by the death of the master or principal.
The contract of employment or hire of services is subject to the general provisions prescribed in Article 624 et seq. and to the provisions of the following Articles.

If the hired person lives in the master's house, the latter must defray the expenses of his care for a period of twenty days if he suffers an illness or an accident not resulting from the fault of the hired person himself.

The master is discharged from the obligation specified in the preceding Article if the hired person is able to obtain such care from a mutual aid society of which he has become a member, or from an insurance company with which he is insured, or from the public assistance department.

Lease of work or service is a contract whereby one of the contracting parties undertakes to place his work at the service of the other party and under his direction, in return for a wage which the latter party undertakes to pay to him, and a contract for work or lease of industry is a contract whereby a person undertakes to complete a specific work for another person in return for a consideration proportionate to the importance of the work. The contract whereby a person practising a craft or a liberal profession undertakes to provide his services to those who contract with him, as well as the contracts whereby teachers undertake to practise their profession for the benefit of an institute or a certain person, are deemed to be of the nature of a lease of industry. A contract of carriage is also of this nature.
The contracts built in the preceding Article are concluded by the mere mutual consent of the two parties.

Such mutual consent shall not be valid unless the contracting parties have the capacity to bind themselves.

As for an interdicted person and a minor, they must act under the supervision of those under whose guardianship they are placed or obtain authorisation from them.
Every agreement whereby a person promises service for the entirety of his life, or for a prolonged period that binds him until the day of his death, is absolutely void.

There shall also be absolutely void every agreement whose object is:

First- Matters that are physically impossible

Second- Teaching occult magical practices and acts contrary to the law, morals, or public order, or performing the said acts.

Advocates or other persons who engage in judicial litigation may not conclude with their clients, either in their own name or in the name of a nominee, any agreement that gives them a share in the outcome of the lawsuit by making their fee a portion of what may be obtained.

(Article 69 of Law 8/1970 - Regulation of the Legal Profession)
The consideration must be determined or determinable.

The stipulation of a wage or consideration is presumed in the following cases, unless there is proof to the contrary:

First- Upon the completion of a work that is not customarily performed gratuitously.

Second- If the work falls within the profession of the person performing it.

Third- If the work is commercial or is performed by a merchant in the course of carrying on his trade.

If the employee enters into an undertaking to work as a labourer, or as a servant, or as an employee in a store, or in a shop, or in a public establishment, the first fifteen days shall be deemed a probationary period during which each of the two parties has the right to cancel the contract at will without paying compensation, provided however that the remuneration due to the employee is paid and he is notified of the dismissal from service two days prior to the rescission - all the foregoing unless the custom of the place or the agreement provides otherwise than the foregoing.

In a hire of work or service, each of the two parties shall necessarily have the right to rescind the contract if the other party does not perform that which is incumbent upon him. The judge may also order rescission upon the request of one of the two parties for other grave reasons.

The employer or master has the right to rescind the contract of hire on account of an illness or injury befalling the employee that prevents him from performing his obligations in a satisfactory manner, after paying him what he has become entitled to for the period of his service.

It shall be incumbent upon the employer or the master, and in general upon every person who employs workers:

1- To see to the provision of the requisite conditions of safety or health in the factories, rooms, and in general in all places which he provides for the workmen, employees, or servants in order that they may be able to execute the hire of work.

2- To see to the implements, machinery, tools, and in general all things which he provides for the workmen, employees, or servants for the execution of the hire of work, so that no danger to their health and life shall arise therefrom other than the danger inherent in carrying out the work in an ordinary manner

3- To take every necessary measure required by the nature of the work and the circumstances in which it is completed, to protect the life of the workmen, employees, or servants and to preserve their health during the works which they perform under his direction for his account. The employer or the master shall be liable for every violation of the provisions of this Article.

The employer or the master shall also be liable for accidents and disasters suffered by the hired worker during his performance of the work entrusted to him, if the accidents and disasters arise from his hirer's violation of the special regulations relating to the exercise of his trade, industry, or profession, or from his failure to observe those regulations.
In the cases provided for in the two preceding Articles, the amount of compensation may be reduced if the cause of the accident was the fault or imprudence of the injured person.

Every agreement or provision intended to exclude or mitigate the liability provided for in the preceding Articles on the part of the master, the employer, or the hirer shall be absolutely null and void.

The hire of work or service shall terminate upon the expiration of the term fixed by the contracting parties. If, upon the termination of the hire, the hired worker remains continuing the work or service without objection from the other party, and the term of the contract was one year at most or less than one year, this contract shall be deemed tacitly renewed for the same term; if the contract was for a term longer than one year, it shall be deemed renewed for one year; and if it was by the month, it shall only be deemed renewed for one month. However, if there was an express dismissal from service, the continuation of the work or service shall not imply tacit renewal.

If the term of the hire is neither fixed in the contract nor inferred from the nature of the work intended to be performed, either of the two parties may request the cessation of work, provided that he gives prior notice to the other party. The period of notice shall be one month if the contract of work has been executed for a period of three years or less, and two months if the contract has been executed for a period exceeding three years.

If the rescission of the contract proceeds from the employer and is not caused by breaches of the obligation of the contract, or a fault committed by the employee, there shall then be due to that employee an indemnity equal to the salary or wage of one month for each commenced year of the first five years and the salary or wage of half a month for each commenced year of the remaining years, and the salary or pay taken as the basis for this indemnity is the last salary or wage that the employee was receiving at the time of the rescission of the contract. And if the employer does not observe the time-limit provided for in the preceding Article, he shall be bound to pay to the employee another indemnity equal to the salary or wage of the time-limit that must elapse or the remaining period of the time-limit, and every prior waiver of the right to indemnity shall be null and void and of no effect.

If, however, the rescission of the contract proceeds from the employee without legitimate cause and he does not observe the time-limit provided for above, he shall be bound to pay the value of the damage sustained by the employer.

And if one of the employees contracts anew to perform a service following the rescission of the first contract of employment contrary to the rules, the new employer shall be jointly and severally liable for the damage sustained by the first employer, in the following two cases:

1- If he employs a worker knowing that he is bound by a contract of employment

2- If he continues to employ a worker after learning that this worker is still bound to another employer by a contract of employment, and in this second case liability shall be lifted from the second employer if it appears, at the time he learns of the existence of the contract of employment which the employee rescinded contrary to the rules, that this contract had terminated ipso jure by the arrival of its term if it was among the contracts concluded for afixed period, or by the expiry of the time-limit if it was among the contracts concluded for an indefinite period, and if a period of 15 days had elapsed since the rescission of the aforementioned contract.

The cessation of the enterprise does not release the employer from respecting his obligations unless there is force majeure.

If, however, a change occurs in the legal status of the employer, particularly if it is by reason of inheritance, sale, merger in the form of the establishment, or conversion into a company, all contracts of employment in force on the day the change occurs shall remain subsisting between the new employer and the personnel of the establishment.

1) - Article 3 of the Law of 27/5/1937, which amended Articles 652 and 656 of the Obligations and Contracts, provided as follows:

"The provisions of this Law shall cover contracts currently in force or the rights of which have not been liquidated on the date of its publication, and shall apply only to the relations of the employer with the employee whom custom has not established employing by the day, and the time-limit shall be eight days if the relations are between a master and his servants, subject to the provisions of Article 653 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts."

In the case provided for in the preceding Article, the employer may refuse the work, and if it has been delivered to him, he may return it in the week following delivery and fix for the maker a sufficient time limit to repair the defect or to supply the lack of certain qualities, if such repair is practicable. If the time limit expires and the maker has not fulfilled his obligation, the employer may choose one of the following options:

1- To have the work repaired by another person and at the expense of the maker, if the repair is still possible.

2- To demand a reduction of the remuneration.

3- Or to demand the rescission of the contract and leave the thing for the account of the person who made it.

All of the foregoing is subject to the reservation of any damages that may be payable where appropriate.

If it was the employer who supplied the materials, he shall be entitled to recover their value.

The provisions of Articles 453, 454 and 455 shall apply to the cases provided for under the preceding numbers 2 and 3.

If the employer takes delivery of a work that contains a defect or lacks one of the required qualities, and is nevertheless aware of the defects therein, and neither returns it nor reserves his rights in accordance with the provisions of the preceding Article, Article 463 shall then be applicable as regards the time limit within which he may submit an objection if it is not proved that he was aware of those defects.

The warranty provided for in Article 663 et seq. up to Article 665 shall cease to apply if the defects were caused by the execution of express instructions given by the employer contrary to the opinion of the contractor or the maker.

The engineer, architect or contractor whom the employer engages directly shall be liable during the five years following the completion of the building or other structure the works of which they directed or executed, if such building or structure collapses in whole or in part or manifestly threatens to collapse due to a deficiency in the materials or a defect in the construction or in the ground.

If the architect did not direct the works, he shall be liable only for the defect appearing in the architectural plan which he prepared.

The aforementioned five-year time limit shall run from the day on which delivery of the work is taken.

The action must be brought within thirty days running from the day of verification of the fact that gives rise to the warranty, failing which it shall be dismissed.
Any stipulation tending to exclude or restrict the warranty provided for in the preceding Articles shall be null and void.
The employer must take delivery of the work if it conforms to the terms of the contract, and remove it at his own expense if it is capable of being removed.

The hire of industry or contract for the undertaking of projects shall be subject to the general provisions laid down in Article 624 and the following articles up to Article 628 inclusive, and to the provisions set out in the following articles.

In a contract for work, the contractor may confine himself to supplying his labour only, the employer supplying the materials where necessary, and he may also supply the materials together with his labour. However, if the materials supplied by the contractor constitute the principal subject-matter of the contract and the labour is merely accessory, there is a sale and not a contract for work.
The contractor must supply the implements and tools necessary for the completion of the work, unless there is a custom or agreement to the contrary.

If it is necessary for the completion of the work that the employer should do something, the contractor shall have the right to call upon him expressly to do it. If the employer fails to perform his obligation after a sufficient time limit, the contractor shall have the option either to maintain the contract or to demand its rescission. In both cases, he may obtain, where appropriate, compensation for the damage which he has sustained.

The employer shall have the right to demand the rescission of the contract after giving formal notice to the contractor:

First- If the contractor persists in delaying the commencement of the work without lawful cause.

Second- If the contractor is in delay in delivery, unless the cause of the non-completion of the work, or of the delay therein, or of the delay in delivery is attributable to a fault on the part of the employer.

If, during the execution of the work, it appears that there are in the materials supplied by the employer or in the land upon which a building or other work is to be erected defects or shortcomings of such a nature as to prevent the proper execution of the work, the contractor must notify the employer thereof without delay. If he fails to do so, he shall be liable for the damage resulting therefrom, unless they are of a kind which a workman such as he could not have known.

A contractor who supplies the materials shall warrant their quality. Where, however, it is the employer who supplies them, the contractor must use them in accordance with the rules of the art and without negligence, inform the employer of the manner in which he has used them, and return to him such part thereof as he has not used.
The contractor must in all cases warrant against the defects and shortcomings resulting from his work. The provisions of Articles 442, 446 and 449 shall apply to this warranty.

In all cases where the workman provides the materials, he shall not be liable for the destruction of the work in whole or in part due to force majeure. However, he may not claim the price if the destruction occurred prior to delivery and the employer was not in default of taking delivery. The risk shall therefore be borne by the workman. In such case, the workman must establish proof that the destruction occurred due to force majeure if the destruction occurred prior to the employer taking delivery of the thing.

In the case where the workman provides only his work or his industry, he shall not be liable for destruction due to force majeure. He may claim his remuneration if the thing perished due to a defect in the materials, or if the employer had taken delivery of it, or was in default of taking delivery of it.

The remuneration shall only fall due after the completion of the work or the labour. Where the remuneration is fixed in instalments on condition that an instalment thereof be paid whenever a period of time elapses or a portion of the work is completed, payment shall fall due upon the expiry of each period or the completion of each portion.

Where the work is interrupted for a cause unrelated to the will of the two parties, the workman shall only be entitled to receive from the remuneration an amount proportionate to the work he has completed, subject to the application of Article 67 relating to the destruction of the materials which he provided.

Whoever undertakes a work in return for a fixed price on the basis of a plan or estimate which he drew up himself or agreed to may not claim an increase on the price on the pretext that the expenses exceeded the sum estimated in the plan or in the estimate, unless the employer himself expressly authorised him to exceed the sum, or there is a provision to the contrary.
Payment must be made at the place where the manufactured thing must be delivered.

The workman shall be entitled to retain the work and the other things which he received from the employer for the performance of the work, until the price or the remuneration and such advances as he may have made, where applicable, are paid to him, unless the contract requires payment at a fixed term. In such case, the workman shall be liable for the thing which he retains, in accordance with the rules applicable to the pledgee.

All those who were employed in the construction of the work shall be entitled to bring a direct action against the owner of the property up to the amount which he owes to the contractor at the time the action is brought.
The name of carriage is reserved for the synallagmatic contract the essential object of which is to secure the conveyance of a person or of a thing from one place to another.

Carriage is merely a species of the hire of industry or of the undertaking of works, and it necessarily has the character of contracts for valuable consideration. The person who practises it is called a carrier, and is more particularly called a transport contractor if he makes this work his habitual profession.

The contract of carriage is perfected when the two parties agree upon its elements and conditions, even prior to the delivery of the thing to the carrier by the consignor, unless the two parties agree expressly or impliedly to defer the conclusion of the contract until after delivery.

Where that which is carried consists of things, the consignor must clearly indicate to the carrier the address of the consignee, the place of delivery, the number of packages, their weight, their contents, the time-limit for delivery and the route to be followed; and where valuable articles are contained in the packages, he must inform the carrier of their existence and of their value.

The carrier is liable for the loss of the things and for their damage or shortage, save in cases arising from force majeure, from an inherent defect in the thing carried, or from the fault of the consignor.

Proof of these exonerating circumstances is required of the carrier, unless he made reservations upon receipt by reason of a defect in the packing of the goods; and such reservation gives rise, in favour of the carrier, to a presumption which the consignor or the consignee is entitled to impugn where necessary.

The consignee has the right to bring a direct action against the carrier by virtue of the contract which the carrier concluded with the consignor; and by such action he is enabled to claim from him delivery or the payment of damages, where appropriate, for the total or partial non-performance of the work.
The carrier must notify the consignee forthwith upon the arrival of the goods.
The carrier has a lien over the things carried for the recovery of the price of carriage and its accessories, and he also has the right to retain them.

If no time limit has been set for restitution, the depositary may return the deposit at any time he wishes, provided that he does not return it at an inopportune time, and that he grants the depositor a sufficient time limit to recover it or to prepare what the circumstances require.

The deposit must be returned at the place where it was deposited unless there is a provision to the contrary, and if it is agreed that it be returned at a place other than the place where it was deposited, the depositor must bear the expense of returning and transporting it.

The depositary must deliver the deposit to the depositor, or to the person in whose name it was deposited, or to the person designated to receive it. He cannot require the depositor to prove his ownership of the deposit. The person designated to receive the deposit has the right to bring an action directly against the depositary to compel him to return the deposit to him.

If the depositor is a person lacking legal capacity or a person whose insolvency has been declared by the court, the deposit may only be returned to the person who legally represents him, even if the loss of capacity or the loss of solvency occurred after the deposit.

If the depositor dies, the depositary may not return the deposit to anyone other than his heir or the person who legally represents him. If there are several heirs, the depositary may choose one of two courses: either he submits the matter to the judge and then acts in accordance with his decision, thereby relieving himself of liability, or he returns to each of the heirs the equivalent of his share.

In this case, he remains liable, and if the deposit is indivisible, the heirs must agree in order to be able to receive it. If there are minors or absentees among them, the deposit cannot be returned except by permission of the judge. If the heirs do not agree or do not obtain such permission, the depositary is discharged of his liability by consigning the deposit in accordance with the provisions on consignment, either of his own accord or pursuant to a judgment issued by the judge upon the request of any interested party. However, if the estate is insolvent or there are legatees, the depositary must in all cases refer the matter to the judge.

The provisions of the preceding Article also apply to the case where the contract of deposit is made by several persons jointly, unless there is an express agreement that the deposit may be returned to one of them or to all of them.

If the deposit was made by a tutor or a guardian in his capacity as tutor or guardian, and he no longer holds this capacity at the time of recovery, the deposit may only be returned to the person whom the depositor represented, if that person is legally capable of receiving it, or to the person who succeeded the tutor or the guardian.

The right to bring an action against the carrier lapses by prescription after one year commencing from the day of delivery in the case of damage, and from the day on which delivery should have taken place in the case of loss of the thing or delay in delivering it.

Contracting for the carriage of persons, like contracting for the carriage of things, is completed by mere consent. It obliges the carrier to convey the passenger safely to the designated place and within the agreed period, and if any contingency occurs, the liability arising from the contract is negated for the carrier upon his establishing proof of the existence of force majeure or of a fault on the part of the injured party.

Baggage which has been registered shall be the subject of a contract of carriage added to the contract for the carriage of the passenger; as for hand baggage, it does not enter into the contract and the carrier shall not be liable therefor unless the injured party establishes proof that he committed a specific fault.

Deposit is a contract whereby the depositary receives from the depositor a movable thing and undertakes to keep it and return it, and the depositary is not entitled to any remuneration for keeping the deposit unless the two parties have agreed to the contrary.
If the deposit is a sum of money or fungible things, and the depositary is authorised to use them, the contract shall be deemed a loan for consumption.

Deposit and the acceptance of a deposit require the capacity to bind oneself on the part of the depositor and the depositary. However, if a person having capacity accepts the deposit of a thing from a person lacking capacity, he is bound to fulfil all the obligations of a depositary.

If a person having capacity places a deposit with a person who does not enjoy capacity, he may demand its return to him if it is still in the hands of the depositary. If, however, the deposit has passed into other hands, he may not bring an action for restitution except to the extent of the value of the gain acquired by the person lacking capacity. Where applicable, the rules relating to the liability of persons lacking capacity when they commit a delict or quasi-delict shall apply.
It is not necessary for the validity of the deposit between the two parties that the depositor be the owner of the deposit or be in lawful possession thereof.

A contract of deposit is concluded by the consent of both parties and the delivery of the thing, and constructive delivery suffices where the thing to be deposited is already in the possession of the depositary for another cause.
The depositary must attend to the preservation of the deposit, in the same manner as he attends to the preservation of his own things, subject to the application of the provisions of Article 713.

The depositary shall not be entitled to substitute another person for himself in the custody of the deposit except in either of the following two cases:

1- If the depositor expressly authorises him

2- If urgent necessity requires such custody.

The depositary shall, save in the case provided for in point (2) of the preceding Article, be liable for the person whom he substitutes for himself unless it is proved that had the deposit remained in his hands it would likewise have suffered loss or deterioration without his committing a fault. However, if the depositary is entitled to substitute another person for himself, he shall only be bound to indemnify in the following two cases:

1- If he chooses a person who does not possess the qualifications fitting him to keep the deposit

2- If he alters the instructions which he had or issues to the person whom he substituted instructions from which the damage arose, even though he chose him well.
The depositor shall be entitled to bring an action directly against the substitute of the depositary as though it were against the depositary himself.

If the depositary uses the deposit or disposes of it without the permission of the depositor, he shall be liable for its loss or deterioration even if the cause thereof was an external event, and he shall likewise in all cases be liable for the loss or deterioration even if it resulted from an unforeseen contingency, if he trades with the deposit. However, he shall retain whatever profit he may then have made in this respect. And if he uses only part of the deposit or disposes of only part thereof, he shall be liable only for that part.

The depositary may not compel the depositor to take back his deposit before the agreed term save for a legitimate cause. However, he must return the deposit whenever the depositor demands it, even though the time fixed for its return has not yet arrived.

A depositary from whom the depositor demands the return of the deposit is deemed to be in default by the mere fact of a delay on his part which no legitimate cause brings forth. And if the deposit is in the interest of a third person, he must not return the deposit save with the authorisation of that person.

The depositary must return the deposit to the depositor even if another person claims it for himself, unless an attachment is levied thereon or an action for recovery of ownership is brought before the courts in respect thereof. In that event, the depositary must inform the depositor without delay of the attachment or the action for recovery of ownership. The depositary shall be put out of the action from the moment he proves that he is merely a depositary. If the duration of the dispute extends beyond the date fixed for the return of the deposit, the depositary may obtain authorisation to consign it for the account of the rightful owner.

The depositary must return the very thing deposited and the accessories that were delivered to him therewith in the condition in which they are, subject to the application of the provisions of Article 714.
The depositary must return with the deposit whatever natural and civil fruits thereof he has collected.

The depositary is liable for every cause of loss or deterioration that could have been avoided:

First- If he receives remuneration for the custody of the deposit

Second- If he accepts deposits by virtue of his profession or his function.

The depositary shall not be liable for the loss or deterioration of the deposit if it results:

1- From the nature of the thing deposited, or from the existence of a defect therein, or from the act of the depositor

2- From force majeure, unless he is in default in returning the deposit. The burden of proving the existence of the circumstances set forth in paragraphs (1) and (2) above mentioned lies upon the depositary if he receives remuneration or accepts deposits by virtue of his profession or his function.
A depositary from whom the deposit has been taken away by force majeure and who has received a sum of money or anything else in substitution therefor is bound to return what he has received.
Where there are several depositaries, they shall be jointly and severally liable in respect of the obligations and rights arising from the deposit, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary.
The depositor must pay to the depositary the expenses of preserving the deposit and indemnify him for the losses he has sustained by reason of the deposit.
The depositary may retain the deposit until he recovers in full all that has become due to him by reason of the deposit.

Sequestration is the deposit of a disputed thing in the hands of a third person. The subject-matter of sequestration may be movable or immovable property, and it is subject to the provisions relating to ordinary deposit and to the following provisions.

Sequestration shall be entrusted to a person whom all interested parties agree to appoint, and he may also be appointed by the judge, and the judge may decide to appoint a sequestrator:

1- For a thing which is the subject of a dispute or the subject of doubtful legal relations, until the dispute or doubt ceases - or for a thing which the debtor tenders to discharge his liability

2- For movable and immovable property which the interested party fears, on legitimate grounds, that the person in possession thereof will misappropriate, destroy or damage

3- For movable property securing the right of the creditor if the creditor proves the insolvency of his debtor or has legitimate grounds giving him cause to fear his flight or his misappropriation of or damage to those things. The rights and obligations of the sequestrator shall be determined in the decision of the court appointing him, failing which they shall be subject to the rules relating to a conventional sequestrator.
Sequestration may not be gratuitous.
The sequestrator shall preserve the thing and manage its affairs. He is bound to make it yield all that it is capable of yielding.

The sequestrator may not perform any act of alienation or transfer except such acts as are necessary in the interest of the sequestered thing. Where the sequestration bears upon perishable things, they may be sold by authorisation of the judge, in which case the subject-matter of the sequestration shall be the proceeds of the sale.

The sequestrator must restore the sequestered thing without delay to the person designated to him by the two parties or by the court, and with respect to its restitution he is subject to the same obligations as those incumbent upon a remunerated depositary.
Where the sequestration is not gratuitous, the sequestrator is liable for every fault in his management in accordance with the rules relating to mandate.
If the receivership is entrusted to several persons, joint and several liability exists by operation of law among them in accordance with the rules relating to agency.

The party to whom the thing is restored must pay the receiver the necessary expenses and the useful expenses which he incurred in good faith and without excess, and pay him the agreed remuneration or that determined by the judge.

If the deposit is voluntary, the receiver may bring an action against all the depositors to compel them to pay the expenses and discharge the remuneration due to him, having regard to the proportion of their interests in the matter.
Loan is of two kinds: loan for use or commodatum, and loan for consumption.

A loan for use or commodatum is a contract whereby a person (called the lender) delivers a thing to another person (referred to as the borrower) so that he may use it for a period of time or for a specified purpose, on condition that he restore that very thing to him. In a loan for use, the lender remains the owner of the thing lent and in legal possession thereof; the borrower has only detention and use.
A loan for use is essentially gratuitous.
The subject-matter of a loan for use may be movable or immovable property.
A loan for use is perfected by the consent of the two parties and by the delivery of the thing lent to the borrower.

In a loan for use, the lender must have the capacity to dispose thereof gratuitously. Thus, a testamentary guardian, a curator, or a legal administrator of the property of another may not lend the things which have been entrusted to their administration.

The borrower must watch carefully over the preservation of the thing lent. He may not entrust its preservation to another person save in case of urgent necessity. Where he contravenes the provision of the preceding paragraph, he shall be liable not only for the fault of that person, but also for contingencies resulting from force majeure.
The borrower may not, in using the thing lent, depart from the manner and extent stipulated in the contract or inferred from custom.

The borrower may use the thing lent himself and may lend it or assign its use to another person gratuitously, unless the loan was concluded in consideration of the person of the borrower or for a specific particular use which precludes him from acting in such manner.
The borrower may not lease out, pledge or dispose of the thing lent save with the permission of the lender.

The borrower must bear:

1- The ordinary expenses for the maintenance of the thing lent.

2- The expenses necessary for the use of the thing lent.
Where several persons borrow a thing together, they shall be jointly and severally liable therefor.
The borrower must return, at the agreed term, the very thing lent together with all accessories and accretions which have accrued thereto since the date of the loan.

Where the loan is for a specified term, the borrower must return the thing lent after using it in accordance with the agreed purpose or with custom. Where the intended purpose thereof has not been specified, the lender may demand its return at any time, unless there is a custom to the contrary.

The lender may demand the return of the loaned thing to him even before the expiry of the period or before the use agreed upon. This shall be in the following cases:

First- If he himself has an urgent and unforeseen need for the loaned thing.

Second- If the borrower misuses it or uses it for a purpose other than that stipulated in the contract.

Third- If he fails to bestow upon it the necessary care.

If the borrower assigns the use of the loaned thing or otherwise disposes of it for the benefit of any person, the lender may bring directly against such person the action which he was entitled to bring against the borrower.
The borrower must return the loaned thing at the place where he received it unless there is a provision to the contrary.
The borrower must bear the expenses of receiving and returning the loaned thing.

The borrower shall not be liable for the loss or deterioration of the loaned thing if they result from his normal use thereof in conformity with the agreement concluded between the two parties. And if the lender alleges that the borrower misused it, he shall be bound to establish proof.

The borrower shall be liable for the deterioration of the loaned thing and for its loss resulting from force majeure:

First- If he misuses it.

Second- If he uses it for a purpose other than that for which it is intended by its nature or pursuant to the agreement.

Third- If he is in default of return.

Fourth- If he neglects to take the necessary precautions for the preservation of the loaned thing or disposes of it for the benefit of another person without the permission of the lender whereas the loan for use was concluded out of consideration relating to his person.

Every agreement which places upon the borrower the risk of contingencies resulting from force majeure, save in the cases provided for in the preceding Article, shall be null and void. And every agreement which provides for exempting him in advance from liability for his fault or his negligence shall also be null and void.

The borrower is entitled to bring an action for damages against the lender in the following two cases:

First- If he has incurred necessary expenses for the preservation of the loaned thing

Second- If the loaned thing had defects which caused harm to the user thereof.

However, the lender shall not be liable:

First- If he was ignorant of the cause that led to the dispossession of the borrowed thing by an action for recovery of ownership, or ignorant of its latent defects.

Second- If the defects or risks were apparent to such an extent that it was easy for the borrower to know of them.

Third- If the lender had warned the borrower of the existence of such defects or risks or of the risk of its dispossession by an action for recovery of ownership.

Fourth- If the damage resulted solely from the fault or negligence of the borrower.
The borrower may retain the borrowed thing until he recovers from the lender the compensation due to him.
The contract of loan for use is dissolved by the death of the borrower. However, the obligations arising therefrom shall pass to his heirs.

The right of the lender to sue the borrower and the right of the borrower to sue the lender in actions arising from the provisions of Articles 734, 735, and 737 shall lapse by prescription upon the expiry of six months. This period shall commence, with respect to the lender, from the day the borrowed thing is returned to him, and with respect to the borrower, from the day of termination of the contract.

A loan for consumption is a contract whereby one of the parties delivers to the other party money or other fungible things on condition that the borrower return to him, at the agreed term, a quantity equivalent thereto in kind and quality.

A loan for consumption is also concluded where a creditor has, owed by another person by way of deposit or otherwise, a sum of money or a quantity of fungible things, and he authorises his debtor to retain such money or things by way of loan.
The lender must possess the capacity necessary to alienate the things which he intends to lend.
A loan for consumption may be contracted in respect of all movable fungible things, whether or not they are consumed by the first use.

If the borrower receives income securities or other financial instruments or goods instead of the agreed money, the value of the loan shall be calculated on the basis of the price of the securities or the price of the goods at the time and place at which delivery took place. Any stipulation to the contrary shall be null and void.
The things lent become the property of the borrower, and the risks thereof shall be borne by him.
The lender is liable for latent defects in the things lent and for eviction therefrom by an action for recovery of ownership, in accordance with the rules laid down in the title on sale.
The borrower must return the equivalent of the thing lent in kind and quality.

The borrower may not be compelled to return what he owes before the maturity of the term fixed under the contract or by usage. However, he may return it before the term, unless such return is prejudicial to the interest of the lender.

If no term has been fixed, the borrower is bound to make restitution upon any demand made to him by the lender, and if the two parties have agreed that the borrower shall only perform when he is able to perform or when the means become available to him, the borrower may then request the judge to fix a date for performance.
The borrower must return the thing lent at the place where the loan was concluded, if there is no agreement to the contrary.
The expenses of taking delivery and of restitution shall be borne by the borrower.
A mandate shall not be valid if its object is the performance of an act which may not be completed through a third party, such as taking an oath.
A mandate may only be given in the form required for the act which is the object of the authorisation, unless there is a legal provision to the contrary.
A mandate may be special or general.

A special mandate is one which is given to the mandatary for one or more specified matters, or which grants him a limited special authority. It confers upon him the right to act only in the matters or acts which it has specified and their necessary accessories, as required by the nature of the act or by custom.

A general mandate for the management of the principal's affairs permits the mandatary only to perform administrative acts; acts of alienation, compromise and arbitration always require a special mandate.

The mandatary is not entitled to exceed the limits specified in the mandate; however, he may depart from the instructions given to him if it was impossible for him to inform the principal beforehand and there were circumstances under which the principal's consent could be presumed. In such case, the mandatary must inform the principal without delay of the modification he has made in the execution of the mandate.
If the mandatary is able to perform the act entrusted to him on terms more advantageous and beneficial than the terms specified in the mandate, the difference shall accrue to the principal.

If several mandataries are appointed by a single mandate and for a single matter, they may not act separately without an express authorisation in that regard. Thus, for example, one of them cannot perform an administrative act in the absence of the other, even if it is impossible for the absent one to assist him in that act. However, the preceding rule shall not apply in the following two cases:

First- In defending before the courts, returning a deposit, paying a liquidated debt due, taking a conservatory measure in the interest of the principal, or performing another urgent matter the neglect of which would cause damage to the principal.

Second- In a mandate concluded between merchants for commercial business. In these two cases, one of the mandataries may validly act alone, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary.

Interest shall not be due in a loan for consumption unless it is stipulated, and if the borrower pays of his own accord interest that is not stipulated or that is in excess of the stipulated interest, he shall not be entitled to recover it or to deduct it from the principal.

If the two parties stipulate the payment of interest and do not specify a rate for it, the borrower must pay the legal interest, and in civil matters the agreed rate of interest must be specified in writing when it is in excess of the legal interest. And if it is not specified in writing, interest shall only be due at the legal rate.

Interest may be charged on the interest of the principal either by bringing an action or pursuant to a special contract created after maturity, and in both cases it is required that the accrued interest pertain to a period of not less than six months, subject to the preservation of the rules and usages relating to commerce.

Mandate is a contract whereby the principal authorises the agent to carry out a matter or several matters or to complete a work or an act or a number of works and acts. And the acceptance of the agent is required, and the acceptance of the mandate may be tacit and inferred from the agent's execution thereof.

A mandate is in principle gratuitous, and there is nothing to prevent the stipulation of remuneration. And it shall not be presumed to be gratuitous in the following cases:

First- If the agent performs, by virtue of his profession or trade, the services to which his mandate relates.

Second- If the mandate is between merchants for commercial transactions.

Third- If custom requires the payment of remuneration for the acts to which the mandate relates.
A mandate may be subject to a condition and may take effect starting from a specified term or until a specified term.
A mandate shall not be valid unless the principal himself has the capacity to perform its object. And this capacity is not required of the agent; rather, it suffices that he be of discernment.

A mandate shall be void:

First- If its object is impossible or not sufficiently determined

Second- If its object is the performance of acts contrary to public order, morals, or the laws.

An agent may not appoint another person as his substitute in the execution of the agency in the following cases:

First - If the principal has expressly conferred this right upon him.

Second - If the conferral of this right upon him arises from the nature of the act or from the circumstances

Third - If the agency is general and absolute.

An agent who does not hold the power of substitution shall be liable for whomever he appoints in his place just as he is liable for his own acts. Where substitution is permitted to him, he shall only be liable if he chose a person who did not possess the attributes required for the agency, or if, despite having made a good choice, he gave his substitute instructions that were the cause of the damage or failed to supervise him when necessity so required.
In all cases, the substitute of the agent shall be directly liable to the principal in the same manner as the agent himself, and shall have the same rights as the agent.
The agent must attend to the execution of the agency with the care of a bonus paterfamilias.

The obligations provided for in the preceding Article must be construed strictly:

First - If the agency is for remuneration

Second - If it is in the interest of a minor, an incapacitated person, or a juristic person.
The agent must inform the principal of all circumstances that might induce him to modify or revoke the agency.

Upon completing the agency, the agent is bound to promptly notify the principal in a manner that enables him to fully ascertain how it was completed. If the principal delays in replying after receiving the notification for longer than is required by the nature of the affair or by established custom, he shall be deemed to have accompanied what the agent has done, even if he exceeded the limits of his authority.

The agent must submit to the principal, at his request at any time - an account of his management, and must deliver to him everything that has accrued to him through the agency in any manner whatsoever, and he must pay interest on the funds the payment of which he has delayed.

The mandatary shall be liable for the things which he has received by way of the mandate, in accordance with the conditions provided for in Articles 696, 697, 711, 712, 714 and 715, and if the mandate is for remuneration, the liability of the mandatary shall be subject to the provisions of Article 713.

If there are several mandataries, joint and several liability shall not exist among them unless it is stipulated; provided that the joint and several liability of the mandataries shall exist ipso jure:

First- When the damage which has befallen the principal arises from a common fault upon which collusion took place among them

Second- When the mandate is indivisible

Third- When the mandate is concluded for commercial business between merchants, and there is no stipulation to the contrary; provided that the mandatary, even if jointly and severally liable with the rest of the mandataries, shall not in any case whatsoever be answerable for what one of them has done which falls outside the scope of the mandate or exceeds its limits.
The principal must provide the mandatary with the funds and all other means necessary for the execution of his mandate, unless there is an agreement or custom to the contrary.

The principal must:
