First- Pay to the mandatary all the money he has advanced and the expenses he has incurred for the execution of the mandate which do not fall outside the scope of what is necessary for this purpose. If he is entitled to remuneration, it must be paid regardless of the result of the work, unless there is a fault attributable to the mandatary.

Second- Relieve the mandatary of the obligations to which he has bound himself as a result of the execution of the mandate.

Provided that the principal shall not be bound by the obligations to which the mandatary has bound himself nor by the losses which he has suffered due to a fault he committed or for reasons extraneous to the mandate.

The mandatary shall not be entitled to the agreed remuneration:

First- If force majeure prevented him from commencing the execution of the mandate

Second- If the matter for which he was appointed mandatary was concluded before he was able to commence it

Third- If the matter for which the mandate was given is not completed. In this last case, commercial or local custom shall be observed; provided that the judge shall be entitled to consider whether the mandatary must be granted compensation, having regard to the circumstances of the case.
If the remuneration is not specified, it shall be determined on the basis of the custom observed in the place where the mandate was concluded, and otherwise according to the circumstances.

If the principal assigns the matter to another person, he shall remain liable towards the mandatary for all the consequences of the mandate in accordance with the provisions of Article 793, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary accepted by the mandatary.

If the mandate is issued by several persons in a matter common to them, each person among them shall be liable towards the mandatary in proportion to his interest in the matter, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary.

The principal shall not be bound by what the agent does beyond the scope of his authority or in excess of its limit, except in the following cases:

First- If he ratified it, even tacitly

Second- If he benefited therefrom

Third- If the agent contracted on terms more advantageous than the terms specified in the instructions he received

Fourth- If the agent contracted on terms more onerous than the terms specified to him in the instructions he received, and that in the following two cases:

1- If the difference is of minor importance

2- If it is in conformity with the tolerance customary in commerce or in the place where the contract was concluded.

The agent who acts without a mandate or exceeds the limit of his mandate is bound to pay damages to the persons with whom he contracted if the contract cannot be performed, and the agent shall not be bound by any warranty if he enabled his co-contractor to have sufficient knowledge of his authority, unless the agent took upon himself the performance of the obligation.

The mandate terminates:

First- By the completion of the business for which it was given.

Second- By the fulfilment of a resolutory condition or by the expiration of the term fixed for the mandate.

Third- By the revocation of the agent by the principal.

Fourth- By the renunciation of the mandate by the agent.

Fifth- By the death of the principal or the agent.

Sixth- By the occurrence of a change in the status of the principal or the agent leading to his loss of legal capacity to exercise his rights, such as interdiction and declaration of bankruptcy, unless the object of the mandate is among the acts that can be completed despite such change.

Seventh- By the impossibility of performance arising from a cause unrelated to the will of the contracting parties.
A mandate given by a juristic person or a company terminates with the cessation of this company or that person.

The principal may revoke the agent whenever he wishes. Any stipulation to the contrary shall be of no effect, whether with respect to the contracting parties or with respect to third parties. The stipulation of remuneration shall not prevent the principal from exercising this right. However, if the mandate was concluded in the interest of the agent or of another person, the principal shall not be entitled to revoke the mandate except with the consent of the party for whose benefit it was concluded.
Revocation may be express or tacit. If the revocation is effected by letter or telegram, it shall not take effect except from the date of the agent's receipt of the notice of his revocation.

If the mandate is given by several persons for a single affair, revocation shall not be permissible except by agreement of all the principals; however, if the affair is divisible, a revocation issued by one of the principals terminates the mandate with respect to the part pertaining to this principal alone. As for general partnerships (collectif) and other companies, every partner who holds the right to confer a mandate in the name of the company is entitled to revoke the mandate.

The agent shall be entitled to retain in his possession the movables or goods of the principal which have been delivered or consigned to him until he recovers what is due to him from the principal in accordance with the provisions of Article 793.

Where the agent contracts in his own name and on his own behalf, the rights arising out of the contract shall vest in him. He shall remain directly bound towards those with whom he contracted as though the transaction concerned him alone to the exclusion of the principal, even if those with whom he contracted knew him to be a nominee or an intermediary acting on commission.

An agent who acts in his capacity as agent and does not exceed the limits of his authority shall incur no personal obligation whatsoever towards the other persons with whom he contracted.

Those persons may not make any claim except against the principal.
A third party shall not be entitled to bring an action against the agent to compel him to perform the mandate unless it was concluded in the interest of that person as well.
Third parties shall be entitled to bring an action against the agent to compel him to accept the performance of the contract where its performance necessarily falls within his mandate.

Where a special mandate exists, any person dealing with the agent in his capacity as agent shall at all times be entitled to require him to produce the instrument of mandate and, where necessary, to obtain an official copy of that instrument, provided that he pays the cost thereof.

Acts validly performed by the agent in the name of the principal and within the limits of his authority shall take effect both in favour of and against the principal as though the principal had performed them himself.

The principal shall be bound to fulfil directly the undertakings entered into by the agent on his behalf within the limits of the authority conferred upon him in the mandate. Restrictive stipulations and secret agreements concluded between the principal and the agent which do not appear from the mandate itself may not be invoked against a third party unless proof is established that such person had knowledge thereof at the time of the contract.

If the agent dies and the heirs are aware of the existence of the agency, they shall notify the principal without delay of the news of the death. They shall also preserve the documents and other papers belonging to the principal and take all measures necessary to safeguard his interests. However, the provisions of this article shall not apply to minor heirs so long as they are without a guardian.

If the principal or the agent revokes the contract of agency suddenly at an inopportune time and without an acceptable reason, he may be held liable to indemnify the other party for damages by reason of his abusive exercise of this right.

The existence of damage and its amount shall be assessed by the judge according to the nature of the agency, the circumstances of the case and local custom.

Partnerships are of two kinds:

First- Partnerships of ownership or quasi-partnerships

Second- Contractual partnerships or partnerships in the proper sense.

When a thing or a right is held in undivided and common ownership among several persons, there arises therefrom a legal entity called a partnership of ownership or a quasi-partnership, which may be voluntary or compulsory.
In case of doubt, the shares of the co-owners shall be deemed equal.

Every co-owner may use the common thing in proportion to his right, provided that he does not use it in a manner contrary to the nature of that thing or the purpose for which it is intended, or contrary to the interest of the co-ownership, or in a manner that prevents the other co-owners from exercising their rights.

No co-owner may make an alteration to the common thing without the express or implied consent of his co-owners. If the provisions of the preceding paragraph are not observed, the following rules shall apply:

First- Partition shall take place when the thing is divisible. If the part in which the alteration was made falls within the share of the co-owner who made it, none of the parties shall have any ground for objection. However, if the alteration falls within the share of another co-owner, that co-owner may choose either to pay the value of the alteration or to compel his co-owner to restore the thing to its original condition.

Second- When the thing is indivisible, the co-owners may compel the person who made the alteration to restore the thing to its original condition and to bear the expense, together with the payment of damages where applicable.

When the thing is by its nature indivisible, a co-owner shall only be entitled to take from its products what corresponds to his share. And it must be leased for the account of all the co-owners even if one of them objects thereto.
Every co-owner must render an account to his co-owners of everything he has received in excess of his share of the produce of the thing held in common.

The co-owners may agree that each of them shall individually enjoy the thing or the right held in common by turns. In such case, each of them may dispose of his own right which he enjoys throughout the period fixed for such enjoyment, whether for consideration or gratuitously, and he shall not then be bound to render an account to his co-owners of what he has collected. However, he may not do anything calculated to diminish or prevent the rights of the remaining co-owners when their turn for enjoyment comes.
Every co-owner must see to the preservation of the thing held in common in the same manner as he sees to his own property.

Every co-owner is entitled to compel the remaining co-owners to contribute in proportion to their shares to the necessary expenses for preserving the thing held in common and keeping it fit for the use for which it is intended. Provided that each of them may release himself from this obligation:

First- By selling his share, reserving the right of preference attaching to co-ownership for the co-owner who incurred the expense or offered to incur it.

Second- By leaving to the said co-owner the right of enjoyment of the thing held in common together with its produce until he recovers what he has paid on behalf of the co-owners.

Third- By applying for partition if it is possible.

If, however, the expense has already been paid, the co-owners shall be liable therefor in proportion to their shares.

Every co-owner is bound towards the others to bear the charges of the thing held in common and the expenses of management and exploitation, and the share of each co-owner in such charges and expenses shall be determined according to his share in that thing.

Useful expenses and luxury expenses incurred by one of the co-owners shall not entitle him to claim any part thereof from his co-owners unless they have expressly or impliedly authorised him to incur them.

The minority of the co-owners shall be bound to accept the decisions taken by the majority with respect to the management of the thing held in common and the manner of enjoying it, provided that the majority holds three-quarters of the interests of which the object of the co-ownership is composed. If the majority does not hold three-quarters thereof, the co-owners may have recourse to the judge, who shall decide what he deems most consistent with the general interest of the co-ownership. He may appoint a manager for it if necessary or order its partition.

Revocation of the mandate, in whole or in part, shall not be effective against a third party in good faith who contracted with the mandatary before knowing of his revocation. However, the mandator shall retain the right of recourse against his mandatary.
Where the law requires a specific form for establishing a mandate, the same form must be used to revoke it.

The mandatary may not renounce the mandate unless he notifies the mandator of his renunciation. The mandatary shall be liable for all damages that such renunciation may cause to the mandator if he fails to take the necessary measures to fully safeguard the interests of his mandator until the mandator himself is able to do what is necessary.

The mandatary may not renounce his mandate where it has been concluded in the interest of a third party, except in the case of illness or another legitimate impediment. In the said case, the mandatary is bound to give notice to the person in whose interest the mandate was given, and to grant him a sufficient period to do what the circumstances require.

The revocation or death of the principal mandatary shall entail the revocation of the person whom he appointed as sub-mandatary, except in the following two cases:

First- Where the sub-mandatary was appointed with the authorisation of the mandator.

Second- Where the principal mandatary had absolute power of disposal or had the right to appoint a sub-mandatary.

The death of the mandator or the change of his status shall terminate the mandate of the principal mandatary and the mandate of his sub-mandatary, except in the following two cases:

First- Where the mandate was given in the interest of the mandatary or in the interest of a third party.

Second- Where the object of the mandate is an act intended to be completed after the death of the mandator, such that the mandatary then stands in the position of a testamentary executor.

The acts performed by the mandatary in the name of the mandator before knowing of his death or of one of the causes that led to the termination of the mandate, shall be deemed valid provided that the third party with whom he contracted was also unaware of such cause.

Where the mandate terminates upon the death of the mandator, his bankruptcy, or his loss of capacity, the mandatary must, if there is danger in delay, complete what he has begun to the extent required by necessity, and perform everything that the circumstances require in the interest of the mandator if there is no heir having capacity or legal representative of the mandator or of the heir. On the other hand, the mandatary shall be entitled to recover what he has advanced or expended for the performance of the mandate in accordance with the rules relating to negotiorum gestio.

The minority shall not be compelled to accept the decisions of the majority if they relate to:

First - Acts of disposition, and also administrative acts if they directly affect ownership

Second - New modifications to the partnership contract or the common thing.

Third - Contracting new obligations. In the aforementioned cases, the opinion of the dissenters must prevail. However, the other co-owners may, where necessary, exercise the right provided for in Article 86.

Each co-owner has an undivided share in the ownership of the common thing and in its products. He may sell that share, assign it, mortgage it, substitute another person for himself in the enjoyment thereof, and dispose of it in any other manner, whether for consideration or without consideration, unless he possesses only a right personal to him.
If one of the co-owners sells his undivided share to another person, the remaining co-owners may invoke the right of pre-emption in accordance with the legal provisions relating thereto.

Co-ownership or quasi-partnership terminates:

First - By the total loss of the common property.

Second - By the assignment by the co-owners of their shares to one of them or by abandoning them to him

Third - By partition.

No one may be compelled to remain in undivided co-ownership, and every co-owner may request partition; however, the court may temporarily stay the action for partition if it is satisfied that the circumstances are unsuitable for carrying it out.

It is permissible to agree to remain in undivided co-ownership for a

fixed period not exceeding five years, and any excess over this limit shall be of no effect. The court may order, even during the fixed period, the termination of the undivided co-ownership if strong supervening reasons appear to it justifying this. Moreover, the court may, even in this case, order the dissolution of the partnership and partition during the period agreed upon for the continuation of the undivided co-ownership.
Partition may not be requested if the object of the co-ownership consists of things which, after their partition, do not remain fit for the use for which they are intended.
Prescription shall not run against an action requesting partition.

A partnership is a reciprocal contract whereby two or several persons participate in a thing with the view to dividing the profit resulting therefrom.

It may, in the cases provided for by law, be established by an act proceeding from the will of a single person.

The participation of employees or representatives of legal persons or partnerships in a portion of the profits, as total or partial remuneration given to them for the services they perform, shall not suffice to confer upon them the capacity of partner.

A partnership may not be contracted:

First - Between a father and a son who is still subject to paternal authority.

Second - Between a guardian and a minor until the minor attains the age of majority and the guardian renders the account of guardianship and final approval thereof is completed.

Third - Between the curator of an incapacitated person or the administrator of a religious establishment, and the persons whose property they administer.

The authorisation by the father or the guardian or curator to the minor or the incapacitated person to engage in commerce shall not suffice to render them capable of contracting with them to form a partnership.

Every partnership must have a lawful object: every partnership whose object is contrary to morals, public policy or the law shall be null ipso jure. Also null ipso jure shall be every partnership whose subject matter consists of things which are not considered property in commerce among people.

A partnership is perfected by the consent of the contracting parties to its establishment and to the other clauses of the contract, save in the case where the law requires a special form. However, if the subject matter of the partnership consists of immovable property or other property susceptible of mortgage, and its term exceeds three years, its contract must be drawn up in writing and registered in the legal form, and furthermore the formalities provided for in Decision No. 188 issued by the High Commissioner on 15 March 1926 must be completed.

The contributions of the partners to the capital may consist of money, movable or immovable property, or incorporeal rights, and may also consist of the industry of one of the partners or of the industry of all of them.
That which is contributed by one of the partners may also consist of the commercial credit which he enjoys.
The things contributed by the partners may differ in value and in nature. In case of doubt, they shall be deemed to have contributed equally.

The share of each partner in the capital must be determined along with a statement of its nature. If it consists of all the present property owned by one of the partners, an inventory thereof must be drawn up. If it consists of things other than money, they must be appraised according to the value they have on the day of their contribution to the property of the partnership; failing which, the partners shall be deemed to have agreed that their current price on the day of their contribution shall be the basis of appraisal. If there is no price, it shall be according to the value determined by experts.

The common fund or capital of the partnership consists of the aggregate of the shares contributed by the partners and of the things purchased therewith for carrying out the business of the partnership. There shall also be included in the capital of the partnership the compensation received for the loss, deterioration or expropriation of a thing belonging to the capital; however, there shall only be added to the property of the partnership out of such compensation an amount equivalent to the value assigned to that thing when it was placed in the partnership pursuant to the contract. The capital of the partnership shall be joint property among the partners, each of whom having an undivided share therein in proportion to what he has contributed to the capital.

A partnership may be formed for a term or for an indefinite duration. If its object is an enterprise of a determinate duration, it shall be deemed to have been formed for the duration for which such enterprise continues.
The partnership begins from the conclusion of the contract, unless the partners agree to fix another date.
Every partner is a debtor to the other partners for everything he has promised to contribute to the partnership. In case of doubt, the partners are deemed to be bound to contribute equal shares.

Every partner must deliver what he is bound to contribute at the appointed time. If there is no fixed time, then immediately upon the conclusion of the contract. Due regard shall be had in this respect to the time limits required by the nature of the thing or by distance. If one of the partners is in default in contributing his share to the capital, the other partners may demand his expulsion from the partnership or compel him to perform what he has undertaken, while reserving their right to claim damages in both cases.

If the share of one of the partners in the capital is a debt owed to him by another person, the liability of such partner shall not be discharged until the day on which the partnership receives the sum in lieu of which that debt was contributed. The partner shall also be liable for damages if the sum is not paid at the date of maturity.

If the share contributed is the ownership of a specific thing, the partner who contributed it shall be bound by the warranty incumbent upon a seller in respect of latent defects and eviction. If what he contributed is limited to the usufruct, the partner shall be bound by the warranty incumbent upon a lessor, and he shall also be bound to warrant the contents of that thing on the same conditions.

A partner who has undertaken to contribute his industry shall be bound to perform the acts which he has promised and to render an account of all the profits which he has realized from the date of the conclusion of the contract by means of that industry which is the object of the partnership. However, he shall not be bound to bring into the partnership patents of invention which he has obtained, unless there is an agreement to the contrary.

If the share of a partner perishes or deteriorates due to force majeure after the contract and before actual or constructive delivery is effected, the following rules shall apply:

First- If what the partner contributes consists of money or other fungible things, or the right of usufruct in a specific thing, the risk of loss or deterioration shall be borne by the partner who is the owner.

Second- If, however, it is a specific thing the ownership of which has been brought into the partnership, all the partners shall bear the risk.

None of the partners shall be bound to renew his share in the capital if it perishes; save for the case mentioned in Article 911, nor shall he be bound to increase it beyond what was fixed in the contract.
A partner may not invoke set-off between damages for which he is liable and profits which the partnership has obtained through him in another matter.

A partner may not substitute another person for himself in the performance of what he has undertaken towards the partnership. He shall in any event be liable for the acts of the persons whom he puts in his place or whose assistance he uses, and for the fault they commit.

A partner may not, without the consent of his partners, carry out for his own account or for the account of a third party acts similar to the acts of the partnership if such competition harms the interests of the partnership. In the event of breach, the partners shall have the right to choose between claiming damages from him and taking for their own account the transactions into which he has entered and demanding payment of the profits which he has realized. All this is without prejudice to the right to seek his expulsion from the partnership. If three months elapse without their choosing one of the aforementioned options, they shall forfeit the right of choice and shall retain only the right to obtain damages where applicable.

The provision of the preceding Article shall not apply if the partner, prior to his entry into the partnership, had an interest in undertakings similar to it or was carrying out acts similar to its acts with the knowledge of his partners and it was not stipulated that he must abandon them, and the said partner may not resort to the courts to compel his partners to give him their consent.

A partner in a partnership with general delegation may not, without a special authorisation set out in the partnership contract or in a subsequent contract:

First- Assign gratuitously. Customary gifts and gratuities are excepted

Second- Guarantee third parties

Third- Lend gratuitously

Fourth- Submit to arbitration

Fifth- Relinquish the establishment, the business concern, or the patent of invention upon which the partnership was contracted.

Sixth- Waive guarantees, unless the waiver is for consideration.

If the partnership contract specifies that all the partners are entitled to assume the management, but that none of them may act separately from the others, the partnership is then described as restricted or as having a restricted mandate. Failing a special provision or custom, every partner in a restricted partnership may perform acts of management, provided that he obtains the consent of his partners, unless it is a matter requiring urgency and the omission of which would result in harm to the partnership.

If it is stipulated in the partnership contract that its decisions shall be taken by a majority, this provision must be understood, in case of doubt, as meaning a majority in number.

If the votes are equally divided into two parts, the opposing side shall prevail. If the two sides differ as to the decision sought to be taken, the matter shall be referred to the court to decide what accords with the general interest of the partnership.

Management may be entrusted to one or several managers, and they may be appointed from among persons who are not members of the partnership. However, they may only be appointed by the majority required by the partnership contract for its decisions.

A partner to whom the management of the partnership has been entrusted pursuant to the contract may perform, notwithstanding the opposition of the remaining partners, all acts of management and even acts of disposition falling within the object of the partnership, in accordance with what is provided for in Article 887, provided that there is no fraud and that the restrictions set out in the contract pursuant to which the authority was granted are observed.
A manager who is appointed from among non-partners shall have the rights conferred upon a mandatory pursuant to Article 777, unless there is a provision to the contrary.

Every partner is bound to exercise such care and diligence in performing his duties towards the partnership as he exercises in the conduct of his own affairs. Any default in this respect shall constitute a fault for which he is liable to the other partners, just as he is liable for the non-performance of the duties arising from the partnership contract and for the abuse of the authority conferred upon him. He shall not be liable for force majeure unless it results from a fault on his part.

Every partner is bound, under the same conditions as an agent, to render an account of:

First- All sums and assets which he takes from the capital of the partnership for the common business.

Second- Everything he has received on the common account or by way of the business that constitutes the object of the partnership.

Third- And in general, every act which he performs on behalf of the partnership.

Any stipulation exempting one of the partners from the duty to render an account shall be null and void.
Every partner may take from the common funds the sum fixed in the contract for his personal expenses. He shall not be entitled to exceed this sum.

Every partner who uses, without the authorisation of the other partners, the common funds or things in his own interest or in the interest of a third party, is bound to restore the sums he has taken and to bring into the funds of the partnership the profits he has realised. The right of the partners to damages and to institute criminal proceedings against him, where appropriate, is nevertheless reserved.

A partner, even if he is a manager, may not, without the consent of the other partners, associate another person in the business of the partnership, unless the contract grants him this right. He may, however, grant a third party an interest in his own share or assign it to him, just as he may assign his share in the capital upon partition- all this unless there is an agreement to the contrary. Where a partner exercises any of the rights recognised to him in the preceding paragraph, no legal relationship is thereby created between the partnership and the interested third party or the assignee of the partner, as these two persons have no right save to the profits and losses accruing to that partner on the basis of the balance sheet. Neither of them may institute any action against the partnership, even by way of subrogation to the partner whose rights have been transferred to them.

A person who substitutes for an outgoing partner with the consent of the other partners or pursuant to a stipulation in the contract- of partnership, takes his place in all rights and obligations in accordance with the conditions derived from the nature of the partnership.

Every partner has the right of action against the remaining partners in proportion to their shares in the partnership:

First- For the sums which he has expended for the preservation of the common things, and the expenses which he has incurred in the interest of all with prudence and without extravagance.

Second- For the obligations which he has contracted in the interest of all with prudence and without extravagance.

An administering partner shall not be entitled to receive special remuneration on account of his administration unless it is expressly stipulated. This provision shall apply to the remaining partners in respect of the work which they perform in the common interest or the special services which they render to the partnership and which do not fall within their obligations as partners.
The obligations of the partnership with respect to the partners shall be divided among them in proportion to what each of them has contributed thereto.

The right to administer the business of the partnership belongs to all the partners jointly, and none of them is entitled to exercise it individually unless he is authorised by the remaining partners.
The right to administer the partnership includes the right to represent it towards third parties unless the contrary is stipulated.

When the partners agree to confer upon each of them a mandate to administer the affairs of the partnership and state that each partner may act without consulting the others, their partnership is then called a partnership of general delegation or mandate.

In a partnership of general delegation, every partner may perform individually all acts of administration which fall within the object of the partnership, even acts of alienation. He may, in particular:

First- Enter on behalf of the partnership into a particular partnership with third parties the object of which is an administrative act or a set of administrative acts.

Second- Advance funds to third persons to carry out an enterprise on behalf of the partnership.

Third- Appoint employees and agents.

Fourth- Appoint and dismiss mandatory agents.

Fifth- Receive payments, rescind contracts, sell for cash, on credit, for a term, or for future delivery the things falling within the object of the partnership, acknowledge debts, bind the partnership by obligations to the extent required by the needs of the administration, constitute a pledge or other form of security to the same extent, accept such a pledge or security, issue or endorse promissory notes "to order" or bills of exchange, accept the return of a thing sold on account of a redhibitory defect when the partner who concluded the sale is absent, represent the partnership in legal proceedings whether as plaintiff or as defendant, and enter into compromises provided that they are advantageous. - All the foregoing unless there is fraud or special restrictions set forth in the partnership contract.

If the partnership has several managers, none of them may, in the absence of a stipulation to the contrary, act without the concurrence of the others save in cases of urgency where delay would be cause for serious harm to the partnership. If a dispute arises, the opinion of the majority must be followed, and if the votes are equally divided into two halves, those opposing shall prevail. However, if the dispute is confined to the method to be followed, reference shall be made in this regard to what all the partners decide. If the branches of management are distributed among the managers, each of them may perform the acts falling within the management of his branch and is in no way entitled to exceed them.

Neither the managers, even if unanimous in opinion, nor the partners, even if their majority so decides, may perform acts other than those falling within the object of the partnership according to its nature and commercial usage. The unanimity of the partners shall be required:

First- To dispose gratuitously of the common property or of any part thereof.

Second- To amend the partnership contract or to depart from its terms.

Third- To perform acts outside the object of the partnership. Every stipulation authorising in advance the managers or the majority to take decisions of this kind without consulting the others shall be void.

In such case, even the partners who are not managers are entitled to take part in the deliberations.

If a dispute arises, the opinion of those opposing must be followed.

Non-managing partners may neither take part in any acts of management nor object to the acts performed by the managers appointed pursuant to the contract, unless they exceed the limits of the acts that constitute the object of the partnership or expressly contravene the contract or the law.

Non-managing partners are entitled to demand at any time an account of the management of the affairs of the partnership and of the state of the common property, and to inspect the books and papers of the partnership and to examine them. Every stipulation to the contrary shall be deemed void. This right is personal and may not be exercised by an agent or other representative save in the case of persons lacking capacity, who may validly be represented by their legal representatives- or in the case of a valid impediment duly established.
A person who is merely a partner in a joint venture is not entitled to inspect the books and papers of the partnership save for a serious reason and with the leave of the judge.

Managers appointed pursuant to the partnership contract may not be dismissed except for legitimate causes and by a decision taken by the unanimous agreement of all the partners. However, the partnership contract may grant this right to the majority or stipulate that the managers appointed pursuant to the contract may be dismissed in the same manner as an agent is dismissed. Mismanagement, the arising of serious disagreement among the managers, the commission by one or several of them of a grave breach of the obligations of their office, and the impossibility of their performing the same shall be deemed legitimate causes. On the other hand, managers appointed pursuant to the partnership contract may not relinquish their offices except for a legally acceptable impediment, failing which they shall be bound to pay damages to the partners. However, where the dismissal of the managers is subject to the will of the partners, they may relinquish their offices subject to the conditions laid down for an agent.

Managing partners who have not been appointed pursuant to the partnership contract shall be subject to dismissal in the same manner as agents. However, their dismissal may only be decided by the majority required for appointment. On the other hand, they shall have the right to relinquish the performance of their offices subject to the conditions laid down for agents. The provisions of this Article shall apply to managers who are not partners.

Where nothing has been decided with respect to the management of the partnership's affairs, it shall be deemed a "limited partnership" and the relations of the partners in this respect shall be subject to the provisions of Article 891.

Where the partnership contract does not specify the share of each partner in the profits and losses, the share of each of them shall be in proportion to what he contributed to the capital of the partnership. Where the contract specifies only the share in the profits, such specification shall apply to the losses, and vice versa. As for the partner who has contributed only his industry, his share shall be determined in proportion to the importance of such industry in relation to the partnership. A partner who, in addition to his industry, has contributed money or other assets shall be entitled to receive a share proportionate to what he has contributed in both respects.

Where the contract provides for granting one of the partners the entirety of the profits, the partnership shall be void. Every stipulation exempting one of the partners from participating in the payment of losses shall result in the nullity of the partnership.

The settlement of the partnership's profits and losses shall take place on the basis of the balance sheet, which must be drawn up together with the inventory, at the end of each calendar year or at the end of each financial year of the partnership.

Prior to any division, one-twentieth of the net profits at the end of the year shall be deducted in order to form the reserve fund until it reaches one-fifth of the capital. If the capital decreases, it must be replenished to the extent of the loss from the profits earned thereafter. The partnership shall cease distributing any profit to the partners until the capital is restored to its original amount in full, unless the partners decide to reduce the capital of the partnership to the amount actually existing.

After deducting what is required by the preceding Article, the share of each partner in the profits shall be liquidated and he shall then be entitled to take it; if he fails to take it, it shall be retained as a deposit for him without his share in the capital of the partnership being increased thereby, unless the remaining partners expressly consent to add it to his share, all of the foregoing being subject to any provision to the contrary.

In the event of a loss, a partner shall not be bound to return to the funds of the partnership the share which he received from the profits of a past year if he took it in good faith pursuant to a lawful balance sheet also drawn up in good faith; however, if the balance sheet was not drawn up in good faith, the partner shall be entitled to bring an action for damages against the managers of the partnership.
If the partnership is established for a specific affair, the final liquidation of the account and the distribution of profits shall only take place after the conclusion of that affair.
If the contract of partnership does not entail joint and several liability, the partners shall be liable towards the creditors in proportion to what each of them has contributed to the partnership.
In a partnership of general mandate, the partners shall be jointly and severally liable for the obligations validly contracted by one of them, unless there is fraud.
A partner who contracts obligations falling outside the scope of his authority or the object for which the partnership was created shall alone be bound by those obligations.
Acts performed by one of the partners outside the limits of his authority shall bind the partnership towards third parties to the extent of the benefit it derived from his act.

Where one of the partners has contributed to the partnership the usufruct of a specific thing, the loss of such thing before or after its delivery entails the dissolution of the partnership among the partners, and the rule of this provision shall apply where it becomes impossible for the partner who promised to contribute his industry to perform the work.

A partnership that is dissolved ipso jure by the expiration of the term fixed for it or by the accomplishment of the object for which it was contracted shall have its term deemed tacitly extended if the partners continue the operations which formed the object of the partnership after the arrival of the agreed term or the accomplishment of the work for which it was contracted, and such tacit extension shall be from year to year.

The personal creditors of one of the partners are entitled to object to the extension of the term of the partnership, provided that they shall only have such right if the amount of their debt is liquidated by virtue of a judgment that has acquired the force of res judicata, and such objection suspends the effect of the extension of the partnership with respect to the objecting parties, and the other partners may decide to expel the partner on whose account the objection was made, and Article 918 has determined the effects of such expulsion.

Each of the partners is entitled to apply for the dissolution of the partnership even before the fixed term, if there are legitimate grounds such as the arising of serious disagreements among the partners, or the failure of one or several of them to fulfil the obligations arising from the contract, or the impossibility of their performing them, and the partners may not waive in advance their right to apply for the dissolution of the partnership in the cases provided for in this Article.

Where the duration of the partnership is not fixed pursuant to the contract or according to the nature of the work, each of the partners may withdraw from the partnership by notifying the other partners of such withdrawal, provided that it is made in good faith and does not occur at an inopportune time. The withdrawal shall not be deemed to be made in good faith if the partner who withdraws intends to appropriate for himself alone the benefit which the partners intended to derive jointly, and the withdrawal shall be deemed to occur at an inopportune time if it takes place after the operations have been commenced and it has consequently become in the interest of the partnership that its dissolution be deferred, and in all cases the withdrawal shall only take effect from the end of the partnership year, and notice thereof must be given at least three months before that date, unless there are serious grounds.

Where it is stipulated that the partnership shall continue, after the death of one of the partners, its operations with his heirs, such stipulation shall have no effect if the heir lacks legal capacity, provided that the competent judge is entitled to authorise minors or persons lacking legal capacity to continue the partnership if they have a substantial interest therein, and to order in such case all the measures required by the circumstances to safeguard their rights.

The partners shall be liable towards a third party - if he is in good faith - for acts of deceit and fraud committed by the head of the instrument representing the partnership, and shall be bound to indemnify him for the damage arising from such acts, whilst reserving their right to bring an action against the person who caused the damage

Whoever enters an established partnership shall be bound, to the extent required by its nature, by the obligations contracted prior to his entry therein, even if the name or style of the partnership has changed, and any agreement to the contrary shall be void with respect to third parties.

The creditors of the partnership may bring actions against the partnership represented in the persons of its managers and against the partners themselves. Provided that the execution of the judgment rendered in their favour must first apply to the property of the partnership.

They shall have priority over such property against the personal creditors of the partners.

If the property of the partnership is insufficient, they may have recourse against the partners to recover what remains due to them of the debt under the conditions required by the nature of the partnership, and each of the partners may then raise, against the creditors of the partnership, the defences personal to him as well as those pertaining to the partnership, including set-off.

The personal creditors of one of the partners may not exercise their rights during the continuance of the partnership save upon that partner's share of the profits realised according to the balance sheet, and not upon his share of the capital. After the expiration or dissolution of the partnership, they shall be entitled to exercise such rights upon his share of the property of the partnership after deduction of the debts. However, they may levy a conservatory attachment upon that share prior to any liquidation.

The partnership shall come to an end:

First - By the arrival of the term fixed for it or by the fulfilment of the condition of cancellation

Second - By the completion of the object for which it was contracted or by the impossibility of completing it

Third - By the loss of the common property or by the loss of a substantial portion thereof after which no useful exploitation can be carried on

Fourth - By the death of one of the partners, or by the declaration of his absence, or by his interdiction for mental infirmity, unless there is an agreement for the continuance of the partnership with his heirs or representatives - for its continuance among the surviving partners

Fifth - By the declaration of bankruptcy or judicial liquidation of one of the partners

Sixth - By the agreement of the partners

Seventh - By the withdrawal of one or more partners, if the duration of the partnership is not fixed pursuant to the contract or according to the nature of the work which was made the object of the partnership

Eighth - By a judgment of the court in the cases provided for by law.

Commercial partnerships shall not be deemed dissolved with respect to third parties prior to the expiry of the term fixed therefor, save after the lapse of one month from the publication of the judgment or other instruments from which the dissolution of the partnership is inferred.

In the case provided for in Article 914 and in all cases in which the partnership is dissolved by reason of the death of one of the partners, his absence, his interdiction, the declaration of his insolvency, or by reason of the minority of one of the heirs, the remaining partners may continue the partnership among themselves by obtaining a judgment from the court ordering the exclusion of the partner who was the cause of the dissolution of the partnership, and in such case the excluded partner, or the heirs of the deceased, or other legal representatives of the deceased, the interdicted, the absent, or the insolvent person, shall be entitled to receive the share of that partner in the partnership property and in the profits after the liquidation thereof is carried out as on the day on which the exclusion was decided. They shall not participate in the profits and losses arising after that date save in so far as they, that is to say the profits and losses, are a direct and necessary consequence of the transactions that preceded the exclusion of the partner whom they succeed, or his absence, his fulfilment, or his insolvency. They shall not be entitled to demand payment of their share save at the date fixed for distribution pursuant to the partnership contract.

If the partnership consists of two persons, the partner who did not cause the dissolution thereof in the cases provided for in Articles 914 and 915 may obtain leave from the judge to pay off the other partner and continue operating the partnership, taking for himself its assets and its liabilities.
The heirs of a deceased partner shall be bound by the obligations incumbent upon the heirs of an agent.

The managers may not, after the dissolution of the partnership, embark upon any new transaction other than the acts necessary for the completion of the business already commenced. If they do so, they shall be personally and jointly and severally liable for the transactions upon which they have embarked, and the effect of this prohibition shall run from the date of the expiry of the term of the partnership, or from the date of the accomplishment of the object for which it was contracted, or the date of the occurrence of the event that led to the dissolution of the partnership pursuant to the law.

Partition among partners in contractual partnerships or co-ownerships shall take place, if they are of full age and have the capacity to dispose of their rights, in accordance with the manner fixed in the deed of constitution of the partnership or the manner upon which they expend, unless they unanimously decide to carry out the liquidation prior to any partition.

All partners, even those who take no part in the management, shall be entitled to participate in the liquidation. The liquidation shall be carried out by all the partners or by a liquidator whom they appoint unanimously if he has not already been appointed pursuant to the partnership contract. If the interested parties fail to agree on the choice of the liquidator, or if there are legitimate grounds preventing the entrusting of the liquidation to the persons designated in the partnership contract, the liquidation shall be carried out through the judiciary, upon the first application submitted by any of the partners.
Pending the appointment of the liquidator, the managers shall be deemed depositaries of the property of the partnership, and they must attend to urgent matters.

It must be stated in all acts undertaken by the dissolved partnership that it is "in liquidation". The clauses of the contract and the provisions of the law relating to active partnerships shall apply to the partnership placed under liquidation, whether with respect to the relations of the partners among themselves or with respect to their relations with third parties, to the extent that such clauses and provisions are applicable to a partnership that is in liquidation and subject to the provisions set forth in this Title.
Where there are several liquidators, they shall not be entitled to act individually unless they have been expressly authorised to do so.

Upon commencing his duties, the liquidator, whether judicial or non-judicial, must draw up jointly with the managers of the partnership the inventory and the balance sheet of its assets and liabilities. He must receive and preserve the books, papers, and assets of the partnership handed over to him by the managers, take note of all operations relating to the liquidation in a journal in chronological order in accordance with the accounting rules used in commerce, and retain all supporting documents and other papers relating to the liquidation.

The liquidator shall represent the partnership placed under liquidation and shall manage its affairs. His mandate shall include all acts necessary to realise its assets and discharge its liabilities, and shall include in particular the power to collect debts, conclude pending cases, take all conservatory measures required by the common interest, publish the notices necessary to call upon creditors to produce their instruments of title, pay the liquidated and due debts of the partnership, carry out the judicial sale of the immovable property of the partnership which cannot be easily partitioned, and sell the goods in stock and the equipment - all of the foregoing subject to the restrictions set out in the instrument appointing him liquidator, and subject to the resolutions unanimously adopted by the partners during the liquidation.

If one of the known creditors fails to appear, the liquidator shall be entitled to deposit the amount due to him if deposit is mandatory. As for debts that have not fallen due or that are disputed, he must retain a sum of money sufficient to discharge them and place it in a safe place.

If the property of the partnership is not sufficient to discharge the debts that have fallen due, the liquidator must demand the necessary sums from the partners if they are bound to provide them pursuant to the nature of the partnership or if they still owe the whole or part of their contribution to the capital. The shares of insolvent partners shall be apportioned among the remaining partners in proportion to the losses for which they are bound to be liable.

The liquidator may borrow and contract other obligations even by way of commercial bill of exchange, endorse negotiable instruments, grant extensions of time, delegate and accept delegation, and pledge or mortgage the property of the partnership, all to the extent required by the interest of the liquidation, unless the contrary is expressly stated in the instrument of his appointment.

The liquidator may not enter into a compromise, submit to arbitration, or waive securities except in return for consideration or other equivalent securities. Likewise, he may not sell for a lump sum the business goodwill which he has been entrusted to liquidate, nor effect a gratuitous assignment, nor embark upon new transactions unless he is expressly authorised to do so. He shall, however, be entitled to carry out new transactions to the extent required by necessity to liquidate pending business. If he contravenes these provisions, he shall be personally liable for the transactions upon which he has embarked. If there are several liquidators, they shall be jointly and severally liable.

The liquidator shall be entitled to appoint another person as his substitute to perform one or more specified acts, and he shall be liable for the persons whom he appoints as his substitutes, in accordance with the rules relating to mandate.
The liquidator, even if appointed by the court, may not contravene the resolutions adopted unanimously by the interested parties regarding the administration of the affairs of the common property.

The liquidator must, upon every request, furnish the partners or the holders of undivided rights with full information as to the state of the liquidation, and place at their disposal the books and papers relating to the liquidation operations.

The liquidator is bound by the obligations incumbent upon a salaried mandatory regarding the rendering of his accounts and the restitution of what he has received by virtue of his mandate. At the close of the liquidation, he must draw up an inventory and a balance sheet of assets and liabilities summarizing all the transactions he has carried out and the final position resulting therefrom.

The mandate of the liquidator shall not be deemed gratuitous. If his remuneration is not fixed, the judge may determine its amount. Interested parties shall retain the right to object to the determined value.

A liquidator who has paid common debts out of his own funds shall only have the right to bring the actions pertaining to the creditors whose debts have been discharged. He shall only have a right of recourse against the partners or the co-owners in proportion to their shares.

After the completion of the liquidation and the rendering of accounts, the liquidator shall deposit the books, papers and documents of the dissolved partnership with the registry of the court or another safe place designated by the court, unless the majority of the partners designate a person to receive them. They must remain preserved in the said place for a period of fifteen years from the date of deposit. Interested parties, their heirs or successors in title, or the liquidators shall be entitled to consult and examine the documents.

If the post of one or several of the liquidators becomes vacant due to death, bankruptcy, interdiction, renunciation or dismissal, the successor shall be appointed in the manner established for their appointment.

The partners may agree to effect the partition in such manner as they deem fit. If among them there is an incapacitated person or an absentee with interrupted absence, the consent of his legal representative shall not suffice; rather, the competent civil judge must rule to ratify the partition for it to become effective.

If the co-owners disagree on the partition, or if there is among them a person lacking legal capacity or an absentee whose absence is intermittent, and the judge does not ratify the amicable partition, each of the co-owners may bring an action before the court against all the co-owners and the holders of real rights whose names are entered in the Land Register, or in the mukhtar's statement in the case of properties that have not been surveyed and demarcated. The court shall seek the assistance of experts to value the property held in common and to partition it in kind without depriving any of the co-owners of the benefit intended therefrom prior to the partition, having regard to the characteristics of each lot and securing its independence, as far as possible, with easements. The following rules shall also be observed:

1 - In contiguous immovable properties - the lots of the co-owners shall be determined by way of consolidation and subdivision.

2 - In non-contiguous immovable properties - they shall be regarded as if they were combined, and the lots shall be determined on the basis of their value and in such a manner that one or more of the co-owners may be allotted one or several parcels.

3 - In the event of the smallness of the shares, and the impossibility of determining the lots on the basis of the smallest of them, the small shares may be combined and joined to one or more lots.

4 - In the event of disparity between the lots - they shall be equalised in cash up to one-fifth of their value.

5 - The selection of the lots shall be carried out - by drawing lots, unless one of the co-owners has an immovable property contiguous to the common immovable property, in which case he shall be given his lot from the contiguous portion.

The judge shall determine the method of drawing lots, having regard to the interest of the co-owners in so far as it requires combining or separating the lots of each of them.

6 - If partition in kind is impossible, the property shall be sold by public auction in accordance with the provisions of the Enforcement Law through the Execution Department, provided that the appraised value is taken as the reserve price for the first bidding.

The bidding may be restricted to the co-owners if they agree thereon.

The creditors of the co-ownership, or the creditors of one of the partitioning co-owners who is afflicted by insolvency, shall be entitled to object to the carrying out of the partition or the sale by auction of the common property in their absence, and they may intervene at their own expense. They shall also be entitled to request the annulment of the partition if it was carried out notwithstanding their objection.
The partitioning co-owners, or any one of them, may stay the action for the annulment of the partition by paying off the creditor or by depositing the amount which he claims.

Creditors to whom notice has been duly sent and who do not appear until after the completion of the partition shall not be entitled to demand its annulment; however, if a sufficient sum has not been left to satisfy their debts, they shall be entitled to recover their rights from the common property if a part thereof remains that has not been subjected to partition; otherwise, they shall be permitted to bring an action against the partitioning partners to the extent determined pursuant to the nature of the partnership, whether it is a contractual partnership or a co-ownership.

Each partitioning party shall be deemed to have been the original owner of the things that fell to his share or that he purchased by auction upon the sale of the common property, and never to have been the owner of the remaining things.
A partition, whether by agreement, statutory, or judicial, may not be annulled except on the ground of mistake, duress, fraud, or lesion.

The partitioning parties shall warrant one another against any disturbance or eviction that may occur due to a cause prior to the partition, and each of them shall be bound, in proportion to his share, to indemnify those entitled to the warranty on the basis of the value of the thing at the time of the partition.

If one of the partitioning parties is insolvent, the amount due from him to the person entitled to the warranty shall be distributed among all the other partitioning parties in proportion to the amount of the share of each of them.

The annulment of the partition on the grounds specified by law shall restore each of the partitioning parties to the position in which he was, legally and practically, when the partition took place, subject to the rights duly acquired for valuable consideration by a third party in good faith, and the action for annulment must be brought within the year following the partition, and shall not be maintainable after the expiry thereof.

Insurance is a contract whereby a person (called the insurer) undertakes certain obligations upon the occurrence of certain contingencies affecting the person of the insured or his property, in consideration of the payment of a sum called the premium or contribution.

The provisions of this Book shall apply to fixed-premium insurance, provided that they shall not apply to mutual insurance companies and insurance syndicates where they are contrary to the laws or regulations established for such companies or syndicates.
Marine insurance shall remain subject to the Commercial Code and to the special laws relating thereto.

Every person having an interest in the preservation of a thing may conclude an insurance contract for it, and this right shall vest in particular in the owner, the operator, the mortgagee or privileged creditor, or the antichresis creditor, and in every person exposed to being liable for the loss or deterioration of the thing in his possession.

An insurance contract may be concluded pursuant to a general or special mandate, or without a mandate for the benefit of a specified person.

In this case, the insurance shall benefit the person for whose benefit it was concluded, even if he only ratifies it after the occurrence of the contingency. An insurance contract may also be concluded for the benefit of an unspecified person, and this clause shall be deemed an insurance contract for the benefit of the person who signs the policy and a stipulation for a third party for the benefit of the person who benefits from this clause, whether known or future. The signatory of the policy relating to insurance concluded for the benefit of an unspecified person shall alone be bound towards the insurer to pay the premium, provided that the defences which the insurer may invoke against the signatory may also be invoked against the person who benefits from the insurance, whoever that person may be.

The duration of the contract shall be specified in the policy, and it may be stipulated that the contract shall automatically be renewed by tacit renewal if the insured does not declare his intention before the expiration of the duration specified in the current policy. The effect of such renewal shall only run from year to year, as the insured retains the right to terminate the contract at any time he wishes, notwithstanding any provision to the contrary.

An insurance contract shall be drawn up in writing in an instrument registered before a notary public or an instrument under private signature. If the instrument is under private signature, there must be drawn up thereof as many original copies as there are contracting parties having distinct interests. Every copy must mention the number of original copies that have been drawn up. Every addition to the original insurance contract and every amendment thereto must be evidenced by an endorsement signed by the contracting parties. These provisions shall not prevent the insurer from being bound towards the insured, even before the delivery of the policy or the additional endorsement, if the insured proves that the insurer accepted the contract pursuant to a cover note.

The contract of insurance shall be dated on the day of its conclusion and shall specify:

1- The insured thing

2- The names of the insurer and the insured and their places of residence

3- The nature of the insured risks

4- The date of commencement of the risks and the date of their termination

5- The insured value

6- The premium or consideration for the insurance

7- The submission of the contracting parties to the award of arbitrators when a dispute arises, if they have agreed thereon. The policy may be made out to a named person, or "to order", or to bearer. A policy drawn up "to order" shall be transferred by way of endorsement, even in blank. The provisions of this Article shall not apply to life insurance contracts except in accordance with the conditions provided for in Article 999.

The insurer is entitled to invoke against the holder of the policy, even if it is drawn up to order or to bearer, the defences pertaining thereto which he could have raised against the original insured had the transfer not taken place.

The insurer shall be liable for loss or damage occurring by force majeure or by an unforeseen event or resulting from a fault on the part of the insured, provided that the insurer shall not be liable for loss or damage occurring by reason of a fault intentionally committed by the insured, even if there is an agreement to the contrary.
The insurer shall guarantee the loss and damage caused by persons for whom the insured is civilly liable, whatever the nature of their fault and whatever its gravity.
The insurer shall not be liable for deterioration, damage or diminution affecting the insured thing as a result of an inherent defect therein.

The insurer shall not be liable for loss or damage caused by a foreign war, civil war, sedition or popular commotion, unless there is an agreement to the contrary, and the burden of proving that the loss or damage arose from one of these causes shall lie upon the insurer. Any stipulation requiring the insured to prove that the damage or loss did not arise from one of these causes shall be void.

The insurer shall not be bound beyond the insured value, but he must, within the limits of that value, pay to the insured what the latter has expended in order to mitigate the damage upon the materialisation of the risk. The insurer shall be bound by this obligation regardless of the result obtained. The judge may decide to reject or reduce the expenses if he deems that they were incurred without sufficient cause or were excessive.

When the whole of the insured thing perishes, the contract of insurance shall terminate ipso jure, and the insured shall not be entitled to claim the recovery of any part of the premium for the current year.

All the provisions of this Title which are not specifically declared to be enforceable notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, or for which non-observance entails nullity, shall merely serve as an interpretation of the intention of the contracting parties, and may be departed from by virtue of an express provision.

The insurer may reinsure with third parties the risks which he has insured, and such reinsurance may cover a specific insurance contract, several contracts, or all the contracts concluded by the insurer; in all cases, the insurer alone shall be liable towards the insured.

Insurance relating to property shall only be a contract of indemnity, and it may not place the insured person, after the occurrence of the contingencies, in a better financial position than that in which he would have been had the contingency not occurred.

Where insurance is concluded for a sum of money exceeding the value of the insured thing and there is fraud or deceit on the part of one of the contracting parties, the contract shall be void with respect to that party, and damages may moreover be awarded to the party in whose favour annulment is pronounced for that reason; where there is neither fraud nor deceit, the contract shall be deemed valid up to the actual value of the insured thing and no more.

The insurer shall not be entitled to collect premiums in respect of the excess amount. However, only the premiums fallen due and the premiums of the current year shall remain definitively acquired by the insurer.

The sums insured under life insurance contracts (insurance in the event of death and insurance in the event of survival) shall be definitively fixed in the policy, and where the insurance is concluded against accidents befalling persons, the sum insured fixed in the policy may likewise not be the subject of dispute.

A single person may not conclude several insurances relating to the same thing and against the same risks for a total sum exceeding the value of the insured thing; where different insurances are concluded without fraud on the same date or on different dates for a total sum exceeding the value of the insured thing, all such contracts shall be valid, and each of them shall produce its effect in proportion to the value assigned to it, provided that the entire value of the insured thing is not exceeded; the provisions of this Article may be set aside by inserting a clause in the policy stipulating the application of the rule of chronological order or prescribing joint and several liability among the insurers.

Where the insurance contract covers only a part of the value of the insured thing, the insured person shall be deemed to have remained his own insurer for the remaining part and shall consequently bear a proportionate part of the damage, unless it is expressly stipulated that the insured person is entitled - within the limits of the sum insured- to receive full compensation if the damage does not exceed the insured value.

Premiums shall be paid at the domicile of the insured, with the exception of the first premium.

Whether the premium is payable at the domicile of the insurer or at the domicile of the insured, the effect of the insurance contract shall be suspended after the lapse of ten days starting from the date of putting the insured on notice for his delay in paying one of the premiums on its due date. The notice shall be effected by sending a registered letter in the name of the insured person or in the name of the person mandated to pay the premiums to their last domicile known to the insurer. It must be declared in this letter that it is sent by way of notice, and the due date of the premium and the text of this article must be mentioned therein.

The insurer shall be entitled, after the lapse of twenty days from the date of expiry of the time-limit specified in the preceding paragraph, to rescind the contract or to demand its performance before the courts. Rescission may be effected by a declaration from the insurer in a registered letter which he sends to the insured person. However, in contracts which stipulate the non-forfeiture of the contract upon the delay of the insured in paying the premium due, the insurer shall be exempted from sending the notice, and the premium due shall be collected automatically from the reserve, and he shall send to the insured a registered letter to that effect.

An insurance contract which has not been rescinded shall resume producing its effects for the future at the hour of noon on the day following the payment of the overdue premium to the insurer and the settlement of the expenses, where applicable.

The time-limits specified in this article shall not include the day of sending the registered letter, and if the last day of one of these time-limits is a holiday, the time-limit shall be extended to the following day.

Those time-limits shall not be extended by reason of distance; however, if the notice is addressed to a place outside Lebanese territory, the time-limit of ten days provided for in the second paragraph of this article shall run only from the day of presentation of the registered letter as established by the registers of the postal administration.

Every clause comprising a shortening of the time-limits specified pursuant to the preceding provisions or an exemption of the insurer from the notice shall be null and void.

The insurer shall have a preferential right over the insured thing for the recovery of the debt of the premium, and if this preference applies to immovable property, it must be registered in the form of a compulsory mortgage, and it shall rank immediately after the preference for judicial expenses, and its effect shall cover only a value equivalent to the premiums of the last two years. It shall apply only if the insurance contract has not been rescinded.

The insurer who has paid the insurance indemnity shall be subrogated ipso jure to the insured in all the rights and actions accruing to him against third parties who by their act caused the damage that gave rise to the liability of the insurer, and the insurer may be discharged from all or part of his liability towards the insured if subrogation to such rights and actions has become impossible by reason of an act of the insured. Notwithstanding the preceding provisions, the insurer shall have no right to bring an action against the insured's children, descendants, ascendants, direct relatives by marriage, agents, employees, workmen or servants, and generally any person who ordinarily resides in the insured's home, except in the case of fraud committed by one of those persons.
The insured may not under any circumstances abandon the insured things.

The insured must:

First- Pay the premiums at the appointed times

Second- Disclose clearly to the insurer at the conclusion of the contract all the circumstances which are of a nature to enable him to assess the risks which he insures

Third- Notify the insurer, in accordance with the provisions of Article 977, of any supervening circumstances which are of a nature to increase the risks

Fourth- Notify the insurer of any casualty that gives rise to his liability, within three days from the date on which he became aware of it. The provisions of the third and fourth paragraphs above mentioned shall not apply to life insurance.

If the insured intends to commit an act of a nature to increase the risks to such an extent that, had the insurer been aware of that increase, he would not have contracted with him or would only have contracted for a higher premium, he shall be obliged, prior to committing that act, to declare it to the insurer by registered letter. If the risks are aggravated without any act on the part of the insured, he must notify the insurer within eight days at most from the date on which he became aware of the aggravation of the risks. In both cases, the insurer shall be entitled to rescind the contract unless the insured agrees to an increase in the premium upon the proposal of the insurer. However, the insurer shall not be entitled to invoke the aggravation of the risks if, after becoming aware thereof in any manner whatsoever, he manifested his intention to maintain the insurance, in particular if he continued to collect the premiums or paid the indemnity after the occurrence of the contingency.

If the schedule of conditions refers to special circumstances which were taken into consideration in fixing the amount of the premium, and which were of a nature to increase the risks, the insured shall be entitled, if those circumstances cease to exist during the course of the insurance, to demand the rescission of the contract if the insurer does not agree to a corresponding reduction of the premium, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary.

If the insured dies or alienates the thing on which the insurance is contracted, the contract of insurance shall continue for the benefit of the heir or the purchaser, provided that he performs the obligations by which the insured was bound towards the insurer pursuant to the contract. However, in the aforementioned case, the insurer, the heir, or the purchaser shall be entitled to rescind the contract concluded by the decedent or the seller, by notifying the other party of his intention. Any agreement stipulating the payment of a sum exceeding the annual premium by way of damages to the insurer if the thing on which the insurance is contracted is sold or the insured dies and the purchaser or the heir elects to rescind the contract as set forth in the second paragraph of this article shall be null and void. Where the insured thing is sold, the seller shall remain bound towards the insurer to pay the premiums that have fallen due, but he shall be discharged from every obligation, even by way of suretyship, in respect of the premiums that have not yet fallen due, as from the date on which he notifies the insurer of the contract of sale by registered letter. If there are several heirs or several purchasers and the contract of insurance continues, they shall be jointly and severally liable for the payment of the premiums.

If the insured falls into bankruptcy or judicial liquidation before the expiry of the term of the insurance, the insurer shall be entitled to rescind the contract after giving formal notice to the insured at his place of residence requiring the provision of a solvent surety within eight days, if the formal notice remains to no avail. The formal notice and the rescission shall be effected by sending a registered letter. The insured shall have the same rights if the insurer falls into bankruptcy or judicial liquidation before the date of expiry of the risks.

If the thing in respect of which the insurance was contracted had perished at the time of the conclusion of the contract or had ceased to be exposed to the risks, the contract of insurance shall be void. In such a case, the insured acting in bad faith must pay to the insurer double the annual premium. If proof of the bad faith of the insurer is established, he must pay to the insured the same value.
