Regardless of the ordinary grounds of annulment, the contract may be annulled by reason of reticence on the part of the insured person or his intentional making of a false declaration if such reticence or falsehood is of a nature to change the subject of the risk or to diminish it in the opinion of the insurer. If the contingency occurs, the rule of this special annulment shall remain applicable even though the risk which the insured concealed or in respect of which he made a false declaration had no effect on its occurrence. The premiums paid shall remain with the insurer, and he shall also be entitled to collect all premiums due by way of damages. However, the concealment or false declaration of the insured shall not entail the nullity of the contract of insurance if proof of the bad faith of the insured is not established. If the concealment or falsehood is discovered before the occurrence of any contingency, the insurer shall be entitled to rescind the contract after the lapse of ten days from the date of service of the formal notice which he sends to the insured by registered letter, unless the insurer agrees to maintain the contract in consideration of an increase in the premium accepted by the insured. If the concealment or falsehood is discovered only after the occurrence of the contingency, the indemnity shall be reduced in proportion to the difference between the rate of the premiums that were paid and the rate of the premiums that ought to have been paid had the risks been completely and accurately declared.

There shall be null and void:

First- All general clauses providing for the forfeiture of the insured's rights for violation by him of laws and regulations, unless such violation constitutes an inexcusable gross fault.

Second- All clauses providing for the forfeiture of the insured's rights merely for his delay in notifying the authorities of the occurrence of the contingency or in producing certain documents, without prejudice to the insurer's right to claim compensation proportionate to the damage resulting from the delay.

The provisions of the first paragraph of this article shall not preclude inserting a provision stipulating the forfeiture of the insured's rights for violation of laws or regulations the full text of which is set forth in the policy.

The insurer must deliver to the insured, or to any person producing a power of attorney from him, an acknowledgment of receipt of the application submitted to him for the conclusion of a new insurance contract or the modification of a previous insurance contract. He must also notify the insured of his affirmative or negative reply to such application within fifteen days at most.

If the insurer violates the provisions of this article, he may be ordered to pay damages to the insured if the latter proves that he suffered damage by reason of such violation.

All rights of action arising from the insurance contract shall lapse by prescription upon the expiry of two years from the event which gives rise to them. However, this time limit shall not run:

First- In the case of concealment or omission of the insured risk, or of a false or inaccurate declaration, except from the day on which the insurer became aware thereof.

Second- Nor shall it run, in the case of the occurrence of the contingency, except from the day on which the interested parties became aware thereof, if they prove that they were ignorant of it until that day; and where the action brought by the insured against the insurer arises from an action brought by a third party, the period of prescription shall run only from the day on which such third party brings his action against the insured or from the day on which he receives compensation from the insured.
The period of prescription may not be shortened by virtue of a clause inserted in the policy.

The two-year period of prescription shall run even against minors, interdicted persons and other persons lacking legal capacity.

Its running may be interrupted by one of the ordinary causes interrupting prescription. Furthermore, prescription relating to an action for recovery of the premium may be interrupted by the insurer sending a registered letter to the insured person.

The fire insurer shall be liable for all damage resulting from conflagration, ignition or simple combustion, but he shall not be liable for damage arising merely from the action of heat or from direct contact with fire or contact with a hot substance, if there is neither a fire nor the beginning of a fire capable of developing into an actual fire.
The insurer shall only cover material damage resulting directly from the fire or the beginning of a fire.

The life insurance policy must contain, in addition to the particulars set out in Article 964:

First - The first name, surname, and date of birth of the insured.

Second - The first name and surname of the beneficiary, if there is a designated beneficiary.

Third - The event or the term upon the occurrence or maturity of which the insurance sum becomes due.

Fourth - The conditions for reduction, if provided for in the contract in accordance with the provisions of Article 1012 and Article 1013.

A life insurance policy may be drawn up "to order", but it may not be made out to bearer.

The endorsement of a life insurance policy drawn up "to order" must state the date, the name of the endorsee, and the signature of the endorser, failing which it shall be null and void. Stating the value paid, however, is not mandatory, and the assignment shall not be effective against the insurer unless notified to him by registered letter or unless the insurer acknowledges in writing to the holder of the policy the right to benefit therefrom.

The insurer may undertake, by virtue of a special clause, to pay the insurance sums in the event that the insured person commits suicide intentionally and voluntarily, or in the event that a sentence of death is executed against him; however, such clause shall have no effect until after the expiry of a period of two years from the conclusion of the contract, and in the event of execution of the death penalty, the date of commission of the offence shall be taken into account for calculating the period.

If the contract does not contain the clause provided for in the preceding Article, or if the suicide or the offence that caused the death sentence occurred before the expiry of the aforementioned two-year period, the insurer must pay to the beneficiaries a sum equal to the amount of the mathematical reserve.

It may be stipulated that the insured sums be paid:

First- In the event of the survival of the insured person on a specified date.

Second- In the event of his death.

Third- Either on a specified date if the insured remains alive, or in the event of his death if it occurs before that date.

The insured capital or annuity may be paid upon the death of the insured person either to his heirs or successors in title, or to a designated beneficiary or several designated beneficiaries. The insurance shall be deemed contracted for the benefit of designated beneficiaries when the insured grants the right of benefit to his wife without designation of name or to his children and descendants born or to be born, and it is not necessary that their names be recorded in the policy or in any subsequent instrument containing the designation of the person entitled to the insured capital.

The children and descendants designated in the foregoing manner shall benefit from the insurance in proportion to their hereditary shares, and this right shall remain theirs even if they renounce the inheritance. If no designated beneficiary is mentioned in the policy or if the beneficiary designated therein refuses, the subscriber of the policy shall have the right to designate the beneficiary or to replace him with another.

This designation or this replacement shall be effected inter vivos by adding an endorsement to the contract or by endorsement if the policy is drawn "to order" - or by way of testamentary disposition.

When the insurance is contracted for the benefit of a designated person, it becomes, upon the acceptance of the beneficiary, irrevocable and may not be revoked. This acceptance may be express or tacit. So long as acceptance has not taken place, the right of revocation is confined to the contracting party of the insurance to the exclusion of his creditors or his legal representatives and to the exclusion of his heirs after his death or his legatees. The acceptance by the beneficiary of the insurance contracted for his benefit or the revocation thereof shall only be effective against the insurer from the date of his knowledge thereof. The allocation of the benefit of the insurance to a designated person shall be deemed subject to the condition of the existence of that person at the date of maturity of the insured capital or annuity, unless the contrary is inferred from the text of the contract or from the circumstances.

The right to benefit from the insurance may be pledged in favour of the creditor of the insured pursuant to an endorsement to the contract or pursuant to a written instrument notified to the insurer. If the policy is drawn "to order", the pledge contracted to secure a debt, even if such debt is non-commercial, may be established pursuant to an endorsement stating that the policy was delivered by way of security.

When an insurance contingent upon death is contracted without the designation of a beneficiary or for the benefit of the heirs of the insured or his successors in title designated in their capacity, the insured capital shall be deemed part of his estate.
Material damages that befall the insured things by reason of relief operations and means of salvage shall be deemed to be direct material damages.

The insurer shall be liable, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, for the loss or disappearance of the insured things during the fire, unless he proves that the loss or disappearance was the result of theft.

The insurer shall not be liable for the destruction or deterioration of the insured thing arising from an inherent defect therein, in accordance with the provisions of Article 968, but he shall guarantee the fire damages resulting from that defect unless he is entitled to apply for the rescission of the contract of insurance in accordance with the provisions of the first paragraph of Article 982.
The insurance shall not cover fire resulting from the eruption of volcanoes, earthquakes, storms, hurricanes and other calamities. However, it shall cover fire resulting from lightning.
Insurance on the life of a person may be contracted by that person or by a third party.

Insurance contingent upon death contracted by a third party in the interest of the insured shall be void if the insured does not declare his acceptance in writing, stating the amount of the insurance.

Likewise, the insured must declare his acceptance in writing upon every assignment of the right to benefit from the contract concluded by a third party in his interest.

No person may contract insurance contingent upon the death of a minor who has not completed the fifteenth year of his age, or an interdicted person, or any other person placed in a lunatic asylum. Every contract contrary to this prohibition shall be void. Annulment shall be pronounced upon the application of the insurer, the person who signed the policy, or the representative of the incapacitated person.

All premiums paid must be refunded in full. Furthermore, the insurer and the signatory of the policy shall be liable to a fine of five pounds to two hundred and fifty Syrian pounds for every insurance they knowingly contracted contrary to this prohibition. However, the provisions of this Article shall not prevent the conclusion of a contract guaranteeing, upon the death of one of the persons specified in the first paragraph of this Article, the refund of the premiums paid in performance of a life insurance contract concluded for one of those persons.

A third party may not contract insurance contingent upon the death of a person placed under judicial supervision without the authorisation of the supervisor. However, such authorisation shall not dispense with the consent of the incapacitated person himself, where applicable.

In the absence of such authorisation or such consent, the annulment of the contract shall be pronounced upon the application of the supervisor, the application of the signatory of the policy, or the application of the insurer, as the case may be.

The sum stipulated to be paid upon the death of the insured to a specified beneficiary does not form part of his estate. The beneficiary, whatever the form of his designation and the date of such designation, is deemed to have been solely entitled to that sum from the day of the contract, even if his acceptance took place after the death of the insured.

The sums paid upon the death of the insured to a specified beneficiary are not, where applicable, subject to the rules of reduction for exceeding the reserved portion pertaining to the heirs of the insured. Nor do these rules apply to the sums paid by the insured by way of insurance premiums, unless they were manifestly excessive in proportion to his financial means or, in particular, in proportion to his income.

The creditors of the insured are not entitled to claim the capital insured for the benefit of a specified person; they are only entitled to recover the premiums in the cases provided for in the second paragraph of the preceding Article.

Any beneficiary may, after accepting the insurance contracted for his benefit, transfer even the benefit of the contract either by way of assignment or by way of endorsement if the policy is drawn "to order". Any transfer, whatever its form, is deemed null and void if the person on whose life the insurance was contracted has not consented thereto in writing.
Each of the spouses may contract an insurance for the benefit of the other reciprocally and by virtue of a single instrument.

The insured alone, to the exclusion of his creditors, is entitled either to maintain the contract or to elect reduction or surrender. If the contract is maintained, it remains in force with all its effects for the benefit of the beneficiary designated in the policy or in an endorsement to the contract. If there is no specified beneficiary, any person is entitled to maintain the contract for his own benefit if the insured consents, provided that such person pays the surrender value to the creditors of the insured.

The insurer has no right to bring an action to claim payment of the premiums. Failure to pay one of the premiums only results in the termination of the insurance contract or the reduction of its effects after fulfilment of the conditions set forth in Article 975. In insurance contracts contingent upon death and concluded for the whole life of the insured without a condition of his survival beyond a known date, and in all contracts in which it is agreed that the insured sum or annuity shall be paid after a specified number of years, non-payment shall have no effect other than reduction, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, if three or more premiums have been paid. Such reduction shall apply in particular either to the amount of the insured sum or annuity or to the duration of the insurance contract.

As for contracts which provide that the contract shall not lapse upon the delay of the insured in paying the premium due, neither the forfeiture nor the reduction provided for in the preceding paragraphs shall apply to them.

Notwithstanding any provision to the contrary, the insurer shall include in the contracts an explicit detailed schedule in figures of the sums provided for by the contract, such as the cash reserve, the reduced insurance, and the sum which the insured is entitled to borrow on his contract, for each year of the years of the contract. He shall also state that he guarantees these sums, undertakes them, and pays what is due to be paid thereof upon the request submitted to him or to the agent of the company in Lebanon without the need to carry out any formality.

The surrender of the contract shall be optional, except in the cases provided for in Articles 1001 and 1015 and in the cases in which the insurer compels the insured to rescission, and advances by the insurer to the insured shall also be optional.

The effect of the contract of insurance shall cease ipso jure if the beneficiary causes the death of the insured intentionally or by an act on his part, unless there is mere fault, and the insurer shall pay the value of the reserve to the heirs of the insured or to his successors in title if the premiums have been paid for three years or more, and if there is only an attempted killing, the insured shall be entitled to revoke the designation of the beneficiary of the insurance even if the perpetrator of the attempt has accepted the insurance concluded for his benefit.

If the beneficiary of the insurance is designated by way of testamentary disposition and the insurer pays the insured sum to a person who, but for the existence of the designation, would have been the beneficiary, the payment shall discharge the liability of the insurer, provided that he is in good faith.

Accident insurance is a contract whereby the insurer undertakes, in return for a premium, to pay a specified capital sum or a known income to the insured person himself, or to his heirs, or to his successors in title, or to designated persons, upon the death of the insured person or his permanent or temporary incapacity for work, if the death or incapacity results from an accident or from an accident of a known type that befell the person of the insured. The insured person may be the signatory to the policy, and it may also be one or more persons for whose benefit the signatory to the policy contracted the insurance. The provisions of this Title relating to life insurance shall apply to accident insurance, save for the exceptional provisions and modifications set forth in the following Articles.
The payment of premiums is compulsory in accident insurance.
The provisions of this Title relating to reduction or surrender in life insurance shall not apply to accident insurance.

Where the insured person is other than the person who signed the policy, it shall suffice to specify his profession or office, contrary to the provisions of Article 998; and in this case, the provisions of Article 996, which prohibit contracting insurance on a minor who has not attained the fifteenth year of his age, shall not apply.
The law grants no right of action in respect of a gaming debt or the payment of a wagering consideration.

Excepted from the provision of the preceding Article are wagers contracted between persons taking part in games relating to practice in arms, and in kinds of racing and athletic games; provided that the judge shall be entitled to dismiss the action if he deems the amount excessive. And in the cases provided for in the first paragraph of this Article, intermediaries legally licensed to collect wagering considerations from persons not taking part in the games shall not be entitled to invoke the provision of the preceding Article.
The loser shall not be entitled to recover what he has voluntarily paid in a game or wager free from any fraud.
The game of "lottery" grants no right of action, unless it is legally authorised.

If a life insurance policy is lost, the following rules shall apply: If the policy is not "to order", the insurer shall deliver to the insured a duplicate thereof against his declaration that he has granted no right whatsoever over the insurance - and the duplicate shall take the place of the lost instrument. If the policy is "to order", the person claiming to have been dispossessed thereof must submit under registered cover a statement containing a summary of the circumstances in which he lost that policy. This statement shall operate as an opposition staying the payment of the capital and its accessories. If a third party appears holding the policy against which opposition was made, the insuring establishment shall notify the opposing party by registered letter and shall temporarily retain possession of the said policy. The opposing party must refer the matter, within the month following the receipt of that letter, to the court of competent jurisdiction to rule upon the ownership of the policy. If he fails to bring his action within the said time limit, the effect of the opposition shall lapse ipso jure, unless there is fraud or an acceptable impediment. If two years have elapsed from the date of the opposition to the policy and no third party holding it has appeared, the opposing party shall be entitled to submit a petition to the President of the court requesting authorisation to obtain a duplicate of the policy. With regard to the insuring establishment, this duplicate shall take the place of the original policy, which shall become unenforceable against it. The person who was dispossessed thereof shall retain the right of recourse against whomsoever it may concern through the ordinary legal channels.

An error as to the age of the insured shall not entail the nullity of the insurance contract unless the true age of the insured exceeds the limit fixed for the insurance contract pursuant to the tariff of the insurer. In all other cases, if the premium paid in consequence of an error of this kind is less than the premium which ought to have been paid, the insured capital or annuity shall be reduced in proportion to the premium paid and the premium corresponding to the true age of the insured. If the contrary is the case, that is to say, if the premium paid in consequence of an error as to the age of the insured is excessive, the insurer shall be bound to refund the excess without any interest being calculated thereon.

If the insurer becomes bankrupt or is placed in judicial liquidation, and if he fails to provide a solvent surety in accordance with the provisions of Article 980, the claim of each of the beneficiaries of current insurance contracts shall be determined, on the day of the judgment declaring bankruptcy or judicial liquidation, at an amount equal to the value of the reserve of each contract calculated without any addition - on - the basis of the tariff of conventional premiums which was in force at the time of the conclusion of the contract.

A life annuity contract is a contract whereby a person (called the debtor of the annuity) undertakes to pay to another person (called the creditor of the annuity), for the duration of his life or the life of another person or several persons, an allowance or an annual annuity in return for certain movable or immovable property assigned at the time of the creation of the annuity obligation; and if the assigned property is immovable, the creation of the annuity shall have no effect, even between the two parties, until after its registration in the Land Register.

An annuity contract may be created upon the life of the person who furnished the capital, or upon the life of a third person or several persons, and it may likewise be created for the benefit of the person or persons upon whose life the contract is made contingent, or for the benefit of another person or several other persons.

An annuity contract shall be void if it was created upon the life of a person who was dead at the time of its creation, or who on that date was afflicted with an illness that led to his death twenty days after the said date.

Non-payment of due instalments does not entitle the creditor of the annuity to claim the recovery of the capital or the assigned property. In this case, he is only entitled to claim the payment of the due instalments and security for future instalments.

The instalment of the year in which the creditor of the annuity dies shall be paid in proportion to the number of days he lived during that year. However, if the agreement provides for payment in advance, the instalment whose period commenced during the life of the creditor must be paid in full.

A person who creates upon his property, without consideration, an annuity for the benefit of another person for the duration of his life is entitled to stipulate at the time of its creation that it shall not be subject to attachment for the satisfaction of debts owed by the creditor of the annuity.
No claim may be made for the annuity if the existence of the person upon whose life the contract was made contingent is not proven.
Compromise is a contract whereby the two parties settle an existing dispute between them or prevent it from arising by mutual concession.
Whoever concludes a settlement must have the capacity to alienate, for valuable consideration, the property included in the settlement.

A settlement may not be concluded in respect of matters relating to personal status or public order, nor in respect of personal rights which are not considered property among persons. However, it is permissible in respect of a pecuniary interest arising from a matter relating to personal status or from an offence.
The two parties may conclude a settlement in respect of rights or things even if their value is unknown to them.
A settlement may not be concluded in respect of the right to maintenance, but it is permissible in respect of the manner of providing maintenance or the manner of paying the accrued instalments.

A settlement is permissible in respect of acquired hereditary rights in return for a consideration that is less than the lawful share prescribed by law, provided that the concerned parties have knowledge of the amount of the estate.

When the settlement involves the creation of rights over immovable property or other property susceptible of mortgage, or the alienation of such rights or the making of a modification therein, it must be concluded in writing. It shall have no effect unless it is registered in the Land Register.

The effect of a settlement is to extinguish definitively the rights and claims in respect of which the settlement was made, and to secure for each of the two parties the ownership of the things delivered to him by the other party or the rights acknowledged to him. A settlement in respect of a debt in return for payment of part of the amount due extinguishes the remaining part of the debt and discharges the debtor.

Each of the contracting parties must warrant to the other the things which he gives to him by way of settlement, and if one of the parties takes delivery by virtue of the settlement of the thing in dispute, and this thing is subsequently evicted from him by an action for recovery of ownership or he finds in it a redhibitory defect, there shall be ground for the rescission of the contract of settlement in whole or in part or for the reduction of the consideration in accordance with the conditions laid down for sale. Where the settlement relates to the grant of the right of enjoyment of a thing for a period of time, the warranty owed by each of the two parties to the other shall be the same warranty owed in the lease of things.
A contract of compromise must be interpreted strictly and, whatever its wording, may be applied only to the disputes and rights upon which the compromise was made.

Whoever compromises upon a right that belonged to him or that he received by virtue of a specific cause, and subsequently acquires this same right from another person or by virtue of another cause, shall not be bound by the provisions of the prior contract of compromise with respect to the right that he has newly acquired.

If one of the two parties refrains from fulfilling the undertakings he made in the contract of compromise, the other party shall be entitled to demand the performance of the contract if possible, failing which he shall be entitled to demand rescission, without prejudice to his right to claim damages in both cases.

A contract of compromise may be impugned:

First- On the ground of duress or fraud.

Second- On the ground of a material mistake bearing upon the person of the other party, his capacity, or the thing that was the subject of the dispute.

Third- On the ground of absence of cause when the compromise is made:

1- Upon a forged instrument

2- Or upon a non-existent cause

3- Or upon a case that had been concluded by a valid compromise or by a judgment not subject to appeal or retrial, of the existence of which one or both of the parties were unaware. Annulment on the grounds set forth above may only be demanded by the party who was acting in good faith.
A compromise may not be impugned on the ground of a mistake of law or on the ground of lesion.

When a compromise is concluded generally in respect of all matters existing between the contracting parties, the discovery of instruments of which they were unaware at the time of the contract and of which they subsequently became aware shall not constitute a ground for the annulment of the contract unless there was fraud on the part of the other party. This rule shall not apply to a compromise concluded by the representative of an incapacitated person where the inducement therefor was the absence of an instrument that was subsequently found.

A compromise is indivisible; the nullity or annulment of part thereof entails the nullity or annulment of the entire contract. However, this rule shall not apply: First- When it appears from the wording of the contract and the nature of the agreement that the contracting parties regard the clauses of the contract as independent and separate parts one from another.

Second- When the nullity results from the incapacity of one of the contracting parties. In this latter case, only the incapacitated person in whose interest the nullity was established may avail himself of the nullity, unless there is an express provision to the contrary.

Nullity or dissolution restores the contracting parties to the same legal position in which they were at the time of the contract and gives each of the contracting parties a right to recover what he gave in execution of the compromise, subject to the exception of rights lawfully acquired for consideration by a third party in good faith, and if the exercise of the relinquished right has become impossible, the value of such right shall be recovered.

If the contract styled a compromise in reality entails a gift, a sale, or any other contract contrary to what is inferred from its wording, its validity and effects shall be assessed in accordance with the provisions governing the contract entailed by the compromise.
Suretyship is a contract whereby a person binds himself towards the creditor to perform the obligation of his debtor if that debtor fails to perform it.

Whoever commissions a person to open a financial credit for a third party, undertaking to be answerable for him, shall be bound in the capacity of a surety for the obligations contracted by the third party up to the amount of the value which he fixed for him. If the surety has not fixed any value, he shall be liable up to the reasonable limit consistent with the standing of the person for whom the credit was opened. The undertaking provided for in the first paragraph of this Article may be revoked so long as the person commissioned to open the credit has not commenced its execution. Such undertaking may only be proved in writing.

No person may constitute himself a surety unless he has the capacity to dispose gratuitously. Suretyship given by a minor shall not be valid, even with the authorisation of his father or his guardian, if he has no interest in the matter which he guarantees.
Suretyship shall only be valid for a valid obligation.

The subject-matter of a suretyship may be a contingent obligation (such as a warranty against dispossession by an action for recovery of ownership) or a future or indeterminate obligation, provided that determination is subsequently possible (such as a suretyship for the sum which will be adjudged against a certain person); in such a case, the obligation of the surety shall be determined by what is due from the principal debtor.
Suretyship shall not be valid for an obligation in which the surety cannot take the place of the principal debtor, such as corporal punishment.
Suretyship shall not be presumed; rather, the intention to stand surety must appear expressly from the instrument.

An undertaking to stand surety for a person does not constitute suretyship, provided however that the promisee shall be entitled to demand the completion of the suretyship, failing which he shall be entitled to claim damages.
Suretyship must be expressly accepted by the creditor.

An obligation may be guaranteed without the knowledge of the principal debtor and against his will. However, a suretyship given notwithstanding the express prohibition of the debtor shall not create a legal relationship between him and the surety; rather, the surety shall be bound towards the creditor alone.
Suretyship may validly be given for a surety just as it may validly be given for the principal debtor.
Suretyship cannot exceed what is owed by the principal debtor, save with respect to the term.

Suretyship may be made subject to a term, that is to say, for a specified period or starting from a specified date. It may also be contracted for part of the debt only or under less onerous conditions.

Where the suretyship is not expressly limited to a specified sum or to a definite part of the debt, the surety shall also guarantee the damages and costs awarded against the principal debtor for non-performance of the obligation. The surety shall not be liable for new obligations contracted by the principal debtor after the creation of the guaranteed commitment; however, where the surety has expressly guaranteed the performance of all commitments undertaken by the debtor by reason of the contract, he shall be liable, in the same manner as the principal debtor, for all the obligations for which such debtor may be liable pursuant to the contract.
Suretyship is gratuitous by its nature, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary.

If the surety accepted by the creditor pursuant to the contract becomes insolvent, another surety must be provided to him or another security equivalent to the suretyship must be given, failing which the creditor shall be entitled to demand immediate payment of his debt or to rescind the contract which he concluded on that condition; whereas if the solvency of the surety becomes insufficient, an additional suretyship or security must be provided. These provisions shall not apply:

First- If the suretyship was given without the knowledge of the debtor or despite him

Second- If the suretyship was given pursuant to an agreement in which the creditor designated the person of the surety.

Suretyship does not entail joint and several liability without an express agreement. If joint and several liability is stipulated or if the suretyship constitutes a commercial act on the part of the surety, its effects shall be subject to the provisions governing joint and several obligations among debtors.
The creditor has no right of action against the surety unless the principal debtor is in default in performing the obligation.

Nevertheless, the following provisions must be observed:

1- If the surety dies before the maturity of the debt, the creditor shall be entitled to sue his heirs immediately without awaiting the date of maturity. If the heirs pay the debt in that case, they shall be entitled to have recourse against the debtor upon the maturity of the principal debt.

2- A declaration of the insolvency of the surety renders the debt due and payable by him even before the date of maturity of the principal debt. In that case, the creditor is entitled to apply for the admission of his debt among the debts of the body of creditors.

3- In the case provided for in Article 114, the creditor shall not be entitled to sue the surety except upon the arrival of the agreed term.

The surety is entitled to require the creditor, at the commencement of the proceedings and prior to any defence on the merits, to first proceed against the principal debtor in respect of his movable and immovable property, and to indicate to him such of it as may be subject to execution, provided that it is situated within the territories subject to the jurisdiction of the courts of the States covered by the French Mandate; in that case, the proceedings against the surety shall be stayed until the exhaustion of proceedings against the property of the debtor, without prejudice, however, to the creditor being authorised to take conservatory measures against the surety; and if the creditor holds a pledge or a right of retention over certain movable property of the debtor, he must satisfy his debt out of it, unless such property is assigned to secure other obligations of the debtor and is insufficient to satisfy all of them.

The surety may not insist on the prior proceeding against the principal debtor:

First- If he has expressly waived this right, and in particular if he has bound himself to the obligation jointly and severally with the principal debtor.

Second- If the principal debtor has fallen into a state of notorious insolvency or his inability to pay has been declared.

Third- If the property against which proceedings may be taken is the subject of litigation, or is mortgaged as security for debts that absorb a large part of its value, or is manifestly insufficient to satisfy the creditor, or if the debtor has only a revocable right over such property.
A surety who insists on the prior proceeding against the debtor must indicate to the creditor the property of the principal debtor and advance the expenses necessary for execution.

Where several persons guarantee the same debt by a single instrument, each of them shall be bound only to the extent of his share and portion, and he shall be entitled to insist against the creditor on the division of the action. There is no joint and several liability among the sureties unless it has been stipulated, or unless each of them has entered into the suretyship separately for the entire debt, or where the suretyship constitutes a commercial act on the part of the sureties.

The surety of a surety shall not be bound towards the creditor unless the principal debtor and all the sureties have fallen into a state of inability to pay, or unless they have been discharged on the basis of personal grounds appertaining to the debtor or to the sureties.

The surety is entitled to raise all the pleas appertaining to the principal debtor, whether personal or real, including those founded on the incapacity of the principal debtor. He shall have this right notwithstanding the opposition of the principal debtor or his waiver of such pleas, and he shall likewise have the right to raise pleas that are strictly personal to the debtor, such as a remission of the debt granted to the person of the debtor.

The surety is entitled to proceed against the principal debtor in order to be discharged from the obligation of suretyship:

First- When the surety is sued judicially for the payment of the debt, or even before any proceedings when the debtor is in default in performing the obligation

Second- When the debtor has undertaken to bring to the surety a deed of discharge from the creditor within a specified term, if that term has fallen due.

If the debtor is unable to produce the deed of discharge, he must pay the debt or give the surety a pledge or sufficient security. A surety who is in one of the cases provided for in Article 1073 is not entitled to avail himself of the benefit of the preceding provisions.
The surety is entitled, in order to be discharged from the debt, to proceed against the creditor if the latter delays in demanding performance of the obligation that has fallen due.

A surety who has discharged the principal obligation may have recourse against the debtor for all that he has paid, even if the suretyship was given without the knowledge of the debtor, and he also has a right of recourse against him for the expenses and damages necessarily arising from the suretyship, and any act by the surety - other than actual performance - which is such as to extinguish the principal obligation and release the debtor, is deemed equivalent to performance and opens to the surety the way of recourse against the debtor for the principal of the debt and the expenses pertaining thereto.

A surety who has discharged the debt is not entitled to have recourse against the principal debtor unless he produces a receipt from the creditor or another document establishing the extinction of the debt, and a surety who has paid before maturity has no recourse against the debtor until the maturity date of the principal obligation.

Where there are several joint and several sureties and one of them pays the whole debt at maturity, he is entitled to have recourse against the other sureties according to the share and portion of each of them, as well as to have recourse against them for the share of whichever of them has become insolvent.

Where the surety and the creditor enter into a compromise, the surety has no right of recourse against the debtor and the other sureties except for what he has actually paid or its equivalent value if there is a specified sum.

A surety who has validly discharged the debt is subrogated to the creditor in all his rights and privileges against the principal debtor to the extent of the sum which he has paid, and against the other sureties to the extent of their shares and portions. However, such subrogation to the creditor does not modify the special agreements concluded between the principal debtor and the surety.

The surety has no right of recourse against the debtor:

First- Where he pays a debt which pertains to him personally, even if it was ostensibly in the name of another

Second- Where the suretyship was given despite the prohibition of the debtor

Third- Where it is inferred from the express admission of the surety or from the circumstances that the suretyship was given gratuitously and without regard therein to a right of recourse against the principal debtor.

The surety is not entitled to have recourse against the principal debtor if he has paid the debt or had judgment rendered against him at last instance without notifying the debtor, provided that the debtor proves that he had discharged the debt or that he has grounds establishing the nullity or extinction of the debt. However, this rule does not apply where it is impossible for the surety to notify the debtor, as where the debtor is absent.
All grounds of nullity or extinction pertaining to the principal obligation extinguish the suretyship.
The obligation of suretyship is extinguished by the same causes which extinguish other obligations, even if those causes have no relation to the principal obligation.
The surety is discharged if his subrogation to the rights of the creditor becomes impossible by reason of an act of the creditor.

Payment of the debt by the surety discharges both the surety and the principal debtor. The same applies to the delegation by the surety of a third person to the creditor if the creditor and the third person accept this delegation - and to the consignment of the thing due if validly made, to giving in payment, and to the novation of the debt between the creditor and the surety.

The release of the debtor from the debt discharges the surety, but the release of the surety does not discharge the debtor. The release of one of the sureties without the consent of the others discharges the latter to the extent of the share of the surety who has been discharged.

Novation of the debt between the creditor and the principal debtor discharges the sureties unless they have consented to guarantee the new debt. However, if the creditor stipulates the accession of the sureties to the new obligation and the latter refuse, the former obligation is not extinguished.

The confusion of the capacities of creditor and principal debtor in the same person discharges the surety, and if this confusion takes place in the person of the principal debtor by reason of the death of the creditor and the principal debtor is one of his heirs along with others, the surety is discharged to the extent of the debtor's share; whereas the confusion of the capacities of creditor and surety in the same person does not discharge the principal debtor, and the confusion of the capacities of principal debtor and surety when one of them becomes the heir of the other extinguishes the suretyship and leaves only the principal debt subsisting. Nevertheless, the creditor retains his right of action against the person who guaranteed the surety, and retains the securities which he took to guarantee the obligation of the surety.

An extension of the term granted by the creditor to the principal debtor avails the surety, unless it was granted by reason of the debtor's insolvency; whereas an extension granted by the creditor to the surety does not avail the principal debtor unless the creditor declares the contrary.
Interruption of prescription with regard to the principal debtor takes effect against the surety, and prescription completed in favour of the principal debtor avails the surety.

Where the creditor voluntarily accepts a thing other than the thing due, in discharge of his debt, the surety, even if jointly and severally liable with the debtor, shall be discharged even if that thing is recovered from the creditor by an action of revendication or is returned by the creditor on account of its latent defects.
The death of the surety does not extinguish the suretyship; rather, the obligation of the surety passes to his heirs.
Suretyship for appearance is an undertaking whereby a person binds himself to produce another person before the judiciary or to bring him upon the maturity of the obligation or when needed.
Suretyship for appearance is not valid on the part of one who does not possess the right to alienate gratuitously.
Suretyship for appearance is only effected by an express declaration.
The surety must bring the person guaranteed to the place designated in the contract, and if no place is designated, the person guaranteed shall be brought to the place of performance of the contract.

The surety is discharged if he brings the person guaranteed or if the person guaranteed appears voluntarily in person on the designated day and at the designated place. Bringing the person guaranteed before the designated day does not suffice to discharge the surety.
The surety is discharged if, on the day of maturity, the person guaranteed is in the custody of the judicial authority for reasons other than the suretyship and the creditor is notified thereof.
The provisions relating to Customs are consolidated in a law, in accordance with the following Articles.

Customs duties may be imposed on goods imported into Lebanon only by decisions of the Higher Council of Customs. The same shall apply in respect of export duties which may be imposed on certain export products.

The customs duties pertaining to the normal import tariff shall apply to goods originating in the countries designated in the decisions of the Lebanese Higher Council of Customs, and may also apply to all or part of the goods originating in certain countries with which special customs agreements have been concluded.
The customs duties pertaining to the maximum import tariff shall apply to all or part of the goods originating in countries which do not benefit from the normal tariff.
Customs duties subject to an agreed tariff shall apply to all or part of the goods originating in certain countries with which special customs agreements have been concluded.
The same decisions, regulations and tariffs shall apply in all ports and customs offices in Lebanon.

The customs duties fixed in the tariffs shall be paid on all goods entering Lebanon, and where applicable, on all those leaving it, save for the exceptions provided for in the following Titles Three and Four.

Goods imported for the account of government departments, whether in their own name or in the name of contractors therefor, shall be subject to the payment of customs duties, in accordance with the procedures provided for in Article 162.

The surety shall be bound by the principal debt if he does not produce the guaranteed person on the appointed day, and he shall be discharged if the guaranteed person appears after this date. However, if a judgment has been rendered against the surety, the appearance of the guaranteed person shall not suffice for the revocation of this judgment. The death of the guaranteed person, his notorious insolvency, and the declaration of his inability to pay shall all discharge the surety.

A surety who has been ordered by judgment to pay for failing to produce the debtor shall be entitled to request the revocation of the judgment if he proves that the guaranteed person was, on the date the judgment was rendered, dead or insolvent. If the surety has executed the judgment rendered against him, he shall be entitled to have recourse against the creditor for the amount of the sum he paid, in accordance with the conditions laid down for the recovery of undue payment.
All provisions of the "Mejelle" and other legislative texts that contravene the Code of Obligations and Contracts or are incompatible with its provisions are repealed and shall remain repealed.
This Law shall enter into force thirty months after its publication in the Official Gazette is completed.

In principle, decisions of the Higher Council of Customs ordering an increase in customs duties shall apply after the lapse of five full days from the date of their signature, unless otherwise provided in the decision ordering the increase. These decisions shall be published by affixing them inside and outside the customs offices and in the place designated for official announcements at the Palace of the Presidency of the Government, and if it happens - that one or more of the aforementioned five days is an official holiday, a number of days equal to the number of days of the official holiday shall be added to this - period.

Notwithstanding the provisions of Articles 12 and 13, and unless a contrary measure is taken, goods of the kinds on which the tariffs have been increased, and which are proven to the Customs Department to have been shipped directly to Lebanon prior to the date of signature of the decision ordering the increase in tariffs, shall benefit from the previous customs duties. The date of shipment must be proven. a- For goods arriving by sea, by means of the bills of lading drawn up at the last port from which the goods were shipped to one of the ports of Lebanon. Only bills of lading certifying that the goods have actually been loaded onto the carrying vessel shall be accepted as an instrument of proof. b - For goods arriving by other routes, by means of the last consignment note made out for Lebanon: a waybill in respect of railways and a cargo manifest in respect of motor transport lines that ensure regular communications between Lebanon and the countries bordering it. The date of the manifest is the date of its receipt by the customs of the shipping country, and it must be certified by the visa of that customs. Goods entering Lebanon after the date of signature of the decision ordering an increase in customs duties, and which fulfil the conditions stipulated above, must, in order to benefit from the duty of the previous tariff, pay these duties within a maximum period not exceeding five full days from the date of their entry into the customs warehouses. This period shall be determined in accordance with the conditions set forth in the third paragraph of Article 13.

Decisions of the Higher Council of Customs containing a reduction in customs duties shall apply, unless these decisions stipulate a contrary measure, after the expiry of a period of two full days starting from the date of their signature, provided that the provisions of the last two paragraphs of Article 13 shall apply.

No reductions in duties other than those provided for by legal regulations may be granted, regardless of the capacity of the declarant or the consignee. Customs officers are prohibited, on pain of being charged with bribery, from: a- Granting exemptions from duties not provided for in decisions and regulations, and any person who benefits from such grants shall be prosecuted as an accomplice. b - Levying duties other than the prescribed duties or duties exceeding them.

The customs duties set out in the specific tariff shall, in principle, be levied in full on the quantities presented to the Customs, irrespective of the nature of the goods subject to this specific tariff, their relative value and their condition. However, where damage to the goods is established, the quantities subject to duties may be reduced in proportion to the established damage, provided that the damaged quantity is destroyed under the supervision of the Customs Department.

(1)- Notwithstanding the provisions of the first paragraph of the tenth Article, importers of motor vehicles who have benefited, upon the importation thereof, and under the conditions provided for in Articles 247, 248, 249, 251, 252 and 254, from exemption from customs duties, and who dispose of them after using them, may be granted by the Customs Administration, upon payment of the duties, a proportional reduction, calculated in accordance with the following method, on the rate of the lowest duty in force on the date of importation or release for consumption: 1- Motor vehicles sold after the lapse of one year from the date of registration of the import declaration with the Customs, a reduction of one quarter of the duty imposed thereon. 2- Motor vehicles sold after the lapse of more than one year and less than two years from the date of registration of the import declaration with the Customs, a reduction of one quarter of the imposed duty and 1/48 thereof for each month following the twelfth month. 3- Motor vehicles sold after the lapse of more than two years from the date of registration of the import declaration with the Customs, a reduction of one half of the imposed duty and 1/48 thereof for each month following the twenty-fourth month. The duty payable in all the cases mentioned above shall not be less than 25 percent of the value of the motor vehicles upon their disposal. If the motor vehicle suffers a major accident resulting in a decrease of fifty percent or more of its value, the duties shall be reduced by an amount equivalent to the decrease in value as determined by the valuation of the insurance companies' experts, or, where necessary, the court-appointed experts.

Where an amendment or change occurs in the tariff, and subject to observance of the provisions of Article 14, the rate of duties to be levied shall be determined on the basis of the date of registration of the declarations of release for consumption at the Customs office.

The duties applicable to goods leaving the warehouse shall be the duties in force upon the lodging of the declaration of entry for consumption. However, goods located in customs stores and warehouses on the date of signature of the decision ordering an increase in tariffs may benefit from the previous duties more favourable to them if they pay such duties within the time limit provided for in Article 13.

When duties are liquidated ipso jure on goods kept in the warehouse, due to the expiry of the storage time limit and failure to obtain a legal extension thereof, the duty shall be applied in accordance with the tariff in force upon the expiry of the legal storage time limit in the warehouse.
Goods misappropriated from the warehouse shall be subject to the duties in force on the day the misappropriation is established.

Where a minor shortage is established when reconciling the warehouse accounts, the duty thereon shall be levied in accordance with the tariff that was in force on the date of the last removal from the warehouse.

Goods transferred from the free zones to the customs territory shall be subject, as the case may be, either to the duties of the ordinary tariff or to the duties of the maximum tariff in force upon the lodging of the consumption declaration, and to the various duties and taxes due.
Goods sent in transit that are declared for consumption at the office of destination shall be subject to the duties in force on the date of the declaration of payment of duties.

Goods in respect of which guaranteed undertaking bonds have been executed for transit, change of warehouse, change of free zone, temporary admission, etc..., and which have not been discharged in whole or in part within the time limit granted for that purpose, shall be subject to the duty in force on the date of registration of these bonds.
Goods sold by the Customs Administration for consumption under the conditions provided for in Chapter Eight of Title Eight below shall be subject to the duties in force on the day of the sale.

All goods entering or leaving Lebanon shall be presented and declared to the customs office, in order to be inspected should the officers so desire and subjected to duties where applicable. - The lodging of the customs declaration by the taxpayers and the payment of duties shall take place at the customs office nearest to the border, except with respect to export goods of the types subject to the control of the customs zone, or perishable goods, which must be declared in accordance with the conditions determined by the Customs Administration, either at internal export offices or at authorised second-line offices.

By administrative orders of the Higher Council of Customs published in the Official Gazette, the customs offices open for the importation and exportation of certain goods or for transactions carried out in accordance with one of the regimes provided for in Titles III and IV below (Articles 167 to 271) may be designated. Certain derogations from these restrictions may be granted within the conditions determined by the Customs Administration.

The materials specified below shall, in principle, only be exempted from customs duties if they are brought in through one of the ports of Lebanon: a- Machinery, supplies and products intended for agriculture and referred to in Article 261. b - Building materials and all supplies for buildings and their maintenance, and mechanical tools, engines, machinery and apparatus of all kinds imported by religious bodies, evangelical missions, and educational and relief institutions referred to in Article 254. Likewise, electrical and non-electrical machinery and apparatus shall, in principle, only benefit from the reduced duty provided for in the tariff if they are imported through one of the ports of Lebanon.

The goods specified below may only be imported through the customs offices of Beirut and Tripoli: a- Playing cards, b - Yarns, fabrics and articles made of cotton, c- Raw silk and yarns, fabrics and articles made of natural silk and of artificial silk, d- Yarns, fabric and articles made of flax, ramie, hemp, burlap (jute) and other vegetable textile materials, e- Pharmaceutical chemical products, various substances and preparations, vegetable products imported for medicinal uses only, compounded medicines, serums and vaccines, pharmaceutical preparations, and dressing articles (water-absorbent cotton, gauze, compresses and bandages), f- Silkworm eggs.

Cotton seeds, from whatever source, with the exception of cotton seeds of Syrian origin, shall not be imported except through the ports of Beirut and Tripoli. The formalities relating to these importations are determined in the decisions in force.

Cinematographic films, of whatever origin, shall not be imported except through the Beirut Customs post. Weights, measures and weighing instruments subject to initial verification pursuant to the provisions of the decisions in force concerning the verification of weights and measures shall not be imported except through the Beirut and Tripoli Customs posts.

Plants or parts of plants (grafts, shoots, flowering bulbs, cut flowers, leaves, fruits, vegetables, tubers, bulbils, roots and seeds), as well as materials of whatever kind that have been used for the packing and transport of these products, may not be imported except through the Customs offices situated within the maritime or land border zones that have the technical officials and the equipment necessary to ensure the control of their importation and, where necessary, their disinfection. The formalities relating to these importations are determined in the decisions in force.
The importation of silkworm eggs of foreign origin is prohibited between the first of May and 15 September of each year.

The animals and animal substances referred to in the decisions in force relating to the veterinary sanitary police may not be imported or exported, by sea, except through the ports of Beirut and Tripoli and under the conditions referred to in these decisions.
Cattle may not be exported except through the Customs offices of Beirut, Tripoli and Masnaa and under the conditions determined in the effective decisions in force.
Lemons and oranges of Lebanese origin may not be exported by sea except through the offices of Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon and Tyre and under the conditions determined in the decisions in force.

Goods that may not be brought in or taken out except through the ports and offices mentioned above for this purpose shall, if an attempt is made to bring them in or take them out through other passages, be subject to the application of the penalties provided for in Article 358 or in Article 362, as the case may be. Provided that if these same goods are presented to the Customs offices under their true designation, those among them that are imported shall be sent back abroad and those intended for exportation shall be returned to the interior, and they may subsequently be exported through the offices open for the formalities of taking out goods of their kind.

The special formalities and restrictions (entry or exit licences, sanitary regulation of livestock, meat and plants, inspections, disinfections, etc...) to which certain goods are subject upon importation or exportation shall be determined by decisions or administrative orders.

In the event of an admixture of cotton yarns subject to different duties (yarn waste), the duties shall be assessed on the basis of the duty applicable to the yarn subject to the highest duty in each package.

Playing cards imported from abroad must be presented in a special wrapper containing a circular hole 35 millimetres in diameter in which the lower part of the ace of clubs appears in order to be stamped with the legal seal, and the number of cards contained therein must be stated on the wrapper of each pack of playing cards.

Edible fatty substances, whether of animal or vegetable origin, shall not be accepted for importation or placement in warehouse unless they are placed in soldered metal containers each holding no more than ten kilogrammes net.

Fabrics of all kinds may not be imported from abroad except in bales, the weight of each of which shall be five hundred kilogrammes net as a maximum limit. If fabrics subject to different duties by reason of the difference in their kinds and classes are found in a single bale, their duties shall be assessed on the basis of the duty applicable to the fabric subject to the highest duty in the bale, unless there are exceptions determined by the Customs Administration.

Importation, passage in transit, transport, exportation and re-exportation are strictly prohibited: 1- For all products illegally bearing a factory or commercial mark or a trade name enjoying lawful protection in Lebanon in accordance with the Paris Union Convention dated 20 March 1883, revised at The Hague on 6 November 1925. 2- For all products bearing a false indication of their origin, in which it is stated directly or indirectly that the producing country or place of origin is one of the countries contracting or acceding to the Madrid Agreement dated 14 April 1891, revised at The Hague on 6 November 1925, or a place situated in one of those countries.

The affixing of marks indicating origin on foreign products entering Lebanon may be made compulsory by special decisions specifying those products. Those decisions shall specify, for each kind of foreign product, the conditions to be observed in affixing the marks of origin as well as all procedures necessary for the application of the regime. Importation and entry into warehouse are strictly prohibited for all foreign products, natural or manufactured, that do not fulfil the conditions imposed pursuant to this Article and the decisions issued for its implementation.

Infractions or attempted infractions of the provisions of Articles 48, 49 and 50 shall be treated as importations or attempted importations of prohibited goods, without a declaration or by way of smuggling, and shall be repressed by the penalties provided for in Article 358. However, the seizure of such goods may be lifted after the destruction of the offending marks, names, signs or indications, or the placing of a correction thereon, or the affixing of the mark indicating origin, in cases where the Customs Service deems one of these measures to be sufficient therein. The importation, by a merchant, of labels, signs, stoppers, containers or other objects bearing a factory or commercial mark, a trade name or an indication of origin entitled to enjoy lawful protection in Lebanon shall be deemed an attempted infraction of the provisions of Article 49, if the merchant does not prove that he has imported products corresponding thereto in kind and quantity.

With the exception of goods that are prohibited in an absolute manner and the goods referred to in Articles 45, 46 and 47, goods whose entry or exit is prohibited and for which a customs declaration has been submitted under their specific designation shall not be seized; rather, goods intended for importation shall be returned abroad and goods requested to be taken out shall be returned to the interior. Importations or exportations, or attempted importations or exportations, of prohibited goods or goods assimilated thereto, without a customs declaration or by way of smuggling, shall be suppressed by the penalties provided for in Article 358.

Every good whose importation or exportation is prohibited for any reason whatsoever, or which is subject to restrictions or to special formalities, shall be deemed prohibited. If importation or exportation is not permitted except on the basis of a licence, permit, certificate, etc., the goods shall be prohibited if they are not accompanied by a legal document or if they are accompanied by a document not applicable to them.

All documents issued or endorsed by the Administration pursuant to which importation or exportation is authorised (licences or documents similar thereto) may not, under any circumstances whatsoever, be sold, lent or assigned to another person, and in general may not be the subject of a transaction, of whatever kind, carried out by the right-holders in whose names these documents were issued. Infringements of the provisions of the preceding paragraph shall be liable to the penalties suppressing importations and exportations of prohibited goods without a customs declaration.

The mere obtaining or attempt to obtain one of the documents referred to in Article 46, whether by way of counterfeiting public seals, or by false declarations, or by any other fraudulent means, shall be deemed an attempted importation without a declaration or exportation without a declaration of prohibited goods and shall be suppressed as the infringement itself.

Importation, entry into a warehouse and into the free zone, and passage in transit are prohibited, in an absolute manner, for all foreign products, whether natural or manufactured, which bear upon themselves or upon their wrappers, cases, bales, envelopes, bands or packings, etc., a factory mark or trade mark, or any name, sign or indication whatsoever, of a nature to create the false impression that these products were manufactured in Lebanon or that their origin is Lebanon.

The importation or re-exportation, on vessels whose tonnage is less than 150 marine tons, of monopolised goods, prohibited goods, and goods subject to exorbitant duties and designated by administrative orders from the Higher Council of Customs published in the Official Gazette, is prohibited. Likewise, cruising in the maritime zone is absolutely prohibited for vessels whose tonnage is less than 150 tons and loaded with goods of the kinds mentioned above, whether declared under a manifest for abroad or undeclared, except in the cases of force majeure set forth below: verified maritime emergencies or breakdown forcing them to cast anchor within the limits of twenty kilometres from the coast and to take refuge in one of the Lebanese ports. In these cases, the masters of the aforementioned vessels must notify, - without delay, the nearest Customs office of their presence and justify the same and sign at the - said office a guaranteed undertaking whereby they undertake to produce, within a specified time limit, - proofs of their arrival at the intended foreign country and their payment there of the import duty. Every infringement of the provisions of this Article shall be deemed an importation or re-exportation without a declaration or an unauthorised transport of prohibited goods and shall be repressed by the penalties provided for in Article 358.
Special prohibitions concerning the importation and exportation of certain goods shall be determined by decisions of the Higher Council of Customs.

Licences permitting the importation or exportation of materials whose importation or exportation is prohibited shall be granted by the Higher Council of Customs, upon the proposal of the competent Ministry. The validity of import licences is fixed at a period of six months, and of export licences at a period of three months. Every operation of entry or exit of licensed goods shall be subject to the payment of a unified fee levied by the Customs Department, amounting to one hundred Lebanese piastres. Exempted from the payment of this fee are: - The Office of the President of the Republic - The institutions referred to in Article 253 - Members of the diplomatic and consular corps referred to in Article 249 - Legations and consulates in respect of what they import in their own name in accordance with the provisions of Article 251 This fee shall remain due in every licensed importation operation that does not benefit from customs exemption.

Goods worked in a third foreign country subject to a less favourable tariff than the tariff applicable to the country of origin shall be subject to the duties of the tariff specific to the third country in accordance with the degree of preparation in which they are at the time of their importation. Goods worked in a third foreign country benefiting from a more favourable tariff than the tariff applicable to the country of origin may pay the duties on the basis of the tariff pertaining to the third country in accordance with the degree of their preparation: a - if they are among the products that have undergone a complete transformation which has caused them to lose the character of their origin; b - if they have been incompletely transformed or completed by the addition of manual labour, provided that such labour has resulted in bringing the imported goods into a category of the tariff subject to heavier duties than those applicable to the raw material. If neither of the two conditions referred to in sub-paragraphs (a) and (b) is fulfilled, the products worked in the third country shall remain subject to the tariff specific to the original origin, according to their condition upon their importation. Every false declaration aimed at subjecting the products mentioned in this Article or in the preceding Article to a more favourable status than their own specific status shall be deemed to constitute a false declaration of origin and shall be repressed by the penalties provided for in Article 358 or in Article 362, as the case may be.

There may be applied, pursuant to special decisions, an additional customs duty, known as the surtax of origin, to the importation of foreign goods, for consumption in Lebanon, whatever their origin may be, arriving from a country other than the country of origin. The special decisions referred to in the preceding paragraph shall designate the countries of provenance to which the surtax of origin is applied and shall determine the rate of this duty. The surtax of origin shall be levied, in general, under the same conditions and according to the same rules as those pursuant to which customs duties are levied. Goods that benefit from the right of drawback of customs duties upon re-exportation shall not benefit from the drawback of the surtax of origin that may be imposed thereon.

Infractions or attempted infractions of the provisions of Article 49 shall fall within the jurisdiction of the ordinary courts that hear civil cases, and the Customs Administration shall institute proceedings by referring the seizure report to the Protection Office. The right of the Customs Administration to settle by compromise shall not apply, and the lifting of the seizure of the goods after the destruction of the offending marks, or the affixing of the correction thereon, shall not be ordered except after the approval of the Property Protection Office. When these infractions are brought before the judiciary, the injured party, notified by the Property Office, shall have the right to intervene in the action, and in this case the seizure of the goods in his favour may be ordered. The costs of safekeeping and other costs advanced by the Customs Service shall be borne by the losing party.

Foreign goods imported into Lebanon and admitted under the ordinary tariff shall be subject to proof of origin, whatever their origin and provenance may be. Proof shall be furnished in the form of original invoices endorsed by the Lebanese consulates and simultaneously comprising proof of the accuracy of the prices and the origin of the goods. As regards goods exported from cities in which there are no Lebanese consulates or persons acting in their stead, it shall suffice for the invoices described above to be endorsed by chambers of commerce or any similar institution accepted by the Higher Council of Customs. These same documents shall be required for goods of any foreign provenance entering across the land borders, if it is manifestly apparent that their origin is a country other than the countries contiguous to Lebanon. The documents proving the origin of goods that may benefit from agreed tariffs are determined by the special customs agreements concluded with the countries that benefit therefrom. The production of false documents of origin shall entail the application of the penalties provided for in Article 358, or in Article 362, as the case may be. The Customs Administration shall determine the derogations from the provisions of this Article.

The production of the document proving origin shall not bind the assessment of the Customs Service, which retains the freedom to contest the authenticity or validity of such document. Every dispute of this kind shall be subject to the arbitration of the statutory experts.

Where any goods are imported by way of a third country, after having been released for consumption in that third country, they shall pay, upon their entry into Lebanon, the tariff applicable to the country of origin or to the exporting country, whichever tariff is higher.

The value of goods subject to "ad valorem" duties, which must be declared to the Customs, is the value of such goods when they are presented to the Customs for the payment of duties thereon. This value shall include the purchase price plus all subsequent expenses up to the presentation of the declaration to the Customs. The purchase price, which must correspond to the normal price in the country of sale, shall be proved by the production of the original invoice specified in Article 53. The production of this invoice is mandatory. By purchase price shall be understood the amount which the buyer has actually paid or which he has entered in his records to the account of the consignor. If the value is expressed in a foreign currency, it must be converted into Lebanese piastres on the basis of the exchange rate on the working day preceding the day of presentation of the declaration. However, in a period of continuous depreciation of one of the kinds of foreign currency, the conversion rate may be fixed by a decision of the Higher Council of Customs which counteracts the effect of the depreciation in exchange or fixes the value subject to customs duty in Lebanese piastres.

In order for the invoice to be accepted at the Customs, there must be mentioned therein a date consistent with the date of shipment of the goods to which it relates from the place of their dispatch. Any period elapsing between the date of shipment of the consignments and the date of drawing up of the invoice must be justified.

The dutiable value relating to goods leaving real warehouses, special real warehouses, or fictitious warehouses, and to goods which have remained in customs stores and warehouses for more than three months, is the value of such goods upon their exit from such warehouses or stores. The Customs may accept the original invoices presented upon the exit of the goods from the warehouses and stores if it considers that the value mentioned in such invoices has not changed since the date on which they were drawn up. The dutiable value relating to goods leaving free zones is the value of such goods in the condition in which they are presented to the Customs at the time of their exit from the free zones, and the assessment of this value shall take place in accordance with the conditions laid down in this Chapter.

The original invoice specified in Articles 53 and 58 to 60, or a true copy thereof certified by the Service, must remain attached to the declaration in order to be kept therewith, unless there is a derogation from this rule within the conditions determined by the Customs Administration.

The submission of invoices shall not bind the assessment of the Customs Department, which retains the freedom to contest the authenticity or accuracy of such invoices. In such a case, the production of agreements, contracts, correspondence, bank account statements, insurance company certificates, catalogues, current price lists, cheques, certificates of proof of value and valuation elements issued by industrial bodies qualified to issue them and worthy of trust, etc., all relating to the customs transactions, may be required, without the assessment of the Customs Department being bound by these documents themselves. Any dispute of this kind shall be subject to the arbitration of the legal experts.
The production of false invoices shall entail the application of the penalties provided for in Article 358 or in Article 362, as the case may be.

For the purpose of applying ad valorem duties to apparatus, separate parts or goods imported under cover of contracts not constituting an outright sale, importers must submit declarations thereof and duties shall be levied thereon as if there were an outright sale, in accordance with the preceding rules relating to the determination of the dutiable value.
