The Customs Department shall have the option to increase, where necessary, the values of the contracts in a manner that renders them commensurate with the true dutiable value.

For the purpose of interpreting tariff decisions, assimilation shall be based on the duty specific to the most similar category and shall be determined by administrative orders issued by the Director General of Customs.

Products composed of materials or elements subject to different duties by reason of the difference in their nature, and for which there is no special tariff in such condition, shall be subject to the customs duty applicable to the element of the mixture subject to the highest duty, unless the constituent parts of the mixture can be easily separated or the matter relates only to accessory parts; by way of exception, the following rules shall apply to the various fabrics of mixed textile materials, knitted and crocheted goods (Bonneterie), and articles made of these textile materials: 1- Mixed fabrics containing more than 20 per cent by weight of natural or artificial silk shall follow the regime of fabrics of natural or artificial silk according to kind. Fabrics containing more than 20 per cent by weight of natural silk and more than- 20 per cent by weight of artificial silk shall follow the regime of fabrics of natural silk, according to - kind. 2- Mixed fabrics containing natural or artificial silk in a proportion by weight equal to 20 per cent or less thereof and containing, in addition, cotton, shall follow the following regimes: a- The regime of cotton fabrics, according to kind, if the proportion of cotton, by weight, exceeds 20 per cent. b - The regime of the fabric predominating in weight according to kind, if the proportion of cotton, by weight, is equal to 20 per cent and less. 3- Mixed fabrics not containing natural or artificial silk, but comprising more than 20 per cent by weight of cotton, shall follow the regime of cotton fabrics, according to kind. 4- Mixed fabrics composed of textile materials other than silk and cotton shall follow the regime of the textile material predominating in weight, according to kind. Also by way of exception, fabrics containing borders of coloured threads shall not be deemed to be made of dyed threads unless the surface area of the coloured threads exceeds 10 per cent of the entire surface area. Every false declaration aimed at obtaining a more favourable regime, for mixed products, than the regime to which they are subject, shall be deemed to constitute a false declaration as to kind and shall be repressed by the penalties provided for in Article 358 or Article 362 as the case may be.

No goods may be imported by sea, whether from a foreign port or from one of the Lebanese ports, without a single manifest, signed by the master of the vessel and stating the number of packages, their marks and numbers, their wrappings of all kinds, the descriptions of the goods, and the places from which they were shipped.

Prohibited goods must be entered in this manifest by their true designation and their types, qualities, and kinds, under pain of the penalties provided for in Article 358, No. 2. These provisions shall apply to the manifest or the documents standing in lieu thereof referred to in Articles 85, 86, 87, 88, 90, and 91.

Customs officers shall have the right to inspect vessels of a tonnage of less than 150 maritime tons, whatever their nationality, whether at anchor or cruising within twenty kilometres of the Lebanese coasts, except in cases of force majeure having a legitimate justification.

Customs officers shall have the right to board, without the assistance of a member of the public police force or any other intermediary, ships of whatever tonnage and flag located in the ports or roadsteads of Lebanon, or entering or leaving such ports, and to remain on board until the completion of their unloading, and to order, upon their departure, the opening of hatches, cabins, compartments, lockers, chests, bales, casks, and other packages or receptacles, and to search by all means all shipments.

The Customs Service is authorised to place under seal, by lead seal or otherwise, monopolised or prohibited goods or goods subject to high duties designated by administrative orders of the Higher Council of Customs published in the Official Gazette, which are in the possession of ships of every tonnage and flag upon their entry into the ports and roadsteads of Lebanon. The master must draw up, upon entry into these ports and roadsteads, a summary list of such goods if no manifest has been drawn up therefor. The provisions of Article 73 shall apply to the operations referred to in this Article.

Customs officers shall have the right, within twenty kilometres of the coasts, to board steamships of a tonnage exceeding 150 tons, whatever their flag, provided that they confine themselves to requesting a copy of the manifest and endorsing the original manifest. They shall not have the right to inspect such ships unless they have specific information as to the presence of goods for smuggling.

If the masters of the vessels referred to in Articles 69 and 70, and where applicable in Article 72, refuse to open the holds, cabins, compartments, and lockers, the customs officers shall request the assistance of a member of the public police force, and such officer must attend the opening of those holds, cabins, compartments, and lockers.

Goods imported by railway under the international transit regime must be accompanied by the waybill which stands in lieu of the manifest, and to which shall be attached the special declarations known as summary sheets stating therein, for each package, its mark, its numbers, the nature of the goods, the gross weight, the volume, etc... if the goods are subject to duties on the basis of weight or measurement or on the basis of another specific unit. As for goods that are subject to duties on the basis of value or prohibited goods, both their gross weight and their value must be declared simultaneously. The provisions of the second paragraph of Article 85 shall apply in their entirety to waybills.

Commercial consignments of goods imported by motor vehicles must be accompanied, on each trip of each vehicle, by a manifest drawn up in accordance with the same conditions laid down for the manifests referred to in the following Article.

Goods imported, under the international transit regime, by authorised motor transport companies must be accompanied, on each trip of each vehicle, by a manifest consisting of a summary schedule of the total goods transported under this regime. There shall be stated in this manifest, in the Arabic language (and where necessary in the French, English or Turkish language), the names of the consignors and of the consignees, the number of packages, their marks, their numbers, the nature of their packings, their gross weight in kilograms, the nature of the goods, their origin, their value, and their quantity by weight, number or volume or, where necessary, by the requisite specific unit. The manifest must bear the signature of the authorised representative of the transport company, the signature of the driver of the vehicle, and the visa of the customs office from which the goods were consigned or of the first Lebanese office through which they entered. This manifest shall be lodged, immediately upon the arrival of the vehicle, at the Lebanese office of destination.
The provisions of Articles 78 and 80 shall apply to these modes of transport.

The inspection of vessels, which takes place under the conditions provided for in Articles 69, 70 and 71, and where applicable in Articles 72 and 73, gives rise to the verification of the contraventions provided for and penalised by Articles 363 to 367.

The master of the ship or the shipping company agent representing him shall, within a maximum period of thirty-six hours following the arrival of the ship at one of the ports, and before the unloading of its cargo, deliver to the customs office, by way of a summary declaration, the original manifest and two copies thereof.

Every original manifest pertaining to a ship that does not make regular voyages and where the shipping companies owning it do not have agents in the ports of Lebanon, as well as every manifest pertaining to a sailing vessel, must be endorsed by the customs authorities at the port of loading.

Every ship, whether laden or empty, is prohibited from departing from one of the Lebanese ports unless it is accompanied by a manifest conforming to the provisions of Article 67 presented to the Customs Department, under pain of the penalties provided for in Article 362.

It is prohibited to mention in the manifest or in the loading lists or waybills as a single unit, several closed packages, grouped together in any manner whatsoever, under pain of the penalties provided for in Article 358.
The masters of vessels are obliged to produce to the customs officers upon entry and departure the bills of lading which they must have in their possession the penalties provided for- in Article 358.

Save for exceptions granted by the Customs Department, no goods may be unloaded from any steamship, barge or boat, or loaded onto any steamship, barge or boat, without a permit from the customs officers and without their presence, under pain of the penalties provided for in Article 358 or in Article 362 as the case may be. Unloading and loading are not permitted, in principle, except during the course of the day and within the precincts of the ports in which there are customs offices, unless there are exceptions granted by the Customs Department. Save in cases of urgent necessity, the loading and unloading of vessels shall take place in sequence according to the date of their summary declaration and to the extent permitted by the premises and the number of officers attached to the customs office

The Customs Administration shall determine, according to the requirements of commercial traffic, the hours of opening and closing of the customs offices and the hours of unloading and loading of vessels.

All goods imported by land must be conducted directly to the first office of entry from the frontier, under penalty of the sanctions provided for, with respect to importation by way of smuggling, in Article 358 in Article 362 as the case may be. It shall be incumbent upon the owners of the goods and their escorts to regulate their course so as to follow the road or route leading directly to the place in which the first and nearest customs office is situated. Administrative orders of the Higher Council of Customs, published in the Official Gazette, shall determine the direct roads and routes for importation and for exportation.

The same penalties shall apply if the goods pass beyond the customs offices without authorisation or if they are introduced into any warehouse before being conducted to these offices. Goods arriving after the closing of the customs offices shall in principle be placed in the premises attached to these offices and shall remain therein without any charge until the opening of the said offices.

Subject to the provisions of the second paragraph of Article 24, all goods exported by land must be brought directly to the office of exit under penalty of the sanctions provided for, with respect to exportation by way of smuggling, in Article 358 or in Article 362, as the case may be. It is prohibited under penalty of the same sanctions, for the owners of the goods and their escorts, to follow deviating roads or routes with the intention of avoiding the customs offices or to pass beyond these offices without authorisation.

Goods imported by railway must be accompanied by a waybill, serving as a manifest, stating the number of packages, their marks and numbers, the wrappings of all kinds and the nature of the goods. These waybills must bear the signature of the authorised agent of the railway company, the signature of the train conductor and the visa of the customs office from which the goods were shipped or the visa of the first Lebanese customs office through which they entered. Immediately upon the arrival of the train, these waybills shall be lodged in duplicate at the first Lebanese customs office through which it enters.

The manifests, or the certified abstracts thereof, pertaining to goods unloaded in the maritime free zone, or the summary documents pertaining to goods placed in the inland free zones, must be submitted to the Customs Administration immediately after the unloading of the goods, by the masters of vessels, shipping companies, or the authorised agents of the companies entrusted with transport under a guaranteed bond. On the other hand, the body entrusted with operating the free zone shall deliver to the Customs Administration, within the 36 hours following the unloading of the goods, a separate list for each vessel, train, or motor vehicle comprising a complete enumeration of the number and nature of the packages, their marks and numbers, and the nature and origin of the goods. The obligations provided for in the two preceding paragraphs shall be incumbent upon the same obligated persons for the shipping or dispatch of goods exiting the free zone.

The carrier must draw up a manifest containing a description of the goods transported by air and their kind, and a true copy of this manifest must remain aboard the aircraft and be presented upon request to the officers entrusted with the policing of movement and to the customs officers.

Aircraft performing international flights must land, upon departure and upon return, at special airports called customs airports. They must cross the borders at designated points. The list of these customs airports and border-crossing points is determined in the decisions in force. However, certain categories of aircraft may, having regard to the nature of their operation, be exempted by an administrative permit from landing at customs airports. The permit shall designate, in this case, the airport of arrival and departure, the air route to be followed, and the signals to be given when crossing the borders.
Every aircraft in flight, wherever its position may be, must comply with the orders issued by police and customs posts and aircraft, whatever the form in which such orders are given.

The commander of the aircraft is entitled to order, en route, the jettisoning of the loaded goods if the jettisoning thereof is necessary for the safety of the aircraft. He must, if a choice is possible, jettison the goods of low value.
The importation of goods by letter post or by postal parcels is admitted under the conditions provided for in the decisions in force.

Every transaction for clearing goods from customs must be mandatorily preceded, pursuant to the provisions of Article 24, by the lodging of a detailed declaration signed by one of the persons enumerated in Article 106. The detailed declaration shall be drawn up in duplicate, on forms printed at the expense of the merchants, and in the form prescribed by the Customs Administration in accordance with specimen forms deposited at its offices. This declaration shall be subject to the fiscal stamp duty applicable under the law in force. The conditions under which the owner of the goods may authorise a licensed customs broker to complete customs formalities are determined in Articles 106 to 118. Customs officers are prohibited from drawing up declarations, except in the cases provided for in Article 119.

Customs declarations must be drawn up in accordance with the wording of the tariff and, where applicable, in accordance with the text granting or imposing a special regime. In particular, items eligible to benefit from a preferential regime must be designated strictly in accordance with the exact wording of the text of the decision granting such regime. The commercial designation of the goods must, where applicable, follow their designation in the tariff.

Customs declarations must contain all the particulars necessary for the application of customs duties, various charges, regulations, formalities, and control measures. They must state: 1- the nature of the goods, their weight, their value, their origin, and the kind, marks, and numbers of the packings, as well as the number of packages, 2- with respect to maritime operations, the name of the vessel, and in other operations, the mode of transport (railway, motor vehicle) and the date of entry of the goods into the warehouse, 3- upon importation, the provenance of the goods and the name, profession, and place of residence of the licensed customs broker and of the real consignee, and upon exportation, the destination of the goods and the name, profession, and place of residence of the licensed customs broker and of the real consignor, 4- regarding goods subject to duties on a basis other than weight and value, the unit specified in the tariff for the collection of duties (area, number, etc...), 5- the request to benefit from the special treatment from which the goods may benefit and the text granting such treatment.

An import declaration may mention only goods pertaining to a single manifest or a single waybill, except with respect to goods leaving a warehouse, for which the declaration may contain several items entered in up to three different registers. It is prohibited to mention in declarations several closed packages, grouped together in any manner whatsoever, as a single unit, under penalty of the sanctions provided for in Article 358.

Exemption from duties, upon the entry or exit of the goods, shall not exempt from submitting the declarations provided for in the preceding Articles to the Customs Administration, under penalty of the sanctions provided for in Article 362.
Customs officers are prohibited from disclosing the declarations to third parties except in compliance with a request from the judicial authority or in execution of judgments issued by the courts.

Declarations drawn up in accordance with the provisions of Articles 96 to 100 shall be registered by the Customs Department, after verifying their conformity with these Articles, under the date of the day on which they are submitted, in the order of their receipt and following an uninterrupted annual series of numbers. Registration of declarations that do not satisfy the aforementioned instructions shall be refused.

Those who have submitted customs declarations may not alter anything therein under any pretext whatsoever, and the truth or falsity of these declarations shall be judged on the basis of what was initially stated therein. However, if the declarant acknowledges, within twenty-four hours from the submission of his declaration, and prior to the inspection, the existence of an error in weight, number, measure, or value, he may rectify it with the permission of the Customs, provided that he presents the very same packages and goods. After the expiry of this time limit, every request in this regard shall be refused. The prohibition provided for in this Article shall not, in principle, cover changes of customs status so long as the duties have not yet been liquidated. In the event of a dispute, changes relating to the status shall only be permitted after the settlement of such dispute. Customs officers are also prohibited from making any modification to the declarations, whatever the reason may be.

The Customs Department may cancel, ipso jure, declarations for which, for a reason attributable to the declarant, the formalities relating thereto have not been completed within a period of fifteen full days starting from the date of registration of these declarations. In the event that the declaration is cancelled ipso jure, the Customs Administration may request the inspection of the goods under the conditions provided for in Articles 120 to 133 and subject to the application of Article 141. Such inspection may be carried out, notwithstanding the provisions of Article 122 of the Law, even in the absence of the declarant or his legally authorised representative, if neither the former nor the latter responds to the written summons addressed to them to attend the inspection.

Owners of imported goods or their customs clearing agents may obtain an authorisation from the Customs Department to examine these goods under its supervision, prior to submitting the declaration, and even to take samples thereof to verify their kind, value, or quantity, and the duties due on these samples shall be paid.

The following shall be admitted to present goods to Customs to place them for consumption or under any other regime: 1- Non-merchant individuals, in whose names packages of goods are, exceptionally, sent by them or to them 2- Merchants or their authorised representatives (clearing commercial employees) for the goods of which they prove that they are the owners, depositaries, or shippers, 3- Professional goods clearers, namely licensed customs brokers.

The persons mentioned in Article 106 shall be required to submit the delivery order, pertaining to the goods, to Customs. The endorsement of the delivery order to the name of a licensed customs broker shall be considered solely as an authorisation to complete the customs formalities. The Customs Administration shall be relieved of all liability resulting from the delivery of the goods to the owner of the delivery order or to the bearer thereof. Customs shall not be required to carry out any verification regarding ownership.

All persons to whom the goods are consigned, or the owners thereof, or the depositaries thereof, or those charged with dispatching them by way of transit shall be liable, within the conditions specified in Article 344, for the acts of their employees, or their agents, or the clearers of their goods, and in general for the acts of every person who undertakes on their behalf the clearance of the goods.

A commercial employee who undertakes clearance through Customs is one who carries out, for the account of a specific commercial establishment, the customs formalities relating to goods consigned to that establishment or shipped by it. He shall not be admitted to work in customs stores unless he is at least twenty-one years of age and has previously submitted a regular power of attorney from the establishment that employs him. The name of that establishment alone shall be mentioned on the declarations, which must either be signed by the establishment in whose name they are drawn up or signed by proxy on its behalf. The power of attorney shall remain valid unless revoked by the principal pursuant to a regular instrument notified to Customs. Local heads of Customs, after the approval of the regional head, shall issue to commercial employees who engage in the clearance of goods a card entitling them to enter customs stores or warehouses, and this card may be withdrawn from them following an infringement or misconduct. In Beirut, this card confers the right to enter the examination hall only, and it may be withdrawn under the conditions mentioned in the preceding paragraph. Merchants, commercial employees, or licensed clearing agents shall not be authorised to enter open or roofed customs warehouses unless accompanied by a customs officer or holding a special permit from the bodies operating the customs stores, warehouses, and free zones bearing the visa of the Customs Service. The Customs Administration or the bodies operating the stores, warehouses, and free zones may order the permanent withdrawal of any permit of this kind under the conditions specified above regarding the cards of licensed clearing agents.

A licensed customs clearing agent is one who carries out at Customs formalities relating to goods that are neither his property nor in his name. The licensed customs clearing agent is liable, towards the persons to whom the goods are consigned, and towards Customs and the bodies operating the customs stores or warehouses or free zones, for the acts of his employees, to whom he is required to deliver a regular power of attorney to be deposited with Customs. A licensed customs clearing agent may not acquire ownership of goods that are not his and for which the customs formalities have not been regularly completed, and he acts at all times for the account of the consignee, whose name the agent is required to declare in the declaration submitted to Customs.

A licensed customs broker shall be entitled to utilize the services of one or more employees, who shall then fall within the category of commercial employees clearing goods through customs and shall be subject to the same obligations. The cards may be withdrawn from such employees subordinate to licensed customs brokers in all cases provided for in Article 116.

The practice of the profession of customs clearance before the customs offices shall be subject to an examination announced by the Directorate General of Customs whenever the need of the service so requires, within the conditions specified by this Law. The right to sit for this examination shall be restricted to the following persons: 1- Employees of customs brokers and commercial employees who have practiced customs clearance work for a period of at least ten years. 2- Customs officers and officers of the bodies operating customs stores or warehouses or free zones, who have been dismissed from service for a non-disciplinary reason after actual service of not less than five years, provided that they prove their need to practice this profession before the committee provided for in the second paragraph of Article 114. However, this committee shall be entitled to meet under the chairmanship of the Director General of Customs to consider the matter of licensing customs officers of the higher cadre or of the technical cadre, who are referred to retirement before reaching the legal age and for non-disciplinary reasons, to practice the profession of clearing goods in the capacity of licensed customs brokers, if they request so in writing and provided that they prove their need for this purpose before the committee provided for in the second paragraph of Article 114 without sitting for the examination provided for in this Article, provided that they shall be subject, in the matter of their suspension or removal from work, to the provisions of Article 116.

Currently registered customs brokers and clearance companies shall continue to practice their profession, even if they do not fulfil all the conditions provided for in this Law, provided that they shall be subject, in the matter of their removal or suspension, to the provisions of this Law.

When the Customs Administration announces the holding of an examination for the profession of licensed customs broker, a person wishing to sit for the examination must submit a written application to the Head of the Customs Region - to which the customs office in which the examination is held belongs, and he must satisfy the following conditions: 1- That he has been Lebanese for at least five years and that he satisfies the conditions provided for in Article 112. 2- That he has completed the twenty-fifth year. 3- That he possesses civil capacity and has not been convicted of a disgraceful offence or of a customs contravention provided for in Articles 358 and 361 4- That he is of good conduct and morals. 5- That he has paid all the taxes due from him to the financial and municipal departments. 6- That none of his relatives up to the fourth degree or any of his relatives by marriage is an employee at the customs post before which he applies to work. The submitted applications shall be laid before a committee composed of:

The Head of the Departments of the Directorate General as Chairman The Head of the Region to which the examination centre belongs as Member The Principal Receiver as Member The Head of Control at the examination centre as Member In the event of the absence of the Chairman or one of the members, or where it is impossible for him to attend the meeting, a replacement for him shall be appointed from among the employees of the upper cadre by a decision of the Director General of Customs

This committee shall meet upon the convocation of its Chairman to examine the applications and shall submit a report containing its opinion on the acceptance or non-acceptance of each of the applicants to the Director General of Customs, who shall rely thereon in issuing his decision accepting the applicants to sit for the examination. The decision of the Director General accepting or rejecting the application shall not be subject to any channel of administrative or judicial review. The holders of accepted applications shall sit for the examination provided for in Article 112 under the supervision of the same committee, and this examination shall comprise two tests: - Preparation of a customs transaction with the assessment of its duties - Mark 20 Coefficient 1 - A general question on customs regulations - Mark 20 - Coefficient 1 Every candidate who does not obtain at least twenty marks in the general total shall be deemed to have failed The committee provided for in the second paragraph of this Article shall meet to mark the tests and shall draw up a formal record of the marking setting out therein the names of the successful candidates and submit it to the Director General of Customs, who shall rely thereon to issue his decision appointing the successful candidates in the examination in the capacity of licensed customs brokers, and the decision of the Director General making the appointment shall not be subject to any channel of administrative or judicial review. The Directorate General shall draw up and publish, after the Director General takes the decision provided for in the preceding paragraph, a schedule of the names of the accepted customs brokers specifying therein the customs post to which each broker belongs, and a broker may not practise his profession in more than one customs post. The Director General of Customs shall determine by an administrative order, and when the need so requires, the number of licensed brokers working in all or some of the customs posts, the Director General of Customs shall give by an administrative order, and when the need so requires, the number of licensed brokers working in all or some of the customs posts. The Head of the Region shall give a card to the customs broker proving his capacity and the customs post in which he is authorised to work and granting him the right of entry to customs warehouses, depots, and free zones.

Upon the death of a licensed customs broker, his adult child, or, if he has several children, one of his adult children with the approval of the other children, may be permitted to practise the profession of clearing goods temporarily and until he sits the examination provided for in Article 114, by a decision of the Director General of Customs taken at the request of the person concerned. The Customs Administration shall fix, where necessary, a date for holding an examination for the children of brokers who have been permitted to practise clearance operations pursuant to the preceding paragraph. The period of training in clearance operations provided for in section 1 of Article 112 shall be waived for the acceptance of the applications of the children of deceased brokers referred to in this Article. Those who pass the examination shall be finally appointed in the capacity of licensed customs brokers. As for those who fail, their right to practise clearance operations shall lapse ipso jure.

The name of a customs broker shall be struck off finally from the roll of licensed brokers, by a decision of the Director General of Customs upon the proposal of the committee provided for in Article 114, if he loses his Lebanese nationality or loses his civil capacity or is convicted of an infamous offence or of a customs offence provided for in Articles 358 and 361, or if his suspension from work is repeated due to the multiplicity of his customs offences, or if he refuses to place the registers kept by him and provided for in Article 118 at the disposal of customs officers for inspection. The Director General of Customs shall be entitled, upon the proposal of the competent Regional Head, to decide to suspend the customs broker temporarily from work for a period not exceeding one year, if he commits acts or offences that do not warrant the final striking off of his name. The decision of the Director General to strike off or suspend from work shall not be subject to any administrative or judicial means of review.

The delivery of the licensed customs broker card shall be conditional upon the deposit of a security the value of which shall be determined by the Director General of Customs and which shall be paid effectively into the Customs fund or for which a guarantee shall be furnished under the conditions determined by the Customs Administration, within a period of three months from the date of notification to the broker of his success in the examination. If this period expires without the deposit of this security, his right to practise clearance operations shall lapse ipso jure.

A customs broker shall keep a register in which he records a summary of the customs transactions which he carries out on behalf of third parties, under the conditions determined by the Customs Administration. Customs officers shall have the authority to inspect these registers at any time whatsoever if the need of the Service so requires, without any refusal or objection on the part of the broker, under penalty of the sanctions provided for in Article 116. A customs broker is prohibited from lending his name or his signature to other brokers or to persons not licensed to practise customs clearance operations, under penalty of the sanctions provided for in Article 116.

In places where there is no licensed customs broker, by way of derogation from the provisions of the last paragraph of Article 96, the parties concerned may entrust customs officers, under the conditions provided for in Article 290, with drawing up their declarations.

After the declarations have been submitted, the goods shall be examined, weighed, measured or counted, in accordance with Article 24, if the customs officers so wish. The right of the Service to inspect covers all the packages mentioned in a single declaration; however, this inspection may be partial or total at the discretion of the Service or in accordance with the instructions given to him. The Service may, if it deems it useful, send the substances subject to inspection to the Administration's chemist for analysis.

The transport of goods within the customs office, their opening, their repacking, their weighing and all operations required for the examination shall be borne by the declarant. Declarants or any third party are prohibited from opening within the customs office any packages other than those designated by the Service for the purpose of their examination.

The examination may only take place in the presence of the declarant designated in Article 106 or in the presence of his legal representative, and they alone shall be liable for any shortage that may be ascertained following the examination.

If the Service is unable to verify, with certainty, the accuracy of the contents of the declaration by examining the goods or the documents submitted, the suspension of the examination may be decided until the Service has gathered the elements necessary to carry out this verification, provided that all useful measures are taken to shorten the duration of the suspension, without the declarant having, as a result thereof, the right to resort to any recourse against the Administration.

Duties must be collected in accordance with the contents of the declaration; however, if the result of the examination reveals a discrepancy between the declaration and the goods, duties shall be collected on the basis of this result.

The provisions of Articles 120 to 124 shall apply in all respects to counter-examinations, which chiefs of examination and customs control officers may carry out for so long as the goods remain under the control of the Service.

Whenever it is necessary to verify that goods imported for consumption are not likely to be harmful to public health, such goods shall be subject to a sanitary examination in addition to the customs examination.

Sanitary examinations shall be carried out by official customs physicians or chemists at offices where there is an official physician or chemist charged with performing the sanitary service or chemical analyses. At other offices, such sanitary examinations shall be carried out by municipal physicians or physicians of the Health Service. No special remuneration shall accrue from these operations.

If the physicians or chemists referred to in the preceding Article consider that it is necessary to subject any substance to analysis, such analysis shall be carried out, after three samples have been taken in the presence of the interested parties, in the nearest laboratory to the office of entry to which the official customs chemist belongs. The tariff for each analysis, or for the counter-analysis referred to in Article 131, is fixed in Article 285. The customs office concerned shall notify the declarants of the results of the analysis within the shortest possible period.
Substances proved to be harmful must be destroyed in the presence of the declarant and at his expense; however, they may be returned to him at his request on condition that they are re-exported.

If the analysis proves that the substances are fit for consumption, the Customs Administration shall bear the expenses of such analysis, and if it proves the contrary, such expenses shall be borne by the importers.

If the declarant objects to the result of the analysis, he may have recourse to a counter-analysis, and for that purpose he must submit an application to the Head of the Local Customs Service within the thirty days following the date on which he was notified of the result of the contested analysis, and pay in advance the costs of the counter-analysis.

The counter-analysis shall be carried out adversarialy in Beirut, on one of the samples taken beforehand, in the presence of the customs physician, by two sworn chemists, one appointed by the Customs and the second appointed by the declarant. In the event of disagreement between the reports of the chemists as to the harmful nature, the customs physician of Beirut shall decide the dispute. If the result is in favour of the declarant, the costs of the counter-analysis shall be refunded to him.
The time required to complete sanitary inspection formalities, including analyses and counter-analyses, shall not be included in the calculation of storage duties.

Travellers entering or leaving Lebanon must, pursuant to Article 24, present themselves at the customs office to declare what they have with them, under penalty of the pecuniary penalty provided for in item 9 of Article 362. Travellers and their baggage shall be subject to the inspection formalities provided for in Articles 120 to 125. The Service may, if it deems fit, carry out a personal search of travellers.

In the absence of special provisions to the contrary, customs duties determined on the basis of weight shall be levied: a- On the gross weight, if the specific duty, per one hundred kilograms, is equal to or less than 331 L.P. in the normal tariff or 662 L.P. in the maximum tariff b - On the net weight, if the specific duty, per one hundred kilograms, exceeds 331 L.P. in the normal tariff or 662 L.P. in the maximum tariff. Exceptionally, certain goods, specifically designated in the tariff decisions, shall pay duties on the basis of their semi-gross weight.

With regard to goods on which duties are levied on the basis of net weight, such duties must be assessed on the basis of the real net weight obtained after deducting from the gross weight the weight of the packings or the real tare. If a single package contains goods subject to duties on the basis of gross weight and goods subject to duties on the basis of net weight, the gross weight of the former shall be determined by apportioning the total gross weight in proportion to the net weights of each kind of goods.

With regard to bales of dry goods containing cotton goods, the person concerned may elect, for drawing up his declaration, either the real net weight or the net weight resulting from the application of a flat-rate tare fixed at four per cent for bales of which the gross weight is one hundred kilos or less and three per cent for bales exceeding that weight. With regard to certain goods the packings of which are of a single form, other flat-rate tare rates may be established by tariff decisions, according to the method of packing and the kind of such goods.

If either party objects to the arbitration and refuses to appoint an expert on its behalf, such expert shall be appointed as of right, upon the request of the second party, by the Single Judge in the district or in the nearest neighbouring locality. The Single Judge of whom this is requested must, within eight days commencing from the day on which the request is submitted, take, in the presence of the requesting party, the regulatory samples necessary for the legal expertise and select, from the official list, the expert charged with representing the second party. When the samples are taken as of right, the seal of the declarant shall be replaced by the seal of the Single Judge charged with representing him.

Other than in the case where the goods are subject to prohibition and if their presence is not necessary for the resolution of the dispute, they shall be delivered, without awaiting the settlement of the dispute, subject to the guarantees determined by the Customs Administration.

If the opinions of the two experts concur, their decision shall be final, and if they differ, they shall refer the arbitration file to a third chosen by the two parties by mutual agreement, or, if they do not agree, appointed by the Higher Council of Customs. The concurring opinions of the two experts or the decision of the third arbitrator are final and not subject to appeal.
The remuneration of the experts shall be disbursed on the basis of the sessions the value of which is determined in the decisions in force. The losing party shall bear all the costs of the expertise.

The procedures to be followed in taking the samples and the conditions for the examination of the disputed goods by the experts, the undertakings of the taxpayers prior to the arbitration, and the drawing up of the judicial documents subsequent to the decision of the experts, shall all be determined by the Customs Administration.

The goods are the pledge for the duties. They cannot be withdrawn from Customs until after the payment, securing or guaranteeing of these duties. The duties shall be paid in cash and without discount in accordance with the provisions set forth in Article 124.

If the goods are subject to duties on the basis of gross weight, the weight of their packings shall be included in the dutiable weight. If the goods are subject to duties on the basis of net weight or if they are exempt from duties, the packings shall be subject separately to their own duties or exempt from duties according to whether or not such packings have a commercial value. If the goods are subject to ad valorem duties, the value on the basis of which the duties are determined must include both the value of the goods and the value of the packings together.

Irrespective of the provisions of Article 271, certain packings having a commercial value may be exempted from duties, either definitively or on condition of their re-exportation, either pursuant to tariff decisions or under the conditions provided for in Article 232.

The application of the provisions of Articles 136 to 139 shall entail carrying out the formalities of the detailed declaration and the formalities of inspection referred to in Articles 96 to 100 and 120 to 125.
The penalties applicable in matters of importation without declaration and importation by way of smuggling, false declarations, are set forth in Articles 358, 361 and 362.

Disputes arising between merchants and the Customs Administration regarding the kind, quality, value or origin of the goods shall be referred to the sworn experts officially accredited to the Administration.

The Higher Council of Customs shall draw up the list of sworn experts upon the proposal of the Director of General Customs, and this list shall include: 1- persons of standing in scientific, industrial, agricultural and commercial circles whose competence is guaranteed and who are chosen from a list drawn up on the basis of proposals by chambers of commerce and associations of merchants and industrialists, 2- officials of the public administrations, with the exception of the Customs Administration, who are qualified to perform the task of arbitrating in disputes falling within their competence. Vacancies arising by reason of death, revocation or resignation shall be filled successively by other experts whose names are proposed and who are appointed under the same conditions.

If a dispute arises between the Customs and merchants, of the kind referred to in Article 142, each of the two parties shall appoint an expert, after a sample of the goods that are the subject of the dispute has been taken, sealed and prepared for examination by the arbitrators. If it is impossible to take samples of the goods by reason of their nature, shape or size, the experts shall examine such goods in situ or shall content themselves with drawings or specifications thereof. The two experts shall make their decision and notify it to the two parties as soon as possible as from the date on which the dispute is referred to them.

However, taxpayers of reputed solvency (ability to pay) may be permitted to withdraw their goods immediately after their inspection and prior to the assessment and payment of duties, under the security of a guaranteed undertaking renewable every year. The secured duties shall be paid upon the expiry of a period of eight clear days commencing from the date of withdrawal of the goods. During this period, the receipts relating to these duties shall be kept with the accountants as cash values in the treasury. The taxpayers shall be required, in consideration of the delay in the collection of these duties and the possible risks to which the Treasury is exposed, to pay, in addition to those amounts, a fee amounting to one per thousand of their value, and this fee shall be divided into three equal parts, one of which shall be given to the Chief Customs Receiver, the second shall be divided equally between the Head of the Office who authorised the credit and the Chief Controller in charge of accounting at the Chief Receivership, whereas the third shall accrue to the Treasury.

Apart from the payment facilities provided for in Article 151, taxpayers who furnish exceptional guarantees of their solvency may be permitted to present, for each daily account the value of which is at least equivalent to one thousand five hundred piastres, guaranteed promissory notes maturing after four months. These notes shall be drawn up in the form prescribed for commercial bills and made out to the order of the Chief Customs Receiver, and their date shall be the very date of the assessment of the duties, and they shall be payable at the seat of the Chief Customs Receivership to which the office receiving these notes by way of payment is attached. The receipts relating to these duties shall be kept with the accountant as cash values in the treasury and must be converted into bills (drafts) within the eight clear days following their entry in the assessment register.

Guaranteed promissory notes maturing after the lapse of four months shall give rise to: a - delay interest at the rate of 8 per cent per annum, the value of which shall be added to the value of the duties due, and the value of the bill (draft) shall consist of both values, b - a fee of 1/3 per cent on the duties due, payable upon the deposit of the note, c - interest at the rate of 9 per cent per annum if not settled at maturity, and this interest shall be calculated on the total value of the bill from the date of maturity until the date of payment, without the need for formal notice. Both the delay interest and the 9 per cent interest shall in all cases accrue to the Treasury.

The Chief Receiver of Customs shall have the right, in order to safeguard the interests entrusted to him, to take a compulsory mortgage on the property of taxpayers or of their guarantors, under the conditions set forth in the third paragraph of Article 131 of Decision No. 3339, dated 12 November 1930, as amended by Decision No. 102/LR, dated 9 August 1932.

The Chief Receiver of Customs shall be the sole judge, under his pecuniary liability, of the possibility of granting credit for duties to a taxpayer and of fixing the value of such duties established. The value fixed in this manner must be submitted to the approval of the Director General of Customs and may not be exceeded in any case.

The Chief Receiver of Customs and the heads of offices shall be liable for the legality of the documents which they accept, for any fault they commit in exceeding the fixed credits, and for collecting the value of guaranteed bills.

The registrars of the Land Registry must, upon a mere written request from the Chief Receiver of Customs, furnish him with all information relating to the status of the real property owned by the taxpayers or their guarantors who apply to benefit from credit for duties or who have benefited from such credit.

Import declarations relating to goods imported under the conditions provided for in Article 8 shall be drawn up in the regulatory forms and under the special conditions determined by the Customs Administration. After the completion of the inspection, the Customs shall have the right to authorise the withdrawal of the goods, for which declarations have been submitted in this manner, immediately, before the payment of duties, under the conditions also determined by the said Administration.

Officers charged with collecting duties shall give a receipt therefor. Receipts shall be drawn up in the name of the declarant, as defined by Article 106, who is legally liable for the payment of the duties. They must state the name of the declarant, the number of the declaration, the details of the sums collected and, where appropriate, whatever the Customs deems useful to state therein. Liquidations for the refund of duties shall be drawn up in the name of the declarant, upon production of the receipt originally given to him, and the Customs shall be discharged from all obligation immediately upon paying to the declarant the sums unduly collected or refunded.

The proceeds of the addition of one-third of one per cent shall be divided into two equal parts, one of which shall be granted to the Principal Customs Receiver as compensation for the financial liability borne by him, and the second part shall accrue to the Treasury.

No persons shall be admitted to benefit from the credit (deferral of payment) of duties, under the liability of the Principal Customs Receiver, other than taxpayers of recognized solvency who furnish as security the guarantee of two merchants or property owners who are also solvent. The two guarantors referred to in the preceding paragraph may, if the taxpayer so wishes, be replaced by a financial institution accepted by the Customs Administration. The guarantor of secured duties is, in the view of the Customs, an actual taxpayer like the principal debtor; therefore, the Treasury shall have, over his movable property, the general priority right provided for in Article 356. If the secured duties are not paid at maturity, the Regional Director of Customs shall pursue the collection thereof under the conditions provided for in Article 323.

The Regional Director of Customs may, furthermore, issue a writ of constraint against the principal debtor or either of his two guarantors. The Regional Director of Customs shall issue this writ with a copy of the instrument establishing the debt of the Administration. In order for this order to be capable of service and enforcement, it must be endorsed by the Single Judge at the seat of the Regional Customs Directorate or the office in which the duties were secured. The endorsement must be placed on the original writ and not on the copy left with the person concerned upon service thereof. The Single Judge may not refuse to endorse the writ of constraint if it is regular in form. The taxpayer against whom a writ of constraint has been issued may file an objection. However, such objection shall not stay enforcement unless the taxpayer deposits a security equivalent to the value of the unpaid instruments. Writs of constraint shall have the effect of judicial judgments and shall be enforced as such, and shall authorize the use of all ordinary methods of enforcement against the movable and immovable property of the taxpayers.

In the event of the inability of either of the two guarantors to fulfill his undertaking, the principal debtor shall be required to present, within two days, another guarantor accepted by the Principal Customs Receiver, or failing that, to pay the duties owed by him, both those due and those not yet due.

No person shall be entitled to claim from the Customs Administration the refund of duties after three years have elapsed from the date of their payment. Securities, of whatever kind, shall be finally converted into duties and proceeds within the time limits and under the conditions determined by the Customs Administration if the concerned parties fail to submit, within the specified time limits, the proofs enabling the discharge of such securities. In all events, the portion exceeding the duties actually due (the balance) may not be claimed after three years have elapsed from the date of payment of the security, unless the delay in discharge is attributable to the Administration. Concessionary companies shall not be entitled to claim the recovery of duties deposited by way of security, and the Administration may undertake the final collection of the secured duties, if more than one year has elapsed between the date of receipt of the works and materials by the Directorate General of Control of Companies and the date of the application submitted to the said Directorate General for obtaining the certificate of use.

The Customs Administration shall be released towards taxpayers, after five years have elapsed from each completed year, from the obligation to keep the registers of receipts and other registers and papers pertaining to the said year, and it may not be compelled to produce these registers and papers if there are cases that are still at risk, even if the said registers and papers are necessary for investigation and for rendering judgments therein.

Prescription against the Treasury for the collection of duties and the privilege granted to the Treasury over the property of taxpayers for the collection of these duties are the subject of Articles 355 and 356.

Goods of foreign origin may be dispatched by way of ordinary transit or international transit, whether these goods have entered through the land or sea borders to exit directly, without taking the sea route, through other land or sea borders, or are dispatched by land from an office, warehouse, or free zone at the borders or in the interior to another office, another warehouse, or another free zone.
Entry and exit operations may only take place through the offices specially designated for that purpose.

Goods bearing false marks of Lebanese origin shall be excluded from transit, in application of Article 48, as well as goods excluded from transit by prohibition decisions taken in application of Article 42.

International transit is restricted to railway companies or authorised motor transport companies and under the responsibility of such companies, within the conditions and reservations determined by the Customs Administration.

The routes over which transport by international transit may be carried out shall be determined by decisions or administrative orders of the Higher Council of Customs, provided that conventions concluded with neighbouring countries are observed where applicable.

Goods consigned under the international transit regime shall in principle be exempted from the formalities relating to the detailed declaration and detailed examination. However, they may be subjected to these formalities, particularly in case of suspicion of fraud or where sealing is impossible. These goods shall be subject to the formalities of the summary declaration provided for in Articles 85 and 96 and to a summary examination.

The nature and extent of the undertakings that must be furnished by the companies referred to in Article 177, the conditions of sealing and escorting the goods, the preparation of railway wagons, motor vehicles and special containers intended for transport by international transit, the transhipment of goods from one means of transport to another en route, the establishment of customs offices, stores and warehouses by those companies, and all the various special provisions shall be determined by the decisions of the Higher Council of Customs or by its administrative orders designating the routes that may be followed for international transit, or shall be regulated by the Customs Administration.

Goods placed in a real warehouse or a real warehouse or a special real warehouse or a fictitious warehouse shall be deemed to be outside the territory of Lebanon with respect to the collection of duties. Upon exit of the goods from these warehouses, they may be declared for all the regimes applicable to directly imported goods, and the duties applicable thereto shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of Article 16 and Article 60.
All entrances to the stores allocated to the real warehouse or to the special real warehouse shall be locked with two different keys, one of which shall remain in the hands of the Customs Department.

Goods shall not be admitted into the actual warehouse, the private actual warehouse, or the fictitious warehouse except under an entry declaration drawn up in accordance with the conditions set forth in Article 96 and the following Articles. Inspection shall be carried out in accordance with the rules referred to in Article 120 and in the following Articles. For the purpose of supervising the movement of goods, the Customs shall keep a special register in which all operations relating thereto are recorded. The accounts entered in this register shall be balanced upon the expiry of the appointed term and may be closed abruptly in order to facilitate supervision by the Service, which may carry out surprise stocktakings to verify the conformity of the contents of the warehouses with the records.

The period of storage of goods is fixed at two years for the actual warehouse and at one year for the actual warehouse and for the fictitious warehouse. The Customs Administration may permit the extension of these time limits provided that the warehoused goods are preserved in good condition.

The conditions for the practical application of the regime of the actual warehouse, the private actual warehouse, or the fictitious warehouse, and the internal formalities which prove necessary for the proper operation of these warehouses, and which are not provided for by this Decision, shall be determined by the Customs Administration.

The regime of the actual warehouse may be put into operation in certain Lebanese ports or cities pursuant to decisions of the Higher Council of Customs designating the places in which it is established and the body entrusted with its management, and determining the conditions of such management, the conditions for the transfer of its concession, the rate of storage charges, and all special provisions relating to each warehouse.

Excluded from the regime of the actual warehouse are products bearing false marks or suspicious marks, types of gunpowder, explosives and similar substances, inflammable substances, goods showing signs of spoilage or damage, goods whose presence in the warehouse exposes it to dangers or which may harm the quality of other products, goods the preservation of which requires special installations, and goods in bulk.

Goods located in the actual warehouse may be assigned in favour of a third party; the assignment shall be recorded in the transfers column, under the names of the new owners, and discharged from the names of the assigning depositors in the registers provided for in Article 183.

Upon the arrival of the goods at the office of destination, they may be assigned all the destinations that would have been possible had these goods been imported directly through this office; the procedure that is to apply finally shall be declared, the declaration shall be drawn up, and the examination shall be carried out in accordance with the rules set out in Article 96 and the following articles.

If the goods are destined for a foreign country, the granting of discharge of guaranteed bonds or the documents replacing them shall be conditional, in principle, upon the production of a certificate from the customs of the country of destination proving that the said customs have taken delivery of the goods. The Administration shall fix a time limit for the submission of this certificate, and it shall be entitled to dispense with its submission and to replace it with other proofs which it shall be for it to determine.
Contraventions of the transit procedure are provided for in Articles 358, 362.

Ordinary transit shall take place by all routes without distinction, on the responsibility of the shipper who signs the transit undertaking. At the customs office of dispatch, the goods dispatched under the ordinary transit procedure shall undergo the same formalities mentioned in Article 96 and the following articles, relating to the detailed declaration, in the form of a guaranteed bond, and to the examination.

The consignment of goods dispatched under the ordinary transit procedure shall require either the deposit of customs duties and other duties by way of security or the signing of guaranteed bonds containing the guarantees determined by the Customs Administration, stating the office of destination and fixing the duration of transport in proportion to the distances. Where the matter relates to goods subject to internal or other duties, the transit principals shall be required to undertake to bear, in the event of non-completion of the transit, the legal penalties in accordance with the special legislation governing these duties, in addition to the customs pecuniary penalties.

Packages of goods dispatched under the ordinary transit procedure shall be subject, under the conditions determined by the Customs Administration, either to simple lead-sealing, or to simple lead-sealing with the taking of a sample of the goods, or to double lead-sealing with double packing. As for goods shipped in bulk, the Customs may authorise the lead-sealing of their containers under the conditions which it determines.

Upon the arrival of the goods at the office of destination, the guaranteed bond or the document replacing it shall be delivered to the Customs, which shall grant discharge only after verifying the integrity of the lead seals and the identity of the packages.

The goods must be re-presented to the Customs Department in compliance with every request made thereby and in the state in which they were upon their entry into the warehouse. Every shortage, even in the event of theft or disaster, shall be subject to the payment of duties, subject to observing the reservations provided for in Articles 199 and 206, and the interested parties may conclude insurance policies covering the price of the warehoused goods, with the customs duties added thereto.

The Customs may require the lead-sealing or sealing of the packages admitted into the private actual warehouse. This same right shall be reserved for the depositor, who shall bear the expenses of this operation in both cases.

The sole operations permitted in the private actual warehouse are the operations intended for the preservation of the goods. The depositor must submit a special application for this purpose indicating therein the nature of the work intended to be carried out, the hour chosen therefor, and the approximate duration of the operation; no authorization shall be granted to carry out any work whatsoever except in the continuous presence of a Customs officer. The applicant shall bear the travel expenses of this officer and his allowance.

Upon the expiry of the period of stay in the private actual warehouse, the provisions of the first paragraph of Article 189 shall apply, provided that, upon the sale of the goods, the amount of the customs duties shall be deducted from the net proceeds of the sale before any other amount.

The beneficiary of the status of the private actual warehouse must contribute to bearing the supervision expenses of the Customs Department by paying a lump sum determined by the Higher Council of Customs upon the proposal of the Director General of Customs. This allowance shall be paid in advance, and shall be subject to annual review. It shall vary according to the importance of the stores and the goods warehoused therein and the general expenses which the necessary verifications cause to the Customs Department.

A concession for a private actual warehouse may only be granted to merchants who provide all the desired guarantees relating to integrity and solvency. They shall sign a guaranteed undertaking within the conditions determined by the Customs Administration.

Every shortage for which the depositor is unable to provide acceptable explanations shall be considered a misappropriation from the private warehouse and shall be subject to the application of the penalties provided for in Article 358. The failure to re-present the warehoused goods is sufficient to characterize the misappropriation legally and to place the misappropriator under liability to the penalties referred to in the preceding paragraph. The Customs Department alone shall have the capacity to assess and determine whether the explanations given by the petitioner are sufficient to absolve him of liability and to charge him solely with the payment of the duties.

The dispatch of goods from an actual warehouse to another actual warehouse or to a customs office, and the re-exportation from the warehouse, shall take place under the guarantee of guaranteed bonds of undertaking. The signatories of these documents must return them endorsed with a certificate of entry into the actual warehouse or of placement for consumption. In the event of re-exportation, the discharge of these documents shall be conditional upon the completion of the formalities provided for in Article 171. And if these various formalities are not completed, the signatories of the guaranteed bonds of undertaking shall be subject to the penalties specified in Article 358 or Article 362, as the case may be.

Foreign goods may be deposited in a private actual warehouse in coastal or inland cities where a customs office exists and an actual warehouse does not exist. In the event of the abolition of the customs office in that centre, the accounts of the private actual warehouse must compulsorily be liquidated within one month.

The concession for a private actual warehouse shall be granted by virtue of an administrative order from the Higher Council of Customs after taking the opinion of the Director General of Customs. The stores must be in good condition and the openings must be equipped with tamper-proof locks, except for the entrance and exit doors closed with a double key within the conditions provided for in Article 182. The Customs Administration shall have the right to refuse any store that appears to it not to fulfil the necessary precautionary guarantees.

The stores designated for the private actual warehouse must be located within the perimeter of the city in which its establishment is licensed. The Customs Administration may narrow this limit to the extent it deems necessary to secure its interests.

The private actual warehouse shall be open to all goods subject to the tariff, regardless of origin, except for goods exempted from duties or prohibited, even if the importation of these latter goods has been specially licensed. Damaged goods shall also be deprived of the right to benefit from the private warehouse regime.

The customs duties payable on goods placed in the private actual warehouse shall be calculated on the basis of the quantities verified to exist upon their entry into the store. However, with regard to goods susceptible to drying out, if the depositor has requested the lead-sealing of the packages before their entry into the warehouse and if the Customs Administration has ascertained that the shortage verified upon removal results from natural causes only, the shortage may be exempted from duties. In the event of doubt as to the causes of the shortage, the Customs Administration may always demand the payment of the full duties applicable to the verified goods.

Upon the expiry of the period prescribed for the real warehouse, these goods shall be re-exported or subjected to duties. Other than in these two cases, a formal notice shall be served upon the depositor requesting the re-exportation of these products or the payment of the customs duties thereon. If the depositor does not fulfil this obligation within one month, the goods shall be sold and the proceeds of the sale, after deducting the value of the customs duties, storage expenses and others, shall be deposited, on trust, in the Customs fund, to be delivered to the owner thereof if he claims the same within the year commencing from the date of the day of the sale, and if he does not claim the same within this period, the proceeds of the sale shall accrue, finally, to the Public Treasury. Goods the importation of which is prohibited may only be sold for the purpose of their re-exportation.

Authorisation shall be granted in the real warehouse and under the continuous supervision of the Customs Service: 1- For the purpose of re-exportation: to mix foreign products with other foreign products or with national goods or with goods that have acquired this status. A special mark shall be placed on the coverings containing mixed products, and these coverings shall be placed after sorting in a special place of the warehouse. 2- For the purpose of all regimes: to strip of coverings, transfer from one container to another, assemble or divide parcels, and carry out all other operations intended for the preservation or improvement of the products. The completion of the operations set out in paragraph 1 and paragraph 2 shall be conditional upon the authorisation of the Customs Service. Mixed products a part of which comprises Lebanese produce shall only be subject to customs duty in respect of the part composed of foreign produce.

The customs duties chargeable on the goods placed in the real warehouse shall be levied on the quantities that entered therein. However, the deficiency ascertained in the real warehouse which results from natural or fortuitous causes shall be exempt from the duties.

If the loss of the goods placed in a real warehouse results from force majeure and is duly ascertained, the depositors shall be exempt from paying the duties. If the goods are insured, it must be proved that the insurance does not cover the value of the goods deposited in the real warehouse including the customs duties.

In the event of theft or damage following a disaster, or any other contingency, the depositor shall be exempt from the duties; however, the Customs shall remain absolved of all liability towards the depositor, and it cannot be held liable for the loss or damage sustained by the goods during their stay in the warehouse.
Individuals, industrial or commercial companies, municipalities, or chambers of commerce may be licensed, upon their request, to establish special actual warehouses for petroleum.

The right to establish these warehouses shall be granted by an administrative order from the Higher Council of Customs, upon the proposal of the Director General of Customs, following the approval of a committee composed of the Governor, the heads of the departments of Customs, Health, and Public Works, and the municipal authority within whose jurisdiction the establishment of such warehouses is sought. This committee shall determine the conditions for establishing the warehouses and the strength of the customs officers required for their supervision. The expenses of this supervision (the expenses of the officers, their housing, their offices, and their supplies) shall remain borne by the concessionaires. In Beirut, this committee shall include a representative of the Port Company and shall determine, in agreement with him, the amount of the royalty that the concessionaires must pay to that company in consideration of its right to the monopoly of storage.

Petroleum warehouses must fulfil the conditions imposed by local regulations with respect to dangerous, unhealthy, and inconvenient establishments. They must be isolated from every building and may not be established within the port zone itself. The openings of the warehouses, except for the entrances, must be fitted with iron gratings.

The sole operations permitted in petroleum warehouses are the changing of packagings, the transfer from one tank to another, and the decanting into new packagings. The tanks must be fitted with a depth gauge that records the quantity of petroleum present therein. The receptacles must not bear any mark whatsoever of a nature to mislead as to the origin or provenance of the products.

Every deficiency shall be subject to the payment of duties, subject to the application, where applicable, of the penalties provided for in Article 206. Every deficiency not exceeding 1 per cent for petroleum and 1.50 per cent for benzine and proved to result from natural causes, and every deficiency resulting from force majeure, shall be exempted from the payment of duty. In this latter case, if themineral oils are insured, it must be proved that the amount of the insurance covers the value of the mineral oils present in the warehouse exclusive of customs duties.
The provisions of Articles 194 and 203 shall apply to special petroleum warehouses.

Certain foreign goods, designated by administrative orders of the Supreme Council of Customs published in the Official Gazette, may be placed under the fictitious bonded warehouse regime, in commercial premises, in coastal and inland towns where a customs office exists, even if a real bonded warehouse or a private real bonded warehouse is located therein. The provisions relating to private real bonded warehouses set out in Articles 195 (second paragraph), 197, 199 (first paragraph), 200, 202, 203, 204, 205 and 206 shall apply to fictitious bonded warehouses.

In every seaport, a part of the dependencies of such port, called a "free zone", may be allocated and isolated from the customs regime. Save in the cases provided for in Article 219, goods of whatever kind and of whatever foreign or national origin may be brought into the free zone, where they shall be deemed to be outside the customs territory. Upon their entry, during their stay in the free zone and upon their exportation or re-exportation, such goods shall, subject where applicable to compliance with the provisions set out in the last paragraph of Article 227, be exempt from all customs and import duties or, where applicable, from export, consumption, quayage and octroi duties and all other duties other than those established in favour of the body charged with operating the free zone. The Customs Administration may not impose any time limit whatsoever with respect to the duration of stay of goods deposited in the free zone.

Free zones shall be established by decision of the Supreme Council of Customs upon the request of the bodies charged with operating the ports, or of duly incorporated companies, or of the local chambers of commerce or the municipalities, as the case may be, after the approval of the Council of Ministers. The decision establishing the free zone shall determine precisely: 1- The boundaries and area of the zone, which may comprise lands forming part of the domain of the State and private properties necessary for the establishment of such zone. 2- The part of the zone that must be allocated for lease to the interested parties. The manner of enclosing the free zone and the means for its supervision, which must be designed and constructed so as to guard against the fraudulent infiltration of goods benefiting from the privileges into the customs territory, as well as the hours of opening and closing, shall be determined in the regulations referred to in Article 216.

The body duly established and entrusted with operating a free zone shall be required to establish and operate, in the places falling within this zone, and within the terms of a regulation or a book of specifications approved in the decision of establishment, the roofed or unroofed warehouses, railway lines, and equipment necessary for storing, transporting, and handling goods. This body must bear all expenses necessary for these works. It shall also bear the additional expenses resulting from the supervision by the Customs Administration of the perimeter of the free zone. The operating body may be authorised, as compensation to it for the preparation expenses placed upon its charge as precedes, to levy, for its own benefit, fees or rental charges the nature and maximum limit of which shall be determined in the decision of establishment. Lessees of plots falling within the free zones shall be entitled to erect installations therein within the conditions specified in the regulation mentioned above.

Free zones may be abolished by decisions issued in the form in which the decisions of establishment are issued. These decisions shall specify the period within which goods must be removed from the free zone. The instruments establishing the free zones shall contain special provisions for all matters relating to the allocation of the lands, buildings, and equipment falling within the free zone, as well as to the measures that the return to the former state may lead to taking.

In free zones, it shall be permitted to carry out, in absolute freedom, all operations of conditioning, cleaning, sorting, mixing, classifying, shifting, sifting, dividing, roasting, pounding, breaking, crushing, and altering goods, and all other transformation operations that may be specified in the decision establishing the free zone or in subsequent decisions. In general, it shall be permissible to mix all foreign products with other foreign products or with national goods or goods having acquired this status.

When goods move from the free zone to the customs territory, such goods shall become subject to the tariff status provided for in Article 20. In all cases where the Customs Administration is unable to ascertain the origin of the goods with certainty, the maximum tariff duties shall be levied on such goods. With respect to goods subject to ad valorem customs duties, the value on which duties are levied shall be determined in accordance with the third paragraph of Article 60.
