In all cases, the adversary shall have the right to answer within a time limit equal to that from which the other party benefited.

The clerk shall draw up a roll of the cases scheduled for a single day and shall post a copy thereof on the notice board designated for announcements at the door of the court prior to the opening of the hearing.

The court clerk shall, within five days after the exchange of written pleadings and the expiry of the time limits prescribed therefor, submit the actions to the President in the order in which they were received for the purpose of fixing a hearing for the trial thereof.

The date of the hearing shall be notified without delay to each of the two parties. Each of them shall be entitled to request the adjournment of the trial to another date:

1- If the notification did not reach him three days prior to the hearing, unless there is a decision to abridge the time limit.

2- If he has an acceptable excuse justifying the adjournment.

The order of the President of the court abridging the time limits shall be entered at the foot of the statement of claim or the pleading, stating the date of the hearing where necessary. In this case, it shall be permissible to serve the statement of claim or the pleading and the summons to appear at the same time.

The provisions relating to the reply and its service shall not be observed.

The summons to appear shall include the following particulars:

1- The name of the court before which appearance is required.

2- The identity of each of the litigants and his domicile or place of residence.

3- The date of the hearing and the hour at which it is to be held.

4- The date of drawing up the document.

At the time appointed for the trial, the President shall consider whether the action is ready for oral argument or should be adjourned to a following one for a legitimate reason. At the first hearing, the judge shall endeavour to reconcile the two parties; if he succeeds in doing so, he shall draw up a record thereof which he shall sign with them and the clerk, and issue a decision ratifying it; the decision ratifying the reconciliation shall have the force of a judgment and shall not be subject to any avenue of recourse, and if the two parties do not reconcile, the trial shall be commenced and the judge may put to them all questions conducive to elucidating the truth.

The floor shall be given to the plaintiff, and then to the defendant. Each of them may be granted the right to reply to the defence of his adversary a second time. Each of them may content himself with referring to the pleadings and documents he has submitted.

The President may put such questions or make such observations as he deems useful. He may bar from speaking any party who proves unable to speak in a useful and proper manner, or who departs from the subject-matter of the action, breaches order, directs an insult at another, or impugns the right of a third party to the litigation.

Litigants and their representatives shall follow a course of gravity and moderation in their statements and shall observe respect for the judiciary. If they breach this duty, the judge shall caution them to respect it and shall bar them from speaking in the event of repetition.

Maintaining order in the hearing and conducting it are vested in its president. He may expel from the courtroom any person who disturbs the order of the hearing or adopts a disrespectful attitude towards the court. He may either refer him to the Public Prosecution or sentence him to a penalty of imprisonment for three days and a fine ranging from ten to fifty pounds. This decision shall be executed immediately and shall not be subject to any recourse.

The court may order of its own motion or upon the request of either party the striking out of offensive expressions contrary to public morals from any document of the pleadings, or require the person from whom it emanated to withdraw the document in its entirety and submit a new copy free from such expressions.

If an offence is committed while the hearing is in session, the president shall order that a record of the incident be drawn up, that such investigative measures as he deems appropriate be taken, and that the perpetrator be arrested and immediately referred to the Public Prosecution.

If the transgression or breach of the order of the hearing is committed by an advocate during the performance of his duty, the president of the court shall draw up a record of the incident, refer it to the Public Prosecution, and notify a copy thereof to the Bar Association.

The trial hearing shall be public unless the court sees fit, of its own motion or upon the request of one of the litigants or of the Public Prosecution, to hold it in camera in order to preserve public order or out of regard for public morals or the sanctity of the family. The decision to hold the trial in camera shall not apply to advocates wearing the robe of advocacy and shall not include the pronouncement of the judgment.

The litigants may agree to settle the dispute existing between them and record their agreement in the trial record and sign it, or have it signed by their authorised representatives.

The court may ratify their agreement if there is no legal impediment preventing the same.
Upon the conclusion of the pleading, the president of the court shall declare the trial closed and appoint a date for issuing the judgment in the action within the shortest possible time limit.

Each of the litigants may submit, after the closure of the trial and within a time limit of three days, a written memorandum to complete or correct certain points. The opposing party shall have a similar time limit to reply thereto from the date of notification.

If a new event occurs or an unknown fact becomes apparent after the conclusion of the trial and the pronouncement of the judgment is scarce, the court may decide of its own motion or upon the request of one of the two parties to reopen the trial and return the case to the pleading roll.

The clerk shall draw up a record for each action, which he shall sign at the end of each hearing together with the President of the Court, and in which he shall record the hour of the opening of the hearing and the hour of its conclusion, the names of the judges, the names of the litigants and their attorneys, the proceedings that took place, the facts that occurred, and the statements which the court orders to be recorded. The record of the trial shall be deemed an official instrument. A clerk who falsifies it in bad faith commits the offence of forgery of official documents.
It shall not be permissible to publish the debates taking place before the courts whenever they relate to cases of defamation and to personal status.
The judge may summon one of the two parties in person, upon the request of the other party or of his own motion, to seek clarification from him personally in the action.
The party summoned in person may object to his interrogation if the points of the interrogation do not relate to the action and are not admissible under Sharia.

If the party summoned in person has an excuse preventing him from attending, the judge may proceed in person, accompanied by the clerk, to the residence of this party and hear him in the presence of the adversary or in his absence after having duly summoned him, and draw up a record of the fact which he shall sign together with the clerk and the two parties or whichever of them attended.

If the party summoned in person refrains from answering the questions or from attending, the judge may assess whether the conduct of this party constitutes an admission by him of the matters regarding which his interrogation is requested or serves as a presumption of their validity that may be corroborated by other evidence.

If the two litigants are unable to bring their witnesses in person, each of them shall advance the expenses of his witnesses as estimated by the judge, and then the witnesses shall be summoned; if one of them fails to answer the summons without a legitimate excuse, the judge shall order that he be brought in and shall sentence him to a fine of one pound to five Lebanese pounds, provided that if, after his attendance, he presents an acceptable excuse, he shall be exempted from the fine.

If the plaintiff or the defendant fails to advance the expenses of his witnesses, or if the witnesses do not attend of their own accord where no advance has been made, he shall be deemed unable to prove his case, unless he adduces other means of proof.

The Sunni judge shall administer the oath to the witness prior to the giving of his testimony that he will uphold the truth (bi-an yaqum al-haqq). The Jaafari judge shall have the option in that regard.
The clerk shall record the statements of the witness in the minutes of the trial, and the witness shall authenticate them by his signature after they have been read out to him in public.

Witnesses residing outside the territorial jurisdiction of the court may be heard by commissioning the judge of the locality in which they are present to hear them in accordance with the procedures set forth above, and the absence of one of the parties after both have been summoned to appear before the commissioned judge shall not prevent the hearing of their testimony.

The judge shall have the right to assess the testimony, and shall have the option to investigate the probity (tazkiyah) of the witnesses secretly and publicly, or by either method, in order to ascertain their uprightness ('adalah).

In matters requiring the report of experts, if the two parties do not agree or if one of them is absent, the judge shall himself appoint the experts from among persons of competence.

The assessment of their report shall ultimately rest with him, and in maintenance (nafaqah) cases the judge may assess the maintenance himself after ascertaining the financial standing of both parties, or he may seek the assistance of experts according to the requirements of the circumstances of the action.

The judge alone shall have the power to select experts to assess maintenance for an orphan out of his funds held in custody in the Orphans' Fund, and he alone shall likewise have the power to select them to ascertain mental deficiency ('atah) and insanity, the fair market rental value (thaman al-mithl) of immovable properties belonging to orphans, the granting of leave to sell them for a Sharia necessity and the inspection thereof, the ascertainment of the values of immovable properties placed as security in lending out their funds, the inspection of waqf immovable properties upon their partition, and similar transactions that do not fall within an action or litigation. The expenses of the experts in all these cases shall be borne by the applicant, the minor, or the waqf, and the interested party must advance the amount of the expenses as determined by the judge.

If one of the litigants requests the oath of the other, the judge shall tender the formula thereof to him if he is present in person; otherwise, he shall summon him to appear in order to take it and shall warn him in the writ of summons that if he fails to appear to take the oath he will deem him to have refused (nakil), and if on the appointed day he fails to appear without a legitimate excuse he shall be deemed to have refused and judgment shall be rendered in favour of his adversary in his action.

If the litigant whose oath is requested resides outside the jurisdiction of the court in Lebanon or in one of the Arab countries, a Sharia judge or whoever acts in his place shall be delegated to administer the oath to him in the presence of his adversary or in his absence after summoning him in accordance with the rules.

However, if he resides in another country, the representative of the Lebanese Government shall be delegated to perform that.

If one of the two litigant parties dies during the trial, his heirs shall be brought to the court at the request of the other, and the trial shall be resumed from the point it had reached.

However, if one of the two litigant parties is a legal adversary, such as an endowment administrator (mutawalli) or a testamentary guardian (wasi), the standing to litigate shall be rectified by the Sharia methods.

If the plaintiff and the defendant fail to appear at the time appointed for the trial, the action shall be struck off the pleading roll. Striking off shall not result in the loss of the effect of the proceedings already carried out therein.

If one of the two parties or one of the members of either party fails to appear at the appointed time, it shall not be permissible for his adversary to submit any new claim unless he notifies him thereof and sends him a second summons granting him a time limit of ten days to reply.

If the defendant fails to appear without an acceptable legitimate excuse, his trial shall proceed by way of representation, and the court shall adjudge the claims of the plaintiff if it finds them lawful in form, admissible, and founded upon a valid basis.

If there are multiple defendants and one or some of them appear at the appointed time while the others fail to appear, the court must summon this latter group for a second time. If their failure to appear continues, the trial shall be deemed adversarial with respect to all.

The defendant or one of the members of the defending party may request the invalidation of the trial or judgment on the merits upon the failure of the plaintiff to appear at the first hearing of the trial; and if there are multiple plaintiffs and some of them fail to appear at the trial and the obligation claimed is indivisible, the request for invalidation shall not be accepted, and instead the merits of the dispute shall be examined.
It shall not be permissible to proceed with the trial in the absence of one of the two parties except after the lapse of one full hour from the opening of the hearings.
If the default of one of the two parties from the trial occurs after his attendance at any previous hearing, the trial shall be deemed adversarial.

The opposition shall be submitted to the court that issued the judgment pursuant to a summons in which the provisions governing the drawing up thereof are observed. It must contain the grounds upon which the opposition is based, under penalty of dismissal.

The time limit for opposition is fifteen days from the date of service. The notice of service must contain a warning of the forfeiture of the right of opposition after the expiry of the aforementioned time limit.
Save for cases of expedited execution, the opposition stays execution if it is registered in accordance with the rules within the legal time limit.

Every judgment in absentia whose service is not requested and whose fees are not paid within three months from the date of its pronouncement shall lapse by prescription. This lapse shall not extend to the formalities and proceedings prior to the judgment.
A judgment rendered pursuant to an opposition is not subject to a new opposition.

By agreement of the two parties, the action may be stayed for a maximum period of one year. This stay shall have no effect on any mandatory time limit prescribed by law for any measure. It is also permissible to agree on striking the action off the pleading roll.

In cases other than those in which the law provides for the stay of the action, the court may order the stay thereof if the course of justice requires suspending its judgment upon the determination of another issue. Once the cause ceases, the course of the action shall be resumed of its own motion or upon the request of one of the two parties, and from the point at which it stood stayed.

The course of the action shall be interrupted:

1- By the death of one of the litigants, or by his loss of capacity to litigate, or by the cessation of the capacity of the person who was pursuing the action on his behalf, unless it is ready for judgment.

2- By any event of force majeure capable of disrupting the trial proceedings.

The interruption of the course of the action shall entail the suspension of the time limits running against both parties and the nullity of the proceedings carried out during the interruption. This interruption shall have no effect unless it is notified through the court to the adversary of the party to whom it relates.

The course of the action shall be resumed by the appearance of the person who has become qualified to litigate at the trial hearing scheduled for examining the action, or by a summons served by him upon his adversary to appear, or by his being summoned to do so by the latter. The court shall rule expeditiously on any dispute arising from an application to resume the course of the action.

The court may grant a party whose representative's mandate has terminated by his death, dismissal therefrom, or withdrawal therefrom a time limit not exceeding fifteen days in order to appoint a new representative.

If the appellant or the objecting party abandons his action for a period of two years from the last valid procedural act, the court must rule that the action has lapsed if the adversary requests that prior to any discussion on the merits and the appellant or objecting party does not present an acceptable excuse.

If the plaintiff abandons his action at first instance without pursuing it for a period of two years without a legitimate excuse, it shall lapse and all formalities carried out therein shall become null and void by operation of law. The judge shall decide the lapse in chambers either of his own motion or upon the request of the defendant, and the judge's decision in this regard shall be subject to objection.

The lapse shall be annulled if it is established that the abandonment was due to a legitimate excuse or that the lapse was effected contrary to the law.

The period for the lapse of the action, in the event of the interruption of its course, shall begin from the day on which notice of the existence of the action is given to the heirs of the deceased, or to the representative of the person lacking capacity, or to the person who replaces the one whose capacity has ceased.

An application for a ruling that the action has lapsed shall be submitted by way of a petition to the court seized thereof by any of the plaintiff's adversaries having an interest. It may also be submitted in the form of a plea in bar if the plaintiff pursues his action after the expiry of the period. If one of the defendants submits it, the remaining defendants shall benefit therefrom.

In the event of a plurality of plaintiffs, it shall not be admissible unless it is directed against all of them.
The period prescribed for the lapse of the action shall run against all persons, even if they lack legal capacity, have diminished legal capacity, or are missing persons.

The plaintiff may, at any stage of the trial, waive the right he claimed or the action he instituted. The party in whose favour judgment was rendered may waive the judgment rendered in his favour. This waiver shall entail the waiver of the right established thereby.

Waiver of the right shall terminate the action. The plaintiff shall bear the costs of the trial and the compensation due to his adversary where applicable. The latter shall be handed the documents pertaining to the claimed right.

If a waiver occurs before the trial hearing is scheduled and before the defendant submits any answer in the case, the President of the Court may accept it and declare the action lapsed without the need to summon the latter or notify him of the waiver.

However, if the waiver occurs after the trial hearing is scheduled, the court shall examine the case and any dispute that may arise regarding the waiver.

If the waiver is limited to the action, it may not be accepted except with the consent of the adversary. Excluded from this is a waiver occurring before the defendant submits his claims, or where such claims are based on a plea of lack of jurisdiction, referral of the case to another court, nullity of the action, or another claim that precludes proceeding with hearing it.
Waiver of the action shall result in the lapse of the action and the lapse of all proceedings, provided that the costs remain borne by the plaintiff.
The rules of procedure before the Supreme Court shall be the same rules of procedure as before the Court of First Instance, with the following modifications:
An appeal shall be lodged with the Supreme Court pursuant to a statement of claim in which the rules prescribed for an initial statement of claim are observed.
The appeal must contain a statement of the appealed judgment, the date of its service, and the grounds of appeal.

The appellant must, under penalty of dismissal of the appeal in form, attach to the appellate summons a complete certified copy of the appealed judgment of first instance, a receipt for having deposited with the Treasury chest a security in the amount of ten thousand Lebanese pounds, and a receipt for the payment of all legal fees determined by the registry of the court in accordance with the law, and if the appellate summons is issued by several appellants united by a community of interest or of defence, a single security and single fees shall suffice.
The fine shall be confiscated for the benefit of the State Treasury in the event that the appeal is dismissed for any reason whatsoever other than its withdrawal.

The time limit for appeal shall be thirty days for all judgments and eight days for decisions of prohibition from travel starting from the date of their issuance if they were rendered in the presence of the parties.

The appellate summons shall be lodged with the registry of the Court of Appeal or the registry of the court that issued the judgment within the appointed period.

It shall be deemed submitted on the date of its lodging with the registry of the court fulfilling all the conditions stipulated in the amended Article 224".

After the lodging of the summons, the President shall appoint a counsellor entrusted with supervising the exchange of pleadings and the completion of deficiencies capable of preparing the action for oral argument and judgment

The respondent may, within a time limit of fifteen days from the date of being served with the appellate summons, submit a cross-appeal by means of a pleading containing the grounds of his challenge to the judgment.

The appeal transfers the action and brings it before the Supreme Court in the state in which it was prior to the issuance of the appealed judgment, to the extent of the claims covered by the appeal.

With the exception of judgments subject to expedited enforcement, the appeal stays the enforcement of the appealed judgment, provided that it has been duly registered within its legal time limit.

The Supreme Court shall hear the action on the basis of the facts, pleas and defences submitted before the Court of First Instance, and on such new evidence, pleas and defences as are submitted to it, even if they result in changing the cause of the claim and adding thereto.

No new claims may be submitted on appeal unless they aim to effect a set-off or constitute a defence to the original claim, or relate to wages, compensation for delay, salaries and all other accessories falling due after the submission of the original claims before the Court of First Instance, and such damages as accrue after the issuance of the appealed judgment.

Nevertheless, a claim arising directly from the original claim or aiming at the same result, even if based on another cause, as well as a claim for a coercive fine, a claim for expedited enforcement, and a claim submitted by a third party or directed against a third party without prejudice to the conditions of intervention, may be admitted.
The provisions governing waiver of the action shall apply to waiver of the appeal, and waiver of the right of appeal shall be valid prior to the issuance of the judgment.
From the moment the appeal is lodged, the Court of First Instance shall be precluded from hearing the interpretation of the judgments issued by it.
If the appealed judgment does not include a decision on the merits of the action, the Supreme Court must, when setting it aside, evoke the case and hear it.

Judgments in the Supreme Court shall be issued by a President and two Associate Judges, either unanimously or by a majority of opinions. In the latter case, the dissenting judge must state his dissent in his own handwriting and sign at the foot of the original of the judgment. The judgment shall be drafted by the President of the Court or by such of its members as he designates, and shall be signed by the members of the Court before it is pronounced at the hearing, and the clerk shall sign it immediately thereafter under pain of nullity."

The President, or such of the members as he delegates, shall read out the judgment in a public hearing in the presence of the adjudicating bench, and the judges who sat during the trial proceedings - with the exception of the Public Prosecutor - must attend the reading of the judgment.

If, between the commencement of the deliberations and the public reading of the judgment, an impediment arises preventing the attendance of one of the judges of whom the Court was composed, the deliberations must be repeated before the newly constituted Court.

The Supreme Court shall examine without bringing the litigants together:

1- Judgments referred to it without appeal and issued against minors, interdicted persons, the Public Treasury (Bayt al-Mal), and the Waqf, and judgments issued against absent persons for the annulment of marriage and separation.

2- Appealed judgments issued in actions for maintenance, nursing wages, custody, service, and the delivery of minors to the custodian. If it finds the judgment of first instance to be in conformity with Sharia provisions and legal rules of procedure, it shall uphold it; otherwise, it shall summon both parties and rule on the action in their presence.
The judgment shall be issued "In the Name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful".
The court may pronounce the judgment publicly forthwith upon the conclusion of the trial or adjourn that to a subsequent hearing.

The judgment shall contain:

1- A statement of the court that issued it and its date.

2- A statement of the names of the judge or judges who issued it.

3- A statement of the names of the litigants, a summary of their claims, the factual evidence and legal arguments advanced, the stages of the action, and the trial proceedings therein.

4- The grounds of the judgment and its operative part. And the legal and Sharia articles relied upon, and whether it was issued in the first or last instance.

5- The signature thereon of the judge or judges who issued it and the clerk before it is read out at the public hearing.
The judgment may include the granting of a time limit for the performance of the obligation.

First: The Sunni judge shall issue his judgment in accordance with the provisions stipulated in the resolutions issued by the Supreme Islamic Sharia Council on the personal status of Sunni Muslims and relating to the organisation of the religious affairs of the denomination pursuant to Article 1 of the provisions of Legislative Decree No. 18/55 as amended by the resolution issued on 21 Dhu al-Qi'dah 1386 corresponding to 2 March 1967, and the Law issued on 28 May 1956 and published in the Official Gazette on 30 May 1956, Issue (22).

In the absence of any text, the Sunni judge shall refer to the Ottoman Family Rights Law issued on 25/10/1917; otherwise, he shall rule in accordance with the most preponderant opinions of the school of Imam Abu Hanifa.

Second: The Jaafari judge shall issue his judgment in accordance with the Jaafari school, and with such provisions of the Family Law as are compatible with this school.

(Article 2 of Law 177 /2011: The provisions of this amendment shall apply to actions that are still pending in first instance and on appeal, and the provisions of this amendment shall not apply to actions in which final and binding judgments have been issued.)

A judgment shall be subject to expedited execution:

1- Without need for a declaration thereof in the judgment.

a- In imposing maintenance for the wife, descendants or ascendants.

b - In delivering a minor or suckling infant to his female custodian.

2- With the requirement of a declaration thereof in the judgment:

a- When the lawsuit is based on an official deed or on an ordinary deed acknowledged by the adversary or on an admission before the session of the judge.

b - In the remuneration for nursing, custody and service.

c- In lawsuits of guardians to annex youths and young girls to them.

And security shall not be required in the cases set forth in the second paragraph of this Article unless the judge orders it in the judgment.
The judge shall have the right, in urgent cases not mentioned in the preceding Article, to order expedited execution, and in this case security must be imposed.
Sharia judgments shall be executed through the Execution Department in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to execution.
A judgment shall be contentious if rendered in an existing dispute between adversaries, and ex parte if rendered without any dispute.

A dispositive judgment is that which decides on the merits of the dispute or on one of its aspects or on a plea or defence relating thereto. And a dispositive judgment shall be final if the litigation in its entirety is terminated therein.

Every decision rendered prior to deciding on the merits of the dispute dealing with one of the measures of investigation or proof or any other measure that facilitates the resolution of the case shall be preparatory.

Every decision ordering the taking of a precautionary measure or an urgent measure called for by the state of the dispute or the circumstances of the lawsuit during the examination thereof shall be provisional.

The judge, when examining other cases of nullity resulting from a violation of formal rules and trial procedure, shall take into consideration the circumstances of the case and the interest of the litigants, and if rectifying the trial or the procedure is possible, the judge may order every measure capable of remedying the defect or flaw within a specified time limit.
The judge may award fair compensation against any person who fails to carry out the rectification assigned to him within the fixed time limit or who causes the defect through his negligence.

Save for matters relating to public policy, nullity shall cease either by a waiver from the person in whose interest it was prescribed to invoke it, or by any act emanating from him that indicates that he considers the measure valid.

No litigant may invoke the nullity of any measure resulting from his own act or the act of his representative, or rely upon a breach of procedures prescribed in the interest of his adversary, except in cases relating to public policy.
The nullity of a trial procedure shall not entail the nullity of the procedures that preceded it or those that followed it if they are independent of it.
The nullity of a judgment may only be ruled upon by way of challenging it in accordance with the legal rules.

The court may rectify of its own motion or upon the request of one of the litigants any purely material clerical or arithmetical errors occurring in the operative part of its judgment, after summoning the litigants and hearing them, unless it has been divested of the case by the exercise of one of the means of recourse. It shall make the rectification on the original copy of the judgment and order that it be recorded in the margin of the rectified judgment. The clerk shall mention the rectification on every copy delivered and shall recover the copies previously delivered in order to destroy them.

If the court exceeds the limits of its jurisdiction in this regard, its decision shall be subject to challenge by the means admissible against the judgment that is the subject of the rectification. However, a decision rejecting the rectification may not be challenged, and independently.

Every litigant having an interest may request the court that issued the judgment to interpret any ambiguity or obscurity occurring in its operative part. The rules governing the filing of an action shall be followed in his request.
A judgment issued by way of interpretation shall be deemed complementary to the interpreted judgment and subject to the avenues of recourse applicable to that judgment.
Upon issuing judgment, the court shall, of its own motion, award the costs of the action against the unsuccessful party.

Where there are several unsuccessful parties, it may apportion the costs among them equally or in proportion to the interest of each of them, at its discretion.

They shall not be jointly and severally liable therefor save by virtue of their joint and several liability in their principal obligation.

Where each of the litigants fails in some of his claims, the court may apportion the costs between them at its discretion or order one of them to bear them. The apportionment shall be made in equal shares if the judgment omits to specify the proportion thereof.
The costs of intervention shall be awarded against the intervener if his application is dismissed.

The costs shall include all judicial fees, stamps, experts' fees, judges' travel expenses, all other judicial disbursements, and advocates' fees.

In assessing the fees, regard shall be had to the difficulties of the action and its importance. Such assessment shall have no effect save as between the litigants.

The clerk of the court shall specify the costs at the foot of the enforceable copy of the judgment or by virtue of a separate schedule. Interested parties may object to the taxation of costs by a petition submitted to the President of the court within a time limit of eight days from the date of service of the statement of costs.

The President of the court shall examine the matter after hearing the parties in interest, and his decision shall not be subject to any recourse.

Any party to litigation whose condition does not enable him to pay the fees, fines, and other judicial costs payable by him in respect of an action, investigation, proceeding, or transaction before the various courts and enforcement departments may apply for legal aid.
Legal aid shall be granted to insolvent Lebanese nationals or foreign nationals residing in Lebanon, provided that the law of their country grants Lebanese nationals the same right.

An application for legal aid shall be exempt from any fee or stamp duty and shall be submitted by a petition to the court competent to hear the action or to the head of the department in charge of the enforcement proceedings. The date for hearing the application shall immediately be set at the foot of the petition, and a copy thereof shall be sent to the Public Prosecution and to the opposing party to state their observations.

The petitioner shall attach to his application:

1- A certificate from the financial departments indicating the direct taxes that he pays.

2- A certificate from the administrative authority having jurisdiction over his place of residence showing his family status, his living conditions, his income, and his inability to pay the costs.

If the applicant is a foreign national, he must also produce a certificate from the representative of his State proving his insolvency and the legal text that grants Lebanese nationals legal aid in his country.

The court may, even if the insolvency of the applicant is established, reject the application when it is manifestly evident to it:

1- That the action is unfounded or has lapsed by the expiry of the statutory time limits.

2- That there is an intent of malice and procrastination in the application.

The decision of the court accepting or rejecting the application shall not be subject to any recourse except an appeal by the Public Prosecution, and the judge of first instance must notify the Public Prosecution of the judgments he issues regarding legal aid.

A recipient of legal aid who has won the action shall continue to enjoy legal aid with respect to the service and enforcement of the judgment and to pleading when avenues of recourse are invoked by his opposing party.

However, if the recipient of legal aid loses the action, he must submit a new application to the authority competent to hear the recourse brought against the judgment rendered against him.
Upon the mere submission of an application for legal aid, the running of the statutory time limits shall be suspended until the issuance of the decision thereon.

When the application is granted, the recipient of legal aid shall be exempted from paying fees of any kind whatsoever and from fines, and the State Treasury shall advance the fees of experts and all other costs due to third parties in accordance with the regulations in force.

The court may, of its own motion or upon the request of the Public Prosecution, the representative of the State Treasury, or one of the opposing parties, and after summoning the recipient of legal aid, revoke its decision:

1- If the condition of the recipient of legal aid has changed and he has become able to pay the costs.

2- If it appears that the statements that were taken as a basis for granting the application were forged or untrue.

In this latter case, the recipient of legal aid shall immediately be ordered to pay the advanced costs and shall be referred to the Public Prosecution for criminal prosecution where appropriate.

Legal aid ceases upon the death of the recipient of legal aid without such cessation having any retroactive effect.

The heirs may, where necessary, submit a new application.

The clerk of the court shall draw up a statement of the fees and expenses due to the Treasury and advanced by it within a period of ten days from the date the judgment becomes final, indicating therein the number of the action or proceeding, the date of the judgment, and the identity of the party ordered to pay the expenses, and shall send a copy thereof to the Ministry of Finance. The President of the Supreme Court may penalise the clerk for his negligence with a fine ranging from five to fifty pounds.

The Treasury may recover from the party ordered to pay the expenses the fees and amounts which it advanced on behalf of his opponent who received legal aid, in accordance with the procedures followed for the collection of direct taxes, and it may recover in the same manner the fees and expenses awarded against the recipient of legal aid if his financial condition improves and he becomes able to settle them.
The Treasury shall have a right of priority in respect of the expenses due to it over all other holders of debts and rights.
The right of the Treasury to claim the expenses shall lapse by prescription upon the expiry of five years from the date the judgment becomes final.

A judicial judgment carries the authority of res judicata, which precludes the renewal of argument regarding its operative part, subject to the preservation of the avenues of recourse and applications relating to interpretation and difficulties of execution.
The existence of res judicata requires the fulfilment of the identity of the litigants, the identity of the cause, and the identity of the subject matter.

The following shall be exempted from the principle of the relativity of res judicata:

1- Matters relating to joint and several or indivisible obligations in the cases provided for in the Civil Law or the Commercial Law.

2- Matters relating to the successors of the litigants.
A judicial judgment alters the rule of limitation that was running in respect of the matter in dispute.

A judgment shall in principle be deemed declaratory of a right, and its effects shall therefore relate back to the date on which that right was claimed before the judiciary; a judgment shall not be deemed constitutive of a right except where it results in the creation of a legal status that did not exist prior to its issuance, in which case its effects shall commence from the date of its pronouncement, such as judgments issued in matters of enforcement, capacity, and a person's civil status, or from the occurrence of its grounds, such as interdiction, for example.

A judicial judgment shall have enforceable effect, provided that it may not be enforced until it has been served upon the judgment debtor; exempted from service are decisions relating to investigation, evidentiary measures, and all other cases provided for by law or in the decision itself on the grounds of necessity or other valid cause.

A judgment may not be compulsorily enforced for so long as it remains subject to ordinary means of recourse, unless it is coupled with expedited enforcement. Conservatory measures may, however, be taken pursuant thereto. Ordinary recourse shall have no suspensive effect on enforcement unless it is lodged within its statutory time limit.

An engrossment valid for enforcement must bear at its foot a formula indicating the same, together with the seal of the court and the signature of the clerk.

Such engrossment shall not be issued unless the judgment is enforceable, and shall be delivered to the party who benefits from its enforcement.

A second engrossment may not be delivered to the same party except in the event of the loss of the first and against security.

The applicant shall be exempted from giving security if the judgment debtor acknowledges that the judgment has not been enforced.

The security shall lapse upon the lapse of the judgment or upon its enforcement without opposition on the part of the latter.

The president of the court that issued the judgment shall hear all disputes relating to the delivery of the first or second enforceable engrossment, pursuant to an action brought in accordance with the rules governing summary proceedings by one of the litigants against the other.

The means of recourse against judgments are divided into two categories:

1- Ordinary means, which are opposition and appeal.

2- Extraordinary means, which are retrial, third-party opposition, and proceedings against judges for liability.

The exercise thereof is conditional upon the person exercising them having an interest therein.

Preparatory judgments and definitive non-final judgments shall not be subject to challenge except together with the final definitive judgment, provided that the plea of inadmissibility is raised before arguing on the merits, with the exception of the following:

1- Judgments issued staying the action.

2- Provisional judgments or judgments coupled with expedited enforcement.

3- Judgments ordering the liquidation of an estate.
A judgment deciding one of the aspects of the action may not be enforced before the judgment becomes irrevocable in respect of the other aspects, unless it is coupled with expedited enforcement.

The time limit for a recourse shall run from the day following service unless the law provides otherwise. With respect to the Public Prosecution, however, the time limit shall run from the day following the pronouncement of the judgment in its presence or from the date of service upon it of the judgment of the single judge of first instance. Service shall be effected upon the judgment debtor in person or at his actual or elected domicile, and the time limit shall run against the person upon whom the judgment has been served.

The running of the time limit for a recourse shall be interrupted by the death of the judgment debtor, and the time limit shall not begin to run anew except from the date of service of the judgment upon the heirs.

Service upon them may be effected at the elected domicile of their decedent. The running of the time limit shall be suspended throughout the time required to decide upon an application for legal aid, and the running of the time limit shall then resume as from the date of issuance of the judgment on the legal aid.
Failure to observe the time limits for a recourse shall entail forfeiture of the right thereto. The court shall rule thereon of its own motion.

The effect of a recourse shall be confined to the party who lodged it and his opponent therein. Nevertheless, a person against whom the time limit for a recourse has expired or who has acquiesced in the judgment may challenge it during the examination of the recourse lodged by one of the judgment debtors, joining him, in the following cases:

1- If the judgment was issued in an indivisible matter or in a joint and several obligation.

2- If the law requires that he be joined as a party with the person lodging the recourse.

3- If the defence of the guarantor and of the party claiming under the guarantee is united in the original action in which judgment was rendered.

All judgments issued by the Sharia courts shall be subject to appeal:

1- At first instance with respect to the value of the claim.

2- In cases of unassessed value or incapable of assessment.

3- In cases of lack of jurisdiction, prescription and res judicata whereby the court is divested of the action.

Decisions and instruments issued by the Sharia courts upon application and without adversary proceedings against anyone in matters of determination of heirs, Sharia authorisation and other matters cannot be appealed, but may be challenged by way of an original action.

It shall be permissible for the Public Prosecutor before the Supreme Court to request that Court to annul the said decisions if they are contrary to Sharia or legal provisions.

Judgments rendered against minors, interdicted persons, the Public Treasury (Bayt al-Mal), and endowment (waqf), as well as judgments rendered against absent persons for the annulment of marriage and separation, shall not be enforceable until they have been confirmed on appeal. If the interested parties do not appeal within the legal time limit, the court shall, within fifteen days from the expiry of that time limit, transmit the case file to the Supreme Court, which shall rule thereon as a matter of urgency; otherwise, the clerk responsible shall be liable to a fine of ten thousand to twenty-five thousand Lebanese pounds. As for judgments for maintenance awarded to minors and interdicted persons out of their own property, if the maintenance for a single person exceeds twenty thousand Lebanese pounds per month, the amount in excess of this value shall not be enforceable until the judgment has been confirmed on appeal.

Article 11: The pecuniary fine set forth in the first paragraph of Article 299 is amended as follows: "from ten thousand to twenty-five thousand Lebanese pounds". - And the second paragraph of the same Article is amended as follows: "if the maintenance for a single person exceeds twenty thousand Lebanese pounds per month, the amount in excess of this value shall not be enforceable until the judgment has been confirmed on appeal".

The time limit for appeal shall commence from the date of service of the judgment if the judgment is deemed adversarial or rendered in absentia not subject to opposition, and from the date of expiry of the time limit for opposition if the judgment is rendered in absentia and subject to opposition.
The time limit for appeal shall be suspended by the death of the party against whom judgment was rendered and shall not resume running until the date of service upon the heirs.

Regardless of the value of the action, judgments may also be appealed on the ground of a substantial nullity therein, or if they are contrary to a prior judgment rendered between the litigants in the same dispute, and if they are rendered on a plea of lack of jurisdiction.

Execution difficulties arising from an appellate decision confirming the judgment of first instance shall be adjudicated by the court of first instance that rendered the judgment, and if it modifies the judgment, they shall be adjudicated by the Supreme Court.

Litigants may petition for a retrial in respect of judgments rendered at last instance by the courts of first instance and by the Supreme Court in the following cases:

1- Where fraud has been committed by the prevailing adversary or by his representative which influenced the rendering of the judgment.

2- Where the judgment was based on a document proven to be forged by the confession of the perpetrator or by a final and conclusive judgment, or was based on testimony, an expert's report, or a translation conclusively proven after the rendering of the judgment to be forged, or was based on a prior decision that was subsequently amended or annulled.

3- Where the petitioner obtained, after the rendering of the judgment, documents decisive to the dispute which his adversary had withheld or prevented from being submitted.

4- Where the judge ruled on matters not claimed.

5- Where the judgment omitted to rule on one of the claims.

The petition for retrial shall be submitted to the court that rendered the judgment by way of a summons following the general rules, stating the date of the contested judgment, the date of its service, the grounds for retrial, and the claims, and accompanied by a receipt evidencing payment of a fine of fifty pounds before the court of first instance and seventy-five pounds before the Supreme Court.

The time limit for the petition for retrial shall be thirty days starting from the date of service of the adversarial judgment, or from the date of expiry of the time limit for opposition to the judgment in absentia, or from the day the fraud became apparent, or the forgery was proven, or the documents decisive to the dispute were discovered, provided that their discovery is established by written evidence.

The respondent may, within a time limit of fifteen days from the date of being served with the petition for retrial, submit a counter-petition for retrial by way of a pleading containing the grounds and the claims.

A petition for retrial may be submitted incidentally before a court other than the court that rendered the contested judgment if it is of equal degree thereto, provided that the time limit prescribed for submitting a principal petition has not expired.
The fine shall be forfeited in the event that the retrial is dismissed, and the petitioner may be ordered to pay compensation where appropriate.

When the court admits the retrial, it shall rule to annul the contested judgment, refund the fine, and adjudicate the merits of the dispute.

The admissibility of the retrial and the merits may be adjudicated by a single judgment.

A party who has petitioned for a retrial may not submit a new petition against the judgment rendered as a result of his challenge, whereas the other party shall have the right to a retrial if he did not discover the ground until after the first petition.

An application for retrial shall not entail a stay of execution of the contested judgment; however, the court may order a stay of execution or the provision of security if there are strong grounds justifying the same.
The court is only required to reconsider the claims covered by the retrial.
With respect to drawing up the summons, service, time limits, exchange of pleadings and trial, the rules in force before the court to which the application for retrial is submitted shall be observed.

Any person who was neither a party to the action nor represented therein may contest the judgment rendered therein within ten years by way of third-party opposition, provided that an interest exists. He may also invoke the relativity of res judicata or avail himself of any other avenue of recourse.

An heir creditor shall not be deemed represented by the person from whom he inherits or by his debtor if the judgment resulted from fraud, deceit or collusion directed against him. In such case, he may contest the judgment rendered against his predecessor in title.

Creditors and debtors under a joint and several or indivisible obligation may file a third-party opposition against a judgment rendered against another creditor or debtor:

1- If they prove that such judgment fraudulently prejudiced their rights.

2- If they have a personal ground or defence.
Where the right to litigate is reserved by law exclusively to a specific person or several specific persons, any person deprived of this right may not resort to third-party opposition.

Third-party opposition shall be submitted to the court that rendered the judgment in accordance with the general rules followed in the action.

It shall not be admitted unless accompanied by a fine equivalent to the fine prescribed for retrial.

Where a judgment is invoked in the course of a pending dispute, an incidental third-party opposition may be lodged against such judgment by way of a pleading if the court hearing the dispute is equal to or higher than the court that rendered the judgment; otherwise, it shall be submitted to the court that issued the judgment by way of a principal action. In the latter case, the court hearing the dispute may decide to proceed with the action or stay it until the third-party opposition is adjudicated.
The opposing party must establish proof that the opposed judgment was rendered unlawfully.

A third-party opposition devolves the action before the court, thereby empowering it with the right to hear it anew, and no one shall benefit from the judgment rendered therein except the person who submitted it, unless the law provides otherwise.

The effects of the judgment rendered in a third-party opposition shall be confined to the opposing party, except in the case of indivisibility where it is impossible to enforce both judgments together.
Opposition to a judgment shall not stay enforcement. However, the court may order such stay for serious reasons, with or without security.

An action for liability against a judge shall be permissible:

1- If fraud or deceit was committed by him in his work, or if he committed bribery.

2- If he committed a denial of justice.

3- If the law imposes upon him, by reason of his negligence, a liability obliging him to pay compensation.

The State shall be liable for the damages awarded. And he has a right of recourse against him.

A judge's denial of justice shall be established by his refusal to perform the required act or to adjudicate the case after being served with formal notice through the court clerk pursuant to two petitions from the interested parties, separated by a time limit of three days in respect of ex parte orders, urgent cases, and conservatory measures, and eight days in respect of other cases.
A clerk who refuses to effect service shall be subject to the penalty of dismissal.

The action for judicial liability set forth in the first paragraph of Article 325 of this Law shall lapse upon the expiry of two months from the day of notification of the judgment or from the day of becoming aware of the ground upon which it is based if it is discovered after the issuance of the judgment.

The action for judicial liability shall be submitted to the Supreme Court by summoning the defendant or defendants in accordance with the ordinary rules of procedure. The plaintiff must produce such documents as he has in his possession in support of his claim and deposit a fine in the amount of one hundred and fifty pounds.
The plaintiff may sign the summons and the pleadings.

The Supreme Court may impose a fine ranging from one hundred thousand to three hundred thousand Lebanese pounds" on an attorney who signs a summons containing insulting expressions against the judge complained of.
The Court shall examine first the admissibility of the action for judicial liability.

When the Court rules that the action is inadmissible or unfounded, it must confiscate the fine as revenue for the Treasury, and it may order the plaintiff to pay compensation in favour of the interested parties.

Once the admission of the claim is decided, the decision shall be notified within a time limit of three days through the Court registry to the defendant, who may submit his reply within fifteen days.

The Court may, where necessary, authorise the submission of additional memoranda, and the execution of the judgment that is the subject of the recourse shall be stayed.

The Court shall examine the matter as a matter of urgency and, if the claim is well-founded, shall award the necessary compensation in favour of the plaintiff and rule for the annulment of the judgment based on fraud, deceit or bribery, or for the annulment of the judge's act.

The trial shall be resumed from the point it had reached prior to its issuance.

The judge shall be incompetent to examine the action or to perform any act relating to the claimant from the date of the issuance of the decision granting leave to admit the action against the judge for liability.

Either spouse may apply for judicial separation on the ground of harm arising from discord or ill-treatment, such as battery, insult, coercion to commit a forbidden act, or engaging in a forbidden act.

Following proof of the harm, the judge may endeavour to effect reconciliation between the spouses and shall grant the two parties a period of not less than one month for reconciliation. If reconciliation is not achieved, the judge shall appoint two arbitrators possessing the qualifications required under Sharia from among the relatives of the spouses, or two arbitrators from outside their relatives in whom he sees the ability to effect reconciliation between them if there is no one from among their relatives or the relatives of either of them who is fit to serve as an arbitrator, from among the arbitrators whose names are entered on the roster.

The two arbitrators shall accurately ascertain the causes of the discord between the spouses, inspect the case file and the defences and documents of both parties, and bring the spouses together in a family council in which they shall exert their utmost effort to reconcile them; if they succeed in effecting reconciliation, they shall draw up a report thereon and submit it to the judge.
The family council shall be attended only by the spouses, the two arbitrators, and any person whose attendance the two arbitrators deem beneficial.

The arbitration shall not be affected by the refusal of either spouse to attend the family council after having been notified of the date and place of the meeting of the council for the second time; rather, the two arbitrators shall continue their mission notwithstanding such absence.

If the two arbitrators are unable to effect reconciliation between the spouses, they shall refer the matter to the judge by means of a detailed report, accompanied by the minutes of the sittings, in which they set forth their viewpoint and their proposals for judicial separation in the light of the proof of fault on the part of either spouse.

If it is established from the report of the two arbitrators that the fault, or the greater part thereof, lies with the husband, the judge shall decree judicial separation and shall order the husband, upon application, to pay all the marital rights.

If it is established that the fault, or the greater part thereof, lies with the wife, he shall decree separation by khul' between them in return for the whole of the dower or a portion thereof proportionate to the fault.

In the event of actual or constructive consummation of the marriage between the spouses, and save in those two cases, the separation by khul' between them may include, in addition to the dower due to her, the engagement gifts, or a portion thereof, according to the discretion of the judge after reviewing the proposal of the two arbitrators.
Separation in the two cases mentioned in the preceding Article shall be deemed an irrevocable divorce.

If the two arbitrators differ in opinion, they shall refer the matter to the judge, who shall appoint two others as arbitrators or join to them a third casting arbitrator from outside their families, administer the oath to him, and notify the two arbitrators thereof; and this arbitral panel shall reconvene the family council and submit its proposals within the time limit fixed by the judge.
The provisions of the preceding Articles of this Chapter shall not apply to the Jaafari Sharia Judiciary.

Each of the two Supreme Sharia Courts shall draw up a list of the names of the arbitrators in suits of dispute and discord, and shall also draw up lists of the names of the experts, judicial receivers, and physicians for all cases relating to the courts subordinate to each of them.

Those persons shall take the oath before the Supreme Court to which they are subordinate to perform their duties with integrity, justice, and fidelity.

It shall be prohibited to select arbitrators from among advocates or Sharia officials. A number of arbitrators, experts, judicial receivers, and physicians shall be allocated to each court of first instance. These lists shall remain in force for a period of three years.

The name of the arbitrator, expert, judicial receiver, or physician shall be struck off temporarily or permanently if it is established that he has committed negligence or fault warranting the same, by a decision issued by the Supreme Sharia Court that placed him on the roll.
The Sharia judge or the authorised marriage official shall conduct the conclusion of the marriage contract.

The marriage contract must include:

A- The name of the two parties, the domicile of each of them, their surname, their sect, their date of birth, the name of their guardian, and as regards the wife, whether she is a virgin or previously married.

B - The conclusion of the contract, its date, and its place.

C- The full names of the witnesses and proxies and the domicile of each of them.

D- The amount of the prompt and deferred dower and what has been received of the prompt dower in cash or trousseau.

E- The signature of the interested parties and the authorised marriage official, and the authentication of the judge.

The Sharia Court shall register the marriage contract verbatim in its official registers after its authentication by the Sharia judge within forty-eight hours of its receipt, and shall also notify the Personal Status Departments thereof within one month from the date of the marriage; and the Chief Clerk of the Sharia Court shall be responsible for any failure in notifying these Departments.
The Court shall issue to each of the two parties, upon their request, a certified copy of the marriage contract registered with it.

In places remote from the seat of the Sharia Court and falling within its jurisdiction, the judge may authorise one of the marriage officiants of his denomination registered on the roll to conclude the marriage contract in accordance with the provisions relating thereto.

After the marriage officiant draws up the contract, he shall send it with its documents to the judge of the court to which he is attached within forty-eight hours from the date of the contract, and the judge shall ensure the registration of the contract in the special register of the court therefor and shall also ensure the sending of a statement thereof to the Department of Statistics and Personal Status.

If the marriage officiant finds an impediment to the marriage contract or an objection arises before him in this regard, he shall refrain from concluding the contract and shall refer the matter to the judge, who shall examine it and decide upon it in accordance with the provisions of the Family Law.
Violation by the marriage officiant of the provisions of the preceding articles shall entail the striking off of his name from the roll, and this shall not preclude criminal prosecution.

Judges, marriage officiants, judicial assistants, and all employees of the Sharia Courts are prohibited from taking any fee for marriage contracts concluded inside the court during or after official working hours, and they are also prohibited from following up on marriage transactions.

The inventory and settlement of an estate is the determination of the property left by a decedent and, where necessary, the distribution and partition of the movable property thereof among the heirs and other right-holders.

The inventory and settlement of an estate shall be permissible in the following cases:

1- If requested by one of the heirs, one of the right-holders in the estate, or the executor of the will.

2- If among the heirs or right-holders in the estate there is a fatherless minor, a legally incapacitated person, or an absentee who has no representative, or if the heirs are unknown.

An application for the inventory and settlement of an estate shall be submitted to the Court of First Instance of the denomination of the deceased within whose jurisdiction the place of opening of the succession falls, and it shall be examined in chambers.

Every claimant of a right in the estate who is prejudiced by the decision ordering its inventory and settlement may apply to the competent court to establish the rights he claims, and the action shall not stay the proceedings for the inventory and settlement of the estate unless the court decides to stay them for serious reasons against security guaranteeing all damages arising therefrom.
The settlement of the estate shall be carried out by an expert appointed by the judge, or a judicial assistant delegated by him for this purpose.

If one of the heirs, the holders of rights in the estate, or the executor of the will requests the settlement of the estate, an inventory showing the property of the estate and the value of each item thereof shall first be made. The judge may order the affixing of seals where necessary.

After making the inventory and assessing the value of the property left behind, the judge shall summon all the heirs as well as all the apparent holders of rights to appear before him at a specified time and submit their documents proving their rights in the estate, and he shall fix, where necessary, a time limit for the heirs and legatees to submit this statement.

After the beneficiaries of the estate have submitted the documents set forth in the preceding Article, the judge shall ask them whether they wish to remain in a state of joint ownership of the movable property or request its liquidation and partition. If all the heirs and holders of rights declare their wish to remain in a state of joint ownership, the judge shall draw up a record thereof and decide to deliver the property of the estate to its beneficiaries against a receipt signed by them.

Property specifically bequeathed shall be delivered to those to whom it was bequeathed, and the creditors of the deceased shall have the right to attach the jointly owned property while reserving their right to claim from the heirs and legatees the share of the debt incumbent upon each of them in proportion to his share.

In the event that the heirs request liquidation or partition, the judge shall decide to publish this request in the Official Gazette and in one or several other newspapers designated by him, and shall order that a copy thereof be posted in the vestibule of the court and in a place near the residence of the deceased.

By this notice, he shall invite everyone who claims a right in the estate and everyone who is owed a debt by it to declare the right he claims and submit his documents within a time limit of six months from the date of publication of the notice in the Official Gazette. If among the property of the estate there is anything feared to be perishable, the judge shall decide to sell it and deposit its price in one of the approved banks.

After the expiry of the period specified for declaring rights and claims, the judge shall draw up a report setting forth the claims submitted by the claimants of rights and shall summon the heirs and the claimants to a hearing at which deliberation shall take place between them regarding an amicable settlement.

If a settlement is reached between the heirs and the claimants, the judge shall ratify it by a decision issued by him in the deliberation chamber; otherwise, he shall require everyone who claims a right to bring his action before the competent judiciary within a time limit which he shall fix.

If the claimant of the right brings his action within the specified time limit, the court shall schedule an urgent hearing at which it shall examine the matter of staying or not staying the liquidation. In all cases, the heirs shall have the right to provide security for the claimed right. In that event, the operations of settling the estate shall continue.
In the event of proceeding with the inventory of the estate, the heirs shall have the right to agree among themselves to divide the assets of the estate in the manner they choose.

If the heirs do not agree on the partition, the judge shall draw up a draft partition and shall seek the assistance of an expert for this purpose where necessary. If the heirs approve this draft, the judge shall ratify it by a decision issued by him in chambers.

If one of the heirs objects to the draft partition and the partition proves impossible, the judge shall then proceed with the liquidation of the movable assets, their sale in accordance with due process, and the distribution of their price among the heirs according to the hereditary share of each of them.
If among the effects left behind there is an industrial, commercial, or agricultural establishment, the Sharia Court may order its liquidation, its sale, and the division of its price.

If a person dies and his heirs are unknown, the Mukhtar of the locality in which he resides shall notify the Sharia Court of First Instance of the deceased's sect of the matter of his death, whereupon it shall decide the matter of his death in chambers and shall also decide to draw up an inventory of the estate and to appoint a curator over it.

After carrying out the inventory, the judge shall deposit in one of the approved banks the cash and valuables that he finds among the assets of the deceased and shall hand over the remaining assets to the curator, who shall undertake their administration under his continuous supervision, and the curator may be required to provide a security.

If among the assets of the estate there is anything feared to perish, the court may decide to sell it and keep its price in one of the officially approved banks.
After the lapse of five years from the death without an heir appearing, the judge shall take a decision in chambers to hand over the assets of the estate to the Islamic Waqfs.

The curator shall submit his account book to the judge, and he shall also submit an account of his administration of the assets of the estate at least once every year, whereupon the judge shall decide to fix the remuneration of the curator and pay it to him, and the remaining assets shall be handed over to the Islamic Waqfs.
If the heir appears after the delivery of the property and proves his right to the inheritance, he shall have recourse against the Islamic Endowments for his property.

If the heir or one of the heirs is absent and has no proxy representing him, the judge may, pursuant to a statement from the Mukhtar of the locality of the deceased or one of the relatives of the absentee, decide in chambers to inventory the estate if he deems its inventorying useful.

If there are multiple heirs and some of them are absent, then after drawing up the inventory, the property of the estate shall be delivered to the present heirs, after taking a guarantee from them securing the share of the absentee; and if those heirs refrain from providing the guarantee, the cash and valuable items, if found, shall be deposited in a bank, and the remaining property shall be delivered to a judicial receiver who shall administer it on behalf of all the heirs and preserve the share of the absentee therein and in the fruits thereof.

This latter procedure shall be followed if the sole heir or all the heirs are absent. And the judicial receiver shall be obliged to provide a guarantee.

If the present heirs or one of them requests the liquidation of the estate and it is possible to ascertain the place of residence of the absent heir, the judge shall serve notice of the request for liquidation upon this heir and fix a time limit for him to appear or to appoint a proxy to represent him; if he neither appears nor is represented, the liquidation may be carried out in the presence of the judicial receiver.

However, if the absent heir is of unknown place of residence, he shall be summoned by way of the service of process for persons of unknown place of residence, and upon the failure of him or a proxy on his behalf to appear, the judicial receiver shall represent him in the liquidation proceedings.

If none of the heirs requests the liquidation of the estate and the absent heir is not represented, the judge shall decide in chambers to sell the items feared to perish or deteriorate, to divide their price and the cash, if found, among the heirs, and to preserve the share of the absentee therein in a bank, and he shall authorise the receiver to participate with the present heirs in administering the remaining common property, collecting the revenues of the share of the absentee therein, and preserving them in the same bank.

The receiver shall submit his account book and shall render an account to the judge of his administration of the property of the absentee at least once every three months, and his remuneration shall be determined by the decision of appointment.

If among the heirs there is a fatherless minor or an legally incapacitated person, the Sharia Court of First Instance may decide of its own motion or pursuant to a notification to inventory the estate.
If the minor or the legally incapacitated person has no legal representative, the court shall decide of its own motion to appoint a guardian over him.

After the inventory is drawn up, the judge shall decide such measures as he deems appropriate to preserve the property of the minor, and thereafter shall decide, according to the exigencies of the case, whether or not to carry out the liquidation, unless a request for liquidation is submitted by another heir.

If it appears to the judge that it is in the interest of the minor or the legally incapacitated person to liquidate and partition the estate, the rules designated in the first Subsection shall apply. The representative of the minor or the legally incapacitated person shall act on his behalf in the proceedings relating to him, provided that the contracts which he signs shall not be executed prior to the judge's ratification thereof.

The death of a Lebanese national or a foreign national residing in Lebanon whose traces have disappeared in Lebanon or outside Lebanon in circumstances in which his perishing is probable and in which his body has not been found may be judicially declared, upon the application of an interested party, in accordance with the following provisions:

1- The application for the declaration of death shall be submitted by way of a petition to the competent court with respect to the denomination to which the person whose death is sought to be declared belongs, and the said court shall adjudicate upon the application in the deliberation chamber, and in order to form its conviction to take the necessary decision it shall rely upon the various Sharia means of proof, including presumptions, publication and notice.

2- On the basis of the result of the said inquiries and investigations, and if the absence and disappearance of trace occurred in circumstances in which perishing is probable, and a period of at least four Hijri years has elapsed since the disappearance, the court shall decide the death of the person who is the subject of the investigations and inquiries and shall rule for the liquidation of his estate, taking into consideration the rights that may accrue to him, and for its division among the right-holders in accordance with the provisions of the Sharia, provided that the said right-holders shall not dispose of the immovable property that has devolved upon them by way of a disposition transferring ownership or establishing real rights thereon during six years starting from the date the judgment takes effect, save for the purpose of maintenance decided by the court.

3- The judgment declaring the death shall be published, in addition to the party provided for by law, by all the means in which the court sees benefit, and shall be notified to the Public Prosecution before the competent Supreme Sharia Court and to this Court without delay.

4- The said judgment shall have the character of a non-contentious judgment subject to modification, opposition and appeal by the Public Prosecution before the Supreme Sharia Court and by every interested party, and in all cases it shall not become enforceable until after its ratification by the Supreme Sharia Court after reviewing the submissions of the Public Prosecution before it, and this ratification procedure shall be accorded the character of urgency.

5- If the person whose death was declared returns and appears during the said six years or after their expiry, his Sharia rights recognised by the denomination to which he belongs shall be applied in respect of him.

6- The provisions provided for in the Ottoman Family Rights Law shall remain in force with respect to the disappearance of the husband, and the provisions recognised by the denomination to which the absent person belongs shall likewise remain in force with respect to cases of absence and disappearance of trace in circumstances other than those in which perishing is probable.

1- In cases where the liquidation of the estate takes place by an agreement among the heirs or between them and the holders of rights in the estate on the division of the estate assets, and the division is executed amicably, such amicable division, even if ratified by the judge, shall not prevent the application of the provisions of Articles 943 and 949 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts. 2- Actions brought by creditors after an amicable or judicial division may only be brought against the heirs and beneficiaries of the estate personally, each to the extent of what he received from the property of the estate.

The Sharia single judge shall assume the administration of the property of incapacitated persons belonging to his confession and residing within his jurisdiction, with a view to developing it, preserving it, and spending on them therefrom.

The incapacitated persons subject to the guardianship specified in the preceding Article are:

A- Orphans under eighteen years of age before the judge decides that they have attained the age of majority.

B - Persons placed under interdiction for imbecility, insanity, or prodigality and squandering.

C- Persons the administration of whose property the Sharia Court temporarily decides to assume pending a ruling on the matter of their interdiction.

One or more judicial assistants, whose number shall be determined in accordance with the requirements of the interest, shall assist the single judge in his duties in administering the property of incapacitated persons.

The single judge shall enjoy the right to:

1- Represent the administration of the property of incapacitated persons.

2- Authorise the guardian to purchase, sell, or exchange movable and immovable property, all under the supervision of the judge, if the benefit of the incapacitated person is established.

3- Register contracts of pledges and mortgages after ascertaining that the sale value is three times the value of the debt.

4- Decide on construction when the benefit of the incapacitated person is proven.
