5- Receive and pay monies through the bank accepted by the Government and designated by the Supreme Sharia Court within the jurisdiction of the Sharia Court of First Instance.

6- Supervise the entries and compare the accounts of the bank and the register in his possession.

7- Execute contracts of pledges and mortgages before all competent authorities directly or through an attorney whom he appoints in order to recover the debt, its accessories, expenses, and fees.

The decisions issued by the judge and the measures taken by him shall be subject to review before the Supreme Sharia Court upon the request of the guardian, one of the guardians, or the Public Prosecutor before the Supreme Sharia Court within a period of fifteen days from the date of their notification to the guardian and the Public Prosecutor, and they shall not be enforceable until after the expiry of the period without review. The Supreme Court shall examine them in council chamber to approve, amend, or annul them and rule on their matter.

If the sale is not completed in accordance with the two preceding articles, the judge shall appoint a new date within a time limit not exceeding two months after the first date. He may broaden the scope of the publication and posting formalities.

The sale at this auction shall be concluded in favour of the person who offers the highest price and pays it immediately.
No person shall be admitted to the auction unless he produces a certificate from the Sharia Court proving that he has deposited in the competent bank an amount equal to the starting price.

If the purchaser refuses or is unable to pay the price, the property intended to be sold shall be put up for sale anew at his responsibility. The auction shall take place immediately if that is practicable, and the defaulting purchaser shall bear the difference between the price which he offered and the price finally fixed.

The record of the sale shall constitute an enforceable instrument for the difference in price as against him.

Where the property intended to be sold consists of shares of any kind whatsoever, negotiable instruments, perpetual annuities and shares of limited partners in companies, and where such shares and instruments are of significance, the Single Judge may seek the assistance of a banker in certain of the sale procedures, and he shall, in light thereof, decide what publicity measures ought to be taken.
The auction in respect of such shares and instruments shall take place under the supervision of the Single Judge in a public hearing.

The sale of immovable property or of a right in rem belonging to an incapacitated person shall take place pursuant to a decision establishing the benefit to the incapacitated person, in accordance with the provisions laid down in the following articles:

The Sharia judicial assistant entrusted with carrying out the preliminary formalities for the sale shall, pursuant to the decision on the beneficial nature of the sale and upon the instruction of the Single Judge, draw up a statement in which he shall set forth:

1- The designated immovable property or properties or rights intended to be sold, including their appurtenances, boundaries and descriptions, and the rights attached thereto and the encumbrances or charges thereon, in accordance with the entries in the Land Register or the documents produced, describing their current condition, with mention of the names of the tenants and the rents, where applicable.

2- By the appraised value estimated by the expert appointed during the preliminary formalities for the decision on the beneficial nature.

3- The place of the auction and the date and time at which it is to be held, specifying the month, day and hour, within a prior period of not less than twenty days.

4- The conditions of sale and the starting price as determined by the Single Judge on the basis of the appraised value.

The judge is prohibited from retaining cash, ornaments, shares, bonds, and all other movables belonging to legally incapacitated persons on the occasion of the administration of their property, and he must deposit all of them in the bank decided to be accredited by the Supreme Sharia Court from among the banks accepted by the State.
The sale of a movable belonging to a legally incapacitated person shall take place in the hall of the house or in the nearest market to the place where the property intended to be sold is located.

The sale shall be announced by publication in the newspapers and by posting on the walls in the square of the city, town, or village, and on the board prepared for announcements at the door of the department, all of that at least eight days before the fixed date, unless the property is subject to perishability or fluctuation of prices, in which case this time limit may be shortened from day to day or from hour to hour.

The judge shall determine the number of publications and announcements in proportion to the value of the property intended to be sold, and he may suffice with the formality of posting if the case does not exceed three hundred pounds or if there is a necessity requiring the acceleration of the sale due to the exposure of the property to perishability or fluctuation of prices.

The judge may decide to sell movable and immovable property after seeking the assistance of technical expertise, and after taking into consideration the estimated value of the property offered for sale, which must not exceed one million Lebanese pounds".

Village mayors may be entrusted with posting the announcements in the places prepared for them, and the posting shall be proven by a record from the clerk, the bailiff, or the town mayor. Publication shall be proven by submitting a copy of the newspaper and annexing it to the file of the sale formality.

The auction shall take place in the presence of the judicial assistant assigned by the judge at the designated time and place, and the property shall be awarded to the last bidder who pays the highest price.

The assistance of the municipal auctioneer or an auctioneer chosen by the judicial assistant assigned to the sale may be sought, and his fee shall be determined from the proceeds and shall be considered part of the expenses of the sale.

The valuation of the property intended to be sold shall take place through an expert appointed by the judge from among the experts registered on the roster, and this shall be indicated in the announcements of the offering for sale. The sale may not be completed unless the price offered reaches two-thirds of the estimated value.

Gold and silver items, jewellery, and precious stones shall be weighed accurately and their value shall be estimated after describing them accurately, and this shall be indicated in the announcements of the offering for sale.

Their sale shall not be completed at a price less than nine-tenths of their value determined according to their weight and the price of their metal.

Within three days from the drawing up of the schedule of conditions provided for in the preceding Article, the judicial assistant entrusted with the preparatory acts for the sale shall send a copy thereof to the Public Prosecutor at the Supreme Sharia Court and to the guardian to state their observations thereon or the grounds for challenging it by way of objection thereto before the Single Judge within a time limit of eight days from the date of service.

Within eight days from the date of the last service, the Sharia Single Judge shall examine the submitted observations and the raised grounds of challenge and shall issue his decision in chambers accepting them, dismissing them, or correcting the schedule of conditions.

The decision of the Single Judge shall be subject to recourse before the Supreme Sharia Court at the request of the Public Prosecutor at the Supreme Sharia Court or at the request of the guardian. The Supreme Sharia Court shall examine the recourse and rule thereon in chambers without summoning anyone, unless it decides otherwise.

The decision of the Single Judge shall not become enforceable until after the ratification of the Supreme Court if the value of the real property sold exceeds ten million Lebanese pounds".

The judicial assistant entrusted with the preparatory formalities for the sale shall draw up an abstract of the schedule of conditions in the form of a notice stating therein:

1- The identity of the incapacitated owner.

2- A description of the real property or properties or the rights in rem to be sold, their appurtenances and their current specifications, the names of the occupants or tenants, the amount of the rents, and the reserve price fixed for each of them.

3- The date and time of the auction by year, month, day, and hour, and the exact place where it is to be held.

4- The expenses payable in addition to the price as estimated by the judge.

The judge shall order the publication of the notice in a widely circulated daily newspaper at the location of the real property, in the Official Gazette, and in the following places:

1- The notice board at the Sharia Court and at the Enforcement Department.

2- The domicile of the incapacitated person.

3- The doors of the real properties to be sold.

4- The door of the municipal hall, and in the absence thereof, on the door of the residence of the mukhtar in the area where the real property is located.

Where necessary, the judge may increase the number of publications at the request of the guardian or the Public Prosecutor.
The formality of advertising by publication and posting must be completed at least ten days prior to the date of the auction.

Publication shall be proved by producing a copy of the issue of the newspaper containing the notice. Posting shall be proved by a record drawn up by the bailiff or the clerk entrusted therewith, containing a statement of the places of posting.

The auction hearing shall be held in public before the Single Sharia Judge in his department or in another place which he has deemed suitable and which was indicated in the notice. The hearing shall be opened by reading out the notice, and then the bailiff shall begin calling for bids, repeating the mention of the property or properties, their appurtenances, their boundaries, their descriptions, the fixed reserve price, and every offer submitted by any of those wishing to purchase.

The Single Judge shall decide to adjudicate the property sold to the last bidder who offered the highest price equal to or exceeding the reserve price.

If no one comes forward to purchase, the sale shall be adjourned for a period ranging between one month and two months, and the notice procedure shall then be carried out anew, and the judge may repeat this action until a person wishing to purchase comes forward, just as he may decide to dispense with the sale.

Every person wishing to participate in the auction shall be required to:

1- Deposit, prior to its commencement, with the Treasury fund or one of the accepted banks, an amount equal to the reserve price, or submit a bank guarantee securing this amount and the expenses.

2- Designate an elected domicile for himself within the seat of the Sharia Court; otherwise, the registry of the court shall be deemed an elected domicile for him.

Every person who participated in the auction and fulfilled the obligation of the deposit or the guarantee, and who was not the last bidder, may withdraw the deposited money or the guarantee immediately upon having been outbid.

The issuance of the adjudication decision shall entail:

1- The performance by the purchaser of the obligations incumbent upon him, and in particular the payment of the price, fees, and expenses without the need for a formal notice or demand, within twenty days.

2- The consideration of the purchaser as owner.

The Single Judge must request the enforcement of the adjudication decision after it has acquired the force of res judicata and the purchaser has paid the price and fees. This registration shall entail the transfer of ownership with respect to third parties.

The adjudication decision shall only be subject to appeal before the Supreme Sharia Court on the following grounds:

1- For a defect in the auction procedures.

2- For a defect in the form of the decision.

3- For a violation of the law in an incidental dispute addressed by the adjudication decision, if it is of such a nature as to affect the validity of the procedures.

Every person shall have the right to offer to the Single Sharia Judge, within the ten days following the adjudication, an increase over the price specified in the adjudication decision of not less than ten percent, and he shall be bound by this offer if no other bidder comes forward to purchase.

If there are multiple offers, consideration shall be given to the highest offer, and to the earliest in the event of equality.

The auction at the risk and expense of the defaulting purchaser shall be conducted and the sale therein shall take place in accordance with the rules observed in the first auction and on the basis of the same schedule of conditions of sale.

The issuance of the decision of adjudication in the auction conducted at the risk and expense of the defaulting purchaser shall result in the cancellation of the rights of the latter and the substitution of the new purchaser in his place with retroactive effect.

If the new auction concludes at a price exceeding the price reached in the first auction, the defaulting purchaser shall not be discharged from his obligations except upon the new purchaser actually paying the price, and he shall not benefit from the difference in price because that accrues to the incapacitated person.

If the adjudication is decided at less than the price fixed in the first adjudication, the defaulting purchaser must pay to the Court of First Instance, for the account of the incapacitated person, the difference together with the expenses necessitated by his default.

This obligation shall be secured by the guarantee or by the amount deposited prior to the auction, and in case of insufficiency, execution shall be levied against him from the remainder of his assets on the basis of the two decisions of adjudication without need for a judgment.

If the judge deems, of his own motion or upon the request of the guardian, that the interest of the incapacitated person requires purchasing immovable property with his movable funds or effecting an exchange for another immovable property, this shall be carried out after the approval of the Supreme Sharia Court.
The purchase of immovable properties shall be permitted at the sale value set by the competent expert or engineer, subject to proof of benefit to the incapacitated person.
In the event of construction, the costs shall be estimated by a competent engineer appointed by the Sharia judge.
Recourse to purchase or construction shall not be permissible unless absolute greater benefit is established.

An overbid shall not be accepted unless the person making it provides an adequate bank guarantee or deposits the full price offered with the Treasury Fund or an approved bank, and the person making the offer shall elect a domicile at the seat of the Sharia Court if he has no domicile within its district.

The judicial assistant entrusted with preparing the sale proceedings shall serve the declaration of the overbid upon the purchaser within three days, failing which he shall be liable to a fine of ten to one hundred pounds.

The publication formalities and sale procedures in respect of the additional auction shall be carried out in accordance with the rules prescribed for the first auction, and the notices shall state the amount of the increase in addition to the sale price.

The issuance of the first adjudication decision resulting from the additional auction shall entail the cancellation of the rights of the first purchaser and the substitution of the second purchaser in his place retroactively. All other effects relating to the first adjudication shall remain in force.
No increase shall be accepted after the adjudication following the additional increase.

The purchaser shall proceed to pay the price and perform his other obligations within eight days from the issuance of the adjudication.

If he defaults, the Sharia Single Judge may, of his own motion or upon the request of the Public Prosecutor or the guardian, put the purchaser on notice to perform his obligations within three days, failing which the sale shall be repeated at his risk and expense.

If the time limit specified in the preceding Article expires to no avail, the Single Judge shall decide to repeat the sale against the purchaser in accordance with the rules observed in the first sale. The notices shall state the upset price, the price at which the adjudication concluded, and the conduct of the sale at the risk and expense of the defaulting purchaser.

The defaulting purchaser shall have the right, up until the second adjudication is decided, to stay the proceedings being conducted at his risk and expense by paying what is due from him as a result of his purchase, the expenses resulting from his delay, and the compensation assessed by the judge on account of the delay as from the time limit specified for payment.

The opinion of the real estate engineer shall be submitted to the Supreme Sharia Court to take the appropriate decision regarding construction and to decide what it deems consistent with the interest of the legally incapacitated person.

The funds of legally incapacitated persons shall be invested by way of real estate mortgage in return for interest in the amount of 12 %, provided that the maximum limit of the value of the mortgage is thirty percent in relation to the sale value of the real property sought to be mortgaged.
The mortgage may only be of the first rank.
The assessment of the sale value of the real property shall be carried out by a specialist expert appointed by the judge from among the experts whose names are listed on the roster.

The report of the expert shall be submitted to the Supreme Sharia Court to decide on ratifying the decision of advantageousness in light thereof and to take what it deems consistent with the interest of the legally incapacitated person.

In the absence of a provision in this Law, the general rules provided for in the Code of Civil Procedure and the legislative texts supplementary thereto shall apply to the extent of their suitability to the organisation of the Sharia Courts. In the centres to which more than one single judge is assigned, the work therein shall be distributed among the judges by a decision of the President of the Supreme Sharia Court to which they belong, and this distribution may be amended when necessary.

Each of the experts, arbitrators, physicians and judicial custodians is prohibited from collecting fees that exceed the amount set for them by the decision of assignment, and every sum that exceeds that limit shall be considered to be in the nature of a bribe, and the name of the perpetrator of the violation shall be struck off the roster and he shall be prosecuted criminally.

Within five years from the date of publication of this Law:

A- Lawsuits for ratification of marriage and filiation and the registration of their documents in the personal status registers shall be exempted from all judicial fees, stamp duty and others, and they shall also be exempted from the transport and travel expenses of the judge and the employees of the Sharia Court.

B - Sharia judges of first instance may travel upon request outside the seat of the court, that is, to the villages and towns falling under their jurisdiction, to hear and examine lawsuits for ratification of marriage and filiation.

The Sharia courts shall be attached to the highest Islamic authority in the executive branch, which shall take charge of the affairs of their employees and their administrative and financial matters.

A full-time civil servant of the Second Category from the confession of the competent court, termed the Director of Judges and Employees Affairs, shall be seconded from the public administrations of the State to perform the administrative and financial duties after consulting the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council.

No person shall be admitted to the cadre of the Sunni Sharia Judiciary unless:

First: He is Lebanese, has completed the twenty-fifth year of his age and has not exceeded the forty-eighth, enjoys civil and political rights, and has not been convicted by the Disciplinary Council of a matter prejudicial to honour.

Second - He holds a licence in Sharia Judiciary, or the High Certificate from Al-Azhar Al-Sharif, or a licence in Law granted by the faculties that teach the rules of Islamic Sharia.

Third - He has succeeded in the competitive examination conducted by the Sharia Judicial Council, and no person shall be admitted to this competitive examination unless he has occupied the post of judicial assistant at the Lebanese Sharia courts for a period of at least two years.

The Sharia Judicial Council may decide to grant an exemption from the two-year requirement for anyone who holds one of the two certificates provided for in the second paragraph of Article 448 of this Law and for anyone who holds the High Certificate from one of the faculties of Al-Azhar Al-Sharif.

No person shall be admitted to the cadre of the Jaafari Sharia Judiciary except one who:

First: Is Lebanese, has completed the twenty-fifth year of his age and has not exceeded the forty-eighth, enjoys civil and political rights, and has not been convicted by the Disciplinary Council of a matter prejudicial to honour.

Second- Has graduated from Al-Najaf Al-Ashraf or any Islamic university, holding therefrom the Certificate of Higher Religious Studies, or a licence in Law granted by the faculties in which the rules of Islamic Sharia are taught.

Third - Has succeeded in the competitive examination conducted by the Sharia Judicial Council, and no person among the holders of a licence in Law shall be admitted to this competitive examination unless a period of not less than two years has elapsed since he obtained this certificate, during which he practised the post of judicial assistant in one of the Lebanese Sharia courts.

Anyone who is an employee in the cadres of the Jaafari Sharia Judiciary, the Jaafari Ifta, and the Supreme Islamic Shia Council shall be exempted from the age requirement."
Former Sharia judges shall be exempted from sitting for the competitive examination, subject to the approval of the Sharia Judicial Council.

The Supreme Sharia Judicial Council shall be composed of the Mufti of the Lebanese Republic as President, and the Presidents of the Supreme Courts, the judges seconded to the Public Prosecution and the inspectors as members, and every decision issued by this Council in respect of a Jaafari or an Alawite shall not be effective unless the majority includes one of the members of his sect."

"The Private Secretary to the Mufti of the Lebanese Republic shall assume the duties of the Secretariat of the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council, and shall receive a lump-sum allowance from the budget of the Sunni Sharia Courts, which shall be determined in the decree appointing him."

"The supervision of the proper functioning of the Sunni, Jaafari and Alawite Sharia Judiciary and of the work of the judges and employees of the Sharia Courts shall be assumed by one non-full-time inspector of at least the eighth grade for each of the courts, who shall be seconded from among the judicial judges of the denomination of the competent court by decree after consulting the opinion of the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council, and he shall be a member of the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council, and his monthly lump-sum allowance shall be determined by the decree of secondment, and each of them shall retain his original post in the cadre to which he belongs, and each of them shall submit his monthly reports to the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council and shall have the right to propose disciplinary penalties and appropriate measures."

The inspector shall propose the referral of the judges and employees of the courts to the Disciplinary Board if there appears to him in the investigations that which requires such referral, and he may decide to suspend the judge or employee referred to the Disciplinary Board from work for a period of ten days pending a decision on his matter in the decree of referral.

Every breach of the duties of office and every act prejudicial to honour, dignity or decency shall constitute a fault punishable disciplinarily. Failure to attend hearings, delay in deciding cases, failure to fix a specific date for the pronouncement of judgment at the close of the hearing, discrimination between litigants, disclosure of the secrecy of deliberations and expression of an opinion on the case before pronouncing judgment shall in particular be considered a breach of the duties of office."

Each of the Presidents of the two Supreme Sharia Courts may

address a warning to the judges subordinate to him.

The Sharia Judicial Council shall examine the disciplining of judges and employees of the Sharia Courts pursuant to the decree of referral.

A counsellor from the Supreme Sharia Court of the denomination of the referred judge, seconded by the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council, shall participate in the composition of the Disciplinary Board.

The President shall appoint a rapporteur from among the members of the Board, and he may himself perform the function of rapporteur. The rapporteur shall conduct the necessary investigations, hear the person concerned and the complainant where necessary, receive the statements of witnesses under oath and submit his report to the Board without delay.

The President shall immediately summon the person concerned to inspect the file and the rapporteur's report and to appear before the Council at the hearing which he appoints for him. The trial shall be conducted in camera. The rapporteur's report shall be read out and the person concerned shall be asked to present his defence regarding the matters imputed to him. The person concerned shall be entitled to be assisted by one lawyer or by one of his colleagues, and if he fails to appear, the Council shall examine the case in the light of the documents alone. The Council shall issue its decision on the same day or adjourn it to the following day at the latest, and this decision shall be reasoned.

The decision of the Council shall not be subject to any avenue of review, including an application for annulment before the State Council, and shall be enforceable of itself upon being notified to the person concerned through administrative channels. This decision shall be notified to the authority of the Sharia judiciary.
It shall not be permissible to publish or announce any of the proceedings of the disciplinary prosecution except the final decision if it includes the penalty of termination of service or dismissal.

The President of the Supreme Sharia Court to which the referred judge belongs shall perform the function of Government Commissioner before the Disciplinary Council. He shall not participate in the judgment.

The disciplinary penalties that may be imposed are:

1- Warning.

2- Reprimand.

3- Delay of promotion for a period not exceeding two years.

4- Demotion in grade.

5- Suspension from work without pay for a period not exceeding one year.

6- Termination of service.

7- Dismissal with deprivation of termination indemnity or retirement pension. In the event of demotion in grade, the judge shall retain his period of seniority for promotion.

In the event of dismissal with deprivation of termination indemnity or retirement pension, the pension deductions shall be refunded to him.
Sharia judges must wear their religious attire.

The cadre of judicial assistants in the Sharia courts is defined in the schedule annexed to this Law, and the rules prescribed for ordinary judicial assistants shall apply to them with respect to the salary scale and promotion.

Each of the two Presidents of the Sunni and Jaafari Supreme Sharia Courts shall be appointed from among the counsellors of those two Courts, or from among the judges who have attained the sixth grade and above, or from among the Sharia scholars attested to for jurisprudence and learning, provided that none of them has exceeded forty-eight years of age.
Sharia judges shall be appointed by decree upon the proposal of the authority of the Sharia Courts after the approval of the Sharia Judicial Council.
The scale of ranks and salaries of judges is set forth in the schedules annexed to this Law.

Sharia judges shall be promoted within their cadre in accordance with the provisions stipulated in the General Civil Servants Regulations, and the Sharia Judicial Council shall act in their regard in the place of the Civil Service Board.

The judges of the Sunni and Jaafari Sharia Courts shall benefit from all allowances and salary supplements established for all judicial judges.
The cadre of the Sharia Courts is determined in the schedules annexed to this Law.

A salary supplement not exceeding fifteen percent in value shall be granted to judges outside the city of Beirut.

The salary supplement provided for in this Article has been fixed as follows:

- /120.000/ L.L. for judges serving originally or by secondment at the seats of the Courts of Jiyeh - Aley and Chhim.

-/160.000/ L.L. for judges serving originally or by secondment at the seats of the Courts of Jbeil Sidon - Baakline and Chtaura.

-/200.000/ L.L. for judges serving originally or by secondment at the seats of the Courts of Tripoli - Zahle and Bar Elias.

-/240.000/ L.L. for judges serving originally at the seats of the remaining Courts.

The amount and conditions of this supplement shall be determined by a decree adopted in the Council of Ministers upon the proposal of the authority of the Sharia Courts. This supplement shall not be included in the calculation of retirement.

The office of the Sharia judiciary may not be combined with any elective office, any remunerated public or private office, or any other profession.

None shall be exempted from this rule except holders of religious offices within the conditions provided for in the Law on the Assignment of Religious Offices.

Judges of the Sharia Courts may be transferred, dismissed, referred to the Disciplinary Board, and placed at the disposal of the authority of the Courts after the approval of the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council, and none of the foregoing shall be permissible with respect to the President of the Supreme Sharia Court except after the approval of two-thirds of the members of the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council present, in the absence of the judge or member concerned, and by a decree adopted in the Council of Ministers.

No person shall be admitted to the cadre of Sharia judicial assistants for clerical positions unless he:

1- Is a Lebanese national who has completed the eighteenth year of his age and is of the denomination of the court concerned.

2- Has not been convicted of a felony or a disgraceful misdemeanour.

3- Holds a Sharia secondary certificate or a bachelor's degree from one of the Sharia faculties, both recognised by the Equivalence Committee formed by the Mufti of the Lebanese Republic, and wears religious attire, if he is Sunni.

4- Holds the Lebanese Baccalaureate certificate, Part Two, or its equivalent, if he is Jaafari.

5- Has passed the competitive examination before the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council.

None shall be exempted therefrom - except for the condition of the Sharia certificate or bachelor's degree - save candidates for restricted sessions decided by the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council upon the proposal of the President of the competent Supreme Sharia Court and the approval of the authority of the Sharia courts for the promotion of personnel in the cadres of employees and wage-earners at the Sharia courts, in which case the conditions approved by the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council, in its capacity as acting in the place of the Civil Service Board, shall be observed.

Adherence to religious attire shall be deemed one of the special conditions for the position of judicial assistant at the Sunni Sharia courts, and violation thereof shall constitute a ground for the loss of one of the conditions of appointment to this position, and this condition shall apply to all judicial assistants in service on the date of entry into force of this Law.

This Law shall apply to the current situation in the Jaafari Sharia courts, in particular the measures taken by the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council in respect of Jaafaris after the date of 24/8/2005.

Save for the exceptions set forth in this Law, the provisions set forth in the Employees Regulations shall apply to judicial assistants, provided that the Supreme Sharia Judicial Council acts in the place of the Civil Service Board.
Judicial assistants in the Sharia courts shall be appointed by decree upon a proposal from the authority of the Sharia courts.
Bailiffs in the Sharia courts shall be appointed from among holders of the primary certificate or its equivalent; as for ushers, the State Employees Regulations shall apply to them.

Bailiffs assigned to effect service of process shall be granted a travel allowance the conditions and amount of which shall be determined by a decree taken upon the proposal of the authority of the Sharia courts. The assignment shall be effected by a decision of the authority of the Sharia courts after consulting the President of the Supreme Sharia Court.

Judicial assistants who breach the duties of office or expose, by their acts, their dignity or the dignity of the office shall be subject to one of the following disciplinary penalties:

1- Warning.

2- Reprimand.

3- Deduction of salary for a period not exceeding fifteen days.

4- Suspension from duty with deduction of salary for a period ranging between three and six months.

5- Demotion in grade.

6- Dismissal with deprivation of dismissal indemnity or retirement pension, provided that this decision is taken unanimously, and if it is taken by a majority, he shall be entitled to half of the dismissal indemnity or retirement pension.

In the event of a reduction in rank or grade, the judicial assistant shall retain the period of his seniority for promotion, and if the penalty of warning and reprimand is imposed upon him twice, whether by the Inspector or the Disciplinary Council, the subsequent penalty may only be a reduction in grade.

Reprimand and deduction of salary may be decided by a decision of the Authority of the Sharia Courts, whereas the other penalties shall be decided by the Disciplinary Council, and the Inspector of the Sharia Courts may impose the penalty of deduction of salary for a period of five days by a decision from him.

The Disciplinary Council for each of the two denominations shall be composed of a counsellor from the Supreme Court as President and two Sharia judges as members, appointed by a decision of the Authority of the Sharia Courts upon the proposal of the President of the competent Supreme Sharia Court, and the judge delegated to the Public Prosecution before the Supreme Court shall perform the function of the Public Prosecution before this Council.

The judicial assistant shall be referred to the Disciplinary Council by a decision of the Authority of the Sharia Courts, and this Council shall convene upon a convocation by its President, the deliberation shall take place in secret, and the decision shall be rendered in a public session and sent to the Authority of the Sharia Courts for execution.
The statements of the judicial assistant referred to the Disciplinary Council shall be heard, or at least he shall be summoned to defend himself, and he may be assisted by only one lawyer.
Every judicial assistant referred to the Disciplinary Council may be temporarily suspended from office in the decision referring him to the Disciplinary Council.

Every judgment for a felony or an infamous misdemeanour that has acquired final and conclusive force shall necessarily entail the dismissal of the convicted judicial assistant.

The misdemeanours considered infamous are in particular:

-Forgery

- Theft

- Fraud breach of trust

-Embezzlement of funds

- Extortion thereof

- Intimidation

- And offences against public morals and decency.

The two current Presidents of the two Supreme Sharia Courts shall be classified in the cadre, each in the grade and salary corresponding to his former salary. If the salary is less than the lowest grade of the grades of the Presidency, he shall be classified in the lowest grade of the grades of the Presidency.

Incumbent Sharia judges and judicial assistants shall be classified within the establishment, each in the grade and salary corresponding to his former salary, in accordance with the schedules annexed to this Law.

The Government is authorised to open, by decree adopted in the Council of Ministers, the necessary appropriations to cover the expenditures and salaries pertaining to the Sharia Courts and to cover them by drawings from the reserve fund.
The two Supreme Sharia Courts shall undertake the operations of liquidating the Orphans' Fund attached to each of them, collecting the debts due and paying them to those entitled thereto.

The funds of the reserve fund that belonged to the Sunni Orphans' Directorate shall be allocated for the erection of a building suitable for the seat of the Sunni Sharia Judiciary in Beirut, to be constructed on real estate properties 3258 and 3365 of the Mousaitbeh cadastral area belonging to the Waqf of the Muslim Scholars, provided that the design and construction works are carried out under the supervision and direction of the President of the Supreme Sunni Sharia Court.
All previous provisions contrary to or inconsistent with the provisions of this Law, which shall enter into force from the date of its publication, are hereby repealed.
The courts are completely independent, vis-a-vis all authorities, in the investigation of actions and the adjudication thereof.

The courts may not examine the validity of the acts of the legislative authority, whether as regards the conformity of laws with the Constitution or as regards the conformity of political treaties with the rules of public international law. Nor may they formulate their judgments in the form of regulations.

No court may abstain from giving judgment on the pretext of the obscurity or insufficiency of the law, failing which it shall be deemed to be in default of rendering justice. Unlawful delay in issuing judgment may also be deemed a default in rendering justice.

Judicial decisions must include a statement of reasons, save in cases excepted by an express text, and must resolve all issues raised by the litigants and provide for each answer reasons appropriate thereto.
The courts may not award more than what is claimed, except in the application of laws relating to public policy.
Deliberation must remain secret in courts composed of several judges, and any disclosure of the secrecy of deliberation shall constitute the offence known as breach of professional secrecy.

The judicial courts in the territory of the Lebanese Republic are: 1- The Peace Court 2- The Civil and Commercial Court of First Instance 3- The Judge of Summary Matters 4- The Court of Appeal and Cassation

Peace judges have the right, save for bankruptcy actions the hearing of which is in the Court of First Instance, to adjudicate at last instance personal actions relating to movables if their value does not exceed fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds, and they have the right to render judgments subject to appeal in such actions if their value does not exceed five hundred and fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds.

They shall also be entitled to adjudicate all actions concerning immovable property where the value thereof does not exceed five hundred and fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds. Their judgments in respect of what has been stated shall always be subject to appeal.

For the purpose of determining the jurisdiction provided for in the preceding Articles 8 and 9 - and for the purpose of this determination alone - the Ottoman gold pound shall always be calculated at the rate of five hundred and fifty Lebanese-Syrian piastres, subject to the application of the rate provided for in Resolution 655 issued by the High Commissioner on 21 December 1921 concerning the settlement of deferred debts.

Whatever is divested from the principal action by way of interest, accretions and consequences, whatever the value thereof may reach, shall also be heard by the Summary Courts together with the principal action.

Magistrates of the Summary Court shall adjudicate the following actions, and their judgments in respect of what has been stated shall not be subject to appeal where the value does not exceed fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds, and shall be subject to appeal whatever their value exceeds: First - Actions concerning the payment of rent for buildings and lands, the facilitation of vacation of leased premises, the rescission of the lease, and the vacation of leased premises, all of this where the annual rent does not exceed five hundred and fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds. Second: Actions for compensation for damage caused to lands, fruits and crops by the act of a human being, whether direct or indirect.

Magistrates of the Summary Court shall adjudicate the following actions, and their judgments therein shall always be subject to appeal: 1- Possessory actions (actions of possession), provided that they are instituted within the time limit provided for in Article 48. 2- Actions aimed at preventing any interference with the right of irrigation. 3- Actions concerning easements encumbering real properties in accordance with Article 56 and following up to Article 91 of Resolution 3339 issued on 12 November 1930. 4- Actions for the demarcation of boundaries where ownership and the instruments establishing it are not the subject of dispute.

Judges of the Summary Court shall hear, subject to appeal, actions for the partition of immovable property where there is no dispute over ownership, and Judges of the Summary Court shall also hear actions for the partition of movable property in accordance with the provisions of the general law.

Where a single plaintiff has several claims against the same defendant in a single action and the value of their aggregate exceeds fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds, the Magistrate shall adjudicate thereon only at first instance, even if the value of one of them is less than this amount. He shall lack jurisdiction to hear them if the value of their aggregate exceeds the limits of his jurisdiction.

When an action is brought against several persons jointly or is brought by several persons jointly pursuant to a common instrument, the value of the common instrument shall remain the basis for determining the amount of jurisdiction in accordance with the rules prescribed in the preceding Articles.

Magistrates shall hear all counterclaims and actions for set-off which by reason of their nature or their value fall within the scope of their jurisdiction, even if their aggregate with the principal claim exceeds the limits of their jurisdiction, and they shall also hear, in addition to the principal action, counterclaims for damages derived exclusively from the principal action, whatever the value of such counterclaims may be.

Where the value of each of the principal claims or the counterclaims or the claim for set-off falls within the jurisdiction of the Magistrate at last instance, the said judge shall adjudicate thereon without right of appeal, and where one of these claims may be adjudicated only subject to appeal, the Magistrate shall adjudicate upon their aggregate only at first instance. Provided that he shall be entitled to adjudicate at last instance if the counterclaim relating to damages and branching exclusively from the principal action alone exceeds his jurisdiction at first instance; whereas if the counterclaim or set-off exceeds the limits of his jurisdiction, he may either retain the hearing of the principal action or direct the two parties to bring the action in its entirety before the Court of First Instance.

The Court of First Instance shall have jurisdiction to hear: At first instance - all actions not referred pursuant to the law to the Magistrates' Courts or to other exceptional courts; On appeal - judgments rendered at first instance by the Magistrates' Courts.

The Civil Court is the ordinary court. Where an action falling within the jurisdiction of the Magistrate's Court is brought before it, the lack of jurisdiction of the Civil Court shall only be relative; whereas if an action falling within the jurisdiction of the Civil Court is brought before the Magistrate's Court, the Magistrate's Court shall lack jurisdiction to hear it absolutely.
A person's capacity to litigate is subject to the law of his State.
The same rule is followed in supervising legally incapacitated persons and in representing them.
The court must, at every stage of the action, ascertain the capacity to litigate, and the validity of the representation of legally incapacitated persons or the validity of the supervision over them.

If the court finds that the courts are unlawful, it may order that the necessary measures be taken to rectify them if rectification is possible, and appoint a time limit for carrying it out. The court shall provisionally continue hearing the action, but it may not issue judgment unless the defect has been remedied or the granted time limit has expired. Damages may be withheld against the party who did not remedy the defect within the appointed period.

If the personal status law to which one of the parties is subject requires a legally incapacitated person to obtain an authorisation from the judiciary, the court before which the action must be brought (the Magistrate's Court or the Civil Court) is the one that grants him this authorisation, and it remains valid for the entire duration of the trial.

The authorisation given to a legally incapacitated person to litigate before the Court of First Instance includes granting the right of defence before the Court of Appeal, but it does not permit bringing an action on appeal, in which case a new authorisation must be obtained; whereas the authorisation to lodge an appeal before the Court of Appeal and Cassation is given by the Civil Court.

If an action is brought against a legally incapacitated person and he does not have a legal representative, the plaintiff is entitled to petition the President of the court to appoint a special representative provisionally in place of the legal representative pending his appointment, and the special representative has no right to waive, to acquiesce, or to settle.

An action is called personal when its object is to establish a debt, it is called a real action when its object is to establish a real right, and the action is called mixed when the plaintiff is able to claim at the same time a debt against the defendant and a real right.

The Civil Court has full jurisdiction: for it is the court of the principal action just as it is the court of the subsidiary action, save for the cases assigned by law to the administrative jurisdiction. However, if there arises in the course of an action falling within the jurisdiction of the Magistrate's Court and brought before it, a matter in the form of a subsidiary action or an incidental action - falling according to the rules within the jurisdiction of the Civil Court, the Magistrate's Court remains incompetent to hear it and must stay judgment in the action and direct the litigants to apply to the Civil Court when deciding the subsidiary or incidental action is indispensable to deciding the principal action.

With regard to personal status, nothing has been amended in the provisions of Article 33 and following up to Article 38 of Legislative Decree No. 6 issued on 3 February 1930 and supplemented by the Law issued on 9 December 1930, for they remain in force.

When the value of the action must be assessed in order to determine jurisdiction or the appealable amount, the assessment shall be made in the following manner: in real actions concerning immovable property - by reference to the value of the real property as shown by the produced documents or by the inspection of experts; in personal actions - by reference to the amount claimed if the object of the action is a judgment for a sum of money. However, if the object of the action is a judgment for the delivery of goods in kind, then by reference to the price of the goods according to market prices on the day the claim is filed, and otherwise according to the price determined by the expert. As for claims whose subject-matter is an indeterminate interest or the performance of something other than money, they shall be deemed equivalent to claims whose value exceeds 550 pounds, save for the exception provided for in the following Article 25.

If the plaintiff is able to claim several debts of distinct origins against the defendant, he may join all the grounds of claim in a single action, and the value of the action shall then be assessed on the basis of the value of the total.

If a single claim has several subject-matters and one of the parties has the right of election therein, the value of the action shall be assessed according to the subject-matter of the highest value; and if the value of one of the subject-matters is determinate, and the value of the other is indeterminate, only the value of the first subject-matter shall be taken into account.

If the subject-matter of the action relates to a periodic obligation, a distinction must be made as to whether the duration of this obligation is limited or unlimited; if it is unlimited, as in the case of a life annuity, the value of the action shall be deemed indeterminate and the provisions of the fourth paragraph of Article 23 shall then apply; however, if the duration of the periodic obligation is determinate, the amounts of the obligations shall be aggregated in order to determine the value of the action.
The rules of procedure in urgent matters are determined pursuant to Article 473 and the articles following it up to Article 487.
The Court of Appeal and Cassation shall hear actions adjudicated by the Courts of First Instance at first instance.
The right to bring an action before the courts is open to every natural or legal person, Lebanese or foreign, to establish and preserve his rights.

The object of the action may be to establish a right the existence of which has been denied, even though no obstacle has been raised against the exercise thereof, and the object of the action may be an inquiry intended to avert a future or potential dispute, or to pursue one of the avenues of recourse.

An action brought in bad faith and with the intent to cause harm must be dismissed, and the plaintiff may be ordered to pay damages in favour of the defendant; conversely, whoever opposes in bad faith a claim the validity of which has been established may be ordered to pay damages in favour of the plaintiff.

In the cases referred to in the preceding Article, the party acting in bad faith may also, in addition to the foregoing, be ordered to pay a fine of ten pounds at least and one hundred pounds at most, which the court shall impose of its own motion.

The Public Prosecutor has the right to bring an action directly in the cases determined by law, and in the same cases he has the right to appeal even if he was not a principal party in the proceedings at first instance.

An action for recovery of possession shall be brought by any possessor who, prior to his dispossession, was exercising material, continuous, peaceful, public, and unequivocal possession, and a lessee, a sharecropper, or a concessionaire in the public domain of the State shall have the right to bring this action under the same conditions.

An action for disturbance of possession requires for its institution the existence of a possessor who has, for at least one year, been exercising possession by himself or through his predecessors in a manner combining the characteristics set forth in the preceding Article.

Actions are divided, in terms of form, into principal claims and incidental claims; the principal claim is that from which the action originates, and the incidental claim is that which arises during the course of the action after its institution.

An incidental claim submitted by the plaintiff in the principal action is called an additional claim, that submitted by the defendant is called a counterclaim, and that brought by or against a third party is called a claim in intervention.

In order for incidental claims to be admissible in this capacity, it is required, first, that they be connected to the principal claim - and the two claims are deemed connected when the decision rendered on one of them is such as to affect the decision that must be rendered on the other; second: that the incidental claims do not fall outside the absolute jurisdiction of the court before which the principal claim is brought. The plea of inadmissibility must be raised prior to any debate on the merits.

Claims that arise during the course of the action and are not such as to broaden or narrow the subject-matter of the principal claim shall not be deemed incidental claims, but rather procedural incidents.

Notwithstanding the provisions of Article 54, the defendant may, up until the closing of the debates, request by way of counterclaim that the plaintiff be ordered to pay damages for his abuse of the right to sue in accordance with Article 31.
The principal claim and the incidental claim shall be adjudicated together.
Actions that do not fall within the categories referred to in the preceding Article, and in particular actions relating to pecuniary rights. They are deemed to be personal actions.
An action is called movable when it is intended to obtain movable property, and it is called immovable when it is intended to obtain immovable property.

Real immovable actions are called petitory when they are intended to establish the ownership of a real right, and are called possessory when they are confined to establishing the possession of a real right.
Whoever brings the petitory action shall not subsequently have the possessory action admitted from him, whereas whoever brings the possessory action and loses it may bring the petitory action.
The court before which the possessory action is brought may not base a judgment on grounds relating to ownership.

The petitory action and the possessory action may not be brought at one and the same time; thus, the court before which an action relating to the right of ownership and to the right of possession together is brought must declare its lack of jurisdiction in respect of the part which it is not entitled to hear.
The possessory action shall not be admitted except within one year commencing from the date on which the interference with the right of possession occurred.

The possessory action is of two kinds: the action for restoration of possession, which requires the existence of a person who has been dispossessed, and the action for interference, which requires the occurrence of an interference with the right of possession that has not reached the extent of dispossession.

If one of the litigants requests the joinder of a third party to the action merely for delay, the court may, when deciding to dismiss the request for compulsory intervention, order the party who joined the third party to the action to pay damages to this person and to the other party, and the provisions of Article 32 may also be applied
Voluntary intervention and compulsory intervention are permissible at first instance and on appeal

If one of the litigants is entitled to compel a person to defend in the proceedings or to indemnify him wholly or partially for the damage to which he is exposed as a result of judgment being rendered against him, he may join that third party to the proceedings by summoning him thereto in warranty
A summons in warranty may be brought before a court lacking relative jurisdiction, but it may not be brought before a court lacking absolute jurisdiction

By way of exception, a summons in warranty shall not be admissible before the court with which the original action was filed, in the following two cases: First: If there is an agreement concluded between the warrantor and the warrantee conferring jurisdiction to hear the warranty case upon another court Second: If an action pertaining to the same warranty has been instituted and remains pending before another court
The person summoned in warranty may himself also summon for his warranty another person bound thereby
The party who summoned a third party in warranty may, if all the litigants consent, withdraw from the proceedings, whereupon the warrantor shall take his place therein
The judgment rendered shall then apply to all the litigants, including the party who withdrew from the proceedings in this manner

Intervention shall be either voluntary or compulsory. It is voluntary when a third party intervenes of his own accord to establish or protect his rights against the litigants or one of them in the principal action, or to support the claims of one of the litigants if their success is in his interest, and intervention is compulsory when the litigants or one of them in the principal action request the attendance of the third party to take part in the hearing of the judgment

The litigants, or whichever of them is the target of the intervention in particular, may, prior to any discussion on the merits, contest the admissibility of the intervention pursuant to the provisions of the 54th Article

If no dispute arises over the admissibility of the intervention, or if it is decided to admit it, the intervener shall be entitled to request the conduct of any investigation he deems useful, even if the litigants have not requested it
The intervener may also raise all grounds of defence that he deems useful

If the voluntary intervention is not based on an interest of significance and is intended solely to delay the judgment, the litigants shall be entitled, whilst opposing its admissibility, and to request, in accordance with the conditions stipulated in the 31st Article, an award of damages in their favour, and the provisions of the 32nd Article may also be applied
The litigants or the party made defendant in the intervention may bring a counterclaim against the intervention
An application for compulsory intervention is the right granted to the litigants to summon a third party so that the case adjudicated between them shall also be adjudicated as against that person

If the litigants do not exercise their right to summon the third party to take part in the hearing of the judgment, the court may decide to summon him of its own motion if it considers that this measure is likely to facilitate adjudication in the principal action or that there is benefit in it for the preservation of the rights of the litigants or of one of them, and the decision taken directly by the court to join the third party in the action shall be notified to that person and to each of the litigants
A defence consists in directly denying the claimant's right or in asserting a claim intended to extinguish that right.
Lapse of time, res judicata, set-off, and a term are means of defence.
As for a defence, it consists in contesting the legality of the proceedings or in requesting a time limit.
Grounds of defence may be raised at any stage of the proceedings.
As for grounds of a plea, they must in general be raised at the commencement of the proceedings.
A plea containing the assertion that the court before which the action is brought is not competent to hear it is called a plea of lack of jurisdiction.
And a plea intended to obtain a time limit is called a dilatory plea.

Pleas must be raised in the following order, failing which they shall be liable to dismissal: First: A plea requiring security, where one of the litigants is required by law or pursuant to a judgment or agreement to provide security guaranteeing the costs of the action or damages for abuse of process that may be awarded. Second: A plea of lack of international jurisdiction. Third: A plea of lack of absolute jurisdiction. Fourth: A plea of lack of relative jurisdiction. Fifth: A plea of lis pendens or connectedness. Sixth: A plea based on the nullity of the writ of summons. Seventh: A plea requesting the transfer of the action for legitimate suspicion. Eighth: A plea requesting the transfer of the action for consanguinity or affinity. Ninth: Dilatory pleas, all of which must be raised at the same time. Tenth: A plea requesting the service of documents.
Jurisdiction is the competence of the court to hear the action

Jurisdiction is of three kinds: 1) International jurisdiction, by virtue of which is determined the State that must provide the adjudicating body 2) Absolute jurisdiction, by virtue of which are determined the classes of courts and the hierarchy of their degrees 3) Relative jurisdiction, by virtue of which is determined the court that is entitled to hear the action among the courts that are of a single class and a single degree, and these three pertinent matters are resolved one after the other

Actions relating to the ownership of immovable property or to real rights in immovable property shall be subject to the court of the place where such property is situated. As for actions relating to the devolution of inheritance, the regime of ownership of immovable property must not be followed therein on the pretext that the estate consists wholly or partly of immovable property. As for the classification of actions into immovable and movable, it must be in accordance with the provisions of Lebanese law
Personal actions and actions relating to family rights must in principle be adjudicated in the courts of the State in which the domicile of the defendant is situated
Provided that actions arising from a delict or quasi-delict shall be adjudicated by the courts of the State in which the delictual act or quasi-delict occurred
Actions arising from the breach of a concession granted or recognised by any State may be brought only before the courts of that State
The rules of absolute jurisdiction are derived from the seventh Article and those following it up to the twenty-eighth Article, relating to judicial organisation
Real actions relating to immovable property shall be heard in the court of the place of the immovable property

And personal actions shall in principle be heard in the court of the place in which the defendant resides, and if he does not have a known domicile his residence shall suffice, and if there are several defendants, the plaintiff is entitled to summon them before the court of the place in which one of them resides, and it is not necessary that the suing of the defendants together be based on a single cause.

Mixed actions may be brought, according to the choice of the plaintiff, either before the court of the place in which the defendant resides, or before the court of the place in which the immovable property is situated.

If the defendant has an elected domicile, the action may be brought in this domicile or in his actual domicile; as for moral persons who have several branches, they shall be deemed as having an elected domicile in each branch thereof in respect of the operations conducted by those branches with a third person.

If there are multiple heirs, actions relating to inheritance among the heirs or between them and the legatees or between them and the creditors of the estate shall be brought, until the completion of the partition, before the court of the place in which the estate was opened.

As for what relates to companies, actions among partners shall be brought before the court of the place in which the head office of the company is situated until the complete termination of its liquidation.
And in respect of life insurance, the action for payment of indemnity shall be brought before the court of the domicile of the plaintiff.

And in respect of fire insurance, the plaintiff shall bring the action for indemnity before the court of the place in which the contingency occurred, and if the subject of the insurance is movable property, the plaintiff is entitled to choose the place in which the fire actually occurred or to consider that the movable property was present in the places of his residence.
And in respect of accident insurance, the action for indemnity shall be brought before the court of the place in which the accident occurred or the court of the domicile of the insured person.
Actions arising out of bankruptcy shall be adjudicated by the court which declared it.
Actions arising out of an offence or a quasi-offence shall be brought before the court of the defendant or the court of the place in which the act giving rise to compensation occurred.

An action in warranty shall follow the ordinary rules relating to jurisdiction if it is brought as an original action; however, if it is submitted in the form of an incidental action, it may be brought before the court before which the original action was brought, provided that such court does not lack absolute jurisdiction to hear it in accordance with the rule laid down in the second paragraph of Article 54.

In commercial matters, the plaintiff shall have the right to bring the action, at his choice, either before the court of the domicile of the defendant, or before the court of the place of conclusion of the contract and delivery of the goods, or before the court of the place of payment.
Actions relating to difficulty in interpreting a judicial judgment shall be brought before the court which issued such judgment.

Actions relating to difficulties in executing a judicial judgment shall be brought before the court which issued the judgment. However, if the judgment issued by an appellate court rules for reversal, difficulties in its execution shall be referred to the appellate court, and if it contains an affirmation, difficulties in its execution shall be referred to the court whose judgment was affirmed.

The litigants shall have the right to agree either the civil court to waive appeal in advance, save in cases in which the subject-matter of the dispute consists of rights not susceptible of compromise.

If one of the litigants raises a plea of lack of jurisdiction, the judge may either adjudicate immediately by a separate decision on the point of jurisdiction, or join the issue of jurisdiction to the merits and adjudicate upon both of them together by a single decision.

If one of the litigants submits a plea of lis pendens or of connectedness, and the judge finds that he is not justified in raising this plea, he may rule by a single decision on the dismissal of the plea and on the merits of the action.
The party who submits a plea of lack of jurisdiction, of lis pendens, or of connectedness must at the same time set forth, in the alternative, his claims with respect to the merits.

A plea requiring security and a plea based on the nullity of the writ of summons must be decided by a separate decision, and this decision must be issued within fifteen days from the closing of the hearing; however, it shall not be subject to review except together with the judgment on the merits.

If the lack of jurisdiction of a court is determined by a decision that has acquired the force of res judicata, and there is no other court that appears to have jurisdiction, recourse must be had to an application for designation of the competent court from the court superior to it in the judicial hierarchy.
The same rule shall be followed if a single action is brought before two courts and each of them has decided that it has jurisdiction by decisions that have acquired the force of res judicata.

The matter shall be referred to the court from which the designation of the competent court is requested by virtue of a simple petition and without joining the adversary in the proceedings; it shall designate in its decision the court having jurisdiction, and no argument shall thereafter be permitted before the court so designated regarding the matter of jurisdiction that has been decided.

When it is impossible to constitute the bench of the court due to the lack of a sufficient number of judges for any reason whatsoever, the plaintiff shall submit a petition to the court superior to it, which shall designate a court of the same category and of the same degree to hear the action in place of the court that could not be constituted, and if there is no court superior to it in the judicial hierarchy, this designation shall be made by the Minister of Justice.
The matter shall proceed in this manner when it becomes impossible for a court to carry out its functions as a result of force majeure, such as a foreign or civil war, a flood, etc...

If a lawsuit is brought before a court after having previously been instituted before another court, what is termed lis pendens arises, and the defendant shall then have the right to request the second court before which the lawsuit was brought to decline to hear it, subject to the application of the provisions of the Law promulgated on 17 February 1928.
The same shall apply in the event of connectedness with another lawsuit that remains pending before a Lebanese court.

If there exists between one of the litigants and two of the judges composing the court, or between one of the litigants and the president of the court, a relationship of consanguinity or affinity in the direct line or in the collateral line up to the fourth degree, the other party shall have the right to request the transfer of the lawsuit to another court in accordance with what is stated in the 112th Article.

The same shall apply where there exists a legitimate suspicion regarding the entire bench of the court. Legitimate suspicion exists where the factual circumstances raise doubt as to the impartiality of the court. The party who requests the transfer of the lawsuit on the ground of legitimate suspicion and whose request is dismissed shall be sentenced to a pecuniary fine of twenty-five to one hundred pounds, and shall also be sentenced to pay damages if he acted in bad faith.

The Public Prosecutor before the Court of Appeal and Cassation shall have the right to request, upon the order of the Minister of Justice, the transfer of the lawsuit from one court to another court for the preservation of public security and in accordance with the provisions of the 112th Article, when the hearing of one of the lawsuits is of such a nature as to cause a disturbance in the district of the court before which the lawsuit is brought.

A judge may be recused: First: If he or his wife has a direct or indirect interest in the lawsuit, even after the dissolution of the marriage contract. Second: If there exists between him and one of the litigants a relationship of consanguinity or affinity in the direct line or in the collateral line up to the fourth degree, even after the dissolution of the marriage from which the affinity resulted. Third: If he is the betrothed of a female litigant. Fourth: If he has previously been a legal representative of one of the litigants. Fifth: If he has previously been a witness in the case. Sixth: If one of the litigants had chosen him as an arbitrator in a previous case. Seventh: If there exists between him and one of the litigants severe enmity.- However, an insult directed by one of the litigants against the judge shall not suffice to render the judge subject to recusal. Eighth: If a civil or criminal lawsuit has been instituted between him and one of the litigants, or one of his relatives by consanguinity or affinity up to the fourth degree, during the preceding five years.
A judge must propose his own recusal of his own accord in the cases set forth in the preceding Article, and each of the litigants may, on the other hand, request his disqualification.

An application for disqualification shall be submitted by a written declaration to the registry of the court, and this declaration shall be referred to the chamber to which the judge sought to be disqualified belongs, and this judge shall not participate in the deliberation. However, if the disqualification of one of the magistrates is requested, the application shall be referred to the Civil Court, and the clerk of the Magistrate's Court must transmit it to the registry of the Civil Court within five days from the date of its filing.

An application for disqualification must be submitted before any discussion on the merits, and not was it subject to imposition. It may be submitted after raising the plea for security for costs, the plea of lack of jurisdiction, the plea of lis pendens, or the plea of connectedness, provided that it must be submitted before dilatory pleas. However, if the ground for disqualification did not occur or did not become known until after the commencement of the discussions, the application shall exceptionally be admissible within eight days from the date on which the ground occurred or became known, and in this case the trial shall be stayed until the disqualification action is adjudicated.
A decision rendered pursuant to a proposal of recusal by the judge or pursuant to an application by one of the litigants shall always be subject to appeal, whatever the value of the action may be.

A party who fails in an application for disqualification shall be sentenced to a fine of twenty-five to one hundred Lebanese-Syrian pounds. In addition thereto, he shall, where appropriate, be ordered to pay damages to the judge whose disqualification was wrongfully sought and to the other party on account of the unlawful delay in the trial.
The court to which the application for disqualification is referred must hear the judge whose disqualification is sought.

If the decision ordering disqualification is appealed, the Court of Appeal shall be entitled, where there is justification for urgency, to order expedited execution, and it shall remit the action to the court before which it was initially brought so that it may adjudicate it without the disqualified judge participating in its bench.

An application for disqualification may be directed not only against the sitting judges of the bench, but may also be directed against experts, against a sole arbitrator or a third arbitrator, and against magistrates of the Public Prosecution when they act in the capacity of an joined party.

No new application for recusal may be directed against the judges of the Court of First Instance or of the Court of Appeal when the number of judges whose recusal has not been requested, or of the judges of their grade, becomes insufficient to constitute the bench that rules upon the case of recusal.

Evidence consists of the means to which one of the litigants resorts in order to convince the judge of the existence of an act from which a right arises, and evidence is adduced to prove a material fact or a legal act.
The plaintiff and the defendant must put forward at the same time during the trial all the pleas and claims upon which they wish to rely, whether principal or subsidiary.

In admitting evidence of a legal act, the provisions of the law in force at the time of the creation of such act shall be observed; whereas the admission of evidence of a material fact shall be governed by the provisions of the law in force at the time of the institution of the action.

The admission of evidence of a legal act shall be subject to the law of the State to which the effects of such act are subject, whereas the admission of evidence of a material fact shall be subject to the law of the State in which the action arises.

The manner of adducing evidence shall be subject to the law of the State in which the taking of evidence is requested; provided that no application may be made for the annulment of evidentiary proceedings conducted in a foreign country on the ground that they are contrary to the foreign law if such proceedings are in conformity with Lebanese law.
No evidence shall be required of the existence of Lebanese law, but evidence must be adduced before the Lebanese courts of the content of every foreign law.
A judge may not base his decision upon what he knows, or believes that he knows, personally about the case.
The judge may decide of his own motion or upon the request of someone to decide that it be brought into the hearing session.
If the dispute concerns movable property, the judge may decide that it be brought into the hearing session.
And if obstacles prevent its transfer, the procedure shall take place as though it were immovable property.

If the dispute concerns real property, the court may decide to inspect it, and this inspection shall be carried out by all members of the court who will participate in the judgment, and the litigants shall be summoned thereto three days prior to its taking place so that they may attend if they wish. The court may also entrust the carrying out of the inspection to a single judge from among the judges who will participate in the judgment.

The decision ordering the inspection may include the appointment of an expert to accompany the judge or judges during the carrying out of the inspection to answer the questions which the judge deems appropriate to put to him.

The clerk shall draw up a record of the facts verified by the judge or judges during the carrying out of the inspection, and the delegated judge or the President shall sign it after ascertaining its accuracy.
The sums expended for the purpose of the inspection shall be added to the costs of the action.

A deed or instrument under private signature, that is, a manuscript created as a legal act, shall have no value unless the signature or signatures which it contains make it possible to establish with certainty that the instrument truly emanates from its author or authors.
A party who does not know how to sign his signature shall replace the signature by affixing his fingerprint.
Save for the exception provided for by law, an instrument under private signature may be written by the hand of a third person or by typewriter, provided that it is signed by its author or authors.

In synallagmatic contracts, the instrument under private signature must be drawn up in a number of originals equal to the number of contracting parties having conflicting interests; provided that a plurality of originals is not required when the contracting parties agree to deposit the sole original in the hands of a third person whom they choose.

In an instrument containing a unilateral obligation, it is not sufficient that it bears the signature of the debtor, but it must also contain the words "good for..." provided for in Article 363 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts, and this rule shall not apply in commercial matters.
If the sum specified in the body of the instrument differs from the sum indicated in the words "good for...", this latter sum shall be deemed valid unless the contrary is proved.

A party against whom an instrument under private signature is invoked and who pleads to the merits without contesting the validity of the signature shall not be admitted thereafter to deny this signature.
The signature affixed to the instrument may be denied before any argument on the merits, in which case the handwriting verification procedure shall take place.
