If the validity of the signature affixed to an instrument under private signature is established, either by the voluntary acknowledgment of the person against whom this instrument is invoked, or following the carrying out of the handwriting verification procedure, this instrument shall acquire, with respect to the contracting parties and with respect to third parties, the probative force of an authentic instrument, subject to the proof of the validity of the date.

An instrument under private signature shall not be deemed to have a certain date except with regard to the contracting parties, and it shall not be deemed to have a certain date with regard to third parties except from the day it is established in an authentic instrument, or from the day of the death of one of the signatories, or from the day its summary is entered in an authentic instrument.

Neither testimony of witnesses nor presumptions shall be admissible against what exceeds or contradicts the content of an instrument under private signature, nor as to what is alleged to have occurred before this instrument, or after it, or during its drawing up - all this subject to the provisions of the laws relating to commerce.

An authentic instrument is an evidentiary written document issued by a competent public officer and drawn up in accordance with the prescribed rules. Whether the authentic character is conferred upon the instrument or not conferred upon it shall be governed by the law of the place in which the instrument was drawn up.

An authentic instrument drawn up contrary to the rules of authentic instruments due to a defect in its form or to the lack of competence of the public officer shall be deemed an instrument under private signature if it contains the signatures of all the concerned contracting parties, even if the rules provided for in Articles 146 and 147 were not observed therein.

An authentic instrument has enforceable force, and it is - until its forgery is alleged - conclusive proof of all the material facts which the public officer ascertained by himself and which it was within his duty to ascertain, such as the place of the contract, its date, the authenticity of the signatures, and the declarations which he attributes to the contracting parties.

An instrument which has the form and external appearance of an authentic instrument must be deemed authentic until the party against whom this instrument is invoked proves the contrary. An authentic instrument is also conclusive proof of the facts declared by the contracting parties which have a direct relation to the contract, until the contrary is proved.
An authentic instrument shall only serve as a commencement of proof in writing with respect to declarations which do not have a direct relation to the subject-matter of the contract.

The evidentiary effect of an authentic instrument, with respect to the declarations of the contracting parties, shall only apply to them and to their successors in title. Conversely, the evidentiary effect of this instrument shall extend to third parties, whether in their favour or against them, with respect to the material facts declared by the public officer and which are deemed established until their forgery is alleged.
Counter-letters intended to modify an authentic instrument or an instrument under private signature shall have effect only between the contracting parties and their universal successors.

The creditors of the contracting parties and their particular successors, to whose prejudice the ostensible instrument was fraudulently drawn up, shall be entitled to bring an action for declaration of simulation and to prove it by all means of proof.
A postal letter shall serve as evidence against its signatory in favour of the addressee, unless the former proves that he neither sent it nor instructed anyone to send it.
If the letter is not confidential, the addressee shall be entitled to make use of it and to assign this right to a third party, and in commercial matters letters shall never be confidential.

In civil matters, a confidential letter may not be produced except by agreement of the sender and the addressee; otherwise, its production shall constitute an unlawful act exposing its perpetrator to an award of damages, and furthermore, the court shall take no account of any postal letter produced before it contrary to the rules.

The sender of a registered letter who proves its receipt by an acknowledgment of receipt from the post office or from the addressee shall be permitted to produce the copy kept in his possession if the addressee refuses to produce the original. Such copy shall be deemed authentic until the contrary is proved.

Whoever obtains, pursuant to the provisions of the preceding Article, a judgment favourable to his interest on the basis of the production of a copy of a letter, and the original subsequently appears and reveals that such alleged copy is untrue, shall be ordered to pay double the value of the damage resulting from his fraudulent act.

Statements written by the creditor indicating discharge on a debt instrument remaining in his possession, or on a copy of such instrument, or on a receipt in the possession of the debtor - shall prove payment until the contrary is proved. Such statements need not be dated or signed.

Every debtor shall be entitled to demand upon discharge, in addition to the receipt instrument, that the creditor return to him the debt instrument, and if the creditor claims that the instrument is no longer in his possession, the debtor shall be entitled to demand that this be expressly noted on the receipt instrument.

Domestic registers and papers shall constitute proof against their author and against his universal successors: 1- When they indicate that a discharge has taken place 2- When they establish a debt in favour of a third party

Compulsory commercial books shall constitute proof: First: against the person who keeps them for the benefit of any person, whether they are kept in due form or not, provided that the party who invokes them shall not be entitled to benefit from them unless he accepts all their entries Second: between merchants for the benefit of the person who keeps them in due form in transactions relating to his trade

If the entries in the books of two merchants are at variance and both of them are kept in due form, the judge shall be entitled to decide, as the case may require, either that the two conflicting proofs cancel each other out or to adopt one to the exclusion of the other.

Proof derived, in actions pending between merchants, from non-compulsory commercial books or from compulsory commercial books kept contrary to due form, may be admitted or rejected by the judge as the case may require.

The production of a copy of an instrument while the original instrument exists shall not dispense with the production of that instrument; the production of the original instrument may be insisted upon at any time.
If the original instrument is lost, it shall be replaced by official copies.

The transcription of an authentic instrument in the official registers shall serve only as a commencement of written proof; it must nevertheless be proved that all the originals kept with the notary public and relating to the year during which the instrument appears to have been drawn up have been lost, or proof must be adduced that the loss of the original of that instrument resulted from a particular event.
If it appears from a copy, in the case set forth in the preceding Article, that the instrument was drawn up in the presence of witnesses, those witnesses must be summoned before the judge.
Confirmation is the waiver by one or several of the contracting parties of the right to invoke the relative nullity with which a legal contract is tainted.
A confirmatory instrument is the writing drawn up to prove confirmation.
A confirmatory instrument must contain a summary of the void contract, the ground for nullity or rescission, and the intention to remedy the defect in the contract.
Confirmation may be proved by means other than written evidence.
A party against whom a written instrument is invoked may immediately either deny the handwriting if it is an instrument under private signature, or allege forgery if it is an authentic instrument.
Any discussion on the merits of a produced instrument entails the forfeiture of the right to deny its handwriting.
A party who has produced a written instrument may not withdraw it from the debate except with the consent of the other party.

Where a party denies the handwriting or signature attributed to him, or declares that he does not recognise the handwriting or signature attributed to a third party, the judge may disregard this plea if he considers it a means merely for procrastination or considers it of no utility in resolving the dispute and the verification of handwriting has not been requested of him pursuant to a written petition; otherwise, he shall mark the instrument and decide to conduct the handwriting verification procedure either by comparing the instruments or by hearing the testimony of witnesses, and where the case so requires, by means of experts. The rules laid down for conducting an inquiry or an expert examination shall apply to handwriting verification procedures.
The documents eligible for comparison in the verification procedure are the same as those eligible for comparison in an action for forgery.

Where it is established that the instrument is authentic, the party who wrongfully denied the handwriting may, save in the case of an excusable error, be sentenced to a fine of ten to fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds, and this shall not preclude, where applicable, the application of the provisions of the Penal Code or the award of damages in favour of the other party.

A party against whom an authentic instrument or an instrument under private signature whose authenticity has been established is invoked may allege the forgery of such instrument, even if there is no forgery entailing a criminal penalty.

Upon the request of the party who wishes to allege forgery, the court shall fix the time-limit within which the party producing the instrument alleged to be forged must declare his intention to make use of it.

The party who produced the instrument alleged to be forged shall be entitled to withdraw it within the time-limit fixed by the court, whereupon the incidental proceeding shall come to an end; its costs, however, shall be borne by the party who withdrew the instrument.
And if he does not withdraw it, the other party shall be entitled to allege forgery pursuant to a declaration submitted to the court registry.

Where the trial is proceeding before the Magistrate's Court, the clerk shall refer this declaration to the registry of the Civil Court, and the Magistrate shall stay judgment on the merits until the judgment of the Civil Court is rendered.

Where the action is before the civil court, it may dismiss the application alleging forgery if it considers that the instrument alleged to be forged has no bearing on the adjudication of the principal action, or if it is manifestly apparent to it that the instrument is genuine and that the allegation of forgery is merely a dilatory measure.
Where the forgery is evident, the court shall be entitled to discard the forged instrument and proceed forthwith to adjudicate on the merits.

Where the application alleging forgery requires examination, the court shall issue a decision declaring a stay of the principal action and ordering the deposit of the original instrument alleged to be forged with the court registry if it has not already been deposited; the deposit must be effected within five days from the date of notification of the decision.
The other party or his counsel may inspect at the court registry the deposited original instrument and obtain a photographic copy thereof against payment of the expenses.

Where the instrument alleged to be forged is not deposited with the court registry within the prescribed period, such instrument shall be excluded from the proceedings, provided however that the court shall be entitled to grant a further time limit.

Where the instrument alleged to be forged is merely a copy of an original instrument held in a public depository or in the possession of a third party, the court shall order the deposit of the original instrument, and such decision shall be notified to the custodian of the public depository or to the third party with whom such instrument was deposited.
Where the custodian of the public depository delays in depositing the instrument within the prescribed period, the Public Prosecution may take or propose such measures as it deems appropriate.

Where the person with whom the instrument was deposited delays in depositing it within the prescribed period, the court may sentence him to a pecuniary fine of ten pounds to one hundred pounds and order him to deposit it, failing which he shall be liable to a coercive fine.

Within the eight days following the deposit of the instrument alleged to be forged, there shall be conducted, in the presence of the litigants or their attorneys, the procedure of describing the instrument and the striking out, addition, interlineation, and other apparent characteristics contained therein, through the care of the judge delegated for this purpose pursuant to the judgment that ordered the deposit; the clerk of the court shall draw up a record of this procedure and the judge shall initial the instrument.
Proof of the forgery of the instrument may be established by all means of evidence.

If the authenticity of the instrument alleged to be forged is established, and the claimant of forgery shall be sentenced to a pecuniary fine of fifty to three hundred pounds, and this shall not preclude, where appropriate, an award of damages in favour of the other party if there was bad faith.
If the forgery of the instrument is established, the court shall decide either to destroy it, or to tear it up or strike it out in whole or in part, or to rectify it or restore its true text.
In all cases, the judgment shall order the return of the instruments that were produced for the purpose of comparison.

The documents that are suitable for comparison are: 1- Signatures affixed to other authentic instruments 2- Handwriting and signatures in acknowledged instruments under private signature 3- The part whose authenticity is not disputed of the instrument undergoing verification is enforceable except after the expiry of the time limit for appeal.
The judgment rendered in the case of a claim of forgery shall not be enforceable except after the expiry of the time limit for appeal.

So long as the instruments alleged to be forged are deposited with the registry of the court, no copy thereof may be delivered except by leave of the court; in all cases, a special annotation indicating the existence of the action for forgery must be placed on the copy, and no enforcement procedure may be carried out in respect of these instruments except by special leave of the court, and such leave shall only be granted in case of necessity.

In all cases, a record shall be drawn up stating the attendance of the litigants and their answers, and if there is a judicial delegation, the record shall be referred within three days to the delegating court through the registries of both courts.

Upon the attendance of the litigants, each of them may be examined separately, and in such case a confrontation between them shall be held afterwards, and the judge alone may put the questions, provided that each party is entitled to specify such questions as he wishes and request the judge to put them to the other party.
If one of the litigants fails to attend and does not present a valid excuse, the judge may deem as established the matters that form the basis of the questions put.
Likewise, if one of the litigants refuses, explicitly or evasively, to give an answer to the questions put to him by the judge.

If one of the litigants confines himself to claiming ignorance or forgetfulness, without it appearing nevertheless that he has adopted the attitude of refusal referred to in the preceding Article, witnesses and presumptions may then be admitted to prove the matters that form the basis of the questions put, even in cases where the law does not permit this mode of proof.

The examination by the judge of the litigants present in person may lead to an admission resulting in full proof, or to statements that constitute only a commencement of proof in writing or serve as a basis for simple presumptions.
An extrajudicial admission, namely an admission made outside the presence of the judge, must be proved in accordance with the general rules relating to proof.
An admission shall be null and void if the person making the admission does not possess sufficient legal capacity or authority.
If criminal proceedings have been instituted on account of the alleged forgery, the civil court shall defer judgment until after the determination of the criminal proceedings.

A criminal judgment of acquittal shall not prevent one of the litigants in a civil dispute from alleging the forgery of the instrument that was the subject of the criminal proceedings, if this judgment sets forth the acquittal of the accused while not establishing the authenticity of the instrument itself.
An admission is the acknowledgment by a party of a matter alleged against him, and an admission is either judicial or extrajudicial.

The judge may, at any stage of the proceedings, just as he may in principle in any subject matter, order the litigants, upon the request of a party among them or of his own motion, to appear before him in person, whether in a public hearing or in the deliberation chamber.

The decision ordering the personal appearance of the litigants shall be served upon them at least three days prior to the date appointed for their appearance, to which the time limit for distance shall be added where necessary.

The personal appearance of the litigants may not be ordered: First- in matters in which neither waiver nor settlement is admissible for reasons relating to public policy. Second- in matters in respect of which the law prohibits the adducing of proof.
The civil court may, by way of exception, delegate the justice of the peace to summon the litigants in person, if it finds that distance or other reasons justify these measures.

If it is established by the report of the physician appointed by the court that the state of health of one of the litigants prevents him from attending the trial hearing, the civil court may, when necessary, order the justice of the peace to proceed to his place of residence and to summon the other party thereto.
A declarant may not retract his admission on the pretext that he did not understand its legal consequences.
The retraction of an admission shall be valid in the case of a material error occurring in respect of a certain act, provided that the person who wishes to retract his admission proves this error.

An admission is termed qualified when it is confined to the act declared by the other party, save that it vitiates its legal consequences by the additional statements which it contains, and this admission constitutes full proof with respect to the principal act, whereas the additional statements shall be deemed established until the contrary is proved.

An admission is termed complex when it relates to both the principal act and another act together, and it shall be indivisible in one case, namely: where the new act presupposes the existence of the principal act, such as where the debtor against whom an action for performance is brought admits that he borrowed the amount claimed, but adds to his admission that he discharged it subsequently; the judge shall deem the act of borrowing to be finally established, whereas he shall deem the discharge to be established until the contrary is proved.

Judicial oaths are of two kinds: First - The decisive oath, which is the oath that one of the litigants directs his opponent to take in order to make judgment in the case dependent thereon. Second - The supplementary oath, which is the oath that the judge of his own motion directs one of the litigants to take.

A decisive oath may only be requested with the leave of the judge, and an oath may not be administered in respect of a criminal act or one contrary to public policy, and in respect of in respect of a contract for the validity of which the law requires a written instrument, nor to deny a fact the occurrence of which an authentic instrument attests in the presence of the public officer who received the contract.
An oath may only be administered in respect of a personal fact relating to the party to whom the oath is directed or in respect of his knowledge of any other fact.
An oath may be administered at any stage of the action, even if there is no prima facie evidence of the claim or of the defence in respect of which the oath is administered.

The judge may not administer the oath directly to the plaintiff as to the value of the thing claimed except if it is impossible to prove it by another means for the amount to which the plaintiff attests by his oath

Contracts or other legal acts intended to create, transfer, modify, or extinguish obligations and rights may not be proved by testimonial evidence if their value exceeds fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds. Rather, a deed before the notary public or a deed under private signature must be drawn up for them

Testimonial evidence shall be admissible: 1- In commercial matters 2- If what is sought to be proved is not a legal act, but a mere material fact such as an offence, a quasi-offence, or a quasi-contract. A legal act concluded between two or several persons is nothing more than a material fact with regard to other persons who have no connection to it. The latter may therefore prove it in this manner 3- If there exists a commencement of written proof, that is, a writing, even if devoid of signature, emanating from the defendant or from one who represents him, which renders the alleged fact plausible 4- If it was impossible for the creditor to obtain written proof, and mere moral impossibility shall suffice, which arises in particular from custom followed in certain professions, or from relations of kinship between ascendants and descendants, or from marital bonds 5- If the creditor proves the loss of the deed by a fortuitous event

In actions the value of which exceeds fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds, testimonial evidence shall remain inadmissible therein even though the value of what is claimed is less than this amount, and accordingly, a claim for an amount of less than fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds may not be proved by testimonial evidence if such amount is the remainder or a part of a debt the value of which exceeds fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds and which is not proved by a written deed
The value of the action must be assessed with regard to the time and place in which the legal act was concluded

If the disputed value exceeds fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds, the plaintiff may neither divide his claim nor waive a portion of his debt so as to render its value less than fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds, since consideration is given to the value of the disputed right and not to the value of the claim

If the plaintiff holds against the defendant several rights that are distinct in origin and cause, and the value of each of them is less than fifty-five Lebanese-Syrian pounds, even though the value of the total exceeds this amount, testimonial evidence shall be admissible from the plaintiff even if he brings a single action to claim his multiple rights

Whoever is required to take the oath and abstains from taking it or from referring it back to his adversary - or the oath is referred back to him and he abstains from taking it, shall lose in his claim or in his defence.
The oath may not be referred back to the adversary if the fact upon which the oath is requested does not concern both parties, but is purely personal to the party from whom the oath was requested.

If the party who was required to take the oath or to whom it was referred back takes it, his adversary shall not be permitted to adduce proof of the falsity of his oath; provided that if the falsity of the oath is established pursuant to a criminal decision, the injured party shall be entitled to claim damages, and this shall not preclude challenging the judgment by the possible legal means of recourse.
The party who required his adversary to take the oath or referred it back to him may not retract if the adversary has declared his readiness to take the oath.
The taking of the oath shall serve as proof only against the party requesting the administration of the oath and his heirs and successors in title, whether in their favour or against them.
The judge shall be entitled to require either of the parties to take the oath, either to make the judgment conditional upon it or to determine the amount that will be awarded.

The judge may not, of his own motion, request the administration of the oath on the claim nor on the defence opposing it unless the following two conditions are met: First- The claim or the defence must not be completely established. Second- They must not be completely devoid of proof. Save in these two cases, the judge must confine himself to accepting the claim or dismissing it.
The oath that the judge requests directly from either of the parties cannot be referred back to the adversary.
It is not necessary for the decision expressly to authorise the defendant to produce witnesses in rebuttal, since every inquiry necessarily entails the admissibility of a counter-inquiry.
The civil court may commission the justice of the peace to conduct the inquiry, but it shall exercise this right only in exceptional circumstances and for reasons of importance.

If the court deems it appropriate to conduct the inquiry and the inspection of the site together, it may delegate one of its judges for this purpose, and the judge shall be accompanied by a clerk who shall draw up a record of what the witnesses testify to and of what the judge verifies directly, and the judge shall be entitled to hear at that site and forthwith the witnesses whom he deems it necessary to summon.
In the cases set out in the two preceding articles, the justice of the peace or the delegated judge shall appoint the place, day, and hour at which the witnesses shall be heard.
The litigants must summon their witnesses through the court registry.

The summons to a witness must include: 1- the designation of each of the litigants by his given name, surname, profession, and residence 2- the designation of the witness to whom the summons is addressed 3- the designation of the place of appearance and the day and hour 4- a warning that failure to appear shall result in the imposition of a pecuniary fine 5- the nature of the action for which the testimony is required And if there is a defect in the designation of the two litigants or of the summoned witnesses, such defect shall not invalidate the summons unless it results in a confusion as to identity worthy of consideration.

If the witness is enlisted in the army or in the navy and is on active service, the president of the court must notify the summons to the commander of his unit, requesting him to grant him leave to appear.

If the witness is imprisoned, the president must inform the director of the prison, who shall take measures to have the witness brought under guard, and if bringing him is not possible, the director of the prison must inform the president of the court without delay.
Testimony shall be requested only from persons possessing the capacity to give it.
Capacity to give testimony shall be lacking either by reason of certain criminal judgments, or for unsoundness of discernment, or for failure to have completed the fifteenth year of age.

Testimony shall likewise not be accepted from ascendants for or against descendants, nor from descendants for or against ascendants, nor from a spouse in respect of his spouse even after the dissolution of the marriage, nor shall the testimony of servants attached to the person of the master be accepted in respect of the master so long as they are in his service, nor the testimony of partners in respect of the partnership, nor the testimony of a surety in respect of the obligations of the principal debtor, nor an agent in respect of the principal, all of the foregoing unless there is a contrary provision of law.

If the judge deems it appropriate to hear a minor who has not completed the fifteenth year of his age and the persons referred to in Article 249, he shall be entitled to hear them by way of information and without putting them on oath.
Every witness is entitled, and indeed is under a duty, to refrain from giving testimony if the question put to him would lead him to disclose a professional secret.
Proof by hearsay testimony is not transmitted except in the exceptional cases in which the law has provided for the admission of such proof as a penalty for negligence or bad faith.

In the cases requiring the hearing of testimonial evidence, the judge shall order the conduct of the inquiry either upon the request of the two parties, or directly of his own motion, and he shall dismiss a request to conduct the inquiry issued by one of the two parties, if the matters sought to be proved by testimonial evidence are neither relevant to the case nor admissible.
The decision ordering the conduct of the inquiry must specify the clarity of the facts sought to be proved and the place, the day and the hour at which the witnesses were heard.
In all other cases without exception, the witness shall be summoned directly without an intermediary.

If it is necessary to hear the testimony of the President of the Republic, the President of the Council of Ministers, the representative of the Mandatory Power, or the Secretary-General of the High Commission, one of the judges of the court who arises to the court before which the action is brought shall be specially delegated.
The summons must reach the witness three days before the time appointed for his appearance, with the addition of the time limit for distance.

If the witness does not appear, the court or the judge delegated for the investigation shall sentence him to a pecuniary fine of from five pounds to fifty pounds, and he shall pay the expenses resulting from his non-appearance, and the judge may summon the witness a second time through the clerk of the court; if he persists in not appearing, he shall be sentenced to a second fine at least equal to the first, and the judge shall have the right to order his arrest and his compulsory production; however, if the witness is on active service in the army or the navy, his arrest shall be requested from the commander of his unit.

The judgments referred to in the preceding Article, rendered against the defaulting witness, may be revoked if he presents excuses worthy of acceptance. If the judgment is maintained, the witness may appeal against it.

If the witness notifies the court or the judge delegated for the investigation, on the day appointed in the writ of summons - of an excuse for his default, the court or the delegated judge may grant him a time limit or decide on rogatory commission or transfer to hear his testimony, and they may also, according to the circumstances, dispense with hearing this witness.

A party may not request the hearing of more than five witnesses on a single fact, and if he summons more than this number, he alone shall bear their expenses. The court or the delegated judge may refuse to hear more than five.

Each of the witnesses shall be heard separately, and the court or the delegated judge shall have the right to bring them together for confrontation afterwards, and so long as the investigations have not ended, the witnesses may not depart without permission from the President or from the judge, failing which they shall be liable to a pecuniary fine of from two pounds to five pounds.
The witness shall first be questioned as to his identity, his age, and any kinship or relationship that may exist between him and either of the two parties.
Before giving testimony, the witness shall take an oath that he will testify to the whole truth and that he will testify to nothing but the truth.

Only the President or the commissioned judge shall examine the witness and put to him all the questions that he deems appropriate, and he shall then ask each of the litigants whether he wishes to put a new question. The judge shall have the discretion as to whether or not the question proposed by one of the parties should be put. The judge's discretion shall not be subject to review, and the witness shall answer without making use of any writing.

The President or the commissioned judge may order one of the litigants to withdraw in order to further ensure the freedom of the witness, and after the testimony has been given, the President or the judge shall summon him back and acquaint him with the testimony given in his absence.

The clerk shall record the testimony of each witness, and upon its conclusion, he shall read it aloud. The judge shall ask the witness whether he adheres to it, and if he answers in the affirmative, he shall call upon him to sign it; if the witness does not know how to sign, the judge shall note this and order him to affix his fingerprint.

Every witness shall be entitled to recover his travel expenses and the special compensation provided for by law, and he may, where necessary, request an advance for his travel expenses, which the court registry shall provide to him, and the clerk shall then recover it without delay from the party who requested that the witness be summoned.

Failure to make a claim within eight days from the date of giving testimony shall forfeit the right of the witness to any compensation. The witness shall submit his request to the judge conducting the investigation by means of a petition filed with the court registry.

The court that rules on the facts is that which assesses the value of the testimonies, and its assessment shall not be subject to review. No investigation may be conducted for the accrediting of witnesses.
The clerk shall, ten days after the date on which the report is filed with the court registry, enter the action on the cause list for pleading.

If it appears to the judge that the expert's report lacks sufficient clarity or contains some deficiency, he may summon the expert to the trial hearing through the court registry and ask him for oral explanations; and if these explanations are found to be insufficient, the judge may order a supplementary investigation through the same expert or through one or several other experts.
The president of the court, or the judge deputising for him, shall fix the expert's fee on the original of the report.

The decision fixing the fee shall be enforceable against the party who requested the technical investigation, and after judgment it shall also be enforceable against the party ordered to pay the costs of the action.

An objection to the decision fixing the fee shall be admissible from either of the litigants within the three days following its service. Such objection shall be submitted by a written declaration to the court registry.

The objection shall stay execution and shall be brought before the council chamber, where all the litigants shall be summoned together with the expert if no judgment at last instance has been rendered binding one of the litigants to pay the costs of the action; however, if such a judgment has been rendered, the party who neither requested the technical investigation nor was ordered to pay the costs shall not be summoned to the council chamber.
The expert's opinion shall not bind the judge, bust if the judgment rules contrary to the expert's opinion, it shall contain special reasons justifying the total or partial rejection of his opinion.
Presumptions are consequences drawn by the legislator or the judge from a known unknown fact.
The judge may grant the expert, at his request, an additional time limit if the expert proves that the time limit initially granted is insufficient.

When the expert refuses the mission entrusted to him, another expert shall be appointed, and this appointment shall be made by a decision of the judge who presides over the court if the case is before a court of first instance or a court of appeal, and if the expert was appointed by the justice of the peace, it is this judge who shall appoint the new expert.

The expert must specify to the litigants, by registered letter, the place where he will commence the work together with the day and hour, and this letter must be sent to the actual domicile of each party among the litigants or to his elected domicile at least six days prior to the technical investigation.
The litigants may attend the proceedings of the technical investigation either alone or with the lawyers, and they may also delegate proxies to attend on their behalf.
The expert must indicate in his report the attendance or absence of the litigants when conducting the proceedings of the technical investigation and record their observations therein.

The expert may gather all the information that he deems useful, and he may in particular question the litigants and hear witnesses, but the hearing of witnesses shall only be for the mere purpose of information, and they shall not take the oath.
When the expert completes his report, he shall deposit it with the registry of the court that commissioned him and shall be given a receipt. The report must be reasoned.

The court clerk must, within the twenty-four hours following the deposit of the report, notify the litigants by registered letter and invite them to attend to inspect it, and the litigants may request the court registry to provide them with a copy thereof.

If the adjudication of the action depends on the investigation of matters requiring technical knowledge, the judge may, of his own motion or upon the request of the litigants, decide to conduct a technical investigation.

It is the court that selects the expert in every case, and it may consult the litigants in this regard, yet it shall not be compelled to select the expert whose appointment they propose, even if they have agreed upon him.
In selecting the expert, the judge shall have regard to his technical knowledge and to his probity. His selection may fall upon a foreigner or upon a woman.

A party who has grounds inducing him to request the recusal of the expert appointed directly by the court must submit his request within three days from the date of his appointment by way of a petition signed by him or by his representative containing the grounds for recusal, and the request for recusal shall be adjudicated without delay, and recusal shall only be accepted for one of the grounds specified in Article 119 or for any other important ground.

The decision ordering the technical investigation must state with full clarity the facts which the judge wishes to clarify, and must include the appointment of the expert and the fixing of a time limit for him to file his report with the registry of the court.
This decision shall be notified to the expert through the clerk of the court within three days from the date of its pronouncement.

The expert shall be entitled, within five days from the date of his notification of the decision, to refuse the mission entrusted to him by a registered letter which he sends to the clerk of the court.

If the expert does not carry out the mission to him after his acceptance thereof or does not deliver his report within the specified time limit, the first of the two parties to act may summon him before the court that appointed him and request his replacement by another and a judgment against him for damages, and in addition thereto, the expert may be sentenced to a pecuniary fine of ten pounds to fifty pounds.

A legal presumption means the presumption which the law attaches to certain acts and facts, which are: First- Acts which the law declares null, on the presumption that they were performed in violation of its provisions, and having regard to their nature alone; Second- Acts in respect of which the law declares that the right of ownership and discharge of liability result from certain specific circumstances; Third- The authority which the law confers upon res judicata.

Res judicata has no authority except with respect to the thing which was the subject-matter of the judgment; the thing claimed must therefore be the same, the claim must be founded on the same cause, the action must be between the same litigants, and it must be brought by them or against them in the same capacity.

A claim for compensation for damage arising from a lawful act shall not be dismissed by a plea founded on res judicata resulting from a decision of a criminal court which confined itself to deciding the question of criminality, and ruled to absolve the defendant from liability or to acquit him.

A legal presumption dispenses the person in whose favour it operates from any proof. No proof shall be admitted against a legal presumption where the law relies upon such presumption to annul certain acts or to bar litigation, unless the law has reserved the admission of proof to the contrary, or unless such proof results from a judicial admission or a judicial oath in all cases that do not pertain to public policy.

Possession of a corporeal movable, if founded on good faith, and peaceful, public and free from ambiguity, shall be deemed accompanied by the right of ownership, and no proof shall be admitted to the contrary of this presumption.

Nevertheless, whoever has lost or had stolen from him movable property may bring an action for recovery of ownership thereof against its possessor within three years starting from the day of its loss or theft, and the possessor shall have a right of recourse against the person from whom he obtained possession of it.

If the possessor of the movable purchased it in a public market or from a seller who sells similar things, he shall not be compelled to restore it to its rightful owner except against the price which he paid, subject to the special legislation applicable to lost or stolen instruments "payable to bearer".

Presumptions which have not been established by the law are left to the insight and wisdom of the judge; he must admit thereof only weighty, precise and concordant presumptions, and he may admit them only in the cases where the law permits the admission of testimonial proof, unless the ground for challenging the contract is fraud or deceit, or the presumption is founded on facts which may be deemed voluntary performance.
If the circumstances require the taking of evidence in a foreign country, the judge may send letters rogatory to the foreign court.

The taking of evidence in foreign countries shall be subject to their local law; however, if procedures conforming to Lebanese law are followed in such taking of evidence, their nullity may not be claimed on the ground of violation of the local law.
The probative force of legal instruments shall be subject to the law of the place in which they were drawn up.

Procedural time limits shall be fixed either in hours, in days, or in months. Time limits fixed in months shall be calculated from the date of their commencement to the corresponding date in the following months, and the duration of a day shall be calculated from midnight to the following midnight.
The day or the hour which marks the commencement of the time limit shall not be included in its calculation.
However, the day or the hour at which the time limit expires shall be included in its calculation.
If the time limit expires on a holiday, it shall automatically be extended to the first working day following it.

An additional time limit for distance shall be added to the original time limit fixed by law if there are at least fifty kilometres between the place in which the person to whom the time limits are granted resides, and the time limits in which the act required to be performed by that person must be completed.
The distance time-limit throughout all the territories of the Levant under the French Mandate shall be one day for every fifty kilometres.

If the person granted the time-limit is abroad, the distance time-limit shall be: - one month for Palestine, Hejaz, Iraq, Iran, Turkey, Transjordan, Egypt, Bulgaria, Greece, and the islands of the Mediterranean Sea that are not further than Malta - forty-five days for Afghanistan, Albania, Hungary, Italy, the Kingdom of the Serbs, the Union of Soviet Republics, and Yugoslavia - two months for the other European countries, the countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea, and India - three months for the other countries, except Oceania, for which the time-limit shall be four months.
Treating the elected domicile as the actual domicile permits the waiver of the distance time-limit.
In principle, no procedural act may validly be carried out on a holiday.
No procedural act may be performed before seven o'clock in the morning or after eight o'clock in the evening, on pain of nullity; however, the litigants may waive reliance on the annulment.

Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding articles, the Justice of the Peace or the President of the Civil Court shall be entitled to authorise, by a decision rendered upon the petition of one of the litigants, the performance of an act on a holiday or outside the legal hours, and such decision shall not be subject to any recourse whatsoever.
All time-limits fixed pursuant to the provisions of this Law for the exercise of any right shall, if exceeded, entail the forfeiture of that right.

The judge shall take into consideration the circumstances of the case and the interest of the litigants when ruling on cases of nullity or on formal irregularities in the procedure arising from non-compliance with the provisions of this Law.

If damage results to one of the litigants or to a third party by reason of a defect in a procedural act, whether the annulment of such act is ordered or not, the injured party shall have the right to claim compensation for such damage from the person through whose fault the defect arose.
The litigants may not appear before the Court of Appeal and the Court of Cassation except with the assistance of an attorney duly registered on the roll of the Bar Association.
The litigants shall have the option between being assisted and not being assisted by an attorney before the Civil Court and the Summary Court.

The appointment of an attorney shall be effected by a power of attorney registered with the Notary Public, subject to the rules set forth in the Part on procedure specific to the Summary Court, and such appointment may include the election of domicile at the office of the attorney if he consents.
Every litigant may revoke the power of attorney granted to the attorney at any stage of the action.
He shall notify the clerk of the court of such revocation and disclose to him, where necessary, the name of the new attorney.
The dismissal of the initially appointed attorney and his replacement by another shall not have retroactive effect.
The written document whereby a person submits an application to a judge or to a court shall be called a petition.

The written instrument by which a party summons another party to appear before the judiciary is called a summons if it is before the Magistrate's Court and a writ of summons if it is before the Court of First Instance or the Court of Appeal, and the writ of summons before the Court of Appeal is also called an appeal.

The petition, the summons, and the writ of summons shall be filed with the court registry, and if there is a specified time limit for submitting them, it is sufficient to file them with the court registry within this time limit.
The petition shall be in writing and subject to stamp duty, and it must be signed by the principal or the lawyer.
The judge to whom a petition is submitted shall reply to it by a decision written at the foot thereof, and the clerk must notify the petitioner thereof.

Every writ of summons before the Court of Appeal and Cassation must be drafted and signed by a lawyer; however, as for the writ of summons before the Court of First Instance and summonses, the litigants have the right to seek the assistance of a lawyer in drafting them or to draft them themselves and file them with the court registry.

The documents of the summons and the writ of summons must adequately contain the designation of the plaintiff and the defendant, the court before which the case is intended to be brought, the time limit for appearance, and the subject-matter of the action; every error or omission in these contents leads to nullity if it is of such a nature as to raise doubt in the mind of the defendant.

In principle, there must be filed with the court registry, of the documents of the summons, the writ of summons, and the appeal, a number of copies equal to the number of defendants having distinct interests, and the filer shall retain a copy for himself.

Upon filing, the clerk shall register the action in a special register of his own called the docket and assign it a serial number, and he shall immediately place this number on the copy intended for the defendant or the copies intended for the defendants and on the copy that remains in the hands of the filer.

Upon filing the petition, writ of summons, statement of claim, or appeal with the court registry, the filer must attach thereto a number, under his signature as being true to the original, and the number of copies or abstracts must be equal to the number of defendants, and they shall be served together with the writ of summons, statement of claim, or appeal. However, copies or abstracts that have previously been served in the proceedings of first instance need not be filed or served on appeal.

The clerk must refrain from entering the action in the Cause List if the plaintiff or his lawyer does not file a sufficient number of copies of the document required to be served and of the supporting documents, and the delivery of the copy bearing the Cause List number to the plaintiff or his lawyer shall be deemed evidence that the clerk has received the required number of copies.

The plaintiff or his lawyer may file with the court registry the originals of the documents that he wishes to use, and such filing is in principle optional for the plaintiff; however, the judge is entitled to order him to do so of his own motion or upon the request of the adversary.
When the original of an instrument is filed with the court registry, the clerk must give a receipt therefor.

Following the filing of the writ of summons, statement of claim, or appeal with the court registry, the clerk must forthwith prepare a file for each action and affix thereto the number entered in the Cause List, and this file shall contain a summary statement of the documents filed, the procedural acts, and the decisions rendered in the action, as well as the record of the trial where applicable.

The litigants or their lawyers may inspect this file at the court registry, and each party or his lawyer is entitled to obtain, against payment of the costs in cash, copies of all or part of the documents after certification under the signature of the clerk that they are true to the original.

Judicial decisions, whether contentious or non-contentious, shall have their originals, signed by the judges who rendered them and by the clerk, recorded by the clerk in a special register for each category thereof, and in principle every person therein, save for the legal exceptions, is entitled to obtain from the clerk of the court, against payment of the expenses, a copy of any judicial decision after the clerk certifies under his signature that it is true to the original, and he gives the party adjudged thereon the following phrase: "A true copy valid for enforcement".

The registers containing the originals of judicial judgments may not be removed from the court registry except pursuant to a special decision from the Chamber of the Court of Appeal and Cassation presided over by the First President, and this decision shall be rendered either ex officio, or upon the request of the Public Prosecution, or upon the request of an interested party, and this decision must specify with full clarity the manner of removing the registers from the court registry and the manner of returning them thereto in the shortest possible time.

All registers kept by the clerks of the courts must be numbered and initialled by the Magistrate or the Assistant Magistrate in the Magistrate's Court, and by the President or one of the judges delegated by him in the Court of First Instance, and by the First President or the Counsellor delegated by him in the Court of Appeal and Cassation.
The Presidents of the courts shall supervise the regularity of the registries attached to their courts.

Writs of summons, petitions of action, and appeals lodged with the court registry, as well as other trial documents, must be served upon the defendant in the following manner: if the principal or his advocate is present within the precincts of the court, the clerk may deliver the document to either of them if he is known to him and consents to receive it; otherwise, service shall be effected at the domicile of the principal, either through the clerk or his assistant, or through the court bailiff, and the copy of the document shall be delivered either to the principal in person or to another person, and in this latter case it shall be delivered inside a sealed envelope bearing on one side the address of the person to be served and on the other side the seal of the court registry.

If the person to be served is not present at his domicile, the notice of service may be delivered to any relative, relation by marriage, or servant present therein, provided that it is inferred from his apparent age that he comprehends the significance of the document delivered to him, and provided that the interest of the person intended to be served does not conflict with the interest of the person receiving the envelope.
Service may be effected at the elected domicile just as it is effected at the real domicile, unless the law provides otherwise.

If a person continuously frequents an office, storehouse, or factory, he may be served therein as though he were at his personal domicile, and if the person intended to be served is absent, the envelope shall be delivered to any employee in the same establishment.

If the person entrusted with service finds no one either at the domicile of the person required to be served or at his office, or if the persons who were found refuse to receive the envelope, exceptional service shall then take place, and likewise if ordinary service is impossible for any reason whatsoever.

After delivery of the document of service, a record shall immediately be drawn up in which shall be stated the place of service and its date, the name of the person served, the name of the person who received the document, and the nature of the document served, and the officer entrusted with service must request the person who received the document or the envelope to sign his signature on the record of service if he knows how to sign, and otherwise it shall suffice to affix his seal or the stamp of his name; and if the person required to be served or the person who received the envelope in his absence refuses to sign or to affix the stamp of his seal or his fingerprint, such refusal shall be indicated by a special endorsement in the record of service.

The process server must deposit the record of service with the registry of the court within forty-eight hours at most, failing which he shall be liable to a fine of five pounds, and this record shall be joined in the record of service.

Exceptional service shall be effected by the clerk sending to the person intended to be served a registered letter with an acknowledgment of receipt inviting him therein to attend at the registry of the court in order to receive in person the document addressed to him, or to send an attorney to receive it on his behalf; and this letter shall be sent to the last known domicile or to the elected domicile if found; and if the addressee refuses to receive the registered letter, the postal officer shall return it to the registry of the court with an indication of his refusal, and in this case service shall be deemed to have taken place and the refused letter shall be joined to the file of the action; and if the officer the post does not find the person intended to be served at the domicile indicated in the letter, he shall endorse the fact and return the letter to the registry of the court, and in this case, as in the case where the domicile of the person required to be served is unknown or his residence is unknown, a copy of the document required to be served must be posted on the door of the hall of the court, and there must also be published, in two of the newspapers that insert judicial notices in the locality or the district, a notice informing the person required to be served of the existence of a service concerning him at the aforementioned court, and the record of service shall be replaced on the posting of the copy on the door of the locality and on the publication of the notice in two newspapers.

Whenever exceptional service is liable to lapse if it is not completed within a specified time limit, the sending of the registered letter or the posting of the document of service on the door of the court shall have the effect of suspending the running of this time limit.

Where service of process is directed to a person residing in a foreign country and his domicile or residence therein is known, service shall be effected by registered letter or in accordance with the forms prescribed by the local law, and where such person is a national of the country in which he has established his domicile or residence, a notice of service must also, in the absence of an international agreement on this matter, be sent to the consul of the said country in the Lebanese Republic, if any, and the date of service shall be calculated from the day on which the registered letter is dispatched.

Where the person to be served lacks legal capacity and has a legal representative, service shall be effected upon such representative, and where the person lacking legal capacity has a judicial supervisor, two notices of service must be sent, one to the person lacking legal capacity and the other to the person who supervises him, and service shall be deemed effected upon completion of the later of the two services.
The clerk commissioned to effect service shall be entitled to delegate the clerk nearest to the place of the person to be served.
The clerk of the Peace Court shall be entitled, upon the request of any person, to proceed with the affixing of seals either in person or through an assistant clerk.
Provided, however, that the Magistrate of the Peace must first authorise him to affix the seals.

The rules laid down in this Part shall govern the procedure before the Peace Courts, and in the absence of an express provision, the general rules laid down in this Law shall apply in so far as they are compatible with the organisation of the aforesaid courts.

A party who wishes to summon his opponent before the Peace Court must draw up a writ of summons and submit it to the competent Magistrate of the Peace, and he shall be entitled to appear in person before the court registry, in which case the clerk shall draw up a record of his declaration, and such declaration must contain the particulars prescribed for writs of summons, and the plaintiff must affix his signature to the declaration or affix his name-seal if he declares that he does not know how to sign.

A plaintiff who resides outside the jurisdiction of the Peace Court must elect a domicile in the locality in which the court sits, and if he fails to do so, all writs of summons, notices, and the final judgment as well may be served upon him at the court registry.

A clerk who fails to observe the rules laid down above, relating to the drawing up of the record of the plaintiff's declaration, shall be subject to disciplinary penalties and shall personally bear the trial fees together with the fees of the judgment and its service.
The clerk shall serve the record of the plaintiff's declaration upon the defendant in accordance with the rules established for the service of summonses.

The Justice of the Peace shall then summon the litigants by registered letter to attend the hearing he has scheduled, and this summons shall be sent within twenty-four hours after the service of the summons or of the record taking its place, and that must take place at least five days prior to the date of the hearing; provided that the judge may, in urgent cases, shorten the period for appearance if the plaintiff so requests, on condition that it be no less than twenty-four hours.

The litigants may attend the hearing and plead in person, and they may appoint an advocate or a relative holding a power of attorney certified by the mukhtar, and their appointment of him may validly be made by an oral declaration at the hearing and without a fee. Persons convicted of a felony or an infamous misdemeanour may not be appointed as attorneys, even if they are relatives of the principal.

The Justice of the Peace must first endeavour to reconcile the litigants; if he succeeds therein, he shall draw up a record of conciliation, and this record must be signed by the litigants and the clerk, and be dated and sealed with the seal of the Justice Court, and the Justice of the Peace must add thereto a clause denoting homologation which he and the clerk shall sign, after which the judge shall read aloud everything written in the presence of the litigants. The record of conciliation appended with the decision of homologation shall be deemed equivalent to a judgment and shall not be subject to any form of review whatsoever, and a copy thereof may be delivered to each party.
If the litigants do not reconcile, the clerk must note that, after which the debate shall begin.

The Justice of the Peace may put to the litigants or their attorneys all questions tending to clarify the debate and may provide thereto all explanations relating to the means of proof which the law places at their disposal.

The litigants shall have the right to appear together and of their own accord before the Justice Court, even if it is relatively incompetent, and to submit to it orally the dispute existing between them without following the rules of procedure, provided that they agree thereon. The Justice of the Peace may then adjudicate immediately or adjourn the case to the ordinary hearing.

The litigants or their attorneys must follow the course of propriety and moderation in their statements and must adhere in all cases to the respect due to the judiciary, and if they breach this duty, the judge shall admonish them to respect it, and upon repetition he shall bar them from speaking.

The magistrate has the right to expel any person who disturbs the peace of order at the hearing, and if anyone directs an insult or a grave contempt at his person, he shall draw up a record against him and may sentence him to a pecuniary fine from five pounds to twenty-five pounds and to imprisonment for three days at most, or to one of these two penalties only, and this decision shall be executed immediately and shall not be subject to any recourse whatsoever.

The action shall be adjudicated without delay if that is possible, failing which it shall be adjourned to an upcoming hearing, and in such case the judgment must be issued within twenty days at most; and if it is decided to conduct an investigation, the judgment must be issued within twenty days after its completion.

The magistrate shall draw up the judgment and mention therein the claims of the litigants, a summary exposition of their defence, and the legal articles relied upon, and the judgment must contain a statement of the grounds; and the magistrate and the clerk shall sign the judgment before its reading at the public hearing, and it shall be mentioned therein that it is issued at first instance or at last resort, and it shall be registered at the court registry in its special register within three days.

If one of the litigants wishes to have witnesses present at the hearing heard, the judge may, if hearing them is relevant to the subject-matter and admissible, hear them immediately without any other formality, and the clerk shall then draw up a record of their testimonies if the action is subject to appeal.

If neither the plaintiff nor an attorney on his behalf attends the first hearing, the defendant shall have the choice between requesting the striking out of the action and requesting its dismissal on the merits.

If neither the defendant nor an attorney on his behalf attends the first hearing, the judge may issue a judgment in absentia or not adjourn the action to another hearing if he knows that the defendant was unable to attend for a significant excuse.

Provided that the effects of the default of the plaintiff or the defendant as set forth in the two preceding Articles shall not take place until after the lapse of one hour from the opening of the hearing at which non-attendance is established.

The writ of summons before the civil court shall be for fifteen days, and the domicile elected by the plaintiff shall be stated therein if he is not resident within the territorial jurisdiction of the court.

The defendant shall, within fifteen days after service upon him of the writ of summons, elect a domicile within the territorial jurisdiction of the court if he is not resident therein, and file with the court registry his statement of defence, that is, a written summary, as brief and complete as possible, of the grounds upon which he relies.
The defendant shall file with the court registry, together with his statement of defence, the original documents supporting it, and the clerk shall give him a receipt.

If neither the plaintiff nor the defendant elects a domicile in accordance with the provisions of the preceding Articles 386 and 387, any service upon them at the court registry, up to the service of the final judgment, shall be valid.
A copy of the defendant's statement of defence and of the documents he has filed shall be served upon the plaintiff within ten days from the date of the filing thereof.

And within the ten days following such service, the plaintiff shall in turn file his submissions, and the defendant shall have the right to inspect them at the court registry or obtain a copy thereof.

No new submission shall be admitted thereafter other than submissions indicating waiver or based on new facts, and the admission of such submissions shall remain possible until the time of the hearing, provided that the court may, where necessary, adjourn the hearings to a subsequent session in order to avoid any surprise.

The clerk shall enter the action on the cause list when the plaintiff files his reply submissions, or when fifteen days have elapsed from the service upon the defendant or from the dispatch of the writ of summons without the defendant having filed his statement of defence.

The memorandum referred to in the preceding Article shall not be admitted if it is submitted directly to the court without passing through the registry, and in addition to the foregoing, the person submitting it in such a case shall be sentenced to a pecuniary fine of five pounds to fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds. Where he is an advocate, he may also be sentenced by prohibiting him from practising the profession for a period of one year at most. These judgments shall be rendered by the court of its own motion.

If a new fact occurs or an unknown fact comes to light after the closure of the hearings and before the pronouncement of the judgment, the court may decide of its own motion or upon the request of one of the parties to reopen the hearing and enter the action anew on the cause list for oral pleadings.

The President shall have the right to decide, as the circumstances require, to conduct the trial in one of the actions before other actions that precede it at the time on the cause list for oral pleadings.

The trial sitting shall in principle be public, provided that the court may decide to hold it in camera of its own motion or upon the request of the Public Prosecution if it sees in the publicity of the hearings a danger to public security or public morals; however, the decision for a trial in camera shall not apply to advocates wearing the robe of advocacy and shall apply only during the hearings, and not at the reading out of the judgment.
The hearings may not be published in the newspapers when they pertain to actions for defamation or to actions relating to personal status.

The clerk shall draw up the record of the trial and affix his signature thereto at the end of every sitting, and shall mention therein the hour of the opening of the sitting and the hour of its closure, the names of the judges of the court and of the Public Prosecution, the actions that were called and in which oral pleadings took place, the names of the advocates and the facts that occurred, and the explanations that the court orders him to enter. The record of the trial is an authentic instrument; the clerk who falsifies it in bad faith commits the offence of forgery in official documents.
The clerk shall notify the lawyers, or the litigants who have not appointed lawyers on their behalf, of the date on which the case will be called for trial at least three days prior to the date.
On the appointed date, the case shall be called for trial. The President may retain it for pleading, or adjourn it to a subsequent hearing according to what is practicable.

If the defendant appears in person or through his lawyer when the case is called, he may petition for its adjournment to a subsequent hearing so as to enable him to file his defence, provided that he shall be sentenced, by reason of his delay, to a pecuniary fine of ten pounds to fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds. No further postponement shall be accepted thereafter.
Leave to speak shall be granted first to the lawyer of the plaintiff, or to the plaintiff if he is pleading in person, and then leave to speak shall be granted to the defendant.

The President may interrupt the pleadings to put the questions that he deems useful or to make the observations that he deems necessary, and he may prohibit one of the litigants or one of the lawyers from speaking if his inability to speak in a useful and proper manner becomes apparent, and the provisions of Articles 378 and 379 shall apply. However, the penalties provided for in the latter Article shall be imposed by the court, not by the President alone.

The President may grant the plaintiff the right of reply or deny it to him, and he may grant against him the right of rejoinder if the case so requires or deny it to him, according to whether he deems that the case has been examined or has not been sufficiently examined, and thereafter he shall grant leave to speak to the Public Prosecution. The Public Prosecutor may request the adjournment of the case to a subsequent hearing in order to prepare his submissions.
The debates shall be closed when the President grants leave to speak to the Public Prosecution.

However, the litigants or their lawyers may submit to the court, within the three days following the closure of the debates, a single written memorandum to complete or rectify certain points, and this memorandum must be submitted through the court registry and at least two copies thereof must be deposited, one of which the registry shall serve upon the adversary without delay, and the adversary shall be given three days to reply thereto.
A judgment rendered against a party ordering the payment of damages may either assess the amount of such damages or declare that it shall be assessed pursuant to a statement.

In this latter case, the party ordered to pay the damages must make an actual tender to the creditor within eight days at the most from the date of service of the judgment; if the creditor does not accept, the debtor may bring an action for verification against him, and if nothing is tendered within the aforementioned period, the creditor shall be entitled to bring an action against the debtor, and the debtor alone shall bear the costs thereof.

Judgments rendered following adversarial proceedings must state that they are provisionally enforceable notwithstanding appeal and without security if the right upheld by those judgments is established by an authentic instrument, by a recognised instrument under private signature, or by an admission, and provisional enforcement may be ordered, with or without security, in cases of urgency, and in commercial matters as well.
Judgments by default may order "provisional enforcement notwithstanding opposition" either with security or without security, in cases of urgency.
Provisional enforcement shall not extend to costs.
Judgments may only be enforced after service upon the opposing party.

Costs shall be assessed in the judgment if their assessment is possible; otherwise, the clerk shall issue an enforceable title therefor upon sight of the decision assessing them issued by the President or the judge deputising for him, without the need for a new action.

All litigants may at all times file an opposition against the decision assessing the costs, within the three days following service of the judgment or the enforceable title or notification of the statement of costs, and such opposition shall be made by a simple declaration to the court registry.

The objection shall be brought before the council chamber of the court that rendered the judgment, pursuant to a simple summons of twenty-four hours sent to the adversary if the circumstances require his attendance, and if the adversary has no actual or potential interest in the rectification of the decision on costs, the objection shall remain admissible, and the objecting party may attend it alone.

In principle, the losing party must be ordered to pay the costs, subject to the following exceptions: 1- A party who has obtained legal aid may not be ordered to pay the costs. 2- The winning party may be ordered to pay all or part of the costs by way of compensation for damages if the judgment holds against him a fault he committed against his adversary.

If there are several losing litigants or if both parties have won their case only partially, the court may apportion the costs in unequal shares as the case may require. If the judgment is confined to ordering the payment of costs and does not include such apportionment, the costs shall then be apportioned in equal shares per capita.
Joint and several liability with respect to the principal judgment necessarily entails joint and several liability with respect to the costs.

The costs of the case shall include the total expenses incurred by the two pleading parties, including the lawyer's fee, which the court shall fix taking into account in fixing it the difficulties of the lawsuit. And this fixing shall have no effect except between the two parties.
If the condition of one of the litigating parties does not enable him to pay the costs of the lawsuit, he may petition for legal aid.

The petition shall be submitted by way of an application exempt from stamp duties (tamgha) and written in three copies deposited with the registry of the civil court that is to hear the lawsuit, or within whose district lies the magistrate court that is to hear the lawsuit; the clerk shall retain one copy and send the second copy to the Public Prosecution, and the third to the adversary.

The petitioner shall attach to his application a certificate from the Finance Administration indicating the direct taxes that he pays, and he may also attach to it any certificate from any authority competent to attest to his poverty, and if one of the certificates is produced collusively and proves to be untrue, and the petitioner and the person who gave him the certificate shall be liable to a pecuniary fine of ten to two hundred L.S. pounds. And to imprisonment from eight days to six months, or to one of these two penalties only. It is the Public Prosecution that shall request the application of the aforementioned penalties either of its own motion or pursuant to a complaint by the adversary.

In civil matters, if the Public Prosecutor is not a principal party to the action, he shall in principle have the option, when the judge grants him leave to speak, either to submit his opinion or to leave the matter to the discretion of the court; however, he must submit his opinion if the court expressly requests him to do so or in the following cases: 1) if the action pertains to an incapacitated person, or to the Government, or to a public administration, or to a public institution 2) if the action relates to personal status 3) if the action concerns the proper administration of justice, such as lack of jurisdiction for instance, or an application for transfer of the action on grounds of kinship or on grounds of legitimate suspicion, or determination of the competent court, or lis pendens, or connexity, or retrial, or complaint against the judgment 4) if an offence is committed during the trial
The court may deliver its judgment forthwith, or during the hearing in which the pleadings took place, or at a subsequent hearing
On the merits, the judgment must be delivered within eight days at the most after the hearing of the closure of the debates

The judgment shall be delivered in accordance with the opinion of the majority of the members of the court, and every dissenting judge must state the grounds of his dissent and enter them in his own handwriting, and affix his signature at the foot of the original of the judgment, and in this case it shall be mentioned in the judgment that it was delivered by a majority of votes and the dissent shall not be mentioned in the copies of the judgment

The judgment shall be drafted by the President of the court or by one of its members designated by the President, and shall then be signed by all the members of the court and the clerk and prior to its pronouncement at the hearing, and the judgment must be registered within three days in the register assigned to judgments kept at the registry of the court

The President, or the most senior of the members in service, shall read out the judgment at a public hearing, and the judges who sat during the debates, with the exception of the Public Prosecutor, must attend the reading of the judgment

If it occurs, between the commencement of the debates and the public reading of the judgment, that an impediment arises preventing the attendance of one of the judges of whom the court was composed - the debates must be repeated before the court as newly constituted
The judgment may contain: either the fixing of a granted period of grace, or the authorisation of provisional enforcement
Whatever the financial condition of the petitioner may be, his petition for legal aid shall be met with refusal if it becomes evident that what he has claimed is unfounded on the merits.

The court entrusted with adjudicating the application for legal protection shall summon the petitioner and his opponent through the clerk to appear before it sitting in the council chamber.
