They shall retain the choice between complying and not complying, and they may confine themselves to sending their observations in writing, and the statements of the Public Prosecution must always be heard.
The decision of the court refusing or accepting the application for legal aid shall not be subject to any recourse except an appeal by the Public Prosecution.

If the court grants legal aid, the clerk must thereupon notify the President of the Bar Association thereof, who shall immediately appoint one of his colleagues to defend the interests of the party who obtained such aid. The assistance provided by the lawyer in this manner shall be gratuitous, and he may not receive a fee except from the opponent who loses the action, provided that this opponent himself has not obtained legal aid; in this case, the lawyer's fee shall be fixed in the judgment, taking into consideration the difficulties of the case. Every attempt aimed at obtaining a fee and every acceptance of such fee - even if not requested by the lawyer - shall be deemed a grave fault entailing disciplinary action, and the enforcement of the penalty for this fault shall be entrusted to the Public Prosecution and to the President of the Bar Association.
The clerical proceedings pertaining to the assisted party shall be gratuitous, and the expenses of the necessary measures pertaining to the investigation shall be borne by the Government.

At any stage of the action, the court that granted the legal aid may revoke its decision if the material circumstances on account of which the aid was granted have changed, or if it becomes evident that they were untrue; in this case, the aid shall be cancelled and its cancellation shall have retroactive effect.
Legal aid shall lapse upon the death of the assisted person, and its lapse shall not have retroactive effect. Nor may his heirs, where applicable, petition for legal aid.

If he wins the action, his opponent who is ordered to pay the expenses must pay them as though the legal aid had not been granted, and he must also, where applicable, refund to the Government the amount of the expenses which it advanced for the measures pertaining to the investigation.

An assisted person who wins the lawsuit shall remain entitled to legal aid with respect to the execution of the judgment, or to the defence when recourse is made to means of review to challenge the judgment
If the assisted person loses the lawsuit, no fee shall be paid for the transactions conducted in his interest, and the advances of the Government shall not be reimbursed

An assisted person who loses the lawsuit may petition the Court of Appeal for legal aid to enable him to have recourse to means of review. This petition shall have the same form and be subject to the same rules as were followed in the first instance lawsuit
A judgment shall, as of right, have the authority of res judicata, and enforceable force

The authority of res judicata shall preclude the renewal of discussion on the operative paragraph of the judicial decision, without prejudice to the right to have recourse to means of review, and to submit applications pertaining to difficulties of interpretation or execution

If a material error occurs in the drafting of the judgment, the judges who issued it may, in all matters, proceed to rectify it either upon the application of one of the litigants or upon the application of the Public Prosecution, unless the lawsuit has been removed from their hands by the exercise of one of the means of review
The litigants concerned in the judgment in which the error occurred shall be summoned to the court through the registry, and they may submit their observations in writing or orally
The rectifying judgment shall be mentioned in the registers of the originals of judgments, in the margin of the rectified judgment
And no copy in which the correction is omitted shall be delivered thereafter; as for the copies delivered previously, the clerk shall retrieve them and then destroy them.
For res judicata to exist, three conditions must be fulfilled: identity of the litigants, identity of the cause, and identity of the subject matter.

The principle of relativity of res judicata admits of the following exceptions: First - With respect to joint and several or indivisible obligations, in the cases provided for in the Civil or Commercial Law. Second - With respect to the successors of the litigants. Third - With respect to decisions issued by a criminal court: the criminal operative part may not be contradicted by a civil or commercial judgment.
The enforcement of foreign judgments is in accordance with the decisions of the High Commissioner.
Every judicial judgment alters the rule of prescription that was running against the disputed right.

Every litigant who has won his case may register upon the immovable properties of his debtor a compulsory mortgage to secure what the judgment has awarded, and for that purpose he is required to submit a petition to the President of the Execution Department within whose district the immovable properties upon which the mortgage is sought to be established are situated. And he must submit with the petition either a copy of the judgment certified by the clerk, or a certificate from the registry containing the operative part of the judgment and including the following: 1- The name, surname, profession, and residence of the creditor, with the designation of an elected domicile in the locality where the court sits. 2- The name, surname, profession, and residence of the debtor. 3- The date of the judgment, mentioning the court that issued it. 4- The amount of the debt. 5- A precise and clear designation of the immovable properties, whether with regard to their nature or their location, in accordance with the particulars derived from the cadastral map and the Land Register.

The President of the Execution Department shall enter his decision at the foot of the petition - and he must in particular take into consideration the amount of the debt and the approximate value of the designated immovable properties, and where necessary, make the allocation of the mortgage intended for a part thereof, or for a single immovable property thereof, or for a portion of such immovable property, if he deems that the portion suffices to pay the principal, interest, and expenses due to the creditor.
If the debt awarded by the judgment has not yet been liquidated, the President of the Execution Department may liquidate it provisionally and fix the amount for which the mortgage shall be allocated.

If the President of the Execution Department rejects the application, the applicant shall be entitled to refer the decision of rejection to the Court of First Instance and to request the appearance of the debtor before it, by a summons of twenty-four hours.

The decision of the President of the Execution Department or the judgment permitting the creation of the mortgage shall be registered in the Land Register, and the compulsory mortgage provided for in Article 453 shall take effect only from the date of such registration.
In principle, the effects of judgments relate back to the date of the summons or the statement of claim.
However, judgments which effect a change in the status or capacity of a person, and judgments rendered in enforcement matters, shall take effect only from the date of their pronouncement.

An application for voluntary intervention shall be effected merely by lodging a statement of claims with the registry of the court. However, such application shall not delay the determination of the principal action if it is in a state permitting judgment to be rendered.
If a dispute arises as to the right to intervene, it shall be adjudicated summarily.
Any party may join a third party in the proceedings to be bound by the judgment. Such summons shall follow the rules observed for the statement of claim at the commencement of proceedings.
The defendant may raise a "plea for a stay" in order to have the time necessary to summon a third party to be bound by the judgment. He may request, for this purpose, a time limit of eight days.
The lapse of the action shall have no effect on the merits of the right.

The President of the Court of First Instance shall rule, in his capacity as Judge of Urgent Matters, on every urgent measure that must be taken in matters subject to and vested in the Head of the Execution Department.

The Judge of Urgent Matters shall also have jurisdiction to examine matters relating to sanitary measures that must be taken for the protection of public health, on condition that such measures do not frustrate any of the rights of the competent administrative authority.

The judge having jurisdiction in urgent matters is the judge of the court competent to examine the merits of the dispute, or the judge of the place in which the subject-matter of the urgent action arose, and the litigants may appear in person or through attorneys.

The action shall be heard at the sitting held for that purpose by the President of the Court of First Instance or the judge acting in his stead, on the day and at the hour appointed by the court, while the time-limit for the summons to appear shall be one clear day.

Provided that if the case requires expedition, the President or the judge acting in his stead may grant leave to summon the litigants either to the court or to his residence, even on official holidays, and in that case the writ of summons may only be issued pursuant to a decision by the Judge of Urgent Matters commissioning one of the bailiffs for that purpose. The writ of summons must be served upon the person himself.
Decisions in urgent matters are enforceable forthwith without security, unless the judge orders the provision of security.

Decisions in urgent matters shall not be subject to opposition, provided that they may be appealed in the matters and cases in which judgments of the Courts of First Instance may be appealed - and they may be appealed within eight days commencing from the date of service. The Court of Appeal shall rule thereon summarily. The appeal shall not stay execution.

The court may, at any stage of the action, decide of its own motion to join a third party to the case, and its decision must appoint the day for the resumption of the debates. The clerk shall send to the third party a writ of summons in accordance with the terms of the decision.

The third party required to intervene in the case upon the request of one of the litigant parties or directly upon the request of the court must submit a defence memorandum within fifteen days commencing from the date of the service he received, and he is bound to submit his statement of defence within the same time limit appointed for the defendant.
The plaintiff may, up to the time fixed for the commencement of the pleadings, waive the right which he claimed, or content himself with discontinuing the action which he instituted.

The waiver of the disputed right terminates the action subject to three conditions, which are: 1- The plaintiff must compensate the defendant for all the costs and various damages caused to him by the action, or undertake to compensate him and provide him with sufficient security 2- The plaintiff must deliver to the defendant the documents relating to the claimed right 3- The instrument of waiver served upon the defendant must be clear and explicit
After the fulfilment of these conditions, the defendant must authorise the clerk to strike the case off the roll.

If the foregoing does not take place and a dispute arises as to the fulfilment of the conditions of the instrument of waiver, the court shall then adjudicate upon the incidental issue. If it is adjudged that the defendant is at fault for not being satisfied with a valid waiver, he shall be ordered to pay the costs of the incidental issue.

A discontinuance confined to the action alone shall have no effect unless the defendant consents thereto, and he may accept such discontinuance only upon conditions, and the action shall not be stayed unless the defendant authorises the clerk to strike it off the roll.

If the plaintiff commences the action, and then abandons it until two years have elapsed without legitimate cause since the last proceeding, it shall lapse and all the proceedings shall become null and void by operation of law, and the principal plaintiff shall be ordered to pay the costs; provided that the lapse of the action shall be precluded if the plaintiff pursues the proceedings and the defendant does not raise a plea for declaration of lapse at the very first act performed to pursue the action.

The Judge of Urgent Matters has jurisdiction to adjudicate cases which, by their nature and value, fall within the competence of the Magistrate, and no urgent case may be brought when the action is before the Court of Appeal.

The originals of decisions issued in urgent matters shall be kept at the registry of the court. The Judge of Urgent Matters has the right, in case of absolute necessity, to order execution upon the original of the decision.
Prior to bringing any action, a petition may be submitted to the Judge of Urgent Matters in order to obtain the appointment of an expert entrusted with a technical inspection.

The decision concerning the appointment of an expert in this manner may require the clerk to send a registered letter to any person to notify him, forty-eight hours prior to the appointed time, of the day, hour, and place at which the expert's inspection will take place. That person may attend the inspection and make all observations he deems useful. A summary of his observations must be included in the expert's report.

The party who requests, prior to bringing any action, an inspection by an expert, is required upon submitting the petition referred to in Article 482, to deposit with the clerk's office a sum sufficient for the expenses of the inspection. These expenses shall remain provisionally at his charge.

If an action is subsequently brought and it is established that the prior inspection was justified, the losing party may be ordered to refund the expenses of the inspection to the person who paid them.
The expert's report shall be deposited with the registry of the court, and the party who requested the inspection may obtain a certified copy of this report.

The litigants may, if they agree, choose the Judge of Urgent Matters as an arbitrator between them, even if the dispute does not fall within the scope of jurisdiction of this judge or the jurisdiction of the court, provided that the subject matter is capable of settlement by compromise, and that the litigants have the capacity required to conclude a compromise; in this case, the decision of the Judge of Urgent Matters shall not be subject to any form of recourse.
Opposition may be lodged immediately following the pronouncement of the default decision.

Opposition shall not be admissible after the expiry of fifteen days commencing from the day of service of the decision, and it must be stated in the writ of service: that after the expiry of the aforementioned time limit the right of opposition shall lapse, failing which the service shall be void.
The time limit for opposition shall not stay execution, save in the cases exhaustively specified by law.
Opposition shall be brought by submitting a summons or a statement of claim to the court that rendered the default decision.

Opposition shall stay the execution of the default judgment unless such judgment authorises expedited execution notwithstanding opposition. Provisional execution notwithstanding opposition may be granted or refused by the judge pursuant to the claims of the plaintiff, with or without security.
Opposition shall not stay execution unless it is duly registered within the statutory period.
Every default decision must be executed within three months commencing from the date of its pronouncement, failing which it shall lapse ipso jure by prescription.
Such lapse by prescription shall apply only to the decision, whereas the preceding proceedings shall remain valid.

An appeal may be lodged against: 1- Decisions rendered at first instance with respect to the value of the action 2- Decisions that pertain to an indeterminate interest or to the quantum of the matter adjudged 3- Decisions ordering the conduct of an investigation if they were rendered at the request of a party and despite the opposition of the other party provided that the decisions stipulated in the third paragraph may only be appealed together with the judgment pertaining to the merits
If the judge characterises the judgment as being rendered at first instance or at last instance, such characterisation shall not bind the Court of Appeal
If a decision omits to sentence one of the litigants to a civil fine in one of the cases in which the law has made such fining mandatory, the Public Prosecution must appeal on this ground alone
During the eight days following the pronouncement of the judgment, no appeal shall be validly lodged and no legal act of execution shall be carried out, except in the case of provisional execution
The time limit for appeal is: - eight days for decisions in urgent matters - and twenty days for judgments of the reconciliation courts - and thirty days for civil judgments

The aforementioned time limit shall commence from the date of service of the judgment upon

the defendant, whether in person or at his actual

elected domicile if the judgment was rendered in adversarial proceedings, and it shall commence from the date of expiry of the period of

persons if the judgment was rendered in default

However, if the appeal is lodged by the Public Prosecution, the time limit shall commence

from the date of the pronouncement of the judgment
The time limit for appeal shall be interrupted by the death of the party against whom judgment was rendered, and shall not resume running except from the date of a new service upon the heirs

The petition of appeal must include a statement of the grounds, and the same rules observed for the summons before the Court of First Instance shall be followed in its drafting and service, as set forth in Article 340 and the articles following it
If neither the plaintiff nor a representative on his behalf attends the first hearing, the defendant may request either the annulment of the proceedings or the dismissal of the claim on the merits.

If a writ of summons to the Reconciliation Court or a writ of summons to the Court of First Instance or the Court of Appeal has been duly sent to the defendant, and he fails to attend in person and fails to appoint a representative on his behalf at the first hearing, the judgment or appellate decision shall be rendered in absentia, subject to the application of the provisions of Article 384 which provides for the rules of procedure before the Reconciliation Court, and the judge shall award the plaintiff his claims, unless they appear to him to be unlawful and unfounded.

The effects of the failure of the plaintiff and the defendant to attend, as set forth in the two preceding Articles, shall not be enforced until the expiry of one hour from the opening of the hearing which they failed to attend.

If the plaintiff himself or his representative attends the first hearing and subsequently fails to appear such that neither he nor anyone representing him attends, the action shall be deemed adversarial, and the defendant may thereupon request either the annulment of the proceedings or judgment on the merits based on the claims previously submitted.
If the defendant himself or his representative attends the first hearing. The action shall be deemed adversarial from that hour even if he subsequently absents himself.
A decision that is rendered in absentia shall be subject to opposition.
A decision that was rendered pursuant to an opposition shall not be subject to a new opposition.

If the action is against several persons and only a party of them absents themselves, the judge must stay the adjudication of the action and send another writ of summons to the defaulting defendants, and after the judgment that is rendered after this summons an adversarial judgment with respect to all the litigants whatever their conduct may be.

Claims for interest, arrears, and all other accessories that have fallen due since the issuance of the judgment, and compensation for damages incurred as a result of the judgment or since its issuance - shall not be deemed new claims, and may be raised on appeal merely by submitting a statement of claims
Intervention in the appellate action shall be admissible from any person who would subsequently be entitled to file a "third-party opposition" against the decision to be issued
The appellate trial shall follow the same rules applicable to the trial before the Civil Court
If an appeal is lodged against a decision that does not include adjudication on the merits, the Appellate Court shall, if it reverses it, adjudicate on the merits as well
Difficulties of interpretation arising from an appellate decision must be submitted to the Appellate Court
Difficulties of execution arising from an appellate decision affirming the judgment of first instance the Appellate, unless this court has decided otherwise
Retrial shall be permissible in respect of judgments issued by the Magistrates' Courts and the Civil Courts at last instance, and in respect of decisions issued by the Court of Appeal and Cassation
The expiry of the time limit for appeal shall not open an avenue for retrial in respect of judgments issued at first instance

When the appellant lodges the petition of appeal with the registry of the Court of Appeal, he must attach thereto a copy of the appealed judgment and a copy of the supporting documents upon which he wishes to rely for the first time in the appeal.

The appellant must also deposit a fine in the amount of ten L.S. pounds if the appealed judgment was issued by a Magistrate's Court and twenty L.L.S. if it was issued by a Court of First Instance. This fine shall become a vested right of the Government if the judgment is not overturned; otherwise, it shall be returned to the appellant. If there are several appellants in a single case, the total of the amounts sought to be deposited may not exceed two hundred L.S. pounds.
The time limit for appeal does not stay execution, except in the cases expressly provided for by law.
An appeal shall not stay execution, unless it is duly registered within the legal time limit.

An appeal shall not stay execution if the judgment has authorised expedited execution; however, the execution shall be invalidated, and damages may be awarded, if it is decided to overturn the judgment.

Expedited execution without security must be ordered when the claim is based on an official instrument or on a private instrument whose signature is acknowledged, and expedited execution may be ordered with or without security in all urgent funds.

If the judgment of first instance omits to order expedited execution in one of the cases in which expedited execution is mandatory, the prevailing party may request it by a petition submitted to the President of the Court of Appeal, which shall order it in a decision issued in the deliberation chamber.

From the moment the application for appeal is lodged with the registry of the Court of Appeal, the Court of First Instance loses the right to adjudicate disputes relating to the interpretation of its decision or to the execution thereof.
The appellate court's examination of the dispute shall be restricted to the grounds set forth in the petition of appeal.
Either party may renounce the right of appeal either after the issuance of the judgment of first instance if he acquiesces therein, or prior to its issuance.
Acquiescence in the judgment shall be express or implied in the judgment, or for another reason, and he may, if the other party appeals, file an incidental appeal.
If one of the parties loses the right of appeal by his acquiescence in the judgment or for another reason, he may, if the other party appeals, file an incidental appeal.

If the incidental appeal is only possible due to the existence of a principal appeal filed prior to it, it shall remain dependent upon this principal appeal: if it is annulled or forfeited by a valid discontinuance, it shall also lapse at the same time.
However, if the incidental appeal is filed within the legal time limits, neither the nullity of the principal appeal nor its forfeiture shall affect it.
Discontinuance of the appeal, like discontinuance of the action, shall be subject to the provisions of Articles 467,471.
No new claim shall be admissible on appeal, unless the purpose thereof is set-off or a defence to the original claim.
A principal "retrial" shall be brought before the court that rendered the impugned judgment. It is not necessary that it be composed of the same judges.

A retrial shall be initiated by a summons or a writ of summons to the Civil Court or the Court of Appeal. The petitioner must, at the time of filing the summons or the writ of summons with the registry, deposit a fine in the amount of twenty L.S. pounds if it is before the Civil Court, and seventy-five L.L.S. if it is before the Court of Appeal. The Government, public departments, and public institutions shall be exempted from this deposit.
A "retrial" has no suspensive effect.

An incidental request for "retrial" shall be submitted pursuant to a statement of claims. In order for it to be admissible - the court before which the principal action is brought must be the same court that rendered - the impugned decision, or another court equal to it or higher than it.

If the court before which the principal action is brought is lower in degree than the court that rendered the impugned decision, the "retrial" cannot be submitted incidentally, and in this case the person who wishes to seek a "retrial" shall have the right to request the court before which the principal action is brought to stay the adjudication thereof so that he may request a principal "retrial" from the court that rendered the impugned decision. The judge may accept or reject the request for a stay as the case may require.
The court before which the request for "retrial" is brought may adjudicate by a single judgment on its admissibility and on the merits together.
The decision dismissing the "retrial" shall also order the petitioner to pay a fine, and where applicable, to pay compensation for damages.
The decision admitting the "retrial" shall revoke the previous decision, replace it, and order the refund of the deposited fine.
The expiry of the time-limit for opposition opens an avenue for retrial in respect of judgments by default.

Retrial shall be permissible in the following cases only: First - Where the opponent of the petitioner personally committed, during the course of the lawsuit, fraud that had an effect on the contested decision. The fraud of the advocate shall be deemed equivalent to the fraud of his client. Second - Where there was an omission to rule on one of the claims. Third - Where the reasons are insufficient. Fourth - Where judgment was given for that which was not claimed, or for more than what was claimed, unless this may be pursuant to a law relating to public policy. Fifth - Where it is subsequently acknowledged or decided that the documents upon which the contested judgment was based were forged, or where the contested judgment was based upon a prior judgment which was subsequently annulled or revoked, or where one of the witnesses, experts or translators was convicted of false testimony or forgery. Where decisive documents appeared after the issuance of the judgment which had been withheld by the opponent of the petitioner or the representative of that opponent. Seventh - Where judgment was issued against the Government or against a public administration or a public institution and it was represented in the lawsuit contrary to the rules of procedure or by way of fraud. Eighth - Where the operative part of the judgment is contradictory to one another. Ninth - Where the Public Prosecution did not submit its opinion in the cases in which its submission is mandatory pursuant to Article 408. Tenth - Where an essential formality was not observed. Eleventh - Where it occurred, as between the litigants themselves acting in the same capacity and on the basis of the reasons, that a contradiction arose between two decisions issued by a single court.

Where contradictory decisions are issued by different courts, only the decision of the highest court among them shall be taken into account. However, where they are issued by two courts of equal degree, only the more recent of the two decisions in date shall be enforced.

The time-limit prescribed for submitting a petition for retrial is, in principle, two months commencing from the date of service of the adversarial judgment or from the date of the time-limit for opposition to the judgment by default.

Where the retrial is based upon a breach of the rules of procedure in the representation of a person lacking legal capacity, the commencement of the time-limit shall be from the date of serving the decision anew after the formality that removed the lack of capacity.

And where the "retrial" is based upon forgery, fraud or the discovery of new documents, the time-limit shall commence from the day of knowledge of the forgery or the fraud or from the day of discovery of the documents, provided that the day of their discovery is established by a written document.

A decision issued pursuant to a petition for "retrial" may also be challenged by a new petition for "retrial". However, this shall only be possible in the cases provided for in Article 541 and on condition that the ground was not discovered until after the first petition.

Judgments and decisions, and decisions of the Judge of Urgent Matters, if they cause prejudice to a person who was neither a party to the action nor represented therein, may be objected to within ten years by way of "third-party opposition".
A party may also confine himself to invoking the relativity of the adjudicated matter, or avail himself of any other means of recourse.

Where the heirs or creditors of a person are duly represented through such person, the case shall be otherwise than the foregoing when the judgment results from fraud directed against them. In this case, the heir or the debtor may avail himself of "third-party opposition" against the judgment rendered against his predecessor in rights, provided that he proves the fraud by all means.

Joint and several creditors and debtors, and creditors and debtors under an indivisible obligation, may avail themselves of "third-party opposition" against a judgment rendered against another creditor or debtor, provided that they prove that this judgment fraudulently prejudiced their rights.
They may also avail themselves of "third-party opposition" if they are able to invoke a ground or defence personal to them.

Where the right to sue is reserved by virtue of the law exclusively to one or several specified persons, the other persons who are deprived of the right to sue shall also be deprived of the right to avail themselves of "third-party opposition".
A principal "third-party opposition" shall be brought before the court that issued the contested decision.

A person aggrieved by a denial of justice shall be required, in order to prove such denial, to submit two successive petitions to the judge or the court, with eight days intervening between the first and the second.
The clerk must refer both petitions to the person or persons concerned, failing which he shall be liable to dismissal.

If the petitioner's request is not answered in any manner within the four days following the filing of the second petition with the court registry, the "action of judicial liability" shall become admissible.

An "action of judicial liability" based on deceit, fraud, or bribery shall become inadmissible after the expiry of two months from the service of the judgment or decision, unless the act upon which it is based became known only after the issuance of the judgment or decision. In such case, the two-month time limit shall commence from the day on which that act became known.
An "action of judicial liability" shall be brought by way of a writ of summons served upon the defendant or defendants.
The plaintiff must, at the time of filing the writ of summons with the court registry, also deposit a fine in the amount of one hundred L.L.S.
If the writ of summons contains professional expressions, the lawyer who signed it shall be liable to pay a fine of 25 to 50 L.L.S. This shall not preclude disciplinary proceedings.
The court before which the "action of judicial liability" is brought shall first examine the admissibility of the request.

Principal "third-party opposition" shall be lodged by filing an action or a summons, and shall be conditional upon the deposit of a fine with the registry of the court equal to the fine payable in a "retrial".
Incidental "third-party opposition" shall be submitted by way of a statement of claims.
The opposing party must establish that the contested decision was issued unlawfully.
"Third-party opposition" vests the court with the right to examine the entire action. The examination of the aforementioned court may not be confined to certain aspects of the first judgment.

A decision which amends the contested decision or orders its revocation, pursuant to a "third-party opposition", shall in principle benefit only the opposing party, and the matter shall be otherwise than the foregoing if the enforcement of the decision issued pursuant to the "third-party opposition" is in fact incompatible with the maintenance of the first decision contrary to the interest of the losing party.

An action for judicial liability brought against magistrates of the peace, or against the courts of first instance or one of their judges, or against one of the judges of the Court of Appeal and Cassation, shall be lodged before the Civil and Commercial Chamber of that court, which must mandatorily be presided over by the First President, and an "action for judicial liability" shall not be admissible if it is directed against one of the chambers of the Court of Appeal and Cassation.
An "action for judicial liability" shall not terminate upon the death of the defendant or defendants, but may be brought against their heirs.
An "action for judicial liability" may be brought in the following two cases: First- in the event of denial of justice Second- in the event of the commission of deceit, fraud or bribery.

If it is decided that the admission of the application is not possible, the plaintiff shall forfeit the fine which he deposited and shall be ordered to pay to the defendant or to each of the defendants an equivalent thereof by way of damages. The matter shall also proceed in this manner if the application which was decided to be admitted is dismissed as unfounded.
If it is decided to admit the application, the decision shall be served upon the defendant or the defendants within three days through the registry of the court.

The defendant or the defendants must submit their written explanations to the registry of the court within fifteen days commencing from the date of service, and the plaintiff may inspect them or take a copy thereof.

Within the eight days following the period of fifteen days provided for in the preceding Article, the action must be set down for hearing, and the Public Prosecution must submit its submissions. The trial may be held in camera.
If the "action for judicial liability" is adjudged to be well-founded, the Court of Appeal shall order the defendant or the defendants to pay what it designates by way of damages.

In the same judgment, the nullity of the act on account of which the denial of justice occurred, or the nullity of the decision which was based on fraud, deceit or bribery and thereby caused damage to the plaintiff, shall be pronounced.

The annulment of the judgment or decision shall restore the litigants to the state in which the proceedings were immediately prior thereto. The trial proceedings shall then be resumed upon the mere filing of a statement of claims.
From the commencement of the "action for judicial liability", the defendant may not perform any act of his office relating to the plaintiff.

All judgments rendered by religious, civil, or commercial courts, and all judgments relating to civil rights rendered by criminal courts, shall be referred to the Execution Department for the purpose of execution. Likewise, all official instruments, and all instruments and decisions the execution of which the law expressly provides shall be entrusted to the aforementioned Department. The party in whose favour judgment has been given may at all times request the said Department to execute the judgment rendered in his favour.

The Execution Departments are attached to the Courts of First Instance, and their Presidents are at the same time Presidents of the said Departments, and in this capacity they may correspond directly with public departments.

Justices of the Peace shall themselves execute their judgments in accordance with the rules provided for in this Law. If the debtor's movable property is insufficient, they may execute the judgments against his immovable property. As for localities in which there are no Courts of First Instance, Justices of the Peace are entitled to execute all judicial decisions, civil judgments, and all instruments provided for in the preceding Article 582.

The Execution Department competent to execute judgments is the Execution Department at the court that rendered them, subject to the exception provided for in Article 58. As for the Execution Department competent to execute official instruments, it is the Department within the jurisdiction of which such instruments were drawn up, or the Department within the jurisdiction of which the debtor's property is located.
Appellate decisions, even those ordering reversal, shall be executed by the Execution Department at the court that rendered the judgment of first instance.

Every Execution Department requested to carry out execution pursuant to the rules of competence set forth above may commission any other Execution Department to take measures relating to property located within the jurisdiction of such Department.

The President of the Execution Department shall adjudicate upon all execution difficulties, particularly those relating to the acceptance of guarantees, in the same manner as in urgent matters in accordance with Article 476 et seq. up to Article 479. In all cases, his decisions shall be appealed directly to the Court of Appeal and Cassation within the time limits and under the conditions provided for in Article 479.

The officer of the Execution Department shall carry out, under the supervision of its President, all acts necessary for execution. He shall receive and distribute the sums of money resulting from the sale of attached property, and he shall be protected against insults and violence in his capacity as a public officer.

If the enforcement officer finds, during an executive attachment, bills of exchange or notes written to the order of the person subjected to attachment, he shall take possession thereof, and then the Chief of the Enforcement Department shall issue a decision authorising the said officer to collect their value; and if their maturity date is distant, the Chief of the Enforcement Department shall order their sale by auction, and shall issue a decision authorising their purchaser to collect their value.

The exemption from attachment provided for in paragraphs 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 of Article 594 shall not apply to the seller who claims the price of things present in the possession of the person subjected to attachment, nor to creditors whose debt arose from the supply of foodstuffs.
Attachment may only be levied on a part of income from work in accordance with the following provisions.

The wages of workmen and the salaries of employees, whether paid from the funds of the State or of any other moral person, or by an individual - may not in principle be attached except up to one-tenth thereof if the total annual wage or salary does not exceed 300 L.S.P. (three hundred). However, if the total annual wage or salary exceeds three hundred L.S.P., the same rule shall remain in force in respect of the first part thereof, which does not exceed three hundred L.S.P.
The aforementioned exemption from attachment shall not apply to suppliers of foodstuffs nor to creditors whose debts arise from the supply of food, except up to the equivalent of one-half.

Small wages and salaries within the meaning intended by the preceding Articles may not be assigned in advance except as to a part thereof not exceeding one-tenth. This one-tenth is other than that which is subject to attachment.

Nor may set-off be effected between them and the debts owed to the employer (spelled with a kasra under the letter dal) by the workman or employee except up to an amount not exceeding one-tenth of those salaries or wages. It is other than that which is subject to attachment and other than the one-tenth subject to assignment.

Nevertheless, the workman or the employee may authorise his employer to deduct a part of his procedure exceeding one-tenth by way of set-off, provided that the employer (spelled with a kasra under the letter dal) must establish proof that this authorisation was voluntary and free.

The enforcement officer shall accept the petitions relating to enforcement and the documents connected therewith, and shall give a detailed receipt therefor, and shall then register each petition in the incoming register with the date and serial number, and shall at the same time prepare a file upon which the same number is written and in which all the documents relating to the enforcement proceeding are collected.
No attachment, even if precautionary, may be levied except for a certain debt that is due for performance.

In principle, attachment may not be levied except for a debt established by an enforceable instrument; however, this rule shall not apply in precautionary attachment nor from attachment in the hands of a third party.
Every attachment carried out contrary to the rules of procedure exposes the attaching party to a claim for damages in accordance with the provisions of Article 31. Article 32 may also be applied.

Attachment, even if precautionary, may not be levied upon the following property: 1- The property of the State and of legal persons of a public character 2- The property of foreign States and of the French State 3- Property intended for consumption and fuel, and the kinds of income necessary for the subsistence of the attached debtor and his family throughout one month 4- The things necessary for the bedding of the attached debtor and his family, or for performing his religious duty, and the clothing necessary for him and for each member of his family 5- Work tools belonging to the attached debtor up to a value of fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds. 6- Books relating to the profession of the attached debtor up to a value of two hundred and fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds. And he shall be given the right of choice therein 7- Instruments and tools used for teaching and the application or practice of sciences and arts up to the value stipulated in the sixth paragraph. And the attached debtor shall be given the right of choice therein 8- One cow or six heads of sheep or ten heads of goats, and the materials necessary to feed these animals for a period of one month 9- Alimentary provisions assigned by the judiciary, maintenance, and cost-of-living allowance 10- Sums or property donated or bequeathed subject to the condition of their non-attachability or inalienability: they may not be attached throughout ten years beginning from the date the donee and the legatee take possession. And the persons who become creditors after the said period are, to the exclusion of others, able to levy attachment upon the property or sums referred to.

Where the enforcement of a judgment is conditional upon the performance of an obligation, or upon the provision of a surety, the applicant must attach to his petition and his instrument the documents proving the performance of the obligation or the provision of the suretyship, and the suretyship may be replaced by the deposit of a sum of money or equivalent financial securities accepted by the judge.

When the debtor's estate comprises property of various kinds, attachment must first be levied upon his debts by way of "attachment in the hands of a third party", then his movables shall be attached by way of "executory attachment" and finally real property shall be attached by way of "real property attachment".
However, those various properties may be attached directly at the same time if it appears that their total value does not exceed the amount of the debt which is the cause of the attachment.

Contrary to the provisions of Article 611, it is permissible on the other hand: 1- For the creditor in any case to attach a specific property of the debtor if the creditor has a mortgage or a privilege specially established over this property 2- If the creditor is in possession of movable property belonging to the debtor and the creditor has a right of privilege over this property, and its value equals or exceeds the amount of the debt - the debtor may then request that this movable property in his possession be attached before any other property.

If the creditor dies before submitting the application for enforcement, the heirs may submit this application after establishing proof of their capacity, and if this capacity is the subject of a dispute, the Head of the Execution Department may, upon the request of the claimant to the inheritance, immediately decide to levy a conservatory attachment.

If the debtor dies before the filing of the application for enforcement, the creditor must renew the service of his enforceable instrument upon the heirs of the debtor if he knows them; however, if he does not know them, or if there is doubt as to their being the heirs, he may request a conservatory attachment, or request the court to appoint a curator for the estate.

A creditor who does not hold an enforceable instrument may submit a petition to the Head of the Department requesting a decision authorising him to levy a conservatory attachment upon the movable and immovable property of the debtor, and the single judge is entitled to order conservatory attachment in personal actions falling within the scope of his jurisdiction.

The Head of the Execution Department or the single judge, in the cases provided for in the preceding Article, may refuse or decide unconditionally to grant leave for the attachment, or make the leave conditional upon the provision of a suretyship by the creditor.
No part of the retirement pensions assigned to a former worker or employee may be attached, except for foodstuffs. In such case, a part thereof not exceeding one half may be attached.

No more than one third of the part exceeding three hundred L.S.P. per year of the salaries of military and civil officials may be attached, except for foodstuffs or for a debt relating to subsistence.

Retirement pensions allocated to former civil and military officials may neither be attached nor assigned, except in the proportion observed in the attachment of wages not exceeding three hundred L.S.P. As for the part that exceeds three hundred L.S.P., up to two thirds thereof may be attached, solely for foodstuffs or a debt relating to subsistence, provided that the rule of non-attachment stipulated in the two preceding paragraphs shall not apply to debts owed to the State incurred by one of the officials on the occasion of the performance of his duties.

When a creditor wishes to obtain the enforcement of an authentic instrument or a judgment, he must lodge with the Enforcement Department a petition requesting enforcement containing the given name of the petitioner, his surname, his domicile and his profession, the designation of the debtor, the amount of the debt, and the property of the debtor sought to be attached - and he must also annex to the petition the authentic instrument the enforcement of which is requested, or a copy bearing the executory formula of the judgment rendered in his favour, and he shall be given a receipt for the petition and the papers annexed thereto.

It is the clerk of the court that rendered the judgment who issues a copy thereof bearing the executory formula, upon which he writes the following phrase: "Delivered as a true copy of the original for the purpose of enforcement": and the copy must bear the signature of the clerk and the seal of the court.

Only one copy bearing the executory formula may be issued; however, if the copy bearing the executory formula is lost by the party to whom it was delivered before he is able to enforce the judgment rendered in his favour, he may obtain another copy pursuant to a summary judgment rendered after summoning all interested parties in accordance with the rules. This party must provide a solvent surety, unless the judgment debtor acknowledges that the judgment has not been enforced - and the surety shall not be discharged unless it lapses by the expiration of the statutory period or is enforced in whole or in part without opposition on the part of the party against whom judgment was rendered.
The clerk must record in the file of every case, the delivery of every copy bearing the executory formula, the date of its delivery, and the name of the person to whom it was delivered.

Precautionary attachment shall be carried out in accordance with the forms observed in executory attachment or real property attachment. However, the officer carrying it out must hold the authorisation decision, and he is bound to produce this decision to the party subject to attachment if he requests it.
Precautionary attachment temporarily produces the effects produced by executory real property attachment.

The effect of precautionary attachment ceases if the attaching party does not bring an action against the party subject to attachment within eight days. With the addition of the distance time limit thereto where required, in order to obtain a judgment to be taken as an executory instrument.

When this judgment is issued establishing the right of the creditor, the precautionary attachment is automatically converted into an executory attachment or a real property attachment, and the proceedings therein shall follow their ordinary course, and the date of service of the judgment shall be reckoned as the date of the executory attachment or the real property attachment.

A person whose property has been precariously attached may obtain from the judge who ordered the attachment a decision lifting it immediately, provided that he furnishes a solvent surety who shall be liable for the debts that necessitated the attachment.

Precautionary attachment leaves the party subject to attachment in possession of his property unless a judicial receiver is appointed at the same time - and he shall continue to enjoy the property attached by way of precaution, and to collect the proceeds thereof.

If the property attached by way of precaution is in the hands of a third party, the officer carrying out the attachment shall deliver to this person a copy of the authorisation decision, and a copy of the record relating to the attachment of the property in his hands.

Attachment in the hands of a third party applies to debts consisting of money or fungible things owed to the debtor subject to attachment by a third party. Among that to which it also applies are securities quoted on the stock exchange and issued in the form of registered or mixed bonds upon tangible movables that are the property of the party subject to attachment, and held by a third party for any reason whatsoever.

If the attaching party is also indebted to the party against whom the attachment is levied and the obligation has not been discharged by way of set-off, the attaching party may attach the property in his own hands. In this case, the President of the Execution Department shall be entitled to order the attaching party to deposit the property with the Execution Department.

If the creditor does not hold an instrument, even an ordinary one, an attachment in the hands of a third party may only be levied pursuant to an authorisation decision issued by the President of the Execution Department upon a petition.

If the debt giving rise to the attachment is not of a specified amount, an attachment in the hands of a third party may only be levied after its amount has been provisionally assessed pursuant to a decision issued by the President of Execution upon a petition.

The decisions issued by the President of Execution upon a petition, whether for the purpose of authorising an attachment in the hands of a third party or for the purpose of provisionally assessing the amount of the debt, may be revoked by him at the request of one of the litigants after hearing the statements of the attaching party and the attached party inter partes, and the case shall be referred for this purpose to the President of Execution in the form in which urgent matters are submitted. The inter partes decision issued in this respect shall be subject to appeal before the Court of Appeal and Cassation.
An attachment in the hands of a third party shall be levied through the Execution Department. It shall serve the writ of attachment upon this person.

The aforementioned writ must include a copy of the instrument. If there is no instrument, it must include a copy of the authorisation decision, and must also include, where applicable, a copy of the provisional assessment decision, the designation of the litigants, and the amount of the debt which was the cause of the attachment.

The writ of attachment shall be served within five days upon the party against whom the attachment is levied, and at the same time he shall be summoned to appear in an action to prove the debt before the court within the territorial jurisdiction of which his domicile falls, and the attached debtor may request the lifting of this attachment by summoning the attaching party before the President of Execution in accordance with the procedure followed in urgent matters.

If the party against whom the attachment is levied or the third party in whose hands the attachment is levied resides outside the territory of the Lebanese Republic, the service of process shall be sent to him in the forms required by the local law.

The action for validation of a garnishment in the hands of a third party shall be brought before the court of the locality in which the attached debtor resides. If the court finds that the garnishment is in conformity with procedure in form and valid in substance, it shall rule that it is valid and order the third-party garnishee - even if he did not attend the trial - to pay the funds into one of the Government treasuries or one of the banks accepted by it.

If there is an action between the attaching creditor and the third party and the garnishee concerning the validity of the declaration of the third party, the court before which the action for validation of the garnishment was brought must adjourn the decision until the amount of the attached debt is determined.

If the debt attached in the hands of a third party is not due for performance, it shall be ordered in the judgment validating the garnishment that this debt be sold by auction through the enforcement officer.
From the issuance of the judgment validating the garnishment, the attaching creditor becomes thereafter secure from the participation of another attaching creditor in the hands of the third party.

The judgment validating the garnishment shall be notified to the third-party garnishee, and this person must send to the Enforcement Department, within five days, the financial instruments and things that hewithholds in his possession; as for the expenses of sending and insurance, they shall be borne by the Enforcement Department.

After the Enforcement Department takes the expenses of the transaction, it shall distribute the funds delivered to it by the third party; it shall first pay the funds of the attaching creditor or attaching creditors, then deliver the balance, if any, to the attached debtor, and proportional distribution shall not take place unless the amount is insufficient to satisfy all the attaching creditors.

If it happens that several garnishments in the hands of a third party are levied upon a single debt before any judgment validating the garnishment, and before any decision from the Enforcement Department comprising the restriction of the priority to the garnishment in the hands of the third party in accordance with the provisions of Article 635 - the creditors shall participate in the distribution, each in proportion to the debt owed to him.

The assignment of the debt owed to the attached debtor renders the garnishment null and void if such assignment took place before the service of the writ of garnishment upon the third-party garnishee.

If, after an attachment in the hands of a third party, and prior to any judgment validating the attachment, and any decision restricting the priority of the attachment - it happens that the debtor assigns to someone the debt attached in the hands of the third party, the assignment shall be null and void in that capacity, provided however that the assignee becomes towards the first attaching creditor in the position of a second attaching creditor and shares with him in proportion to what is owed to him of the debt.

If, after the first attachment in the hands of a third party and prior to any judgment validating the attachment and any decision restricting the priority of the attachment - it happens that an assignment of the debt took place first and then a second attachment, the assignee shall take his share at the time of distribution with the first attaching creditor and shall have priority over the second attaching creditor, and the distribution shall be effected in the following manner: first, the share of the first attaching creditor shall be determined by conducting a proportional distribution among the three interested parties, and then the surplus shall be given to the assignee in preference to the second attaching creditor (1).
The attachment of a registered security in the hands of a third party entails prohibiting the disposal of the principal and of the interest.
The judgment validating the attachment shall order the sale of the registered security by public auction. The purchaser may take the interest accrued thereon since the date of the attachment.

The sale of a registered security by auction shall be conducted in the same manner as the sale of a bearer security is conducted. After the adjudication, the court shall issue, upon the request of the enforcement officer, a judgment ordering the legal person that issued the registered security either to transfer it into the name of the person who purchased it at the auction, or to convert it into a bearer security, as the said purchaser wishes. If it is converted into a bearer security, the legal person that issued it must deliver it to the enforcement department, whereupon its purchaser shall come and receive it therefrom, provided that the department shall not deliver it to him until after payment of the expenses.

The legal person that transferred the security into the name of its purchaser from the conditions or converted this security into a bearer security pursuant to the provisions of the preceding Article, shall not be subject to what the judgment imposed upon it.

The attachment of an annuity in the hands of a third party shall be subject to the same rules to which the attachment of a registered security is subject. However, the auction in respect thereof shall be conducted through the offices of the officer of the enforcement department at the court within the jurisdiction of which the debtor resides.

If the attachment falls upon movables belonging to the attached debtor, which are in the possession of a third party, the writ of attachment that is served upon the third party entails the disposal of all those movables, and the third party shall be the custodian thereof.

Service of the attachment upon the garnishee renders the debt ordered to be attached impounded in its entirety for the benefit of the attaching creditor, subject to the reservation of the unattachable portion of such debt.

However, the attached debtor may submit a petition to the Head of the Execution Department requesting the lifting of the attachment over a portion of the property attached in the hands of a third party, and the decision issued in this regard may then authorise the garnishee to pay lawfully to the attached debtor, out of the debt attached in his hands, the portion that exceeds the amount of the debt which was the cause of the attachment, and pursuant to that decision the attaching creditor acquires a right of priority over the portion of the debt that remains with the third party, and on the other hand this third party becomes immune from all liability with respect to the portion which he paid to the attached debtor by permission of the judge.
The garnishee may in any case deposit of his own accord, in one of the Government treasuries or one of the banks approved by it, the amount of the debt which he owes to the attached debtor.

The third party must, within five days after being served with the writ of attachment, to which the distance time-limit shall be added - send to the Execution Department a registered letter accompanied by an acknowledgment of receipt, containing a declaration indicating the true amount which he owes to the attached debtor. If he does not send this declaration within the statutory time-limit, he shall become liable towards the attaching creditor for the amount which was the cause of the attachment.

The attaching creditor may contest the validity of the declaration made by the garnishee. Such contestation is effected by submitting a writ of summons to the court of the locality in which the third party resides. If it appears that this third party acted in bad faith, he shall be sentenced to a fine varying between ten pounds and fifty Lebanese-Syrian pounds, without prejudice to the damages to which the attaching creditor is entitled by reason of the delay and expenses caused by the conduct of this third party.

If a discrepancy arises between the amount declared by the garnishee and the amount specified by the attaching creditor, or if the attaching creditor has not specified any figure for the amount of the debt which is the subject of the attachment - the execution officer must, upon receiving the declaration of the garnishee, notify the matter to the attaching creditor in order to enable him to contest, where necessary, the declaration of that third party in accordance with what is set forth in the preceding Article.

The enforcement officer shall draw up a record of attachment, and this record must contain an enumeration of all attachable movables and a clear description thereof insofar as possible. The said officer, or whoever he delegates, must open the boxes, cabinets and parcels that he discovers.

The record must provide for the appointment of a custodian, and the debtor subject to attachment may himself be a custodian. If a person other than the debtor subject to attachment is appointed for custody, a fee shall be allocated to him out of the general expenses relating to the attachment.

When appointing the custodian, the enforcement officer must explain to him the liability incumbent upon him and warn him that any intentional destruction or embezzlement of the attached items exposes its perpetrator to imprisonment from two months to two years and to a fine from ten pounds to one hundred L.S.P.

If there are found among the attached items money, or metallic currency or paper currency, and bearer financial securities, or manufactured articles or precious stones, these items, even though described in the record, shall not be left in the hands of the custodian; rather, the enforcement officer must transport them and deposit them with the Execution Department.
A copy of the record of attachment shall be left in the hands of the custodian.

Within the five days following the drawing up of the record of attachment, the enforcement officer shall fix the place, the day, and the hour at which the attached movables will be sold by public auction, with the exception of financial securities made out to bearer.

The sale shall be preceded by the formality of publication through the newspapers designated for the publication of judicial notices, and by means of notices posted on the walls of the city and its suburbs; as for the number of notices inserted and posted, it shall be in accordance with the value of the movables intended to be sold. The enforcement officer shall fix this number under the supervision of the Head of the Execution Department.
The Head of the Execution Department shall also decide whether it is appropriate to display the movables to the public prior to their sale.
The garnishee, when submitting the declaration provided for in Article 637, must submit a detailed statement of the movables in his possession.

If the validity of that declaration is the subject of a dispute, the head of the Execution Department may authorise the officer himself, or whomever he deputises in his stead, to enter the residence of the garnishee to levy attachment on the movables that are the property of the party subject to attachment.

If the third party attempts in bad faith to conceal the movables that are the property of the party subject to attachment, he shall be liable to the penalties provided for the misappropriation or destruction of attached items.

After notifying the party subject to attachment of the notice of attachment in the hands of the third party, the head of the Execution Department shall appoint the day on which the attached movables shall be sold by auction; this sale must be preceded by the publication procedure followed in matters of executory attachment, and the same formalities must be observed therein.

The enforcement officer himself shall conduct the sale if the movables are within the territorial jurisdiction of the court; however, if they are within the territorial jurisdiction of another court, and transporting them would entail incurring useless expenses, the sale shall be conducted through the offices of the officer of the Execution Department competent for that court.

Notifying the third party in whose hands the movables are attached of the appointment of the day and hour at which those movables will be taken for the purpose of selling them must take place two days before their removal, and by registered letter.

Executory attachment shall apply to the movable corporeal property of the debtor remaining in his possession. Transferable securities and those made out to bearer shall be deemed movable corporeal property.
There must be an enforceable title in order to be able to effect an executory attachment.
An executive attachment shall be null and void if it is not preceded by a formal notice. This formal notice must be served upon the debtor at least twenty-four hours prior to the attachment.

However, the creditor may submit a petition to the Head of the Execution Department requesting authorisation to serve the formal notice and draw up the attachment record at the same time. If he obtains this authorisation, the expenses of the attachment remain at the same time. If he obtains this authorisation, the expenses of the attachment record shall remain definitively borne by the attaching party alone and if the debtor makes payment within twenty-four hours from the date of the attachment.

The party against whom the attachment is levied may object to the formal notice or to the attachment record by a petition submitted to the Head of the Execution Department. This judge must examine therein whether this objection has a character of significance requiring its referral to the court for scrutiny, failing which he shall dismiss it forthwith.

If it appears that the objection has a measure of validity, the Head of the Execution Department shall order the stay of proceedings for eight days to enable the objecting party to bring the case before the civil court by way of a summons.

If he does not bring his action before the court within the aforementioned time limit, he shall be sentenced to a fine varying between ten pounds and one hundred L.S.P. This judgment shall not preclude the payment of damages to the attaching party, and the said fine shall be imposed by a mere decision issued by the Head of the Execution Department of his own motion.

In order to carry out the executive attachment, the execution officer shall proceed with two witnesses to the location of the movable property sought to be attached, and he shall be entitled to enter the debtor's house after stating his official capacity.

If the debtor refuses to allow the execution officer to enter his residence, or if this officer calls out and no one answers him, he may use force in order to be able to enter the residence. To achieve this purpose he may, where necessary, request the assistance of the public force.

A person who unlawfully resists the execution officer after he states and proves his official capacity shall be liable on this ground alone to a fine of five L.S.P. pounds and to imprisonment from three days to fifteen days, or to either of these two penalties alone. This shall not preclude more severe penalties where offences specified in the Penal Code are committed.
The publication of notices in newspapers and the affixing thereof on walls must take place at least eight days and at most fifteen days prior to the day fixed for the sale.

The place of sale shall be - according to the circumstances, either the sale hall, if one exists, or the square of the main market, or the place where the items were located at the time of attachment.

The measures taken by the enforcement officer may be amended by the head of enforcement of his own motion or upon the request of any interested party, and if the sale is postponed, the formality must be renewed, and postponement shall only be ordered for an important reason.

Shortly before the sale, the enforcement officer shall proceed to compare the attached movables with the attachment record, and by this comparison the burden of liability shall be lifted from the custodian or the liability attaching to him shall be determined by showing what has been lost of the items.

On the day, at the place, and at the hour fixed in the notices published in the newspapers and affixed on the walls, the enforcement officer shall commence the public auction. The said officer may be assisted by an auctioneer if the head of the enforcement department permits him to do so.

The enforcement officer shall draw up without delay a record of the sale in which he shall record the formalities that take place and the incidents that may occur, and it must include the name of each purchaser and the amount reached by the price of each item and each lot.

If there is among the attached items an item of great value, it must be appraised by an expert prior to the sale pursuant to an order from the head of the enforcement department. It may not be sold for a price that is more than twenty per cent less than the price fixed by the expert, and the amount of the appraisal must be stated in the notices preceding the sale.

Gold and silver items shall be weighed prior to the sale and their weight shall be stated together with the price of gold and silver in the notices, and they may not be sold for a price that is more than ten per cent less than their value fixed according to their weight and the price of their metal.

With respect to the things that could not be sold in accordance with the provisions of the two preceding Articles, the auction therefor shall be renewed on a date appointed by the enforcement officer, and this date must be between the fifteenth day and the thirtieth day following the first sale.

Prior to the second auction, the publication formality that was followed prior to the first auction shall be followed. However, the head of the Enforcement Department may order that the publication formality be made wider in scope. The price that was set as a minimum at the time of the first auction must be mentioned therein.
When the second auction is held, the things shall be sold to the final bidder, whatever the price he offered.

In every sale by auction of movables attached by way of executive attachment, the price must be paid forthwith; if the enforcement officer grants a time limit to the buyer, he shall be personally liable for payment.

If the latter refuses or is unable to pay the price, the movable shall be put up at his liability in a new auction to be held forthwith if that is possible. If the price of the movable in the second auction does not reach the amount that had been offered by the defaulting buyer, this buyer shall bear the difference between the two prices.
The sale must be discontinued when the value of the sales by auction reaches an amount sufficient to pay the expenses and to satisfy the attaching party and the opposing creditors.

In principle, the other creditors of the party subject to attachment may not request the levying of a second attachment upon the same movables; rather, they may limit themselves to lodging an opposition with the enforcement officer.

This opposition shall be lodged with the Enforcement Department either in writing or by an oral declaration of which a record shall be drawn up forthwith. The cause of the debt and its amount must be stated in this opposition.

Where, following the first executory attachment, another creditor of the attached debtor alleges that the attachment was not comprehensive and that there are other movables belonging to the attached debtor which were not covered by the first attachment, such creditor may request that a new executory attachment be carried out.
Where this second attachment does not result in the discovery of a new movable, the costs thereof shall be borne by the creditor who erred in his request.

On the contrary, where new movables are attached pursuant to the second attachment, on the contrary, it shall be deemed to be ordinary attachment costs which the execution officer is entitled to recover from the proceeds of the sale.

Where the movables attached pursuant to the second executory attachment are located in a place other than the place in which the movables first attached are located, the President of the Execution Department shall then decide, as the case may require, whether it is appropriate to gather all the movables in order to hold a single auction or to hold two separate auctions.
Whoever purchases in good faith a movable at an auction held following attachment shall become the irrevocable owner thereof as from the payment and taking delivery.
Where movable property belonging to a third party is attached by error, the true owner may, up until the sale takes place, file an objection thereto before the execution officer.

The execution officer shall thereupon summon, by registered letters accompanied by acknowledgements of receipt, each of the objector, the attaching creditor and the attached debtor to appear before the President of the Execution Department within three days at least and six days at most.

Where all the interested parties acknowledge that the movable property is the property of the objector, it shall be released from the attachment and delivered to its true owner; where, however, they disagree, such property shall be temporarily excluded from the sale and deposited with the Execution Department or at another place designated by the judge, and the interested parties shall be instructed to litigate before the court of competent jurisdiction (the Civil Court or the Court of Peace); where, however, it appears that the claim of ownership is unfounded, the attaching creditor may request leave from the President of the Department to disregard it.

The true owner whose movable property has been erroneously attached may, even after the sale by auction, bring an action for revendication against the purchaser if the purchaser has not taken delivery thereof or was in bad faith.

Transferable financial instruments made out to bearer, regardless of the place where they were subjected to executive attachment, may only be sold by auction through the care of the Execution Department in Beirut, and the other Execution Departments must, where necessary, send them by post to the said Department in insured envelopes with their value declared; and registered instruments shall be treated in this manner after garnishment in the hands of a third party, as stated in Articles 651, 652.

The sale of securities traded on the stock exchange, by public auction, whether registered or to bearer - shall take place in a special sitting held by the Civil Court in Beirut, and shall be preceded by the publication formality in the same manner provided for in Article 678 and within the time limit specified in Article 680.

The sale of securities traded on the stock exchange by public auction may only be carried out through the officer of the Execution Department in Beirut, and this officer may, if the sale is of importance, request from the President of the aforementioned Department the assistance of a banker.

Officers of the Execution Departments may not purchase by auction in sales the affairs of which they conduct - neither in person, nor through interposed persons, nor in the capacity of agents. If they do so, they shall be liable to a fine of ten pounds up to one hundred L.S.P. and to disciplinary penalties, and this rule shall apply to every auction pertaining to the attachment of movable or immovable property.

If a creditor holds a priority right over corporeal movables that were removed without consent and thus came into the possession of a third party, this creditor may request the Execution Department at the place where the movables are located to authorise him to levy a revendication attachment thereon.

In the cases where the true owner is entitled, pursuant to the Civil Law, to bring an action for revendication of movable property against the holder thereof - that owner may also request authorisation to levy a revendication attachment.
In revendication attachment, the rules followed in precautionary attachment shall be observed.
Upon the filing of this petition, the enforcement officer shall send a formal notice to the debtor
Upon the submission of this petition, the enforcement officer shall send a formal notice to the debtor.
If the owner of the real property or the holder of the real property right is at the same time a personal debtor to the attaching party, this formal notice shall be sufficient

If the situation is contrary to the foregoing, the enforcement officer must send - in addition to the formal notice to the personal debtor - a notification to the owner of the real property or the holder of the real property right

The formal notice must expressly contain a statement that if payment is not made, attachment of the real property shall be initiated.
