He may in this respect request, through the Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation, from the Appellate Public Prosecutor in all governorates, to initiate the public prosecution action before the investigating judges or to bring charges directly before the competent courts.

The Financial Public Prosecutor may seek the assistance of specialists in banking, tax and financial affairs, after administering to them the legal oath of expertise, to carry out the technical and specialised duties with which he entrusts them, unless they are sworn experts.

The Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation may request, of his own motion or upon the request of the Financial Public Prosecutor, through the Minister of Justice to the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, that the Central Inspection Board be assigned to conduct any investigation in the financial cases entrusted to him for consideration.

The Financial Public Prosecution shall be responsible for keeping a special judicial record relating to all companies concerned by Decree No. 3094 dated 25/01/1993. All criminal judgments issued against them shall be recorded therein.

The chief clerks of the competent courts must notify the Financial Public Prosecution of every criminal judgment that was issued or is issued against the company for the purpose of recording it, in the special judicial record for companies, within three months from the date of its issuance.

The Appellate Public Prosecution is charged with:

a - Investigating offences that are of the category of a misdemeanour or a felony and prosecuting those who participated in committing them. It may directly request the assistance of the security forces when performing its duties. Upon learning of the occurrence of a serious offence, it must immediately inform the Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation and execute his instructions.

b - Initiating and pursuing the public right action.

c - Representing the Public Prosecution before the Courts of Appeal and the Criminal Courts and executing the judgments issued by them.

d - Issuing a search and investigation notice, in the event that the person complained against or the suspect is not found or his place of residence is unknown, containing his full identity and the offence attributed to him.

- Upon executing the search and investigation notice, the Public Prosecution that issued it must be contacted immediately.

- The search and investigation notice shall lapse ipso jure after the passage of ten days from the date of its issuance unless the Public Prosecutor decides to extend it for a period of thirty days after which it shall lapse ipso jure.

e - Abating criminal judgments or preventing or suspending their execution in accordance with the provisions of Article 147 of the Penal Code.

f - All other duties entrusted to it in this Law and in other laws.

The Advocate General at the Court of Appeal may perform the duties of the Appellate Public Prosecutor specified in this Law.

Special Rules of Inquiry and Investigation

1 - Upon receipt by the Public Prosecution of a complaint or notification concerning the offences provided for in Article 401, the said Public Prosecution shall, within a time-limit of 48 hours, decide either to shelve the complaint or to institute proceedings before the Investigating Judge without conducting any inquiry or preliminary investigation in this regard except in person, with the exception of the decisions necessary to preserve and seize evidence and to commission a forensic physician to examine the presumed victim of torture if the enclosures to the complaint or notification do not include a medical report of that kind.

2 - The Investigating Judge seised of the case shall personally undertake all measures of investigation concerning the acts provided for in Article 401 of the Criminal Code, without delegating the Judicial Police or any other security agency to carry out any measure with the exception of technical missions.

3 - Any of the Public Prosecution, the investigating judiciary or the courts may, as a matter of urgency, take the measures and decisions aimed at ensuring the protection of the complainant and witnesses from all kinds of ill-treatment or intimidation resulting from the complaints and notifications received by them, and the treatment of victims of torture during their hearing and the trial in a manner that preserves the evidence and presumptions and takes into account their psychological condition arising from their exposure to torture.

The Public Prosecution takes cognisance of offences by one or more of the following means:

a - Investigations which it conducts itself.

b - Reports which reach it from an official authority or from an official who has learned of the occurrence of an offence during the performance of his duties or in the course or on the occasion of the performance thereof.

He has the right to conduct an investigation in public administrations and institutions without the right to bring charges.

c - Preliminary inquiries carried out by the Judicial Police when commissioned to investigate offences and the records which they draw up upon learning of the occurrence thereof.

d - Complaints and notifications which reach it directly or through the Public Prosecution at the Court of Cassation or its assistants.

e - Any lawful means enabling it to obtain information about the offence.

The Appellate Public Prosecution brings charges for the offence and specifies the names of the defendants.

It may bring charges against a person unknown before the Investigating Judge, thereby setting the public prosecution in motion by its indictment.

A complaint means that which is issued by an injured person or his representative, whereas an information originates from an informant who learned of the offence or heard thereof.

No information shall be accepted unless it is submitted in writing and signed at the foot thereof by its author or his representative.

Both the complaint and the information must state the name of the complainant or the informant, clearly and in full, and his place of residence.

Every person who witnesses an assault against public security or against a person's safety, life or property must inform thereof the Appellate Public Prosecutor or one of his assistants having jurisdiction over the place where the offence occurred, the place where its perpetrator was arrested, or his place of residence.

If he refrains without a legitimate excuse from giving information, he shall be prosecuted before the Criminal Single Judge having jurisdiction over the place where the offence occurred and shall be punished by a fine of a minimum of two hundred thousand pounds and a maximum of two million pounds.

An offence shall be deemed flagrant:

A - An offence that is witnessed as it occurs.

B - An offence whose perpetrator is apprehended during or immediately upon its commission.

C - An offence in which the suspect is pursued upon theHue and cry of the people.

D - An offence that is discovered immediately upon the completion of its commission at a time when its traces clearly indicate it.

E - An offence in which articles, weapons or papers are seized in the possession of a person from which it is inferred that he is its perpetrator, within twenty-four hours of its occurrence.

An offence that occurs inside a house, where its owner or one of its occupants requests, within a period of twenty-four hours from the date of its discovery, the Public Prosecution to investigate it, whether it is a felony or a misdemeanour, shall be treated as a flagrant offence.

If a flagrant felony occurs, the Public Prosecutor or the Advocate General must proceed, immediately upon being notified thereof, to the place of its occurrence, the First Investigating Judge or the Investigating Judge on duty notice of his proceeding without being obliged to wait for him to commence performing:

A - Drawing up a record establishing therein what he witnessed of its traces and describing the place of its occurrence and whatever evidence appeared to him of the circumstances in which it took place.

B - Seizing the weapons and all other criminal materials used in its commission and all articles that assist in revealing the truth, and interrogating the suspect regarding the seized articles after presenting them to him.

C - Hearing the persons who witnessed the offence or who have information thereof after administering to them the statutory witness oath.

Every statement shall be recorded in a record signed by the Public Prosecutor or the Advocate General, the clerk and the witness. Upon the refusal of the latter to sign, mention thereof shall be made in the record.

The Public Prosecutor may enter the home of the suspect to search for items which he estimates will assist in shedding light on the investigation.

He may seize whatever thereof he finds, draw up a record of what he has seized describing it accurately and in detail, and decide to preserve the seized items according to their nature, and the search shall be conducted in the presence of the suspect or the defendant.

If he is not present, or refuses to attend, or is in hiding, the search shall be conducted in the presence of his representative, or two adult members of his family, or two witnesses chosen by the Public Prosecutor.

After completing the search operation and the seizure of the items, the Public Prosecutor shall present the seized items to the suspect, the defendant, his representative, or those previously mentioned, and shall request each of them to sign the record establishing the same; if he refuses, he shall note this in the record.

If the Public Prosecutor finds prohibited items during the search, he shall seize them even if they are not among the items resulting from the offence, or used therein, or related thereto, and shall draw up a separate record thereof.

The Public Prosecutor may commission a judicial police officer to conduct the search in the home of the suspect or the defendant under his supervision and oversight and in accordance with the procedures followed by the Public Prosecutor himself.

Entry into homes to search or look for the perpetrator shall not be permitted except between the hours of five in the morning and eight at night.

Unless the homeowner explicitly consents thereto outside this period. However, the Public Prosecutor or the commissioned judicial police officer may conduct the search and look for the suspect at any time in public places or in homes that have acquired this character by practice.

If the nature of the offence or its effects require the assistance of one or more experts to clarify certain technical or artistic matters, the Public Prosecutor shall appoint the competent expert and define his mission accurately.

If the condition of the victim requires a medical examination or an autopsy, the Public Prosecutor shall summon the forensic physician or the specialist physician and charge him with the mission required to be executed accurately and clearly.

The expert or physician shall not commence his mission until after he takes the oath to perform it in accordance with the dictates of conscience and honour.

He shall not be entitled to exceed the mission defined for him.

After he completes it, he shall draw up a report in which he mentions the authority that appointed him, the mission defined for him, the measures he carried out, and the conclusion he reached.

The Public Prosecutor shall undertake any other investigative measures which he deems necessary in order to gather useful information concerning the felony, to secure evidence thereof, and to uncover its perpetrators or accomplices.

The measures must be lawful and free from the defects of moral or physical coercion.

He must record in the minutes which he draws up all the measures which he has undertaken, and must specify in these minutes the time at which the measure commenced, the time at which it concluded, and every means used in its execution. He shall then sign each of the minutes together with the clerk whose assistance he engaged.

The Public Prosecutor must cease pursuing his investigations into the flagrant offence upon the arrival of the Investigating Judge and must hand over to him the minutes which he has drawn up and the items which he has seized, save for those which do not relate to the offence and which were seized by reason of their being prohibited by their nature.

He must bring a prosecution before him for the offence committed against any person in respect of whom evidence or suspicions have been established regarding his participation in its commission.

If the time-limit for flagrancy expires without the Investigating Judge having attended, the Public Prosecutor must conclude his investigations therein and refer the papers to the Investigating Judge accompanied by his prosecution.

The Single Judge must, upon the occurrence of a flagrant offence within the territorial jurisdiction of his division, proceed to the scene to initiate the investigation therein, if neither the Public Prosecutor nor the Investigating Judge has attended there, and must follow the procedures prescribed for the Public Prosecutor in this regard.

He shall cease pursuing his investigations upon the arrival of either of them.

When he completes his investigations, he shall refer them to the Public Prosecutor.

The functions of the Judicial Police shall be exercised, under the supervision of the Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation, by the Public Prosecutors and the Advocates General.

The following persons shall assist the Public Prosecution and operate under its supervision in performing the functions of the Judicial Police, each within the limits of his jurisdiction provided for in this Law and in the special laws applicable to him:

1- Governors and District Commissioners.

2 - The Director General of the Internal Security Forces, officers of the Internal Security Forces and of the Judicial Police, non-commissioned officers serving in territorial sectors, and heads of posts of the Internal Security Forces.

3 - The Director General of General Security, officers of General Security, investigative non-commissioned officers of General Security, the Director General of State Security, the Deputy Director General, officers of State Security, and investigative non-commissioned officers of State Security.

4 - Village mukhtars.

5 - Commanders of sea vessels and commanders of aircraft and aerial vehicles.

6 - Officers of the Fire Brigade and heads of Civil Defence centres with respect to offences committed against the environment.

7 - Forest rangers, village watchmen, and guards of archaeological sites duly commissioned, with respect to offences committed against the environment.

Village watchmen, inspection employees at the Ministry of Health, forest and consumer protection inspectors, employees competent for inspection in the Customs, in the Tobacco and Tombac Monopoly Administration, in ports and airports, and at the Ministry of Tourism, and night watchmen may, each within the limits of his jurisdiction and in accordance with the regulations he is entrusted with enforcing, record contraventions, establish them in duly drawn-up minutes, and refer them to the competent Single Judge.

In the case of a flagrant offence, the Judicial Police shall carry out the measures carried out by the Public Prosecutor when it is impossible for him to undertake them himself, and the judicial police officer shall observe in his measures the procedures prescribed by the law for the Public Prosecutor when conducting the investigation of a flagrant offence.

Outside the case of a flagrant offence, the Judicial Police shall also, upon assignment by the Public Prosecution, investigate offences of the category of felony or misdemeanour that are the subject of complaints and reports referred to it by the Public Prosecution.

The Public Prosecutor or the Advocate General may prohibit any person found at the scene of the felony from leaving it. Whoever violates the prohibition decision shall be prosecuted before the Single Judge having jurisdiction over the place where the offence was committed and shall be punished by a fine ranging between two hundred thousand and two million pounds.

If there is found, among those present, a person against whom strong suspicions exist, the Public Prosecutor or the Advocate General shall order his arrest, interrogate him, and keep him detained pending the investigation for a period not exceeding forty-eight hours, unless he deems that the investigation necessitates an additional time limit, in which case he shall decide to extend his detention for a similar period.

The interrogated person shall enjoy the rights provided for in Article 47 of this Law, and the Public Prosecutor or the Advocate General must inform him of all of them, record in the minutes his position as to whether or not to avail himself thereof, and obtain his signature thereon, under penalty of nullity of the interrogation and the proceedings subsequent thereto.

If the suspect manages to abscond from view or was not present at the commencement of the investigation, the Public Prosecutor or the Advocate General shall issue a warrant to bring him in. When he appears before him, he shall interrogate him immediately after informing him of his rights provided for in Article 47, recording in the minutes his position on availing himself thereof or not, and obtaining his signature thereon, under penalty of nullity of the interrogation and the proceedings subsequent thereto.

An information shall not be deemed a sufficient ground for issuing a warrant to bring in a person who has a known domicile.

The proceedings pertaining to a flagrant felony shall cease upon the expiry of a period of eight days from their commencement.

If the flagrant offence is in the nature of a felony, and the necessities of the investigation require keeping the suspect detained for a longer period, the extension of the time-limit up to four days at most shall be effected by a reasoned written decision of the Appellate Public Prosecutor, which he shall issue after inspecting the file and verifying the justifications for the extension.

The suspect or his counsel or any member of his family shall have the right to request, during the additional time-limit, the assignment of a physician to examine him. The Public Prosecutor shall appoint the competent physician immediately upon the submission of the request to him, and the physician shall conduct the examination without the presence of the judicial police officer and submit his report to the Public Prosecutor immediately thereafter within a period not exceeding twenty-four hours. In all cases, the period of detention shall be deducted from the penalty that may be imposed.

The judicial police officer shall abide by complete secrecy in all the measures that he undertakes. If it is established that he disclosed the contents of the documents or letters that he seized or any of the secrets that the suspect is keen to keep confidential, he shall be prosecuted before the Criminal Single Judge within whose jurisdiction the complained-of act falls and shall be punished by imprisonment from one month to one year and by a fine from two hundred thousand to two million pounds, or by either of these two penalties.

If the judicial police officer considers that there are papers or objects useful to the investigation in the possession of a person against whom strong suspicions do not exist, it shall be for the Public Prosecutor or the Investigating Judge, to the exclusion of the mechanical officer, to conduct the search in the house of this person unless the latter consents without coercion that the judicial police officer conduct the search.

Every search conducted by the judicial police in one of the houses, contrary to the rules determined by the law for the Public Prosecutor in a flagrant felony, shall be null and void. The judicial police officer who enters the house contrary to these rules and conducts the search therein shall be subject to prosecution for the misdemeanour provided for in Article 375 of the Penal Code; however, the nullity in this regard shall be limited to the void measure and shall not extend beyond it to the rest of the investigation measures.

If the Public Prosecutor or the Investigating Judge attends, the judicial police officer shall cease pursuing his measures unless either of them assigns him in writing to pursue them. The assignment may include the interrogation of the suspect.

The judicial police officer shall not have the right, after the state of the flagrant offence has ended, to conduct any additional investigation; rather, he must refer the records that he drew up to the Public Prosecutor immediately upon the end of this state together with the items that he seized during the search.

Where a flagrant offence is committed, the judicial police officer shall immediately proceed to the place of its commission and inform the competent Public Prosecutor thereof.

The judicial police officer shall, under the supervision of the Public Prosecution, carry out the following measures:

1 - He shall preserve the traces, features and indications liable to disappear and everything that assists in establishing the truth, including electronic evidence, subject to the provisions of Law No. 81/2019 in respect of personal data. By seizing the weapons and materials used in the offence or resulting therefrom.

2 - He shall hear the witnesses without administering the oath to them. He shall conduct inquiries, arrest any person against whom strong suspicions exist of having committed the offence or contributed thereto, conduct a search of his home, and seize any criminal materials or prohibited items found by him. He shall seek the assistance of experts where necessary.

3 - He may interrogate the suspect provided that he gives his statements of a conscious and free will and without the use of any form of coercion against him. If he maintains silence, he may not be coerced to speak.

The person interrogated shall enjoy the rights provided for in Article 47 of this Law, and the judicial police officer conducting the investigation under the supervision of the Public Prosecution must inform him of all of them, record in the minutes his position as to whether or not to avail himself thereof, and obtain his signature thereon, on pain of nullity of the interrogation and the measures subsequent thereto.

The judicial police officer who undertakes the investigation of the flagrant offence must abide by the instructions of the competent Public Prosecutor and keep him informed of the course thereof.

If the competent Public Prosecutor commissions the judicial police officer with certain acts falling within his competence, he must abide by the terms of the commission.

Any person may, in the case of a flagrant offence, whether a felony or a misdemeanour punishable by imprisonment, arrest the perpetrator caught in the act thereof and bring him to the nearest judicial police station.

If the flagrant offence is of the nature of a misdemeanour punishable by imprisonment for at least one year, the judicial police officer may arrest the suspect and investigate the misdemeanour under the supervision of the Public Prosecutor.

The Public Prosecutor may decide to detain the defendant in the misdemeanour and refer him directly before the Single Judge to be tried in accordance with the procedures provided for in this Law.

If the judicial police officer violates the rules relating to the detention of the defendant or the suspect, he shall be subject to prosecution for the offence of unlawful deprivation of liberty provided for and punishable under Article 367 of the Penal Code, in addition to the disciplinary penalty, whether the offence is flagrant or non-flagrant.

The Public Prosecutor may conduct the preliminary investigation himself.

The person interrogated shall enjoy the rights provided for in Article 47 of this Law, and the Public Prosecutor or the Advocate General must inform him of all of them, record in the minutes his position as to whether or not to avail himself thereof, and obtain his signature thereon, on pain of nullity of the interrogation and the procedures subsequent thereto.

With the exception of the interrogation of the suspect or the person complained against, if he does not conduct the investigation himself, he shall examine the preliminary investigations conducted by the judicial police officer. If he finds that the offence is of the nature of a felony or that it is a misdemeanour requiring an expansion of the investigation, he shall bring charges in respect thereof before the Investigating Judge.

If the investigation into the misdemeanour is sufficient, he shall bring charges in respect thereof before the competent Single Judge.

The Public Prosecutor may decide to file the papers of the preliminary investigation if it appears to him that the act does not constitute an offence, or that the evidence of the commission of the offence is insufficient, or that the public action has lapsed for one of the reasons provided for in Article 10 of this Law.

A Public Prosecutor who has brought charges in a given case shall not be entitled to conduct the investigation or adjudicate therein.

At the seat and within the jurisdiction of every Court of Appeal there shall be an investigation department composed of a First Investigating Judge and Investigating Judges.

The First Investigating Judge shall head the investigation department.

The indictment sheet by which the Public Prosecution brings charges in respect of offences shall be referred to the First Investigating Judge. Direct actions brought by persons harmed by offences, accompanied by their personal claims, shall also be submitted to him.

The First Investigating Judge shall himself conduct the investigation in important cases and shall distribute the other cases among the Investigating Judges in his department.

He shall supervise the proper functioning of the work in his department.

The First Investigating Judge shall assign one or more Investigating Judges to cases of environmental offences, in addition to the tasks entrusted to him.

An investigating judge to whom a case is referred may not refuse to investigate it.

However, he shall have the right to offer his recusal from hearing it. Each of the parties to the dispute shall have the right to request his disqualification.

The rules set forth in this regard in the Code of Civil Procedure shall apply to both the request for recusal and the disqualification.

If any impediment prevents the investigating judge from performing his function, the First President of the Court of Appeal shall delegate a judge to perform it.

An investigating judge who undertakes the investigation in a given case may not adjudicate it or participate in adjudicating it.

The investigation shall remain confidential unless the case is referred to the trial court, with the exception of matters relating to the committal order.

Anyone who discloses the confidentiality of the investigation shall be subject to prosecution before the Single Judge within whose jurisdiction the complained-of act falls and shall be punished by imprisonment from one month to one year and by a fine from one hundred thousand to one million pounds, or by either of these two penalties.

The Indictment Chamber shall be the appellate authority for the decisions of the investigating judge.

It alone shall exercise the power of indictment for a felony and shall exercise the right of avocation in the cases specified by law.

If a flagrant felony occurs, the investigating judge must proceed to the place of its occurrence and initiate the investigation therein without waiting for the Public Prosecutor. If the Public Prosecutor attends, he shall not have the right to participate with him in the investigation or to conduct a parallel investigation in the same case.

However, he shall have the right to submit such requests as he deems fit.

If he had preceded him to the scene of the crime and initiated the investigation, he must cease pursuing it and comply with the provisions of Article 36 of this Law.

The investigating judge must be accompanied, upon proceeding to the scene of the crime, by the clerk of his department.

If he seeks the assistance of a clerk from among the members of the judicial police, he must administer the oath to him to perform his work with honesty and fidelity and to preserve the confidentiality of the investigation.

In a flagrant felony, the investigating judge shall exercise all the powers enjoyed by the Public Prosecutor.

He shall perform all the acts and procedures entrusted to him and provided for in Articles 31, 32, 33, 34 and 35 of this Law.

Upon the completion of the measures required by the investigation into the flagrant felony, the Investigating Judge shall transmit the papers to the Public Public Prosecutor, who shall bring charges against the suspects and submit his requisitions.

Following the prosecution brought by the Public Prosecution, the Investigating Judge shall exercise his functions in accordance with the ordinary procedures. The Public Prosecutor shall have the right to examine the investigation file at any time and to submit his requisitions in writing.

The Investigating Judge shall examine them and decide whether to accept or reject them. If he rejects them, he shall be required to inform the Prosecutor thereof, and the latter shall have the right to appeal any decision contrary to his requisition before the Indictment Chamber.

The Investigating Judge shall be bound by the ruling of the Indictment Chamber resulting from the appeal.

Where a flagrant misdemeanour occurs that is punishable by imprisonment of at least one year, the Public Prosecutor may request the Investigating Judge to proceed to the scene of its occurrence to conduct the investigation locally.

In the investigation, the Investigating Judge shall observe the procedures followed in a flagrant felony.

The Investigating Judge shall not be entitled to commence the investigation, outside the case of a flagrant offence, unless he is seised of the public action pursuant to a prosecution brought by the Public Prosecution, or a direct complaint in which the injured plaintiff assumes the capacity of a civil party, or a decision designating the competent court, or a decision transferring the action.

The Investigating Judge shall be seised of the public action in rem. He may interrogate as a defendant any person suspected of having committed the offence, whether as a principal, co-principal, accessory, or instigator, without being dependent in respect thereof on a prosecution brought by the Public Prosecution.

If criminal acts unconnected with the act prosecuted are discovered during the investigation, he shall refer the file to the Public Prosecutor to bring charges in respect of those acts.

Where, however, the discovered acts are connected with the act prosecuted, no prior prosecution shall be required for him to investigate them.

The Investigating Judge shall be bound to follow lawful means while carrying out all investigative measures conducive to uncovering the truth. He shall record in writing everything that he carries out among them.

Where the investigation requires conducting a physical inspection of the scene of the offence, the Investigating Judge shall proceed thereto by his proceeding without waiting for him and shall conduct the inspection in accordance with the procedures.

Judicial police officers, in their capacity as assistants to the Public Prosecution, shall undertake the tasks assigned to them by the Public Prosecution, including investigating non-flagrant offences, gathering information thereon, and conducting inquiries aimed at uncovering their perpetrators and participants in their commission and gathering evidence against them, along with what that requires in terms of seizing criminal items, conducting physical inspections of the scenes of offences, and scientific and technical studies on the traces and features left behind by them, and hearing the statements of witnesses without administering the oath to them and the property of the persons complained against or the suspects.

If the suspects or persons complained against refrain from speaking or remain silent, this shall be noted in the record, and they shall not be entitled to compel them to speak or interrogate them, under pain of nullity of their statements.

The suspect or person complained against, before his statements are heard in a flagrant or non-flagrant offence, and whether the person conducting the investigation is the Public Prosecution or the Judicial Police, and immediately upon his detention for the necessities of the investigation, shall enjoy the following rights:

1 - To contact a lawyer of his choice and a member of his family, his employer, or an acquaintance of his.

2 - To be assisted by a lawyer to attend his interrogation or the hearing of his statements and to meet with him.

The person conducting the investigation must, prior to commencing the interrogation or the hearing, inform the suspect or person complained against of these two rights, record in the record his position regarding whether or not to avail himself of them, and obtain his signature thereon.

The appointment of the lawyer shall take place by virtue of a declaration recorded in the record without the need for a duly executed power of attorney, provided that he produces a formal power of attorney at the first investigation or trial hearing.

- The meeting between the suspect or person complained against and the lawyer shall take place in a manner that guarantees the confidentiality of the conversation between them, provided that its duration is thirty minutes at most. The date and time of the start of the meeting and the time of its conclusion shall be recorded in the record, and it shall be signed by both the lawyer and the suspect or person complained against.

If he requests a period of time to appoint a lawyer, he shall be granted a period of twenty-four hours for that purpose.

They must inform the Public Prosecution of the measures they take and abide by its instructions, and they shall not be entitled to search a house or a person except after obtaining prior permission from the Public Prosecution. Where permission to search is granted to them, they must observe the procedures prescribed by law for the Public Prosecutor in a flagrant offence. Every search they conduct in violation of these procedures shall be null and void; however, the nullity shall be limited to the search process and shall not extend to other procedures independent thereof.

They are prohibited from detaining the suspect in their lockups except by a decision of the Public Prosecution and within a period not exceeding forty-eight hours. It may be extended for a similar period only upon the approval of the Public Prosecution.

The period of his detention shall be calculated as part of the duration of his remand in custody.

After the expiry of the period of detention, the Public Prosecution may not take any measure of any kind whatsoever against the detained person, and the members of the Judicial Police must transfer the detainee from the detention centre in which he was interrogated to any other centre not affiliated with the same unit, provided that this is recorded in the record prior to its closure, under pain of nullity.

The suspect or person complained against, before his statements are heard in a flagrant or non-flagrant offence, and whether the person conducting the investigation is the Public Prosecution or the Judicial Police, and immediately upon his detention for the necessities of the investigation, shall enjoy the following rights:

1 - To contact a lawyer of his choice and a member of his family, his employer, or an acquaintance of his.

2 - To be assisted by a lawyer to attend his interrogation or the hearing of his statements and to meet with him.

The person conducting the investigation must, prior to commencing the interrogation or the hearing, inform the suspect or person complained against of these two rights, record in the record his position regarding whether or not to avail himself of them, and obtain his signature thereon.

The appointment of the lawyer shall take place by virtue of a declaration recorded in the record without the need for a duly executed power of attorney, provided that he produces a formal power of attorney at the first investigation or trial hearing.

- The meeting between the suspect or person complained against and the lawyer shall take place in a manner that guarantees the confidentiality of the conversation between them, provided that its duration is thirty minutes at most. The date and time of the start of the meeting and the time of its conclusion shall be recorded in the record, and it shall be signed by both the lawyer and the suspect or person complained against.

If he requests a period of time to appoint a lawyer, he shall be granted a period of twenty-four hours for that purpose.

If the lawyer is not present, the suspect or person complained against and the lawyer shall be granted in a manner that guarantees the confidentiality of the conversation between them, provided that its duration is thirty minutes at most, the date and time of the start of the meeting and the time of its conclusion shall be recorded in the record, and it shall be signed by both the lawyer and the suspect or person complained against.

If he requests a period of time to appoint a lawyer, he shall be granted a period of twenty-four hours for that purpose.

If the lawyer is not present, the suspect or person complained against shall be granted a period of two hours in order to attend.

- The investigation may not be commenced in the absence of the lawyer except in the case of a flagrant offence and when there is an extreme necessity justifying not waiting, provided that it is explained in detail in the record.

If the lawyer does not attend after the expiry of the time limit, the interrogation shall be commenced immediately.

If he attends late, he shall join the investigation from the point it has reached after being informed of the content of his client's statements.

In all cases, he shall be entitled, upon the conclusion of the hearing of his client's statements, to put to the latter the questions he deems appropriate and that are exclusively connected to the subject of the investigation.

- If the suspect or person complained against is unable to appoint a lawyer for financial reasons, the judge supervising the investigation shall appoint a lawyer for him through a delegate appointed specifically for this purpose by each of the Bar Associations of Beirut and Tripoli.

The procedures for the assistance of a lawyer must be recorded in the record.

3 - Promptness in hearing his statements and non-procrastination in doing so.

4 - Not administering the oath to him prior to beginning to hear his statements.

5 - Informing him of the capacity on the basis of which he is being interrogated, of the suspicions existing against him, and of the evidence supporting them so that he may be able to execute them and defend himself.

The person conducting the investigation shall not be obliged to give him the legal characterisation of the facts.

6 - To be assisted by a sworn interpreter if he is not proficient in the Arabic language, and for every foreigner from a state whose official language is not the Arabic language, provided that the interpreter is appointed as quickly as possible. An unsworn interpreter may be used, provided that he does not commence his mission until after he takes the oath to perform his work honestly and faithfully.

7 - To submit a request directly, or through his counsel or a member of his family, to the Public Prosecutor, to have him examined by a forensic physician specialised in physical or mental health to examine him at the expense of the Public Treasury. The Public Prosecutor shall appoint a physician for him immediately upon the submission of the request to him. The physician must conduct the physical or mental examination without the presence of any of the judicial police officers, and submit his report to the Public Prosecutor within a period not exceeding twenty-four hours. The Public Prosecutor shall notify the applicant of a copy of this report immediately upon his receipt thereof, and the detainee and any of those previously mentioned shall have the right to submit a request for a physical or mental medical examination whenever they deem it necessary.

The Public Prosecutor shall not be entitled to refuse to grant a repeat request for a medical examination except in the case of abuse of the right by the suspect or person complained against, and provided that his decision of refusal is sufficiently reasoned.

The Judicial Police must inform the suspect, prior to hearing his statements and immediately upon his detention, in a flagrant and non-flagrant offence, of his rights set forth above and record this measure in the record, under pain of its nullity and the nullity of the procedures subsequent thereto.

In all cases, the procedures of the interrogation or the hearing of the statements of the person complained against must be recorded in audio and video starting from the moment his rights mentioned in this Article are read out to him, provided that the recordings are attached to the record of the preliminary investigations under pain of nullity of the record and the procedures subsequent thereto.

Subject to the principle of the confidentiality of the investigation, the right to examine the content of the recording shall belong solely to the judge supervising the investigation, the person interrogated and his counsel, and the plaintiff and his counsel.

In addition to the disciplinary penalty, the person conducting the investigation, whether the person conducting the investigation is a judge of the Public Prosecution or a member of the Judicial Police, shall be liable to a penalty of imprisonment for a term ranging between three months and one year and a fine ranging between two million Lebanese pounds and ten million Lebanese pounds in the event that he fails to observe any of the fundamental guarantees mentioned in this Article, without any prior permission from any authority.

The Public Prosecutor shall state in his indictment before the First Investigating Judge the legal characterisation of the offence and the identity of each of the participants in its commission, specify the place and time of the occurrence of the criminal act, and define his requests.

If he has not succeeded in ascertaining all the participants in the offence, he shall bring charges against those of them who are known, failing which he shall bring charges against an unknown person. The public action is set in motion by his indictment, whether he undertakes this himself or one of the Advocates General carries it out.

The Public Prosecutor shall attach to his indictment the papers, minutes and documents that support it.

The Investigating Judge may not refuse to proceed with the public action set in motion by the indictment of the Public Prosecutor unless it is established to him that the act alleged does not constitute a criminal offence or that the public action therein has lapsed for one of the reasons for its lapse.

He shall not take his decision until after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecutor.

He may decide to stay proceedings in the public action by a decision taken by him after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecutor, if he finds that another Investigating Judge has previously taken cognisance of the same investigation or of an investigation into a connected offence.

The Public Prosecutor may request the Investigating Judge to relinquish cognisance of the action if the conditions of lis pendens are met therein or if there is a connection between it and another action under investigation, whereupon it shall be joined to that action.

The Investigating Judge may not decide to annul the indictment of the Appellate Public Prosecution if he finds a defect therein capable of rendering his cognisance of the action invalid.

However, he may decide to abstain from the investigation on account of this defect.

The Public Prosecutor, if he does not rectify the defect, shall appeal the decision of the Investigating Judge before the Indictment Chamber.

The Investigating Judge may, after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution, decide that he lacks jurisdiction to hear the case if it is established that it falls outside the scope of his territorial or subject-matter competence or by reason of the capacity of the defendant.

His decision in this regard is subject to appeal before the Indictment Chamber.

The Public Prosecutor may subsequently bring charges in respect of acts which he omitted to include in his original indictment and against any person whom he omitted in that indictment or in his subsequent indictment.

The Investigating Judge shall interrogate those persons in the capacity of defendants and shall give effect to this capacity in all investigation proceedings.

A person harmed by the offence may submit to the Investigating Judge a civil claim ancillary to the public prosecution initiated by the indictment of the Public Prosecution. He must elect an address for service in the city or town in which the seat of the Investigating Judge is located unless he has an actual residence in either of them. If he fails to do so, he may not object to the failure to serve upon him the documents that must legally be served upon him.

He may be exempted wholly or partially from the costs of the action, even if it is decided to bar the trial of the defendant, where it appears that he did not abuse his right to bring the claim.

If he is a foreigner, he shall be required to furnish security the amount and nature of which shall be assessed by the Investigating Judge. He may be exempted from the security if there is found in his action that which justifies this exemption.

Every person harmed by a felony or misdemeanour may submit a complaint directly to the First Investigating Judge having jurisdiction over the place where the offence was committed, the residence of the defendant, or the place of his arrest, and constitute himself a civil party therein.

The complaint shall be registered with the registry of the First Investigating Judge, who shall decide to require the person submitting it to pay an advance deposit comprising the judicial fees and expenses, provided that it does not exceed one per cent of the value of the action. In addition thereto, the complainant, if he is a foreigner, shall be required to furnish cash or real estate security the amount of which he shall specify in his decision.

The complainant shall be exempted from paying the advance deposit if the act alleged is of the nature of a felony.

If the act is of the nature of a misdemeanour, the Investigating Judge may exempt the complainant from paying the advance deposit if his financial situation does not enable him to do so. He may also exempt the foreign complainant from paying the security for the same reason by a reasoned decision.

A complaint in which the complainant constitutes himself a civil party and pays what he is required to pay, unless paid therefrom, shall automatically set the public prosecution in motion. If one of these two conditions is not met therein, it shall be deemed to constitute a notice of an offence and shall be referred to the Public Prosecutor to take a position on setting the public prosecution in motion.

The complainant may withdraw his action. If he does so within two working days from the date of his complaint, he shall not be liable for the expenses subsequent to his withdrawal.

His withdrawal shall not affect the course of the public prosecution except in actions in which the dropping of the civil action leads to the dropping of the public prosecution.

Both the defendant, or his counsel without the attendance of his client, and the Public Prosecution shall be entitled to raise, once prior to the interrogation of the defendant, one or more of the following pleas:

1 - The plea of lack of jurisdiction.

2 - The plea of abatement of the public action due to one of the grounds for abatement specified by law.

3 - The plea of inadmissibility of the action for a reason preventing the hearing thereof or proceeding therewith prior to examining its merits.

4 - The plea that the alleged act does not constitute an offence punishable by law.

5 - The plea of lis pendens or connectedness.

6 - The plea of res judicata.

7 - The plea of nullity of one or more of the investigation procedures.

The Investigating Judge shall, after hearing the civil party and seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution, rule on the plea within one week from the date of its submission. Each of the parties to the action may appeal his decision.

The Investigating Judge shall verify the identity of the defendant, recording his first name, surname, age, place of birth, the names of his parents, his place of residence, his social and family status, and his judicial record.

He may seek the assistance of specialists in psychiatry as well as in somatic medicine for the purpose of ascertaining the personality of the defendant.

If the latter or his counsel requests that he be examined mentally or physically, the Investigating Judge shall not be entitled to reject his request except by a reasoned decision.

The Investigating Judge shall interrogate the defendant in his chambers, unless it is impossible for the latter to appear there due to illness, disability, or another excuse worthy of acceptance.

When the impediment is established, the Investigating Judge shall move from his chambers accompanied by his clerk to the place where he is able to interrogate the defendant in accordance with the rules set forth hereinafter.

The Investigating Judge shall, upon the first appearance of the defendant before him, inform him of the offence attributed to him by summarising its facts for him and acquainting him with the evidence available to him or the suspicions existing against him so that he may refute them and defend himself.

The Investigating Judge shall not be obliged to give him the legal characterisation of the facts.

The Investigating Judge shall advise him of his rights, particularly his right to be assisted by a single lawyer during the interrogation.

If the Investigating Judge omits to inform the defendant of the offence attributed to him, in accordance with what has been set forth above, or to advise him of his right to be assisted by a lawyer, this shall result in the nullity of the interrogation as a piece of evidence.

The First Investigating Judge shall personally undertake the investigation into the direct complaint, and he may refer it to one of the investigating judges within his jurisdiction.

The judge seized of the direct complaint shall commence the investigation therein after seeking the opinion of the Appellate Public Prosecution.

However, he shall not be bound by its opinion if it entails a refusal to proceed with the public action previously initiated by the civil claim in accordance with the provisions of the fourth paragraph of Article 68 of this Law.

He shall serve a copy of the complaint and its attachments upon the defendant at least twenty-four hours prior to his interrogation.

The Public Prosecutor may contest the standing of the civil claimant to bring the claim prior to proceeding with the investigation. The defendant or his counsel may raise this plea prior to the interrogation.

The Investigating Judge shall, after serving this plea upon the civil claimant and granting him a period of 24 hours to reply, rule thereon after seeking the opinion of the Appellate Public Prosecution.

The Public Prosecutor may, if he finds that the complaint is unclear, request the Investigating Judge to commence the investigation before he takes a position in respect thereof. In such case, the Investigating Judge shall interrogate the persons named in the complaint as defendants and hear the witnesses. He shall then refer the file to the Public Prosecutor to take a position on the prosecution.

The Investigating Judge may, if evidence becomes available against those whom he heard as witnesses of their participation in the offence, interrogate them as defendants, provided that he complies with the provisions of Article 61 of this Law.

If the Investigating Judge decides to dismiss the proceedings against the person named by the complainant, the defendant may claim, before the Criminal Single Judge, compensation for his damages and losses against the civil claimant who abused his right to litigate. Provided that he files his action, under pain of inadmissibility, within a period of three months from the date on which the decision dismissing the proceedings against him is served upon him.

By way of exception to the provisions of Articles 78 and 79 of this Law, the investigating judge may, by a reasoned decision, commence the interrogation of the defendant immediately in the event of the existence of a trace or evidence which is feared may disappear.

He may interrogate the defendant without an attorney in the case of an offence in flagrante delicto and an offence treated as such.

If the counsel of the defendant attends the interrogation, he may not put any question to his client or the adversary except through the investigating judge, and he may make certain observations and object to what he deems incompatible with the rules of investigation in the questions put by the investigating judge.

If the investigating judge does not grant permission to the attorney to speak, or to put the question, or to make observations or objections, he shall record that in the minutes of the interrogation.

The Public Prosecutor or one of his assistants may attend the interrogation of the defendant, and he may during the same put questions and make observations through the investigating judge.

If the defendant is not proficient in the Arabic language, the investigating judge shall appoint for him an interpreter who shall not commence his mission except after taking an oath to perform his work with honesty and fidelity.

If the defendant is mute or deaf or unable to speak, the investigating judge shall seek the assistance of a person who is able to communicate with him by sign language or otherwise, after taking an oath to observe honesty and fidelity in his work.

If the deaf or mute person knows how to write, his interrogation shall be conducted by way of recording the questions in writing and recording his answer thereto.

Provided that the sheet on which he answers the questions shall be attached to the minutes of the interrogation.

The civil party, the person civilly liable, and the guarantor may attend the interrogation of the defendant, or each of them may instruct an attorney for this purpose. Each of them may put questions and make observations through the investigating judge.

If there are multiple defendants, none of them or his counsel may attend the interrogation of a person other than his client except in the case where a confrontation is conducted between them.

If the Investigating Judge has interrogated the defendant concerning a criminal act, considering it a misdemeanour, and it subsequently appears to him that the classification applicable to it is that of a felony, he must interrogate him again and caution him that he has the right to the assistance of an advocate if he has not already appointed an advocate to assist him in the action.

Subject to the penultimate paragraph of Article 81 of this Law, the defendant, the civil party, the person vicariously liable and the guarantor, or their attorneys, may attend the investigative acts except for the hearing of witnesses. Each of them must be served with his summons at least twenty-four hours prior to the investigative act that concerns him, failing which the act carried out in his absence shall be null and void.

If the person among them whom it was decided to summon attends without objecting to the manner in which he was served or to the non-observance of the twenty-four-hour time limit, the investigative act that concerns him shall be deemed valid.

Each of the person vicariously liable and the guarantor must elect an address for service within or the town in which the office of the Investigating Judge is located, unless he has an actual residence in either of them, in order to be served thereat with that which must be served upon him, the documents legally required to be served upon him.

Each of the aforementioned persons must notify the Investigating Judge in writing of any change that may occur to his actual or elected residence. If he fails to do so, service upon him at the address stated in the case file shall be valid.

The Investigating Judge may decide to prohibit communication with the detained defendant for a period not exceeding five days. The prohibition shall not include his advocate.

If the arrest warrant is executed against the defendant detained in absentia, the Investigating Judge must, immediately upon receiving the notice of arrest, have the detained defendant brought before him and interrogate him concerning the acts attributed to him, provided that in his interrogation he observes the procedures previously set forth.

If a defendant residing outside the jurisdiction of the office of the Investigating Judge presents a legitimate excuse preventing him from appearing at his office, the Investigating Judge may delegate to interrogate him the Investigating Judge within whose jurisdiction the defendant's residence falls or the Single Judge within whose jurisdiction the defendant's residence falls.

It shall not be permissible to delegate a judicial police officer for this purpose.

The Investigating Judge may not conclude the investigation unless he has interrogated the defendant, unless he is unable to do so due to his flight, or if he assesses that the evidence gathered by him in the action is sufficient to bar his trial regardless of the interrogation.

If the action requires hearing the testimony of the President of the Republic, the Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, or the President of the Council of Ministers, the Investigating Judge shall proceed with his clerk to his official residence and hear his testimony.

The investigating judge shall observe the principle of the freedom of will of the defendant during his interrogation and shall ensure that he gives his statement free from any external influence upon him, whether moral or material.

If the defendant refuses to answer and remains silent, the investigating judge shall not be entitled to compel him to speak.

If the defendant feigns suffering from a physical, psychological, or mental illness during his interrogation, recourse may be had to medical expertise to ascertain his true condition.

If the defendant refuses the assistance of an attorney, the investigating judge shall not be obliged to appoint an attorney for him. This shall be recorded in the minutes under penalty of nullity of the interrogation and the proceedings subsequent thereto.

He shall interrogate him without an attorney and proceed with the investigation measures.

If he chooses an attorney to defend him, the investigating judge may not interrogate him or proceed with the investigation measures except after the attendance of the attorney and his inspection of all investigation acts other than the statements of witnesses, under penalty of invalidation of the interrogation and the proceedings subsequent thereto.

If the defendant is unable to brief an attorney, the investigating judge shall appoint an attorney for him or entrust his appointment to the President of the Bar Association. The defendant may, at any time during the investigation, notify the investigating judge of the name of the attorney whom he has briefed to defend him.

If he chooses several attorneys for this purpose, he must notify the investigating judge of the name of the attorney to whom the notice to appear shall be addressed.

The attorney shall be summoned by a notice sent to him at least one day prior to the interrogation. The clerk of the investigating judge shall record this measure in the minutes, stating the date on which the notice was sent.

If the attorney was not served with his notice to appear prior to the date of the hearing, his attendance at the interrogation, without objecting to the procedure of his service, shall preclude the invalidation of the interrogation.

If the retained attorney fails to attend despite having been duly notified of the date of the hearing, without a legitimate excuse, the investigating judge may proceed with the interrogation.

The investigating judge shall, prior to every interrogation subsequent to the first interrogation, ask the defendant whether his consent to be interrogated without the assistance of an attorney continues to stand, and shall record this in the minutes under penalty of nullity of this interrogation and the proceedings subsequent thereto.

The defendant may communicate freely with his retained attorney throughout the duration of the investigation. Communications between them shall be confidential.

No evidence resulting from a breach of the principle of confidentiality shall be admitted.

The Investigating Judge shall summon the persons whose names are mentioned in the complaint, information, or investigations, and any person whom he considers to have information useful to the investigation.

- He shall not be bound to summon a witness named by the civil party or the defendant if he deems that there is no utility in hearing him. However, if he refuses to hear a witness named by the Public Prosecution, he shall issue a reasoned decision to that effect.

- The summons shall be served on the witness at least twenty-four hours prior to the time of the hearing fixed for hearing him.

- Members of the diplomatic and consular corps shall be served with their summonses through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Emigrants.

- Military personnel shall be served with their summonses through their respective commands.

- If the witness resides abroad, he shall be served with his summons by registered letter with acknowledgment of receipt.

- If he is detained, he shall be brought under escort.

Prior to being heard, the witness shall produce the summons that was served upon him, and this shall be recorded in the minutes. If he appears prior to being served with his summons, he shall not be entitled to refrain from giving his statement on the pretext that he was not served with the date of his summons.

The Investigating Judge shall, in the presence of his clerk, hear each witness

separately.

After the Investigating Judge asks the witness for his first name, surname, the names of his parents, his age, his occupation, and his place of residence or domicile, and whether he is married to one of the parties, a servant of either of them, or one of their relatives, and the degree of kinship, he shall administer to him the following oath:

"I swear by Almighty God to testify to the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth," and this shall be recorded in the minutes.

The witness shall give his statement orally, and he may rely on documents to support it.

The statement of each witness shall be recorded in minutes containing the text of the questions addressed to him and his answers thereto.

The witness's statement shall be read out to him, and he shall endorse it and sign each page thereof. If he refuses or is unable to sign, mention thereof shall be made in the minutes.

The number of pages comprising the witness's statement shall be stated at the foot of the minutes. The Investigating Judge and his clerk shall sign each page thereof, and the names of the persons heard and the date of their hearing shall be recorded in the foundational minutes.

If seized incriminating materials or objects are presented to the witness, this shall be recorded in the minutes.

The same procedures shall be followed in hearing the statement of each of the civil party, the defendant, the person civilly liable, the guarantor, and the expert.

Only the party prejudiced by a breach of any of the procedures set forth above may request the annulment of the minutes.

If the witness is not proficient in the Arabic language, the Investigating Judge shall appoint an interpreter for him, who shall perform his mission after taking an oath to carry it out truthfully and faithfully, unless he is a sworn interpreter.

The Investigating Judge may, if the young man resides outside the territorial jurisdiction of his department, delegate to hear his testimony the Investigating Judge or the Single Judge within the territorial jurisdiction of whose department the place of residence of the witness is located.

The delegating judge shall specify to the delegated judge the facts regarding which the witness must be questioned with sufficient accuracy and clarity.

The delegated judge shall hear the testimony of the witness in due form after administering the oath to him and shall send the record in which his testimony is recorded in a sealed envelope to the delegating judge as soon as possible.

Every person duly notified of the obligation to appear before the Investigating Judge to give his testimony shall be bound to appear before him.

If he fails to do so without a legitimate excuse, the Investigating Judge shall repeat his summons to a subsequent hearing after imposing on him a fine ranging between fifty thousand and one hundred thousand pounds.

If he fails a second time to appear, he shall issue a subpoena against him.

If the witness claims illness and produces a medical report proving it in justification of his failure to appear, the Investigating Judge may reject this excuse if it appears to him that it is not serious, or appoint another physician or a medical committee to examine the witness and to state whether his health condition prevents him from appearing.

If it appears to him that the report is false, he shall draw up a record thereof and refer it to the Public Prosecution to prosecute the witness and the physician who drew up the report pursuant to Article 466 of the Penal Code.

If the excuse is other than illness, and it appears to the Investigating Judge that it is false, he shall draw up a report thereof and refer it to the Public Prosecution to prosecute the witness pursuant to Article 407 of the Penal Code.

The Investigating Judge may, if it is impossible for the witness to appear at his office due to illness, disability or force majeure, proceed to the place of his presence to hear his testimony in the presence of his clerk.

The Investigating Judge may, in the absence of his clerk or one of the clerks of the investigation department, the Public Prosecution or the courts, seek the assistance of one of the non-commissioned officers of the Internal Security Forces to record the testimony of the witness after administering the oath to him to perform his duty truthfully and faithfully.

If no clerk is available to him to record the record, he may perform this task himself.

The record that he draws up in this latter case shall not be null and void.

Where a witness asserts a falsehood, denies the truth, or conceals part or all of what he knows of the facts of the case about which he is questioned, the Investigating Judge shall refer the record in which his statement was entered to the Appellate Public Prosecution so that it may prosecute him for the offence of perjury provided for in Article 408 of the Criminal Code.

No scraping may occur in the investigation record, nor may any interlineation or addition be inserted therein.

Where it is necessary to strike out or add a word, the Investigating Judge, the clerk and the witness must certify and sign the striking out, interlineation and addition in the margin of the record.

Every uncertified interlineation, striking out or addition shall be deemed null and void, and shall be subject to the provisions of the last paragraph of Article 87 of this Law.

The Investigating Judge shall hear minors who have not completed eighteen years of age by way of information.

Where a minor who has passed fifteen years of age has taken the legal oath, his statement shall not be void and he shall not be prosecuted for the offence of perjury.

The ascendants and descendants of the defendant, his brothers and sisters, his relatives by marriage of the same degree as brothers and sisters, his spouse even after divorce, and informers whom the law grants financial rewards for giving information shall be barred from testifying.

The Investigating Judge may hear the statement of each of those persons by way of information.

A witness shall not be exempted from giving his statement unless he proves that he is legally bound to maintain secrecy.

Where the Investigating Judge considers that the witness's plea of professional secrecy or banking secrecy is legally unfounded, he shall, after seeking the opinion of the Appellate Public Prosecution, issue a reasoned decision rejecting his plea.

The witness may appeal the decision within a time limit of twenty-four hours from the date on which he is notified thereof.

Every person who possesses information that sheds light on the investigation must come forward to give his testimony before the Investigating Judge.

If he fails to do so, a fine ranging between one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand pounds shall be imposed upon him, to be collected from him in the manner in which public funds are collected.

Where such information is capable of proving the innocence of the defendant, anyone who fails to state it or to submit the evidence thereof shall be prosecuted pursuant to the amended Article 567 of the Criminal Code.

The Investigating Judge shall determine a travel allowance for the witness and shall order whichever of the parties requested him to pay it.

Where the action is brought in the name of the public right, it shall be disbursed from the Treasury fund.

Every search conducted contrary to the procedures set forth above shall be null and void.

The investigation measures based thereon shall consequently be null and void.

Nullity shall not preclude taking into account information obtained that benefits the investigation, as a result of the search, if accompanied by evidence corroborating it. The measure shall not be invalidated if the aggrieved party consents thereto.

The investigating judge may issue a summons calling the civil party, the defendant, the witness, the civilly liable party or the guarantor to the hearing which he schedules and in which he specifies the day and hour.

The defendant must attend the office of the investigating judge after being served with his summons and appear before him.

If he fails to attend, without presenting a legitimate excuse, or if the investigating judge fears his flight, he shall issue a warrant to bring him in against him containing a written order to the security forces to secure his production within twenty-four hours from the scheduled time of the hearing.

The Public Prosecution shall undertake the tasks of executing the warrant to bring in.

The Investigating Judge may move with his clerk to carry out an on-site inspection of the scene of the offence or to search one of the residences in search of incriminating materials or objects that shed light on the investigation. He shall inform the Public Prosecutor of his movement.

If he accompanies him, he shall carry out the measures of inspection and search in his presence; otherwise, he shall carry them out alone. The inspection or search shall be completed in the presence of the civil party and the defendant.

If either of them does not attend or is unable to attend, it shall take place in the presence of his representative, or two witnesses from the members of his family, or two witnesses chosen by the Investigating Judge.

The Investigating Judge shall draw up a detailed record of the measures of inspection or search, which he shall sign with his clerk and all those present.

If, during the search, he seizes incriminating materials or objects useful to the investigation, he shall describe each of them and state its nature with sufficient precision.

He shall preserve the seized materials and objects according to their nature, seal them with the seal of the Investigation Department, and affix to them a slip of paper stating the seized contents, which the Investigating Judge shall sign with his clerk and those present.

If the seized items consist of ledgers, papers, and statements of accounts, they shall be placed in envelopes stamped with the seal of the Department and preserved in the Investigation Department after affixing the statement of their contents.

If the seized items consist of bullion or banknotes or financial papers, they shall be placed in envelopes stamped with the seal of the Department and preserved in the safe of the Palace of Justice after affixing the statement of their contents.

If confidential documents are seized during the search, they shall be numbered and no one other than the Investigating Judge and their owner may inspect them.

They shall be preserved in envelopes stamped with the seal of the Department, and a statement shall be affixed to them stating that they are confidential and indicating their count and their numbers.

If among the seized objects there is that which cannot be transported to the Investigation Department or the depository of trusts at the Palace of Justice, by reason of its size or its dangerous nature, the Investigating Judge shall deliver it to whomever he deems appropriate to preserve it, pursuant to a record which he shall sign with his clerk, the owner of the seized object, and the person who received it.

Save in the case of a flagrant offence, the Investigating Judge does not have the right, when prosecuting a lawyer, to search his office until after he has informed the President of the Bar Association of the matter. During his search, he shall not breach professional secrecy.

The President of the Bar Association or whomever he delegates may attend the search operations.

Communications conducted by the suspect lawyer may not be intercepted except by a judicial decision and after informing the President of the Bar Association.

If the Investigating Judge finds during the search prohibited articles the acquisition or possession of which constitutes an offence of the category of a misdemeanour or a felony, he shall seize them, even if they are unrelated to the offence which he is investigating, and draw up a record thereof which he shall sign with his clerk and with whoever attended the search, and send them with the record to the Public Prosecution.

The seals of the seized and preserved articles shall not be broken except in the presence of the Investigating Judge, his clerk, the defendant or his counsel, and the person in whose residence the search took place or in whose presence it was conducted. In the event that any of these fails to attend, they shall be broken in his absence, provided that he has been notified of the date and time of the taking place of this formality.

The Investigating Judge may examine telegrams and letters and retain such of them as he deems necessary to reveal the truth or the disclosure of which to third parties would be detrimental to the investigation.

He shall not be entitled to disclose the contents of any seized telegram or letter without the consent of the party concerned.

The Investigating Judge may not examine correspondence exchanged between the defendant and his counsel, the lawyer.

If the Investigating Judge considers that retaining the seized articles or some of them is of no use to the investigation, he shall return them to the rightful claimant if his right is free from any judicial dispute.

If there is a serious dispute regarding the right of ownership or possession of the seized article which can be returned, the Investigating Judge shall defer the return operation until after the adjudication of the dispute.

If the civil party or the defendant requests the restitution of one of the seized articles, the Investigating Judge shall rule on the request after ascertaining the position of the adversary in the action and the opinion of the Public Prosecution.

His decision in this regard shall be subject to appeal within a period of twenty-four hours from the date of its notification to the party aggrieved thereby among the parties to the dispute in the action.

If the Investigating Judge sees fit to conduct a search of a residence located outside his jurisdiction, he shall commission by letters rogatory for this measure the Investigating Judge within whose jurisdiction the residence is located or the Single Judge in the same jurisdiction.

He shall specify the mission for him with precision and detail.

The commissioned judge must execute this mission and follow the rules of procedure in seizing incriminating materials or articles that are of use to the investigation, and draw up a record thereof which he shall sign with his clerk and with the householder or two witnesses, and refer it with the seized items to the commissioning judge within an envelope stamped with the seal of his office and having affixed thereto a statement of the contents of the seized items.

Save in the case of a person previously sentenced to a penalty of a duration of at least one year, the duration of detention in a misdemeanour may not exceed two months. It may be extended by a similar period as a maximum in the case of extreme necessity.

Save in felonies of homicide, narcotics, assault on State security, felonies of comprehensive danger, crimes of terrorism, and the case of a detainee previously sentenced to a criminal penalty, the duration of detention in a felony may not exceed six months, which may be renewed once by a reasoned decision.

The Investigating Judge may decide to prohibit the defendant from travelling for a period not exceeding two months in a misdemeanour and one year in a felony from the date of his release on bail or his release without bail.

Whoever is arrested in execution of an in absentia detention decision shall be brought without delay to the Public Prosecution at the seat of the Investigating Judge who issued the decision, and it shall give the official who executed the decision a receipt for taking delivery of the detainee, send him to the place of detention, and inform the Investigating Judge of the matter. The Investigating Judge shall decide to have the detainee brought before him immediately and shall interrogate him in accordance with the provisions of Articles 74 et seq. of this Law.

Whoever from the security forces is tasked with executing the in absentia detention decision shall enter the house in respect of which he has available evidence that the defendant detained in absentia has taken refuge therein.

However, it may only be entered during the period extending between five o'clock in the morning and eight o'clock at night.

The procedures specified in this paragraph shall apply upon the execution of a warrant to bring.

The Investigating Judge may decide, during the investigation proceedings, whatever the type of offence, to withdraw the arrest warrant with the approval of the Public Prosecutor.
