Provided that the defendant elects a domicile in the city or town in which the seat of the Investigating Judge is located, unless he has a real domicile in either of them, in order to be notified therein of all proceedings relating to the investigation and the enforcement of the judgment.

The investigating judge shall immediately interrogate a defendant summoned by a writ of summons. As for a defendant brought pursuant to a warrant to bring in, he shall interrogate him within twenty-four hours from the time the warrant to bring in is executed against him.

Upon the expiry of the twenty-four hours, the head of the detention facility shall, of his own accord, bring the defendant before the Public Prosecutor, who shall request the investigating judge to interrogate him. If he refuses, is absent, or is prevented from interrogating him by a lawful impediment, the Public Prosecutor shall request the First Investigating Judge to interrogate him or to assign one of the investigating judges to do so.

If it is impossible to interrogate him, the Public Prosecutor shall order his immediate release.

If his detention continues for more than twenty-four hours without his being brought before the Public Prosecutor, such remand in custody shall be deemed an arbitrary act and the official responsible therefor shall be prosecuted for the offence of deprivation of personal liberty.

After the investigating judge interrogates the defendant and obtains the opinion of the Public Prosecution, he may issue an order remanding him in custody, provided that the offence attributed to him is punishable by imprisonment for more than one year or that he has previously been sentenced to a felony penalty or to imprisonment for more than three months without stay of execution.

The remand order must be reasoned and the investigating judge must state therein the factual and material grounds upon which he relied to issue his order, provided that remand in custody is the sole means to preserve the evidence or the material traces of the offence, or to prevent the exercise of coercion upon witnesses or victims, or to prevent the defendant from making any contact with his accomplices, accessories, or instigators in the offence, or that the purpose of the remand in custody is to protect the defendant himself, or to put an end to the effect of the offence, or the desire to guard against its recurrence, or to prevent the defendant from fleeing, or to spare public order any disturbance resulting from the offence.

The writ of summons of the defendant, the warrant to bring him in, and the order remanding him in custody must each contain a statement of the date of its issuance, a statement of his identity, the description of the offence attributed to him, the legal article applicable thereto, the signature of the investigating judge who issued it, and the seal of his office.

The defendant shall be served with both the warrant to bring in and the remand order, even if he is detained for another offence, upon the execution of either of them against him, and he shall be left a copy of the document of service.

If the rules of procedure specified above for the warrant to bring in and the remand order are not observed, the clerk shall be fined an amount of two million pounds at most by a decision of the court before which the violation is raised. The defendant may appeal the order remanding him in custody within twenty-four hours from the date he is served therewith.

Appealing the order shall not stay its execution.

If the defendant has absconded, the investigating judge may issue against him a reasoned order remanding him in custody in absentia.

If it is impossible to execute the remand order in absentia against the defendant, service thereof upon him shall be effected by posting a copy on the door of his last residence in the presence of the mukhtar of the locality or two witnesses from among the neighbours, and a record thereof shall be drawn up.

The Investigating Judge may, whatever the nature of the offence, and after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution, substitute the detention of the defendant by placing him under judicial supervision, and by binding him to one or more of the obligations that he deems necessary for the enforcement of the supervision.

Among which:

أ - Undertaking to reside in a city, town, or village, being prohibited from leaving it, and electing a place of residence therein.

ب - Refraining from frequenting certain premises or places.

ج - Depositing the passport with the registry of the Investigation Department and notifying the General Directorate of General Security thereof.

د - Undertaking not to go beyond the supervision area and proving presence periodically at the supervision centre.

ه ـ Refraining from practising certain professions which the Investigating Judge prohibits him from practising throughout the duration of the supervision.

و - Submitting to medical and laboratory examinations periodically during a period determined by the Investigating Judge.

ز - Providing a guarantee bond the amount of which is determined by the Investigating Judge.

The Investigating Judge may modify the obligations of supervision that he has imposed whenever he deems it appropriate.

If the defendant breaches one of the obligations of supervision imposed upon him, the Investigating Judge may decide, after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution, to issue a detention warrant against him and to confiscate the bond in favour of the Treasury.

The defendant placed under judicial supervision may request that the supervision be lifted from him.

The Investigating Judge shall rule on his request, after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution, within three days at most from the date of its registration in the registry of the Investigation Department.

His decision is subject to appeal before the Indictment Chamber in accordance with the procedures followed in appealing the decisions of the Investigating Judge.

If the offence is of the nature of a misdemeanour, and the maximum penalty does not exceed imprisonment for a period of two years, and the defendant is Lebanese and has a domicile in Lebanon, he shall be released as of right after the lapse of five days from the date of his detention, provided that he has not been previously sentenced to the penalty of a disgraceful offence or to the penalty of imprisonment for a period of at least one year.

The released defendant shall undertake to attend all investigation acts, trial proceedings, and the enforcement of the judgment.

In all other offences, and if the conditions for release as of right are not met, the investigating judge may, after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution, decide to release the detained defendant, if he applies for it and undertakes in his application to attend all investigation and trial proceedings and the enforcement of the judgment, with or without bail.

Bail shall cover:

A - The attendance of the defendant at the investigation and trial proceedings and the saving of the judgment.

B - Fines, fees and judicial expenses.

C - The expenses advanced by the civil party.

D - A portion of the personal damages.

The investigating judge shall determine the amount and type of bail and the sum allocated to each of its parts, and he may amend its amount or type when necessary.

The defendant or his counsel shall submit the application for release to the investigating judge prior to the issuance of the committal order.

A copy of the application shall be served upon the civil party at his elected domicile to submit his observations thereon within a period of twenty-four hours from the date of service upon him.

The application shall be referred, after the expiry of a period of twenty-four hours from the service upon the civil party, to the Public Prosecutor to state his position thereon. The investigating judge shall take his decision in accordance with the opinion of the Public Prosecution or contrary thereto immediately upon the return of the file to him.

The civil party may appeal before the Indictment Chamber against the decision granting release within a period of twenty-four hours from the date he is notified thereof. The defendant may appeal against the decision dismissing his application for release within twenty-four hours from the date he is notified thereof.

The Public Prosecution may appeal against the decision within a period of twenty-four hours from the date of its issuance.

An appeal against a decision granting release shall stay its execution.

The appeal shall be lodged through the investigating judge.

The released defendant shall be required to elect a domicile in the city or town in which the seat of the investigating judge is located, unless he has an actual domicile in either of them.

Bail may consist of cash, State bonds, or a bank, commercial, or real estate guarantee.

If it consists of cash or State bonds, it shall be deposited with the treasury of the Palace of Justice against a receipt.

If it consists of a bank guarantee, it shall be effected by producing a deed of guarantee duly issued by the guarantor bank, which shall be placed in the case file. The date of its receipt, by day and hour, the name of the guarantor bank, the amount stated in the deed of guarantee, and the number of such deed shall be recorded in the foundational record.

If the bail consists of a commercial guarantee, it shall be effected by producing a deed of guarantee issued by the commercial entity, whether an individual, an establishment, or a company.

The name of the guarantor, his address, and the amount stated in the deed shall be registered in the foundational record before the Investigating Judge. A notation of the deed of guarantee shall also be entered in the Commercial Register in the file of the guarantor.

If the bail consists of a real estate guarantee, it shall be accompanied by a report of a sworn expert specifying the number of the real property, its location, its area, and a detailed valuation of its price.

A notation of this bail shall be entered on the real property folio of the property.

The original deed of guarantee and the report shall be kept in the treasury of the Palace of Justice. Mention thereof shall be noted in the foundational record.

Both the civil party and the defendant may, within the time limit provided for in Article 116 of this Law, appeal the part of the release decision relating to the amount of the bail.

If the released defendant attends the investigation and trial proceedings and presents himself for the enforcement of the judgment, the first part of the bail shall be refunded to him.

However, if he fails to attend any of the investigation or trial proceedings or fails to submit to the enforcement of the judgment, the first part of the bail shall be forfeited in favour of the Treasury.

If a decision barring the trial of the defendant is issued, the bail shall be refunded to him in full.

If a decision is issued declaring the public prosecution action against him abated by reason of death, the first part of the bail shall be refunded to his heirs.

If a decision is issued declaring the offence attributed to him extinguished by general amnesty or special pardon, the first part of the bail shall be refunded to him.

If a dispute arises regarding the application of this Article, it shall be adjudicated, upon the petition of the interested party, in chambers by the authority seized of the action or which rendered judgment therein.
The Public Prosecution shall be in charge of enforcing parts (a and b) of the bail, and parts (c and d) shall be enforced through the Enforcement Department after the judgment becomes final.

If, following the release of the defendant, grave grounds arise requiring his re-arrest, the Investigating Judge may issue a decision ordering his arrest after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution. Where the decision to release him was issued by the Indictment Chamber upon reversing the Investigating Judge's decision rejecting the application, the Investigating Judge shall refer the case file to the Indictment Chamber for it to take a position on his decision ordering the re-arrest of the defendant.

However, this shall not stay the execution of his decision.

If the Indictment Chamber rules to reverse his decision, it shall release the defendant.

After the Investigating Judge concludes the investigative acts, he shall refer the file to the Public Prosecution for it to submit its final submissions therein.

The Public Prosecution shall submit within one week at most.

If the Public Prosecution requests an expansion of the investigation, it shall specify the deficiencies and the investigative acts that it deems necessary. The Investigating Judge may execute its request or refuse it.

If he refuses it, he shall state the grounds for the refusal.

The Public Prosecution may appeal the decision of refusal.

If the Indictment Chamber reverses it, it may assume jurisdiction over the subject-matter of the request or refer the case file to the First Investigating Judge to pursue the investigation or to assign it to another Investigating Judge.

If, however, it upholds it, it shall return the file to him so that he may issue the committal order after the Public Prosecution submits its final submissions.

If the Investigating Judge decides to bar the trial of the defendant, he shall base his decision either on a legal ground or on a factual ground.

The ground shall be legal where the alleged act does not correspond to any penal legal characterisation, or where, after the allegation of the act, a new law is enacted that strips it of any criminal character, or where the criminal nature of such act has ceased by reason of one of the legal grounds of justification, or where the public prosecution in respect of the alleged act has lapsed by reason of one of the grounds of lapse prescribed by law.

The ground shall be factual where the investigation has not established that the alleged offence actually occurred, or where there is insufficient evidence of a causal link between the alleged offence and the defendant, or where the public prosecution was initiated against an unknown person whom the investigation failed to uncover or whose identity it failed to ascertain. In this latter case, the Investigating Judge shall decide to issue a warrant for permanent inquiry with a view to ascertaining the perpetrator or uncovering his identity.

If the Investigating Judge decides to bar the trial of the defendant, he shall order his immediate release if he is in custody. An appeal against this decision shall not stay its execution.

If the Investigating Judge decides that the act alleged is of the nature of a contravention or a misdemeanour that does not entail imprisonment, he shall immediately release the defendant if he is detained and refer the case file to the Single Judge through the Public Prosecution.

The Public Prosecutor shall, in a case in which a committal order for a misdemeanour or a contravention has been issued, send the case file to the competent Single Judge within three days of its being lodged with him, accompanied by an inventory of items prepared by the Investigation Department.

If the Investigating Judge considers that the act which he has investigated is of the nature of a felony, he shall issue an order in which he sets out the facts of the case, the evidence available therein and the legal characterisation applicable thereto.

He shall refer the file to the Public Prosecution for it to lodge it with the Indictment Chamber in its capacity as the authority vested with the power of indictment.

If the Investigating Judge decides that the felonious characterisation alleged does not apply to the facts available in the case, but rather that a misdemeanour characterisation applies thereto, the Public Prosecutor may appeal his decision.

The civil party shall not have the right to appeal this decision.

The decision of the Investigating Judge, whether referring the case to the Single Judge or considering the act to be of the nature of a felony, must include the defendant's given name, surname, age, place of birth, the names of his parents, his nationality, his civil register number, his place of residence, his occupation, the date of his arrest and of his release, and a clear statement of the facts, the evidence and the legal characterisation.

After the Public Prosecutor refers the file of the action, accompanied by his report, to the Indictment Chamber, it shall take objective cognisance thereof. If it finds that the investigation of the action is complete and that there is no utility in expanding it, it shall issue one of the following decisions:

أ- A decision barring the trial of the defendant and releasing him if it appears to it that the evidence is insufficient to indict him for a felony, or that the act attributed to him does not constitute an offence, or that the criminal character has ceased to attach to it due to one of the grounds of justification or by the enactment of a new law amending the previous law, or that the public action has lapsed due to one of the grounds of lapse specified in the law.

ب - A decision deeming the act a misdemeanour or a contravention, pursuant to which it refers the defendant to the Criminal Single Judge and releases him if it deems the act a contravention or a misdemeanour that does not entail a penalty of imprisonment of more than one year.

ج - A decision indicting the defendant if it appears to it that the facts and the evidence thereof are sufficient to indict him, after giving the act attributed to him a felonious characterisation.

It shall order in its decision the referral of the accused to the Court of Assizes to be tried for that with which he is indicted, and shall issue a warrant of arrest against him.

The decision of indictment must include the names of the members of the Indictment Chamber, the submissions of the Public Prosecution, a clear and precise account of the facts of the case, a detailed statement of the evidence connecting the crime to the act of the defendant, a reasoned legal characterisation, a specification of the legal provisions that apply to the facts, and the issuance of a warrant for the arrest of the accused, and it must also include the name and surname of the accused, his date of birth, the names of his parents, his register number, his place of residence, his profession, his nationality, the date of his detention, and the date of his release on bail if it occurred.

Each of the President of the Chamber and its two counsellors shall sign the decision of indictment. The warrant of arrest must include the name and surname of the accused, his date of birth, the names of his parents, his place of residence, his profession, his nationality, the type of felony attributed to him, the legal provision applicable thereto, and the order to the security forces to detain the accused in execution thereof.

If the Indictment Chamber issues its decision referring the accused before the Court of Assizes and omits to issue a warrant of arrest against him, it may issue this warrant upon the request of the Public Prosecution.

If new evidence emerges, after the issuance of a decision barring trial of the defendant, the investigation shall be reopened if the decision was based on a factual ground.

Considered as new evidence are witness statements, documents and records that were not placed in the hands of the investigating judge and that are capable of affecting the conclusion which he reached.

The new evidence shall be submitted to the Public Prosecutor, who shall assess whether it is useful and sufficient to request the renewal of the investigation.

If it appears to him that it fulfils the aforementioned purpose, in a request from the investigating judge to conduct the investigation anew.

The investigating judge must investigate the new evidence and issue such warrants as he deems necessary.

He shall interrogate the defendant without a subsequent prosecution by the Public Prosecution and shall observe the established procedures in the acts of investigation.

If the investigating judge sees fit, after resuming the acts of investigation, to revoke the decision barring trial, he shall decide, after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution, to charge the defendant with a misdemeanour or to consider his act to be of the nature of a felony.

However, if the new investigation does not lead to anything requiring the amendment of the first decision barring trial, he shall issue a decision maintaining it.

If the decision barring trial was issued by the Indictment Chamber, it shall undertake, upon the request of the Public Prosecutor, the renewal of the investigation, which shall be conducted by its President or by one of its counsellors whom he delegates in accordance with the procedures followed before the investigating judge.

A civil chamber at the Court of Appeal shall assume the functions of the Indictment Chamber.

They are:

1 - The indicting authority in a felony.

2 - The appellate authority for the decisions of the investigating judge and for the decisions falling within its jurisdiction pursuant to special laws.

3 - The right of evocation.

4 - Adjudicating applications for rehabilitation.

If the investigating judge considers in his final decision that the act complained of is of the nature of a felony, he shall refer the case file to the Public Prosecution to lodge it with the Indictment Chamber, and the Public Prosecution shall draw up within five days a report in which it sets out its submissions.

Each of the civil party and the accused may submit, within the same time limit, a memorandum in which he presents the facts of the case, the evidence, the legal characterization and the submissions at which he arrives.

If the Indictment Chamber finds a deficiency or ambiguity in the investigation, its President shall conduct a supplementary investigation or assign one of his Associate Judges to do so.

The supplementary investigation shall observe the rules of procedure governing the acts of the Investigating Judge in this regard.

Upon completion of the supplementary investigation, the case file shall be referred to the Public Prosecution to submit its opinion in light of the new developments in the action. The Indictment Chamber shall then take the appropriate decision therein.

The Indictment Chamber shall issue a single decision of indictment in respect of connected offences. If some of them are of the nature of a misdemeanour, it shall refer the case in its entirety to the Criminal Court.

Offences shall be deemed connected:

a - If they are committed by several persons assembled together at the same time.

b - If they are committed by multiple persons at different times and places in execution of an agreement between them.

c - If some of them are in preparation for others, or paved the way for their commission, or facilitated or executed them, or were committed to conceal their criminal results or to keep their perpetrators free from prosecution.

d - If several persons participated in concealing the items resulting from the offence in whole or in part.

The Indictment Chamber may, regardless of the conclusion reached in the decision of the Investigating Judge referred to it, examine all felonies and the misdemeanours connected therewith, of its own motion or at the request of the Public Prosecutor, and take the appropriate decision in respect thereof.

It may conduct any additional investigative act of its own motion or at the request of the Public Prosecutor, the defendant or the civil party.

The Indictment Chamber is the competent appellate authority to hear appeals brought against the decisions of the Investigating Judge.

1- The Public Prosecution may appeal all investigation decisions issued contrary to its request, whether administrative, investigative, or judicial, as well as the decision withdrawing an arrest warrant for failure to meet its conditions, within a time limit of twenty-four hours from the date the decision is issued.

2 - The defendant may appeal the following decisions of the Investigating Judge:

a - A decision dismissing an application for his release.

b- A decision dismissing one or more of the defences provided for in Article 73 of this Law.

3 - The civil party may appeal the following decisions:

a - A decision upholding one or more of the defences provided for in Article 73 of this Law, where it is prejudicial to his interest.

b - A decision leaving the defendant free or releasing him as of right or on bail.

c - A decision barring the trial of the defendant.

d - A decision characterising the alleged act as a contravention.

e - A decision withdrawing a warrant for the arrest of the defendant where it is contrary to procedure.

A person civilly liable or a guarantor may only appeal, among the decisions of the Investigating Judge, a decision ruling on jurisdiction.

The time limit for appeal is twenty-four hours.

In respect of the civil party, the defendant, the person civilly liable, and the guarantor, it runs from the date he is notified of the decision at his elected domicile within the city in which the department of the Investigating Judge is located, unless he has an actual domicile therein.

An appeal shall be lodged directly with the Indictment Chamber or through the Investigating Judge.

The Indictment Chamber shall rule on an appeal against a decision of the Investigating Judge within a time limit of ten days at most from the time the file is deposited with it.

An appeal before the Indictment Chamber has a devolutive effect within the scope of its subject matter.

If it is filed within the statutory time limit, sets out the legal grounds and claims, and is signed by a lawyer admitted to appeal, the Indictment Chamber shall decide to admit the appeal in form and, on the merits, to uphold, set aside, or amend the appealed decision.

An appeal lodged by the civil party against a decision barring the trial of the defendant sets the public prosecution in motion anew and brings it before the Indictment Chamber.

If the Indictment Chamber decides to bar the trial of the defendant, he may claim compensation for his losses and damages in accordance with the provisions of Article 72 of this Law.

If the Public Prosecution or the civil claimant appeals the decision ordering the release of the defendant, or leaving him at liberty, or revoking the warrant for his arrest that is contrary to procedure, the appeal shall stay the execution of the decision until it is adjudicated within a time limit of twenty-four hours.

If this time limit expires without the Indictment Chamber having taken its decision, the Public Prosecutor shall release him ipso jure.

If the Indictment Chamber reverses the decision of the Investigating Judge leaving the defendant at liberty, it may issue an arrest warrant against him.

If the Chamber reverses the decision of the Investigating Judge dismissing the application for the release of the defendant, the released person shall elect a domicile in the city or town in which the seat of the Indictment Chamber is located, unless he has an actual domicile therein.

If the Investigating Judge issues a decision whereby he deems the act of the defendant to be of the nature of a felony, the Indictment Chamber may, without the need for a prosecution by the Public Prosecution, examine all the offences disclosed by the investigation and connected with the original offence, and deal with all the persons against whom there is evidence of their participation in those offences.

As for offences not connected with the original offence, the institution of the public prosecution in respect thereof requires a prosecution by the Public Prosecution.

If an appeal is lodged against a decision of the Investigating Judge in which he abstained from taking a measure or performing an investigative act, and the Indictment Chamber reverses his decision, it shall undertake to perform the measure or act in place of the Investigating Judge and may assume jurisdiction over the merits of the case.

If it examines an appeal against a decision issued by the Investigating Judge barring trial or discontinuing the proceedings for one or more of the grounds set forth in Article 73 of this Law, and decides to reverse it, it may assume jurisdiction over the merits of the case.

If the Indictment Chamber does not assume jurisdiction over the merits of the case, it shall refer the file to the First Investigating Judge to pursue the investigation therein or to refer it to another Investigating Judge.

If the Indictment Chamber assumes jurisdiction over the merits of the case, it shall undertake the investigations and the issuance of warrants to bring in or of arrest, as the case may require, and it may delegate one of its members to perform these acts.

The investigations conducted by the President or the delegated Judge shall be subject to the very same rules of procedure that govern the investigation before the Investigating Judge, and each of them may commission an Investigating Judge or a Single Judge to perform certain investigative acts in accordance with the provisions that govern letters rogatory issued by the Investigating Judge.

Upon completion of the investigations conducted by the Indictment Chamber itself or through one of its members, it shall return the case file to the Public Prosecution to submit its opinion anew on the merits of the case. It shall then issue its decision after examining the case and the additional investigations.

Decisions of the Indictment Chamber may not be appealed before the Court of Cassation except on the grounds set out in Articles 306 and 307 of this Law.

The time limit for appealing decisions of the Indictment Chamber shall be fifteen days. It shall run in respect of the Public Prosecution from the date of their issuance, and in respect of each of the civil party, the defendant, the civilly liable party, and the guarantor from the date on which he is served in accordance with the procedures set out in Articles 147 and 148 of this Law, and he shall be deemed served if it is established that he became aware thereof.

Every person convicted of a felony or a misdemeanour may be rehabilitated. The decision to that effect shall be issued by the Indictment Chamber within whose jurisdiction the place of residence of the convicted person falls, upon his application.

The rehabilitation provided for in Articles 159 and 160 of the Penal Code shall take place in accordance with the following procedures:

a - The convicted person shall submit an application for rehabilitation to the Indictment Chamber. There must be attached thereto a copy of the judgment rendered against him and a judicial record dated no more than one month prior to the date of submission of the application.

b - The Indictment Chamber shall delegate one of its members to verify that the application satisfies the legal conditions, and he shall draw up a report which he shall submit to the Chamber.

The Indictment Chamber shall transmit the application together with the report to the Public Prosecution to submit its opinion.

If the Indictment Chamber decides to grant the application, it shall communicate a certified copy of its decision to the Appellate Public Prosecutor, who shall transmit it to the Judicial Record Department for enforcement.

If the Indictment Chamber decides to reject the application for rehabilitation, the applicant may not submit it anew before the expiry of six months from the date on which he was served with the decision of rejection.

Writs of summons, warrants, judgments and decisions issued by the judiciary shall be served, and judicial measures shall be enforced, through special security detachments that report directly to the Public Prosecutor, the First Investigating Judge, and the presidents of the competent chambers and courts, and that shall be answerable to the president of the judicial authority who entrusts or tasks them with carrying out any service of process or enforcing any measure in the event that they fail to do so within the specified time.

The person effecting service shall not be entitled to serve himself, his spouse, their ascendants, their descendants, their relatives by marriage, or their other relatives up to the fourth degree. The certificate of service must state the name of the party requesting service, the name and address of the process server and the date of his assignment, and the name and address of the person to be served.

If the person is a legal person, it shall be served at its head office.

In addition to the foregoing, the certificate of service must state the criminal act that is the subject of the prosecution, investigation or trial, the legal provision that penalises it, the judicial authority seised of the action, and the capacity of the person to be served: civil claimant, defendant, person civilly liable, guarantor, witness, etc.

The person tasked with service must execute that with which he was tasked without delay and must exert his utmost effort to serve the intended person in person.

The person intended to be served must sign the original copy of the certificate of service and receive a copy thereof.

If he abstains from signing, is unable to do so, or refuses to receive the copy, the person effecting service shall note that on the original copy.

If the person intended to be served is not present at his place of residence or dwelling, service upon him shall be effected through one of the members of his family, his servants, or any other person residing with him in the same dwelling, provided that his appearance indicates that he is of age.

It is also required that his interest not be in conflict with the interest of the person to be served.

If he abstains from stating his name and his relationship to the person intended to be served, or from receiving a copy thereof, the process server shall record his abstention and leave for him a copy of the certificate of service.

If the person to be served is a legal person, service upon it shall be effected through its legal representative, the person authorised to sign on its behalf, or any person having capacity to accept service on its behalf. A copy of the certificate of service shall be left for the person served.

Members of the diplomatic and consular corps shall be served with their writs of summons through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Military personnel shall be served with their writs of summons through the commanders of their units.

If the Single Judge considers that the case, in a flagrant misdemeanour, is not ready for judgment, he shall decide to adjourn it to another date not exceeding ten days. He may release the defendant of his own motion in the absence of a personal claim or upon an application by him, with or without bail, if he finds that there is no necessity for his continued detention, provided that the released defendant elects a place of residence in the town or city in which the seat of the Single Judge is located.

He may, in this case, decide to ban him from travel if he sees a necessity therefor for a period not exceeding two months.

If the defendant applies for his release, a copy of his application shall be served on the civil party at his actual place of residence within the jurisdiction of the Single Judge or his elected place of residence therein, and he shall submit his observations thereon within a time limit of twenty-four hours from the date of service upon him.

The Single Judge shall render his decision either granting the request or rejecting it within a similar time limit.

Both the civil party and the defendant may appeal the decision of the Single Judge before the Court of Appeal within twenty-four hours from the date it is served upon him.

The Public Prosecution may appeal it within a time limit of twenty-four hours from the date of its issuance.

The Single Judge shall be seized of the action by one of the following means:

a - The prosecution of the Public Prosecution.

b - The direct action brought by the injured party in which he assumes the capacity of a civil party.

c - The indictment decision issued by the Investigating Judge or the Indictment Chamber.

d - The action for damages based on a decision barring trial, acquittal or dismissal of proceedings.

e - The decision designating the competent court or transferring the action.

f - The case of a misdemeanour committed during the holding of the trial hearing.

g - Contraventions established in official records.

The Public Prosecutor shall bring a prosecution before the Single Judge for a misdemeanour against a person whose identity has been determined.

The prosecution shall include a description of the misdemeanour prosecuted and of the place of its commission, and there shall be attached to it the preliminary investigations, the complaint and all the documents justifying the prosecution.

The Public Prosecutor may subsequently bring a prosecution against a person whom he omitted to prosecute for as long as the action remains pending before the Single Judge. The latter may draw his attention to his omission to prosecute a person against whom evidence is available without binding him thereby.

The Public Prosecutor may request the case file in order to examine it, provided that he returns it within three days at most from the date on which it was deposited with him.

The Public Prosecutor must sign the document bearing his prosecution, and he may not retract or waive his prosecution.

He may not bring a prosecution for the same offence against the same person before the Single Judge if he has previously prosecuted it before the Investigating Judge.

Where a person is arrested in flagrante delicto in a flagrant misdemeanour punishable by imprisonment, he shall be brought before the Public Prosecutor, who shall interrogate him, prosecute him and refer him to the Single Judge to be tried before him forthwith or on the following day, subject to Article 108 of this Law, and the Public Prosecutor may issue against him, prior to his referral, a remand warrant executable immediately.

Where the defendant requests a postponement before the Single Judge in order to retain a lawyer, he shall grant him a period of three days at most, which shall not be subject to extension.

The Public Prosecutor shall specify the names of the witnesses in a flagrant misdemeanour.

The Single Judge may decide to notify them orally of the date of the hearing through the Judicial Police, the Security Forces or the Process Servers Department.

Where any of them refuses to appear, the Single Judge may issue a warrant to bring against him.

If the person to be served has no place of residence or dwelling, or if the process server finds no one to accept service on his behalf at his place of residence or dwelling, he shall be served by affixing a copy of the service document firmly to the door of his last dwelling, delivering a second copy thereof to the mukhtar having jurisdiction over his last dwelling, and affixing a third copy to the door of the judicial authority ordering the service.

The process server shall record these procedures on the original copy of the document and return it to the authority that issued it.

If the person to be served has no last dwelling, it shall suffice for the process server to affix a copy of the service document to the door of the judicial authority ordering the service.

Service must be effected at least three days prior to the date set for the appearance of the person served before the judicial authority ordering the service, unless otherwise provided by law.

If the service is addressed to a person residing in a foreign country, it shall be effected by registered letter with acknowledgment of receipt, or through the Lebanese embassy or consulate in the said country, or in accordance with the rules prescribed by local law.

If service proves impossible, the court may deem the person to whom the service is addressed to be of unknown abode, and he shall be served in accordance with the provisions of Article 148 of this Law. If the procedures for service, including the time limit for service, are not observed, the judicial authority shall declare the nullity of the service in the event that the person to be served fails to appear, and order that service be repeated anew in accordance with Article 148 of this Law.

If he appears and requests the adjournment of the hearing to another date, before raising any plea or defence in the action, the judge seized of the case shall decide to adjourn it and notify him of its new date; if he does not request this, the service upon him shall be deemed valid. If the judicial authority declares the nullity of the service for a reason attributable to the act of the process server, it shall fine him an amount equivalent to the costs of service and shall order him, where appropriate, to pay damages to the injured party.

The hour and day on which service takes place shall not be counted in calculating the time limit for service.

If the time limit expires on an official holiday or outside official working hours, it shall be extended to the first working day following it.

The Single Judge shall hear cases of misdemeanours and contraventions, except those excluded by a special provision.

The Public Prosecution shall not be represented before him.

Any person harmed by a misdemeanour may file a direct complaint in which he assumes the capacity of a civil claimant before the Single Judge within whose territorial jurisdiction the place where the offence was committed, the place of residence of the defendant, or the place where he was arrested is located.

The complaint shall be registered with the registry of the Single Judge, who shall decide to require the person filing it to pay an advance deposit covering the judicial fees and expenses, provided that it does not exceed one per cent of the value of the claim.

In addition to that, he shall require the complainant, if he is a foreign national, to furnish security the type and amount of which he shall determine in his decision.

The judge may exempt the complainant from paying the advance deposit if his financial situation does not enable him to pay. He may also exempt the foreign complainant from furnishing the security for the same reason by a reasoned decision. A complaint in which the complainant assumes the capacity of a civil claimant and pays what he is required to pay, unless he is exempted therefrom, sets the public prosecution in motion. If either of these two conditions is not met therein, it shall be deemed to constitute a notice of an offence.

In such a case, the judge shall decide to refer it to the Public Prosecutor for him to take a position on setting the public action in motion.

The complainant may withdraw his complaint.

If he does so within two working days from the date of its filing, he shall not be liable for the expenses subsequent to his withdrawal.

His withdrawal shall not affect the course of the public action except in actions in which the dropping of the civil action leads to the dropping of the public prosecution.

If the public action is set in motion by the prosecution of the Public Prosecution, the harmed person may claim his civil rights ancillary thereto.

In all cases, the civil claimant must elect an address for service within the boundaries of the city or town in which the seat of the court is located and notify the court in writing of this address.

The Single Judge shall fix the trial hearing and summon thereto the claimant, the defendant, the witnesses, the person civilly liable, and the guarantor.

The Single Judge shall serve upon the defendant a copy of the direct complaint together with its attachments at least three days prior to the date of the hearing.

The defendant or his counsel, without the attendance of his client, may:

1- Raise, prior to the interrogation, one or more of the defences provided for in Article 73 of this Law.

The Single Judge must serve upon the civil claimant a copy of the memorandum submitted by the defendant or his counsel in this regard and grant him a period of five days at most to reply thereto.

Upon the expiry of the time limit, he shall rule upon the defence raised.

The Public Prosecutor may appeal against this decision within a period of twenty-four hours from the date of its issuance.

The defendant or his counsel, as well as the civil claimant or his counsel, may appeal against the decision within a period of twenty-four hours from the date it is served upon him.

2 - Request the stay of execution of the effect of the arrest warrant in absentia issued against him by the Investigating Judge pending the issuance of the judgment in the action.

The Judge may render, with or without bail, a decision staying the execution of the arrest warrant in absentia, subject to an undertaking by the defendant to attend the trial hearings.

In the event of his absence from any of these hearings without a legitimate excuse, the Judge may revoke his decision staying the execution.

The decision ordering the stay of execution or the revocation thereof shall not be subject to any avenue of recourse.

Where the Investigating Judge decides to indict the defendant for a misdemeanour or a contravention, the Public Prosecution shall refer the case file to the Single Judge within three days of its being lodged with it, unless it appeals against the indictment decision.

It shall likewise refer to him within the same time limit the indictment decision issued by the Indictment Chamber.

The Single Judge shall be seised of the action on the basis of the indictment decision.

Where the Investigating Judge decides to bar the trial of the defendant, on a ground of law or of fact, the latter may claim, against the civil claimant, compensation for his loss and damage before the competent Criminal Single Judge in accordance with the provisions of Article 72 of this Law.

The Single Judge shall be seised of the action when it is referred to him pursuant to a decision issued by the Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation following the determination of an application for the designation of the competent court or the transfer of the action.

Where the Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation decides to annul the decision of the Single Judge declaring his lack of jurisdiction to hear the action, it shall remit the action to him or to another Single Judge within the same judicial district to hear it.

Where a misdemeanour occurs during a trial hearing before the Single Judge, he shall forthwith draw up a record in which he interrogates the perpetrator and hears the witnesses, if necessary, and shall impose at the very same hearing the penalty warranted by the misdemeanour.

If he imposes a penalty of imprisonment, he may issue a warrant for the arrest of the convicted person to be executed immediately.

His decision shall be subject to appeal.

Where the act committed during the trial is of a felonious characterisation, he shall take a decision to arrest the perpetrator, draw up a report of what occurred, and refer it to the Public Prosecution appended with an indication of the arrest of the perpetrator.

The Criminal Single Judge shall be seised of contraventions established in records drawn up by those entrusted by special laws with the matter of drawing them up and referring them to the competent court.

After the action is received at the chamber of the Single Judge, the clerk of the court shall draw up a record thereof, the judge shall fix the date of the hearing, and the clerk shall then draw up the writs of summons for each of the plaintiff, the defendant, the civilly liable party and the guarantor, and dispatch them to be served upon him.

Service of his writ of summons must be effected three days prior to the commencement of the trial.

The judge may, in urgent cases, decide to shorten the time limit.

Where any of those mentioned appears before the court merely upon learning of the date of the hearing, he may not invoke the non-service of the writ of summons or the non-observance of the three-day time limit.

Subject to the provisions of Article 165 of this Law, a defendant who has been served with the date of the hearing must appear in person before the court.

Where the defendant is a legal person, it shall appear through the person of its legal representative or through an attorney-at-law acting as its counsel.

The defendant must appear in person or send an attorney-at-law on his behalf if the maximum penalty for the offence attributed to him does not exceed one year of imprisonment.

In such case, the trial shall be deemed adversarial with respect to him. If he does not appear in person or is not represented by an attorney-at-law, he shall be tried in absentia.

Where the judge finds it necessary for the defendant to appear in person before him, he shall notify him through his counsel of the date of the hearing fixed for his interrogation, provided that his decision includes the date of the hearing by day and hour.

If the defendant is absent therefrom, the judge may take his absence as a presumption of the validity of what is attributed to him.

Where the penalty for the offence attributed to the defendant exceeds one year of imprisonment, and he does not appear in person despite having been served with the date of the hearing, he shall be tried in absentia.

Where the defendant is detained, has been served with the date of the hearing, and his refusal to attend it without a legitimate excuse is established, the trial shall be conducted in absentia with respect to him.
Where the offence attributed to the defendant is wholly covered by a general amnesty, he may be represented by an attorney-at-law at the trial.

Each of the civil party, the person civilly liable and the guarantor shall only be represented at the trial by an attorney.

If the civil party fails to appear at the trial hearing without an acceptable excuse and is not represented by an attorney despite having been duly notified, he shall be tried in absentia and the public action shall proceed.

The judgment rendered as a result of the trial shall not be subject to opposition by him, but shall be subject to appeal.

If the civil party attends one of the trial hearings and submits his claims therein, then absents himself from the remaining hearings without an acceptable excuse, the court may award him personal damages even if it tried him in absentia deemed adversarial.

If the person civilly liable or the guarantor absents himself from the trial hearing, and is not represented by an attorney and does not and submits an acceptable excuse despite having been duly notified, he shall be tried in absentia.

The judgment rendered as a result of the trial shall not be subject to opposition, but shall be subject to appeal.
If the defendant attends the trial hearing and then absents himself without an acceptable excuse from the subsequent hearings, the trial shall be deemed adversarial with respect to him.

If the defendant is unable to attend the court for an important health reason, and there are reasons justifying not adjourning his trial, the single judge may move to the place of his presence twenty-four hours after serving him in person with the decision to interrogate him.

He shall draw up a record of his proceedings and sign with his clerk and the defendant on each of its pages.

If the defendant absents himself from the trial after this interrogation and the health excuse continues, he may be represented by an attorney; otherwise, he shall be tried in a manner deemed adversarial.

The civil party or his legal representative may attend these proceedings after being duly notified of their date.

The judgment in absentia must be served upon the convicted person in accordance with the rules of service specified in this Law before sending the extract of this judgment for enforcement.

The judgment in absentia rendered against the convicted person shall not be enforced unless he has been served with it in accordance with the rules specified in Articles 147 et seq. of this Law.

The person convicted in absentia has the right to file an opposition to the judgment in absentia within a time limit of ten days from the date of its service upon him, by means of a petition submitted to the court that rendered the judgment in absentia. If the aforementioned provisions were not observed in serving him, he has the right to file an opposition to it throughout the limitation period of the penalty imposed.

If the convicted person is not served with the judgment in absentia, this judgment shall be considered the last judicial measure, and the limitation period for the public action shall begin to run from its issuance.

The civil part of the judgment rendered in absentia shall become final and binding upon completion of the procedures for its service in accordance with the provisions governing service in the Code of Civil Procedure, and the party awarded personal damages shall obtain an enforceable copy which shall be executed in accordance with the provisions governing the execution of civil judgments.

If, as a result of an appeal against the judgment rendered in absentia after the execution of the civil part thereof, the acquittal of the convicted person or the dismissal of proceedings against him is declared, he shall be entitled to request that the executing party be ordered to return what he received and to pay damages.

A person convicted in absentia shall be entitled to file an opposition against the judgment rendered in absentia

against him in its entirety, or to limit his opposition to the civil obligations and damages awarded.

The opposing party may attend the trial hearings in person or send an attorney on his behalf if the term of the penalty to which he was sentenced does not exceed one year of imprisonment, or if his opposition is limited to the civil obligations and damages awarded.

If he appears, and his opposition was submitted within the legal time limit and satisfies its formal conditions, the judge shall decide to set aside the judgment rendered in absentia and deem it null and void. The trial shall be conducted anew in accordance with the ordinary rules of procedure.

If the opposing party fails to appear at the first hearing without an acceptable excuse, the judge shall decide, subject to the second paragraph of this Article, to dismiss the opposition on formal grounds.

His decision shall not be subject to opposition, but shall be subject to appeal, which shall extend to the initial judgment rendered in absentia.

The time limit for appeal shall run from the date of service of the judgment rendered as a result of the opposition.

If the defendant is justified in his opposition, he shall be exempted from the costs of the trial in absentia; otherwise, he shall be ordered to pay them.

The court may, when it decides to dismiss the opposition on formal grounds, sentence the opposing party to pay a fine ranging between five hundred thousand and one million pounds.

The Single Judge shall hear the action in personam, that is, in respect of the persons prosecuted as defendants.

He shall not be entitled to address others unless a subsequent prosecution is brought against them prior to the determination of the action.

He must, where evidence is available against persons other than the defendants, draw up a report on the matter and refer it to the Public Prosecutor without delay.

The Single Judge shall examine the facts set out in the indictment of the Public Prosecution, the direct complaint, or the committal order.

He may address the circumstances and facts that accompanied the alleged offence and that are likely to affect its characterisation.

The Single Judge shall not be bound by the legal characterisation given to the alleged criminal act.

If he considers that the alleged offence constitutes a felony, he shall declare his lack of jurisdiction to hear the action.

If the Single Judge declares his lack of jurisdiction, on the ground that the act alleged is of the nature of a felony, he shall refer the file of the action to the Public Prosecution.

He may issue a warrant of arrest against the defendant if the action was brought directly before him.

However, if it was referred to him pursuant to a prosecution by the Public Prosecution or on the basis of a charging decision, he shall suffice with declaring his lack of competence and referring the action to the Public Prosecution.

The trial shall be conducted publicly and orally, on pain of nullity, unless the Single Judge decides to conduct it in camera for the sake of preserving public order or public morals.

Minors may, in all cases, be barred from attending it.

The offences alleged may be proved by all means of proof unless there is a provision to the contrary.

The judge may not base his judgment save on the evidence made available to him, provided that it has been subjected to public adversarial debate during the trial.

The judge shall assess the evidence with a view to establishing his personal conviction.

At the commencement of the trial, the clerk shall read out the prosecution of the Public Prosecution or the charging decision, or summarise the facts set out in the direct complaint and the evidence set out against the defendant.

The judge shall hear the statements of the civil claimant or his counsel.

Thereafter, he shall interrogate the defendant in the presence of his defence counsel if he has appointed a lawyer to assist him in the action.

If the defendant refuses to answer and maintains silence, neither the judge nor the claimant shall be entitled to compel him to speak. The judge may not take his silence as a presumption to convict him.

The parties to the action may request witnesses whom they name, and the Single Judge may summon any witness whom he sees benefit in hearing.

He shall not be heard until after he has been administered the oath, the text (literally: deficiency) of which is as follows:

"I swear by Almighty God to testify to the truth and nothing but the truth". The administration of this oath to him shall be recorded in the minutes of the trial.

After the judge finishes hearing the witness, the civil claimant or his counsel and the defendant or his counsel may put to him, through the judge, questions relating to the case.

The judge may refuse to put any question that he does not deem useful. In the event of insistence on putting it, he must record the question and the decision rejecting it.

Every witness must be served with his summons three days prior to the date of the hearing.

If the witness appears before the court, merely upon learning that he is summoned to testify before it, he may not invoke the failure to serve him with his summons or the failure to observe the three-day time limit.

No party to the action shall have the right to object to the hearing of a witness who has begun giving his testimony after having taken the oath.

The statement of one of the defendants against his accomplices in the offence shall not constitute sufficient evidence in proof.

Rather, its assessment shall be a matter for the judge in the light of the evidence available to him.

If it appears to the judge that the witness is giving false testimony, he shall instruct the security forces to place him in the custody cell of the police station and shall draw up a report which he shall submit to the Public Prosecutor in this regard, indicating therein that the witness has been placed in the custody cell.

The Public Prosecutor may prosecute this witness for the offence of perjury in accordance with the rules of procedure.
The witness shall sign the record of his testimony after it has been read out to him.

Records and reports joined to the case file shall not carry probative force unless they are valid in form and the person who drew them up prepared them within the limits of his duties and competence and recorded therein what he personally saw, heard or verified.

If the record is one upon which the law requires reliance until its forgery is proven, the judge must give effect to it.

He may not allow testimonial evidence to be adduced against what is contrary to it. If the record is one upon which the law confers probative force until the contrary of what is stated therein is proven, the defendant may prove what is contrary to it by written evidence or by testimony.

Upon the completion of what the judge deems necessary to form his conviction, he shall hear the claims of the civil claimant or the pleading of his counsel, then he shall hear the defendant or the pleading of his counsel, and then the person civilly liable and the guarantor, if any, or his counsel, provided that the defendant shall have the last word.

The defendant may plead in his own defence even in the presence of his counsel.

The Single Judge may decide to release the detained defendant after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution.

The defendant shall submit the application for his release to the Single Judge in two copies.

A copy thereof shall be served upon the civil claimant, where there is one, at his elected domicile unless he has an actual domicile within the town or city in which the seat of the court is located. If he has not elected a domicile, he shall be served at the court registry.

The civil claimant may object to the application within a time limit of twenty-four hours from the date on which it is served upon him.

Upon the expiry of the time limit, the Single Judge shall rule on the application.

If he decides to release the defendant, the civil claimant may appeal his decision before the Court of Appeal to which the Single Judge is attached within a time limit of twenty-four hours from the date on which he is notified thereof.

If he decides to dismiss the application, the defendant may appeal the decision from the date on which he is notified within the same time limit.

The Public Prosecutor may appeal the decision of the Single Judge within a time limit of twenty-four hours from the date of its issuance. An appeal by the civil claimant or the Public Prosecutor lodged within the legal time limit shall stay the execution of the decision.

Either the civil claimant or the defendant may appeal, within the time limits mentioned above, the part relating to the amount of bail in the release decision.

The provisions of Article 108 of this Law shall apply to the period of detention and the travel ban.

The Single Judge may issue a detention warrant against the defendant if he convicts him in his presence and sentences him to a penalty of imprisonment of more than one year at least, provided that the detention decision is reasoned.

The detention warrant shall remain in force notwithstanding an appeal against the judgment.

After the closing of the trial, the Single Judge shall deliver his judgment at the end of the hearing or at a subsequent hearing.

The judgment must be signed by the judge and by the clerk and bear at its foot the date of its issuance, and it must contain a clear statement of the facts established by the judge, an examination of the evidence supporting them, sufficient precision in the reasons and grounds warranting it, and the legal articles applicable to the offence.

The legal basis pursuant to which the Single Judge became seised of the action must be mentioned therein.

The judge must rule on the defences and issues raised before him by the parties to the action.

He must rule on the public action and on the civil action, if it was brought accessorily to the public action or by way of a direct complaint, and deliver his judgment in public.

He may not address in his judgment facts that have not been alleged or persons against whom no claim has been brought.

After having the remaining witnesses leave, the judge shall ask the witness, prior to administering to him the oath provided for in the preceding Article, for his first name, surname, date of birth, the names of his parents, his nationality, his civil registry number, and his place of residence, and whether any relationship of kinship or dispute exists between him and the defendant.

In principle, the testimony of the ascendants, descendants, brothers and sisters of the defendant, those in the same degree by affinity, and the husband and wife, even after divorce, shall not be admitted.

The judge may hear the testimony of any of these persons if neither the civil party nor the defendant objects thereto, and the testimony of these persons shall not be null and void.

However, an objection by either of them to hearing such persons shall not prevent the judge from hearing them by way of information.

The testimony of a minor who has not completed the eighteenth year of his age shall only be admitted by way of information. A person who is under seven years of age shall only be heard by way of information and pursuant to a reasoned decision.

If the witness fails to appear, despite having been duly served with his summons, and does not submit an acceptable excuse, the judge may order him to pay a fine ranging between one hundred thousand and five hundred thousand pounds.

A witness upon whom a fine has been imposed may request the judge to exempt him therefrom if he presents a legitimate excuse. The judge may decide to compel the attendance of a witness who has failed to appear for the second time after having been served, even if he has previously been fined.

The judge may decide of his own motion or at the request of one of the parties to the proceedings to hear a witness who is present in the courtroom.

If the witness is not proficient in the Arabic language, or is deaf or mute, the judge shall appoint an interpreter for him and administer to him the oath to perform the mission truthfully and faithfully.

Testimony shall bear upon the facts of the alleged offence, its circumstances, and the nature of the defendant's participation therein.

If the witness summoned before the Single Judge is the person who reported the occurrence of the offence to the competent authority, the judge shall note this matter prior to hearing him.

If the witness is an informer who gave notice of the offence in return for remuneration that he received, the judge may hear him by way of information.

The witness shall give his statement orally.

Neither the plaintiff nor the defendant, nor the counsel of either of them, may interrupt him.

The witness may seek the permission of the judge to make use of documents or papers when giving his testimony.

The judge may retain the witness outside the courtroom after hearing him in order to call him a second time and hear him anew, or to confront him with other witnesses.

The judge shall show the witness the incriminating materials and evidentiary items and question him thereon, and he may read out to him his statement from the preliminary or investigative inquiry and seek clarification from him thereon and as to whether he confirms it.

Where it becomes apparent to the Single Judge that the facts he has established are of a felony nature, he shall declare that he lacks jurisdiction to hear them and shall refer the case file to the Public Prosecution.

Where it becomes apparent to him during the investigation of the action that there are offences in respect of which no claim has been brought or persons against whom no claim has been brought, he shall refer the case file to the Public Prosecution so that it may bring a claim in respect of the acts or against the persons pursuant to its original claim or in an independent action.

Where it becomes apparent to the Single Judge that the misdemeanour in respect of which the claim is brought satisfies all its constituent elements and that the evidence is sufficient as to the existence of the causal link between it and the act of the defendant, he shall establish the same, specify the legal articles applicable thereto, convict the defendant and sentence him to the prescribed penalty, and award all civil damages and obligations to the civil party if he has requested them and the conditions for awarding them are met.

Where the penalty imposed is a fine or a suspended sentence of imprisonment, he shall order the release of the convicted person if he is in custody.

Where it becomes apparent to the Judge that the evidence of the defendant's participation in the commission of the misdemeanour in respect of which the claim is brought is insufficient, he shall render a judgment declaring the acquittal of the latter and shall release him forthwith if he is in custody.

Upon rendering a judgment acquitting the defendant, he shall award him damages against the civil party if he has requested the same, where the civil party has exceeded his right to litigate.

Where the defendant does not request compensation for the harm suffered by him during the course of the criminal trial and up until its conclusion, it shall remain open to him to request it before the same authority in an independent action within a time limit of three months from the date of service upon him of the judgment of acquittal or the decision upholding it.

Where it becomes apparent to the Single Judge that the act in respect of which the claim is brought does not constitute a criminal offence, or that it is exempt from punishment, or is not punishable by imprisonment, or that its criminal character has ceased to exist for any of the reasons causing it to cease, or that the action has lapsed for any of the reasons causing it to lapse, he shall render a judgment annulling the prosecution against the defendant and shall release him forthwith if he is in custody.

The provisions of the preceding Article shall be observed in respect of a claim for damages.

Where it becomes apparent to the Single Judge that the act constitutes a contravention, he shall rule thereon and award compensation to the injured party if he has requested it.

He shall decide to release the defendant forthwith if he is in custody.

The costs of the action shall be awarded against the unsuccessful party.

The civil party may be exempted from all or part of the costs if it becomes apparent to the Judge that he acted in good faith, unless he initiated the public prosecution by his direct complaint.

The Single Judge may rule on applications for the restitution of seized items even if he has adjudicated the merits of the case and is consequently functus officio in respect thereof, unless his judgment is the subject of a challenge.

The decision ordering the restitution of the seized items or refusing their restitution shall be subject to appeal.
The Single Judge may make part of the compensation awarded to the civil party provisionally enforceable, even if his judgment is subject to appeal.

Summary proceedings shall apply to contraventions of municipal, health and traffic regulations.

When a contravention of the said regulations occurs, whether it entails a contravention penalty or a misdemeanour penalty, the official report establishing it shall be sent to the Single Judge, who shall impose the penalty legally entailed by the act without summoning the defendant.

The judge shall issue his judgment within a time-limit of ten days, unless the law prescribes a shorter period.

The facts established by the official report shall be deemed true unless it appears that there is a breach of procedure in the drawing up thereof.

The judge shall characterize the facts, specify the legal article applicable thereto and impose the penalty on the defendant, unless it appears to him:

A - That the act attributed to the defendant does not constitute an offence or is wholly exempt from punishment.

B - That he lacks jurisdiction to hear the contravention.

C - That the public prosecution has abated for any of the causes of abatement thereof.

If he decides to declare his lack of jurisdiction, he shall refer the case file administratively to the competent Single Judge.

The decision issued by the Single Judge in one of the said contraventions shall be deemed enforceable unless the convicted person lodges, within a time-limit of ten days from the date of being notified thereof, an objection thereto in accordance with the ordinary rules of procedure.

The Public Prosecutor may object to the decision within a time-limit of ten days from the date of its issuance in accordance with the ordinary rules of procedure.

If the objection is dismissed as to form, the penalty imposed shall be ordered to be increased by up to one half thereof as a maximum.
The summary proceedings provided for above shall not apply when there is a civil party in the action.

After the judgment becomes final and reasoned, whether due to the expiry of the period for objection, the withdrawal by the objecting party of his objection, or the dismissal of the objection, the clerk shall send an extract of the judgment bearing at its foot the phrase "valid for execution" to the Public Prosecution within a time-limit of five days from the judgment becoming irrevocable.

If the clerk fails to observe the provisions of this article, he shall be fined, pursuant to a decision issued by the Single Judge, an amount ranging between one hundred thousand and five hundred thousand Pounds.

The convicted defendant may appeal the judgment of first instance, whether with respect to its ruling on the penalty or on the compensation.

He may appeal the judgment ruling for his acquittal if it ordered him to pay all or part of the judicial costs and the judgment that ruled in his favour for compensation for the plaintiff's abuse of his right to bring an action.

The civilly liable party or the guarantor may appeal the judgment that ordered him, jointly and severally with the defendant adjudged guilty, to pay compensation to the civil party.

He may appeal this judgment alone even if the defendant has acquiesced in it. In this latter case, he alone shall benefit from his appeal.

The civil party may appeal the part of the judgment relating to the civil action. If the civil action has been dismissed pursuant to a judgment of acquittal, he may appeal the judgment ordering its dismissal even if the judgment of acquittal has become final due to the failure of the Public Prosecution to appeal.

He may appeal the clause of the judgment ordering him to pay compensation to the defendant.

The Appellate Public Prosecution may appeal judgments with respect to what relates therein to the public action.

The Cassation Public Prosecution may request in writing from the Appellate Public Prosecution to appeal a judgment of first instance that ruled to acquit the defendant, or to annul the proceedings against him, or to extinguish the public right action against him, or to declare the court's lack of jurisdiction to hear the action.

Judgments rendered in misdemeanour cases shall be subject to appeal.

Judgments rendered in contraventions shall not be subject to appeal unless they rule for:

a - Imprisonment, disciplinary detention, or a fine exceeding five hundred thousand Lira.

b - An additional or accessory penalty, or personal compensation exceeding five hundred thousand Lira.

c - The dismissal of one of the pleas provided for in Article 73 of this Law.

d - A penalty for a contravention connected with a misdemeanour.

Decisions that do not dispose of the merits of the dispute may only be appealed together with the final judgment.

Exempted from this principle are decisions that adjudicate upon one or more of the pleas provided for in Article 73 of this Law, decisions of release, and decisions by which the Single Judge terminates the action without addressing the merits.

Each of the civil claimant, the defendant, the person civilly liable and the guarantor may appeal the judgment of first instance within a period of fifteen days from the date of its issuance if it is adversarial, and from the date of service thereof upon him if it is deemed adversarial, in absentia, or ruling on the dismissal of the opposition in form.

The Appellate Public Prosecutor may appeal the judgment within a period of one month from the date of its issuance.

In order to characterise the judgment as in absentia or adversarial, the rules mentioned in Articles 165 to 170 of this Law shall apply.
If the judgment is not issued on the date fixed in the closing hearing for its issuance, each of the parties to the action may appeal it within fifteen days from the date of service thereof upon him.

Any of the parties to the action who has not appealed the judgment of first instance within the period of fifteen days may lodge an incidental appeal within a period of five days from the date he is notified of the date of the first appellate hearing, if one of the parties to the action has appealed it by way of a principal appeal.

The dismissal of the principal appeal on a formal ground shall entail the dismissal of the incidental appeal.

The appeal shall be lodged, through an attorney-at-law admitted to the Court of Appeal, with the Court of Appeal to which the judge who issued the appealed judgment is attached, or through him. The appeal must include the grounds raised by the person lodging it and his claims.

If the appeal is lodged through the Single Judge who issued the appealed judgment, he must forward the appeal together with the file of the action within a period of three days from the date of its lodging.

If the convicted person is detained, the Public Prosecution may order his transfer to the place of detention located at the Court of Appeal.

If the term of his sentence expires before his appeal is adjudicated, the Public Prosecution shall release him immediately.

The judgment of first instance may not be executed before the expiry of the period for appeal, nor before the adjudication thereof when it is appealed.

The appeal shall stay the execution of the appealed judgment.

However, any provisional advance on account of compensation awarded by the Single Judge to the civil claimant shall be enforceable forthwith, unless the Court of Appeal decides otherwise within the framework of examining the appealed judgment of first instance.

The detention warrant issued by the Single Judge pursuant to Article 193 of this Law shall remain in force unless the Court of Appeal decides to release the detainee.

An appeal by the Public Prosecutor brings the public action in its entirety before the Court of Appeal unless it is directed against a specific part thereof, in which case its effect shall be limited thereto.

As for an appeal lodged by the defendant, it binds the Court of Appeal within the limits of the part of the appealed judgment against which the appeal was lodged.

The Court of Appeal may not examine new facts that are capable of constituting offences and that were not submitted to the Single Judge who rendered the appealed judgment.

Where the defendant appeals the judgment of first instance to the exclusion of the other parties, the Court of Appeal may not increase the penalty imposed upon him or the damages awarded in favour of the civil party.

An appeal by the civil party alone brings before the Court of Appeal the civil aspect of the action.

The Court of Appeal may not reduce the damages awarded to him.

The Court of Appeal shall set a date for the trial and shall adhere before it to the ordinary rules governing trial before the Single Judge. The Public Prosecution shall be represented before it by the Public Prosecutor or by one of the Advocates General.
