It shall hear the claims of the civil party or his counsel if either is present, the pleadings of the representative of the Public Prosecution, and then the pleadings of defence counsel and the defendant himself if he so requests.

If it is satisfied with the facts and evidence contained in the case file, it shall close the trial and render judgment at the end of the hearing or set another date for rendering it.

If the Court finds cause to expand the investigation, it shall summon the witnesses and carry out the investigative measures that it deems useful, conducting them in a public hearing, or assign one of its members to conduct a supplementary investigation in accordance with the ordinary rules.

Upon completion of the supplementary investigation, its documents shall be joined to the case file, and all parties thereto may inspect it and debate it in a public hearing.

After the Court of Appeal completes the investigative measures before it, it shall issue a decision reversing the appealed judgment, amending it, or affirming it with respect to the outcome it reached after substituting the reasoning it adopts for the reasoning contained therein.

If the Court reverses the appealed judgment and rules to declare the acquittal of the defendant or to annul the prosecution against him, it shall rule at the same time to release him if he is detained and to dismiss the civil action.

A defendant in respect of whom a ruling has been rendered declaring his acquittal or discontinuing the prosecution against him may claim from the claimant who abused his right to litigate compensation for the damage he sustained in accordance with the provisions of Article 197 of this Law.

Where the Public Prosecution appeals the judgment of first instance, the entire action shall be devolved upon the Court of Appeal.

Where it appears to the Court that the facts established in the action carry a felony characterisation, it shall decide to set aside the judgment under appeal and declare its lack of jurisdiction.

It may issue a warrant of arrest against the defendant and remit the case file to the Public Prosecution for referral to the Investigating Judge.

Any conflict of jurisdiction shall be resolved, once its decision becomes final, by way of determination of the competent court.

Where it is established to the Court of Appeal that the Single Judge who rendered the judgment under appeal lacked jurisdiction to hear the action, it shall confine itself to setting aside the judgment for lack of jurisdiction and remitting the case file to the Public Prosecution to take the requisite action.
Where it appears to the Court of Appeal that the act which is the subject of the action is in the nature of a contravention, it shall adjudicate upon it after setting aside the judgment under appeal.

Where the Court of Appeal sets aside the judgment under appeal for violation of the law or for breach of essential rules of procedure, it shall assume jurisdiction over the merits of the action and adjudicate upon it.

Opposition may be lodged against a judgment in absentia rendered by the Court of Appeal in accordance with the rules governing opposition to a judgment in absentia rendered by the Single Judge and within the same time limit.

The Court of Appeal may decide, after seeking the opinion of the Public Prosecution, to release the detained defendant.

Its decision shall not be subject to any avenue of recourse.

The Criminal Court shall be composed of a President and two Associate Judges.

It shall sit in the presence of the Public Prosecutor or the Advocate General and the Clerk.

It shall be seised of the action pursuant to an indictment decision accompanied by the claim of the Public Prosecution.

The Court shall hear offences carrying a felony characterisation and misdemeanours connected therewith.

It may not hear any criminal act not covered by the indictment decision or try any person not indicted therein. It may alter the legal characterisation of the acts which are the subject of the indictment decision.

No person who has previously performed in the action an act of prosecution or investigation, or who was a member of the Indictment Chamber that drew up the indictment decision therein, may participate in the composition of the Criminal Court.

The civil claimant before the Criminal Court shall be required to appoint an advocate to represent him.

Where there are multiple participants in the commission of a single felony or connected felonies, and separate indictments have been issued against each of them or against some of them to the exclusion of the others, the President of the Court may decide to join the indictments into a single action.
Where the indictment includes unconnected felonies, the President of the Court may decide to commence by trying the accused for some of these felonies and subsequently trying them for the others.

The President of the Criminal Court shall decide to fix the date of the trial and to summon the civil claimant and the witnesses thereto, and shall also issue a time-limit order granting the accused who was released during the preliminary investigation a period to surrender himself to the Court within twenty-four hours prior to the commencement of the trial.

The time-limit shall run against him from the date on which he is served with this order in accordance with the provisions of Articles 147, 148 and 149 of this Law.

If he surrenders himself within the time-limit, he shall be tried in person and the arrest warrant shall be executed against him.

If he fails to do so, he shall be tried in absentia and the special procedures for the trial of a fugitive from justice shall be applied against him.

The names of the President of the Court, its assessors, the representative of the Public Prosecution, and the clerk, as well as the hour of the opening of the sitting, must be recorded in the minutes of the trial at the beginning of each sitting, and they, with the exception of the representative of the Public Prosecution, must sign the minutes at the end of each sitting.

If any one of them omits to sign, the sitting shall be null and void.

All measures of investigation and trial shall be recorded in the minutes. The President shall dictate to the clerk what must be recorded.

The Public Prosecutor shall prepare a list of the witnesses for the public action and shall undertake to serve the accused with a copy thereof and of the indictment decision.

After completing the service procedure, the Public Prosecution shall send the case file to the Criminal Court after ordering that the detained accused be brought to the place of detention located at its premises.

A trial held without the witnesses for the public action, as well as the judgment rendered as a result thereof, shall be subject to annulment.

The President of the Court, or whichever of its assessors he delegates, shall interrogate the accused after he is brought before him and prior to the trial sitting.

If the accused is not detained, the President of the Court shall issue an order of time-limit against him calling upon him to surrender himself within twenty-four hours from the commencement of the trial.

If he surrenders himself within the said time-limit, he shall remain detained until a decision ordering his release is issued.

If he abstains from doing so without an acceptable excuse, he shall be deemed a fugitive from justice and the arrest warrant issued against him shall be put into execution.

If he has not appointed a lawyer, the President or the delegated assessor must request the President of the Bar Association to appoint a lawyer to undertake his defence within twenty-four hours from the time of his notification, or undertake to appoint him himself.

Minutes of the preliminary interrogation shall be drawn up and signed by the President or the delegated assessor, the accused, and the clerk.

The preliminary interrogation shall cover asking the accused whether he has been served with the indictment decision and the list of witnesses for the public action and whether he has appointed a lawyer to assist him in the trial, and asking him about his social status and his observations regarding the charge attributed to him and the investigations conducted therein.

If he has not appointed a lawyer, the President or the delegated assessor must request the President of the Bar Association to appoint a lawyer to undertake his defence within twenty-four hours from the time of his notification, or undertake to appoint him himself.

Minutes of the preliminary interrogation shall be drawn up and signed by the President or the delegated assessor, the accused, and the clerk.
All parties may inspect the case file and take a copy thereof.

The Court shall take, before deciding on the merits of the action, the following decisions:

a - The decision determining the plea of lack of jurisdiction on the ground that the accused was a minor on the date of the occurrence of the felony with which he is charged.

If the Court rules to declare its lack of jurisdiction, and there is another accused in the action, the severance procedure shall be carried out and it shall refer the file of the minor to the Public Prosecution to file it with the Juvenile Court.

b - The decision determining one or more of the formal pleas raised by the parties to the action.

c - The decision determining the substantive grounds of defence.

d - The decision ordering the stay of execution of the arrest warrant until the constitution of the adversarial proceedings before the Court is complete, if the accused was released during the stage of the preliminary investigation.

e - The decision releasing the detained accused.

It is required for release that the accused elect a chosen domicile for himself within the town or city in which the seat of the Court is located in order to be served therein with its papers and notices, that he surrender himself to it within twenty-four hours prior to the convening of each hearing, and that he pay the bail decided by the Court, provided that he remains detained from the hearing of the conclusion of the trial until the issuance of the judgment.

If he fails to appear at any hearing without an acceptable excuse, he shall be deemed a fugitive from justice and the special rules for the trial of a fugitive shall apply to him. The Court may decide to bar the released accused from travel until the issuance and execution of the judgment.

The Court may not take its decision deciding on the application for release until after it has sought the opinion of the Public Prosecution.

The Court shall observe the provisions of Article 108 of this Law.

The decision determining the application for the release of the accused shall not be subject to any avenue of review.

The parties to the action may, prior to the commencement of the trial and during it, request a month whom they name. The Public Prosecutor and the civil party must be served with a list of the names of the witnesses whom the accused names at least twenty-four hours prior to the time appointed for hearing them.

The accused must also be served with a list of the names of the witnesses whom the civil party or the Public Prosecutor names within the same time limit.

The President of the Court may decide of his own motion to summon the experts who carried out technical assignments in the action to seek clarification from them thereon, and the witnesses whom he sees benefit in hearing.

Each of the accused and the civil party shall bear the expenses of summoning and travel of the witnesses whom he named.

The trial before the Criminal Court shall be conducted in public unless the President decides to conduct it in secret to preserve time or public morals.

The trial hearings shall continue day after day until the determination of the action unless the status of the action necessitates the adjournment of one of these hearings, in which case it shall be to a near date.

Minutes of the trial proceedings shall be drawn up and signed by the panel of the Court together with the clerk.

If the civil party fails to attend the trial without a legitimate excuse, he shall be tried in absentia and the action shall proceed in the name of the public right.

If he attends one of its hearings, and submits his claims therein, the Court may award him personal damages.

The trial shall be conducted orally.

The President may decide to record it by audio or visual means.

All the evidence that will be relied upon to determine the action must be subjected to public debate between the parties, the incriminating articles must be exhibited, and the minutes proving their seizure must be read out.

Each of the parties may take a position thereon.

The accused shall appear before the Court, at the hearing scheduled for his trial, unfettered. He shall be guarded by members of the security forces to prevent his escape. The President shall ask him about his first name, his surname, the names of his parents, his nationality, the date and place of his birth, his civil status register number, his place of residence, the nature of his work, his educational level, whether he is married or single, whether he has been previously convicted, the nature of the offence of which he was convicted, and whether he has served his sentence.

He shall also ask him whether he has instructed a lawyer to defend him.

The trial shall not be conducted in the absence of the lawyer of the accused.

If the accused has not appointed a lawyer for himself, the President of the Court may request the President of the Bar Association to assign a lawyer to defend the accused or may undertake to appoint one himself.

If the accused insists on refusing the assignment of any lawyer to defend him, his trial shall in this case be conducted without a lawyer.

If the President of the Court finds, prior to commencing the trial, that the elements of the case are incomplete, he shall decide to conduct a supplementary investigation in the presence of the parties, which he shall undertake himself or delegate one of the associate judges to perform for this purpose.

Upon completion of the supplementary investigation, the records drawn up therein shall be joined to the case file.

The President of the Court shall supervise the maintenance of order inside the courtroom and shall take the necessary measures for the proper conduct of the trial.

Members of the security forces charged with maintaining security in the court shall obey his orders in this regard.

If any person present causes a commotion in the courtroom, the President may order his expulsion therefrom.

If he resists the execution of the order, the President may order his detention for a period of twenty-four hours.

If he commits an act that constitutes a misdemeanour, a record of his act shall be drawn up, and the Court shall then examine it immediately, try him in person, and sentence him to the penalty forthwith.

The President shall enjoy discretionary power authorizing him to take such measures as he deems necessary to uncover the truth, provided that they do not betray a preconceived opinion on his part regarding the case.

The President shall conduct the hearing and the deliberations in accordance with the order he deems appropriate.

He may reject any request that would prolong the trial to no avail. He shall hear the witnesses after putting them under oath, unless one of the parties to the case objects to the hearing of some of them on legal grounds, in which case he shall decide to dispense with hearing the witness or to hear him by way of information, and he may decide to fine a witness who abstains from appearing after having been duly summoned in an amount ranging between one hundred thousand and five hundred thousand pounds. A witness upon whom a fine has been imposed may request the President to exempt him therefrom if he presents an acceptable excuse.

The President of the Court may decide to compel the attendance of a witness who fails to appear for the second time after having been notified, even if he has previously been fined. The President may decide to join the papers and documents that he deems necessary to reveal the truth. He shall read them out together with the letters and documents contained in the case file.

He may refer to the preliminary or initial investigation to discuss statements contained therein, seek the assistance of experts to clarify technical points, and commission, to hear a witness residing outside his district, the investigating judge within whose jurisdiction the witness's place of residence or dwelling is located.

The President shall caution the accused as to the obligation to listen to the facts set forth in the indictment decision.

The President, or the Associate Judge whom he designates, shall read out the indictment decision clearly.

Neither the civil party, nor the representative of the Public Prosecution, nor the accused may interrupt the reading with any remark that he may make. After the reading, the President shall summarise to the accused the facts set forth against him in the indictment decision, the evidence supporting them and their legal characterisation; thereafter, the civil party shall reiterate the purport of his claim and state his demands or waive his rights in the action, and after him the representative of the Public Prosecution shall explain the grounds of the indictment and submit the list of witnesses for the public right. The clerk of the court shall read out the list in public.

Subject to Article 244, each of the civil party, the representative of the Public Prosecution and the accused shall be entitled to object to the hearing of a witness whose name was not included in the list notified to him. The court shall rule on the objection in the same hearing or in the subsequent hearing.

The President of the court may decide, pursuant to his discretionary power, to hear all the witnesses whose names are included in the lists or some of them to the exclusion of others, and he may hear one or more witnesses whose names were not included in the lists of witnesses.

Before the President of the court interrogates the accused, he shall order that the witnesses be brought into the room designated for them, where certain members of the security forces shall guard them therein and prevent them from disclosing what they will state in their testimonies.

After the witnesses have been brought in, the President shall proceed to ask the accused whether he confesses to the charge attributed to him.

Following that, he shall continue his interrogation after observing his ability to understand the questions put to him and that he is making his statements with sufficient freedom.

If the accused refuses to answer and remains silent, he may not be compelled to speak.

If he is afflicted with a physical, psychological or mental illness, or feigns the same during his interrogation, the court shall, of its own motion or at the request of any of the parties, seek the assistance of medical expertise to ascertain the truth of his condition.

The physician appointed to examine him shall record in his report that which pertains to the condition he is required to diagnose.

He may not exploit his mission to induce the accused to disclose to him information relating to the offence for which he is being tried.

After the President concludes the interrogation of the accused, each of the Associate Judges of the court, the civil party, the representative of the Public Prosecution and defence counsel shall be entitled to put questions to him through the President, who enjoys the right to disallow any question he deems unavailing or unproductive in uncovering the truth.

The questions and answers shall be recorded in the trial record with sufficient accuracy and clarity.

If the accused is mute or deaf, the President of the Court shall seek the assistance of a person capable of communicating with him by sign language or otherwise, after administering to him an oath to observe truthfulness and honesty in his work. If the deaf or mute person knows how to write, his interrogation shall be conducted by recording the questions in writing and recording the answers thereto.

If the accused does not understand the Arabic language, the President of the Court shall appoint for him a competent interpreter and shall administer to him the legal oath to perform his work truthfully and honestly.

After the interrogation of the accused, his statement shall be read out to him clearly, and he shall confirm it or make observations thereon where necessary, which shall be recorded in the minutes of the trial.

After the completion of the interrogation of the accused, the President shall summon each of the witnesses to give his testimony separately from the others. The witness shall be asked for his name, the names of his parents, his place of residence or domicile, his age, the extent of his acquaintance or relationship with both the accused and the civil party, and whether he is related to either of them and, if so, in what degree. He shall then administer to him the following oath:

"I swear by Almighty God to testify to the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth."

Thereafter, he shall give his testimony orally, and the clerk shall record it in the minutes of the trial.

If the witness does not take the oath in the formula specified above, his statement shall be null and void, unless the President exempts him from taking the oath after it is established that he belongs to a religious denomination that forbids him from taking an oath.

The Court shall hear, by way of information, each of the following:

(a) - The ascendants and descendants of the accused.

(b) - His full brothers and sisters, or his half-brothers and half-sisters, or his relatives by marriage who are of the same degree.

(c) - The spouse of the accused, even after divorce.

(d) - The civil party.

(e) A minor under eighteen years of age.

The Court may hear the testimony of each of these persons after administering to him the legal oath if none of the parties to the proceedings objects thereto.

The testimony of an informer who notified the competent authority of the offence without remuneration or reward for his information shall be admissible.

For this purpose, the Public Prosecutor must state the capacity of the informer prior to his being heard.

If the informer received remuneration for his information or any reward, his testimony shall not be admissible if one of the parties to the proceedings objects thereto.

It shall remain open to the President of the Court to hear him by way of information.

A judicial police officer shall be prohibited, when giving his statement, from mentioning the name of the informer.

No person who is bound by professional secrecy shall be compelled to give testimony if the subject matter of the testimony discloses a secret which he is entrusted to keep.

If the witness invokes professional secrecy and a dispute arises concerning his reliance thereon, the Court shall decide the dispute in the light of the law governing his profession and the nature of his work therein.
The court may hear a witness who attended without having been summoned if his name appears on one of the lists of witnesses scheduled to be heard.

A witness may not be interrupted while giving his testimony.

Each of the civil party, the representative of the Public Prosecution, the associate judges of the court and the accused may put questions to the witness through the President.

The President of the court may decide to refuse to put any question that does not serve to reveal the truth.

When the witness finishes making his statements, the President shall ask him whether the accused standing in the dock is the person to whom he referred in his testimony.

He shall then ask the accused for his position regarding the deposition of the witness.

He may conduct any confrontation that he deems necessary between the accused and the witness to reveal the truth.

The deposition of the witness shall be read out publicly, and he shall confirm it.

After giving his testimony, a witness may not leave the courtroom unless the President authorises him to do so.

If a discrepancy or alteration appears between the testimony of the witness and his statements in the preliminary or preparatory investigation, the President shall order the clerk of the court to record the same. Each of the civil party, the representative of the Public Prosecution and the accused may request that such discrepancy or alteration be recorded in the minutes of the trial. If such discrepancy or alteration in the deposition of the witness gives reason to believe that the witness is lying in his deposition, the President of the court may order, of his own motion or at the request of those aforementioned, that he be detained. The representative of the Public Prosecution shall bring charges of perjury against him.

Such charges shall be entered in the minutes of the trial.

Thereupon, the President of the court, or one of its associate judges delegated by him, shall investigate the witness in respect of the offence of perjury with which he is charged. The person entrusted with the investigation shall interrogate the defendant witness and gather the evidence of the offence charged without expressing his opinion on the investigation that he conducted.

After concluding his investigation, he shall refer it to the Public Prosecution, which shall submit its opinion thereon and refer it to the Indictment Chamber.

That Chamber may issue the decision as to whether or not to indict.

If it decides to indict the witness for the felony of perjury, the court shall adjudicate thereon before or together with the original action. The decision of the Indictment Chamber shall be subject to cassation before the Court of Cassation.

Where charges of perjury are brought, in the manner set out in the preceding article, each of the representative of the Public Prosecution, the civil party and the accused may request the adjournment of the hearing in the original action until the action for perjury is adjudicated upon. The court shall rule upon the request.

It may also decide the same of its own motion.

After a witness has given his testimony, the President of the Court may order, of his own motion or at the request of the representative of the Public Prosecution, the accused, or the civil party, that any of the witnesses he wishes be removed from the courtroom, and then that one or more of those who left be brought back in to give his testimony anew separately, or in the presence of the others, or in the presence of some of them, and to conduct a confrontation between them, and to present the seized incriminating items to them and discuss them with the accused.

The President of the Court may, before hearing a witness or during his hearing, temporarily remove the accused from the courtroom in order to seek clarification from the witness alone or jointly with others. Counsel for the accused shall remain present during the proceeding of seeking clarification from the witness.

However, if counsel leaves, his departure shall not result in the invalidation of the statement given in his absence. Nevertheless, the Court may not continue the trial until the accused has been returned to the courtroom and informed of the statement given in his absence.

If the accused, during the hearing of a witness or during the trial, causes a commotion or disturbance in the courtroom, the President of the Court shall warn him to put an end to his act. If he persists therein, he shall order that he be removed from the Court and kept outside it, and shall continue the trial in his absence.

After the conclusion of the hearing, the President of the Court shall order that the accused be notified of the proceedings that took place after his removal, and his notification shall be recorded in the minutes of the trial.

A witness against whom a decision imposing a fine has been issued may file an objection thereto before the Court. The Court shall assess the excuse he puts forward and rule on the objection by a decision not subject to any means of recourse.

The fine imposed shall be enforced in the manner in which judgments imposing fines are enforced.

If the Court decides to dispense with repeating the summoning of a witness upon whom it has been unable to duly serve a summons, it shall read out his preliminary or initial statement publicly and submit it to debate.

If it appears that the witness did not take the oath before giving his testimony, the President of the Court may summon him a second time, administer the oath to him in a public hearing, and ask him whether he confirms his previous testimony. If he confirms it, the Court may then rely upon it in its judgment.
If the witness is deaf or mute, or does not have a command of the Arabic language, the provisions of Article 254 of this Law shall apply in hearing his statement.

If the Court decides to move to the scene of the crime, it shall set a date of which it shall notify all the parties to the action.

If one of them fails to attend at the appointed time, it shall conduct the inspection in his absence, and he may examine it in the case file.

The President of the Court, or any of his associate judges whom he delegates, may conduct a supplementary investigation in the action pending before the Court, and may draw up a record of the inspection of traces liable to disappear that are capable of assisting in revealing the truth, or may hear the testimony of a witness at the point of death.

The person delegated to conduct the investigation shall draw up records establishing the information he has seized or heard and shall send them to the Court, which shall submit them to public debate.

After the Court finishes hearing the witnesses, gathering the evidence and submitting it to debate, it shall give the floor to the civil party, who shall state his claims. Then the representative of the Public Prosecution shall plead and put forward such evidence and arguments as he deems fit, concluding by specifying his demands.

Thereafter, defence counsel shall plead on behalf of his client and shall also specify his claims. The Court shall then hear the final statement of the accused and decide to close the trial.

The civil party, the representative of the Public Prosecution and the accused may each request, after the close of the trial, that it be reopened, after stating the grounds supporting his request.

The Court shall decide to grant the request if it appears to it to be serious and worthy of acceptance or if it contains important grounds that necessitate renewed debate.

After the President of the Court declares the close of the trial, he and his associate judges alone shall retire to the deliberation room and deliberate on the action, and examine the indictment decision, the final investigation conducted by the Court, the documents and records joined to the case file, the claims of the civil party, the pleading of the representative of the Public Prosecution, the pleading of counsel for the accused, and the final statement of the accused.

The Court shall then deliberate on everything it has examined and shall issue its judgment on the same day or within a period not exceeding ten days, unanimously or by a majority of opinions, signed by the President, the associate judges and the clerk.

The omission by one of the members of the Court to sign the judgment shall render it liable to annulment.

If one of the members of the Court dissents from the judgment, he shall record his dissent and sign it.

If it is established to the Court that the act occurred, that the criminal characterization is satisfied therein, and that there is sufficient evidence to attribute it to the accused, it shall rule to convict him of the felony and specify the penalty it imposes upon him.

It shall also award damages to the civil party if he has requested them.

It shall order the confiscation of the seized items, or their restitution if there is no ground for their confiscation. It may also impose one or more precautionary measures and one or more ancillary or supplementary penalties. The Court may order the merger of principal penalties in accordance with the provisions of Article 205 of the Penal Code.

If the court finds that the evidence available in the case file does not suffice to convict the accused, it shall rule to declare his acquittal. If it finds that the act attributed to the accused does not constitute an offence or does not warrant a penalty, it shall rule to discontinue the proceedings against him.

If it finds that the elements of the felony attributed to the accused are incomplete and that the act constitutes a misdemeanour, it shall amend the legal characterization set out in the indictment decision, adjudge the misdemeanour against the accused, and impose its penalty upon him. The judgment of the Criminal Court must include the following:

a - A citation of the indictment decision pursuant to which the court was seized of the case, and a reference to the prosecution brought by the Public Prosecution before it in accordance with the indictment decision.

b - A clear summary of the claims of the civil party and of the pleadings of each of the representative of the Public Prosecution and the counsel for the accused, and a reference to what the accused stated in his final statement.

c - A clear summary of the facts drawn from the indictment decision and from the trial proceedings.

d - A detailed examination of the evidence and the grounds warranting conviction or the absence thereof.

e - A statement of the nature of the offence, a determination of the legal characterization applicable thereto, and a citation of the legal article that establishes it.

f - A determination of the penalty following conviction.

g- A fixing of the amount of personal damages.

h - An order to pay the fees of the case and its legal expenses.

The court must set out in its judgment the material aggravating circumstances, then the excuses, then the personal aggravating circumstances, and then the mitigating circumstances. The court must, if a ground of justification is present in the act of the accused, ascertain its fulfilment before deciding that the criminal character of this act is negated and consequently that the accused is not liable.

It must, in all cases, rule upon every plea that it previously joined to the merits, upon every ground of defence, and upon every request of the parties to the case.

Its judgment must be sufficiently reasoned, free from ambiguity, obscurity, or contradiction.

If the court considers that the act attributed to the accused does not constitute a felony, but rather a misdemeanour or a contravention, or if the legal text is amended such that the characterization of the act becomes of the nature of a misdemeanour or a contravention, the court shall retain jurisdiction over the action and rule thereon.

The fees and expenses of the action shall be awarded against the civil party upon a judgment declaring the acquittal of the accused or the discontinuance of proceedings against him. He may be exempted therefrom in whole or in part if it is established that he acted in good faith and that it was the Public Prosecution that initiated the public action.

However, if the civil party initiated the public action by his direct complaint in which he assumed the capacity of a civil party, he may not be exempted.

If he had advanced a sum of money in his civil claim, the amount exceeding the fees and expenses of the action shall be refunded to him.

The judgment issued by the Criminal Court shall be recorded in a special register of judgments.

The original of the judgment shall be kept in the file of the action, and the panel that issued it shall sign it at the foot of its entry in the register, in addition to the clerk.

Where the Indictment Chamber decides to indict a person, it shall issue an arrest warrant against him.

The Public Prosecution shall undertake the tasks of serving the accused with a copy of the indictment instrument, of the list of witnesses for the public action, and of the arrest warrant in accordance with the procedures set forth in Articles 147, 148 and 149 of this Law, and shall refer the file of the action to the Criminal Court accompanied by its claim in accordance with the indictment decision.

No claim may be made contrary to what is stated in the indictment clause.

Immediately upon receipt of the file by the court, its President shall schedule a hearing to examine it.

He shall issue a time-limit order whereby he calls upon the accused to surrender himself to the court within twenty-four hours prior to the commencement of the trial. If he is served with this order and refrains from surrendering himself, the court shall decide to try him in absentia and consider him a fugitive from justice, and shall issue an order to execute the arrest warrant issued against him, and shall rule to divest him of his civil rights, prohibit him from disposing of his property and from bringing any action not related to his personal status throughout the duration of his flight, and appoint a curator to administer the property of the fugitive throughout this period.

The curator shall not be entitled to dispose of the property of the convicted person except by special permission from the Criminal Court.

The Public Prosecution shall notify the Real Estate Registry of the court's decision to that effect in order to enter a caveat thereof ex officio on the real property folios of the properties of the accused.

The President of the Court or whichever of his Associate Judges he assigns shall read out the judgment in a public sitting attended by the representative of the Public Prosecution, the accused and the civil party. If the accused or the civil party fails to attend it, the reading out shall take place in his absence.

The Court Clerk shall sign the judgment after it is read out. He shall then draw up a record of the reading out of the judgment, dictated to him by the President, in which a summary of the judgment may be stated.

The President, the two Associate Judges and the Clerk shall sign this record.

If the convicted accused causes, upon the reading out of the judgment, a commotion, noise or disturbance, the President shall order his removal from the courtroom and proceed with the reading out of the judgment in his absence.

If what the convicted accused caused constitutes a criminal act in the nature of a misdemeanour, the President shall draw up a record thereof, and the Court shall examine the misdemeanour act and sentence him to the penalty for the offence forthwith. He may defend himself at his trial for the misdemeanour which he committed.

If the Court rules to acquit the accused or to discontinue the proceedings against him, it shall adjudge that he be released forthwith unless he is detained for another cause.

He may not thereafter be prosecuted for the same act even if it is given another classification.

If it appears to the Court, in the course of the trial, that the accused committed an offence not covered by the bill of indictment, it must rule to send him in detention, if the act is in the nature of a felony, to the Public Prosecution in order to prosecute him therefor and refer him to the competent judicial authority.

If the act is in the nature of a misdemeanour, it shall draw up a report thereon and refer it to the Public Prosecution.

If it appears to it that the person who committed the act attributed to the accused is another person, it shall decide, after adjudging the acquittal of the accused, to send the case file to the Public Prosecution in order to prosecute the suspect and refer him before the competent judicial authority.

The accused may claim, until the declaration of the close of the trial, compensation for his damage against the civil party for exceeding the bounds of good faith in his action, or for abusing the right to bring an action, or for committing a fault in exercising it.

The Criminal Court shall award him adequate compensation for his damage when it delivers a judgment declaring his acquittal or discontinuing the proceedings against him.

If the judgment declaring the acquittal of the accused is founded on the absence of evidence, or on the insufficiency thereof, or on doubt, the civil party may claim from him before the Criminal Court compensation for the damage caused by his fault and inferred from the acts set forth in the bill of indictment.

If he omits to claim compensation during the trial and up to its close, it shall remain open to him to claim it in accordance with the provisions of the preceding Article.

The decision on the time-limits shall be notified to the accused by publishing it and posting it for a period of ten days on the door of his last residence, in the square of his town, and on the door of the courtroom.

If he has no known domicile or residence in Lebanon, he shall be notified exceptionally by publishing the decision at the expense of the State in two local newspapers designated by the Court and in the Official Gazette, and it shall also be published by posting it on the door of the registry of the Criminal Court.

The fugitive accused shall not be entitled to be represented in the trial in absentia by a counsel on his behalf. However, such counsel may submit an excuse on behalf of his client after proving his mandate on his behalf. If the Court accepts the excuse, after verifying its validity, it shall adjourn the trial to another date.

If the accused does not surrender himself within twenty-four hours prior to the new date to the Court, the trial in absentia shall be resumed against him.

After the Court decides to try the accused in absentia, the President shall order the reading aloud of the indictment decision, the certificate of notification of the decision on the time-limits, and the record proving its publication and posting.

It shall then hear the statements of the civil party and the submissions of the representative of the Public Prosecution and shall close the trial.

The Court shall rule, after forming its conviction, either to acquit the accused or to convict him and impose the penalty upon him, and to confirm the placement of his immovable and movable property under the administration of the curator whom it appoints if he was not appointed during the trial, and it shall confirm therein its insistence on the execution of the arrest warrant against him.

The accused shall remain deprived of his civil rights from the date of the issuance of the judgment until the lapse of the penalty to which he is sentenced by prescription, or his surrender of himself, or his death.

The Public Prosecution shall undertake the publication of an abstract of the judgment in the Official Gazette and in one of the local daily newspapers within eight days from the date of its issuance. A copy thereof shall be posted on the door of the last residence of the accused, another in the square of his town, and a third on the door of the courtroom of the Criminal Court. This abstract shall also be notified to the Land Registry Registrar. The judgment shall become enforceable from the day following its publication in the Official Gazette.

For as long as the property of the absconding convicted person remains under the administration of the curator, his wife, his children, his parents, and those whom he is legally bound to support shall be entitled to submit a petition against the curator to the Judge of Urgent Matters whose seat is located within the jurisdiction of the Criminal Court that rendered the judgment, requesting therein a monthly maintenance allowance from his property, whereupon he shall issue a decision determining the amount of such maintenance allowance, taking into account the situation of each of the petitioners and the extent of his need therefor.

The civil claimant shall be entitled to obtain from the same Judge of Urgent Matters, against the curator, a decision granting him a provisional advance from the damages awarded to him. The decision shall be enforced through the Execution Department against the immovable and movable property of the convicted person.

If the court finds that the investigations are insufficient to convict the absconding accused, it shall delegate one of its members to conduct a supplementary investigation in accordance with the ordinary rules of procedure, which shall be joined to the case file, and it shall then render a judgment in the case.

If it becomes apparent to it that the evidence against him is insufficient, it shall rule to declare his acquittal, or to discontinue the prosecution against him if it deems that the act of which he was accused does not constitute an offence or does not warrant punishment, or to declare his non-liability if it ascertains that he benefits from a ground of justification.

It may also modify the legal characterization of the act that is the subject of the indictment decision, deem it a misdemeanour, adjudicate the action, and sentence him to a misdemeanour penalty.

A judgment convicting a fugitive accused of a felony shall not be subject to opposition or to challenge before the Court of Cassation.

If the Felony Court characterises the act set out in the indictment decision as a misdemeanour, the person sentenced in absentia shall be entitled to file an opposition against this judgment before it. The rules of procedure followed before the Misdemeanour Court of Appeal shall apply to this opposition.

If the Court rules to exempt the convicted person from punishment in a felony and orders him to pay personal compensation, he shall be entitled to file an opposition against the judgment in respect of the order to pay compensation within fifteen days from the date of being notified thereof.

If the civil action has not lapsed, for any of the reasons for its lapse, following the lapse of the public prosecution action in the felony by the ten-year statute of limitations, the person ordered to pay personal compensation shall be entitled to file an opposition against the judgment, as against the civil claimant, within a period of fifteen days from the date of being notified thereof.

In all cases where an opposition is filed against the amount of the personal compensation awarded, the Court must observe the bases for assessing compensation provided for in Articles 133 and 134 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts.

The civil part of the judgment in absentia shall become final after the completion of the procedures for notifying it in accordance with the provisions in force in the Code of Civil Procedure. The party awarded personal compensation shall obtain an enforceable copy in accordance with the rules governing the enforcement of civil judgments.

If the person sentenced in absentia is declared innocent in the felony judgment or the prosecution against him is annulled, he may have recourse against the enforcing party by way of an action for unjust enrichment.

If the fugitive convicted person surrenders himself or is arrested before the penalty imposed lapses by the statute of limitations, the Court shall decide to declare the lapse of the judgment in absentia issued against him and of all the measures it conducted as from the date the case was brought before it.

It shall also decide to try the accused in accordance with the ordinary rules of procedure provided for in Articles 236 et seq. of this Law.

The judgment in the action shall be issued in accordance with these rules of procedure.

If it is impossible to hear certain witnesses before the Court, their statements in the preliminary or initial investigation shall suffice after being read out publicly and submitted for adversarial debate.
The decision of one of the accused may not be a ground for adjourning the trial or delaying the examination of the action in respect of the remaining accused.
If the fugitive convicted accused is arrested and denies his identity, the Felony Court that issued the judgment against him shall undertake the verification of his identity.

If the penalty stated in the contested judgment is that prescribed by the law for the offence, the convicted person may not request its cassation on the ground of an error occurring in the citation of the applied legal article.
The civil claimant may challenge the personal damages awarded by the judgment that are less than what he requested.

With the exception of the case where the judgment is issued by a bench not constituted in accordance with the law and decisions relating to jurisdiction, to the lapse of the public right of action by prescription or by general amnesty, or to the bar to prosecution due to res judicata, cassation in misdemeanour cases shall only be admissible for one of the grounds provided for in Article 296 of this Law, subject to the existence of a difference in the legal characterisation of the act between the judges of the first instance and the judges of the second instance.

Subject to the provisions of the preceding Article, the Public Prosecution alone may request the cassation of decisions issued by the Court of Appeal in contraventions with respect to the legal characterisation given to them if it considers that they have the characterisation of a misdemeanour.
A person who challenges an appellate decision shall not be entitled to raise grounds that fall outside the content of this decision or outside the scope of the trial that led to its issuance.
The Court of Cassation may not decide to stay the execution of a decision imposing a misdemeanour or contravention penalty unless it quashes it.

With the exception of decisions issued by a bench not constituted in accordance with the law and decisions relating to jurisdiction, to the lapse of the public right of action by prescription or by general amnesty, or to the bar to prosecution by virtue of the authority of res judicata, final decisions of the Indictment Chamber shall not be subject to cassation unless the condition of a difference in the legal characterisation of the act between the Investigating Judge and the Indictment Chamber is met, and for one of the following grounds:

1 - Violation of the law or error in its interpretation or in its application.

2 - Omission of procedures prescribed under penalty of nullity or breach of fundamental rules in the investigation.

3 - Distortion of the facts or of the clear content of the documents produced in the case file.

4 - Failure to rule on a plea or a ground of defence or on a request submitted by one of the parties to the action.

5 - Lack of legal basis or insufficiency of reasoning.

Without being restricted by the grounds for cassation stated in the preceding Article, it shall be permissible:

أ - For the civil claimant to challenge the indictment decision ruling his civil action inadmissible on the ground of his lack of standing to bring the action.

ب - For both the civil claimant and the Public Prosecution to challenge decisions ruling to bar the trial of the defendant.
An accused who is a fugitive from justice shall not have the right to appeal against the decision of indictment before the Court of Cassation unless he surrenders himself.

If the Court of Cassation dismisses the petition for cassation, it shall order the forfeiture of the security deposit, and it may order the petitioner to pay a fine ranging between one hundred thousand and five hundred thousand pounds if it appears to it that he abused his right to litigate.
When the decision of indictment becomes final and irrevocable and orders the referral of the accused to the Criminal Court, it vests it with jurisdiction.

In all cases, it shall not be permissible to petition for the cassation of preparatory decisions or decisions preceding the final decision or judgment except after its issuance and together with it. Excluded from this are decisions or judgments that rule on one or more of the defences provided for in Article 73 of this Law.

The Criminal Court of Cassation must verify whether the impugned decision or judgment contains anything that would stay the course of the investigation or trial and take a decision thereon.

No person who was not a party to an action shall have the right to petition for the cassation of the judgment or decision rendered therein. The petitioner in cassation must have standing and interest in his petition, under penalty of its inadmissibility.

The right to petition for cassation belongs to the Public Prosecution at the Court of Cassation, the Appellate Public Prosecution, the Financial Public Prosecution, the civil party, the convicted person, the person civilly liable, and the guarantor.

The appeal of the Public Prosecution must be directed at the part of the judgment relating to the public action, the appeal of the convicted person must cover the penalty, personal damages, and costs ordered against him by the judgment, and the appeal of the civil party must be confined to the part of the judgment relating to the civil action. Each of the person civilly liable and the guarantor may appeal against the judgment or decision that ordered him to pay personal damages.

If one of the convicted persons petitions for the cassation of the judgment or decision to the exclusion of the other parties, the Court of Cassation shall not be permitted to increase the penalty to which he was sentenced or the damages awarded against him.
Each party to the action may confine his appeal to one part of the judgment or decision that is independent of its other parts.

The Court of Cassation shall hear the following:

a - Applications for cassation of judgments rendered by the Criminal Courts and decisions rendered by the Criminal Courts of Appeal and by the Indictment Chamber.

b - Other applications for cassation falling within its jurisdiction pursuant to special laws.

c - Applications for retrial in criminal actions.

d - Applications for the designation of the competent court.

e- Applications for the transfer of the action.

f- Offences committed by judges.

Judgments rendered by the Criminal Courts shall be subject to cassation on one of the following grounds:

a - The judgment was rendered by a bench that was not constituted in accordance with the provisions of the law.

b - Violation of the law or error in its interpretation or in its application.

c - Violation of the rules of jurisdiction.

d - Omission of formalities prescribed under pain of nullity or breach of essential rules in the trial.

e - Ruling on a criminal act not covered by the indictment decision or against a person not indicted therein.

f- Failure to rule on a plea, a ground of defence, or a claim submitted by one of the parties to the action, or ruling beyond what was claimed.

g- Failure to state the reasons for the judgment, contradiction between its reasoning and the operative part, or contradiction within the operative part itself.

h - Distortion of the facts or of the clear content of the documents produced in the case file.

i - Lack of legal basis.

j - Judgments imposing the death penalty.
No party to the action shall be entitled to challenge the judgment on the ground of violation of a legal rule established for the benefit of another.

Both the Public Prosecution and the convicted person may apply for the quashing of the judgment on one or more of the grounds for cassation set forth in Article 296 of this Law. If it is quashed upon the application of either of them, the public action shall devolve before the Court of Cassation, which shall follow at trial the procedure applicable before the Criminal Court and proceed to determine the action.

The effect of an application for cassation submitted by the civil party shall be confined to the civil aspect of the contested judgment or decision.

If the contested judgment orders the acquittal of the accused, the dismissal of prosecutions against him, or his lack of responsibility, he shall not be tried in custody before the Court of Cassation unless it decides to remand him in custody by a reasoned decision.

Provided that the provisions of Article 108 of this Law are observed.

If the contested judgment orders the conviction for a felony or for a misdemeanour of the accused, and the Public Prosecution applies for the quashing of the judgment, he shall be tried in custody, subject to the provisions of Article 108 of this Law.

An application for cassation from a person sentenced to a felony penalty shall be admissible if he is in custody or has served the sentence imposed.

The Court of Cassation may not release a convicted person who is in custody before it quashes the contested judgment.

Each of the convicted person, the civil claimant, the person civilly liable and the guarantor may request the cassation of the adversarial judgment rendered by the Criminal Court and the adversarial decision rendered by the Misdemeanour Court of Appeal within fifteen days from the date of its issuance.

Each of the Financial or Appellate Public Prosecution may request the cassation of either the adversarial judgment or decision within a time limit of one month from the date of its issuance.

The Cassation Public Prosecution may request its cassation within a time limit of two months from the date of its issuance. A judgment in absentia rendered against an accused who is a fugitive from justice shall not be subject to cassation.

Each of the parties to the action shall have the right to request the cassation of the decision rendered by the Misdemeanour Court of Appeal as a result of an opposition within the time limits specified in the first and second paragraphs of this Article.

The time limit shall run against each of the convicted person, the civil claimant, the person civilly liable and the guarantor from the date of service upon him of the judgment rendered as a result of the opposition if it was not adversarial.

It shall run against each of the Appellate Public Prosecution and the Cassation Public Prosecution from the date of its issuance.

The application for cassation shall be submitted to the registry of the Court of Cassation or to the registry of the court that rendered the impugned judgment. If it is submitted to the latter, it must refer it and the case file to the Public Prosecution attached to it within five days at most from the date of its submission, and the latter shall immediately transmit it to the Cassation Public Prosecution for referral to the Court of Cassation.

If the application for cassation is submitted directly to the Court of Cassation, it shall request that the file be transmitted to it through the Cassation Public Prosecution.

Subject to the time limit provided for in Article 316 of this Law, the application for cassation must, under penalty of its dismissal in form, satisfy the following conditions jointly:

a - It shall include the names of the litigants, the name of the court that rendered the judgment, the judgment sought to be quashed and the grounds for cassation.

b - It shall be signed by an attorney at the Court of Appeal and have attached to it his power of attorney or a certified copy thereof, a certified copy of the judgment or decision sought to be appealed in cassation exempted from the proportional fee, and a receipt for the deposit with the Treasury Fund of a security in the amount of two hundred thousand pounds.

The Public Prosecution shall be exempted from producing a copy of the impugned judgment with its petition and from paying the security fee and judicial fees.

The applicant for cassation may submit, within five days from the expiry of the time limit for cassation, a brief detailing the grounds of cassation which he has raised. He shall not be entitled to include new grounds therein.

The petitioner for cassation shall be deemed to have elected domicile at the office of his counsel. Any service effected at that office shall produce its legal effects if the formal procedural requirements are observed therein. The application for cassation shall be registered in a special register.

Each party to the action may inspect it and obtain a certified true copy thereof.

The security deposit shall be refunded to the applicant if his application is accepted or if he withdraws it before a decision is rendered thereon, and shall be forfeited to the Treasury if it is decided to dismiss the application for cassation.

The convicted person or the civil party shall be exempted from the security deposit fee in felony cases.

He shall also be exempted therefrom in misdemeanour cases if he submits a certificate of indigence.

The Public Prosecution shall be exempted from paying all fees and expenses for submitting an application for cassation.

The respondent in cassation must be served with a copy of the application and its annexes and a copy of the explanatory brief within three days from the date of submission of each of them, and he may submit his observations and requests within a time limit of ten days from the date of service upon him.

The Court shall examine the application for cassation and the case file. If it finds that the application has been submitted within the statutory time limit and satisfies all other formal requirements, it shall admit it in form. It shall then examine the grounds of appeal set forth therein.

If the contested decision is quashed, it shall decide to retry the case in a public hearing in order to examine the action and rule on the merits thereof.

The rules of procedure applicable before the court that rendered the contested judgment shall be followed at the trial.

It shall render its decision in the action.

If it dismisses the appeal, it shall rule to uphold the contested judgment or decision, to forfeit the amount of the security deposit, and to order the applicant to pay a fine ranging between two hundred thousand and one million pounds if it appears to the Court that he abused his right to litigate.

If the civil party submits the application for cassation alone, this shall result in bringing the civil action alone before the Court.

The Court of Cassation may not reduce the damages awarded.

If the application for cassation is submitted by one of the persons convicted of the same offence, and the Court of Cassation admits his appeal in form and on the merits, and holds that the elements of the offence in the act adjudicated by the contested judgment are not satisfied, the remaining convicted persons shall benefit from the effect of the quashed judgment. In such case, the Public Prosecution at the Court of Cassation shall recall the extract of the judgment issued against each of them.
After quashing the contested judgment or decision, the Court of Cassation shall apply the provisions of Articles 276 and 277 of this Law where the cases provided for in either of them are met.

If the Court of Cassation rules to dismiss the petition for cassation in form or on the merits, the clerk of the court shall draw up an abstract of this decision, which the President of the Court shall sign and refer, within three days from the date of its issuance, to the Public Prosecution at the Court of Cassation, which shall lodge it with the Appellate Public Prosecution at the court that issued the contested judgment for its execution.

Subject to the provisions relating to retrial or those set forth in Articles 741 et seq. of the Code of Civil Procedure, the decisions of the Court of Cassation shall not be subject to any avenue of recourse.

If a judgment is issued by the Criminal Court or a decision is issued by the Court of Appeal and each of them has become final due to the expiry of the time limit for cassation, the Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation may, either of his own motion or at the request of the Minister of Justice, request that it be quashed in the interest of the law only, within a time limit of one year from its issuance.

If the Court of Cassation rules to annul the contested judgment or decision, the convicted person shall benefit from this annulment without being prejudiced by it.

The judgment shall remain standing in all cases in favour of the civil party.

The Court of Cassation is the competent authority to hear applications for retrial.

- An application for retrial may be made, in felony and misdemeanour cases, regardless of the court that adjudicated them and the penalty it imposed, in the following cases:

a - If a person is convicted of a crime of homicide and sufficient evidence subsequently appears that the person alleged to have been killed is still alive.

b - If a person is convicted of a felony or of a misdemeanour and another person is subsequently convicted of the same offence and in the same capacity, provided that there results therefrom evidence of the innocence of one of the two convicted persons.

c - If a person is convicted on the basis of the testimony of another person which is subsequently proven by a final judgment to be false.

d - If there occurs or appears after the judgment a new act or documents that were unknown during the trial and which are of a nature to constitute evidence of the innocence of the convicted person.

The lapse of the imposed penalty by prescription shall not preclude the hearing of the application for retrial.

- The convicted person shall submit the application for retrial to the Criminal Chamber at the Court of Cassation or to the Judicial Council, each according to its jurisdiction, through the Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation, within one year starting from the day on which he became aware of the ground requiring the retrial, under penalty of dismissal of the application.

- It may be submitted by his legal representative if he lacks capacity or if his absence is established by a judicial judgment, or by one of his heirs or one of the legatees in the event of his death.

- There must be attached to the application a certified true copy, exempt from fees, of the judgment against which retrial is sought and of the evidence upon which he relies, a copy of the power of attorney of the lawyer who signed the application, and a financial receipt for the payment of a security deposit in the amount of two hundred thousand pounds.

- The Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation shall refer the application to the competent Criminal Chamber at the Court of Cassation or to the Judicial Council, accompanied by his submissions, within a period of one week.

When the Court of Cassation admits the application for retrial in form, it shall examine the merits of the case.

It may conduct an additional investigation where necessary.

If the court examining the application for retrial annuls the contested judgment in respect of one of the living convicted persons due to the cessation of the criminal character of the act for which he was convicted or because the convicted person is exempt from punishment, it shall suffice with such annulment.

If the annulment is based on the cessation of the criminal character of the act, the remaining convicted persons shall benefit therefrom.

If the application for retrial is submitted after the death of the convicted person or his loss of capacity, through one of the persons mentioned in Article 329 of this Law, the court shall examine the application.

If it rules to annul the contested judgment and to declare the acquittal of the convicted person or to annul the prosecutions against him, it shall order the publication of its judgment on the notice board of the court, in the place where the offence occurred, in the place of residence of the convicted person, in the Official Gazette, and in two local daily newspapers.

The State shall bear the publication expenses.

If the acquittal of the convicted person or the annulment of the prosecutions against him is ruled, the judgment shall have retroactive effect whereby all effects of the previous judgment shall be cancelled, save for rights acquired in good faith.

The court may rule, upon the request of the applicant for retrial, to compensate him for the damage sustained by him from the previous judgment.

If the convicted person dies, the right to claim compensation shall pass to his heirs or legatees.

The court shall assess the compensation in accordance with the rules provided for in the Code of Obligations and Contracts.

The State shall bear the awarded compensation. It may have recourse in respect thereof against anyone who caused the issuance of the previous judgment.

The applicant for reconsideration shall advance the costs of the action until a decision is rendered on his application.

Subsequent costs, however, shall be paid by the State.

The Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation shall undertake the task of designating the competent authority in the event of a conflict of jurisdiction between judicial authorities.

Where an offence is committed and two investigating magistrates initiate an investigation therein or two courts commence hearing it after each of the two authorities has deemed itself competent to hear it, or where each of the two investigating magistrates or the two courts decides that it lacks jurisdiction to hear it, or where a court decides that it lacks jurisdiction to hear an action referred to it pursuant to a decision issued by the Investigating Magistrate or the Indictment Chamber, and the conflict over jurisdiction results in a stay of the course of justice owing to the two contradictory decisions having become final in the very same case, this conflict shall be resolved by way of designating the competent authority.

The provisions of this Article shall apply where a conflict arises between an ordinary court and an exceptional court.

Each of the Public Prosecution, the civil party and the defendant may apply for the designation of the authority pursuant to a petition submitted to the Court of Cassation, which shall request the Public Prosecution to lodge with it copies of the documents pertaining to the action before the two judicial authorities between which the conflict has arisen.

A copy of the application for the designation of the authority must be served upon each of the parties to the action, and each of them may reply thereto within ten days from its service upon him.

When the two judicial authorities between which the conflict has arisen are served with the application for the designation of the authority, they shall stay the issuance of a final decision in the action.

Provisional measures and investigations, however, may be pursued until the issuance of the decision designating the competent authority.

The Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation shall examine the application for the designation of the authority after the return of the expiry of the ten-day time limit.

It shall take a decision in the deliberation room designating the competent judicial authority within a time limit not exceeding one month.

It may at the same time annul the proceedings and acts carried out by the judicial authority that has been divested of the action. Its decision shall not be subject to any avenue of recourse. The two judicial authorities between which the conflict has arisen shall be bound to comply with the decision.

Where the civil party or the defendant is not justified in his application, he shall be fined an amount ranging between two hundred thousand and one million Pounds and ordered to pay compensation to his opponent if the latter so requests.

One of the Criminal Chambers of the Court of Cassation shall undertake the task of adjudicating a request to transfer the action from one judicial authority to another judicial authority.

It shall decide to divest a judicial authority, in investigation or judgment, of the action and refer it to another authority of the same degree to continue examining it, either due to the impossibility of constituting the originally competent authority, or due to the interruption of the course of the investigation or trial, or for the preservation of public safety, or out of concern for the proper administration of justice, or on grounds of legitimate suspicion.

The Public Prosecutor before the Court of Cassation alone may request the transfer of the action for the preservation of public safety if the judicial authority sought to be divested of the action is one of the Criminal Chambers of Cassation, in which case the Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation shall adjudicate the request.

The Public Prosecutor before the Court of Cassation may petition for the transfer of the action proprio motu or upon the request of the Appellate Public Prosecutor, the Financial Public Prosecutor, the civil party, the defendant, or the Minister of Justice on the grounds set forth in the first paragraph.

The transfer request must be notified to all parties to the action. Each of them may reply to it within ten days from its notification thereof.

The filing of the petition shall not stay the course of the action unless the Court of Cassation decides otherwise.

If two investigating judges within the same jurisdiction are seized of connected offences, the First Investigating Judge may designate one of them to continue the course of the investigation.

If the two investigating judges belong to two different jurisdictions, the competent Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation shall appoint, upon the request of the Public Prosecutor before the Court of Cassation, the investigating judge who shall continue examining the action.

Every decision issued by the Court of Cassation transferring the action shall be notified through the Public Prosecution before the Court of Cassation to the parties to the action.

Its decision shall not be subject to any avenue of recourse.

If the Court of Cassation rules to dismiss the request, its decision shall not preclude the filing of another request on a ground relating to facts that emerged on a date subsequent to the first request.

If the civil party or the defendant files a request to transfer the action, and the Court of Cassation rules to dismiss it, it may order the applicant to pay a fine ranging between two hundred thousand and one million pounds and award compensation to the adversary if requested.

In all these cases, the decision of the Court of Cassation shall not be subject to any avenue of recourse.
The Court of Cassation shall have jurisdiction to examine offences committed by judges, whether outside their functions or arising therefrom or on the occasion thereof.

The investigations shall be submitted to a panel composed of three judges of at least the grade of the defendant judge.

They shall be appointed by the Supreme Judicial Council.

The panel shall be presided over by the judge of the highest grade or by whomever the First President of the Court of Cassation designates to preside over it.

The panel shall assume the functions of the Indictment Chamber. In its decision, it shall refer the accused judge to one of the Criminal Chambers of the Court of Cassation if he is among the judges mentioned in Article 345 of this Law, and to the Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation if he is among the judges mentioned in Article 346 of this Law.

If the panel finds that the evidence is insufficient for indictment or that the criminal elements are not satisfied, it shall decide to bar the trial of the defendant judge.

All decisions issued by the panel shall not be subject to any form of recourse.

In offences of judges arising out of their functions, the provisions of Articles 344 to 350 inclusive of this Law shall apply.

All of these provisions shall apply to the judges of the State Council, the judges of the Court of Accounts, and retired judges in an honorary position.

A person harmed by a criminal act attributed to a judge may claim compensation therefor ancillary to the public action. He shall not have the right to bring a direct claim whereby he initiates the public right action.

If the criminal act committed does not arise out of the function or on the occasion thereof, the claim for compensation shall be brought against the defendant judge.

If, however, it arises out of the function or on the occasion thereof, the harmed person may bring his action against the State and the judge or against either of them.

If the judge who is a defendant in a misdemeanour or a felony, whether arising out of the function or outside it, has a co-perpetrator, accomplice, instigator or harbourer, the prosecution, investigation and trial shall encompass both of them.

If the investigation does not succeed in ascertaining the identity of the co-perpetrator, accomplice, instigator or harbourer, or if his prosecution proves impossible or is delayed, that shall not affect the prosecution of the judge and the hearing of his case.

If one of the judges of the Courts of First Instance, or one of the investigating judges, or one of the Advocates General before the Appellate, Financial, or Military Public Prosecution, or one of the counsellors of the Courts of Appeal, or one of the counsellors of the Administrative Courts or the Court of Audit, or one of the assistant counsellors before the State Council commits, outside his duties, a criminal act of the nature of a misdemeanour, the Public Prosecution before the Court of Cassation shall prosecute him ex officio or upon the complaint of the injured party.

The action shall be brought before the Criminal Chamber of the Court of Cassation.

If the misdemeanour is attributed to one of the Presidents of the Chambers of Appeal, or to the Public Prosecutor before the Court of Appeal, or the Financial Public Prosecutor, or the Government Commissioner, or to one of the judges of the Court of Cassation or one of the members of the Public Prosecution before it, or to the First Investigating Judge, the Public Prosecution before the Court of Cassation shall prosecute him, ex officio or upon the complaint of the injured party, and the action shall be brought before the Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation.

If the act attributed to the judge, whatever his rank, is of the nature of a felony, the First President of the Court of Cassation shall appoint a judge of at least the rank of the defendant to conduct the investigation with him. The Public Prosecutor before the Court of Cassation shall assume the function of public prosecution and the exercise of the public action.

If the matter requires the detention of the judge charged with a felony, the judge assigned to conduct the investigation with him shall issue the warrant of detention against him.

However, it shall not be enforceable except after the approval of the First President of the Court of Cassation thereon.

The detention of the judge shall take place in a special location determined by the Public General Prosecutor before the Court of Cassation.

The judge entrusted with the investigation must seek the opinion of the Public Prosecutor before the Court of Cassation in all cases in which the law requires the investigating judge to seek the opinion of the Appellate Public Prosecution. The judge assigned to the investigation may substitute for the detention of the defendant judge supervision measures capable of restricting his freedom of movement or travel.

If he breaches any of them, or if the investigator finds that they are unavailing, he shall issue a warrant for his detention in accordance with the provisions of Article 348 of this Law.

The judge entrusted with the investigation shall apply the procedures followed before the investigating judge in felony cases.
