Immediately upon the issuance of the decree establishing the institution, the provisions resulting from the effect of the approved alignment plan or the declaration of public utility shall apply to the entire area subject to the master plan.

B - Subject to the exceptions set forth in paragraph C below of this Article, registered certificates representing the value of the rights accruing to each of them, determined as a sum of money or an area or both, shall be delivered to the owners, tenants, and operators of the real properties located within the scope of the public institution. These certificates shall be transferable after the expiry of one year from their delivery to their holders, except where there exist real rights, other than agreements, over the real property subject to acquisition or the commercial establishment situated thereon, in which case the transfer shall only be valid with the express approval of the holders of these rights to the transfer.

In this case, the right of pre-emption in respect of certificates representing the value of real properties that were held in co-ownership, and the right of priority provided for in Article ten of Legislative Decree No. 11 dated 11/7/1967 in respect of certificates representing the value of commercial establishments, shall remain reserved. The provisions of the legislation relating to the acquisition of real property ownership by non-Lebanese shall apply to the transfer of certificates representing the rights of owners.

C - By way of exception to paragraph B above, the public institution may, by a decree adopted in the Council of Ministers, be granted the right to pay in cash the rights accruing to the following categories of tenants and operators:

1- Tenants and operators the nature of whose commercial business is not consistent with the designated use prescribed in the planning scheme laid down for the area in which their leased premises are situated.

2 - Tenants and operators whose rights do not exceed a specific amount determined by the said decree.

In all these cases, the institution shall be subrogated to the holders of the rights in all of their rights.

D - The public institution shall settle the rights of the owners after the rearrangement of the area by transferring ownership to each owner of a real property or shares in a real property, built or unbuilt, the value of which is equivalent to the value of his rights represented by the certificate delivered to him, after deducting this owner's share of the portion accruing to the Administration free of charge pursuant to paragraph A above of this Article. The owner shall have the option between:

1- Obtaining an unbuilt real property or shares in an unbuilt real property, in which case he shall be required to undertake, alone or jointly with neighbouring owners, construction on the real property licensed to him within the time limits and conditions determined by the construction programme and the book of specifications prepared by the public institution.

2- Obtaining co-ownership rights in a built real property, in which case the public institution shall undertake construction directly or through third parties in accordance with the conditions it deems appropriate.

E - The rights of tenants and operators of premises intended for lease located within the scope of the public institution shall be settled by delivering to each of them, after the rearrangement and reconstruction of the area, new leased premises equivalent in nature and value to the leased premises which he occupied and in the nearest possible location to such leased premises, without this entailing the payment of any additional key money.

The rent of the new leased premises shall be determined by agreement between the owner and the tenant, and in the absence of agreement, the owner shall have the right to request the competent court to determine the fair rent without being bound by any maximum limit.

The public institution shall determine the procedures for executing the transactions of redistributing the real properties and the premises intended for lease among the various holders of rights, and shall also determine, where necessary, the manner of achieving balance between the rights of each of them and the real properties or premises allocated to them.

G- Rights of pledge, mortgage, privilege, and attachment encumbering the real property or the commercial establishment situated within the scope of the public institution shall be struck off upon the transfer of ownership of the real property to this institution, and these rights shall be transferred, with the same prior rank that each of them had, to the certificate referred to in paragraph B of item - "Second" of this Article of this Legislative Decree, and thereafter, where necessary, to the real property or the leased premises allocated to the owner or tenant after the rearrangement of the area.

Built or unbuilt lands covered by subdivision may neither be sold nor leased, nor may buildings be erected, except after obtaining the subdivision permit, executing the provisions imposed upon the subdivider pursuant to the decision of the said permit, and obtaining the certificate of conformity.

In the event that the execution of works in stages is permitted, the sale, lease, or erection of buildings may take place in the arranged parts of the subdivision, if the permit decision provides for that.

The conformity of the subdivision with the provisions in force shall be established by a certificate issued by the departments and sections of the Directorate General of Urban Planning or by the technical departments in each of the municipalities of Beirut and Tripoli, after the execution of the subdivision project and its installations on the ground and prior to final registration at the Land Registry Secretariat.

The subdivision permit shall be issued by the Directorate General of Urban Planning, or by the departments and sections affiliated thereto in the centres of the Governorates and Districts, or by the technical departments in the municipalities of Beirut and Tripoli.

When the Directorate General of Urban Planning or the technical departments in the municipalities of Beirut and Tripoli consider that the subdivision application in unplanned areas must be rejected because the subdivision project is located in an area far from residential places, or in a wooded area, or in an area of distinctive natural scenery, or that the granting of the permit must be made conditional upon the execution of arrangements or works differing by their nature or by their importance from ordinary arrangements and works, the matter shall be decided after consulting the Higher Council of Urban Planning.

If the building is subdivided into different rights (apartments and floors), each subdivided apartment bearing a special number and owned by a natural or legal person independent of the others shall be considered as an independent real property, with respect to the Building Law.

When a subdivision permit application is rejected, or the permit is granted on condition of complying with provisions which the owner of the subdivision considers unlawful, excessive, or inappropriate, he may refer the matter within a period of three months starting from the date of his notification of the decision to the Minister of Public Works and Transport, and this shall not preclude the judicial recourses to which he may resort.

The Minister shall decide on the matter after seeking the opinion of the Higher Council of Urban Planning.

All works executed contrary to the provisions of the enforced plans and regulations must be demolished or brought by the offender into conformity with the provisions of the law following a formal notice specifying the time limit for execution addressed to the offender by the Head of the Executive Authority in the municipality, or the Governor, or the District Commissioner where there is no municipality; if the offender does not comply by the end of the time limit, the works necessary to remove the violation shall be executed ex officio at his expense and under his responsibility.

The amount due shall be determined by the authority that addressed the formal notice and shall be collected by the tax departments at the Ministry of Finance in accordance with the rules followed in the collection of taxes and fees.

The offender shall in addition be punished by a fine ranging from 5000 to 50000 Lebanese pounds and by imprisonment from one day to 15 days, or by either of these two penalties.

Every person who carries out a subdivision without obtaining the permit required by this Legislative Decree, or every person who executes a subdivision without complying with the special provisions required by the subdivision permit, shall be punished by a fine from 5000 to 50000 and by imprisonment from one day to 15 days, or by either of these two penalties.

The violations mentioned in Articles 36 and 37 of this Legislative Decree shall be recorded by the officials and persons authorised to record violations within the municipality concerned, or by the members of the Internal Security Forces authorised to do so.

Every person who carries out, at the request of the Administration and for its account, urban planning studies, shall be considered bound by professional secrecy, and shall be subject, in the event of violating these provisions, to prosecution in accordance with the Penal Code.

If the texts regulating real estate affairs contain conditions special to land use, such as consolidation, subdivision, construction and exploitation, that are stricter than the conditions specified in the Building Law and in the zoning regulations, the conditions set out in the texts regulating real estate affairs shall apply.

The owner of a real property or a group of real properties may impose conditions for land use, consolidation, subdivision, construction and exploitation that are stricter than what is specified in the Building Law and in the zoning regulations in order to secure better harmony for the building complex and to improve its quality and architectural forms.

These conditions shall be registered at the request of the owner in the Land Register after their approval by the Director General of Urban Planning, and he may not revoke them after their registration.

With a view to facilitating urban arrangement, municipalities may be granted loans and aid from the State budget, within the limits of the appropriations allocated for this purpose in the budget.

The amounts and methods of allocation of these loans and aid shall be determined by a decree taken in the Council of Ministers upon the proposal of the Minister of Public Works and Transport.

All provisions contrary to this Legislative Decree are hereby repealed, including the Urban Planning Law promulgated on 24 September 1962 and its amendments, with the exception of those relating to the establishment of the Directorate General of Urban Planning.

Plans, regulations and measures adopted pursuant to the provisions referred to in this Article shall remain in force so long as they have not been repealed or amended in accordance with the provisions of this Legislative Decree.

The details of application of this Legislative Decree shall be determined - where necessary - by decrees adopted in the Council of Ministers upon the proposal of the Minister of Public Works and Transport.
This Legislative Decree shall enter into force immediately upon its publication in the Official Gazette.
The Code of Civil Procedure is promulgated and placed into execution in the text annexed to this Legislative Decree.
This Legislative Decree shall be published in the Official Gazette and shall take effect in accordance with Article 1033 of the text annexed hereto.

The judiciary is an independent authority in relation to the other authorities in the investigation and adjudication of actions; its independence shall not be restricted by any limitation not provided for by the Constitution.

The courts must abide by the principle of the hierarchy of norms. In the event of conflict between the provisions of international treaties and the provisions of ordinary law, the former shall take precedence over the latter in the sphere of application. The courts may not declare the nullity of the acts of the legislative authority on the ground of the non-conformity of ordinary laws with the Constitution or international treaties.
A judge may not cast his judgments in the form of regulations.

A judge may not, under penalty of being deemed to have committed a denial of justice:

1- Refrain from giving judgment on the pretext of the ambiguity or absence of the text.

2- Delay without cause the issuance of judgment.

In the event of ambiguity of the text, the judge shall interpret it in the sense that gives it an effect consistent with its purpose and ensures harmony between it and the other texts.

In the event of absence of the text, the judge shall rely on general principles, custom and equity.

New laws of procedure shall apply immediately to such actions as have not been adjudicated or such procedural acts as have not been completed prior to the date of their entry into force. Excluded therefrom are:

1- Laws modifying jurisdiction where the date of their entry into force is subsequent to the closing of the trial in the action or to the issuance of a judgment adjudicating a question relating to the merits.

2- Laws modifying time limits where the time limit had commenced to run prior to their entry into force.

3- Laws governing means of recourse in respect of judgments or arbitral awards issued prior to the date of their entry into force where such laws abolish or establish one of those means.

4- Laws governing compulsory execution in respect of judgments and decisions issued prior to the date of their entry into force where such laws permit or prohibit execution.
The general rules in the Code of Civil Procedure shall be followed if there is a deficiency in the other procedural laws and rules.

An action is the right vested in every person having a claim to submit it to the judiciary for judgment to be rendered in his favour on the subject-matter thereof. With respect to the adversary, it is the right to put forward grounds of defence or pleas aimed at refuting that claim, and the right to bring an action and the right of defence shall belong to every Lebanese or foreign natural or legal person.
The Public Prosecution shall have the right to bring an action in the cases specified by law, and in cases relating to public order upon the occurrence of facts or acts capable of prejudicing it.

Actions shall be available to every person having an existing legal interest, or to any person who aims thereby to establish a right the existence of which has been denied, or to take precautions to avert an imminent or future harm, or to ascertain a right where the loss of the proof thereof is feared when it is disputed, with the exception of the cases in which the law restricts to persons whose standing it defines the right to submit a claim, to refute it, or to defend a specific interest. No claim, plea, or defence issued by or against a person having no standing shall be admissible.

The right to bring an action and the right of defence are restricted by the proper exercise thereof; thus, any claim, defence, or plea- is pleaded put forward abusively shall be dismissed and shall render the person who submitted it liable to pay compensation for the damage caused thereby.
The abusive litigant shall be sentenced to a fine of forty thousand pounds at least and two million pounds at most, which the court shall order of its own motion.

Capacity to litigate shall be governed by the law of the State of the litigant. The law of the State of persons lacking capacity, of persons of diminished capacity, or of missing persons shall govern with respect to the supervision over them and their representation.

The court shall, at every stage of the proceedings, verify the capacity to litigate and the validity of the representation of persons lacking capacity, of persons of diminished capacity, or of missing persons.

If the personal status law to which one of the litigants is subject requires the representative of persons lacking capacity, of persons of diminished capacity, or of missing persons to obtain authorisation from the judiciary to litigate, the court before which the action must be brought may grant him such authorisation, and it shall remain valid throughout all stages of the proceedings and enforcement.

If the action is brought against an legally incapacitated person or a person of diminished capacity or against a missing person who has no legal representative, or if it is brought against a litigant who turns out to be deceased or who died during the proceedings and it proved impossible to ascertain his heirs, the court seized of the action may carry out the notifications by way of publication in the Official Gazette and in two local daily newspapers designated by it.

After the lapse of two months from the last publication, the court shall appoint a special representative to stand in the place of the legal representative or the heirs if no legal representative appears on behalf of the heirs or on behalf of the legally incapacitated person or the missing person; the special representative shall retain this capacity throughout all stages of the proceedings and before the execution departments until a legal representative is appointed or the heirs are ascertained.

The special representative shall not be entitled to make an admission, waive, forfeit, conclude a settlement, or acquiesce.

The fees of the special representative shall be fixed by a decision of the court that appointed him and shall be considered part of the costs of the action.

The nature of an action is determined with regard to the right that it protects; it is personal if the right is personal, in rem if it is in rem, and mixed if its subject matter encompasses both rights together or if it aims at executing a contract based on a right in rem or cancelling, rescinding, or annulling this contract. As for actions that do not fall within the categories referred to in the first paragraph, particularly those relating to non-pecuniary rights, they shall be deemed to have the status of personal actions.

Actions are movable if the subject matter of the right that they aim to protect is movable, and they are immovable when they relate to a right in rem over immovable property or to the possession thereof.
Immovable actions in rem are divided, according to the purpose intended thereby, into petitory actions and possessory actions.
The classification of actions is subject to the provisions of Lebanese law.

Possessory actions are of two types:

1- The action to prevent disturbance, which aims at preventing infringement upon possession.

2- The action for recovery of possession, which aims at the recovery by the possessor of possession that was usurped from him by force.

It is required for the action to prevent disturbance:

1- That the plaintiff be in possession, by himself or through his predecessor in title, of a principal immovable right in rem, by way of a peaceful, public, unambiguous, and continuous possession for at least one year prior to the disturbance. Possession shall not be deemed to have ceased if the exercise of actual control over the right was prevented by a temporary impediment arising from force majeure.

2- That a disturbance to the plaintiff in his possession has occurred through an act liable to restrict his exercise of that possession, whether this act was completed or was commenced through works leading to the disturbance of his possession, and whether these works took place on immovable property that is in the possession of the plaintiff or took place on immovable property belonging to a third party and were liable to cause damage to that immovable property.

An action for recovery of possession requires:

1- That the plaintiff be in material possession of a principal real right in immovable property fulfilling the conditions prescribed for it in the first paragraph of the preceding Article, with the exception of the condition that it have continued for a period of at least one year prior to the dispossession.

2- That the plaintiff's possession have been taken from him so that he was deprived of the enjoyment thereof.

A possessory action of either kind shall also be admissible from a precarious possessor such as a depositary, a pledgee, a lessee, a sharecropper and a concessionaire in the public domain of the State, with the exception of the case in which the action is brought against the person from whom the precarious possessor derived his rights.

A possessory action shall only be admissible within one year from the date of the occurrence of the interference or usurpation unless it remained clandestine or its cause was tainted with ambiguity or equivocation, in which case the one-year time-limit shall run from the date on which the possessor discovered the interference or became certain thereof.

A possessory action and a petitory action may not be joined. Whoever brings a petitory action shall be deemed to have waived the possessory action unless his possession is infringed during the examination of the petitory action, or if he brings the petitory action in the alternative together with the possessory action, in which case it shall be examined when judgment is rendered dismissing the possessory action.
The defendant in a possessory action may not bring a petitory action until after the removal of the infringement committed by him.

The judge who examines a possessory action may not address the substantive right or base his judgment on grounds or documents relating to that right unless he relies thereon to assess the nature of the possession and the fulfilment of its legal conditions. The judgment in a possessory action shall be provisionally enforceable.

Claims are divided into two categories:

1- Originating claims by which the proceedings are commenced.

2- Incidental claims submitted during the proceedings.

An incidental claim submitted by the plaintiff is called an additional claim. An incidental claim submitted by the defendant against the plaintiff is called a counterclaim. And a claim submitted by a third party against one of the litigants to a third party outside the litigation is called a third-party joinder.

Every claim presented during the proceedings which does not have the effect of broadening or narrowing the subject-matter of the originating claim shall be deemed a procedural incident.

The admissibility of an incidental claim requires:

1- That it be connected to the principal claim, meaning that the decision determined for one of them is such as to affect the decision that must be determined for the other. A claim for set-off shall, however, be excepted therefrom.

2- That the consideration thereof does not fall outside the functional or subject-matter jurisdiction of the court hearing the principal claim, and that it does not fall within the jurisdiction of an arbitral tribunal.
The plaintiff may submit incidental claims seeking to rectify the principal claim, to supplement it, or to amend its object or its cause.

The defendant may submit incidental claims that fulfil the conditions of Article 30, and in particular the following claims:

1- A claim for set-off.

2- A claim for compensation for damage sustained by him as a result of the principal claim or of one of the procedural acts of the trial.

3- Any claim seeking to obtain a benefit other than the mere dismissal of the claims of his opponent.
The plaintiff may, in reply to incidental claims submitted by the defendant, put forward incidental claims, provided that they arise from the cause upon which the claims of the defendant are based.

The principal claim and the incidental claim shall be adjudicated together, unless the court deems it appropriate, for the proper administration of justice, to adjudicate one of them before the other. However, in the case of a claim for set-off between two connected debts that are certain in principle, where one of them is unliquidated or not due, the judge must establish the principle of set-off in the single judgment and order the measures leading to the settlement of the accounts.
Each of the parties may submit claims seeking the adoption of conservatory or provisional measures.
The intervention or joinder of a third party in the trial shall be permissible, whereby he becomes a party thereto.

Voluntary intervention shall be principal when a third party intervenes of his own accord in the trial to establish or protect his rights vis-à-vis the parties or one of them, requesting judgment in his own favour on a claim connected to the claims of the parties. It shall be accessory when it seeks to support the claims of one of the parties if granting them is in the interest of the intervener.

A third party may be joined to the proceedings at the request of one of the litigants for the purpose of making the judgment binding upon him. He may also be joined for the purpose of rendering judgment against him upon claims connected with the claims of one of the litigants, or for the purpose of indemnity.
An application for intervention or joinder shall be submitted by way of a pleading served upon the interested parties, including the person sought to be joined.
For intervention or joinder to be admissible, it is required that the intervener or the applicant for joinder have a personal and legitimate interest.

Intervention or joinder is permissible at all stages of the proceedings and until the closure thereof. It is permissible before the court of first instance and before the court of appeal. Before the court of cassation, only accessory voluntary intervention is admissible, subject to the provisions of Articles 624, 625, 726 and 727.

The litigants and the third party sought to be joined must contest the admissibility as to form of the intervention or joinder prior to arguing on the merits. The court may, in such case, adjudicate upon the application by a separate decision or together with the judgment on the merits. Where no dispute arises as to the admissibility of the intervention or where the court decides to admit it, the intervener or the joined party shall be entitled to request the conduct of any measure of inquiry that he deems useful, even if the litigants have not requested it.

Where the intervention or joinder is not grounded upon a material interest and is intended solely to delay the adjudication of the action, the litigants shall be entitled, in addition to their opposition to its admissibility, to claim, in accordance with the provisions of Article 10 of this Law, an award of damages in their favour, and the court may also impose a fine in accordance with the provisions of Article 11.
The claim set forth in the intervention or joinder may be met with a counterclaim.

The court may of its own motion decide to join a third party to the proceedings if it considers that such measure would facilitate judgment in the principal action and lead to the manifestation of the truth, and that it is beneficial for the preservation of the rights of the litigants or one of them, or the rights of the person decided to be joined. The court registry shall serve the decision of joinder upon the third party.

The court may order each of the litigants to serve his documents upon the third party and fix a time limit for the latter to reply.

The impleader of a third party as guarantor before the court seized of the principal action shall not be admissible in the following cases:

1- If the warranty action falls outside its functional or subject-matter jurisdiction.

2- If there exists between the guarantor and the guaranteed party an agreement conferring jurisdiction to hear the warranty case upon another court or an arbitral tribunal.

3- If there is an action relating to the same warranty still pending before another court.
For the person summoned for the purpose of warranty, or he also summons for his warranty another person bound thereby.

A litigant who has summoned a person as his guarantor may withdraw from the proceedings with the consent of the litigants so that this person may take his place therein. He may return to the proceedings whenever he sees an interest for himself in doing so. The judgment rendered shall be enforceable against all parties and against the party who withdrew from the proceedings.

If the guaranteed party withdraws from the proceedings, he shall bear neither the costs of the action nor the damages awarded against the guarantor, except in the event of the insolvency of the latter.
A defence on the merits is any ground by which a litigant seeks to have his opponent's claim dismissed as unfounded after examining the right at issue on the merits.
Grounds of defence on the merits may be raised at any stage of the proceedings.

A procedural plea is any ground by which a litigant seeks a declaration that the proceedings are unlawful, have lapsed, or that their course is stayed. Considered as procedural pleas are the plea of lack of jurisdiction, lis pendens, connectedness, or the nullity of the summons or other procedural acts, the request for transfer of the action for legitimate suspicion or for consanguinity or affinity, and pleas for a stay granting a time-limit.

Procedural pleas must be raised at the commencement of the proceedings and prior to arguing on the merits or raising pleas of inadmissibility, unless they arise from a cause that appeared thereafter, and subject to the exceptions referred to in the following articles. A request for service of documents shall not constitute a ground for the inadmissibility of a procedural plea. If the jurisdiction is functional, subject-matter, or mandatory territorial jurisdiction, the plea of its absence may be raised at all stages of the proceedings. The court must raise it of its own motion.
The plea of lis pendens shall be available when the same action is brought before two different courts both of which are competent to hear them.

The plea of connectedness shall be available when there are two actions comprising connected claims pending before two different courts, each of which is competent to hear the action brought before it.

The court before which a plea of lis pendens or connectedness with an action previously brought before another court has been raised must decline jurisdiction over the action and refer it to that court, with the exception of the case where the court before which the action was subsequently brought has issued a decision adjudicating upon one of the points of the dispute, or where it is hearing the principal action whilst the other is hearing an action based on an obligation of incidental warranty, in which case the action must then be referred by the court before which it was first brought and before which the plea is raised to the second court.

If the two courts are of two different degrees, the plea of lis pendens or of connectedness shall not be admissible before the court of the higher degree.

In all cases, where lis pendens or connectedness exists between an action pending before the Single Judge and another pending before the Chamber of First Instance, the plea shall be raised before the Single Judge, who must then refer the action to the Chamber.

The plea of connectedness may be raised at any stage of the proceedings, unless it becomes apparent that it was raised at a late time with the intention of prolonging the duration of the proceedings, in which case the court shall decide to reject it.

The plea of nullity of judicial acts for a defect in form shall be raised immediately upon their completion and the adversary's becoming aware of them. However, the nullity shall be cured if the adversary who raises it has invoked, after the completion of the act, defences on the merits or a plea of inadmissibility, without relying upon the nullity.

All grounds of nullity of judicial acts that have been completed shall be raised simultaneously, under penalty of inadmissibility of the ground that was not raised in this manner.

The nullity of any procedural act may not be declared for a defect of form unless there is an express provision to that effect in the law or the defect results from the violation of a substantial formality or one relating to public policy, and provided that the party invoking the nullity proves that he has suffered prejudice as a result of the said defect.

The nullity shall lapse if the person in whose interest it was prescribed waives it expressly or impliedly, except in cases where the nullity relates to public policy.

The nullity shall also lapse in all cases by a subsequent regularisation of the procedural act, even after such nullity has been invoked, provided that the regularisation takes place within the time limit prescribed by law for performing the procedural act and provided that no prejudice arises therefrom.

If the procedural act does not have a time limit of forfeiture fixed by law, the court shall fix a suitable time limit for its regularisation, and the procedural act shall only take effect from the date of its regularisation.

The following shall constitute substantive defects resulting in the nullity of a judicial procedural act:

1- Lack of capacity to litigate.

2- Lack of authority of the parties or of one of the persons appearing in the proceedings as a representative of a legal person or of a person lacking procedural capacity.

3- Lack of capacity or authority of a person representing one of the parties.

Pleas of nullity based on the violation of substantive rules relating to judicial procedural acts may be raised at any stage of the proceedings. However, it shall be for the judge to award damages against the party who refrained from raising them at an early stage with the intent to delay and prolong the duration of the proceedings.

The pleas of nullity referred to in the first paragraph shall be admissible even if there is no express provision regarding such nullity, and the occurrence of prejudice to the party raising the plea shall not be required.

The court must raise of its own motion these pleas of nullity if they relate to public policy. It may raise of its own motion the nullity resulting from the lack of capacity to litigate.

In cases where the regularisation of the defect leading to nullity is possible, the declaration of nullity shall not be ordered if the cause thereof has ceased to exist at the time the judge renders judgment.

A plea of inadmissibility is any ground by which a party seeks to have his opponent's claim declared inadmissible without examining its merits, for lack of his right of action.

Pleas of inadmissibility include the plea of lack of standing, lack of interest, res judicata, or the expiry of the time limits for judicial procedural acts. The plea of prescription shall be deemed a plea of inadmissibility, subject to special provisions such as the provisions of Article 361 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts.

In assessing the value of the dispute, regard shall be had to:

1- The value of the principal claim, without regard to any interest, expenses, damages and other accessories falling due after the institution of the action.

2- The aggregate of connected claims, whether arising from a single legal cause or from different causes, and whether submitted in a single proceeding or in different proceedings subsequently joined, and whatever the number of parties in such proceeding or proceedings. However, where the claims are not connected, regard shall be had to the value of each claim separately.

3- The value of the entire right, where the claim is for a part thereof and the dispute is raised over the entire right.

4- The value of the joint instrument, whether the co-holders therein are creditors or debtors.

5- The value of the principal debt in disputes arising between the attaching creditor and the attached debtor regarding the validity of the attachment or any provisional measure over movable property, or in disputes arising between holders of privileges, pledges or mortgages and their debtor. Where the dispute is between the aforementioned persons and a third party over the revendication of the attached items or the pledged or mortgaged property, regard shall be had to the value thereof.

6- The value of the right established in the instrument, where the action is brought for its annulment, revocation or rescission.

7- The value of the immovable property, where the dispute concerns the right of ownership or the right of disposal (tasarruf) in Amiri lands. In all cases, regard shall be had to the value of constructions and plantations even if their removal is claimed.

8- The value of the goods according to their price on the day the claim is brought.

9- The total income where it is based on obligations of a fixed duration. However, where it is fixed for the duration of life, it shall be deemed of indeterminate value...
In actions arising from alternative obligations, regard shall be had to the claim of the highest value.

Jurisdiction is of four kinds:

1- International jurisdiction: whereby the State that must provide the adjudicating body is determined.

2- Functional jurisdiction: whereby the judicial authority competent to hear the action is determined.

3- Subject-matter jurisdiction: whereby the category and degree of the court that hears the action from among the courts belonging to a single judicial authority are determined.

4- Territorial jurisdiction: whereby the court having the authority to hear the action from among the courts of the same category and degree is determined.

Pleas of inadmissibility may be raised at any stage of the proceedings. However, the judge may award damages against a party who refrained from raising them at an early stage, with the intent of delaying and prolonging the duration of the proceedings.

The court shall raise a plea of inadmissibility when it relates to public policy, particularly if it results from failure to observe the time limits for recourse or from the impermissibility of using the means of recourse.

The court may raise of its own motion a plea of inadmissibility resulting from the lack of standing or interest.

If the ground giving rise to the plea of inadmissibility is capable of rectification, such plea shall be dismissed if the ground has ceased to exist at the time the court renders judgment. The same shall apply if the person having standing to sue has become a party to the action before the expiry of the forfeiture time limits.

A defendant who invokes any plea entailing the dismissal of the action as to form, its inadmissibility, or the annulment of the proceedings shall submit his defence and claims on the merits in the alternative.
The court may rule on the pleas separately or join them to the merits.
The court may rule on the pleas and grounds of defence raised before it, with the exception of those that raise an issue falling within the exclusive jurisdiction of another judicial authority.
In assessing the value of the dispute, regard shall be had to the claims set forth in the statement of claim and the written submissions.

The Lebanese civil courts shall have jurisdiction to hear disputes arising from a marriage contract concluded in a foreign country between two Lebanese nationals or between a Lebanese national and a foreigner in the civil form prescribed by the law of that country. The provisions of the laws relating to the jurisdiction of the Sharia and Druze courts shall be observed if both spouses belong to the Mohammedan communities and at least one of them is a Lebanese national.
Lack of jurisdiction of the Lebanese courts shall be subject to the rules of internal territorial lack of jurisdiction, and shall be relative unless it relates to a case of mandatory jurisdiction.
Functional jurisdiction shall be determined pursuant to the laws and regulations in respect of the various judicial authorities, such as the confessional or Sharia judiciary.
Functional jurisdiction shall be deemed to have the status of subject-matter jurisdiction unless there is a provision to the contrary.

Judicial authority shall be exercised by:

First- Courts of First Instance.

Second- Courts of Appeal.

Third- The Court of Cassation.
Special courts shall exceptionally hear certain disputes in accordance with the laws and regulations established for them and the provisions of this Law that do not conflict therewith.

The Court of First Instance shall be composed of chambers consisting of a President and two members, and of sections in which single judges exercise judicial authority.

The chamber of the Court of First Instance shall be referred to in the following provisions as the Primary Chamber.

The Single Judge heard the following civil and commercial cases:

1- Personal actions and actions relating to movable or immovable property the value of which does not exceed one hundred million Lebanese pounds.

2- Civil status actions, with the exception of matters relating to nationality.

3- Applications for the determination of heirs, unless opposed by a dispute over the designation of the heirs or the determination of the hereditary shares.

4- Actions relating to lease contracts of movable and immovable property and free management, whatever the value of the rent or consideration, and actions relating to occupancy together with all claims and defences incidental to such actions.

5- Possessory actions.

6- Actions to prevent interference with the right of irrigation.

7- Actions relating to easements.

8- Actions for the demarcation of boundaries.

9- Actions of summary jurisdiction.

The jurisdiction vested in the Real Estate Judge shall be observed.

The First President of the Court of Cassation shall adjudicate, by a decision not subject to appeal, upon disputes arising from the decision on the distribution of work among the chambers of the said Court.

The First President of the Court of Appeal shall adjudicate, by a decision not subject to appeal, upon disputes arising from the decision on the distribution of work among the chambers of the said Court and upon disputes arising from the decision on distribution among the chambers and sections in the Court of First Instance.

The decision of the aforementioned First President is of a purely administrative nature and does not affect the merits.

The international jurisdiction of the Lebanese courts shall in principle be subject to the provisions relating to internal jurisdiction without distinction between a Lebanese national and a foreigner.
The Lebanese courts shall have jurisdiction to hear matters of personal status if the parties concerned are Lebanese nationals.
The Lebanese courts shall have jurisdiction to hear any case relating to a Lebanese national or to interests situated in Lebanon if there are no other courts having jurisdiction.

An action relating to the validity or breach of a concession prohibited or recognised by the Lebanese State shall be brought before the Lebanese courts, subject to the provisions of Article 762 (new), third paragraph, and Article 809, second paragraph.

In addition to the cases provided for in the preceding Articles, and subject to the provisions of Legislative Decree No. 34 dated 5 August 1967, the Lebanese courts shall have jurisdiction to hear actions brought against any Lebanese or foreign person who has no real or elected domicile or residence in Lebanon in the following cases:

1- If the action relates to property situated in Lebanon at the time of service of the claim, or to a contract concluded in Lebanon, or where performance of one of the principal obligations arising therefrom was stipulated to take place in Lebanon.

2- If the subject-matter of the application is a provisional or conservatory measure to be executed in Lebanon.

3- If the subject-matter of the action is the delivery of a minor to the person entitled to have custody of him, where the former is present in Lebanon or the latter is resident therein.

4- If the action relates to the filiation of a minor, or to paternal authority or guardianship over him, or to curatorship over the property of a person sought to be placed under interdiction or provided with judicial assistance, where the minor or the person sought to be placed under interdiction or provided with judicial assistance is in Lebanon.

5- If the subject-matter of the action is an opposition to a marriage contract intended to be concluded in Lebanon.

The Single Judge, in his capacity as President of the Execution Department, shall handle matters of execution and adjudicate the merits of difficulties relating to execution procedures; as for difficulties not relating to such procedures, he may take provisional measures in respect thereof in accordance with the procedure followed before the summary affairs judiciary.

The Single Judge shall adjudicate all claims and claims for set-off that fall by virtue of their nature or their value within the scope of his jurisdiction, even if the total thereof together with the principal claim exceeds the limits of that jurisdiction. He shall also adjudicate together with the principal action claims for damages arising out of the principal action whatever the value of such claims may reach. Likewise, he shall adjudicate the interest, accessions and consequences branching out of the right that is the subject of the principal action whatever their value may reach.

If the counterclaim falls by reason of its value outside the jurisdiction of the Single Judge and enters into the jurisdiction of the Chamber of First Instance, the Single Judge shall confine himself to deciding the principal action alone. However, if he finds that the judgment on the counterclaim is such as to affect the resolution that will be decided for the principal action, he shall decide to refer that action together with the counterclaim to the Chamber of First Instance, which shall decide them both together, unless the litigants agree that the Single Judge himself shall decide them both.

The Chamber of First Instance is the ordinary court and has general jurisdiction in civil and commercial cases, and nothing is excluded from this jurisdiction save what is left by a special provision to another court.

If an action is brought before the Chamber of First Instance and jurisdiction to adjudicate it belongs to the Single Judge attached with it to the same Court of First Instance, the Chamber shall declare its lack of jurisdiction and refer the action administratively to the Single Judge. The same rule shall apply when an action that falls within the jurisdiction of the Chamber of First Instance is brought before the Single Judge, whereupon it shall be incumbent upon him to refer it administratively to the latter.

However, the litigants shall be entitled, after the bringing of the action, to agree that the judicial authority before which it was brought shall decide it, even if that authority is not the one having jurisdiction according to its value.

If the Chamber of First Instance finds that the action brought before it is to be adjudicated, according to the decision on the distribution of work, by another chamber of the chambers of the same Court of First Instance, it shall decide to refer it administratively to that other chamber; likewise, if the Single Judge finds that the action brought before him is to be adjudicated by another Single Judge of the judges of the same Court of First Instance, he shall decide to refer it administratively to the latter.
The presidents of the chambers shall exercise the powers vested in them by law, and their decisions shall be subject to objection before the chamber over which they preside.

The Court of Appeal shall hear challenges against judgments and decisions subject to appeal that are rendered within its territorial jurisdiction:

1- By courts of first instance in civil and commercial matters.

2- By enforcement departments and special committees and councils in the cases provided for by law.

It shall also hear petitions for the recusal of judges of courts of first instance from hearing cases, and any other petition or challenge that the law entrusts it to hear.

The Court of Cassation shall hear:

1- Petitions for cassation against final judgments rendered by Courts of Appeal in civil and commercial matters.

2- Petitions for the transfer of an action from one court to another in the cases provided for in Article 116 of this Law.

3- Every other petition the hearing of which is entrusted to it by law.

The Court of Cassation, sitting in its Plenary Assembly convened with the quorum specified in the Law on the Organisation of the Judiciary, shall hear:

1- An action brought against the State regarding liability arising from the acts of judicial judges.

2- Every case the resolution of which raises the establishment of an important legal principle or would give rise to contradiction with prior judgments, in which case the case shall be referred to it by a decision of the chamber before which the action is pending.

3- Petitions for the designation of the competent authority upon the occurrence of a positive or negative conflict of jurisdiction:

a- Between two judicial courts.

b- Between a judicial court and a Sharia or confessional court.

c- Between a Sharia court and a confessional court.

d- Between two different confessional or Sharia courts.

4- An objection against an irrevocable decision rendered by a confessional or Sharia court for lack of jurisdiction of that court or for its violation of essential formalities relating to public policy.

5- A petition for cassation of judgments in the interest of the law submitted by the Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation.
Territorial jurisdiction is of two kinds: ordinary, which is of a relative character, and exceptional, which is of a mandatory character.

Jurisdiction shall lie with the court within whose district the domicile of the defendant is located, unless the law provides otherwise. Where there are multiple defendants, jurisdiction shall lie with the court within whose district the domicile of one of them is located, provided that the latter is originally implicated. It is not required that the claims against the defendants be based on a single cause of action; rather, it suffices that they be connected.

The place of residence shall be deemed equivalent to the domicile in the absence thereof. The elected domicile shall be deemed equivalent to the real domicile.

If the intention of the defendants is merely to divest the natural judiciary of jurisdiction to the detriment of the adversary, it shall be objected to for the dismissal of his claim for lack of territorial jurisdiction and for ordering him to pay the compensation provided for in Article 10 of this Law.

In real property actions in rem, including actions for possession and partition of real property, jurisdiction shall lie with the court within whose district the real property is located. Where there are multiple real properties, jurisdiction shall lie with the court of the place of one of them.

In mixed actions, as well as in actions relating to compensation for the principal real property right due to its loss, damage thereto, or the lapse of the right to claim it in kind, or relating to the lease of real property, jurisdiction shall lie, at the option of the plaintiff, with the court of the place of the real property or with the court of the domicile of the defendant.

In actions relating to a civil or commercial contract, jurisdiction shall lie with the court of the real domicile of the defendant or the elected domicile, or with the court within whose district the contract was concluded and in which the performance of one of the principal obligations arising therefrom was stipulated, or with the court within whose district the performance of the contract in its entirety was stipulated.

The election of domicile shall be binding upon the heirs of the contracting parties.

In actions relating to a legal person, jurisdiction shall lie with the court within whose district its principal office is located, whether the action is brought against the legal person, by it against one of its members, or by one of its members against another.

An action may be brought before the court within whose district a branch of the legal person is located in disputes arising from contracting with such branch or from its operations.

In actions arising from a delict or quasi-delict, jurisdiction shall lie with the court of the domicile of the defendant or with the court within whose district the harmful act or the damage giving rise to compensation occurred.
In actions relating to an alimony debt, jurisdiction shall lie with the court within whose district the domicile of the defendant or the domicile of the plaintiff is located.
In actions relating to the marital bond, the competent court shall be the court having jurisdiction over the last domicile of the defendant in Lebanon.

Where there are multiple heirs and until the partition is completed, actions relating to inheritance among the heirs, or between them and the legatees, or between them and the creditors of the estate, shall be brought before the court of the place where the succession was opened.

If the succession was opened in a foreign country and comprises immovable properties situated in Lebanon, disputes relating to such immovable properties as set forth in the first paragraph shall fall within the jurisdiction of the court of the place where such immovable properties are situated.

If the defendant has neither a domicile nor a place of residence in Lebanon and jurisdiction lies with the Lebanese courts, and it is not possible to designate the competent court in accordance with the rules set forth in this Law, jurisdiction shall lie with the court of the plaintiff's domicile or place of residence. If the latter has neither a domicile nor a place of residence, jurisdiction shall lie with the Court of Beirut.
The territorial jurisdiction of the courts designated in the following articles shall be mandatory jurisdiction.
In actions arising out of bankruptcy, jurisdiction shall lie with the court that declared the bankruptcy.
In actions relating to life insurance, jurisdiction shall lie with the court of the domicile of the insured.
In actions relating to accident insurance, jurisdiction shall lie with the court of the place where the accident occurred or the court of the domicile of the insured.
In actions relating to fire insurance, jurisdiction shall lie with the court of the place where the fire occurred.
In actions which the law requires to be brought before a specifically designated court, jurisdiction shall lie exclusively with that court.

The litigants, or any of them, may request the disqualification of a judge for any of the following grounds:

1- Where he, his spouse, or his betrothed has a direct or indirect interest in the action, even after the dissolution of the marriage contract or the betrothal.

2- Where there exists between him and any of the litigants, or his counsel in the litigation, or his legal representative, a relationship by blood or marriage in the direct line or in the collateral line up to the fourth degree, even after the dissolution of the marriage that gave rise to the relationship by marriage.

3- Where he has a relationship by blood or marriage up to the fourth degree with any of the members of the board of directors of the company concerned or with any of its managers, and such member or manager has a personal interest in the action.

4- Where he is, or previously was, an agent for any of the litigants or a legal representative thereof, or where any of the litigants had chosen him as an arbitrator in a previous case.

5- Where he, or any of his relatives by blood or marriage up to the fourth degree, has previously heard the action as a judge, an expert, or an arbitrator, or has given testimony therein. An exception is made for the case in which he hears an opposition, a third-party opposition, or a retrial against a judgment in which he or any of his aforementioned relatives by blood or marriage participated.

6- Where he has expressed an opinion in the specific action, even if that occurred prior to his appointment to the judiciary. Proof of this matter shall only be valid by written evidence or by the admission of the judge.

7- Where there exists between him and the litigants enmity or affection with which it is likely that he will be unable to adjudicate without partiality. A judge shall not be subject to disqualification by reason of contempt directed at him by any of the litigants.

8- Where any of the litigants is a creditor, a debtor, or a servant of the judge or of any of his relatives up to the second degree.
A judge must submit his recusal of his own motion in the cases set forth in the preceding Article.
A judge may, in cases other than the aforementioned cases of disqualification, if he feels uneasiness in hearing the action for any reason, submit his recusal.

A submission of recusal or a request for disqualification concerning judges of the courts of first instance shall be submitted to the Court of Appeal to which those courts are subordinate, which shall examine it in the deliberation chamber, and its decision shall not be subject to any recourse.

A submission of recusal or a request for disqualification concerning judges of the Court of Appeal shall be submitted to the same Court of Appeal, where a chamber among its chambers appointed by the First President of this Court shall examine it, and its decision issued in the deliberation chamber shall not be subject to any recourse.

A submission of recusal or a request for disqualification concerning judges of the Court of Cassation shall be submitted to this Court, where a chamber among its chambers appointed by the First President of the Court of Cassation shall examine it.

The territorial jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal shall be confined to hearing appeals against judgments rendered by the courts and judicial authorities located within its district, unless a contrary provision exists.

Every interested party may apply to the Court of Cassation in its Plenary Assembly to designate the competent authority:

1- If one of the courts rules that it lacks jurisdiction to hear an action by a decision that has acquired finality without there being another competent court.

2- If an action is brought before two or more different courts and each of them rules that it has jurisdiction or that it lacks jurisdiction by a decision that has acquired finality.

The Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation may decide, where necessary, immediately upon the submission of the application to it, to stay the proceedings before the court hearing the action. The Plenary Assembly shall adjudicate the application to designate the competent authority expeditiously after the lapse of ten days from notifying the adversary to submit his reply. It shall designate in its decision the competent court and refer the file to it.

An action shall be transferred from one court to another court of the same degree:

1- If it is impossible to constitute the bench of the court due to the lack of a sufficient number of judges or due to the impossibility of the court performing its functions by reason of force majeure.

2- If there exists between one of the adversaries and the single judge, or two of the judges of whom the court is composed, or its president, consanguinity or affinity in the direct line or in the collateral line up to the fourth degree.

3- If there exists a ground justifying doubt as to the impartiality of the court.

4- If hearing the action before one of the courts is likely to cause a disturbance of public security.

The application for transfer was submitted to the Court of Cassation by one of the adversaries in the first three cases of the preceding Article and is notified to the judge or judges of the court from whose court the transfer of the action is requested.

It is submitted by the Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation in the fourth case.

The applicant in the third case of the preceding Article must attach to his application a receipt proving that he has deposited a security in the amount of forty thousand Lebanese pounds, which shall be forfeited when judgment is rendered dismissing the application.

The Court of Cassation shall hear the application for the transfer of the action expeditiously without the need to join the adversaries in the proceedings, and it shall designate in its decision the court to which the action is transferred, which shall be of the same category and degree, and the file shall be referred to it. In the third case of Article 116, it may request from the judge or judges of the court from which the transfer of the action is requested a statement of their observations.
The course of the proceedings shall be stayed by the mere submission of the application for the transfer of the action in the second and third cases of Article 116.

The application for recusal shall be submitted, under penalty of inadmissibility, prior to the discussion on the merits, unless the ground therefor occurred or became known thereafter, in which case it must be submitted within eight days from the occurrence of the ground therefor or from the knowledge thereof.

Upon the judge sought to be recused being notified of the application for recusal, he must cease proceeding with the consideration of the case until the application is adjudicated.

However, the court considering the application for recusal may, in case of necessity, decide to proceed with the trial without the participation therein of the judge sought to be recused.

The judge and the adversaries shall be notified of the application for recusal, and each of them may submit his observations within a time limit of three days.

The application shall be adjudicated in the deliberation chamber without summoning the adversaries.

Whoever appears to be unjustified in the application for recusal shall be sentenced to a fine ranging between two hundred thousand and eight hundred thousand Lebanese pounds. He may also be sentenced to pay compensation to the judge sought to be recused and to the adversary harmed by the delay of the trial.

The provisions on withdrawal and recusal shall apply to the judges of the Public Prosecution, arbitrators, and experts.

The application for the recusal of a member of the Public Prosecution shall be considered by the court to which he is attached according to the judicial organisation.

The application for the recusal of an arbitrator shall be considered by the First Instance Chamber having jurisdiction to hear the action, or within the district of which is located the judge having jurisdiction to hear the action in the absence of arbitration.

The application for the recusal of experts shall be considered by the court that appointed them.
If the application for recusal or the multiple applications for recusal render it impossible to constitute the bench of the court, the provisions on the transfer of the action shall apply.

In no court may judges related to one another by consanguinity or affinity up to the fourth degree be combined in a single chamber to hear one of the actions, failing which the judgment shall be subject to annulment through the legal means of recourse.

Proof is the establishment of evidence before the judiciary of a legal fact or act upon either of which a claim, plea, or defence is based. Every person is required or to assist the judiciary for the purpose of bringing out the truth.
The burden of proof falls upon the one who alleges the fact or the act. That which is sought to be proved must be relevant to the dispute and admissible to be proved.

Every party to the trial must put forward at the same time all the means of proof upon which he relies in respect of each fact that he alleges. The parties must abide in proving by the principles of probity.
The court must notify of its own motion the operative part of the judgments ordering measures to the parties who were not notified of the date appointed for their delivery.

The court may order of its own motion the conduct of any investigation in completion of the evidence invoked by the parties. The court shall conduct the investigation itself or commission one of its judges to conduct it.

If the place where the investigation must be conducted is distant from the seat of the court, it may commission the single judge within whose jurisdiction that place lies. The court shall appoint the time limit within which the commissioned judge must carry out his mission.

The commissioned judge shall rule upon the incidents that arise during the investigation. His decisions may be objected to before the commissioning court without the objection having an effect suspending the course of the investigation.

The court or the commissioned judge has the right to resort to audio, visual or audiovisual recording for all or some of the operations of the investigation undertaken by either of them.

The recording shall be kept at the registry, and each party may request to be delivered a copy thereof against payment of the expense. The reproduction shall take place either at the registry or at the Ministry of Justice.

The court may revoke the measures of proof that it has ordered if circumstances arise that justify such revocation and render the ordered proof unavailing.

The court may disregard the result of the measure provided that it states the reasons therefor in the judgment.

The admissibility of evidence of legal acts is subject to the provisions in force at the time of the creation of those acts.

The admissibility of evidence of material acts is subject to the provisions in force at the time of the institution of the action.

In all cases, the procedures of proof are subject to the provisions of the law at the time they are carried out.

Evidence of legal acts may be established in accordance with the law of the State that applies to the effects of those acts or in accordance with the law of the State in which they were created. The admissibility of evidence of material acts is subject to the law of the judge hearing the dispute. The probative force of instruments is subject to the law of the place in which they were created.

Evidentiary procedures shall be governed by the law of the judge before whom they are carried out, provided that evidentiary procedures carried out in a foreign State shall be recognised if they conform to the provisions of Lebanese law, even if they contravene the foreign law. A foreign court may be commissioned by letters rogatory to take evidentiary procedures required for the hearing of the action.

A judge may not rule on the basis of his personal knowledge in the action. Knowledge derived from the judge's experience in general affairs with which everyone is presumed to be familiar shall not be deemed personal knowledge upon which the judge is prohibited from basing his judgment.

Proof of the existence of Lebanese law shall not be required. As for proving the content of foreign law, it shall be required from the party invoking it, unless the judge has knowledge thereof. Where the content of the foreign law cannot be ascertained, the judge shall rule in accordance with Lebanese law.

An authentic instrument is one in which a public official or a person entrusted with a public service establishes, within the limits of his authority and competence, what has taken place at his hands what he has received of declarations from the concerned parties in accordance with the prescribed rules. Reference shall be made to the law of the place where the instrument was drawn up in determining whether or not to confer the authentic character upon it.

If the instrument does not acquire its authentic character due to a defect in its form or due to the lack of capacity or competence of the public official, it shall be deemed equivalent to a private instrument if it contains the signatures of the concerned parties, even if the rule provided for in Article 152 of this Law was not observed therein, unless the authentic character is required for the existence of the legal act.
An instrument that has the form and outward appearance of an authentic instrument shall be deemed authentic until the contrary is proven by the person against whom it is invoked.

An authentic instrument has enforceable force, and is conclusive evidence against all persons as to the matters recorded therein which were performed by the public official or which occurred on the part of the concerned parties in his presence within the limits of his authority and competence. The effect of the authentic instrument shall extend to the heirs of its parties and their successors. A plea of forgery of an authentic instrument shall suspend its evidentiary and enforceable force.

The content of the declarations of the contracting parties set forth in the authentic instrument shall be conclusive evidence against them and against their successors, and shall be deemed true unless the contrary is proven. An authentic instrument shall only serve as a commencement of proof in writing with respect to declarations that are not directly related to the subject-matter of the contract.
An official copy of an authentic instrument shall be deemed to be in conformity therewith unless one of the parties disputes the same, in which event such copy shall be collated with the original.

Where the original of an authentic instrument is lost, reliance must be placed on its official copy. Where all of its official copies are lost, its entry in the official registers shall serve as a commencement of proof in writing, subject to verification of the loss of the authentic instrument and of its copies. Where it appears from the entries in those registers that the instrument was drawn up in the presence of witnesses, those witnesses must be summoned before the court.

A private instrument is an instrument bearing a private signature and shall be deemed to emanate from the person who signed it unless he expressly denies the handwriting, signature, or fingerprint attributed to him where he does not know how to sign. As for an heir or a successor, he shall not be required to make a denial. It shall be sufficient for him to take an oath that he does not know that the handwriting, signature, or fingerprint belongs to the person from whom he derived the right.
A person against whom a private instrument is invoked and who argues its merits shall not be permitted to deny the handwriting, signature, or fingerprint.

In synallagmatic contracts, the original copies must be made in as many counterparts as there are parties thereto having conflicting interests, unless they agree to deposit a single copy with a third party of their choice. Where this rule is not observed, the instrument shall serve only as a commencement of proof in writing of the existence of the contract.

Notwithstanding the provisions of Article 363 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts, an instrument containing a unilateral obligation is not required to include the words "good for". The sum written in words shall prevail in proof over the sum written in figures unless the contrary is proved.

Where a private instrument is acknowledged by the person from whom it emanates, or a judgment is rendered holding his signature or fingerprint thereon to be authentic, the instrument shall become conclusive evidence as against all persons, provided that it shall not be conclusive evidence as against third parties with respect to its date save from the time when such date becomes certain, and a private instrument shall have a certain date in the following cases:

1- From the day on which it is endorsed by a competent public officer.

2- From the day on which its contents are established in an authentic instrument or in another document having a certain date.

3- From the day of the death of one of the persons who left on the instrument an acknowledged trace of handwriting, signature, or fingerprint, or from the day on which it becomes impossible for one of those persons to write or affix a fingerprint by reason of a physical infirmity preventing him from writing.
Secret documents intended to modify an authentic or private instrument shall produce effect only as between the contracting parties and their universal successors.

The creditors of the contracting parties and their particular successors in title, to whose detriment an ostensible instrument has been fraudulently drawn up, may prove its simulation by all means of proof.

An instrument confirming a prior instrument shall constitute proof in favour of the party invoking it, unless the opposing party proves the inaccuracy of this instrument by producing the original instrument or by another written document whose authenticity is established.

Signed letters shall have the probative value of a private instrument in favour of the addressee, unless the sender proves that he did not send the letter and did not instruct anyone to send it. Telegrams shall also have this value if their original deposited at the telegraph and post office- is signed by their sender. A telegram shall be deemed to conform to its original until proof to the contrary is established.
If a letter is not confidential, the addressee may use it and assign it to third parties. A letter shall not be confidential in commercial matters.
In civil matters, no reliance shall be placed on confidential letters submitted to the court without the agreement of the addressee.

If a registered letter whose delivery is established by a postal acknowledgment of receipt or by a receipt from the addressee is in the form of an open card or if the address is written on the back of the letter itself, the sender may prove its contents by producing the copy kept by him, and the copy shall be deemed authentic if the addressee refuses to produce the letter which he received. In other cases, it shall be incumbent upon the sender to prove the contents of the letter, in the event of its denial by the addressee, in accordance with the general rules of proof.

Whoever obtains, pursuant to the provisions of the preceding Article, a judgment based upon his production of a copy of the letter, and the original subsequently appears and it becomes evident therefrom that this copy is inaccurate, shall be ordered to pay compensation for the damage resulting from the judgment.

Statements written by the creditor indicating discharge of liability on an instrument that has remained in his possession, or on a copy of this instrument, or on a receipt in the possession of the debtor, shall, until proof to the contrary, be deemed proof against the creditor to establish payment, even if such statements are neither dated nor signed.

The debtor shall have the right to demand upon performance, in addition to the receipt instrument, the delivery to him of the debt instrument or a declaration by the creditor in the receipt that the instrument no longer remains in his possession.

Domestic registers and papers shall be conclusive evidence against their author and his universal successors:

1- When they indicate that a performance has taken place.

2- When they establish a debt in favour of a third party.

Mandatory commercial books shall be conclusive evidence:

1- Against their owner in favour of any person, whether they are regular or not. However, a person who wishes to derive evidence from them for himself may not divide what is stated therein and exclude therefrom what is contrary to his claim.

2- In favour of their owner in transactions pertaining to his trade, if they are regular and the dispute is between him and a merchant.

An instrument confirming a prior instrument shall be deemed conclusive evidence for the person who invokes it unless the adversary proves the inaccuracy of this instrument by producing the original instrument or by another written document whose authenticity is established.

The judge may, in a dispute existing between merchants, accept or reject, according to the circumstances of the case, the evidence derived from non-mandatory commercial books or from irregular mandatory commercial books.

The books of merchants shall not be conclusive evidence against non-merchants. However, the particulars recorded therein concerning what was supplied by the merchants shall serve as a basis permitting the judge to administer the suppletory oath to either of the two adversaries in matters that may be proven by testimony.

The court may assess the effect resulting from erasure, scraping, interlineation, and other material defects in the paper or instrument as to forfeiting or diminishing its probative value. If the authenticity of the instrument - or the paper - is a matter of doubt in the view of the court, it may of its own motion summon the public official from whom it issued or the person who wrote it - to state what clarifies the truth of the matter therein.

Denial of handwriting, signature, or fingerprint shall apply to non-official papers and instruments, whereas an allegation of forgery shall apply to all official and non-official papers and instruments.

Jurisdiction over the verification of handwriting shall vest in the judge or the court before which the principal action is brought when the verification is requested incidentally. Jurisdiction shall vest in the Chamber of First Instance when the verification is requested as a principal claim.

Jurisdiction to hear an allegation of forgery shall vest in the court before which the principal action is brought when the forgery is alleged incidentally before the Chamber of First Instance or the Court of Appeal. In other cases, jurisdiction to hear an allegation of forgery shall vest in the Chamber of First Instance.

If the party to whom the instrument or document is attributed denies the handwriting, signature, or fingerprint contained therein, or declares that he does not know the handwriting, signature, or fingerprint attributed to a third party, the judge may disregard this defence if he deems it a means of mere delay or deems it unavailing in the dispute and has not been requested to carry out the verification of handwriting. Otherwise, he shall endorse the document or instrument with the phrase "ne varietur" (not to be altered), sign it, and decide to conduct the verification of handwriting either himself by comparison between the documents or instruments, or through experts. The testimony of witnesses may be heard to prove that the writing, signing, or fingerprinting took place in their presence.

The documents eligible for comparison are:

1- Signatures or fingerprints made on official documents or instruments.

2- Handwriting and signatures or fingerprints in acknowledged private instruments.

3- The part of the instrument undergoing verification whose authenticity is not contested.

4- The handwriting, signature, or fingerprint written or affixed before the judge during the investigation.

The judge may order the production of the official documents or instruments required for comparison from the authority holding them, or proceed with an expert appointed by him to their location to examine them without removing them.
