If the judge decides to summon the party who denied the handwriting or signature attributed to him on the document or instrument to appear in person at a specified time to provide a handwriting sample and he fails to appear without an acceptable excuse, the document or instrument may be adjudged authentic.

If it appears, as a result of the verification, that the instrument is authentic, the party who wrongfully denied the handwriting may, save in the case of an excusable error, be sentenced to a pecuniary fine from two hundred thousand pounds to two million Lebanese pounds, and to compensation for damages.

If the allegation of forgery requires an investigation, the court shall issue a decision to that effect containing a statement of the facts into which the court has accepted to investigate, and ordering the deposit of the original instrument alleged to be forged with the court registry within five days from the date of notification of the decision, if it has not already been deposited therein. From the issuance of the decision to investigate, the enforceability of the instrument shall be suspended until the issue of forgery is adjudicated, without prejudice to conservatory measures.
The other adversary or his counsel may inspect the deposited original instrument at the court registry and take a copy thereof.

If the instrument alleged to be forged is not deposited with the court registry within the appointed time limit, this instrument shall be excluded from the debate unless the court decides to grant another time limit.

If the instrument alleged to be forged is only a copy of an original instrument located in an official department or in a public depository in the possession of a third party, the court shall decide to require the deposit of the original instrument, and this decision shall be notified to the person holding this instrument so that it may be sent to the court within the specified time limit.

If the public official or person performing a public service delays in depositing the instrument located in his department, the court may communicate with the Public Prosecution to take legal measures against him.

If the person with whom the instrument was deposited delays in depositing it within the appointed period, the court may sentence him to a pecuniary fine of twenty thousand to two hundred thousand Lebanese pounds and order him to deposit it under pain of a coercive fine which it shall determine.

Within the eight days following the deposit of the instrument alleged to be forged with the registry, the procedure of describing this instrument and the striking out, additions, interlineations and other apparent characteristics it contains shall take place in the presence of the adversaries or their counsel, under the supervision of the President of the court or the judge delegated for this purpose pursuant to the decision ordering the deposit, and the clerk of the court shall draw up a record of this procedure, and the President or the delegated judge shall place the phrase "ne varietur" on the instrument and sign it.

The forgery of the instrument may be proven by all means of proof, and in particular by having recourse to experts appointed by the court, by hearing the testimony of witnesses, and by comparing the handwriting or signature with other papers or instruments.

Any person in possession of a document or an ordinary instrument may bring an action against the person to whom the instrument or document is attributed so that he may acknowledge that it is in his handwriting or bears his signature or his fingerprint, even if the obligation contained therein is not due for performance, and this shall be done by way of an original action. If the defendant appears and acknowledges it, the court shall record his acknowledgment and all costs shall be borne by the plaintiff. The instrument - or the document - shall be deemed acknowledged if the defendant remains silent or does not deny it or does not attribute it to another person. If the defendant fails to appear after having been served with the date in person and has not submitted an answer denying the validity of the claim, the court shall rule in his absence that the handwriting, signature, or fingerprint is authentic. However, if the defendant denies the handwriting, signature, or fingerprint, verification shall be carried out in accordance with the foregoing rules. This provision shall also apply to the case where the defendant is absent without having been served in person.
A party against whom an official instrument or an ordinary instrument is invoked may allege the forgery of such instrument at any stage of the proceedings.

A party who wishes to allege forgery may request the judge or the court before which the original action is brought to fix a time limit for the other party who produced the instrument to declare either that he insists on using it or that he waives reliance upon it. If the court - or the judge - finds that the instrument has a bearing on the judgment in the dispute, it shall grant this request and fix the time limit. If the other party declares that he waives reliance upon the instrument, the incidental proceeding shall terminate, and he shall bear its expenses and recover the instrument. If he declares that he insists on using the instrument, or if the time limit expires without a declaration from him that he waives reliance upon it and recovers it, his opponent shall be entitled to allege forgery.

A party shall allege the forgery of the instrument by a petition or a pleading submitted to the registry of the court in which he specifies all the points of the alleged forgery, failing which the allegation of forgery - shall be null and void. If the proceedings are taking place before a judge or a court other than the Chamber of First Instance, the clerk shall refer the petition or the pleading to the registry of this Chamber which has jurisdiction to hear the allegation of forgery, and the judge or the court shall stay the hearing of the original action until this allegation is decided. If the original action is brought before the Chamber of First Instance, the allegation of forgery before it shall entail a stay of the proceedings until the allegation of forgery is decided.
The clerk of the Chamber shall serve a copy of the petition or the pleading upon the other party. The President of the Chamber shall send another copy to the Public Prosecution.

The documents eligible for comparison in a forgery claim shall be the same documents that are eligible for comparison in the handwriting verification procedure in accordance with the provisions of Article 175.

The defendant in the forgery claim may terminate the proceedings of the claim at any stage thereof by waiving the impugned instrument. In such case, the court may decide to seize or retain the instrument if the claimant in the forgery claim so requests for a legitimate interest.

If the forfeiture of the right of the claimant in the forgery claim to his claim or the dismissal thereof is decided, he shall be sentenced to a fine of two hundred thousand to two million Lebanese pounds, and to damages in favour of the other party where applicable. He shall not be sentenced to any of the foregoing if part of what he claimed is proven.
If the court establishes in its judgment the forgery of the instrument, it shall decide to destroy it, strike out the forged parts therein, rectify it, or restore its authentic text.
In all cases, the judgment shall order the return of the instruments produced for the purpose of comparison.
The judgment rendered in a forgery claim case shall not be enforceable until it becomes final and binding.

As long as the instruments alleged to be forged are deposited with the court registry, no copy thereof may be delivered except by leave of the court. In all cases, a special endorsement indicating the existence of the forgery claim must be placed on the copy.

If a criminal action has been instituted on account of the alleged forgery, the civil court shall stay the proceedings pending before it until the criminal action is adjudicated, unless it is possible to adjudicate the civil action without taking into consideration the instrument alleged to be forged in the criminal proceedings.

A criminal judgment of acquittal shall not prevent one of the litigants in a civil dispute from alleging the forgery of the instrument that was the subject of the criminal action, if such judgment is based on the acquittal of the defendant yet does not establish the validity of the instrument itself.

The court may, even if forgery is not alleged before it through the foregoing procedures, rule on the rejection and nullity of any instrument if it clearly appears to it from its condition or from the circumstances of the action that it is forged. It must, in such case, state in its judgment the circumstances and presumptions from which it ascertained the same.

Any person who fears that a forged instrument may be invoked against him may sue the person holding that instrument and the person benefiting therefrom to hear judgment pronounced as to its forgery, and this shall be done by way of an original action brought in accordance with the ordinary rules of procedure. In investigating and adjudicating this action, the court shall observe the rules provided for in this Sub-section and in the preceding Sub-section.

A litigant may request that his opponent be compelled to produce any document decisive in the dispute that is in his possession in the following cases:

1- If the law permits demanding that he submit or deliver it.

2- If it is common to him and his opponent. A document shall be considered common, in particular, if it is drawn up in the interest of both litigants or if it establishes their mutual obligations and rights.

3- If his opponent has relied upon it at any stage of the trial.

The applicant must state in the application, under pain of rejection:

1- The description of the document and its content in as much detail as possible.

2- The fact for which the document is adduced as evidence.

3- The evidence establishing that the opponent is in possession thereof.

4- The ground for compelling the opponent to submit it.

If the claimant proves his application, or the opponent admits that the document is in his possession, or remains silent, the court shall order the submission of the document forthwith or within a specified time limit. However, if the opponent denies it and the applicant does not submit sufficient proof of the validity of the application, the denying party must take an oath that the document does not exist, or that he does not know of its existence or its location, and that he has not concealed it or neglected to search for it in order to deprive his opponent of adducing it as evidence. The judge may modify the formula of the oath according to the requirements of the case.
If the opponent fails to submit the document at the appointed time or refuses to take the oath- the court may rely upon the admission of the applicant and upon the copy he has produced.

If a litigant submits a document to be adduced as evidence at the trial, he may not withdraw it except with the consent of his opponent and by a written permission from the judge or the president of the court, after a copy thereof is kept in the case file, endorsed by the chief clerk as conforming to the original.
It shall be for the judge to assess the probative value of an extrajudicial admission according to the means adopted to prove this admission.

An extrajudicial admission may be inferred from a statement of the adversary recorded by his act on a magnetic tape. In the event that the adversary denies the statement attributed to him, the judge may resort to the verification of the voice through an expert.

The court may, at any stage of the trial, decide, of its own motion or upon request, that the adversaries or one of them shall appear in person to be interrogated in a public hearing or in the deliberation chamber. Interrogation shall not be permissible regarding matters in which waiver or settlement is not valid or which the law prohibits adducing evidence to prove.
The court may undertake the interrogation of the adversaries itself or delegate one of its judges to carry it out.

If the court finds that the case does not require an interrogation or that the facts regarding which the adversary is sought to be interrogated are not relevant or are not admissible to be proved, it shall reject the request for interrogation.

If the adversary lacks capacity or has defective capacity, the person who represents him may be interrogated, and the court may question the adversary in person if he is discerning regarding the matters in which he is authorised. With respect to legal persons, the interrogation may be directed to the person who legally represents them. The interrogation of the representatives of the adversaries shall be conducted regarding the acts carried out at their hands or of which they had knowledge in this capacity of theirs.
In all events, the person sought to be interrogated must have the capacity to dispose of the disputed right.

The decision for interrogation shall be notified to the person decided to be interrogated at least three days prior to the date appointed for his appearance, unless he is present at the trial hearing and accepts to be interrogated immediately or there is extreme urgency in the case.
If a party has an excuse preventing him from appearing in person before the court for examination, the court may delegate one of its judges to examine him in the presence of the other party.
If a party has an excuse preventing him from appearing in person before the court for examination, the court may delegate one of its judges to examine him in the presence of the other party.

The examination of a party shall be conducted in the presence of his opponent, unless the circumstances require that each of them be examined in the absence of the other, after which a confrontation between them shall take place at the request of either of them or if the court deems it necessary. The failure of one of the parties to appear shall not prevent the examination of the other party.
The parties may be examined in the presence of a technical expert. They may also be confronted with the witnesses.

The president of the court or the delegated judge shall put the questions relating to the subject matter of the examination. He shall also ask the questions which he deems useful and which one of the parties requests him to put to the other party.
The party being examined shall answer in person the questions put to him without relying on any written text.

A record of the questions asked and the answers given shall be drawn up and signed by the president of the court, the judge delegated to conduct the examination, or the single judge, and by the parties examined. If the person being examined refuses to answer or to sign, his refusal and the reason therefor shall be stated in the record.

If a party fails to appear for examination without an acceptable excuse, or refuses to answer without lawful justification, the court may take such failure to appear or refusal as grounds for deeming the facts in respect of which it was decided to examine him to be established.

The court may, while examining the case, order that a person be joined to the trial in order to compel him to produce a document in his possession. It may also order, of its own motion or at the request of the litigants, that documents be brought from official departments if it is impossible for them to do so.

The court may impose a fine from forty thousand to four hundred thousand Lebanese pounds. On any person who fails to execute an order issued by it to produce a document within the specified time limit. This judgment is not subject to appeal, provided that it remains for the court to exempt the person against whom judgment was rendered from the fine if he presents an acceptable excuse.

An admission is the acknowledgment by a litigant of a fact or a legal act either of which is alleged against him. It is judicial if made before the judiciary during the examination of a dispute relating to this fact or act. It is extra-judicial if made otherwise, in which case it is proved in accordance with the general rules of evidence.
A judicial admission is conclusive proof against the party making the admission.
An admission may not be divided against the person making it unless it bears upon multiple facts and the existence of one of those facts does not necessarily entail the existence of the other facts.

An admission is called qualified when it is confined to the fact declared by the other litigant, except that it vitiates its legal consequences by the additional statements it contains. This admission constitutes full proof with respect to the original fact, whereas the additional statements are deemed established until the contrary is proved.

An admission is called complex when it bears simultaneously upon the original fact and upon another fact. It is indivisible in one case, namely where the new fact presupposes the existence of the original fact, such as where a debtor against whom an action for payment is brought acknowledges that he borrowed the amount claimed, but adds to his acknowledgment that he subsequently paid it. The court then considers the act of borrowing as definitively established, whereas the payment is deemed established until the contrary is proved.
The revocation of an admission is not valid except for an error of fact, provided that the party making the admission proves that.

If the interrogated adversary pleads forgetfulness or ignorance and it does not nonetheless appear that he has adopted the stance of refusal referred to in the preceding Article, the court may admit the testimony of witnesses and presumptions to prove the facts that are the subject of the interrogation, even if such evidence is not originally admissible.
If the interrogation does not lead to an admission, a commencement of proof in writing or a simple presumption may be inferred therefrom.

Judicial oaths are of two kinds:

The decisive oath, and the supplementary oath.

The decisive oath is that which an adversary directs to his adversary in order to resolve the dispute thereby. However, taking it shall only be permissible with the leave of the court. The decision issued by the court admitting or refusing the administration of the oath shall be subject to appeal separately even before the issuance of the judgment on the merits.

The taking of the oath shall be in the formula determined by the court. With regard to the taking of the oath by a mute person and his refusal to take it, his customary sign shall be taken into account if he does not know how to write. If he knows how to write, his taking of the oath and his refusal to take it shall be effected in writing.

An oath may not be administered in respect of a criminal act or an act contrary to public order or morals, nor in respect of a contract for the validity of which the law requires a written instrument, nor to deny a fact which an authentic instrument states to have occurred in the presence of the public officer before whom the legal act was performed, or to deny a fact established by an irrebuttable legal presumption that does not admit of proof to the contrary.
The court may amend the formula of the oath tendered by the adversary so that it bears clearly and precisely upon the fact in respect of which the oath is required to be taken.
The fact upon which the oath bears must relate personally to the party to whom it is directed. If it is not personal to him, it shall bear solely upon his knowledge or lack of knowledge thereof.

A legal representative may not tender the decisive oath or refer it back to the person who tendered it to him regarding matters of which he is permitted to dispose. An agent may not tender this oath or refer it back unless he holds a power of attorney for that.

The decisive oath may be tendered at any stage of the trial. It may be tendered in the alternative, in which case it shall be administered after the court decides to reject the evidence submitted primarily for its illegality, insufficiency or futility.

The person to whom the oath is tendered may refer it back to his adversary, unless it relates to a fact in which both adversaries did not participate, but rather is exclusive to the person to whom it is tendered. Whoever has the oath tendered to him and declines to take it without referring it back to his adversary, and whoever has the oath referred back to him and declines to take it, shall lose what he claimed.
Whoever tendered the oath or referred it back may not retract therefrom once his adversary has accepted to take the oath.

If the court decides to administer the oath and the person to whom it is tendered is present in person, the court may administer the oath to him immediately. If he is not present, he must be summoned to appear to take it in the form decided by the court and on the day it fixes for him. If he appears and refuses to take it, or fails to appear without an excuse after having been served personally, he shall be deemed to have declined.

If the person to whom the oath is tendered has an excuse preventing him from appearing, the court shall move or delegate one of its judges to administer the oath to him, in the presence of the other adversary or after summoning him in accordance with the rules.
A record of the taking of the oath shall be drawn up, signed by the person taking the oath, the president of the court or the delegated judge, and the clerk.

An adversary may not prove the falsity of the oath after it is taken by the adversary to whom it was tendered or referred back. However, if the falsity of the oath is established by a criminal judgment, the adversary who suffered damage therefrom may claim compensation without prejudice to any right he may have to challenge the judgment rendered against him by the possible means of recourse.
The taking of an oath shall be conclusive proof only against the person who tendered it, referred it back, or refused to take it, and against his heirs and successors.

The suppletory oath is that which the court directs of its own motion to one of the litigants in order to complete the evidence submitted by him and be able to rule on the merits of the lawsuit or to determine the value of what will be adjudicated.
It is a condition for directing the suppletory oath that there shall not be complete evidence in the lawsuit, and that the lawsuit shall not be devoid of any evidence.
The litigant to whom the suppletory oath has been directed may not refer it back to the other litigant.

The court may not direct the suppletory oath to the plaintiff to determine the value of the subject-matter of the claim unless it is impossible to determine this value by another means. In this case, the court shall fix a maximum limit for the value in respect of which the plaintiff is to be believed upon his oath.

The testimony of witnesses shall not be admissible:

1- To prove contracts and other legal acts intended to create, transfer, modify, or extinguish rights and obligations, if their value exceeds five hundred thousand Lebanese pounds or if their value is indeterminate.

2- To prove that which contradicts or exceeds what is contained in a written instrument, even if the value of the matter in dispute does not exceed five hundred thousand Lebanese pounds. The litigants may waive adherence to this rule expressly or impliedly.

The determining factor in the admissibility of testimony shall be the value of the right in dispute and not the value of the claim. Therefore, proof by the testimony of witnesses shall not be permissible, even if the value of the claim does not exceed five hundred thousand Lebanese pounds, in the following two cases:

1- If what is claimed is the remainder or a part of a disputed right whose value exceeds five hundred thousand Lebanese pounds and which is not established by a written instrument.

2- If the litigant divided his claim or waived a part of his right after having claimed it in full in order to make the value of the claim not exceed five hundred thousand Lebanese pounds. If the excess of the value over five hundred thousand Lebanese pounds results from adding interest and accessories to the principal, proof by testimony shall be admissible.

If the claim comprises multiple demands arising from multiple sources, proof by the testimony of witnesses shall be permissible in every demand whose value does not exceed five hundred thousand pounds, even if these demands in their aggregate exceed this value and even if their origin is a relationship between the same litigants or acts of the same nature.

Proof by witness testimony shall be permissible regardless of the value of the subject matter of the claim in the following matters and cases:

1- Commercial matters.

2- Material acts. A legal act shall be deemed equivalent to a material act with respect to persons other than its parties and their successors against whom it is invoked.

3- Where there is prima facie written evidence, namely a writing, even if unsigned, emanating from the adversary against whom it is invoked or from his representative, which renders the existence of the alleged legal act probable..

4- Where it was impossible for the creditor to obtain written evidence. Mere moral impossibility shall suffice, and it arises in particular from the custom followed in certain professions or from relationships of kinship between ascendants and descendants, or between collaterals up to the third degree, or between spouses, or between one of the spouses and the parents of the other spouse, or between a fiancé and his fiancée.

5- Where the loss of the written instrument due to an extraneous cause not attributable to the party is established.

6- Where the existence of fraud upon the law in order to conclude a contract contrary to public order or to a mandatory provision is established.
A right shall be assessed according to its value at the time and place in which the legal act was concluded.

The following shall not be competent to give testimony:

1- Any person who has not completed the fifteenth year of his age.

2- Any person who is not of sound mind.

3- Any person against whom criminal judgments have been rendered depriving him of the capacity to testify.

The testimony of witnesses shall not be admissible between ascendants and descendants, nor between spouses even after the dissolution of the marriage contract. Nor shall the testimony of domestic servants constantly attending the person of their employer be admissible in favour of the latter for so long as they remain in his service, nor the testimony of an agent in favour of his principal, nor the testimony of a partner concerning matters relating to the partnership, nor that of a surety concerning the obligations of the principal debtor.
The statements of the persons referred to in the two preceding Articles may be heard without oath by way of information.
Testimony based on common repute shall not be admissible except in the cases provided for by law.

Public sector employees, even after leaving office, shall be prohibited from testifying as to matters which came to their knowledge during the performance of their duties and which were not intended to be disclosed to the public, unless the authority grants them permission to testify upon the request of the court or upon the request of one of the parties. The permission of the authority shall be granted to a Minister by the Council of Ministers and to employees by the competent Minister.

No person among advocates, agents, physicians or others who has learned, by way of his profession or craft, of a fact or of information may disclose it, even after the termination of his service or the cessation of his capacity, unless its mention to him disclosed an intention to commit a felony or a misdemeanour. Nevertheless, the aforementioned persons must give testimony regarding that fact or information whenever requested to do so by the person who confided it to them, provided that this does not prejudice the provisions of the special laws applicable to them.

Neither spouse may disclose, without the consent of the other, what the latter communicated to him during the marriage, even after its dissolution, except in the event that a lawsuit is brought by one of them against the other or a lawsuit is instituted against one of them by reason of a felony or a misdemeanour committed by him against the other.

The litigant who requests proof by the testimony of witnesses shall state the facts which he wishes to prove in his written request or orally at the hearing, and shall name his witnesses, provided that their number does not exceed five for a single fact unless the court authorises him to do so.

The decision ordering the conduct of the investigation must include:

1- The designation of the facts that must be proved.

2- The summoning of the witnesses designated by the party requesting the investigation and the fixing of the date of the hearing at which they will be heard.

The court may, of its own motion, decide to hear witnesses in the cases in which the law permits proof by the testimony of witnesses whenever it sees therein a benefit to the truth. It may also, in all cases in which it decides to allow proof by the testimony of witnesses, summon to testify whomever it deems necessary to hear his testimony in order to manifest the truth.

The investigation shall be conducted before the court. It may, where necessary, delegate one of its judges to conduct it, and fix for him the time limit within which it must be completed. The delegated judge may decide to extend this time limit when needed, and shall notify the court thereof. During the investigation, the delegated judge shall exercise the authority assigned to him in Article 135 of this Law.
Permission granted to one of the litigants to prove a fact by the testimony of witnesses necessarily and without a decision entails that the other litigant has the right to disprove it by this means.

The court shall provisionally fix the investigation and oblige the party requesting the investigation to deposit the amount which it fixes. When the court decides of its own motion to summon witnesses to hear them, it shall designate in its decision the person who must advance their expenses and shall fix a time limit for depositing them.

If the court finds benefit in conducting both the investigation and the inspection together, it may delegate one of its judges for this purpose. The delegated judge shall perform the mission, and he may hear at the place of inspection, and immediately, any witnesses other than those named by the litigants whom he deems necessary to hear, or summon these witnesses to hear them at another time appointed by him.

The witness summons must include:

1- The designation of the court before which the testimony is to be given.

2- The designation of each of the litigants by his name, surname, profession, and residence.

3- The designation of the witness to whom the summons is addressed.

4- The designation of the place of appearance, the day, and the hour.

5- The nature of the lawsuit in which the testimony is requested.

6- A warning of the penalty to which a witness who fails to appear is subject. If there is a defect in the designation of the litigants or the summoned witnesses, such defect shall not invalidate the summons unless it results in serious doubt as to their identity.
If the witness is enlisted in the army and on active duty, the summons shall be addressed to him through the commander of his unit to authorise him to appear.
If the witness is imprisoned, the court must request the prison director to bring him under guard, and if bringing him is not possible, the prison director must inform the court without delay.
In all other cases without exception, the witness shall be summoned directly without any intermediary.

If it is necessary to hear the testimony of the President of the Republic, the Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, or the Prime Minister, the court or the judge delegated by it shall proceed to him to hear his statements, and the clerk shall record them in a report which he shall attach to the case file.

The summons must reach the witness at least three days before the time appointed for his appearance, unless the court issues a decision to shorten the time limit. Pursuant to a decision of the court, the summons may be sent by registered telegram with an acknowledgment of receipt in case of urgency.

If the witness fails to appear, he shall be sentenced to a fine of ten thousand to one hundred thousand Lebanese pounds, ' and to pay the expenses resulting from his failure to appear. The court may summon the witness a second time, and if he persists in failing to appear, he shall be sentenced to a second fine ranging between the amount of the first fine and double thereof, and the court shall have the right to order that he be brought by force through the armed forces. However, if the witness is on active duty in the army, his appearance shall be requested from the commander of his unit.
The judgment imposing the fine referred to in the preceding Article may be revoked if the witness who failed to appear presents an excuse worthy of acceptance.

If the witness puts forward an acceptable excuse that prevented him from appearing at the time appointed for hearing him, the court may grant him a time limit, or decide upon delegation or moving to hear his testimony. It may also, according to the circumstances, dispense with hearing this witness.

If the witness appears and refuses without a legal justification to take the oath and to answer, he shall be sentenced to a fine of two hundred thousand to two million Lebanese pounds unless the adversary who named him waives the hearing of his testimony.

The testimony of each witness shall be heard individually in the presence of the adversaries, and the court shall have the right to bring them together for confrontation thereafter. So long as the investigations have not ended, the witness may not leave except with the permission of the court, failing which he shall be subject to a fine of twenty thousand to forty thousand Lebanese pounds.

The witness shall be asked first about his given name, surname, age, profession and place of residence, and about any relationship of employment or otherwise between him and the adversaries, and about whether penal judgments disqualifying him from the capacity to testify have been rendered against him.

The witness shall, prior to giving testimony, take the oath that he will testify to the whole truth and testify to nothing but the truth, failing which his testimony shall be null and void. As for the persons who are heard without taking the oath in accordance with the provisions of Article 261, the judge or the President of the court shall impress upon them their duty to tell the truth.

Questions shall be directed to the witness by the President of the court or the delegated judge concerning the facts relating to the dispute and which may be proved by testimony, even if they were not specified in the decision ordering the investigation. The President may put to the witness the questions requested to be put by the judges of the court or the adversaries if he deems them useful in uncovering the truth.

The adversaries shall not interrupt the speech of the witness and shall not attempt to influence him or direct questions directly to him while he is giving testimony, under penalty of their expulsion from the hall in which the hearing is held.

The President of the Court or the delegated judge may, where necessary, hear the witnesses anew or conduct a confrontation among them or between them and the adversaries, and may hear them in the presence of a technical expert. The witnesses shall remain at the disposal of the President or the delegated judge until the conclusion of the investigation hearing, and they may request to be heard anew to provide additional information modifying the testimony they have given.

The President of the Court or the delegated judge may order one of the adversaries to step out in order to further secure the freedom of the witness, provided that he re-enters after the giving of the testimony and it is read out to him.

Testimony shall be given orally, and no recourse to any writing shall be permitted except by leave of the court or the delegated judge and where the nature of the dispute justifies this. If the witness is ignorant of the Arabic language, he shall give his testimony in the language he knows, and it shall be translated through an interpreter appointed by the President of the Court or the delegated judge, who shall administer the oath to him to perform the translation with truthfulness and fidelity.
Whoever is unable to speak shall give the testimony if it is possible for him to make his meaning clear in writing or by sign.

The answers of the witness shall be recorded in the minutes of the hearing in their entirety without alteration therein, and shall then be read out to the person who made them, and he may introduce into them whatever amendment he sees fit, and the amendment shall be mentioned following the text of the testimony. Every question directed to the witness and any remarks regarding his testimony shall likewise be recorded in the minutes. The witness shall sign the minutes, and if he refuses to sign, that fact and its reason shall be mentioned in the minutes.
The court shall assess the expenses of the witnesses upon their request, and they shall receive what is assessed for them out of the amount deposited on account of the expenses.

Failure to claim the expenses specified in the preceding Article within eight days from the date of giving the testimony shall forfeit the right of the witness thereto, and the advanced amount shall be refunded to whichever of the adversaries paid it.
The assessment of the value of the testimony of witnesses on the merits shall rest absolutely with the court.

Any person who fears losing the opportunity to call a witness on a matter that has not yet been brought before the judiciary and is likely to be brought before it may request, in the presence of the concerned parties, that the said witness be heard. This request shall be submitted by the ordinary means to the judge of urgent matters, and all its expenses shall be borne by the party who submitted it, and once necessity is established, the judge shall decide to hear the witness whenever the fact is one that may be proved by the testimony of witnesses.

In this case, it shall neither be permissible to deliver a copy of the record of the inquiry nor to submit it to the judiciary unless the court of the merits, upon examining it, deems that the fact may be proved by the testimony of witnesses. The adversary may object before it to the admission of this evidence, and may also request the hearing of rebuttal witnesses in his interest.
The foregoing rules shall be followed in this inquiry, except as provided for in Articles 269 and 270.
Presumptions are conclusions drawn, by operation of law or at the discretion of the judge, from a known fact to infer an unknown fact.
Presumptions are of two kinds: legal presumptions and judicial presumptions.

A legal presumption is one provided for by law, and it relieves the person in whose favour it is established of any other means of proof. However, this presumption may be rebutted by proof to the contrary, unless there is a provision to the contrary.

A judicial presumption is one not provided for by law, and which the judge deduces from the circumstances and facts of the action by virtue of his discretionary power.

Proof by judicial presumptions shall only be permissible in the cases in which proof by the testimony of witnesses is permissible. Such proof shall be permissible in particular when the presumption is drawn from facts that may be considered a voluntary performance, in whole or in part, of the alleged obligation.

Final judgments are conclusive evidence as to the rights adjudicated therein, and no evidence rebutting this conclusive authority may be admitted. However, such judgments shall only have this conclusive authority in a dispute that has arisen between the same adversaries without their capacities having changed, and that involves the same subject matter and cause. The court may raise this conclusive authority of its own motion.

The judge of urgent matters may, in the case set forth in the preceding Article, commission one of the experts to proceed to the site, carry out an inspection and hear witnesses without oath, and in such case he shall appoint a hearing to hear the observations of the adversaries on the expert's report and works. The rules provided for in the Chapter relating to expertise shall be followed.

The court may decide to appoint an expert to carry out an inspection, to render a technical consultation, or to conduct a technical investigation concerning a matter that requires technical knowledge.

The expert shall be chosen from among the experts appointed on a special roster, and he may, by a reasoned decision, be chosen from among others, even from among foreigners. Regard shall be had in choosing the expert to his technical knowledge in relation to the subject-matter of the investigation. If the expert's name is not entered on the roster, he must take an oath before the court that appointed him to perform his work with honesty and faithfulness, failing which the work shall be null and void.

The expert shall personally carry out the mission entrusted to him. However, he may seek the assistance of persons working for him under his supervision and control. If the expert is a legal person, its legal representative shall indicate to the court the name of the natural person or natural persons who shall assume, within the scope of that person and in its name, the execution of the mission. The assignment of such persons shall be subject to the approval of the court.

An expert may be recused for the same grounds as justify the recusal of a judge. If the expert is a legal person, the application for recusal may be directed against the natural person or persons who assume the execution of the mission and whom the court has approved. The application for recusal shall be submitted to the court that appointed the expert. If a ground for recusal arises in respect of the expert, he must of his own motion submit his withdrawal to the court that appointed him.

The adversary shall submit the application for recusal within a time limit of three days from the date of service upon him of the extract of the decision appointing the expert or from the date of his knowledge of the ground for recusal, by a petition in which he states the grounds for recusal and which shall be served upon the expert and upon the other adversary, and each of them shall be entitled to submit his observations within three days. The court shall rule on the application for recusal within a similar time limit without summoning the adversaries. The judgment rendered thereon shall not be subject to any recourse.

In the event of acceptance of the recusal or withdrawal, or of the expert's refusal of the mission, or of the impossibility of serving it upon him, or of the existence of any legal impediment, the court shall proceed to replace the expert. The court may also, of its own motion or upon the application of the adversaries, decide to replace an expert who fails to perform his duties, after hearing his statements unless the court decides to dispense therewith for futility.
The court that appointed the expert may decide to broaden or narrow the mission that it entrusted him to perform.
The civil judge shall not be bound by the criminal judgment except in respect of the facts upon which that judgment has adjudicated and where its adjudication thereon was necessary.

If the criminal judgment rules to absolve the defendant of liability, confining itself to examining the act from the standpoint of criminalization without negating its occurrence, it shall not preclude pursuing the defendant before the civil judiciary for compensation.

Possession of a movable in good faith and in a public, peaceful, and unambiguous manner is conclusive proof of its ownership which may not be rebutted by any evidence. Nevertheless, a person who has lost or had stolen from him movable property may claim recovery of title thereto against the person who possesses it, within three years commencing from the day of its loss or theft. The possessor shall have a right of recourse against the person from whom he received it.

If the possessor of the movable purchased it in a public market or from a seller who sells similar items, he shall not be compelled to return it to its rightful owner except against the price that he paid, subject to the special provisions relating to instruments made out to bearer.

The court may decide, of its own motion or upon the request of one of the adversaries, to proceed to inspect the disputed thing. It may delegate one of its judges for this purpose. If the dispute relates to movable property and its transport is possible, the court may decide to have it brought before it to inspect it unless it deems that it is more conducive to the investigation to inspect it in its place. The decision ordering the inspection shall state the appointed time at which it shall take place.

If the court decides to inspect the disputed thing at the place where it is located, the adversaries must be summoned to attend the inspection at least three days prior to its appointed time unless the court decides to shorten the time limit. The court, or the person whom it delegates from among its judges, may appoint an expert to assist it in the inspection. It, or the delegated judge, may hear the adversaries and such witnesses whose hearing is necessary, and the summoning of these persons to attend shall be effected, even if orally, by the clerk of the court.

The clerk shall draw up a record of the inspection in which he shall record the facts ascertained by the court or the delegated judge, and the president of the court or the delegated judge and the clerk shall sign it, and this record shall be joined to the case file.

Any person who fears the loss of the features of a fact that is likely to become the subject of a dispute before the judiciary may request the judge of urgent matters to proceed to an inspection. The judge may decide, where necessary, to summon the interested parties to attend the inspection. The provisions set forth in the preceding Articles shall be observed.

The expert shall carry out the mission with honesty, fidelity and impartiality. He shall express his opinion on the matters into which he has been entrusted to investigate, and shall not address other matters unless the litigants agree in writing thereto. He may not express an assessment of a legal nature.
The expert shall abide by the time limits set for him.
The court may not entrust the expert with the mission of conciliation between the litigants.

The expert may obtain oral or written information from any person, provided that he states his first name, surname, profession and place of residence, and, where applicable, the relationship of consanguinity or affinity or any other relationship existing between him and the litigants. The court may thereafter hear the testimony of this person if it deems it useful for the investigation.
The expert may request from the litigants or third parties the delivery to him of any document that assists in carrying out the mission. The court may order this where necessary.

The expert must state in the report containing his opinion all the information that would enlighten the court on the matters required to be investigated. He is prohibited from disclosing other information of which he has become aware during the execution of his mission.

The court may at any time summon the expert to complete or clarify incomplete or ambiguous information in his report, whether in writing or orally at the hearing. The expert may request the court to hear him at any time.
The opinion of the expert does not bind the court, nor does the information contained in his report.

The opinion of the expert, the disclosure of which leads to the infringement of the tranquility of private life or of any other legitimate interest, may not be adduced as evidence regarding matters outside the scope of the dispute unless the court authorises this or the litigant concerned agrees thereto.
The expert is prohibited from receiving directly from one of the litigants, and in any form whatsoever, a remuneration, even by way of payment of expenses, unless the court decides this.

The court may appoint an expert whose mission it restricts to inspecting the disputed thing. The expert shall refrain from expressing an opinion on the factual or legal consequences that may result from the inspection with which he is entrusted.
The clerk of the court shall notify the expert of the decision issued appointing him and specifying his mission.
The expert shall record the facts that he inspects in a report which he submits to the court, unless the latter decides that the information be submitted orally to it.

The court shall fix the time limit within which the expert must deposit his report or the date of the hearing at which he submits his information orally. It shall order the litigants or one of them to pay in advance an advance on account of the fees of the expert, the amount of which it shall fix.

The expert shall deposit his report with the registry of the court, and it shall be joined to the file of the case. If the expert submits his information orally, it shall be recorded in the minutes of the hearing.
The court shall fix the remuneration for the fees of the expert immediately upon the execution of the mission.

The judge of urgent matters may, upon a petition submitted to him by an interested party prior to the institution of any action, order the appointment of an expert to conduct a technical inspection by a decision taken at the foot of the petition, even without summoning the other adversary. The rules provided for in the preceding Articles shall be followed.

If a purely technical issue that does not require complex investigations is raised in the action, the court may commission an expert to provide a consultation to it regarding such issue. The consultation shall be given orally unless the court decides that it be submitted in writing.
The clerk of the court shall notify the expert of the decision issued appointing him and defining his mission.

The court shall fix the date of the hearing at which the consultation shall be given orally, or the time limit within which the written consultation must be filed. It shall order the adversaries, or one of them, to advance a deposit on account of the expert's fees, the amount of which it shall fix.

If the consultation is given orally, its content shall be recorded in the minutes of the hearing, which must be signed by the expert. However, if it is given in writing, it shall be filed with the registry of the court and joined to the file of the case.
The court shall fix the remuneration of the expert's fees immediately upon the execution of the mission.
Recourse to a technical investigation through an expert shall only be had in the case where an inspection or a consultation is not sufficient to enlighten the conviction of the court.

The technical investigation may cover taking a measure upon the human body - such as a blood test - provided that it is not contrary to the rules of the art or conducive to significant harm. The court may draw from the refusal of one of the adversaries to submit to this measure a presumption as to the validity of the condition or fact sought to be proved.

The decision ordering the technical investigation shall include:

1- The name and surname of the expert and other particulars indicating his identity.

2- The name of the judge commissioned to supervise his work, where necessary.

3- A statement of the matters in which his expertise is sought, and the urgent measures which he is authorised to take.

4- The amount required to be deposited with the court fund on account of the expert's expenses and fees, the litigant ordered to deposit this amount, the period within which the deposit is to be made, and the amount that may be withdrawn for his expenses and fees.

5- Specification of the period within which the expert must file his report.

6- Adjournment of the trial to a specified date pending receipt of the expert's report.

If the litigant abstains from depositing the amount he is ordered to deposit within the period specified in accordance with the provisions of the preceding Article, the court may draw such consequences as it deems fit from this abstention.

Following the deposit of the aforementioned amount, the registry shall serve upon the expert a copy of the decision ordering the investigation within a period of three days and invite him to assume his mission. The expert shall have the right to inspect the case file at the registry even before accepting the mission, provided that no papers therefrom are handed over to him.

The expert may, within three days from the date he is served with the decision, request to be exempted from the mission, and the president of the court that appointed him or the judge who appointed him may exempt him therefrom if he deems that the reasons he has put forward are acceptable. In urgent actions, the court may decide in its judgment to shorten this period.

Article 348- If the expert does not carry out his mission after having accepted it, or delays in submitting his report within the appointed period, a formal notice shall be addressed to him to complete his work within a new appropriate period. If he fails to do so and does not put forward an acceptable excuse, he shall be replaced by another and fined a pecuniary penalty from forty thousand to two hundred thousand Lebanese pounds and ordered to refund to the court registry the amount he may have received on account of his expenses or fees, in addition to the disciplinary penalty that may be imposed upon him and the compensation that may be due to the injured party. The judgment issued replacing the expert and ordering him to refund what he received on account of his expenses and fees shall not be subject to appeal.

If the delay arises from the fault of the litigant, he shall be sentenced to a fine from forty thousand to two hundred thousand Lebanese pounds, and a judgment may be rendered forfeiting his right to invoke the decision issued appointing the expert. A copy of every judgment imposing a fine that issues the expert who defaults on performing his duties shall be served upon the Supreme Judicial Council to be joined to his file and thereafter to issue the appropriate disciplinary penalties against him.

The expert shall fix a date for the commencement of his work not exceeding the fifteen days following the notification to him of the decision appointing him, and he shall summon the adversaries by registered letters or by telegrams with acknowledgement of receipt sent at least seven days before that date, informing them therein of the place, day, and hour of the first meeting. In cases of urgency, the judgment may provide for the commencement of the work within the three days following the date of notification to the expert of the decision appointing him at the latest, and in such case the adversaries shall be summoned by a telegram with acknowledgement of receipt at least twenty-four hours before the first meeting. In cases of extreme urgency, the judgment may provide for the immediate commencement of the mission and the summoning of the adversaries by telegram to attend forthwith. The expert shall notify the time and place at which he commences the mission to the judge delegated to supervise the investigation, if one has been appointed. Failure to summon the adversaries shall entail the nullity of the expert's work.

The adversaries may attend the technical investigation proceedings in person or through their lawyers. They shall deliver to the expert without delay all documents which he deems necessary for the execution of his mission. If they fail to do so, he shall inform the court of the matter, and it shall take a decision either compelling the adversaries to produce the documents under penalty of a coercive fine where necessary, or authorising the expert to dispense with the production of the documents, or also to file his report in the current state.

The expert shall take into consideration the observations and requests of the adversaries, and if they are submitted to him in writing, he shall annex them to the report if the adversaries so request. He must indicate in the report the conclusion he has drawn therefrom.
The expert may, of his own motion, seek the opinion of another expert, but only in respect of a technical matter requiring a specialisation different from his own.

If an obstacle impedes the expert's work and prevents its continuation, or if it appears necessary to expand the scope of his mission, he shall submit a report thereon to the court. The court may take the appropriate decision in the light thereof and may extend, where necessary, the time limit within which the expert must submit the report.

The court may order the deposit of an additional sum on account of the expert's expenses and fees if it becomes apparent that the sum originally deposited is insufficient. It may authorise the expert to receive a payment on account.

Article 355 - If a settlement takes place between the adversaries and the expert verifies it, he shall submit a report thereon to the court indicating the same and that his mission has consequently become without object. The adversaries may request the court to homologate the settlement in order to grant it executory force.

The judge shall give the proper legal characterisation to the disputed facts and acts without being bound by the characterisation given to them by the litigants. He may raise of his own motion pure legal grounds regardless of the legal basis invoked by the litigants. However, he may not alter the characterisation or the legal basis where the litigants, by their express agreement and concerning rights of which they have free disposal, have bound him by a characterisation and points of law to which they intended to restrict the debate.
The judge may request from the litigants, concerning the facts or the points of law, the clarifications that he deems necessary to adjudicate the dispute.
No judgment may in any event be rendered against a litigant who has not been heard or enabled to present his defence.

The judge must, in all circumstances, observe and enforce the observance of the adversarial principle. He may not rely in his judgment on grounds or clarifications put forward by one of the litigants or on documents produced by him unless he has enabled the other litigants to debate them adversarially. Nor may he base his judgment on legal grounds that he has raised of his own motion without having invited the litigants beforehand to submit their observations thereon.

Where the law permits or necessity requires the ordering of a measure without the knowledge of a litigant, the latter shall have the right to challenge the decision prejudicial to him by the appropriate means.
Conciliation between the litigants falls within the mission of the judge.
The trial shall be public unless the law requires or permits that it be conducted in camera or in the deliberation chamber.
The judge is not required to have recourse to an interpreter if he knows the language spoken by the litigants.
The opinion of the expert shall not bind the court. Where the judgment is contrary to the opinion of the expert, in part or in whole, the reasons justifying such departure must be stated.

The parties alone shall have the right to institute the action save in the cases where the law provides otherwise, and they shall conduct the proceedings of the trial together with the burdens incumbent upon them, in accordance with the forms and formalities and within the prescribed time-limits. They may bring the trial to an end before it terminates by the rendering of the judgment or pursuant to the law.
The judge shall oversee the proper conduct of the trial and, to that end, shall have the right to grant time-limits and to take the necessary measures.

The subject-matter of the dispute shall be determined by the claims of the parties set forth in the summons and the pleadings. It may be modified by incidental claims fulfilling the conditions set out in Article 30.
The judge must rule in his judgment on all that is claimed and only on what is claimed.
The parties must adduce the facts upon which they base their claims.

The judge may not base his judgment on facts outside the scope of the trial. However, he may take into consideration the facts appearing in the trial even if the parties have not specifically invoked them to support their claims or defences.
The judge shall decide the dispute in accordance with the legal rules applicable thereto.

The expert shall draw up a record of his operations comprising a statement of the attendance of the litigants and their statements and observations signed by them unless they have an impediment thereto, which shall be mentioned in the record, and also comprising a statement of the expert's operations in detail and the statements of the persons whom he heard of his own motion or at the request of the litigants, and their signatures.

The expert must draw up a report in which he includes the result of his operations, his opinion, and the grounds upon which he relies in justifying this opinion, with accuracy and clarity. Where there are multiple experts and they differ in opinion, they must draw up a single report and state therein the opinion of each of them and the reasons therefor. Where the expert seeks the assistance of the opinion of another expert in a specialisation that differs from his own specialisation, this opinion shall be annexed to the report.
The expert must file his report, accompanied by the record, with the court registry against a receipt, and request by virtue of a detailed statement the assessment of his fees and expenses.

The court registry shall send to each of the litigants a copy of the expert's report immediately upon its filing, and they may submit their observations thereon within a time limit of ten days from the date of service. The court may shorten or extend this time limit where necessary.

Where it appears to the court that the expert's report is incomplete or unclear, it may summon the expert to seek clarification from him, and it may also resort to additional expertise. In the event of not adopting the expert's report in whole or in part due to a defect in its form or a deficiency in its substance resulting from the negligence or error of the expert, it may order the expert to refund what he received by way of remuneration and expenses or assign him to conduct a new or additional investigation without remuneration, and notify the matter to the Supreme Judicial Council. Where it appears to the court that the report contains gross errors, it shall refer a copy thereof to the Supreme Judicial Council to be placed in the expert's file and thereafter for the issuance of the appropriate disciplinary penalties against him.

The expert's fees and expenses shall be determined by a decision of the President of the court that appointed him or of the single judge who appointed him. The expert, as well as the litigants, shall have the right to object to this decision before the authority that appointed him within a time limit of three days from the date of service. The objection shall be submitted by virtue of a petition to the court registry, and it shall rule thereon in the council chamber after summoning the litigants. The judgment rendered as a result of the objection shall not be subject to any means of recourse. However, an expert registered on the roster who is assigned to carry out the investigation in the interest of a litigant who has been granted legal aid shall be bound to perform the mission free of charge. Nevertheless, it shall remain open to him to claim his remuneration from the other litigant if the latter is ordered to pay the costs of the action, or from the litigant who was granted legal aid after he becomes solvent.

The parties shall be assisted by an attorney as a representative in cases in which the value of the claim exceeds one million Lebanese pounds, or which have no determinate value, and in other cases in which the law requires the assistance of an attorney.

Article 379- The appointment of an attorney as representative in the action or proceeding shall be effected pursuant to an official instrument. However, in cases the value of which does not exceed one million Lebanese pounds, the appointment before the court of first instance may be effected pursuant to a power of attorney drawn up before the Mukhtar or by a declaration by the principal recorded in the minutes of the trial hearing.

The appointment of an attorney as representative confers upon him the authority to perform the acts and procedures necessary to institute and pursue the action or to defend therein at all levels of litigation and avenues of recourse, to take conservatory measures, to serve and be served with judgments and the procedures for their enforcement, and to receive judicial fees, expenses and securities, without prejudice to that for which the law requires a special authorisation. Any restriction in the instrument of power of attorney contrary to the foregoing may not be invoked against the other party.

Without a special authorisation, it shall not be valid to acknowledge the claimed right, to waive it, to compromise or arbitrate thereon, to accept, tender or refer back the oath, to discontinue the proceeding, to waive the judgment or any of the avenues of recourse against it, to lift an attachment, to waive securities notwithstanding the subsistence of the debt, to allege forgery, to recuse an expert, to make or accept an actual tender, or to perform any other act for which the law requires a special authorisation.

By the mere appointment of an attorney as representative, his office becomes an elected domicile for his principal in all matters relating to the procedures of the proceeding in which he used his power of attorney and the procedures for the enforcement of the judgments rendered as a result of such proceeding. He may not thereupon refuse service. Service shall be valid when made upon the representative attorney and upon any of his partner or associate attorneys or upon any of the employees working in his office.
Where there are multiple representatives, each of them may act individually without regard to any contrary provision in the instrument of power of attorney.
The representative may substitute another attorney for himself unless he is expressly prohibited from substitution in the power of attorney.

The principal of an attorney may revoke the power of attorney and dismiss his representative; however, such revocation or dismissal shall not take effect vis-a-vis the judiciary except after it is notified to the court registry. In such case, the principal shall appoint a new attorney, and if he fails to do so, all procedures may be served upon him at the court registry unless he has a known domicile or has elected a domicile within the territorial jurisdiction of the court, in which case he shall be served at such domicile.

An advocate may withdraw from his mandate provided that he notifies this withdrawal to his client and to the court registry. He must continue to carry out the acts of the mandate until another advocate is appointed in his place or the expiry of a reasonable period for such appointment, provided that it does not exceed fifteen days from the date of notifying the client of the withdrawal. In the event that the client fails to appoint another advocate within the aforementioned time limit, the provisions of the second paragraph of the preceding Article shall apply.
The court registry shall consist of a chief registrar, clerks, and bailiffs who are subject to special regulations. The president of the court shall supervise them and distribute the work among them.
The registry officials shall perform the duties imposed upon them pursuant to this Law and other special laws and regulations.

The chief registrar, or whichever clerk deputises for him, shall receive all writs of summons, petitions, pleadings, and documents, issue a receipt therefor, and register them after collecting the legal fees. He shall arrange a separate file for each case in accordance with the provisions of Article 448.
Under pain of nullity, the court must be assisted in trial, investigation, and inspection hearings by a clerk who shall draw up and sign the minutes.

The adversaries or their representatives may inspect the case file at the court registry and obtain copies of the papers and documents after the chief registrar or the clerk certifies their conformity with the original, upon payment of the expenses.

The court clerks shall arrange and keep the case files, and organise the hearing rolls, the trial minutes, and the registers designated for the entry of actions and the recording of judgments and decisions, whether contentious or non-contentious.
All registers shall be numbered, and their first and last pages shall be initialled by the president of the court or by a judge delegated by him for this purpose.

The Chief Clerk or the clerk whom he deputises shall deliver to the prevailing party in whose favour judgment was rendered a copy of the judgment bearing the phrase "Certified true copy valid for enforcement" and appended with his signature, after collecting the fees and verifying the enforceability of the judgment. He may also, after the fees have been paid, deliver in return for payment of the expenses a certified true copy to any person whomsoever, save for the legal exceptions.

The registers containing the originals of judgments and decisions may not be removed from the registry of any court of first instance or of appeal except pursuant to a special decision issued by the First President of the Court of Appeal, nor may such registers be removed from the registry of the Court of Cassation except pursuant to a decision issued by the First President of that Court, upon the request of the Public Prosecution or any interested party. This decision shall specify the manner of removing the registers and returning them in the shortest possible time.

Clerks and bailiffs may not perform any measure falling within the limits of their functions in actions concerning themselves or their spouses, relatives by blood, or relatives by marriage up to the fourth degree, under pain of nullity.

Notice to the concerned parties of the contents of the trial papers and its measures shall be effected by way of service. The rules of service provided for in this Chapter may be followed even where the law provides for another manner of notifying the concerned parties of the contents of the papers or the measures.
Service shall be effected by the hand of a bailiff. It may also be effected through members of the police or gendarmerie. It may likewise be effected through the clerk in the registry.

The papers required to be served shall be delivered to the person himself at his domicile, his residence, his place of work, or any other place in which he is found. They may be delivered at the elected domicile in the cases specified by law. If the bailiff does not know the person required to be served, he shall deliver the papers at the domicile or residence of the latter to the person who declares that he is the person intended by the service; outside the domicile or residence, however, he shall not deliver the papers to the person intended to be served until after inspecting official papers from him proving his identity. The bailiff shall note in the record of service the declaration of the person served or the aforementioned manner of proving his identity, while inserting the number of the identity document.

In the event of the refusal of the person required to be notified or the person with whom is taken

an elected domicile to receive the papers, the bailiff shall leave them for him.

Receipt of service shall then be deemed to have been legally effected, even if he refuses

to sign the record.

If the bailiff does not find the person to be served at his domicile or residence, he may deliver the document to any person who declares that he is his agent or works in his service or is among those residing with him from among the spouses, relatives, and relatives by marriage whose appearance indicates that they have completed the eighteenth year of their age, provided that the interest of the person to be served is conflicting with their interest.

In the event that one of the persons mentioned above refuses to receive

the documents, the bailiff shall leave them for him, and service shall then be deemed to have taken place

legally, even if he refuses to sign the record.

If the law requires the adversary to elect a chosen domicile and he fails to do so, or if the statement of such domicile is incomplete or incorrect, he may be served at the registry of the court with all the documents that could validly be served upon him at the chosen domicile, with the exception of the final judgment. Service of the documents shall be made to the chief clerk, and the bailiff shall draw up a record thereof in accordance with the conditions stipulated in Article 405, and a copy of the served document shall be posted on the notice board of the court.

Save as otherwise provided in special laws, documents shall be served in the following manner:

1- With respect to the State and other public persons: service shall be made to the person who represents it by law or to the person acting in his stead.

2- With respect to companies, associations, and other legal persons: service shall be made at the head office of the legal person, or at its branch referred to in Article 101 paragraph 2, or at the branch of the foreign legal person located in Lebanon, or at the office of its agent, to its legal representative or to the person in charge of the branch or to the agent or to any person who declares that he deputizes for any of them, and if none of them is present, to one of the members or employees present. If the legal person has no head office, branch, or agency office, the documents shall be served upon the legal representative or the agent in person or at his domicile. In the event that the persons mentioned in the two preceding sentences refuse service, the provisions of Article 399 paragraph 4 shall apply with respect to the legal representative or the agent, and the provisions of Article 401 shall apply with respect to the other persons.

3- With respect to members of the army: service shall be made through the unit command.

4- With respect to prisoners: service shall be made through the director of the prison.

5- With respect to seamen of merchant ships or persons working thereon: service shall be made through the master.

6- With respect to a person lacking capacity, a person of diminished capacity, or a missing person: service shall be made to his statutory representative. If the person of diminished capacity has a judicial supervisor, a copy of the document shall be served and another copy to the judicial supervisor, and the time limits shall run as of the date of the last service.
If there are multiple agents or representatives of the person to be served, service may be made to one of them.

The record of service must contain the following particulars:

1- A statement of the place of service and the date of its occurrence by day, month, year and hour.

2- The forename, surname, profession or office, and domicile of the party requesting service, and the forename, surname, profession or office, and domicile of the person representing him.

3- The name of the court that ordered the execution of the service.

4- The nature of the document being served.

5- The forename, surname, profession or office, and domicile of the person served, and if his domicile is not known at the time of service, the last domicile he had.

6- The name and capacity of the person to whom the document required to be served was delivered.

7- A statement of the delivery of the document required to be served to the person who received it and the taking of his signature. In the event of his refusal to receive the document or to sign, an indication of such refusal and its reason in the record, as well as an indication therein that the document required to be served was left for the person required to be served in person.

8- The name of the bailiff who carried out the service and his signature. Where applicable, the bailiff must also state in the record of service the particulars referred to in Articles 399 and 401. Where the service upon the adversary or another interested party concerns a judgment or a judicial or non-contentious decision, the time limit for opposition, third-party opposition, appeal or cassation must be stated in the instrument of service.

The bailiff or the person carrying out the service must lodge the record of service with the court registry within forty-eight hours at most, failing which he shall be liable to a fine of twenty thousand to forty thousand Lebanese pounds, to be imposed by the court. This record shall be joined to the case file.
If ordinary service is impossible for any reason, recourse shall be had to exceptional service after the court has verified the existence of such impossibility.

If the person required to be served has no known domicile, exceptional service shall be carried out after the court has verified this matter. The court shall verify that the person required to be served is of unknown domicile on the basis of a thorough and complete investigation carried out by the process server with the relatives, neighbours and acquaintances of the person required to be served and the mukhtar of the locality where he used to reside, and in the light of the clarifications provided to him by the party requesting service in this regard.

Extraordinary service shall be effected by the court registry sending, within an envelope sealed with its seal, a registered letter with acknowledgment of receipt to the last known domicile or residence that the person sought to be served may have and to his elected domicile if any exists, summoning him therein to appear at the registry to receive the document addressed to him. The envelope addressed to the elected domicile must mention the person to whom the letter may be delivered. If the addressee refuses to receive the letter, the postal officer shall return it without delay to the court registry endorsed with a note of his refusal, and it shall be joined to the case file to serve as proof that service has been effected. If the postal officer does not find the person to whom service is addressed at the indicated domicile, he shall record the fact and return the letter to the court registry.
