In this case, as in the case where the person sought to be served has no known domicile, residence, or elected domicile, a copy of the document sought to be served shall be posted on the notice board of the court for a period of twenty days, and an announcement notifying the person sought to be served of the existence of a service concerning him at the court shall be published in a daily newspaper among the newspapers designated for judicial announcements, and service shall be completed upon the expiry of twenty days from the posting of the copy and the publication of the announcement. The record of service shall be replaced by a certificate from the clerk attesting thereto.

Where service is subject to lapse if it is not effected within a specified time limit, delivering the document sought to be served to the bailiff shall have the effect of suspending the running of this time limit.

Service of documents directly between lawyers shall be valid, provided that the document sought to be served is sent to the other lawyer in two copies, and he immediately returns one of them, which must be submitted to the court, to his colleague after placing the date thereon and signing it by way of acknowledgment of service.

If the place of service is outside the territorial jurisdiction of the court, its president may send the documents sought to be served to the president of the court within whose territorial jurisdiction service is requested.

If service is addressed to a person residing in a foreign country, it shall be effected by a registered letter with acknowledgment of receipt, or through the Lebanese embassy or consulate in the said country, or in accordance with the rules prescribed in the local law. If service proves impossible, the court may deem the person to whom service is addressed to be of unknown domicile, and service upon him shall be effected by the extraordinary method.

If service is addressed to a representative of a foreign State or of an international organisation or body, or to one of their envoys in Lebanon, it shall be effected through the Ministries of Justice and Foreign Affairs in Lebanon by means of a letter in two copies, the second copy of which the party served shall return, dated and signed by it, to the court ordering the service.
The court shall summon the applicant for legal aid and his adversary to appear before it in the deliberation chamber, and it may examine the application even in their absence.
The court registry shall serve the two adversaries and the Public Prosecution with the contents of the decision rendered by the court, and this decision shall not be subject to any recourse.
The decision issued granting legal aid shall be served upon the President of the Bar Association, who shall appoint a lawyer to defend the interests of the person who obtained such aid.

The assistance provided by the lawyer in this manner shall be free of charge, and he may not receive or attempt to receive any fee or any benefit from the person whose interests he defends. However, the court may order the other adversary, in the event that he loses the action, to pay the advocacy fee if he has not been granted legal aid.
The registry formalities pertaining to the aided person shall be free of charge, and the expenses of the necessary measures pertaining to the investigation shall be borne by the State Treasury.

In all cases, even prior to the institution of the principal action, the court that granted legal aid may revoke its decision of its own motion or upon the request of the Public Prosecution or the Ministry of Finance if the circumstances for which the aid was granted have changed or have proved to be untrue. In this latter case, the aid shall be cancelled with retroactive effect.
Legal aid shall lapse upon the death of the aided person, and its lapse shall not have retroactive effect. The heirs of the aided person may apply for legal aid where necessary.
If the aided person wins the action, his adversary shall be ordered to pay the costs, including the costs advanced for the measures pertaining to the investigation.

No trial or enforcement measure may validly be carried out, and it shall be deemed null and void if carried out:

1- On official holidays.

2- Before seven o'clock in the morning and after eight o'clock in the evening, unless the person for whom the measure is intended accepts it, or the measure is a continuation of what was commenced during the legal time.

There shall be exempted from the provisions of the preceding article:

1- Measures in summary matters.

2- Measures which the court orders to be carried out in view of circumstances justifying urgency.
If the condition of one of the litigants does not enable him to pay the trial fees and expenses, he may apply to be granted legal aid.

Legal aid shall be granted to natural persons of Lebanese nationality, as well as to foreigners habitually resident in Lebanon subject to reciprocity. Such aid may exceptionally be granted to legal persons that do not seek profit and whose centre of management or operations is in Lebanon.

Legal aid may be applied for in order to institute a first-instance action or to defend therein. It may also be applied for, even if submitted for the first time, in order to exercise means of recourse. The submission of this application within the time limit for recourse shall result in suspending that time limit until the notification of the decision issued in respect thereof to the applicant for aid.

The application for aid shall be submitted by way of a petition exempt from fees and fiscal stamp drawn up in three copies, and lodged with the registry of the court that will hear the action; the clerk shall retain one copy, send the second to the opponent, who may submit his written observations within five days, and send the third copy to the Public Prosecution, which may also express an opinion within a time limit of five days. If the action is to be brought before the Single Judge, the application for aid shall be submitted to the First Instance Chamber within whose district the judge is located.

There shall be attached to the application a certificate from the Revenue and Treasury Departments at the Ministry of Finance (Directorate General of Finance) indicating the direct taxes paid by the applicant for aid, and a certificate from any local authority proving his indigence.

Whatever the financial condition of the applicant for aid may be, his application shall be dismissed if it clearly appears that his claim or defence is inadmissible or unfounded. An application for aid submitted to the Court of Cassation may be refused if the petition for cassation is devoid of any mention of a serious ground for cassation.

Where the law prescribes a time limit for bringing an action, lodging an appeal or performing any procedural act, such time limit shall run from the date of the act, event, decision or service which the law deems to set it running.
Where the law prescribes that a time limit must expire before a procedural act is taken, the procedural act may not take place before the expiry of the last day of that time limit.

Time limits for judicial proceedings shall be fixed in days, months or years, or also in hours. A time limit fixed in days shall be calculated from midnight of the commencement of the time limit until midnight of the day appointed for its expiry. A time limit fixed in months or years shall be calculated from the day of its commencement in a given month or year until the corresponding day in the month or year in which the time limit expires. Where there is no corresponding day, the time limit shall expire on the last day of the month. A time limit fixed in hours shall be calculated from the hour at which it commenced until the hour appointed for its expiry.

The day of service or of the occurrence of the matter which the law deems to set the time limit running shall not be included in the calculation of a time limit appointed in days, months or years. Likewise, the hour at which it commenced shall not be included in the calculation of a time limit appointed in hours. The time limit shall expire upon the expiry of the last day or the last hour thereof.
Where the end of a time limit falls on an official holiday, it shall be extended to the first working day following it.

Where the person to whom the procedural act is directed resides outside Lebanon, there shall be added to the original time limit:

1- Thirty days if he resides in one of the Arab States or in Turkey or Cyprus.

2- Sixty days if he resides in other countries. These time limits may, by order of the judge or the court, be reduced according to the ease of communications and circumstances of urgency. Any person who is temporarily present in Lebanon and is served in person shall not benefit from distance time limits.

An elected domicile appointed in an express agreement or arising from the mandate of an advocate shall be deemed equivalent to the actual domicile with respect to distance time limits. The court registry shall also be deemed equivalent to such domicile when service is effected therein in accordance with the provisions of Articles 402 and 405.
Exceeding any of the time limits appointed in this Law for the exercise of a right shall result in the forfeiture of that right.
A litigant who has been granted legal aid shall remain entitled to benefit therefrom for the enforcement of the judgment or for defending himself when avenues of challenge are exercised against it.

If the aided party loses the lawsuit, no fee shall be collected from him for the measures carried out in his interest, and he shall not be bound to refund the sums advanced by the State Treasury unless his solvency is subsequently proved or established.
The head of the Enforcement Department may grant legal aid for the purpose of enforcement in accordance with the preceding rules.

Disputes shall be brought before the Court of First Instance:

- Either by a statement of claim addressed by the plaintiff to his adversary setting forth the matters in respect of which judgment is requested.

- Or by a joint petition in which two disputing parties set forth the subject-matter of an existing dispute between them and request that it be adjudicated.

Where the dispute is brought by a joint petition, such petition must contain the following:

1- The name of the court to which it is submitted.

2- The given name, surname, profession or occupation, and domicile of each of the disputants, and if a legal person, an indication of its form, name or trade name, principal place of business, and the name of its legal representative.

3- A detailed statement of the subject-matter of the dispute and the issues in contention between the disputants, together with the claims of each of them and the evidence or arguments which he invokes in support of such claims.

4- A statement of the documents upon which each of the disputants bases his claims and the grounds of his defence or his arguments, and the attachment of copies of such documents to the petition.

5- The date of submission of the petition and the signature of each of the disputing parties, or the signature of their counsel in cases where representation by counsel is mandatory, with an indication of the date of the power of attorney and the authority that authenticated it, and the attachment of a copy thereof to the petition.

Upon the filing of the joint petition with the court registry and its registration after collection of the fee, it shall be submitted immediately to the president, who shall forthwith fix a hearing date to be notified to each of the parties without delay through the clerk.

In the event of a claim by one adversary against another, the action shall be instituted by a statement of claim containing the following particulars:

1- The name of the court before which the action is brought.

2- The name of each of the plaintiff and the defendant, his surname, his profession or occupation, and his domicile, and, where applicable, the name of his legal representative, his surname, his profession or occupation, his capacity, and his domicile; if it is a legal person, an indication of its form, its name or trade name, its principal place of business, and the name of its legal representative; and the mention of the name and identity of the proxy lawyer, where there is one, while attaching a copy of the power of attorney to the statement of claim.

3- The facts of the action, its grounds, the evidence supporting it, and the claims of the plaintiff, which must be set forth in a clear and detailed manner, whether they are principal, ancillary, or alternative claims, in the claims paragraph with which the statement of claim concludes.

4- The date of submission of the statement of claim, and the signature of the plaintiff or his legal representative, or the signature of the proxy lawyer if representation through him is mandatory.

5- A list of the documents attached to the statement of claim.

- If the plaintiff does not have a domicile within the territorial jurisdiction of the court, he must elect a chosen domicile for himself in this area, unless he is represented by a lawyer, in which case his office shall be deemed a chosen domicile for him and he may be served therein wherever this office is located.

The plaintiff shall submit the statement of claim to the court registry attached with the documents supporting it, and shall deposit a number of copies thereof equal to the number of defendants, and shall attach to each copy copies of the documents certified by his signature as being in conformity with the original.

The statement of claim shall be registered, after collection of the fee, on the same day in a special register under a serial number according to the priority of its submission, and the seal of the court shall be affixed to it and to the documents attached to it, and the registration number and its date shall be mentioned thereon, and the copies of the statement of claim shall be endorsed accordingly.

The statement of claim with the documents attached to it shall be delivered to the clerk inside a special file indicating on its outside the name of the court, the names of the adversaries, the registration number of the statement of claim, and the date of the year, and numbering all the papers kept in the file with consecutive numbers, and a list of their items and their numbers shall be entered on their outside.

The defendant must, within fifteen days from being served with the summons, submit a pleading therein on the action and attach thereto all the documents supporting his reply, and it must include mention of the name and identity of each of the defendant and the plaintiff in accordance with the provisions of Article 445, and the statement of the claims in a clear and detailed manner in the claims paragraph with which the pleading concludes.

The defendant must also, if he does not have a domicile within the jurisdiction of the court, elect a chosen domicile for himself within this jurisdiction unless he is represented by a lawyer, in which case his office shall be deemed a chosen domicile for him and he may be served therein wherever this office is located.

If one of the adversaries does not elect his chosen domicile in accordance with the preceding provisions, or if his statement of this domicile is incomplete or incorrect such that service is impossible, all papers may be served upon him at the court registry in accordance with the text of Article 402. The chief clerk must immediately post the served paper on the court's noticeboard throughout the time limit fixed for replying, appearing, seeking recourse, or executing orders, and he shall draw up a record thereof establishing the posting of the paper and another record of its removal.

The chief clerk or the clerk shall give a receipt for the judicial papers delivered to him and shall send copies thereof for service within a time limit of twenty-four hours at most, under penalty of disciplinary sanction in the event of delay without an acceptable excuse.

The plaintiff may reply to the defendant's pleading within ten days from the date of being served therewith by way of a pleading served upon the defendant, who is entitled to reply thereto within a similar time limit.

After the expiry of the time limits fixed in the preceding articles, none of the adversaries may submit any pleading unless he invokes an acceptable excuse or a reason justifying the submission of a new pleading, and in this case the president of the court or the judge shall fix a time limit for submitting this pleading and replying thereto where necessary.

In the event of multiple pleadings, each of the adversaries must set out at the conclusion of his final pleading a paragraph containing his claims, including the claims that he set out in a previous pleading or pleadings, and the court shall not be required to rule upon claims set out in contravention of these provisions.

The court may shorten the time limits for the exchange of pleadings in cases that require urgency, provided that the time limit it fixes is not less than twenty-four hours. It may, in other cases, extend those time limits upon the request of one of the adversaries if it finds a justification therefor. The court shall issue its decision to shorten or extend the time limits in the deliberation room.

The parties may submit a joint written declaration stating that they are satisfied with the written defences set out in their submissions. If the court considers that there is no necessity to hear oral pleadings or to conduct any investigation and that the case is ready for judgment, it may adjudicate thereon without fixing a hearing for pleading. In this case, a date must be fixed for rendering the judgment within thirty days from the date of submission of the written declaration, and a letter must be sent by registered mail to each of the parties to inform him of this date, and a delay in the arrival of this letter to the concerned parties or to one of them shall not be deemed a ground for delaying the rendering of the judgment. If the judgment is not rendered on the aforementioned date, a new date must be fixed for rendering it and notified to the parties.

On the date fixed for examining the case before the court of first instance, the parties shall appear in person if the value of the matter in dispute does not exceed one million Lebanese Pounds. Advocates whom they appoint as their representatives may also appear on their behalf.

In other cases, however, they may only appear through advocates representing them in accordance with the provisions of Articles 378 to 386, unless the parties themselves are advocates. If a party appears and refuses to appoint an advocate, the case shall be examined in his absence and the judgment shall be deemed adversarial.

If the plaintiff and the defendant fail to appear at the hearing without an acceptable excuse, the court shall decide to strike the case off the roll. The decision to strike off is a special measure of judicial administration and does not prevent the parties or one of them from requesting the restoration of the case to the roll and proceeding with it from the point it had reached prior to being struck off.
If the plaintiff or the defendant appears at any hearing, the trial shall be deemed adversarial with respect to him even if he fails to appear thereafter.

If the plaintiff is absent from the first hearing without an acceptable excuse after having been notified of the date of the hearing, the defendant may request either

the striking of the action off the pleading roll, or judgment on the merits, or the lapse of the statement of claim.

If the defendant requests judgment on the merits or the lapse of the statement of claim, the case shall be adjourned to a second hearing of the date of which the plaintiff shall be notified. If the plaintiff is absent from the second hearing without an acceptable excuse, the court must grant the defendant's request and its judgment shall be rendered as quasi-adversarial with respect to the plaintiff, provided that, in the event of the lapse of the statement of claim, the plaintiff may bring the action anew if he is still within the legal time limit.

On the day following the expiry of the time limits for submitting the written pleadings, the Chief Clerk or the clerk shall refer the file to the President of the Court, who shall delegate one of its judges to examine it in order to complete it where necessary and prepare the case for oral argument within a time limit which he shall set for him and which shall be extendable when needed. It shall be for the President of the Court to undertake this work himself. The President or the delegated judge, as well as the single judge, after examining the file, may take the measures he deems appropriate for the aforementioned purpose. He may direct the adversaries to submit the necessary clarifications in fact or in law regarding their claims or defences and to produce the documents upon which they based them, observing their right to discuss any new documents or papers submitted to him. He may also hear the adversaries in an effort to conciliate and effect a settlement between them, in the presence of their counsel the lawyers or without their presence in accordance with the request of the adversaries. In all the foregoing cases, he shall set a time limit for the execution of the decision he takes and warn the adversaries that, in the event of non-execution of this decision, the case shall be heard in the state in which it stands.

Immediately upon the completion of the task set forth in the preceding Article, the delegated judge shall return the file of the case to the court registry, and the President shall, if no settlement has taken place between the adversaries, appoint the date of the hearing at which the case shall be heard.
In any event, it shall be for the court, if it finds a necessity to conduct an investigation, to delegate one of its judges to carry it out in accordance with the provisions of Article 135.

In cases whose value does not exceed eight hundred thousand Lebanese pounds and in urgent cases, the judge may appoint the date of the hearing immediately upon the registration of the statement of claim and hear the adversaries at the first hearing without the need for the exchange of written pleadings.

The President of the Court or whichever of its judges he delegates, as well as the single judge, may invite the two disputing parties to his chambers and endeavour to conciliate between them; if they agree on a settlement, even if partial, he shall draw up a record establishing it, obtain their signatures thereon, and issue a decision ratifying this settlement, which shall be enforceable. In the event that the two parties refuse the settlement, he shall draw up a record establishing this refusal.
The two parties may, at any time during the trial, settle, even partially, and request the court or the single judge to issue a decision ratifying this settlement.
If the absent party appears at the same hearing or at a subsequent hearing, the decision issued trying him in absentia shall be deemed as if it had never been.

The court may not accept new additional or counter claims, or new evidence submitted by the appearing party against the absent party, unless they are notified to the latter and he is given a time limit to submit his reply or his observations regarding them.

If a default judgment is issued and its notification is not requested and the fees thereon are not paid within three months from the date of its pronouncement, it shall be deemed lapsed ipso jure. The lapse shall only cover the judgment, whereas the proceedings prior to it shall remain standing.
The Public Prosecution shall have the right to institute the action in the cases set forth in Article 8, and it shall have in these cases the rights that parties have.

The intervention or joinder of the Public Prosecution in the action provided for in Article 8 shall be permissible at any stage of the trial, whereupon it shall become a principal party to the dispute.

The court may, at any stage of the trial, order that the case file be sent to the Public Prosecution for the purpose of its intervention in the cases provided for in Article 8. The intervention of the Public Prosecution in this case shall be mandatory.

The Public Prosecution shall give its opinion in its capacity as an joined party in the following cases:

1- The cases set forth in Article 8 when the Public Prosecution is not a principal party in the trial.

2- Actions brought against the State regarding liability arising from the acts of judges.

3- A request for the designation of the competent authority. The Public Prosecution must, in the cases specified in item (1) of the first paragraph, give its opinion before the Court of First Instance and the Court of Appeal within ten days from the date the file is deposited with it by the court, otherwise it shall be dispensed with and the file shall be returned to the court without delay.

The Public Prosecution is not required to appear before the Court of First Instance even if it is a principal party or a joined party before it, and it shall, depending on the circumstances, submit the summons, pleadings, memoranda, and evidence to the court, or receive them from it, or give a written opinion when necessary. In the event of the attendance of the Public Prosecution, it shall be represented by one of the Advocates General. The Public Prosecution shall be represented before the Court of Appeal if it is a principal party in the trial, provided that it is not required to attend when it confines itself to giving a written opinion in the case.

1- Where there is a plurality of plaintiffs and all of them are absent from the first hearing, the provisions of the preceding Article shall apply.

2- Where some of the plaintiffs appear and the others are absent without an acceptable excuse, the defendant may request a declaration of the lapse of the summons in respect of those who are absent if the subject-matter of the claim is divisible, or request judgment on the merits, and the provisions of the first paragraph of the preceding Article shall apply to those who are absent. Where the subject-matter of the claim is indivisible, the request of the defendant shall be limited to judgment on the merits, and the same aforementioned provisions shall apply.

3- Where some of the plaintiffs appear and the others are absent with an acceptable excuse, the case must be adjourned to a subsequent hearing of the date of which they shall be notified. Thereafter, the provisions of the second paragraph of this Article may be applied.

Where the defendant alone fails to appear at the first hearing without an acceptable excuse, and the date of the hearing was served on his person or he had submitted a pleading containing his defence, the court shall render an adversarial judgment on the merits. It shall not grant the claims of the plaintiff unless it finds them lawful in form, admissible, and shown to be on a sound basis. Where the defendant was not served in person and did not submit a pleading containing his defence, the court may, of its own motion or upon the request of the plaintiff in non-urgent cases, adjourn the examination of the case to a subsequent hearing of the date of which the defendant shall be notified.

The judgment shall be rendered in default against the defendant if it is not subject to appeal, service was not effected on his person, and he did not submit a pleading containing his defence, and in such case it shall be subject to opposition. However, if the judgment is subject to appeal, or if service was effected on the person of the defendant, or if the latter submitted a pleading containing his defence, the judgment shall be deemed adversarial in such case.

Where there is a plurality of defendants in the same subject-matter and one or some of them fail to appear at the first hearing without an acceptable excuse, the judgment shall be deemed adversarial against all of them if it is subject to appeal or if those who failed to appear were served in person. Where the judgment is not subject to appeal, those who failed to appear and were not served in person must be re-served. The judgment rendered thereafter shall be deemed adversarial towards all whenever one of the defendants has appeared or was served in person the first or second time. In the converse case, the judgment shall be in default.
The court must ascertain the validity of the service on the party who failed to appear; if it finds it defective, it shall order that it be re-effected validly for a subsequent hearing.
Failure to appear may not be recorded against one of the parties until one hour has elapsed from the time appointed for the trial.

In all trials in which the Public Prosecution is a joined party, the litigants may not, after it has submitted its statements and requests, request the floor or submit new briefs. However, they may submit to the court a written statement to correct the facts mentioned by the Public Prosecution. Nevertheless, the court may, in exceptional circumstances in which it deems fit to accept new documents or supplementary briefs, authorise their submission and the reopening of the pleading, and the Public Prosecution shall have the last word.

In the cases set forth in Article 8, the Public Prosecution shall have the right to appeal even if it was not a principal party in the first-instance trial, provided that the time limit for appeal in such case does not exceed six months from the date of issuance of the judgment, whether it has been notified or not.

The clerk of the court shall prepare a list of the cases to be heard at each session, arranged according to their serial numbers and the hours appointed for hearing them. This list shall be presented to the president of the court, and a copy thereof shall be posted on the board designated for that purpose at the door of the court before the opening of the session.
The date of the session shall be notified to the litigants at least three days prior to its occurrence.

Trial sessions shall be public on pain of nullity, unless the court deems fit, of its own motion or upon the request of one of the litigants, to hold them in camera in order to preserve public policy or out of regard for public morals or family privacy, but the judgment in such case shall inevitably be read out.
The session in the deliberation chamber shall be held non-publicly. In the deliberation chamber, the court shall examine ex parte matters as well as contentious matters expressly designated by law.

The proceedings of the trial may not be published in newspapers in cases of defamation and in respect of what is prohibited from publication pursuant to Article 420 of the Penal Code and pursuant to the provisions of the Publications Law.

The litigants shall be called at the hour appointed for the trial through a bailiff. If the defendant appears in person or through his lawyer representative in a case not subject to the exchange of briefs in accordance with the provisions of Article 459, he may request its adjournment to a subsequent session to enable him to submit his defences. If the defendant appears in person in a case in which a lawyer must be appointed to represent him, and a reason has arisen preventing him from doing so of which the court is convinced, he shall be entitled to request an adjournment to a subsequent session in order to appoint a lawyer and submit a brief of his defence.

Subject to the provisions of the Legal Profession Law, the President of the sitting shall order that a record be drawn up of any offence committed during the sitting and of the investigative measures he deems fit to take, and shall then order that the papers be referred to the Public Prosecution to take the necessary action thereon. If the offence committed is a felony or a misdemeanour, he may, where necessary, order the arrest of the person who committed it.

Subject to the provisions of the Legal Profession Law, the court may try any person who, during a sitting held by it, commits a misdemeanour constituting an assault against its bench, one of its members, or one of its officers, and shall immediately sentence him to the penalty. The court may also try any person who gives false testimony at the sitting and sentence him to the penalty prescribed for false testimony. The judgment of the court in these cases shall be enforceable even if it is appealed.

After the conclusion of the oral pleadings, the President of the court shall decide to close the trial and shall fix a date for delivering the judgment within a time-limit not exceeding six weeks. If it is not delivered on the appointed date, he must fix another date for that purpose, which shall be notified to the litigants.

Each of the litigants may submit, within one week following the closure of the trial, a written memorandum to supplement and clarify the points set out in the written submissions.

The memorandum shall be submitted through the court registry, and copies thereof shall be deposited in a number equal to that of the litigants, who shall - on their own responsibility - take service thereof at the court registry within a time-limit of three days following the one-week time-limit provided for in the first paragraph. They may submit a reply memorandum within a time-limit of one week from the date on which they were served.

The time-limits set out in this Article shall be reduced to two days in cases pending before the summary jurisdiction.

If a new fact occurs or an unknown fact comes to light after the closure of the trial and before the pronouncement of the judgment, the court may decide, of its own motion or at the request of one of the litigants, to reopen the trial and re-enter the case on the roll of pleadings.

Actions provided for in item /1/ of Article 86 of the Code of Civil Procedure promulgated by Legislative Decree No. 90 dated 16/9/1983, the value of which does not exceed an amount equivalent to thirty times the minimum wage, shall be subject to the simplified procedure, provided that the principal amount specified in the statement of claim shall be taken into account.

Subject to the remaining provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure that are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Law, the plaintiff shall submit the writ of summons of his action pursuant to the simplified procedure provided for in this Chapter, and shall set out in the body of his writ of summons the submissions he has and attach thereto all the documents in his possession.

The President shall grant the floor to the plaintiff or his representative first, then grant the floor to the defendant or his representative, and finally to the interveners; in all cases, the defendant shall have the final word, subject to the provisions of Article 480.
If, prior to the close of the trial, the composition of the court is changed in whole or in part of its members, the oral arguments must be repeated before the new bench.

The parties may request the court, at any stage of the trial, to record what they have agreed upon in the minutes of the hearing, and it shall be signed by them or by their representatives. If they have put what they agreed upon in writing, the written agreement shall be annexed to the minutes of the hearing and its contents shall be recorded therein. In both cases, the court shall issue an enforceable decision ratifying the agreement.

The clerk shall draw up minutes for each trial, which he shall sign together with the President at the end of each hearing, and in which he shall state the hour of opening the hearing and the hour of its closing, the name or names of the judge or judges, the names of the parties and their representatives, the occurrences that took place, and the statements which the President orders him to record. The minutes of the trial are an official instrument, and the forgery thereof shall constitute forgery of official documents.
Maintaining order in the hearing and conducting it are vested in its President. Every order issued by him to that end shall be executed immediately.

The President may address to the parties or their representatives such questions as he deems useful, make such observations as he deems necessary, and draw the attention of those pleading to the necessity of addressing an issue which they have neglected to address. He may prohibit a person pleading from speaking if he adopts in his pleading an unhelpful or improper course.

The President may expel from the courtroom anyone who disturbs its order; if he fails to comply, the court may apply to him the provisions of Article 418 of the Penal Code. If the act that necessitated his expulsion constitutes an offence carrying a penalty more severe than the penalty prescribed in the said Article, the President shall draw up a record against him and refer him to the Public Prosecution for prosecution. He may issue a detention order to be executed immediately.

The court may order, of its own motion or upon the request of one of the parties, the striking out of offensive expressions or those contrary to public morals or public policy from any document of the trial, or direct the person from whom they emanated to withdraw the document in which they appeared and replace it with a document free of such expressions, under penalty of having it removed from the file.
Decisions joining or severing proceedings are measures of judicial administration.
A stay of proceedings may be ordered upon the agreement of the parties not to proceed therewith for a period not exceeding six months from the date of the court's approval of such agreement.

In cases other than those in which the law provides for a mandatory or permissive stay of proceedings, the court may decide to stay them for a specified period or until the occurrence of a contingency which it specifies in its decision. It may revoke the decision to stay or shorten its period. Upon the cessation of the cause of the stay, the parties may resume the proceedings.

The proceedings shall be interrupted, unless they have been closed, in the following cases:

1- The death of one of the parties in transferable actions.

2- The loss by one of the parties of the capacity to litigate.

3- The cessation of the capacity of the person who was representing the party in the action as a legal representative thereof. The interruption shall take effect by operation of law from the notification of its cause to the other party.

The proceedings shall not be interrupted by the death of a party's counsel, nor by the termination of his mandate by dismissal, withdrawal, or any other cause, and the court may grant the party a reasonable time limit to appoint new counsel.

The interruption of the proceedings shall entail all running time limits and the nullity of all procedural acts carried out during the interruption, unless the party to whom the cause of interruption relates waives, expressly or impliedly, the right to invoke the nullity.

The proceedings shall be resumed by serving notice upon the person who replaces the party who died or lost his capacity to litigate, or who replaces the person whose capacity ceased, at the request of the other party, or by serving notice upon the latter at the request of those persons. The proceedings shall likewise be resumed if the heir of the deceased, or the person who replaces the party who lost his capacity to litigate or the person whose capacity ceased, attends the hearing that was scheduled for considering them and proceeds therewith.

If the proceedings, whatever their subject matter, are left without prosecution for a period of two years from the last valid procedural act performed therein, each of the parties may request that they be declared lapsed.

The defendant must submit his answer to the action within a time limit not exceeding one week from the date of service, and he may not submit any answer outside this time limit, nor may the judge grant him an additional time limit or accept an answer from him received outside that time limit except by a reasoned decision and for substantial grounds, provided that the additional time limit does not exceed five days.

Immediately upon the expiry of the time limit specified in the preceding Article, the judge shall examine the papers and issue his judgment on the basis of the data contained therein within a time limit not exceeding two weeks from the aforementioned date.

If the judge finds cause to interrogate the parties, hear witnesses, or seek the assistance of technical expertise, he must immediately take the appropriate measure and specify in his decision a time limit for carrying out the measure not exceeding one week.
Each of the two parties shall have the right to comment on the interrogation, testimony, or expertise within a time limit of three days from the date of service.
After the expiry of this three-day time limit, the judge must adjudicate the case by a final judgment within a time limit not exceeding one week.
The judgment of the judge shall be provisionally enforceable by operation of law, and shall be subject to appeal within a time limit of fifteen days from the date of service.

The Court of Appeal must adhere, in the event that the judgment is appealed before it, to the same summary procedures provided for in this Chapter, and it may not order a stay of execution unless it appears to it that there are new grounds justifying it. The decision issued by the Court of Appeal shall not be subject to any means of recourse.

The court may, of its own motion or upon the request of the litigants, decide to join two or more proceedings pending before it if there exists a connection between them requiring, for the proper administration of justice, that they be investigated and adjudicated together. The court may also decide to sever the proceeding pending before it into two or more proceedings.

In the case of interruption, the period for lapse of the proceedings shall not run except as from the procedural step by which the court is resumed. In the case of stay of the proceedings, however, the period for lapse shall continue to run unless the stay has been prescribed by law or ordered by the judiciary for a specified period or until the occurrence of a specified contingency, in which case the period shall be interrupted and shall not resume running except as from the expiry of the period or the occurrence of the contingency.

The application for the lapse of the proceedings shall be submitted to the court before which the action is brought, by a petition notified to the adversary or by a plea raised against the adversary who undertakes any procedural step to proceed with the proceedings after the expiry of the two years. The petition must be submitted or the plea of lapse of the proceedings invoked, on pain of inadmissibility, prior to raising any claim, plea or defence or undertaking any procedural step relating to the proceedings.

1- The lapse of the proceedings shall mandatorily bepronounced when its conditions are met, but the court may not pronounce it of its own motion.

2- If the court ascertains, by the means of proof available to it, that the proceedings have been left unpursued for a period of five years as from the last valid procedural step taken therein, it may decide to declare their lapse of its own motion without summoning the litigants, by an ex parte decision enforceable on its original.

3- Every annotation of an action or attachment, whatever its nature and source, shall be struck off after the lapse of ten years from its entry on the real estate register sheet if the interested party does not proceed to renew the entry by a petition exempt from fees submitted to the court before which the action is pending or to the President of the competent Execution Department.

4- The application for striking off the annotation of the action or attachment shall be submitted by a petition to the President of the Chamber of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the real property is situated. The President of the Chamber of First Instance shall conduct a thorough and comprehensive investigation and shall order the publication of an abstract of the petition in the Official Gazette and in two local newspapers designated by him. He shall take his decision after the lapse of twenty days from the publication, either accepting the application if it appears that the file of the action or attachment is lost, or dismissing the application if it appears that the file of the action or attachment still exists. The decision to strike off shall be issued on an ex parte basis and shall be enforceable on its original.

5- The provisions of paragraphs 3 and 4 of this Article shall apply after the lapse of one year from the entry into force of this Law.

The period suspended pursuant to Law No. 50/90 dated 23/05/1991 shall not be included in the calculation of the ten-year period.
Discontinuance may be express or implied, as may be the consent of the defendant.

Discontinuance of the proceedings entails the annulment of all the measures thereof, including the summons, and the ordering of the discontinuing party to pay the costs. However, it does not lead to the annulment of the effect resulting from the interruption of prescription, nor does it prejudice the right in respect of which the action is brought.

Discontinuance of the appeal does not require the consent of the respondent unless it is coupled with reservations or the latter has previously submitted an incidental claim or a cross-appeal. Such discontinuance necessarily implies the appellant's acquiescence in the judgment. However, it shall be deemed null and void if another party subsequently files an appeal in accordance with the applicable rules.

Discontinuance of the opposition does not require the consent of the respondent to the opposition, the original plaintiff, unless the latter has previously submitted an additional claim. Such discontinuance made without reservation implies the opposing party's acquiescence in the judgment.

Where the discontinuance is confined to a specific measure or one of the documents of the proceedings, the consent of the other party shall not be required for its completion unless that party has a legitimate interest in such measure or such document. Such discontinuance entails considering the measure - or the document - as though it had never been.
Waiver of a judgment entails waiver of the right established therein.

The plaintiff may, at any stage of the proceedings, waive the right claimed. Such waiver extinguishes the right, terminates the action, and obliges the plaintiff to pay the costs and any compensation due to his opponent where applicable. He must deliver to the latter the documents relating to the right claimed. A partial waiver of a right, whether express or implied, does not in itself imply a total waiver of that right.

Deliberation for the pronouncement of judgments shall take place, on pain of nullity, among the judges in whose presence the oral pleadings were heard and the proceedings were closed. Deliberation shall be secret.

Where one of the parties to the proceedings consists of multiple persons and one or some of them submit an application for the abatement of the proceedings or a plea of their abatement, all of them shall benefit therefrom. Where a step interrupting the time-limit for abatement is directed against one or some of them, the time-limit shall be interrupted in respect of all of them. Where a party consists of multiple persons, the application for abatement or the plea thereof must be submitted against all of them. Where one or some of them direct a step interrupting the time-limit for abatement, the remainder shall benefit therefrom.

A judgment declaring the abatement of the proceedings shall entail the lapse of all steps thereof, including the writ of summons, and the lapse of judgments rendered therein ordering evidentiary measures. However, it shall not entail the lapse of the effect resulting from the interruption of prescription, nor shall it extinguish the right, final judgments, the steps upon which such judgments are based, admissions made by the litigants, or oaths taken by them. The litigants may rely upon measures of inquiry and expert works that have been carried out, unless they are null in themselves.

Once the abatement of an appeal or an opposition is adjudged, the contested judgment, even if not served, shall be deemed a conclusive judgment. Once the abatement of an application for retrial is adjudged prior to the judgment admitting the application, such application itself shall lapse; whereas if it is adjudged after the judgment admitting it, the foregoing rules governing appeal or first instance, as the case may be, shall apply.

The period prescribed for the abatement of the proceedings shall run against all natural and legal persons, including persons lacking or of defective capacity, while retaining their right of recourse against their guardians or administrators.
Article 517- The costs of the proceedings adjudged to have abated shall be borne by the party who instituted the action.
The plaintiff may discontinue the proceedings at any stage thereof.

Discontinuance shall not be complete save with the consent of the defendant. However, such consent shall cease to be required if, at the time of discontinuance, the defendant has not submitted an answer containing a defence on the merits, a plea of inadmissibility, or a counterclaim.
No account shall be taken of the defendant's objection if it is not founded upon a legitimate ground.
Judgments shall be issued unanimously or by a majority of opinions. In the latter case, the dissenting judge must record his dissent.
The judges shall sign the judgment before its pronouncement, and the clerk shall sign it immediately thereafter; otherwise, the judgment shall be null and void.
Following the conclusion of the pleading, the court may pronounce the judgment at the hearing, and it may adjourn its issuance to another near hearing which it shall fix.

If the circumstances require adjourning the issuance of the judgment a second time, the court shall declare this at the hearing while appointing the day on which it shall be pronounced and stating the reasons for the adjournment in the record.

The pronouncement of the judgment shall be made by the president or by one of the judges who participated with him in the deliberation, at a hearing at which the attendance of all of them is not required. The pronouncement of the judgment shall be made in public; otherwise, the judgment shall be null and void, unless the law provides otherwise.
The pronouncement of the judgment may be confined to reading its operative part.
The judgment shall be issued at the seat of the court unless there is a provision to the contrary. The date of the pronouncement of the judgment shall be the date of the judgment itself.
The clerk shall draw up a record to establish the pronouncement of the judgment, which shall be signed by the president and the clerk.

Upon delivering the judgment that terminates the litigation, the court shall, of its own motion, rule on the costs of the trial. The losing party to the litigation shall be ordered to pay the costs of the trial. Where there are multiple losing parties, the costs may be ordered to be divided among them equally or in proportion to the interest of each of them, as assessed by the court. Where they are ordered to pay the costs without specifying the proportion to be borne by each of them, the costs shall be divided among them equally. The parties shall be ordered to pay the costs jointly and severally if they are jointly and severally liable under their original obligation as adjudicated.

The court may order the winning party to bear all or part of the costs if the right was acknowledged by the judgment debtor prior to the bringing of the action, or if the judgment creditor caused, by his fault, additional or useless costs, or if he left his opponent in ignorance of the decisive documents in the dispute that were in his possession or of the content of those documents.
Where each of the parties fails in part of his claims, the court may apportion the costs between them in such manner as it sees fit or order one of them to bear them.
The intervener shall be ordered to pay the costs of the intervention if his intervention is ruled inadmissible or if his claims are dismissed.
An attorney may be ordered personally to pay the costs relating to a trial, proceedings, or an enforcement measure that he undertook beyond the limits of his mandate.

The costs relating to an unjustified trial, proceedings, or enforcement measure shall be borne by the attorney or judicial assistant who undertook it, without prejudice to any damages that may be claimed where applicable. This shall also apply to the costs relating to a trial, proceedings, or enforcement measure rendered void as a result of a fault committed by him.

The amount of the costs shall be determined in the judgment that disposes of the case; failing such determination, the chief clerk of the court shall state the same at the foot of the enforceable copy of the judgment or in a subsequent statement which shall constitute an enforceable instrument.

An objection to the decision fixing the costs may be lodged within three days from the service of the judgment or of the statement of costs, by means of a declaration made to the court registry, exempt from fees.

The judgment shall contain the following particulars:

1- Its issuance in the name of the Lebanese People, provided that this is expressly mentioned therein.

2- The name of the court that issued it.

3- The names of the judges who participated in issuing it.

4- The name of the representative of the Public Prosecution who may have given his opinion in the case.

5- The place and date of its issuance.

6 - The names of the litigants, their surnames and their capacities.

7- The names of the representatives of the litigants.

8- The presence and absence of the litigants.

9- A summary of the claims and grounds therefor, and of the grounds of defence or pleas, submitted by them.

10- A summary of the evidence and legal arguments relied upon by the litigants.

11- The opinion of the Public Prosecution, where there is one.

12- The reasons for the judgment and its operative part.

- The particulars set out in numbers 2, 6, 9 and 12 listed above shall be mandatory on pain of nullity of the judgment.

The judgment shall also contain, on pain of nullity, a determination of all the issues raised by the litigants and shall state the reasons appropriate thereto.

The omission or inaccuracy of one of the mandatory particulars shall not entail the nullity of the judgment if it is established by the papers or by the record of the trial or by any other means that the provisions of the law were observed in fact.

The court may, within the limits of the provisions of the law, decide in the judgment it issues to grant the judgment debtor a time limit for its enforcement, provided that it states the reasons that led it to do so. The time limit granted shall run from the date of the judgment if it was rendered in the presence of the parties, and otherwise from the date of its service. The granting of the time limit shall not preclude the taking of conservatory measures.

The time limit set out in the preceding Article may not be granted, and if granted it shall be revoked upon the request of the litigant:

1- In the event of the bankruptcy or insolvency of the judgment debtor.

2- In the event that the judgment debtor commits an act that led to the diminution of the special securities he gave to the judgment creditor under a contract, or fails to provide to the latter the securities he undertook towards him under a contract.

3- In the event of the attachment of the property of the judgment debtor and part thereof by other creditors.
The costs of the proceedings shall include judicial fees, witnesses' compensation, experts' fees, the expenses of procedures whose tariff is officially fixed, and attorneys' fees.

The objection shall be submitted to the court that rendered the judgment, which shall examine it in the deliberation chamber after summoning the parties or the objecting party to appear within a period of twenty-four hours where circumstances require such summons.
A party granted legal aid shall not be ordered to pay the costs of the trial.

The court shall award compensation for any damage arising from a claim, defence or plea intended for vexation. Where it deems it inequitable to leave expenses not included in the costs of the trial to be borne by one of the parties who incurred them, it may order the other party to pay him such amount as it determines.
A judgment is contentious if rendered in an existing dispute between parties, and non-contentious if rendered without any existing dispute.

A definitive judgment is one that adjudicates the merits of the dispute as defined in Article 365, or that adjudicates an aspect thereof or a plea or defence related thereto and is definitive with respect to what it has adjudicated. A definitive judgment divests the court of the case. A definitive judgment is final when it is not or is no longer subject to appeal by ordinary means of recourse. A judgment is irrevocable - or absolute - if it is no longer subject to appeal by any of the ordinary or extraordinary means of recourse.

Every decision rendered prior to adjudicating the merits of the dispute and dealing with a measure of inquiry or evidence is interlocutory. An interlocutory decision shall not have the authority of res judicata with respect to the merits of the dispute. However, the court shall be bound by it unless a new or previously unknown fact arises or the court discovers matters that necessitate amending or revoking it.
Every decision ordering a conservatory measure or an urgent measure required by the circumstances of the case during its examination is provisional.

Definitive judgments have, from the time they are rendered, the authority of res judicata with respect to every dispute adjudicated therein in accordance with Article 302. They also have enforceable force in accordance with the provisions of Article 564. The effect of judgments extends to the successors of the parties and operates in favour of the co-obligees of the judgment creditors under a joint and several obligation or an indivisible obligation in accordance with the rules prescribed by law in this regard.

A judgment acquires enforceable force from the date of its issuance if it is final, or from the date on which it becomes final, unless the judgment debtor is granted a period for execution or the judgment creditor is granted expedited execution.

The Chief Clerk, or the clerk whom he delegates, shall deliver the copy of the judgment valid for execution, stamped with the seal of the court and signed by him, after appending to it the phrase "certified true copy valid for execution", to the adversary who derives a benefit from the execution of the judgment, after verifying that the judgment is permissible to be executed. A second executory copy may not be delivered to the same adversary except in the event of the loss of the first copy. The court that issued the judgment shall rule expeditiously on the request and on the disputes relating thereto after summoning the adversaries.

Judgments may not be compulsorily executed except after their service, with the exception of what is provided for by the law or the operative part of the judgment as being required to be executed on its original.

Proof of the enforceable character of the judgment shall be deduced from its content when it is not subject to any recourse suspending execution or when it is coupled with expedited execution. In other cases, such proof shall be deduced from the acquiescence of the judgment debtor, or from the service of the judgment and from a certificate showing, by comparison with such service, that no opposition or appeal was lodged within the legal time limit. Every adversary shall have the right to request from the clerk of the court before which a recourse may be brought the delivery to him of a certificate showing that no opposition or appeal has occurred, or showing the date of the lodging of the recourse in the event of its occurrence.
Judgments issued by foreign courts shall be executed in Lebanon in the cases and in accordance with the conditions specified in this Law.

The courts may, even of their own motion, order a coercive fine to ensure the execution of the judgments issued by them. The coercive fine shall be considered distinct from compensatory damages, and shall be provisional or definitive, and shall in principle be deemed provisional unless the court declares its definitive character. In the event of partial or total non-execution or delay in execution, the court that ordered the fine shall proceed to liquidate it. The court may not modify the amount of the definitive fine upon its liquidation, unless it is proven that the non-execution of the judicial judgment resulted from force majeure. However, it may modify or cancel the provisional fine even if non-execution is proven.

Decisions rendered in a matter other than nationality and which may have an effect thereon shall not automatically produce their effect on nationality and shall not bind the court having jurisdiction to hear matters relating thereto.

Whatever the limitation period applicable to the disputed right may be, such period shall be ten years in respect of the right established in the judgment. Limitation shall not run against a judgment denying the existence of a claimed right, nor against a judgment establishing a right that is not subject to lapse by limitation.

Whatever the limitation period applicable to the disputed right may be, such period shall be ten years in respect of the right established in the judgment. Limitation shall not run against a judgment that clears the existence of a claimed right, nor against a judgment establishing a right that is not subject to lapse by limitation. Article 559- A judgment shall in principle be deemed declaratory of a right, and its effects shall relate back to the date on which the right was claimed before the judiciary; however, a judgment that effects a change in the status of a person or in his capacity, or a judgment rendered in enforcement matters, shall be deemed constitutive and shall have no effect except from the date of its pronouncement.

The court shall undertake the correction of purely material errors, whether clerical or arithmetical, occurring in its judgment, by a decision issued of its own motion or upon request after summoning the parties and hearing them, unless the judgment has been challenged by one of the ordinary means of recourse. An application for the correction of material errors shall not be subject to any fee. The clerk of the court shall enter the correction on the original copy of the judgment, and he and the president of the court shall sign it and record it in the margin of the judgment in the register, and he shall destroy the previously delivered copy after recovering it. Service of the judgment issued making the correction shall be effected in the same manner as the judgment itself.

A judgment issued making a correction may be challenged if the court exceeded the limits provided for in the first paragraph of the preceding Article, by the means of recourse admissible against the judgment that is the subject of the correction. As for a judgment refusing the correction, it may not be challenged independently.

The parties may request the court that rendered the judgment to interpret any ambiguity or obscurity occurring therein, unless such judgment has been challenged by one of the means of recourse. The application shall be submitted in accordance with the rules prescribed for bringing an action. The judgment issued providing the interpretation shall be deemed in all respects supplementary to the judgment it interprets, and the rules relating to the means of recourse that apply to that judgment shall apply to it.
If the court omits to rule on certain substantive claims, the interested party may bring a new action in respect thereof if he has not challenged the judgment.

If the judgment subject to expedited execution is appealed, the Court of Appeal may in all cases decide, upon the request of the interested adversary, to stay the expedited execution if it is clear that the consequences that will result from the execution exceed reasonable limits in view of the circumstances of the case, or if the grounds of the challenge against the judgment make its reversal likely. The court may, when it decides to stay execution, require the provision of security or order whatever it deems sufficient to safeguard the right of the judgment creditor. The court shall decide to stay execution in cases where the law prohibits expediting execution. The foregoing powers are also established, in the event of an opposition, for the court to which such challenge is submitted.
Expedited execution does not include the costs of the trial, fees, fine and compensation for damages caused by the lawsuit.

The Single Judge may hear, in his capacity as a Judge of Urgent Matters, applications for taking urgent measures in civil and commercial matters without prejudice to the merits of the right, while reserving the special jurisdiction established for the President of the Execution Department. He may in the same capacity take measures aimed at removing a manifest trespass against rights or lawful situations. In the case where the existence of the debt is not subject to serious dispute, the Judge of Urgent Matters may grant the creditor a provisional advance on account of his right.

The territorially competent judge in urgent matters is: - either the Single Judge within whose jurisdiction, or within the jurisdiction of the Chamber of First Instance or any other court within whose district he is located, the merits of the dispute fall, - or the Single Judge within whose district the subject matter of the urgent lawsuit arose.

No request may be made to take any measure from the Judge of Urgent Matters relating to a case pending before the Court of Appeal unless the judgment of first instance was issued in favour of the person requesting the taking of that measure which is not inconsistent with this judgment.

The urgent lawsuit shall be heard at the hearing held by the judge on the day and at the hour that he appoints. The time limit for the summons to appear shall be one full day unless the judge decides to shorten this time limit. The judge may authorise summoning the adversaries within the time limit that he appoints either to the court, to the site of the dispute, or to his residence, even on official holidays and outside legal working hours, in which case he shallcommission one of the bailiffs to serve the statement of claim and the decision shortening the time limit.
The Judge of Urgent Matters shall issue his decision in the lawsuit brought before him without delay.

Provisional execution may not be initiated unless it is ordered in the judgment, except in cases where the judgment is subject to provisional execution by operation of law. Considered subject to provisional execution by operation of law are, in particular, decisions rendered in urgent matters, decisions or orders rendered on petitions, decisions ordering interim or conservatory measures within the scope of the proceedings, and any other judgment or decision for which the law prescribes provisional execution.

The court shall mandatorily order provisional execution, upon the request of the interested party, in the following cases:

1- If the judgment was rendered on the basis of a prior final judgment or one covered by provisional execution, or was rendered in execution of such judgment.

2- If the judgment is based on an authentic instrument, an acknowledged private instrument, or an admission.

The court may order provisional execution, upon the request of the interested party, in commercial matters and in matters involving urgency. Provisional execution may be ordered for the entirety of the award or for a part thereof. In the cases specified in the first paragraph, the court may order the deposit of the awarded amount with an approved bank, while authorising provisional execution in the event of non-deposit.
Subject to the provisions of Articles 575 and 576, provisional execution may only be ordered in the judgment to which such execution pertains.

Provisional execution may be made conditional upon the provision of sufficient security guaranteeing any obligation of restitution or compensation that may arise from the execution in the event that the judgment is overturned and the action is dismissed. The court may at any time authorise the replacement of the original security with an equivalent security.

If provisional execution was not requested when it is mandatory, or if it was requested and the court omitted to rule thereon, the interested party may request the Court of Appeal, whether by an independent petition, within a principal appeal filed by him, or in his reply to his opponent's appeal, to issue a decision ordering provisional execution. The said court shall rule on his request expeditiously and in chambers after his opponent's reply thereto or the expiry of the time limit for reply fixed by it. Where such request is submitted by an independent petition, the said petition shall not be subject to the fee and security deposit.
If the judgment dismisses the request for provisional execution, it may be appealed in this respect, and the court of second instance shall rule on this appeal in chambers and expeditiously.
Decisions relating to provisional and conservatory measures shall be enforced upon their original.
In cases requiring that a provisional or conservatory measure be taken without summoning and hearing the opponent, the provisions relating to orders on petitions shall apply.

Non-contentious decisions shall be issued without adversarial proceedings in matters which the law requires to be subjected to judicial supervision by reason of their nature or the capacity of the petitioner.
A non-contentious application shall be submitted by way of a petition to the competent judge or court and shall be examined in chambers.

The judge shall undertake the investigation of his own motion in private and shall carry out all inquiries which he deems useful. He may hear any person who can enlighten him regarding the subject-matter of the application, or whose interests may be affected by the decision issued by him.
The judge may base his decision on all the facts relating to the application before him, even if the petitioner has not invoked them.

The decision shall be issued in chambers or in private unless the law provides that it be pronounced in public. It shall contain appropriate reasoning. The judge or the court may order its enforcement upon its original.

A non-contentious decision shall not have the authority of res judicata. Subject to the following provisions, the judge who issued it shall be entitled to revoke or amend it, upon the application of an interested party, if new circumstances arise or grounds become apparent which were not known when it was issued, provided that this does not prejudice a right acquired in good faith by a third party on the basis of the said decision.

The decision of the judge of urgent matters shall not have the authority of res judicata with respect to the merits of the right. However, he may not amend or revoke it unless new circumstances arise that justify doing so.

The decision of the judge of urgent matters shall be provisionally enforceable without security unless the judge orders the provision of security. In case of necessity, he may order that the decision be executed on its original copy.

The decision of the judge of urgent matters shall not be subject to opposition. However, it may be appealed in matters in which judgments of the courts of first instance may be appealed, within eight days from the date of service of the decision, and the Court of Appeal shall rule thereon in accordance with the summary procedure. The appeal shall not stay execution.
The judge of urgent matters may order the imposition of a coercive fine upon the party who refrains from executing his decision. He may also liquidate it provisionally.
The originals of the decisions of the judge of urgent matters shall be kept at his registry.

The trial judge hearing the action, as well as the judge of urgent matters subject to the provisions of Article 581, may take, upon the request of one of the parties, with or without security, all provisional and conservatory measures capable of preserving rights and preventing damage, such as affixing seals, taking an inventory of assets, imposing judicial receivership, selling perishable property, and recording the state of affairs.

The rules and procedures prescribed for appealing the decisions of the judge of urgent matters shall apply to the appeal of adversarial decisions rendered in accordance with the provisions of the preceding Article and to the time limit for appealing them.
Decisions relating to provisional and conservatory measures may be revoked or amended if the circumstances that justify them change.

The judge may authorise a third party to inspect the case file under his supervision and to obtain a copy thereof after establishing his legitimate interest therein and within the limits of such interest.

Article 601:

Subject to the provisions of Article 86, paragraph 1, item 3, a third party prejudiced by the issuance of a non-contentious decision (decision on a petition) may file an opposition thereto within eight days from the date on which such decision or any measure of execution thereof is notified to him, before the judge or the court that issued it, by way of a petition setting forth the grounds of the opposition and notified to the beneficiary of the decision together with a summons for him to appear before the judge or the court. Where the decision was issued by the President of the Chamber of First Instance, the opposition shall be filed before the said Chamber.

The time limit for opposition for the State and public institutions of an administrative nature shall be thirty days from the date of notification.

Where the non-contentious decision or any of the measures of execution thereof has not been notified to the third party prejudiced thereby, the latter may challenge it by way of opposition in accordance with the provisions of the preceding paragraph throughout the limitation period applicable to his right.

The opposition shall be examined through contentious proceedings and as a matter of urgency.

A prejudiced third party shall be entitled to bring an action for the annulment of the non-contentious decision on the ground of its violation of the law before the court having jurisdiction to examine the merits, throughout the limitation period applicable to the basis of his right. However, where the decision or a measure of execution thereof has been notified, the time limit for bringing the said action shall be thirty days from the date of such notification.

A petitioner who submitted a non-contentious application and whose application was rejected may challenge the rejection decision. If the decision was issued by the President of the Chamber of First Instance, the challenge shall be submitted by way of objection before this Chamber within eight days from the date of notification.

If the decision was issued by the Single Judge or by the Chamber of First Instance, the challenge shall be submitted by way of appeal before the Court of Appeal within eight days from the date of notification.

This time limit shall be thirty days with respect to the State and public institutions of an administrative nature."

The appeal shall be submitted through the registry of the Judge or the Court that issued the decision. After examining it, the Judge or the Court may revoke or amend the decision; otherwise, the case file shall be referred to the Court of Appeal. The registry of the Judge or the Court shall notify the interested party of the order of reconsideration or referral without delay.

The Court of Appeal shall adjudicate the challenge in accordance with the procedures followed in non-contentious matters before the court of first instance.

A third-party challenge against the decision issued on appeal shall be admissible in accordance with the provisions of Articles 601 and 602.

Orders on petitions are provisional decisions issued without adversarial proceedings in cases where it is permissible to issue an order without summoning and hearing the adversary. They shall be subject to the following provisions, subject to special texts.

The application shall be submitted to the Judge of Urgent Matters unless the law provides otherwise, in which case the application shall be submitted to the President of the competent court. Where a dispute is pending before the judiciary, the application shall be submitted, as the case may be, to the Single Judge or the President of the Chamber of First Instance or of Appeal, and the provisions of Article 581 shall be observed.

The application shall be submitted to the Judge or the President of the competent court by a petition in two copies containing the facts of the application and its grounds, and the designation of an elected domicile for the applicant within the jurisdiction of the court if he does not have a real domicile therein mentioned in the petition, and the documents supporting the application shall be attached thereto. In cases of extreme urgency, the petition may be submitted to the Judge at his residence and outside official working hours.

The Judge must issue his order by writing it on one of the two copies of the petition submitted to him within a time limit of two days at most. He must state the reasons upon which he based the order.
The court registry must deliver to the applicant the second copy of the petition with a copy of the order written thereon, on the day following its issuance at the latest.
The order shall be enforceable immediately upon its original by operation of law and without security, unless the Judge stipulates, in the text of the order, the provision of security.

The provisions of Articles 596, 597, and 599 to 603 shall apply to orders on petitions; however, third-party opposition shall be heard in accordance with the procedure followed before the judge of urgent matters. An opposition against an order issued by the President of the Appellate Chamber shall be submitted to this Chamber.
Referring the case to the court of the merits shall not prevent the judge who issued the order from revoking or amending it.

An order issued on a petition shall lapse if it is not submitted for execution within thirty days from the date of its issuance where no challenge is lodged against it, or from the date of issuance of the decision rejecting such challenge where one is lodged. Such lapse shall not prevent the obtaining of a new order.
The annulment of a judgment may only be requested by using the means of challenge specified by law, subject to the provisions of Article 602.
