A judgment may only be challenged by the party against whom judgment was rendered or by the party harmed thereby. A challenge shall not be admissible from a party who has acquiesced in the judgment or a party who has been awarded all of his claims, unless the law provides otherwise.

Judgments issued during the trial may only be challenged together with the judgment that terminates the trial. Excepted therefrom are:

1- A judgment ordering a stay of the trial.

2- A judgment ruling on the inadmissibility of an application for intervention or joinder of a third party.

3- A judgment admitting or rejecting the administration of a decisive oath.

4- A judgment ordering the partition or sale of common property, or the liquidation of a company or an estate.

5- A judgment deciding one of the points or aspects of the dispute when it is subject to expedited execution prior to deciding the other points or aspects.

6- Provisional judgments. Challenging such judgments shall not divest the court that issued the judgment of jurisdiction over the remaining points or aspects of the dispute and shall not prevent the continuation of the trial in all matters not connected with the challenged judgment.

The time limit upon the expiry of which the right to challenge lapses shall run from the date of service of the judgment, unless the law provides for another date from which it begins to run. The time limit shall run against both the party requesting service and the party served simultaneously.

Where a judgment is issued jointly and severally or in an indivisible matter among the parties against whom judgment was rendered, service effected upon one of them shall cause the time limit to run against him alone. Where a judgment is issued in favour of several adversaries jointly and severally or in an indivisible matter, each of them shall be entitled to invoke the service effected by one of them.

None shall benefit from a challenge save the one who lodged it, and it may not be invoked save against the one against whom it was lodged. However, if the judgment was rendered in an indivisible subject-matter, or in a joint and several obligation, or in an action in which the law requires the joinder of specific persons, any judgment debtor who let the time-limit for challenging lapse or who acquiesced in the judgment may intervene in the challenge lodged within the time-limit by another, joining himself thereto. If he fails to do so, the court shall order the challenger to join him as a party to the proceedings. Where the challenge is lodged against one of the judgment creditors within the time-limit, the remaining judgment creditors must be joined therein.

In any event, where the challenge is lodged by one of the judgment debtors in an indivisible subject-matter or in a joint and several obligation and the decision in such challenge is rendered in his favour, the remaining judgment debtors shall benefit from this decision even if they did not intervene or were not joined in the challenge."

The guarantor and the party claiming under the guarantee shall benefit from a challenge lodged by either of them against the judgment rendered in the principal action if their defence therein is united. Where a challenge is lodged against either of them, the other may be joined therein.
An error in the characterization given by the court to the judgment rendered by it shall not affect the right to challenge it.
Decisions relating to judicial administration shall not be subject to any challenge.
Where a challenge or the defence therein is lodged abusively, the party lodging it shall be ordered to pay damages and the fine provided for in Articles 10 and 11.

Where contradictory judgments are rendered by different courts and have become final and binding, only the judgment rendered by the highest court among them shall prevail. However, where they are rendered by the same court or by courts of equal degree, only the judgment most recent in date shall be enforced.

The avenues of challenge against a judgment are of two kinds:

1- Ordinary avenues, which are opposition and appeal.

2- Extraordinary avenues, which are third-party opposition, retrial, and petition for cassation, to which is appended an action against the State in respect of liability arising from the acts of judges. In principle, they shall not have the effect of staying the enforcement of the judgment.

Opposition is a challenge aimed at having the court retract a judgment rendered by it in absentia. Opposition shall not be admissible save from a party against whom judgment was rendered in absentia in accordance with the provisions of Article 468, paragraph 3.
Failure to observe the time limits for appealing judgments shall result in the forfeiture of the right to appeal, and the court shall declare such forfeiture of its own motion.

The time limit for appeal shall be interrupted by the death of the unsuccessful party, by the loss of his capacity to litigate, or by the cessation of the capacity of the person who was representing him in the action as his legal representative, and the time limit shall not run anew except after service of the judgment upon the person who replaces the party who died or lost his capacity to litigate, or who replaces the person whose capacity to represent him ceased.

If the successful party dies during the time limit for appeal, this time limit shall not be interrupted, and the unsuccessful party must lodge his appeal within it. Such appeal shall be valid even if it is directed against the successful party or against his heirs collectively without mentioning their names and capacities and has been sent to them at the last domicile of their ancestor. Once the appeal has been lodged and sent in the manner set forth above, it must be re-served upon all the heirs by their names and capacities in person or at the domicile of each of them, or by any other method of service permitted by law, prior to the hearing scheduled for examining the appeal or within the time limit set by the court for that purpose, and after the appellant has been served with the judgment of determination of heirs or has obtained the issuance of this judgment. If the successful party loses his capacity to litigate, or if the capacity ceases or the death occurs of the person who was representing him as his legal representative during the time limit for appeal, this time limit shall not be interrupted, and the unsuccessful party must lodge the appeal within it. Such appeal shall be valid even if directed and served upon the person who lost his capacity or whose capacity ceased, provided that it is re-served upon the person who replaces the party, in person or at his domicile or by any other method of service permitted by law, prior to the hearing scheduled for examining an appeal or within the time limit set by the court for that purpose. The time limit for an incidental appeal shall not run against the respondent except from the second service effected in the manner set forth in the two preceding paragraphs.
The successful party upon whom the appeal is served shall be presumed, for the needs of this service, to be residing at the address which he designated in the instrument of service of the judgment.
The time limit for appeal shall be suspended by the submission of an application for legal aid and until the service of the decision adjudicating this application.

The time limit for appeal shall not run against the Public Prosecution except from the date it is served. In every case in which the Public Prosecution is represented or expresses an opinion, the registry must without delay serve upon it a copy of the judgment rendered without awaiting the payment of its fees. The provisions of Article 481 shall be observed.
The time limit for opposition shall be fifteen days from the date of service of the judgment.

An opposition shall be submitted by way of a writ of summons to the court that rendered the contested judgment, and the rules prescribed for the writ of summons of a lawsuit shall be observed therein. It must include a statement of the grounds, failing which it shall be null and void.

An opposition brings the dispute anew before the court with respect to the points adjudicated in the default judgment so that they may be decided anew in fact and in law. The contested judgment shall not be set aside except by the issuance of a judgment revoking it.
The trial in the opposition shall proceed in accordance with the rules and procedures followed before the court that rendered the opposed judgment.
The court hearing the opposition shall assess, anew, the admissibility of the claims of the plaintiff and the opponent in relation to the original claim in accordance with the ordinary rules.
A new opposition shall not be admitted from a person against whom judgment has been rendered by default a second time.
An appeal is a recourse submitted to the court of second instance for the purpose of annulling or amending a judgment rendered by the court of first instance.
All judgments rendered by the courts of first instance shall be subject to appeal, except those excluded therefrom by a provision in the law.

Having regard to the value of the matter in dispute, judgments deciding a dispute of a specified value not exceeding three million Lebanese pounds shall not be subject to appeal.

The value of the matter in dispute as at the date of lodging the appeal shall be taken into consideration.

The provisions of the second paragraph of this Article shall apply to pending actions and shall take effect immediately upon the publication of this Law.

Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding Article, an appeal shall be permissible even if the value of the dispute therein does not exceed eight hundred thousand Lebanese pounds if it is based on one of the following grounds:

1- Lack of functional or subject-matter jurisdiction.

2 - Nullity of the judgment due to a defect therein or nullity of the essential proceedings upon which the judgment was based.

3- Contradiction in the operative part of the judgment which renders its enforcement impossible.

4- Omission to adjudicate upon one of the claims.

5- Awarding that which was not claimed or more than what was claimed.
An appeal may be lodged immediately upon the issuance of the final judgment and prior to its service, provided that the fee has been paid.

With the exception of cases in which the law prescribes a time limit for appeal, such time limit shall be:

- Eight days from the date of service of the judgment to appeal judgments of the Judge of Urgent Matters, judgments deciding enforcement difficulties issued by the Head of the Enforcement Department, and decisions ordering provisional measures.

- Thirty days from the date of service of the adversarial judgment to appeal all other judgments issued by the courts of first instance.

Where no special provision prescribes the time at which the time limit for appeal commences, such time limit shall commence from the date of service of the judgment.

In the event of multiple judgments issued in a single case, those among them that are subject to appeal may be appealed separately or appealed together with the final judgment within the time limits prescribed by law.
An appeal may be lodged by any party to the proceedings having an interest therein, provided that he has not waived it.

An appeal may only be directed against parties before the court of first instance, subject to the special rules governing ex parte decisions. An appeal may be directed against any of the parties to the proceedings of first instance.

The respondent may lodge against the appellant an incidental appeal challenging the appealed judgment even after acquiescence therein or the expiry of the time limit for appealing it. If multiple judgments have been issued in the case and the principal appeal covers only one of those judgments, the incidental appeal may cover that judgment and all other judgments even after acquiescence therein or the expiry of the time limits for appealing them.

Where the opposing party appeals a judgment not covered by his appeal, the principal appellant may in turn file a supplementary appeal challenging this judgment and any other judgment rendered in the litigation that was not covered by his prior appeal.

Furthermore, after having covered certain aspects of the judgment in his appeal while his opposing party's incidental appeal covered the other aspects thereof, he may file a supplementary appeal challenging all other aspects of the judgment not covered by his principal appeal.

An incidental appeal may also be filed against another respondent or any party to the proceedings before the Court of First Instance, even if not a respondent, where the party filing the incidental appeal had asserted claims against him in the proceedings at first instance that were dismissed.

A party against whom an incidental appeal is directed may file a counter-incidental appeal, even after his acquiescence in the judgment or the expiry of the time limit for appealing it.

A person against whom the appeal was not directed, and who was a party to the proceedings at first instance, may file an incidental appeal against a judgment in which he has acquiesced or for which the time limit for appeal has expired, whenever he stands to be prejudiced by the principal appeal or the incidental appeal filed by another person.

An incidental appeal or a supplementary appeal must be filed in the first pleading submitted by the party lodging it. However, an incidental appeal filed by a person other than the respondent shall remain admissible until the closing of the proceedings.

If the incidental appeal or the supplementary appeal is filed after the acquiescence of the party lodging it or after the expiry of the time limit for the principal appeal, its admissibility shall be conditional upon the survival of the appeal from which it arose; if that appeal is not admitted in form or is withdrawn by the appellant, the incidental appeal or the supplementary appeal shall lapse, subject to the provisions of Article 523.

Intervention in the appeal shall be permissible for any interested person, provided that he was neither a party nor represented in the proceedings at first instance, or that he appeared therein in another capacity. It shall also be permissible to join the aforementioned person in the appeal.

In matters in which compromise is valid, the right to appeal may be waived. A waiver shall not be valid prior to the institution of the action, but shall be permissible after its institution. It is effected by an express agreement prior to the rendering of the judgment, and is effected after the rendering thereof by express or implied acquiescence therein. Voluntary execution of the judgment without reservation shall be deemed an acquiescence therein.

The inquiry into the action and its preparation for pleading shall be conducted by an appellate judge delegated by the President of the Court of Appeal for this purpose, in accordance with the provisions of Article 456. The delegated appellate judge may verify whether the appeal was lodged within the time limit, and if he finds that it was submitted after the expiry thereof, he shall immediately refer the matter to the court to take a decision thereon. He shall also refer to the court the question of staying the execution of the appealed judgment which was erroneously characterised as final.
An appeal submits anew the adjudicated case before the Court of Appeal to be decided anew in fact and in law.

The Court of Appeal's examination of the dispute shall be confined to the grounds expressly or impliedly addressed by the appeal and those connected therewith. The entire case shall devolve upon the Court of Appeal if the appeal is not confined to certain grounds only, or if it seeks the annulment of the judgment, or if the subject-matter of the dispute is indivisible.

The adversaries may invoke on appeal, in support of the claims submitted by them before the court of first instance, new grounds, pleas and defences, and may submit new documents and evidence.

A request by an adversary seeking the affirmation of the appealed judgment shall be deemed an adoption by him of the grounds of that judgment that do not conflict with what he advances on appeal.

.

No new claim shall be admissible on appeal unless it is a counterclaim, or a claim ancillary to or impliedly included in the original claim, or if it seeks set-off, or if it is in the nature of a defence to rebut the claims of the adversary, or if it aims to adjudicate issues arising from the intervention of a third party or from the occurrence or discovery of a certain fact. Claims seeking the very same outcome requested before the court of first instance shall also be admissible even if based on a new legal ground.

However, new claims shall remain admissible if the adversary does not object to their admissibility.

Claims for interest, arrears, "rentals" and other accessories that have fallen due since the rendering of the judgment, and a claim for compensation for damage incurred as a result of the judgment or since its rendering, shall not be deemed new claims and may be advanced on appeal as additional claims by way of a written submission.

If a final judgment dismissing the action for a reason not relating to the merits is appealed, the Court of Appeal shall, if it reverses such judgment, examine the merits. The same rule shall apply where a judgment relating to the merits is reversed on account of the nullity of the trial proceedings or of the judgment.
The Court of Appeal may at any time order a stay of execution of judgments that were erroneously characterised as final.
After hearing the pleadings, the opinion of the Public Prosecution shall be sought in the cases provided for by law.
An appellate decision that affirms a judgment of first instance shall be deemed to adopt the grounds of such judgment that do not conflict with its own grounds.

An extraordinary challenge and the time limit prescribed for exercising it shall not stay execution unless the law provides otherwise or the court decides to stay execution for serious reasons, with or without security.
Extraordinary means of challenge may only be exercised in the cases specified by law.

The challenger must deposit the security amount provided for in the Judicial Fees Law. This security shall be forfeited in favour of the State Treasury in the event that the challenger fails in his challenge, and shall be refunded to him in the event that judgment is rendered in his favour, even partially, or in the event that he withdraws the challenge prior to judgment being rendered thereon.

Third-party opposition is a challenge aimed at retracting or amending a judgment in favour of the opposing third party. Third-party opposition submits the dispute anew with respect to the opposing party on the aspects of the judgment that it addresses, to be adjudicated anew in fact and in law.

All judgments are subject to third-party opposition unless the law provides otherwise. An appellate decision is also subject to third-party opposition even if it has become final by the dismissal of a petition for cassation filed against it.
Third-party opposition is permissible for every person having an interest who was neither a party nor represented in the proceedings in which the challenged judgment was rendered.

From the moment the appeal is lodged, the court of first instance loses the right to rule on difficulties relating to the interpretation of its judgment and difficulties relating to its enforcement that concern the merits, or on the correction of clerical errors contained therein, and jurisdiction to examine these matters reverts to the Court of Appeal during the examination of the case. As for difficulties that arise after the rendering of the appellate judgment, the right to examine them reverts to the court of first instance where the judgment is upheld, and to the Court of Appeal where it is reversed.

Article 655:

An appeal shall be lodged by way of a statement of claim filed with the registry of the court to which it is submitted, and the rules prescribed for a statement of claim before the court of first instance shall be observed therein. It must be signed by an appellate lawyer and must include a statement of the appealed judgment specifying the court that rendered it and its date, the grounds of appeal, and the relief sought. A certified true copy of the appealed judgment must be attached thereto, as must the documents supporting the appeal unless they are already filed in the case file in which the contested judgment was rendered.

The grounds of appeal must be stated expressly, and a reference in respect thereof to the submissions filed in the first-instance proceedings shall not suffice.

Where the appeal is a principal appeal, the appellant shall deposit the security deposit provided for in the Judicial Fees Law.

This security deposit shall be forfeited to the State Treasury if the appeal is dismissed, and shall be refunded to the appellant if his claims are granted in whole or in part or if he withdraws his appeal.

Article 656:

The registry of the Court of Appeal shall request the joinder of the file of the first-instance proceedings on the day following the day on which the appeal is lodged. The registry of the court that rendered the judgment shall send this file within seven days at most from the date of its request, and this time limit shall be reduced to three days in summary proceedings, unless the Court of Appeal sets shorter time limits. That court shall sentence anyone who neglects to request the joinder of the file or to send it within the time limit to a fine of ten thousand to forty thousand Lebanese pounds, by a judgment not subject to any recourse.

The rules and procedures followed before the court of first instance with respect to the exchange of submissions, time limits, service, trial proceedings, and the rendering of judgments shall apply in appeal, unless the law provides otherwise. The appellate decision shall be rendered in absentia and shall be subject to opposition where the respondent fails to appear, service was not effected on him in person or on his lawyer-representative, and he has not filed a statement of his defence.

Third-party opposition shall be permissible for creditors and other successors to challenge every judgment issued against their predecessor-in-title if it is tainted by fraud or deceit directed against them, or if they invoke grounds or defences specific to themselves.

If the law restricts the right to sue to one or several specified persons, no other persons who are deprived of the right to sue shall be entitled to challenge the judgment by way of third-party opposition.

If the judgment is indivisible with respect to several adversaries therein, a challenge by way of third-party opposition shall not be admissible unless all of those adversaries are summoned to the proceedings.
A person who does not resort to third-party opposition may invoke the relativity of res judicata.
Third-party opposition is of two kinds: principal and incidental.

The time limit for third-party opposition against judicial judgments shall be set at two months from the date on which the opposing party is served with the judgment or with any measure for its enforcement. If such service has not taken place, the right of opposition shall remain standing, unless the law provides otherwise, until the right of the opposing party lapses by prescription, provided that incidental third-party opposition shall be admissible without being bound by a time limit.

Principal third-party opposition shall be submitted to the court that issued the challenged judgment by a statement of claim filed with its registry. The rules and procedures followed before that court shall apply in respect thereof.

Incidental third-party opposition shall be submitted to the court before which the opposed judgment, in which the opposing party was neither an adversary nor represented, is invoked against the latter in the course of other proceedings, where that court to which the opposition is submitted is of the same degree as, or of a higher degree than, the court that issued the opposed judgment and the dispute in which the judgment was issued falls within its jurisdiction. If either of the two aforementioned conditions is lacking, the opposition must be submitted in a principal manner to the court that issued the judgment.
An incidental third-party opposition shall be submitted by way of a statement of claims containing a statement of the grounds of the opposition.

The court before which the judgment contested by way of third-party opposition is invoked may decide, according to the circumstances, either to disregard this challenge and proceed with the trial, or to stay the proceedings until the third-party opposition is adjudicated by a final judgment.
The opposing party must establish proof that the contested decision was issued incorrectly in fact or in law.

The judgment issued in a third-party opposition in accordance with the claims set forth therein shall order the revocation of the opposed judgment or its amendment within the limits of what affects the rights of the opposing party. The original judgment shall retain its effects between the litigants therein, even with respect to the parts thereof that were annulled. However, the judgment issued in the third-party opposition shall have the authority of res judicata towards all the litigants who were summoned to the trial pursuant to the provisions of Article 676.
A judgment issued in a third-party opposition shall be subject to challenge by the same means by which judgments of the court that issued it are challenged.

Third-party opposition shall be permissible against criminal judgments with respect to civil disputes addressed and adjudicated therein as ancillary to the public prosecution. A principal opposition shall be submitted before the civil court located in the district of the criminal court that issued the judgment, equal to it in degree, and having jurisdiction with regard to the value of the matter in dispute. All other provisions set forth in this Law shall apply to the third-party opposition in this case.
An application for retrial is a challenge aimed at revoking a judgment possessing definitive character as defined by Article 553, for the purpose of examining the dispute anew in fact and in law.
An application for retrial may only be made by the litigants in the judgment or those represented therein.

Article 690:

A petition for retrial may not be filed except for one of the following causes:

1- Where fraud has emanated from the party in whose favour judgment was rendered or from his representative, which affected the rendering of the judgment, and which the petitioner for retrial discovered thereafter.

2- Where the petitioner for retrial has obtained, after the rendering of the judgment, decisive documents in the dispute which the party in whose favour judgment was rendered had withheld or prevented from being submitted.

3- Where, after the judgment, an acknowledgment of the forgery of the documents upon which it was founded has occurred, or where their forgery has been adjudged.

4- Where the judgment was based on an oath, testimony, expert statements, or a translation which was adjudged, after its rendering, to be false or forged.

5- Where the judgment was based on a prior judgment which was subsequently adjudged to be annulled, amended, or revoked, subject to the provisions of Article 733, paragraphs 2 and 3.

In all the cases set forth in the preceding Article, the petition for retrial shall not be admissible unless the petitioner was unable, without fault on his part, to invoke, by means of exercising an ordinary recourse, the cause upon which he relies before the judgment became final.

The time limit for a petition for retrial is thirty days, commencing from the day on which the petitioner became aware of the cause upon which he founds the petition for retrial, provided that the contested judgment has been rendered or has become final and has been notified to him prior to his knowledge of the said cause. However, if it is notified to him thereafter, the time limit shall run only from the date of notification of the judgment to him if it is final, or from the date on which the judgment became final after notification, subject to the provisions of the preceding Article. The burden of proving the date of his knowledge of the cause upon which he founds his petition shall lie upon the petitioner for retrial.
The petitioner for retrial must summon thereto all the adversaries in the contested judgment, under penalty of inadmissibility of his petition.

A petition for retrial shall be submitted to the court that rendered the judgment by a writ of summons lodged with the registry of that court, in which the rules prescribed for the writ of summons before the court of first instance shall be observed. It must include a statement of the contested judgment, its date, the causes for retrial, and the claims, failing which it shall be null and void.
The rules and procedures followed before the court to which it is submitted shall apply to the examination of the petition for retrial.

The adversary against whom the petition for retrial is directed may, in turn, submit within fifteen days from his notification of such petition, an incidental petition for retrial by virtue of a pleading containing a statement of the causes and the claims.

If a plaintiff brings a principal action based on a prior judgment and the time limit for challenging that judgment by a petition for retrial has not expired, the defendant may submit an incidental petition for retrial provided that the action is brought before the court that rendered that judgment or another court of the same degree or higher than it. If the court before which the action is brought is of a lower degree than the court that rendered the judgment, the petition for retrial must be submitted by way of a principal application to that latter court, and in this case the petitioner for retrial shall have the right to request the court hearing the principal action to stay its adjudication thereof until the principal petition for retrial is submitted and judgment is rendered thereon. The court may decide, according to the circumstances of the case, to accept this request or to reject it and continue hearing the principal action.

The court to which the petition for retrial has been submitted may rule first on the admissibility of this petition and then examine the merits. It may rule on the acceptance of the petition for retrial and on the merits in a single judgment if the parties have submitted their claims on the merits before it.
The decision issued accepting the petition for retrial shall order the revocation of the impugned judgment and the refund of the deposited security amount.

The acceptance of the petition for retrial shall entail the re-examination of the points covered by this petition and what is connected therewith by virtue of correlation or indivisibility and what is a necessary consequence of the retrial.

A petition for retrial shall not be admissible against a judgment that was challenged by a prior petition for retrial, except for a ground that emerged at a time subsequent to the judgment rendered on the first challenge.
The judgment rendered rejecting a petition for retrial or the judgment rendered on the merits of the dispute after the acceptance of this petition may not be challenged by a petition for retrial.
An appeal by way of cassation is a challenge brought before the Supreme Court for the purpose of quashing a decision on account of its violation of legal rules.

Decisions issued by the Courts of Appeal that terminate the litigation shall be subject to appeal by way of cassation, unless there is a provision to the contrary. Decisions issued by the Court of Appeal prior to the decision terminating the litigation shall be subject to appeal by way of cassation in accordance with the provisions of Article 615.

No appeal by way of cassation may be lodged against decisions rendered in cases in which the value of the claim does not exceed six million Lebanese pounds, and where the value does not exceed this limit, the appeal shall not be admissible save on the second, third, fourth, fifth and eighth grounds of the grounds set out in Article 708 of this Law.

Account shall be taken of the value of the matter in dispute as at the date of filing the appeal in cassation.

The provisions of the second paragraph of this Article shall apply to pending actions and shall take effect immediately upon the publication of this Law.

The time limit for an appeal by way of cassation shall be two months unless a special provision to the contrary is made.

Where no special provision specifies the time at which the time limit for an appeal by way of cassation begins to run, such time limit shall begin from the date of service of the decision. In the event of multiple appellate decisions rendered in a single case, those thereof which are subject to cassation may be appealed in cassation separately or together with the final decision within the time limit prescribed by law.
An appeal by way of cassation may be lodged prior to being served with the appellate decision, subject to payment of the fees thereof.

The respondent in cassation may submit, within a time limit of thirty days from the date of being served with the principal appeal, an incidental appeal against the decision covered by the principal appeal, even after acquiescence therein or the expiry of the time limit for cassation.

Where multiple decisions have been rendered in the case and the principal appeal covers only one decision among them, the incidental appeal may cover that decision as well as all the other decisions, even after acquiescence therein or the expiry of the time limits for appealing against them.

The principal appellant may, in the event that his opponent appeals against a decision not covered by the principal appeal, appeal in turn by way of a supplementary petition for cassation against that decision and any other decision not covered by his previous petition. He may likewise, after having covered in his principal appeal certain aspects of the decision whilst his opponent's incidental appeal covered the other aspects thereof, submit a supplementary appeal against the remaining aspects of the decision not covered by his principal appeal. The supplementary appeal in both preceding cases shall be submitted within a time limit of fifteen days from the date on which the party submitting it is served with the incidental appeal.

An incidental appeal may also be submitted, within the same time limit specified in the first paragraph of Article 712, against another party to the principal appeal or any party to the appellate proceedings even if not a respondent in cassation, provided that the party submitting the incidental appeal had directed claims against him in the appellate proceedings which were adjudged to be dismissed. Any party against whom an incidental appeal is directed may submit a counter-incidental appeal even after his acquiescence in the decision or the expiry of the time limit for appeal, within fifteen days from his being served with the incidental appeal.

A person against whom the appeal is not directed and who was an adversary in the appellate proceedings may lodge an incidental appeal against the decision in which he acquiesced, even if the time limit for appealing against it has expired, whenever he would be prejudiced by the principal appeal or by the incidental appeal lodged by another. The appeal shall remain admissible in this case for as long as the decision in the case has not been issued.

An incidental or supplementary appeal shall be lodged by way of a pleading: if it is lodged after the acquiescence of the person raising it or after the expiry of the time limit for the principal appeal, its admissibility shall be contingent upon the survival of the appeal from which it arose; if that appeal is not admitted as to form or if the appellant withdraws it, the incidental or supplementary appeal shall lapse, subject to the provisions of Article 736.

A principal appeal shall be lodged by a petition filed with the registry of the Court of Cassation, and it may be lodged through the Court of Appeal that issued the contested decision, which shall refer it together with the file of the papers of the case to the Court of Cassation after registering the contested decision in the special register.

A petition for cassation must be signed by an attorney at the Court of Appeal, and must include, in addition to the particulars relating to the names of the adversaries, their capacities, and the domicile of each of them, an indication of the contested decision by stating the court from which it was issued and its date, and a statement of the grounds for cassation and the prayers for relief. A certified true copy of the contested decision must be attached to it, and the documents supporting the appeal must likewise be attached to it unless they are filed in the file of the case in which the decision sought to be quashed was issued.

There must be filed with the petition for cassation a number of copies equal to the number of adversaries for the purpose of serving them upon them, unless they are represented by a single attorney, in which case the filing of a single copy shall suffice.

The principal petitioner in cassation shall deposit with the judiciary fund the amount of the security deposit determined by the Judicial Fees Law, and shall submit with the petition for cassation the receipt evidencing this deposit. In the event of multiple petitioners in cassation having a common interest in a single petition, a single security deposit shall suffice. Any person exempted therefrom by a statutory provision shall be exempted from depositing the security deposit.

A petition for cassation shall not be admissible if it does not fulfil its legal requirements. However, the petitioner may rectify his petition and complete the deficiencies if the time limit for requesting cassation has not expired, failing which his right to rectify or to complete the deficiencies shall be forfeited.
An appeal by way of cassation against default decisions shall not be permissible except after the expiry of the time-limit for filing an opposition thereto.

Article 706 - An appeal by way of cassation shall be permissible even if the contested decision was rendered in favour of or against a person who was not a party to the proceedings.

In non-contentious matters, an appeal by way of cassation shall be permissible even without adversary proceedings.

The Public Prosecutor before the Court of Cassation may, of his own motion or at the request of the Minister of Justice, appeal by way of cassation in the interest of the law against any decision subject to cassation which none of the parties has sought to have quashed within the legal time-limit, or in respect of which the parties have waived the request for cassation, where the decision is based on a violation of the law or on an error in its application or interpretation. He may also appeal by way of opposition and in the interest of the law against the decisions and on the grounds set forth in Article 95, item 4. The appeal by way of cassation or opposition shall be lodged within a time-limit of one year from the date of issuance of the decision by means of a petition signed by the Public Prosecutor. The court shall examine the appeal in the deliberation chamber without summoning the parties. The parties shall not benefit from this appeal.

Article 708 - An appeal by way of cassation shall be permissible on the following grounds:

(1) Violation of the law or error in its application or interpretation. The appellant must specify the text, legal principle or legal rule that was violated or in the application or interpretation of which the error occurred, and the aspects of the violation or error.

(2) Violation of the rules of functional or subject-matter jurisdiction.

(3) Contradiction in the operative part of a single decision such that its enforcement is impossible.

(4) Omission to rule on one of the claims.

(5) Awarding what the parties did not claim or more than they claimed.

(6) Lack of legal basis for the contested decision, such that its factual grounds are insufficient or unclear to support the legal solution decided therein.

(7) Distortion of the content of documents by stating facts contrary to what is contained therein or by contradicting the clear and explicit meaning of their texts.

(8) Contradiction between two judgments rendered at last instance in the same action by two different courts or by a single court.

Article 722- If the petition for cassation has been lodged with the registry of the court that rendered the impugned decision, the said registry must send all the documents relating to the appeal to the Court of Cassation on the day following the submission of the petition. And the registry of the Court of Cassation must request, within two days of the lodging of the petition for cassation or its arrival thereat, the joining of the case file with all its items. And the registry of the court that rendered the decision must send the file within seven days at most from the date on which it was requested. And the Court of Cassation shall sentence whoever neglects to request the joining of the file or to send it within the time limit to a fine of ten thousand to forty thousand Lebanese pounds.

Article 723 : An appeal by way of cassation does not stay the enforcement of the impugned decision prior to the quashing of the said decision, unless the Court of Cassation decides to stay enforcement against a security of which it determines the types and the amount. However, the Court of Cassation may not decide to stay the enforcement of decisions relating to maintenance and custody and decisions enforceable forthwith, save where there is an important ground that justifies it. With the exception of the cases specified in the preceding paragraph, the Execution Department must, when the party enforced against proves that he included an application for a stay of enforcement within the appeal submitted by him, desist from proceeding with enforcement until the Court of Cassation renders its decision on the said application within the time limit set in the following paragraph. Upon receipt of the application, the Court of Cassation must immediately serve it upon the respondent in cassation, and the latter shall be granted a time limit of one week to reply thereto, and the Court of Cassation must adjudicate the application for a stay of enforcement within a time limit of one month from the date of the expiry thereof, failing which enforcement shall proceed. The Court of Cassation may allow enforcement to proceed upon the application of the judgment creditor, provided that he deposits the adjudged sum in an accepted bank or provides a security guaranteeing the consequences of such enforcement in the event that the decision sought to be enforced is quashed
The petitioner in cassation may, within thirty days of the lodging of his petition, submit a pleading detailing- therein the grounds of appeal invoked.

The respondent in cassation may submit, within thirty days from the date of service, a pleading replying to the petition for cassation, and he may also submit another pleading within a similar time limit replying therein to the detailed pleading. The applicant for cassation has the right to reply within fifteen days, and his opponent has the right of final reply within a similar time limit.

Article 726: The respondent in cassation may, even after the expiry of the time limit for cassation, join in the appeal any opponent in the case in which the impugned decision was rendered against whom the appeal was not directed, if he has an established interest in joining him.

The parties shall revert, with respect to the points covered by the cassation, to the status in which they were prior to the issuance of the quashed decision. Cassation shall entail, without the need for a new decision, the annulment of all subsequent judgments and proceedings following the quashed decision if they were issued on the basis thereof or as an application or enforcement thereof, or if they were linked thereto by an inevitable link.

The petitioner in cassation shall have the right, upon the mere issuance of the cassation decision, to request the restitution of the funds that he paid in enforcement of the quashed decision, without attributing any fault to the respondent as a result of the enforcement.

If the cassation is limited to a part of the decision, it shall remain enforceable in the other parts unless they are consequent upon the quashed part.

In the event that the impugned decision is quashed, the Court of Cassation may rule directly on the merits of the case if it is ready for judgment; otherwise, it shall set a date for hearing the pleadings or for conducting such investigation as it deems necessary. In this case, the rules of procedure followed before the Court of Appeal shall apply, and the parties may submit new claims, defences, and pleas to the extent that they are admissible on appeal. The Court of Cassation shall adjudicate the case anew in fact and in law, with the exception of the aspects not covered by the cassation.
If the action requires an investigation, the Court of Cassation shall specify the matters covered by the investigation and assign one of its reporting judges to carry it out.

A discontinuance of an appeal before the Court of Cassation shall not be complete except with the consent of the respondent where it contains reservations or where the respondent has previously lodged an incidental appeal. No account shall be taken of the respondent's objection if it is not based on a legitimate ground. Discontinuance shall necessarily imply the appellant's acquiescence in the decision. However, it shall be deemed null and void if another party subsequently lodges an appeal in accordance with the applicable rules. The discontinuing party shall bear the costs of the appeal which he discontinued, unless otherwise agreed.

An allegation of forgery of any private or official document submitted to the Court of Cassation shall be subject to the provisions of Articles 180 to 202. The chamber of the Court of Cassation seized of the appeal in which the document alleged to be forged was submitted shall hear the forgery action. The decision issued in the forgery action shall be subject to challenge by way of retrial and third-party opposition.

The rules, effects and procedures observed before the Court of Cassation shall apply to petitions for cassation examined by the Plenary Assembly, unless a text provides otherwise, and none of the decisions rendered by the Plenary Assembly, whatever their subject matter, shall be susceptible to any avenue of recourse, including a suit against the State regarding liability arising from the acts of judges.. The rules of procedure before the Court of Cassation shall be followed, with the exception of the time limit for recourse, in the cases specified in item 3 of Article 95.

The rules of procedure before the Court of Cassation shall also be followed in the cases set forth in item /4/ of Article /95/, including the time limit for recourse, which shall run as from the date of notification of the decision that is the subject of the opposition.

The opposition shall not stay the enforcement of the contested decision unless the Plenary Assembly decides to stay enforcement against a security whose type and amount it shall determine. However, the Plenary Assembly may not stay the enforcement of decisions relating to maintenance and custody and decisions subject to expedited enforcement except where there exists an important reason justifying it.

The Public Prosecution shall be represented in the public trial in the person of the Public Prosecutor or such Advocates General as he may delegate, and shall express its opinion in the cases submitted.

Subject to the provisions of Article 6 of the Law of 21 October 1980 relating to the examination of individual labour disputes and disputes arising from the application of the Social Security Law, the grounds, rules of procedure and effects of cassation provided for in this Law shall apply to recourse against judgments rendered by the Arbitral Labour Boards. Appellate decisions rendered in demarcation and census cases shall be subject to recourse by way of cassation in accordance with the rules provided for in this Section.
The word "cassation" (al-naqd) shall be replaced by the word "cassation" (al-tamyiz) in any text in which it appears in this meaning.

A suit against the State regarding liability arising from the acts of a judge, whether he is among those who exercise adjudication, investigation or the Public Prosecution, shall be permissible in all cases in which a special text permits such suit and in the following cases:

1- Denial of justice.

2- Deceit or fraud.

3- Bribery.

4- Gross fault which a judge who attends to his duties with ordinary care is presumed not to commit.

Article 727 - Any adversary in the case in which the contested decision was rendered, against whom the appeal was not directed, may intervene in the proceedings of this appeal to request a ruling dismissing it. His intervention shall be effected by filing a pleading containing his defence, accompanied by the supporting documents, with the registry of the Court of Cassation prior to the adjudication of the appeal.

New grounds shall not be admissible before the Court of Cassation unless they are purely legal grounds or arise from the decision sought to be quashed, unless a provision to the contrary is stipulated.

Article 729 - Within three days following the submission of the petition for cassation, the President of the Chamber hearing the case shall appoint one of its counsellors to supervise the proceedings and alert the adversaries to any deficiency therein so that it may be completed within the statutory time limits, and who shall then prepare, within three months from the expiry of the time limits for the exchange of pleadings, a report setting out the facts of the case, the grounds of appeal, and the legal solutions he proposes, and the report shall remain confidential with respect to the adversaries until the issuance of the final decision. The President of the Chamber may undertake these duties himself.
Article 730 - The file of the appeal shall be referred to the Public Prosecution to give its opinion within fifteen days, in the cases provided for in Article 478.

Article 731: The Court of Cassation shall examine in the deliberation chamber, first, the admissibility of the appeal as to form and the existence of the grounds for cassation. If it decides to dismiss the appeal, it shall rule to affirm the contested decision. The Court of Cassation may dismiss the appeal by substituting a purely legal ground for an erroneous ground in the decision, or also by disregarding an erroneous legal ground therein which it deems superfluous. It may quash the contested decision by adopting of its own motion a purely legal ground relating to public policy. Where the Court adopts a purely legal ground of its own motion, the provisions of Article 373, paragraph 3, shall be observed.

Article 732: Subject to the provisions of Article 737, paragraph 3, and the provisions relating to actions brought against the State in respect of liability arising from the acts of judicial magistrates, decisions rendered by the Court of Cassation may not be challenged by any means of recourse.

Before bringing an action against the State on grounds of a judge's denial of justice, the injured party shall serve notice upon the judge twice to perform his duty by way of two petitions separated from one another by seven days, addressed to him through the clerk of the court, and the clerk shall refer the same to him within a time limit of twenty-four hours under pain of disciplinary penalties in the event of his delay. Upon the expiry of ten days from the filing of the second petition without the judge responding to the petitioner's request in any manner, the proceedings against the State shall become admissible.
The Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation shall hear the action brought against the State in the aforementioned cases.

The action shall be submitted within a time limit of two months from the date of service of the judgment or measure or the date on which the conditions of denial of justice are fulfilled in accordance with the provisions of Article 742, unless it is based on fraud, deceit or bribery and such ground was only known after the service of the judgment or measure, in which case the time limit shall run from the date of knowledge of that ground.

The action shall be submitted by way of a statement of claim addressed to the State, and it shall include a statement of the judgment or act complained of by the plaintiff, the ground or grounds upon which he bases the action, and the evidence supporting it. The parties in whose favour judgment was rendered shall be joined in the proceedings.

The statement of claim shall not be admissible unless it is signed by an attorney expressly authorised to bring the said action. However, if the interested party is unable to appoint an attorney and the President of the Bar Association refuses to assign an attorney to bring the action pursuant to the Legal Profession Law, the interested party may, after proving such refusal, sign the statement of claim himself.
The plaintiff shall deposit with his statement of claim a security deposit equivalent to the security deposit for a petition in cassation.

If the statement of claim contains insulting expressions not justified by the right of defence, its signatory shall be liable to pay a fine of four hundred thousand pounds to eight hundred thousand Lebanese pounds. The Plenary Assembly shall adjudge the same, and this shall not preclude disciplinary or criminal prosecution.

The submission of the statement of claim against the State shall not entail a stay of execution of the judgment complained of; however, it shall be for the Plenary Assembly to decide to stay execution or to permit it in accordance with the rules and conditions provided for in Article 723.

The Plenary Assembly shall first examine whether the action satisfies its legal conditions and the seriousness of its grounds, and consequently its admissibility. If the action is ruled inadmissible or if the claim is dismissed on the merits, the plaintiff shall forfeit the security deposit he lodged and damages assessed by the Plenary Assembly shall be awarded in favour of the defendant.

The judge to whom the cause of action is attributed may intervene in the proceedings at any time to submit his statements and request an award of damages in his favour against the plaintiff, where appropriate. He may only be joined to the proceedings by a decision of the Plenary Assembly upon the request of the defendant.

From the time the statement of claim is filed, the judge to whom the cause of action is attributed may not perform any act of his office relating to the plaintiff.

If the action is ruled admissible, the decision shall be served upon the defendant within three days, and the defendant may submit a written answer within fifteen days from the date of service. This answer shall be served upon the plaintiff, who shall be entitled to reply thereto within a similar time limit. After the plaintiff submits his reply, the defendant may submit its final rejoinder within a time limit of fifteen days from being served with the reply, following which a hearing for oral argument shall be scheduled and the proceedings shall be held in camera. The Public Prosecution shall deliver its opinion in writing or orally.

Where the claim based on denial of justice is upheld, the defendant shall be ordered to pay damages to the plaintiff for the harm caused to him and the original action shall be referred to another judge to examine it.

Where the action shown to be based on deceit, fraud, bribery, or gross error is upheld, the judgment or the complained-of measure shall be declared null and void and damages shall be awarded to the plaintiff for the harm caused to him.

The annulment of the judgment or of the complained-of measure shall restore the case to the state in which it stood immediately prior to the judgment or the complained-of measure, and the proceedings shall be resumed on the basis of a statement of claims.

The judge whose judgment or issued measure was annulled shall not participate in examining the original action and shall be recused from examining it by operation of law. If the action was brought in respect of a judgment or measure issued by a chamber of the court, the action shall be referred to another chamber following the annulment of the judgment or measure.

If the impugned judgment or decision is executed before the issuance of the decision in the action brought against the State, and a contrary judgment or decision is subsequently issued which proves impossible to execute for any reason, the aggrieved party may resort again to the court that issued the judgment or decision which proved impossible to execute, with a request for compensation against the other adversary for the damage caused to him for which he has not been compensated on account thereof. The judgment or decision issued on the request for compensation shall be subject to the same avenues of challenge to which the judgment or decision that proved impossible to execute is subject.

In the event that a judgment is issued against the State for compensation, it shall have the right of recourse therefor against the judge before the Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation. The State shall also have the right of recourse against the adversary in whose favour the annulled judgment or decision referred to in Article 757 was executed, to the extent of the compensation that it may have borne as a result of such execution pursuant to Article 754, and it shall bring the action therefor before the Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation.

If a judgment is issued against the State, it may, in the cases set forth in items 2, 3 and 4 of Article 741, bring an action taking issue with the judge before the Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation, within the time limits and in accordance with the procedures provided for in this Section, taking into account that the State is a plaintiff, with a view to annulling the said judgment and subsequently examining the case anew in accordance with the provisions of Articles 755 and 756. The State may claim from the judge, in the very same action, appropriate compensation in the event of the annulment of the judgment, and it shall have the right of recourse against the other adversary in accordance with the provisions of Article 757.
Judgments issued in an action brought against or by the State shall be notified to the Supreme Judicial Council and to the Judicial Inspection Authority.

The provisions of this Fourth Section (Articles 741 to 760) shall apply immediately upon the publication of this Law in the Official Gazette to all actions taking issue with judges pending before the Plenary Assembly of the Court of Cassation. The plaintiff shall have a time limit of two months to regularise his action in accordance with these provisions, commencing from the publication of this Law.

The contracting parties may insert in the commercial or civil contract concluded between them a clause stipulating that all disputes capable of settlement by compromise that arise from the validity, interpretation, or execution of this contract shall be resolved by way of arbitration. The State and persons of public law, whatever the nature of the contract that is the subject of the dispute, may resort to arbitration. As of the date of entry into force of this amending law, the arbitration clause or arbitration agreement shall not be effective in administrative contracts except after its authorization by a decree adopted in the Council of Ministers upon the proposal of the competent minister with respect to the State, or the tutelage authority with respect to legal persons of public law.

The arbitration clause shall not be valid unless it is written in the main contract or in a document to which this contract refers. It must include, under pain of its nullity, the appointment of the arbitrator or arbitrators in person or by their capacities, or a statement of the manner in which they are to be appointed.

If, after the dispute arises, an obstacle stands in the way of appointing the arbitrator or arbitrators by the act of the litigants or upon applying the manner of their appointment, the request for their appointment shall be made to the President of the Chamber of First Instance. If the President of the Chamber of First Instance finds that the arbitration clause is manifestly null or that it is insufficient to allow the appointment of the arbitrator or arbitrators, he shall issue a decision establishing that and declaring that there is no ground for appointing them. A null arbitration clause shall be deemed as if it had never been.

An arbitration contract is a contract whereby the parties thereto agree to resolve a dispute capable of settlement by compromise that has arisen between them by way of the arbitration of one or several persons.

An arbitration contract may only be proven in writing. It must include, under pain of its nullity, the specification of the subject of the dispute and the appointment of the arbitrator or arbitrators in person or by their capacities, or a statement of the manner in which they are to be appointed. An arbitration contract shall be deemed lapsed if the arbitrator appointed therein refuses the mission entrusted to him.

The litigants may agree to resolve a dispute by way of arbitration even if it is the subject of a lawsuit brought before the judiciary. They may also agree that the resolution shall be in accordance with the provisions of a foreign law or a foreign custom.

The mission of an arbitrator may not be entrusted to anyone other than a natural person, and if the arbitration appoints a legal person, its mission shall be limited to organizing the arbitration. An arbitrator may not be a minor, an interdicted person, a person deprived of his civil rights, or a bankrupt unless he has been rehabilitated.

The arbitrator's acceptance of the mission entrusted to him is required, and such acceptance shall be established in writing. If a ground for recusal exists in the person of the arbitrator, he must inform the parties thereof, and in this case he may not accept the mission except with the approval of those parties. After accepting the mission, the arbitrator may not withdraw without a serious reason, failing which he may be ordered to pay compensation to the injured party.

Arbitrators may not be dismissed except by the mutual consent of all the parties, nor may they be recused from adjudicating except for reasons that arise or appear after their appointment. Recusal shall be requested on the same grounds as those on which a judge is recused. The request for recusal shall be submitted to the Chamber of First Instance within the jurisdiction of which the agreed seat of arbitration is located, and failing that, to the Chamber of First Instance in Beirut, within a time-limit of fifteen days from the date on which the applicant for recusal became aware of the appointment of the arbitrator or the date on which the ground for recusal appeared thereafter. The decision of the court in this respect is not subject to any appeal.

Where there are multiple arbitrators, their number must in all cases be odd, failing which the arbitration shall be null and void. If the parties appoint two arbitrators or an even number of arbitrators, another arbitrator must be added to them, to be chosen in accordance with what the parties have determined, and failing that, by agreement of the arbitrators concerned, and if they do not agree, he shall be appointed by a decision of the President of the Chamber of First Instance.

Where a natural or legal person is appointed to organise the arbitration, the mission of arbitration shall be entrusted to one or several arbitrators accepted by all the parties. If such acceptance does not take place, the person entrusted with organising the arbitration shall invite each party to appoint one arbitrator and shall himself, where necessary, undertake the appointment of the arbitrator required to complete the arbitral tribunal. If the parties fail to appoint an arbitrator, the person entrusted with organising the arbitration shall appoint him. Direct recourse may be had to the appointment of the arbitrators in accordance with the provisions of the second paragraph.

If no time-limit is fixed in the arbitration agreement, whether a clause or a contract, the arbitrators must carry out their mission within six months at most from the date on which the last arbitrator accepted his mission. The contractual or statutory time-limit may be extended either by agreement of the parties or by a decision of the President of the Chamber of First Instance issued upon the request of one of the parties or of the arbitral tribunal.

In the cases provided for in Articles 764, 771 and 773, the President of the Chamber of First Instance referred to in Article 770, paragraph 2, shall issue his decision expeditiously upon the request of one of the parties or of the arbitral tribunal. This decision shall not be subject to any recourse. However, the aforementioned decision may be appealed when the President has declared therein that there are no grounds for appointing the arbitrator or arbitrators for one of the reasons specified in the second paragraph of Article 764. The Court of Appeal shall hear the recourse expeditiously.

The parties may agree in the arbitration clause, in the arbitration submission agreement, or in a separate contract that the arbitration shall be ordinary or ex aequo et bono (absolute), and the arbitrator or arbitrators may also be authorised to conciliate between the parties.

In case of doubt as to the characterisation of the arbitration, it shall be deemed to be an ordinary arbitration. In ordinary arbitration, the arbitrator or arbitrators shall apply the rules of law and the ordinary rules of procedure, with the exception of those that are incompatible with the rules of arbitration, in particular the rules set out in this Title. The parties may exempt the arbitrator or arbitrators from applying the ordinary rules of procedure or some of them, with the exception of those relating to public policy and provided that they are compatible with the rules and procedures of arbitration. In particular, the exemption may not cover the principles provided for in Articles 365 to 368 to 371 to 374. The aforementioned exemption shall only be established by an express provision in the arbitration agreement or in a separate agreement.

In ex aequo et bono (absolute) arbitration, the arbitrator or arbitrators shall be exempted from applying the rules of law and the ordinary rules of procedure and shall rule in accordance with equity. Rules of law relating to public policy and the fundamental principles of procedure, in particular those relating to the right of defence and the reasoning of the award, as well as the rules specific to the regime of arbitration, shall be excluded from this exemption. Ex aequo et bono (absolute) arbitration shall only be established pursuant to an express provision in the arbitration agreement or in a separate agreement.
The dispute shall be submitted to the arbitrator or arbitrators by the parties jointly or by the most diligent among them.
An arbitral award shall, from the moment of its issuance, have the authority of res judicata in respect of the dispute which it has adjudicated.

An arbitral award shall not be enforceable except by an order on petition issued by the President of the Chamber of First Instance with whose registry the original of the award was deposited, upon the request of the interested parties, after perusal of the award and the arbitration agreement.

If the dispute which is the subject of the arbitration falls within the jurisdiction of the administrative judiciary, exequatur shall be granted by the President of the State Council. In the event that it is refused, his decision may be opposed before the Litigation Council.

The dispute which is the subject of this paragraph shall be understood to mean a dispute which may arise between the contracting parties in an administrative contract concerning the interpretation or execution of such contract, excluding applications for annulment for excess of power, which shall remain exclusively within the jurisdiction of the administrative judiciary.

Exequatur shall be affixed to the deposited original of the arbitral award and to the original submitted by the applicant for such exequatur, and the latter original shall be returned to him immediately thereafter. A decision refusing exequatur must include a statement of the reasons. Exequatur may not be refused except for one of the grounds for annulment provided for in Article 800.

The rules relating to the provisional enforcement of judgments shall apply to arbitral awards. In the event of an appeal or recourse by way of annulment, the President of the Appellate Chamber before which the recourse is brought shall grant exequatur to the arbitral award coupled with provisional enforcement. The Court of Appeal may order provisional enforcement in the cases and under the conditions specified in Article 575.

An arbitral award shall not be subject to opposition. Recourse against this award may be had by way of third-party opposition before the court which would have had jurisdiction to hear the action had there been no arbitration, subject to the provisions of Article 681, paragraph 1.

An arbitral award shall be subject to appeal unless the parties have waived appeal in the arbitration agreement. An arbitral award rendered by an amiable compositeur shall not be subject to appeal unless the parties have expressly reserved the right to bring such recourse in the arbitration agreement, in which case the Court of Appeal shall hear the case as an amiable compositeur.

The arbitrators shall conduct the investigation jointly unless the arbitration agreement authorises them to delegate one of their number for this purpose. The arbitrators shall hear the statements of third parties without administering the oath to them. The arbitrators shall refer to the judge or the president of the court that would have had jurisdiction to hear the dispute had there been no arbitration in order to carry out the following: 1- Sentencing any witness who fails to appear or who refuses to answer to the penalties prescribed in this Law. 2- Ordering letters rogatory.
Where any evidence is in the possession of one of the parties, the arbitrators may order him to produce it.

Subject to what may be provided for by a special agreement between the parties, the arbitral proceedings shall terminate:

1- By the dismissal of the arbitrator, his death, the arising of an impediment preventing him from performing his duties, or his deprivation of the exercise of his civil rights.

2- By the abstention or recusal of the arbitrator from sitting.

3- By the expiry of the time limit for arbitration.
The interruption of the arbitral proceedings shall be subject to the provisions of Articles 505 to 508.

Unless there is an agreement to the contrary, the arbitrator may rule on an incidental plea of verification of handwriting in accordance with the provisions of Articles 174 to 178. Where an allegation of forgery is made against an instrument produced in the proceedings before the arbitrator, the latter shall stay the proceedings until this incidental plea is determined by a decision of the First Instance Chamber that would have had jurisdiction to hear the dispute, or within whose district sits the judge who would have had jurisdiction to hear the dispute, had there been no arbitration. The time limit for arbitration shall be suspended and shall not resume running until after the arbitrators have been notified of the judgment rendered on the incidental plea.

Where, during the arbitration, a preliminary question is raised that falls outside the jurisdiction of the arbitrators, or an instrument is challenged, or criminal proceedings are instituted relating to the forgery thereof or to a criminal incident connected with the dispute, the arbitrators shall stay their work and the time limit fixed for rendering the award shall be suspended until the arbitrators are notified of the final judgment rendered on that preliminary question.

Where one of the parties contests before the arbitrator the principle or extent of the jurisdiction vested in him to hear the case brought before him, it shall be for him to rule on such contestation.
Intervention by a third party in the dispute before the arbitrators shall not be permissible unless the parties agree thereto.

The arbitrator or arbitrators shall determine the date on which the case is deemed under examination or deliberation in preparation for issuing the award therein. From that date, it shall no longer be permissible to submit any claim, ground, observation or document unless at the request of the arbitrator or arbitrators.
Where there are multiple arbitrators, deliberation among them shall take place in secret, and the award shall be issued unanimously or by a majority of votes.

The arbitrators shall adjudicate the dispute in accordance with the rules set forth in Article 776 unless the parties have vested them in the arbitration agreement with the authority to adjudicate it as amiable compositeurs, in which case they shall apply the rules set forth in Article 777.

In the course of an existing arbitral dispute, the arbitrator may order such provisional or conservatory measures as he deems required by the nature of the dispute in accordance with Article 589 of this Law. The arbitrator may issue interim awards, and he may also adjudicate part of the claims prior to issuing the award terminating the litigation.

The arbitral award must contain:

1- The name of the arbitrator or the names of the arbitrators who issued it.

2- The place and date of its issuance.

3- The names of the parties, their titles, their capacities and the names of their representatives.

4- A summary of the facts, claims and supporting evidence submitted by the parties.

5- The reasons for the award and its operative part.

The arbitral award shall be signed by the arbitrator or arbitrators who issued it. If a minority of them refuses to sign, the other arbitrators shall mention that fact, and the award shall have the same effect as if it had been signed by all of them.

Upon the issuance of the arbitral award, the case is removed from the jurisdiction of the arbitrator. Nevertheless, the arbitrator retains the authority to interpret the award, to correct any omission or errors occurring therein, and to supplement it where it has omitted and to adjudicate one of the claims. The provisions of Articles 560 to 563 shall apply in this respect. However, the interpretation, correction or supplementation of the award by the arbitrator shall only be permissible within the time limit fixed for him to adjudicate the dispute, and after that time limit, the interpretation or correction of the award shall be undertaken by the court that would have had jurisdiction in the absence of arbitration.

For the purpose of granting exequatur to the arbitral award, the original of this award must be deposited with the registry of the Chamber of First Instance referred to in Article 770 paragraph 2, whether by one of the arbitrators or by the most diligent party. A copy of the arbitration agreement certified as conforming to its original by the arbitrators, a competent official authority, or the Chief Clerk after inspecting that original shall be attached to the original of the said award. The clerk of the court shall draw up a record of this deposit.

The decision issued granting leave for enforcement shall not be subject to any recourse. However, an appeal against the arbitral award or an action for its annulment shall automatically entail, within the limits of the dispute brought before the Court of Appeal, recourse against the decision granting leave for enforcement or divestiture of the jurisdiction of the judge competent to issue it.

The decision issued refusing leave for enforcement shall be subject to appeal within thirty days from the date of its notification. In such case, the Court of Appeal shall, at the request of the parties, examine the grounds that they could have invoked against the arbitral award by way of appeal or annulment, as the case may be.

The dismissal of the appeal or the dismissal of the action for annulment, in whole or in part, shall confer leave for enforcement upon the arbitral award or upon the clauses thereof not affected by the reversal or annulment.

The arbitral award shall be subject to recourse by way of retrial on the grounds and under the conditions prescribed for recourse against judgments by such means.

Such recourse shall be submitted to the Court of Appeal within the jurisdiction of which the arbitral award was rendered, and the decision rendered by the Court of Appeal shall be subject to recourse by way of cassation and by way of third-party opposition.

Arbitration that relates to the interests of international trade shall be deemed international. The State and all other public legal persons shall have the right to resort to international arbitration.

The arbitration agreement may appoint, directly or by reference to arbitration rules, the arbitrator or arbitrators, or determine therein the method of their appointment. If any difficulty arises in the appointment of the arbitrator or arbitrators in an arbitration taking place in Lebanon or in which the application of the Lebanese Code of Procedure is adopted, the most diligent party may, in the absence of a clause to the contrary, request the appointment by a decision issued by the President of the Chamber of First Instance in accordance with the conditions set forth in Article 774. Whenever necessary in the application of the rules of international arbitration, the Court of Beirut shall take the place of the court of the seat of arbitration taking place abroad.

The arbitration agreement may determine, directly or by reference to arbitration rules, the procedure to be followed in the arbitral proceedings. It may also subject these proceedings to a specific procedural law designated in the agreement. In the absence of a provision in the agreement, the arbitrator shall apply, as required by the circumstances, such procedure as he deems appropriate, either directly or by reference to a specific law or to arbitration rules.

Where international arbitration is governed by Lebanese law, the provisions of Articles 762 to 792 shall apply thereto only in the absence of special agreements and subject to the provisions of Articles 810 and 811.

The arbitrator shall decide the dispute in accordance with the rules of law chosen by the parties, or, failing that, in accordance with such rules as he deems appropriate.
