The duration of the substituted imprisonment shall be determined in the judgment imposing the penalty, or otherwise by a special decision, on the basis that one day of this penalty is equivalent to a fine ranging between two thousand pounds and ten thousand pounds.

The substituted imprisonment may not exceed one year nor the maximum limit of the original penalty of imprisonment entailed by the offence, and if the convicted person has a known attachable income, recourse may be had to compulsory enforcement prior to imprisonment.

Every partial payment made before or during the imprisonment and every amount recovered shall be deducted from this penalty according to the proportion determined by the judgment as set forth in the second paragraph of this Article.

The penalty of imprisonment shall not be executed against a pregnant woman who is not detained until six weeks after she gives birth. Spouses who are sentenced to this penalty for a term of less than one year and who are not detained shall serve it consecutively, if they have in their custody a child under eighteen years of age and prove that they have a fixed place of residence.

The following shall be imprisoned in separate places:

1- Persons sentenced to hard labour for life, for a fixed term,

2- Persons sentenced to detention for life, for a fixed term,

3- Persons sentenced to imprisonment with labour,

4- Persons sentenced to simple imprisonment.

All proceeds from the work of the convicted person shall be divided under the supervision of the Public Prosecutor in charge of execution among each of the convicted person, the persons whom he supports, the civil party, and the State for the purpose of recovering fines, judicial expenses, and prison administration expenses, according to a proportion determined in accordance with the nature of the judgment, provided that the share of each of the family of the convicted person and the civil party is not less than one-third of the value of the monthly proceeds.

When the civil party recovers the compensation due to him, the shares allocated to the convicted person and the persons whom he supports shall be progressively increased in proportion to his rehabilitation.

The custodial precautionary measures are:

1- Confinement in a precautionary asylum,

2- Relegation,

3- Confinement in a workhouse.

The liberty-restricting precautionary measures are:

1- Prohibition from frequenting taverns,

2- Prohibition of residence,

3- Supervised liberty,

4- Patronage,

5- Expulsion from the country.

The rights-depriving precautionary measures are:

1- Forfeiture of paternal authority or guardianship,

2- Prohibition from practising an occupation,

3- Prohibition from carrying a weapon.

The precautionary measures in rem are:

1- Real confiscation,

2- Preventive bond,

3- Closure of the establishment,

4- Suspension of a legal entity from operating or its dissolution.
Whoever is sentenced to confinement in a precautionary asylum shall be detained in a hospital designated by decree and shall receive the care required by his condition.

The physician of the asylum must draw up a report on the condition of the convicted person every six months.

He must also be visited at least once a year by a physician appointed by the court that ordered the confinement.

Whoever is sentenced to a custodial or liberty-restricting penalty, or to relegation, or to supervised liberty, or to prohibition of residence, or to a preventive bond, and it is established that during the execution of a sentence he has been afflicted with insanity, shall be confined in a precautionary asylum where he shall receive the care required by his condition.

The duration of the confinement may not exceed the remaining time of the penalty or of the precautionary measure the execution of which was suspended, unless the convicted person is a danger to public safety.

When the judge orders his release, he shall decide whether the whole or part of the duration of the confinement must be deducted from the term of the penalty or of the precautionary measure.

The duration of relegation ranges between three years and fifteen years. Relegation shall be executed in a work institution or in an agricultural colony designated by decree. The convicted person shall be placed in one of these two institutions in accordance with his qualifications and his urban or rural upbringing. Articles 57 and 58 shall apply to those sentenced to relegation.
If the convicted person leaves, for any duration whatsoever, the institution in which he was detained, he shall be liable to imprisonment with labour from one year to three years.

The duration of detention in a workhouse may not be less than three months nor exceed three years. The convicted person shall be subject to the regime prescribed in Articles 57 and 58. If the convicted person leaves the workhouse for any duration whatsoever, he shall be punished by imprisonment with labour from three months to one year.

If a felony or a misdemeanour is committed under the influence of alcoholic beverages, the judge may prohibit the convicted person from frequenting taverns in which these beverages are sold for a period ranging between one year and three years, under penalty of imprisonment from ten days to three months. The same punishment shall be imposed upon the seller and his employees who serve spirituous beverages to the convicted person having knowledge of the prohibition imposed upon him.

Prohibition of residence is the ban on the convicted person from being present after his release in the places specified by the judgment. Residence is prohibited, by operation of law, in the district in which the felony or misdemeanour was committed and the district in which the victim or his relatives by blood or marriage up to the fourth degree reside, unless the judge decides otherwise.

The duration of prohibition of residence shall range between one year and fifteen years. Whoever is sentenced to a felony penalty depriving of or restricting liberty shall be subject as of right to prohibition of residence for a duration equal to the duration of the penalty imposed. Whoever is sentenced to death, to perpetual hard labour or to perpetual detention and is exempted from his penalty by a general amnesty, or whose penalty has lapsed by prescription or has been reduced or commuted to another penalty, shall be subject as of right to prohibition of residence for fifteen years. A person sentenced to a misdemeanour penalty shall not be subject to prohibition of residence unless the law contains an express provision that imposes or permits this prohibition. All of the foregoing shall apply unless the judge decides to increase or reduce the duration of the prohibition within the limits set forth in the first paragraph, or to exempt the convicted person therefrom.

Every violation of the prohibition of residence shall be punished by imprisonment from three months to three years, and the judge may substitute supervised liberty for the prohibition of residence for a duration not less than what remains of the prohibition of residence.

The purpose of supervised liberty is to ascertain the rehabilitation of the convicted person and to facilitate his reintegration into society. The person under supervision shall be subject to the prohibition of frequenting taverns and to the prohibition of residence.

He must refrain from frequenting places prohibited by laws and regulations and must comply with the provisions imposed upon him by the judge, for fear of recidivism, and these provisions may be modified during the execution of the measure.

The duration of supervised liberty shall range between one year and five years unless a special provision to the contrary is contained in the law. If there are no special bodies for supervision, the police shall undertake the matter thereof.

A report on the conduct of the convicted person shall be submitted to the judge at least once every three months.

Whoever is sentenced to supervision and violates the provisions imposed upon him by the law or the judge, or habitually evades supervision, shall be sentenced to imprisonment with labour from three months to three years unless the law provides for another penalty.

Patronage shall be entrusted to institutions recognised by the State.

The institution must provide work for the convicted person. Its delegates shall prudently supervise his manner of living and extend advice and assistance to him.

The peculium of the released prisoner may be handed over to it to be used in his interest in the best manner.

A report on the condition and conduct of the convicted person must be submitted to the judicial body that ordered the measure at least once every three months.

Every foreigner sentenced to a felony penalty may be expelled from Lebanese territory pursuant to a special clause - in the judgment, and if he is sentenced to a misdemeanour penalty, he may only be expelled in the cases provided for by the law. Deportation from the country shall be ordered for life or for a period ranging between three and fifteen years.

A foreigner whose deportation has been ordered must leave Lebanese territory by his own means within a period of fifteen days. Every violation of a deportation measure, whether judicial or administrative, shall be punishable by imprisonment from one month to six months.

Forfeiture of guardianship or tutorship entails deprivation of all rights over the child or the orphan and over his property. Forfeiture shall be total or partial, and shall be general or confined to one child or orphan or to several children and orphans. The exercise of guardianship or tutorship shall pass to a tutor in accordance with the provisions of personal status.

A father, mother or tutor may be deprived of guardianship or tutorship if they are sentenced to a felony penalty and it is established that they are unworthy of exercising their authority over the child or the orphan.

These persons shall be subject to the same measure:

1- If they are sentenced to a felony or misdemeanour penalty for an offence they committed against the child, descendant or orphan, or in participation with him.

2- If the minor in their custody committed a felony or misdemeanour resulting from their negligence in his upbringing or from their habitual neglect in supervising him.

Forfeiture of parental authority or guardianship shall be for life or for a term ranging between three years and fifteen years, and it may not in any case be ordered for a duration shorter than the penalty or precautionary measure depriving of liberty to which the father, the mother, or the guardian has been sentenced.

Any person may be prohibited from practising an art, a profession, a trade, or any occupation contingent upon the approval of the authority or upon obtaining a certificate if he is sentenced to a felony or misdemeanour penalty for an offence committed in breach of the duties of the profession or the obligations inherent to that occupation.

If the practice of the occupation is possible independently of any condition or licence, prohibition from practising it may only be ordered in the cases provided for by the law. In press cases, the publisher shall be subject to prohibition even if his practice of the occupation is not contingent upon a licence.

The prohibition imposed upon him or upon the owner shall result in the suspension of the newspaper for the same duration as the prohibition.

The duration of the prohibition shall range between one month and two years.

It may be ordered for life if the offender had been sentenced to temporary prohibition by a final decision upon which five years have not elapsed, or if the law explicitly provides therefor.

Practising the prohibited occupation, even if carried out through an intermediary or on behalf of a third party, shall be punishable by imprisonment for up to three months and by a fine of up to two hundred thousand pounds.

Deprivation of the right to carry arms may be ordered for life or for a duration ranging between three years and fifteen years.

Any person subject to this measure may not obtain a licence to acquire or carry arms, and the licence that was in his possession shall be revoked, and the fee he paid shall not be refunded to him.

Every sentence to a felony or misdemeanour penalty for an offence committed by means of arms or with violence shall entail deprivation of the right to carry arms for a duration of three years, unless the decision of the judgment provides otherwise.

There shall be confiscated from among things that whose manufacture, acquisition, sale, or use is unlawful, even if it does not belong to the defendant or the convicted person or if the prosecution does not result in a judgment. If that which must be confiscated has not been seized, the convicted person or the defendant shall be granted a time limit to surrender it under pain of paying double its value as determined by the judge.

The court may, where necessary, seek the assistance of an expert to estimate the value that must be paid, and the estimated value shall be recovered in the manner followed in the recovery of a fine.

A precautionary bond is the deposit of a sum of money or public bonds, or the furnishing of a solvent surety or an insurance contract, as a guarantee of the good conduct of the convicted person or in prevention of another offence.

A bond may not be imposed for one year at least and for five years at most unless the law includes a special provision.

The judge shall specify in the judgment the amount of the sum to be deposited or the amount of the sum that must be guaranteed by the insurance contract or the surety, and it may not be less than five thousand pounds or exceed four hundred thousand pounds.

Supervised liberty shall by operation of law replace the precautionary bond for the same period if it is not furnished before the date fixed by the judge within ten days. If the precautionary bond is imposed on a moral entity, it may be recovered by attachment; and if the assets found do not satisfy the fixed value except by suspending the lawful activity of the entity, its dissolution may be adjudged.

A precautionary bond may be imposed:

1- In the case of conviction for threat or intimidation.

2- In the case of conviction for incitement to a felony that did not lead to a result.

3- If there is ground to fear that the convicted person will return to harming the victim or the members of his family or damaging their property.

4- In the two cases of stay of execution or stay of an enforceable judgment.

5- In the referral of a judgment against a moral entity for an offence that entails the imposition of supervised liberty.

The bond shall be refunded, the insurance cancelled and the surety discharged if during the probation period the act sought to be prevented is not committed.

In the contrary case, the bond shall be collected and allocated in priority to personal compensations, then to fees, then to fines, and whatever remains thereof shall be confiscated for the benefit of

the State.

The closure of the premises in which an offence was committed by the act of its owner or with his consent may be adjudged for one month at least and two years at most if the law permits that by an express provision; and closure, whatever its cause, shall by operation of law entail prohibiting the convicted person from practising the same work in accordance with what is stated in Article 94.

The closure of the premises adjudged on account of criminal acts or acts offending public morals shall entail prohibiting the convicted person, any member of his family, or any person who acquired ownership of or leased the premises with knowledge of its matter from practising the same work therein. The prohibition shall not cover the owner of the real property, or those who have a privilege, a mortgage right or a debt over the premises, if they remained uninvolved in the offence.

If the closure of the premises is adjudged because the operator commenced operating it in his place of residence without a licence, he shall be ordered to vacate the premises, without prejudice to the right of the lessor in good faith to rescind the lease contract and to all damages.
If this measure is adjudged on account of the incapacity of the operator, its effects shall be confined to him.
The convicted person and any third party shall be liable to the penalties provided for in Article 95 if they violate the provisions of the preceding Articles.

Any syndicate and any company or association and any moral entity, with the exception of public administrations, may be suspended if its directors, members of its management, its representatives, or its workers commit in its name or by one of its means a felony or an intentional misdemeanour punishable by at least two years of imprisonment.

The aforementioned entities may be dissolved in the cases referred to in the preceding Article:

1- If they have not complied with the legal obligations of incorporation,

2- If the purpose of their incorporation is contrary to the laws or if they in fact pursue such a purpose,

3- If they have violated the legal provisions provided for under pain of dissolution,

4- If they had been suspended pursuant to a final decision on which five years have not elapsed.

Suspension shall be pronounced for at least one month and at most two years, and it entails the cessation of all the operations of the entity even if the name is changed and the directors or members of the management are different, and it prevents the assignment of the premises subject to preserving the rights of third parties in good faith, and dissolution entails the liquidation of the property of the moral entity, and deprives the directors or members of the management and every person personally responsible for the offence of the capacity to incorporate or manage a similar entity.
Every violation of the preceding provisions shall be punishable by imprisonment from one month to six months and by a fine ranging between one hundred thousand pounds and two million pounds.

Notwithstanding any other text, and with the exception of the penalty of imprisonment substituted for a fine, a day of a penalty or precautionary measure shall be calculated as 24 hours, and a month as 30 days unless the penalty pronounced is less than one year of imprisonment, in which case the month shall be calculated as 20 days.

However, if the penalty pronounced is imprisonment for one year or more, that year shall be calculated as nine months from day to corresponding day in accordance with the Gregorian calendar.

Persons sentenced to penalties of indeterminate duration shall not benefit from the provisions of this text, nor shall habitual offenders and recidivists defined in accordance with the provisions of Article 258 et seq. of the Penal Code benefit from the provisions of this text after the entry into force of the law, provided that the judgment or decision being executed states this description.

Every penalty depriving of or restricting liberty shall be calculated from the day on which its execution commenced pursuant to the judgment that has become final.

If penalties depriving of liberty and penalties restricting liberty concur, the former penalties shall be executed first.

The period of civil degradation shall run from the day on which the judgment becomes final, and if the decision was issued in absentia, it shall be calculated from the date of the last record of posting executed pursuant to Article 67. Prohibition from certain civil rights ordered as an accessory measure in accordance with Article 66, shall be enforced from the expiry of the period of the original penalty of deprivation or restriction of liberty.

The effects of a judgment ordering confinement in a precautionary shelter shall be enforced immediately without regard to any other penalty or any other precautionary measure that deprives or restricts liberty. Precautionary measures of deprivation or restriction of liberty, with the exception of confinement in a precautionary shelter, shall be enforced after penalties of deprivation of liberty. Penalties of restriction of liberty shall be enforced after precautionary measures of deprivation of liberty. If precautionary measures of deprivation of liberty and precautionary measures of restriction of liberty concur, enforcement of the former shall begin in the following order:

- Confinement in a precautionary shelter, isolation, confinement in a workhouse, provided that the effects of expulsion from the country shall be enforced without regard to any other precautionary measure or any penalty of deprivation of rights.

Prohibition from practising an occupation, prohibition from carrying arms, and precautionary recognisance shall be enforced after the expiry of the period of penalties and precautionary measures of deprivation of liberty.

As for the remaining precautionary and in rem measures or measures of deprivation of rights, their effects shall be enforced from the day on which the judgment becomes final.

Preventive detention shall always be counted in the period of penalties of deprivation or restriction of liberty, and shall be deducted from the fine in the amount determined by the judge in accordance with the provisions of Articles 54, 62 and 64, and shall be deducted from the period of precautionary measures of deprivation of liberty if the judge expressly so orders in the judgment.

The civil obligations that the criminal judge may award are:

1- Restitution,

2- Damages,

3- Publication of the judgment,

4- Costs.

Restitution consists of restoring the situation to what it was before the offence. Whenever restitution is possible, it must be ordered ex officio.

The provisions of the civil law shall apply to the restitution of what was in the possession of a third party.

The criminal court hearing one of the offences provided for in Articles 689 and 692 and from 695 to 697 must order ex officio, even if it rules for acquittal, the restitution of all misappropriated funds, rights or shares to the body of creditors.

The provisions of Articles 134 to 136 inclusive of the Code of Obligations and Contracts shall apply to damages, and they shall be awarded at the request of the civil claimant.

In the event of acquittal, they may be awarded at the request of the defendant or at the request of the party summoned as civilly liable if it appears that the civil claimant committed an abuse in bringing his action.

The judge may decide that the damages he awards, for a felony or misdemeanour that resulted in death or in permanent incapacity for work, shall be paid as a life annuity to the victim or to his heirs if they so request.

The public action shall lapse, consequent upon the waiver of the civil right, if such waiver takes place before the final and conclusive judgment in the action and if it is express, unconditional, and issued by all the civil claimants where there are several of them, in the following offences:

1- In contraventions committed against individuals or against their property.

2- In offences of defamation and slander committed against individuals other than officials of public administrations and institutions, municipalities, the army, constituted bodies, and sitting judges by reason of their functions, and against deputies and ministers, and against the Head of State in all cases.

3- In offences of battery, wounding/embarrassment, and harm committed against individuals if the act did not lead to incapacity or led to an incapacity for work not exceeding ten days.

4- In all misdemeanours occurring between spouses prior to their legal separation, or occurring between ascendants and descendants, or between the father, the mother, and the adopted child.

5- In the misdemeanours provided for in Articles 650, 651, 658, 666, the first paragraph of Article 667, 670, 671, and 673.

In the offences set forth in the preceding paragraph, and where there are several defendants, the waiver of the civil right in respect of one of them shall lead to the lapse of the public action in respect of all the defendants in the same offence.

As for all other offences, the civil claimant may restrict his waiver of his civil rights to one or more of the defendants without such waiver affecting the public action; however, the legal consequences provided for in Article 32 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts shall ensue.

Objects subject to confiscation pursuant to Article 69 may be awarded to the civil claimant at his request, on account of the damages due to him and up to the amount thereof.

If the object decided to be confiscated has not been seized, the judge may order, at the request of the civil claimant, its delivery under pain of the coercive fine provided for in Article 251 of the Code of Obligations and Contracts, or order the offender to pay the equivalent value.

The judge may, if the civil claimant so requests and if his interest so requires, order the publication of the judgment in its entirety or the publication of a summary thereof in one or several newspapers at the expense of the convicted person, and he may, if the accused so requests and if his interest so requires, order the publication of the judgment of acquittal under the same conditions at the expense of the civil claimant if it appears that he was abusive in his action.

Costs shall be borne by the losing party. Where there are multiple convicted persons, the fees shall be payable by them in equal shares unless the judge decides otherwise. All costs that are of no avail to the action shall remain borne by the person who caused them exclusively, even if he is not the losing party. This shall be without prejudice to the provisions of the Commercial Code relating to bankruptcy proceedings.

The Public Prosecution shall apply the rule of payment by instalments set forth in Article 53 to judicial fees and costs. The complainant or the claimant shall be adjudged exempt from fees and costs if the offence that gave rise to the investigation actually occurred, but the investigation was unable to identify its perpetrator. In the event of the death, absence or minority of the convicted person, the fees and costs shall be collected through the Ministry of Finance in accordance with the rule for the collection of public funds.

A civil claimant who waives his action within twenty-four hours shall not be liable for the costs incurred since the notification of such waiver to the Public Prosecution and the defendant. Of the costs occasioned by a civil action that is ruled inadmissible, that part which was of no avail to the case shall remain borne by the civil claimant.

Every offence that causes damage to another person, whether material or moral, shall oblige the perpetrator to pay compensation. Civil obligations shall be incumbent upon the perpetrator of the offence who has benefited from one of the grounds for exemption.
An offence committed in a state of necessity shall render civilly liable the person for whose benefit it took place, to the extent of the damage he averted.

The obligation of restitution is indivisible. All persons convicted of a single offence shall bear the other civil obligations jointly and severally. Joint and several liability shall not extend to costs unless the persons convicted of a single offence were tried in the same action, and the judge may in any case exempt from joint and several liability those convicted of paying the costs.

Persons civilly liable shall be summoned to the trial and shall be held jointly and severally liable with the perpetrator of the offence for the restitutions and costs due to the State, and they shall be adjudged liable for the remaining civil obligations if the civil claimant so requests.

The Misdemeanour Court and the Criminal Court of Appeal, when examining one of the misdemeanours provided for in the chapters on counterfeiting and bankruptcy, and the Criminal Court examining any offence whatsoever, may sentence the defendant or the accused, upon pronouncing an acquittal, to all civil obligations requested by the injured party if the act constitutes a civil delict or a civil quasi-delict.

If a fine and civil obligations concur and the property of the convicted person is insufficient, the proceeds collected shall be distributed in accordance with the following order:

1- Civil obligations awarded in favour of the injured party,

2- Costs due to the State,

3- The fine.
Damages and costs may be paid in instalments in accordance with the provisions of Article 300 of the Code of Contracts and Obligations.

Recourse may be had to coercive imprisonment pursuant to the Code of Civil Procedure and in execution of civil obligations other than publication in newspapers and restitution of what has been ordered to be restored, and in the case of a joint and several judgment, the convicted person may only be imprisoned for the share attributable to him.

Persons coercively imprisoned shall be detained in special places.

The causes that extinguish criminal judgments or prevent or suspend their execution are the following:

1- Death of the convicted person,

2 - General amnesty,

3 - Special pardon,

4 - (Repealed)

5 - Rehabilitation.

6 - Prescription .

7 - Stay of execution.

8 - (Repealed).

-With the exception of rehabilitation, the Appellate Public Prosecutor shall decide the extinction of judgments rendered within the scope of his jurisdiction.

The causes that extinguish criminal judgments or prevent or suspend their execution shall have no effect on civil obligations, which remain subject to the provisions of the Code of Obligations and Contracts.

All criminal effects of the judgment shall cease upon the death of the convicted person.

It shall prevent the recovery of fines and the publication and posting of the judgment ordered in accordance with Articles 67 and 68, and shall have no effect on personal confiscation if the confiscated items have been awarded to the civil claimant, nor on confiscation in rem, nor on the closure of premises pursuant to Article 104.

A general amnesty is issued by the legislative authority, and extinguishes every penalty, whether principal, accessory or additional, and does not include precautionary measures and reformative measures unless the amnesty law expressly provides therefor; fines collected and items confiscated pursuant to Article 69 shall not be returned.

(Repealed by the Law of 5 February 1948)

In the absence of an express provision in the amnesty law, the pardoned penalties shall be taken into account for the application of the provisions relating to stays of execution, suspension of the enforceable judgment, rehabilitation, recidivism and habitual criminality. A general amnesty shall not preclude an application for a retrial.

A special pardon shall be granted by the Head of State after consulting the Pardon Committee, a convicted person may not refuse the benefit of the pardon, the pardon may be conditional and may be made subject to one or more of the obligations specified in Article 70, if the act committed is a felony, compensation must be paid to the civil party in accordance with the third paragraph of Article 170 within a time limit not exceeding three years.

A special pardon is personal, and may consist in commuting the penalty or in remitting or reducing, wholly or partially, the term of the penalty or the precautionary measure, and the pardon shall not cover accessory or additional penalties and precautionary measures imposed in addition to a principal penalty except by virtue of an express provision in the decree granting it.

No person against whom an irrevocable judgment has not been rendered may obtain a pardon, a stay of execution and the suspension of an enforceable judgment shall not preclude the obtaining of a pardon.

The remission of a penalty or of a precautionary measure shall be equivalent to its execution, the effect of the remitted or commuted penalty shall continue for the application of the provisions relating to stays of execution, suspension of the enforceable judgment, rehabilitation, recidivism and habitual criminality.

Every convicted person who again commits an offence exposing him to the penalties for recidivism, or who is proven by a judicial judgment to have breached one of the duties imposed by Article 152, shall forfeit the grant of pardon.

The limitation period for the death penalty and life felony penalties shall be twenty-five years.

The limitation period for temporary felony penalties shall be double the term of the penalty imposed by the court, and it may not exceed twenty years or be less than ten years.

The limitation period for any other felony penalty shall be ten years, and this period shall also apply to any misdemeanour penalty imposed for a felony.

The limitation period shall run from the date of the judgment if rendered in absentia, and from the date it becomes final if rendered in the presence of the parties and the convicted person is not in custody, and otherwise from the day he evades enforcement.

If the convicted person evades the enforcement of a custodial penalty or a penalty restricting liberty, half of the term of the penalty that was enforced against him shall be deducted from the limitation period.

The limitation period for misdemeanour penalties shall be double the term of the penalty imposed by the court, and it may not exceed ten years and be less than five years.

The limitation period for any other misdemeanour penalty shall be five years.

The limitation period shall run:

- In a judgment rendered in the presence of the parties, from the date of its issuance if it is at the last instance, and from the date it becomes final if it is at the first instance.

- And in a judgment rendered in absentia, from the service of notice upon the convicted person in person or at his place of residence.

If the convicted person is in custody, then from the day he escapes from enforcement, and in this case half of the term of the penalty that was enforced against him shall be deducted from the limitation period.
The limitation period for contravention penalties shall be two years, commencing in the manner stated in the preceding Article.

The limitation period for precautionary measures shall be three years. The limitation period shall not commence except from the day on which the precautionary measure became enforceable pursuant to Articles 115 and 116, or after the limitation of the penalty to which this measure was attached, provided that no decision is issued by the judge prior to the expiry of seven years as aforesaid establishing that the convicted person remains a danger to public safety; in this case, he shall order that the precautionary measure be enforced.

The limitation period shall be calculated from day to corresponding day, excluding the first day. The limitation period shall be suspended by any legal or material impediment that prevented the enforcement of the penalty or measure and did not arise from the will of the convicted person. The limitation period shall be interrupted by:

1- The appearance of the convicted person or any act carried out by the authority for the purpose of enforcement.

2- The commission by the convicted person of another offence equivalent to the offence that entailed the penalty or measure, or a more serious offence.

Provided that the limitation period may not in any case be extended to more than double its term.

Any person sentenced to a felony or misdemeanour penalty may be granted rehabilitation by a judicial decision if he fulfils the following conditions:

1- That seven years in the case of a felony and three years in the case of a misdemeanour have elapsed since his execution of the penalty and any custodial precautionary measure that may accompany it, or since its lapse in respect of him by prescription.

If the penalty imposed is civic degradation, the period shall run from the day on which the decision became final, and where a sentence of supplementary imprisonment is passed, from the expiry of the term of this penalty; if the penalty imposed is a fine, the period shall run from the day of payment or the expiry of the term of the substituted imprisonment; if the convicted person is a recidivist within the legal meaning or has previously been granted rehabilitation, the period shall be doubled.

2- That no subsequent judgment imposing a felony or misdemeanour penalty has been issued against him; any subsequent judgment imposing either of these two penalties shall interrupt the running of the period;

3- That the civil obligations entailed by the judgment have been executed, remitted, or lapsed by prescription, or that the convicted person proves that he was in a state in which he was unable to discharge those obligations; a bankrupt must prove that he has discharged the debt in principal, interest, and costs, or that he has been exempted therefrom.

4- That it is established from the prison records and from an inquiry into the conduct of the convicted person after his release that he has truly reformed.

Any person sentenced to a custodial or liberty-restricting misdemeanour penalty shall be rehabilitated by operation of law if he is not sentenced within seven years from the expiry of his penalty by another judgment to imprisonment, compulsory residence, or a more severe penalty; any person sentenced to a misdemeanour fine shall be rehabilitated by operation of law if he is not sentenced by another judgment to a misdemeanour fine or a more severe penalty within five years from payment or the end of the period of substituted imprisonment.

Rehabilitation shall annul for the future the effects of all judgments rendered and shall extinguish accessory or supplementary penalties, precautionary measures, and any incapacity resulting therefrom, and the aforementioned judgments may not subsequently be counted for recidivism or habitual criminality or preclude a stay of execution.

Prescription shall bar the execution of penalties and precautionary measures; however, prescription shall not run in respect of penalties and precautionary measures that deprive of rights, or in respect of prohibition of residence and confiscation in kind.

The mere issuance of a judgment in the action, even if at first instance, shall suspend the running of prescription on the public prosecution, which shall not resume running except in accordance with the provisions of Article 163 et seq. of the Penal Code.

When imposing a misdemeanour or contravention penalty, the judge may order the stay of its execution if the convicted person has not previously been sentenced to a penalty of the same kind or a more severe one. The convicted person shall not be granted a stay of execution if he does not have a real place of residence in Lebanon or if his judicial or administrative expulsion has been decided. A stay of execution shall not suspend the execution of additional or ancillary penalties or precautionary measures.

The judge may make the stay of execution conditional upon one or more of the following obligations:

1- That the convicted person provide a precautionary surety.

2- That he be subject to supervision.

3- That the civil claimant obtain the whole or part of his compensation within a period not exceeding two years in the case of a misdemeanour or six months in the case of a contravention.

Every person shall forfeit the benefit of the stay of execution if, within a period of five years or two years, according to whether he was sentenced to a misdemeanour or contravention penalty, he commits another offence for which he is sentenced to a penalty of the same kind or a more severe penalty, or if it is established against him by a judgment that he breached the obligations imposed by the judge pursuant to the preceding Article.

If the time of execution is not revoked, the judgment shall be deemed void upon the expiry of the probation period, and additional penalties and precautionary measures shall cease to have effect, with the exception of confinement in a precautionary asylum, confiscation in kind, and the closure of premises provided for in Article 104.

However, the stay of execution may be revoked even after the expiry of the probation period if the revocation action or the prosecution of the new offence was initiated before the expiry of the said period.

The stay of an enforceable judgment cannot be granted if there is a custodial precautionary measure that must be executed upon the convicted person after the expiry of the term of his penalty, and it shall have no effect on ancillary and additional penalties; a person sentenced to hard labour or detention shall remain under legal interdiction until the expiry of his penalty unless the judge decides otherwise.

An offence is a felony, a misdemeanour, or a contravention according to whether it is punishable by a felony, misdemeanour, or contravention penalty. The maximum limit of the most severe penalty prescribed by law shall be taken into account in the legal classification.
The legal classification shall not change if the prescribed penalty is substituted by a lighter penalty upon the admission of mitigating reasons or mitigating excuses.

If an act has several classifications, they shall all be mentioned in the judgment, provided that the judge imposes the most severe penalty. However, if both a general provision of the penal law and a special provision apply to the act, the special provision shall prevail.
An act which is punishable for interfering with the will of another shall not be deemed an offence if committed with his consent - prior to or concomitant with its occurrence.
Intent is the will to commit the offence as defined by the law.
An offence shall be deemed intentional even if the criminal result arising from the act or omission exceeds the intent of the perpetrator, if he had foreseen its occurrence and accepted the risk.
Fault exists where the harmful act results from negligence, lack of precaution, or non-observance of laws and regulations.

An offence shall be unintentional whether the perpetrator did not foresee the result of his faulty act or omission when he was able or had a duty to foresee it, or whether he foresaw it and reckoned that it was within his power to avoid it.
Motive is the cause that prompts the perpetrator to the act, or the ultimate purpose that he seeks. It shall not be an element of incrimination except in the cases specified by the law.

If the judge establishes that the motive was honourable, he shall impose the following penalties:

- Detention for life instead of death,

- Detention for life or for fifteen years instead of hard labour for life,

- Temporary detention instead of temporary hard labour,

- Simple imprisonment instead of imprisonment with labour,

The judge may, in addition, exempt the convicted person from the posting and publication of the judgment imposed as a penalty.

A motive shall be honourable if it is characterised by chivalry and magnanimity and is devoid of selfishness, personal considerations, and material benefit.

If an offence punishable by detention for life or temporary detention or by simple imprisonment was inspired by an ignoble motive, the judge shall substitute: hard labour for life for detention for life, temporary hard labour for temporary detention, imprisonment with labour for simple imprisonment.

A single act shall not be prosecuted more than once. However, if the criminal consequences of the act are aggravated after the first prosecution such that it becomes subject to a more severe classification, it shall be prosecuted under that classification and only the more severe penalty shall be enforced; if the penalty previously adjudged has been enforced, it shall be deducted from the new penalty.
An act committed in the exercise of a right without excess shall not constitute an offence.

After the exercise of a right is every act required by an immediate necessity to ward off an unjust and unprovoked assault against one's person or property or the person or property of another, and natural persons and legal persons shall be equal in protection. If excess occurs in defence, the perpetrator of the offence may be exempted from the penalty under the conditions set forth in Article 228.

An act committed in execution of a statutory provision or of a lawful order issued by the authority shall not constitute an offence.

If the order issued is unlawful, the perpetrator shall be justified if the law did not permit him to verify its lawfulness.

The following paragraph was added pursuant to the Law promulgated by Decree No. 15739 dated 11/3/1964:

Shall also be deemed a lawful order a written order given by:

1 - The President of the Judicial Inspection Board.

2 - The President of the Central Inspection Board.

3 - The Director General of the Internal Security Forces.

4 - The Director General of General Security.

Each within the scope of his competence.

To a public official to feign participation in one of the offences of bribery punishable under Articles 351 to 356 of the Penal Code, for the purpose of discovering the perpetrators of such offences, provided that the justification for such participation is the detection of this type of offence, and that the activity of the person charged with this order does not exceed the intended purpose.

Special provisions regarding unlawful orders

"No person prosecuted for one of the offences specified in Article 401 of this Law may invoke any pretext to justify his act, such as a state of necessity, the requirements of national security, orders from a higher authority, or any other pretext.

Orders to torture issued by a public official of any rank, corps, or authority whatsoever shall under no circumstances be deemed lawful orders".

An act permitted by law shall not constitute an offence. The law permits:

1) Forms of non-violent discipline exercised by fathers and mothers over their children, provided that they leave no trace on the children's bodies nor cause harm to their physical or mental health.

2) Surgical operations and medical treatments conforming to the rules of the art, provided that they are performed with the consent of the patient or the consent of his legal representatives or in cases of urgent necessity,

3) Acts of violence that occur during sports games if the rules of play are observed.

Where all the acts aimed at committing a felony have been completed, yet they have produced no effect owing to circumstances unrelated to the will of the perpetrator, the penalties may be reduced as follows:

- The death penalty may be commuted to hard labour for life or for a fixed term of ten to twenty years.

- Hard labour for life may be commuted to hard labour for a fixed term of seven to twenty years.

- Detention for life may be commuted to detention for a fixed term of seven to twenty years.

- Any other penalty may be reduced by up to one half.

The penalties mentioned in this Article may be reduced by up to two thirds if the perpetrator, of his own free will, prevents the result of his act.

Neither an attempted misdemeanour nor an unconsummated misdemeanour shall be punishable save in the cases expressly provided for by law.

The penalty prescribed for a consummated misdemeanour may be reduced by up to one half in the case of an attempted misdemeanour and by up to one third in the case of a frustrated misdemeanour.

An attempt shall be punishable even if it was impossible to attain the intended aim owing to a material circumstance unknown to the perpetrator; provided, however, that the perpetrator shall not be punished in such case if he committed his act out of lack of understanding. Likewise, a person who commits an act under the mistaken belief that it constitutes an offence shall not be punished.

The causal link between an act or omission on the one hand, and the criminal result on the other hand, shall not be negated by the concurrence of other pre-existing, concomitant or supervening causes, whether the perpetrator was unaware of them or whether they were independent of his act.

It shall be otherwise where the supervening cause is independent and sufficient in itself to bring about the criminal result.

In such case, the perpetrator shall be liable only to the penalty for the act which he committed.

Where several felonies or misdemeanours are established, a penalty shall be pronounced for each offence, and only the severest penalty shall be enforced.

Provided that the penalties imposed may be cumulated in such a manner that the aggregate of the fixed-term penalties shall not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for the severest offence by more than one half thereof.

Where no ruling has been given for the merger or cumulation of the penalties imposed, the matter shall be referred to the judge for determination.

Where an offence takes effect against a person other than the one against whom it was intended, the perpetrator shall be punished as though he had committed the act against the person whom he intended.

Where both are harmed, the penalty mentioned in the preceding paragraph may be increased by one half.
Contraventional penalties shall necessarily be cumulated.

Additional penalties and precautionary measures shall be cumulated even if the principal penalties are merged, unless the judge rules otherwise.

Where the principal penalties are cumulated, the accessory penalties attached thereto shall be cumulated by operation of law.

The following shall be deemed means of publication:

1) Acts and gestures if they take place in a public place or a place open to the public or exposed to view, or if they are witnessed, through the fault of the perpetrator, by anyone who has no involvement in the act,

2) Speech or shouting, whether uttered aloud or transmitted by mechanical means, such that in both cases they are heard by anyone who has no involvement in the act,

3) Writing, drawings, manual and photographic pictures, films, badges and imagery of all kinds, if displayed in a public place or a place open to the public or exposed to view, or if sold, offered for sale or distributed to one or more persons.

No one shall be sentenced to a penalty unless he committed the act with awareness and will.

Legal entities shall be criminally liable for the acts of their directors, management members, representatives and employees when they perform such acts in the name of the said entities or by one of their means.

They may only be sentenced to a fine, confiscation and publication of the judgment.

If the law provides for a principal penalty other than a fine, the said penalty shall be replaced by a fine and imposed upon the legal entity within the limits specified in Articles 53, 60 and 63.

No precautionary measure shall be imposed upon anyone unless he constitutes a danger to public safety.

Precautionary measures shall be ordered after verifying the state of danger, except in cases where the law presumes the existence of danger.

Every person or legal entity that has committed an offence shall be deemed a danger to society if it is feared that he may commit other acts punishable by law.

Legal entities shall only be subject to precautionary measures in rem. .
The perpetrator of an offence is anyone who brings into existence the elements that constitute the offence or contributes directly to its execution.

Every co-perpetrator in an offence shall be subject to the penalty prescribed therefor by law. The penalty for anyone who organised the participation in the offence or directed the action of those who took part therein shall be increased in accordance with the conditions set forth in Article 257.

The two co-perpetrators in an offence committed by speech transmitted by mechanical means, as set forth in the second paragraph of Article 209, or in an offence committed by one of the means mentioned in the second paragraph of the same Article, shall be the author of the speech or writing and the publisher, unless the former proves that publication took place without his consent.
When an offence is committed by means of newspapers, the publication director shall be deemed the publisher, and if there is no director, then the editor or the editor-in-chief of the newspaper.
If an offence not punishable by a fine is committed from a motive of gain, both this penalty and the penalty prescribed by law shall be imposed together.

Political offences are intentional offences committed by the perpetrator from a political motive.

They are also offences committed against public and individual political rights, unless the perpetrator was driven by a base selfish motive.

Complex offences or offences closely connected with political offences shall be deemed political offences, unless they are among the gravest felonies in terms of morality and ordinary law, such as homicide, grievous bodily harm, attacks on property by arson, explosion or flooding, and aggravated thefts, particularly those committed with weapons and violence, as well as attempts to commit such felonies.

In time of civil war or insurrection, however, complex or closely connected offences shall not be deemed political unless the customs of war do not prohibit them and they do not constitute acts of barbarity or vandalism.

If the judge ascertains that the offence is of a political nature, he shall impose the following penalties:

- Detention for life instead of death or hard labour for life.

- Temporary detention, banishment, felony compulsory residence or civic degradation instead of temporary hard labour.

- Simple imprisonment or misdemeanour compulsory residence instead of imprisonment with labour.

These provisions shall not apply to offences against the external security of the State.

If the judge ascertains that an offence punishable by a political penalty was committed from a base selfish motive, he shall substitute for the penalty prescribed by law the corresponding penalty set forth in the preceding Article. However, detention for life may only be commuted to hard labour for life.

Every attempt to commit a felony that has begun with acts aimed directly at committing it shall be deemed as the felony itself if its completion was prevented only by circumstances beyond the perpetrator's will.

However, the penalties specified in the law may be reduced as follows:

- The penalty of death may be replaced by hard labour for life or by temporary hard labour for seven to twenty years.

- Hard labour for life may be replaced by temporary hard labour for at least five years.

- Detention for life may be replaced by temporary detention for at least five years.

- Any other penalty may be reduced by one half to two thirds, and whoever begins to commit an act and voluntarily desists therefrom shall be punished only for the acts that he committed and that in themselves constituted offences.

The effects of the material causes capable of aggravating, reducing or exempting from the penalty shall apply to every one of the co-perpetrators of the offence and the accomplices therein.

The effects of the personal or mixed aggravating circumstances that facilitated the commission of the offence shall also apply to them.

As for any other circumstances, their effect shall extend only to the person to whom they relate.

Any person who induces or attempts to induce another person by any means whatsoever to commit an offence shall be deemed an instigator.

The liability of the instigator is independent of the liability of the person instigated to commit the offence.

The instigator shall be subject to the penalty for the offence which he intended to be committed, whether the offence was consummated, attempted or abortive.

If the instigation to commit a felony or a misdemeanour does not lead to an outcome, the penalty shall be reduced in the proportion specified in Article 220 in paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 thereof.

Instigation to commit a contravention shall not be punishable if it is not accepted.

Precautionary measures shall be imposed on the instigator as though he were the perpetrator of the offence.

The following shall be deemed an accomplice to a felony or a misdemeanour:

1- Anyone who gives instructions for its commission, even if such instructions did not assist in the act.

2 - Anyone who strengthens the resolve of the perpetrator by any means.

3 - Anyone who accepts, for the sake of a material or moral interest, the offer of the perpetrator to commit the offence.

4 - Anyone who aids or abets the perpetrator in the acts that prepared or facilitated the offence.

5 - Anyone who was in agreement with the perpetrator or one of the accomplices prior to the commission of the offence and contributed to concealing its traces, or hiding or disposing of the things resulting therefrom, or concealing one or more of the persons who participated therein from the reach of justice.

6 - Anyone who, having knowledge of the criminal conduct of malefactors whose habit is highway robbery or the commission of acts of violence against State security or public safety, or against persons or property, provides them with food, shelter, a hiding place or a meeting place.

An accomplice without whose assistance the offence would not have been committed shall be punished as though he himself were the perpetrator, whereas other accomplices shall be punished with hard labour for life or for a fixed term of ten to twenty years if the perpetrator is punishable with death; and if the punishment of the perpetrator is hard labour for life or detention for life, the accomplices shall be sentenced to the same penalty for a term of seven to fifteen years; and in other cases, the penalty of the perpetrator shall be imposed on them after its duration is reduced by one sixth to one third.

Precautionary measures may be imposed on them as though they themselves were the perpetrators of the offence.

Whoever, save in the case provided for in the fifth paragraph of Article 219, knowingly proceeds to conceal or dispose of things belonging to the ownership of another, which were stripped, embezzled, or obtained by a felony or a misdemeanour, shall be punished by imprisonment from three months to two years and by a fine from twenty thousand pounds to four hundred thousand pounds.

Provided that if the concealed or disposed-of things result from a misdemeanour, the penalty cannot exceed two-thirds of the maximum limit of the penalty for the aforementioned misdemeanour.

Whoever, save in the cases provided for in the 5th and 6th paragraphs of Article 219, proceeds to conceal a person whom he knows to have committed a felony, or helps him to hide from the face of justice, shall be punished by imprisonment from three months to two years.

Exempted from the penalty are the ascendants or descendants of the concealed felons, their husbands or wives even if divorced, their brothers or sisters, or their relatives by marriage of the same degrees.

No one may plead his ignorance of the criminal law or his erroneous interpretation thereof. However, the following shall be deemed an impediment to punishment:

1- Ignorance or mistake relating to a civil or administrative law upon which the imposition of the penalty depends,

2 - Ignorance of a new law if the offence was committed within the three days that followed its publication,

3 - Ignorance of a foreigner who arrived in Lebanon at most three days earlier of the existence of an offence contrary to positive laws that is not punished by the laws of his country or the laws of the country in which he was residing.

No one shall be punished as a perpetrator, instigator, or accomplice in an intentional offence who proceeded to commit the act by reason of a material mistake relating to one of the constituent elements of the offence.

If the mistake relates to one of the aggravating circumstances, the offender shall not be liable therefor, and on the contrary he shall benefit from the excuse of whose existence he was ignorant.

These provisions shall apply in the case of a mistake relating to the identity of the victim.
A mistake relating to an act constituting an unintentional offence shall not be an impediment to punishment unless it did not result from the fault of the perpetrator.

No public official, agent, or employee in the Government who ordered the execution of an act or proceeded to commit an act punished by the law shall be punished if he believed, by reason of a material mistake, that he was obeying the lawful order of his superiors in matters falling within their competence in which obedience to them was incumbent upon him.

There shall be no punishment upon whoever was compelled by a physical or moral force which he had no way to resist.

Whoever found himself in that state through his own fault shall be punished, where applicable, as a perpetrator of an unintentional offence.

Any person who, at the time of committing the act, due to a fortuitous event or force majeure, was in a state of intoxication resulting from alcohol or narcotics that deprived him of consciousness or will shall be exempted from the penalty. If the state of intoxication resulted from the fault of the perpetrator, he shall be liable for every unintentional offence he committed, and he shall be liable for the intentional offence if he foresaw, at the time he placed himself in that state due to his fault, the possibility of his committing criminal acts.

And if he intentionally placed himself in that state in order to commit the offence, his penalty shall be aggravated in accordance with Article 257.

If the state of intoxication resulting from force majeure or a fortuitous event weakened the perpetrator's power of consciousness or will to a great extent, the penalty may be commuted or reduced in accordance with the provisions of Article 251.

In this law, a child means one who has completed the seventh year of his age and has not yet completed the eighteenth year, an adolescent means one who has completed the twelfth year and has not yet completed the fifteenth year, and a youth means one who has completed the fifteenth year and has not completed the eighteenth year.
There shall be no excuse for an offence except in the cases specified by the law.

An absolving excuse exempts the offender from all punishment.

However, reform measures and precautionary measures, with the exception of solitary confinement, may be imposed upon him where appropriate.

When the law provides for a mitigating excuse:

- If the act is a felony entailing the death penalty, hard labour for life, or detention for life, the penalty shall be commuted to imprisonment for one year at least and seven years at most.

- And if the act constitutes one of the other felonies, imprisonment shall be from six months to five years.

- And if the act is a misdemeanour, the penalty shall not exceed six months.

- And if the act is a contravention, the judge may reduce the penalty to half of the petty fine.

The beneficiary of the mitigating excuse may be subjected to the precautionary measures, with the exception of solitary confinement, to which he would have been exposed had he been sentenced to the penalty provided for by the law.
The perpetrator of an offence who committed it in a fit of extreme anger resulting from an unjust and somewhat grave act committed by the victim shall benefit from the mitigating excuse.

Where mitigating circumstances exist in a case, the court shall pass sentence:

- Instead of death, to hard labour for life or fixed-term hard labour for a term of seven to twenty years.

- And instead of hard labour for life, to fixed-term hard labour for no less than five years.

- And instead of detention for life, to fixed-term detention for no less than five years, and it may reduce any other felony penalty down to three years if its minimum limit exceeds that.

And it may reduce the penalty by half if its minimum limit does not exceed three years, or substitute for it, by a reasoned decision, imprisonment for at least one year, save in the case of recidivism.

Where the court admits mitigating circumstances in favour of a person who has committed a misdemeanour, it may reduce the penalty to its minimum limit set out in Articles 51, 52 and 53, and it may substitute a fine for imprisonment and for compulsory residence, or commute, save in the case of recidivism, the misdemeanour penalty to a petty offence penalty by a reasoned decision.

A sentence of the minimum limit of the penalty set out in Articles 60 and 61, or of a fine, may be passed upon a person who has committed a petty offence in which mitigating circumstances are found to exist.
In the case of recidivism, the decision granting mitigating circumstances must be accompanied by special reasoning, whether in felonies, misdemeanours or petty offences.

Where the law does not specify the effect of an aggravating circumstance, the said circumstance shall entail the aggravation of the penalty in the following manner:

Death shall be substituted for hard labour for life, every fixed-term penalty shall be increased by one third to one half, and the fine shall be doubled.

Whoever has been sentenced to hard labour for life by a final judgment and commits another felony carrying the same penalty shall be sentenced to death.

And whoever has been sentenced by a final judgment to fixed-term hard labour or fixed-term detention and commits another felony carrying the same penalty before the lapse of fifteen years from the expiry of the penalty or its limitation by lapse of time shall be sentenced to the punishment that he deserves with the addition of an equal term thereof.

Where appropriate, the maximum limit of this punishment may be raised to double thereof, namely thirty years.

Where the second offence carries a sentence of banishment, compulsory residence or civic degradation, the offender shall be sentenced to the penalty immediately above it by one degree according to the order set out in Article 38.

Reverential fear and states of emotion and passion shall not preclude punishment.

However, where the perpetrator of the offence exceeds the exercise of the right of legitimate defence, he shall not be punished if he committed the act in an outburst of violent emotion whereby the power of his consciousness or his will was nullified.

The perpetrator shall not be punished for an act by which necessity compelled him to ward off from himself or from another or from his property or the property of another a grave and imminent danger that he did not intentionally cause, provided that the act is proportionate to the danger.
A person who is required by law to expose himself to danger shall not be deemed to be in a state of necessity.
Any person who was in a state of insanity that deprived him of consciousness or will shall be exempt from punishment.

Any person proved to have committed a felony or an intentional misdemeanour punishable by imprisonment for two years, and adjudged not to be responsible by reason of loss of reason, shall be confined, pursuant to a special paragraph of the judgment of acquittal, in a precautionary asylum.

Where the misdemeanour is unintentional or is punishable by imprisonment for less than two years, the perpetrator shall be ordered to be confined in the precautionary asylum if it is proved that he is a danger to public safety, and the confinement shall continue until the recovery of the insane person is proved by a decision issued by the court that ordered the confinement, and supervised liberty may be imposed upon the confined person upon his release.

Any person who, at the time of committing the act, was afflicted with a hereditary or acquired mental infirmity that diminished the power of consciousness or of choice in his acts shall benefit by law from the commutation or reduction of his penalty in accordance with the provisions of Article 251.

Any person sentenced to a felony or misdemeanour penalty depriving of or restricting liberty who benefited by law from the commutation or reduction of the penalty by reason of mental deficiency, and any person sentenced to one of these penalties who is proved to be possessed or addicted to narcotics or alcohol and to be a danger to public safety, shall be ordered in the judgment to be confined in a place in the precautionary asylum to be treated therein during the term of the penalty.

A convicted person who is released from the precautionary asylum after his recovery proved by a decision of the court that ordered his confinement shall have the remaining term of his penalty executed against him.

Where the convicted person remains, after the expiry of the term of his penalty, a danger to public safety, he shall be detained in the precautionary asylum pursuant to a decision of the same court for a period not exceeding five years if he was sentenced for a felony and two years if he was sentenced for a misdemeanour, and the confined person shall be released before the expiry of the fixed term if a subsequent decision is issued proving that he is no longer a danger, and supervised liberty may be imposed upon the confined person after his release.

Whoever has been sentenced by a final judgment for a felony to a felony or misdemeanour penalty and commits, before the lapse of seven years from the expiry of the penalty or its prescription by limitation of time, a felony or a misdemeanour punishable by imprisonment, shall be liable to the maximum prescribed penalty up to double thereof.

The same shall apply if the first sentence reached at least one year of imprisonment and was pronounced for a misdemeanour of the same category as the second misdemeanour.

Where the penalty previously pronounced was less than one year, the recidivist shall be sentenced to imprisonment for a term at least equal to double the previous penalty, provided that this increase of the minimum limit shall not exceed double the penalty prescribed by law.

Simple imprisonment shall be substituted for compulsory residence if the first judgment pronounced a felony penalty or a misdemeanour penalty other than a fine.

The fine shall be doubled if it was preceded by a sentence to any misdemeanour penalty whatsoever.

If recidivism occurs a second time, a sentence of imprisonment for up to three months and a fine together may be pronounced.

The misdemeanours set forth in each of the following items shall be deemed to be of a single category for the application of the penalties for recidivism set out in the preceding Article, whether the perpetrator thereof has the capacity of principal, instigator, or accomplice:

1- Intentional misdemeanours provided for in a single chapter of this Law.

2- Misdemeanours contrary to morals (Title VII).

3- Intentional misdemeanours committed against persons (Title VIII).

4- Acts of violence, whether physical or verbal, committed against individuals or members of the authorities or the public force.

5- Unintentional homicide and wounding.

6- The misdemeanours mentioned in the Title on dangerous persons.

7- Intentional misdemeanours committed against property.

8- Concealment of things resulting from a misdemeanour or concealment of the persons who committed it, and that misdemeanour itself.

9- Political misdemeanours or those deemed political pursuant to Articles 196 and 197.

10- Misdemeanours committed out of a single dishonourable motive.

An offender who has been sentenced by a final judgment within a period not reaching one year for the same contravention or for any other contravention of the provisions of a single regulation shall be punished by double the penalty prescribed by law; if recidivism occurs a second time within the same period, a sentence of custodial detention and a fine together may be pronounced in all cases where a fine alone is prescribed.
A habitual criminal is one whose criminal knowledge reveals a permanent psychological predisposition, whether innate or acquired, to commit felonies or misdemeanours.

Whoever is sentenced to a penalty other than a fine for an intentional felony or misdemeanour and is sentenced, before the lapse of five years from the expiration of the term of his penalty or the running of the statute of limitations thereon, to a penalty of deprivation of liberty for a period of at least one year for another intentional felony or misdemeanour, shall be sentenced to confinement in isolation if his habitual criminality and that he is a danger to public safety are established.

Every habitual criminal sentenced to a penalty other than a fine pursuant to Articles 258 and 259 shall be deemed by operation of law to be a danger to public safety and shall be sentenced to confinement in isolation if he is sentenced to a penalty of deprivation of liberty on account of another legal recidivism.

The same shall apply in respect of every habitual criminal against whom there have been issued, within fifteen years not counting the period which he spent in the execution of penalties and precautionary measures:

Either four judgments of imprisonment for felonies committed with an excuse or for intentional misdemeanours, provided that each of the last three offences was committed after the judgment in the preceding offence became final, or two judgments such as the judgments set out in the preceding paragraph and a judgment of a felony penalty, whether the felony occurred before the misdemeanour or after it.

Every person sentenced to confinement in isolation who commits, during his stay in prison or within the five years following his release, an intentional felony or misdemeanour for which he is sentenced to imprisonment for one year or to a more severe penalty shall be liable to confinement in isolation for at least seven years.

Deprivation of civil rights, prohibition of residence and expulsion from the country may be adjudged against anyone whose habitual criminality is established or anyone who is sentenced as a recidivist to a misdemeanour penalty of deprivation of liberty.

A habitual criminal and a recidivist sentenced to compulsory residence or to imprisonment or to a more severe penalty shall, upon his release, be subjected to the measure of supervised liberty for a period of five years, unless the judge decides to increase its period or reduce it or substitute compulsory residence for it, or exempt the convicted person therefrom; the prohibition of residence adjudged pursuant to Article 82, paragraphs 2 and 3 thereof, shall be merged into the measure of supervised liberty for the period adjudged.

The provisions on aggravating or mitigating circumstances of the penalty shall apply in the following order:

Material aggravating circumstances.

Excuses.

Personal aggravating circumstances.

Mitigating circumstances.
The judge shall specify in the judgment the effect of each of the aggravating or mitigating circumstances on the penalty adjudged.
Every agreement concluded between two or more persons to commit a felony by specified means is called a conspiracy.
An attack against the security of the State is consummated whether the act constituting the offence is complete, incomplete, or at the stage of an attempt.

Any person who takes part in a conspiracy against the security of the State and informs the authorities thereof prior to the commencement of any act preparatory to execution shall be exempted from punishment.

If such an act has been committed or commenced, the excuse shall only be mitigating.

An offender who informs the authorities of a conspiracy or of another felony against the security of the State prior to its completion, or who enables the arrest - even after the initiation of prosecutions - of the other offenders or of those whose hiding place he knows, shall likewise benefit from a mitigating excuse.

The provisions of this Article shall not apply to an instigator.

Every Lebanese who bears arms against Lebanon in the ranks of the enemy shall be punished with death, every Lebanese who, even though he does not belong to a hostile army, commits acts of aggression against Lebanon in time of war shall be punished with hard labour for life, every Lebanese who enlists in any capacity whatsoever in a hostile army and does not separate from it prior to any act of aggression against Lebanon shall be punished with temporary hard labour, even if he has acquired a foreign nationality through his enlistment.

Every Lebanese who studies intrigues with a foreign State or contacts it in order to induce it to initiate aggression against Lebanon or to provide it with the means therefor shall be punished with hard labour for life, and if his act leads to a result, he shall be punished with death.
Every Lebanese who plots intrigues with the enemy or contacts him in order to assist him in any manner whatsoever in the victory of his forces shall be punished with death.

Every Lebanese who, by any means whatsoever and with the intent to paralyse national defence, causes damage to installations, factories, ships, aircraft, implements, munitions, provisions, means of communication and, in general, all things of a military character or intended for the use of the army or its affiliated forces, shall be punished with hard labour for life, the death penalty shall be imposed if the act occurs in time of war or when its outbreak is expected, or if it results in the loss of a life.

Every Lebanese who attempts by acts, speeches, writings or otherwise to sever a part of the Lebanese territory in order to annex it to a foreign State or to vest in that State a right or privilege exclusive to the Lebanese State shall be punished with temporary detention for at least five years, if the perpetrator, at the time of committing the act, belonged to one of the associations or organisations referred to in Articles 298 and 318, he shall be punished with detention for life.

Every Lebanese who provides lodging, food or clothing to a spy, to an enemy soldier operating for reconnaissance or to an enemy agent, or helps him to escape, or establishes contact with one of those spies, soldiers or agents while aware of his status, shall be punished with temporary hard labour.

Every Lebanese who facilitates the escape of a prisoner of war or one of the interned enemy nationals shall be punished with temporary detention.
The penalties prescribed in this Subdivision shall also be imposed if the act is committed against a State bound to Lebanon by a treaty of alliance or an international instrument taking its place.
Foreigners who have a domicile or actual residence in Lebanon shall be treated in the same manner as Lebanese within the meaning intended in Articles 274 to 278.

Whoever enters or attempts to enter a prohibited place, with the intent of obtaining objects, documents or information that must remain secret out of concern for the safety of the State, shall be punished with imprisonment for at least one year, and if he acts with the intent of espionage, with temporary hard labour.

Whoever steals objects, documents or information such as those mentioned in the preceding Article, or obtains them, shall be punished with temporary hard labour; if the felony is committed for the benefit of a foreign State, the penalty shall be hard labour for life.

Whoever has in his possession certain documents or information such as those mentioned in Article 281 and communicates or discloses the same without legitimate cause shall be punished with imprisonment from two months to two years.
