7- The manner of investing the funds of the Cooperative.

The Government Commissioner to the Board of Directors of the Cooperative shall be appointed upon the proposal of the Minister of Finance by a decree adopted in the Council of Ministers, and he shall participate in the meetings of the Board of Directors and have the right to vote therein.

The Government Commissioner shall enjoy the right to object to the decisions of the Board of Directors when he considers that they are liable to cause a disturbance in the financial conditions of the Cooperative or in the soundness of its resources, or that exorbitant burdens on the Public Treasury may arise therefrom.

The Government Commissioner must, in this case, request the Board of Directors to reconsider the objected decision in a new session to be held at most eight days after the first session; if the Board confirms its first decision, the Government Commissioner may stay the execution in order to submit the matter, within three days from the date of the holding of the session, to the supervisory authority to take the appropriate decision.

If the supervisory authority confirms the decision of the Board of Directors, the Government Commissioner must, in the event that he insists on the objection, inform the Minister of Finance of the matter within five days from the date of his notification of the decision of the supervisory authority, by means of a detailed memorandum explaining the nature of the objected decision, the reasons for his objection, and both points of view of the Board of Directors and the supervisory authority.

The Minister of Finance may, within at most one week from the date of receipt of the memorandum, decide on the matter; if he upholds the objected decision of the Board of Directors, this decision shall become enforceable, and otherwise he shall submit the matter to the Council of Ministers to take the final decision.

In the event that no decision is taken on the said decision within a period of forty days from the date of the objection of the Government Commissioner thereto, the supervisory authority may consider this decision to be enforceable by operation of law.

The regulations referred to in Article 17 of this Law shall be amended, where necessary, upon a proposal from the Board of Directors and following the approval of the supervisory

authority.

The amendment shall be issued by a reasoned decision of the supervisory authority.

The President of the Civil Service Board shall provisionally assign, by a decision issued by him, the employees and experts whose assistance the Cooperative seeks, and shall determine their duties, and their allowances or wages, until the regulations of the Cooperative are established and its administrative and technical bodies commence their work.
The uninvested cash funds of the Cooperative that exceed daily needs shall be deposited in the Treasury fund or deposited in the bank in which the Treasury deposits its funds.

The Cooperative and its transactions shall be exempted:

1- From all fees imposed on contracts.

2- From fees for the registration of contracts of its properties or its real property rights in rem.

3- From income taxes.

4- From advertising fees and municipal fees.

5- From judicial fees in lawsuits instituted by it in fulfillment of its purposes and in defense of its interests.

6- From fees, taxes, and stamp duties, in respect of all acts carried out by it to execute its mission and manage its affairs.

7- From postage stamp fees in respect of its correspondence within the country.

As for contracts concluded by it with third parties, the third parties shall pay the fees and taxes thereof.
The debts owed to the Cooperative by affiliates shall be considered privileged debts and shall rank immediately after amounts due to the State as taxes.

All employees' cooperatives, cooperation funds of all kinds, and mutual aid institutions and associations shall be dissolved, and the regulations of the Cooperative shall determine the manner of dissolution and liquidation.
If the State dissolves the Cooperative, it shall assume all its debts and obligations towards the employees and third parties.

A grant that may be awarded to the cooperatives of the Army, the Internal Security Forces, and General Security shall be determined by a decree adopted in the Council of Ministers, in the event that these cooperatives provide to the dependents of their affiliates the same health services that the State Employees' Cooperative provides to the dependents of its members, provided that the members of the aforementioned cooperatives contribute to the financing thereof at the rate contributed by the members of the State Employees' Cooperative in return for these services.

The value of the grant shall be determined in the decree as a percentage of the salaries of the members of these cooperatives equivalent to the estimated percentage of the grant that the State awards to the Employees' Cooperative in return for these health services.
All previous provisions that are contrary to this Law or inconsistent with its content are hereby repealed.
This Law shall be published in the Official Gazette.

The provisions of this Decree shall apply to:

(a) All activities of construction, installation, dismantling, demolition, excavation works and the erection of buildings or structures of all types, as well as the alteration of their structure, their renovation, repair and maintenance, and their cleaning and painting, including any activity, work or transport operation carried out on any construction site, starting from the preparation of the site until the completion of the project.

(b) All civil engineering works, including for example excavation works and the erection of airports, docks, wharves, ports and dams, river and marine protection structures and landslide protection structures, roads including highways, railways, bridges, viaducts and tunnels, and work above or under water.

(c) Works relating to the provision of services, such as the laying of telecommunications lines and drainage, sewerage, water, electricity and gas networks, as well as the alteration of their structure, their repair, maintenance and demolition.

Every building intended to be constructed, demolished, restored or maintained must observe the following conditions:

1. It shall be safeguarded and a barrier shall be placed around the property on which these works are taking place to prevent the passage or entry of persons not assigned to the work or who have no direct relation to the property.

2. It shall be provided with the necessary machinery, equipment and installations made of sound and durable material according to their type and manufacture and in good working and usable condition, according to the requirements of the worksite and under the supervision of a responsible person.

Sufficient and suitable scaffolds shall be erected to carry out works that cannot be safely performed by means of ladders or by other means, and such scaffolds shall not be erected, dismantled or altered except under the supervision of a competent and responsible person and by skilled workers trained for this work.
The materials used in the erection of scaffolds shall be of good quality and of sufficient load-bearing strength so as to be capable of withstanding the loads and the movement of work thereon.

The wooden parts used for scaffolds and for gangways must be of good quality, stripped of their outer bark, and of long fibre, and they must not be painted or treated in any manner likely to conceal their defects.

The width of scaffolds and gangways must not be less than one metre so as to allow the safe passage of workers, and such scaffolds and gangways must be surrounded by side guardrails when their height exceeds one and a half metres from the ground surface level, and they must not be crowded with building materials and hand tools.

The height of the side barriers shall be at least 90 (ninety) cm from the level of the floor of the scaffolds and walkways, and these barriers shall be fixed onto closely spaced posts, provided that at mid-distance a crossbar fixed between the top of the barrier and the floor of the walkway is provided for.
The metal parts of the scaffolds and walkways shall not be corroded, cracked or affected by defects that affect their strength.
Nails made of cast iron shall not be used.
Sturdy canopies made of solid materials shall be installed above the walkways to protect passers-by or those working on them from the danger of falling objects.

1 - Everyone who works outside or inside the building shall be equipped with safety belts, and in particular workers installing external and internal pipes and fittings, plastering, cladding and finishing workers, and those who work on scaffolds.

2 - A competent person shall inspect the scaffolds in the cases required by maintenance works weekly, and whenever the need arises.

When digging any trench or pit, it is required:

a - That the digging operation always begin from top to bottom, provided that the sides have a sufficient slope according to the nature of the ground and the requirements of the craft, and are shored if they so require.

b - To shore the sides with sturdy horizontal and vertical wooden or metal beams that prevent the collapse of earth onto the workers performing the work.

c - To secure safe walkways to carry out the removal of earth, or to divert them if they pass through the property.

d - To shore adjacent structures or those that pass through the property on which the work is being carried out.
Earth shall be kept away from the edges of excavations to avoid pressure on the sides, and the necessary precautions shall be taken to prevent water from seeping into them.

a- Demolition operations shall always begin from the upper floors, provided that the walls and protruding parts of the building that are feared to fall are shored.

b - The surrounding environment shall be protected from demolition dust and from waste or debris resulting from the demolition of the building, and work shall be done to dispose of them by appropriate means.

c - All operations shall be carried out under the supervision of an engineer who shall be responsible for them.

a - Debris shall be transported and lifted by means of lifting machines and inclined chutes, and may not under any circumstances be thrown from the top of the building.

b - The manual lifting of excessive loads that entail a risk to the safety and health of workers shall be avoided by lightening them or by using mechanical devices.
The site where excavations are taking place and the site prepared for collecting lifted debris and earth shall be surrounded by a barrier preventing passers-by from approaching or entering it.

It is prohibited for any person to work on a roof that exposes him to falling due to its slope or its flat condition or due to the weather condition unless the necessary precautions are taken to prevent the falling of persons or materials.
Only workers of long experience, and who possess the necessary physical and psychological qualities, shall be employed in work on sloping roofs.

1 - Roofs shall be equipped, as far as possible, with the following:

a - Suitable fencing of sufficient height.

b - Suitable ladders and climbing boards that are firmly fixed.

c - A suitable working platform resting on safe and sturdy bases or supports, provided that its width is not less than 40 (forty) cm.

2 - Employees performing the work shall be provided with protective belts or with sufficient ropes to tie them to a fixed point on the roof.

The following shall be observed in lifting and hauling machines:

a - Every machine intended for workers or for materials used shall be of sturdy manufacture and sound construction, and the necessary maintenance and the preservation of the regularity of its operation shall be provided for it.

b - As far as practicable, every machine must be thoroughly inspected in its place once every week by the person in charge of operating it or a competent person, and the owner or user of the machine shall produce the inspection record to the competent bodies at the Ministry of Labour upon request.

c - The necessary precautions shall be taken to prevent any person from jumping or approaching the moving parts of the machine.

d - A statement of its maximum load assigned to it by the manufacturer shall be placed on every machine in a conspicuous place and in a language understood by all workers in the project, and it is prohibited to load any machine with more than its specified safe load.

e - Machines and machinery intended for transporting work vertically or horizontally shall be equipped with doors that are securely closed throughout the period of their movement.

f - Chains, hauling and lifting wires, ropes, and the like shall be of good manufacture and shall not be loaded beyond their capacity.

g - No person may be raised, lowered, or carried by means of a lifting appliance unless it is manufactured, installed, and used for this purpose. Excluded from this are emergency cases in which serious personal injuries or deaths are likely to occur and in which the use of the lifting appliance is safe and under the supervision of the competent engineer.
All ladders used on the worksite must be made of sound material and of sufficient strength to bear the weights that pass over them.
The wooden parts used for ladders must be made of a good grade and with long fibres, and shall not be painted or treated in any manner likely to conceal their defects.
In ladders made of wooden material, the quantity and type of load shall be observed, such that every ladder must be proportionate to the load it is supposed to bear.
Rungs shall be fixed into recesses in the uprights by means of nails, glue, and the like, and the dimensions between one rung and another must not exceed 40 (forty) cm.
Every ladder must be equipped with non-slip bases, and precautionary measures must be taken to ensure safety in terms of its installation, fixing, use, and supervision.

Adequate precautions shall be taken in any excavation, shaft, earthwork, underground works or tunnel:

(a) By using suitable shoring or otherwise so as to prevent employees from being exposed to the risk of falling or dislodgement of earth, rock or any other material.

(b) To guard against dangers arising from the fall of persons, materials or objects or from the inrush of water into any excavation, shaft, earthwork, underground pit or tunnel.

(c) To secure adequate ventilation at every workplace so as to maintain an atmosphere fit for respiration and to keep any fumes, gases, vapours, dust or other impurities at levels where they are not dangerous or injurious to health and are within the limits prescribed by the laws and regulations in force.

(d) To enable employees to reach safety in the event of an outbreak of fire or an inrush of water or materials.

(e) To avoid exposing employees to potential underground hazards such as the circulation of fluids or the presence of pockets of gas, by undertaking appropriate investigations to locate them.

1 - Every cofferdam and caisson intended for work under water shall be:

(a) Of good construction, of suitable and sound material and of adequate strength.

(b) Provided with adequate means for workers to reach safety in the event of an inrush of water or materials.

2 - The construction, positioning, modification or dismantling of a cofferdam or caisson shall take place only under the immediate supervision of a competent person.

3 - Every cofferdam and caisson shall be inspected by a competent person at intervals prescribed by the competent authority.

1 - The erection of structural frames and their components, formwork, falsework and shoring shall be carried out only under the supervision of a competent person.

2 - Adequate precautions shall be taken to protect employees against any risk arising from the temporary weakness or instability of a structure.

3 - Formwork, falsework and shoring shall be so designed, constructed and maintained that it will safely support all loads that may be imposed on it.

No work shall be carried out in compressed air except by workers whose physical fitness has been established by a medical examination and in the presence of a competent person to supervise the conduct of the operations.

All precautions shall be taken where work is done over or in close proximity to water, in order to:

1 - Prevent employees from falling into the water.

2 - Rescue employees in danger of drowning.

3 - Provide safe and sufficient transport.

4 - Provide the necessary life-saving equipment (life jacket...).

The necessary precautions shall be taken to protect employees from the hazards of falling, falling objects, flying splinters and electrical hazards by providing them with protective equipment or preventive means such as goggles, gloves, helmets, belts, footwear and other protective clothing. Employees who use electrical equipment must wear special insulating footwear, provided that the use of these electrical machines and equipment is prohibited in wet or water-covered locations.

Before the commencement of construction works, and during their progress, the necessary measures shall be taken to verify the absence of live electrical wires or apparatus beneath, above or on the surface of the worksite, in order to prevent employees from being exposed to danger on account thereof.
All shafts and openings shall be surrounded by side barriers of a height of not less than 90 (ninety) cm to prevent persons or objects from falling into them.

a - The employer shall bear the responsibility of ensuring the provision of first aid consisting of the necessary medicines and bandages and trained persons where possible, throughout working hours, and it shall be incumbent upon him to make arrangements for transporting workers who suffer an accident or sudden illness to medical care centres throughout working hours.

b - The employer must notify the Ministry of Labour of work injuries within a period not exceeding 24 hours from the occurrence of the accident.

1 - All appropriate precautions shall be taken to ensure that all workplaces are safe and free from the risk of harming the safety and health of employees.

2 - Safe means of access to and egress from all workplaces shall be provided, maintained and marked with signs indicating them where necessary.

3 - All appropriate precautions shall be taken to protect persons present on or near a construction site from all risks that may be caused by such site.

1 - Clear markings shall be placed on hazardous substances and they shall be provided with identification labels showing their characteristics and instructions for their use.

2 - The competent administrations shall determine the harmful substances the use of which must be prohibited in the construction industry and which shall be replaced by harmless or less hazardous substances.

a - Every employee has the right to remove himself from danger when he has strong reason to believe that there is an imminent and serious danger to his safety or health, and the employee shall immediately inform his supervisor thereof.

b - The employer shall, in the event of an imminent danger to the safety of employees, take immediate measures to stop work and evacuate employees where necessary.

1 - With regard to installations, machinery and equipment, including both manual and mechanical tools, they must:

a) Be of good design and construction, taking into account the principles of ergonomics as far as possible.

b) Be maintained in good working order at all times.

c) Be used solely for the work for which they were designed, unless a competent person has assessed their use for purposes other than those for which they were originally designed and it has been proven to him that such use is safe.

d) Be operated by employees who have received appropriate training.

2) The manufacturer or the employer shall provide adequate instructions for safe use in a form understood by their users.

3 - Installations and equipment operated by compressed air shall be inspected and tested by a competent person, in the cases and at the times determined by the competent bodies, and the results of such inspections shall be produced upon request to the inspector concerned.

The employer shall take all possible measures to ensure:

1 - The avoidance of the risk of fire.

2 - The rapid and effective fighting of any fire that breaks out.

3 - The rapid and safe evacuation of persons.

c - The availability of sufficient and suitable places for storing flammable liquids, solids and gases.

d - The provision of fire-fighting extinguishers that are serviceable, sufficient in number, located in places easily accessible to and usable by workers, as well as proficiency in their use.

Explosives shall not be stored, transported, handled or used except:

1 - In accordance with the conditions determined by the laws and regulations in force.

2 - By a competent person, who must take the necessary measures to ensure that workers and other persons are not exposed to the risk of injury.

Employees shall receive an adequate and appropriate measure of:

1 - Information on potential safety and health risks to which they may be exposed at their workplace.

2 - Guidance and training regarding the means available for preventing, combating and protecting against such risks.

All worksites must be provided with sufficient and suitable lighting to illuminate all workplaces and passages of employees, provided that dangerous places are signalled by a red lamp, particularly at every corner of the worksite.
Specialist employees must be entrusted with watching over dangerous places and places in which a danger may occur should employees lose their way.

The continuation of dangerous work at night is prohibited on construction and public works sites that shall be determined subsequently by a decision of the Minister of Labour, in order to preserve the safety of workers on these sites.

Every employee or person having a connection with the worksite shall cooperate with the employer in implementing the provisions of this Decree, namely:

a - By not defacing, moving or disabling protective devices and precautions unless permitted to do so.

b - By following and executing all instructions relating to prevention during work, and using and maintaining the devices handed over to him.

c - By entering and leaving the workplace solely through the accesses designated for that purpose.

1 - The employer shall provide to the employees, at his own expense, personal protective equipment and appropriate protective clothing to ward off hazards and avert harm.

2 - The employees shall be bound to use the clothing and equipment referred to in the preceding paragraph.

1 - The employer shall provide pure potable water at every construction site or at a close distance therefrom.

2 - The employer shall secure sanitary facilities, places for washing, changing clothes and keeping them away from dust and contamination, and places for taking meals.
The details of the implementation of this Decree shall be determined by a decision of the Minister of Labour.

Every infringement of the provisions of this Decree and of the decisions issued for its implementation, whether committed by the building owner, the person responsible for the kindergarten, the contractor or their representative, shall be punishable in accordance with the provisions of the Law issued on 17 September 1962 relating to the repeal of Articles 107 and 108 and the provisions of Article 109 of the Labour Law.

The Labour, Prevention and Safety Inspection Service at the Ministry of Labour shall be entrusted with supervising the monitoring of the execution of the provisions of this Decree, including the provisions of the relevant International and Arab Labour Conventions that have been ratified.
Decree No. 7380 dated 22 May 1967 relating to the regulation of protection, prevention and safety at work in construction worksites is hereby repealed.
This Decree shall be published and notified wherever needed.

Presidency of the Council of Ministers Report of the President of the Central Inspection on the activities of the Central Inspection for the year 2003 His Excellency the President of the Council of Ministers Subject: The Annual Report on the activities of the Central Inspection for the year 2003 Reference: Legislative Decree No. 115 dated 12/6/1959 (Establishment of the Central Inspection). I am pleased to submit to Your Excellency the sixth report in the series of annual reports that we have prepared since we assumed the duties of the Presidency of the Central Inspection at the beginning of the year 1999, which is the last report that we prepare due to the termination of our services on the first of the month of July 2004 During the five years that we spent at the Presidency of the Central Inspection, we strove hard to make the Central Inspection a productive and effective administration whose sole concern is improving the administrative conditions of the public administrations, public institutions, and municipalities that are subject to the jurisdiction of the Central Inspection. We sought to modernise the Central Inspection through a new draft law that we prepared in cooperation with the competent authorities, but unfortunately this draft remains under examination before you for more than sixteen months. This report has been prepared in accordance with Circular No. 23/2003 dated 2/9/2003 issued by Your Excellency and relating to the manner of preparing annual reports, and we hope that it will shed light on the activities and achievements of the Central Inspection during the past year. I extend to Your Excellency my sincere thanks for what I have received from you during the last three years, and I wish you all the best and progress for the advancement of the nation.

Pursuant to the provisions of paragraph (a) of item 3 of Article 11 of Legislative Decree No. 115/59, read in conjunction with item 4 of Article 12 thereof, and after reviewing the letters of the Presidency of the Central Inspection addressed to the competent General Inspectorates and to the public administrations and public institutions, and the replies received thereto. The Central Inspection Board decided to request all General Inspectorates in the Central Inspection to accord the utmost importance, when inspectors carry out the annual programme for the year 2003 entrusted to them, to the following fundamental elements: 1 - Activating administrative work: directing the administration to establish organisational indicators for the various fundamental areas of work it undertakes, clearly showing the extent to which the administration discharges the tasks entrusted to it, with the aim of identifying areas of deficiency in order to address them, and raising the level of administrative performance, particularly in the field of serving the citizen and completing transactions within the time limits set for them. 2 - Sound financial management: with respect to the assessment of taxes, collection of fees, and enhancement of revenue collection, and monitoring the use of public resources such as auditing contracts and the extent of the need for them, in order to prevent waste of public funds and to improve the position of the Treasury. 3 - Internal self-control: verifying the exercise by hierarchical superiors of their duties with respect to supervising their subordinates, overseeing the works and tasks entrusted to them, regulating work in the units subordinate to them, making proper use of equipment and software, and setting an example in complying with laws and regulations. 4 - Personnel management and human resources development: stating the status of human resources with respect to surplus, or the status of persons employed irregularly, utilising the competence of those working therein and the extent of their dedication to their work, and the discharge by Directors General of their leadership role and their coordination of work among the various administrative units in a manner that ensures raising the level of performance. 5 - Institutional performance evaluation: the undertaking by the General Inspectorates, each within its competence, of an evaluation of institutional performance with complete precision and clarity, by encompassing the elements and data referred to above, and comparing the results of the administration's work with the objectives and programmes set for it in accordance with the performance standards and indicators adopted pursuant to special forms. 6 - Following up on the implementation of the circulars issued by His Excellency the President of the Council of Ministers, in particular Circular No. 14/97, No. 1/98, No. 5/98, No. 12/99, No. 28/99, No. 43/99, No. 48/99, No. 26/2001, No. 40/2001, No. 27/2002 and No. 32/2002, duly notified at the time to all General Inspectorates. The Central Inspection Board has set a special inspection programme for each General Inspectorate as follows:

2 - Tasks completed within the scope of technical inspection Educational inspectors supervised the competence of the members of the teaching staff, and evaluated the technical performance of learning processes, in the various school subjects, and upon examining the lesson attendance reports during the academic year 2002/2003, which amounted to /4222/ reports, the following became evident: - Non-completion of the prescribed curricula in most educational subjects, and in all classes; therefore, the inspectors, the representatives of the technical committees, participating in the workshop launched by the Center for Educational Research and Development to review the educational curricula, are preparing to work on reducing the study content in many subjects, and rearranging the themes and lessons. - Non-achievement of the educational objectives in the required manner; as their achievement in a good manner does not exceed 27,65%, whereas the percentage of objectives achieved in an acceptable manner amounts to 62,74%. - Failure to follow active methods, in most cases, and the continued prevalence of rote instruction among teachers, in a manner that necessitates continuous training and constant follow-up of their work in schools.

3 - Follow-up on the Works of the Directorate General of Education: Public schools in the academic year 2002/2003 comprised more than /351/ thousand pupils, and more than /40/ thousand teachers working therein. The Educational Inspection followed up on the works of the Directorate General of Education in numerous matters, the most important of which are: Workflow in public schools: The workflow in public schools is marred by some impediment resulting from the following matters: - Transfers of members of the teaching staff: A number of decisions and administrative memorandums were issued by the Ministry of Education and Higher Education ordering the transfer of 603 teachers, of those who could be enumerated, from one school to another during the academic year 2002/2003, among whom 145 teachers were transferred to schools that do not need them, and 159 teachers were transferred from schools that cannot dispense with their services. Table of transfer cases that could be enumerated within the scope of basic education schools during the year 2003: (see the table) And this table shows that 304 teachers were transferred without regard for the public interest. As 145 teachers were transferred from surplus to surplus and 159 teachers from need to surplus.

Table of the comprehensive movement of transfers: (see the table) The Educational Inspection studied these transfers and drew up a unified report on the results reached, which was referred to the competent authorities at the Ministry of Education and Higher Education to examine its content and work towards: - Restricting transfers to surplus teachers in the public education cadre in order to secure needs. - Refraining from arranging new contracting, whether in respect of contracting with new teachers or increasing the hours of veteran contractors. - Returning those among them seconded to teacher training colleges, the office of the Minister of Education and Higher Education, and the offices of other ministries to schools in need of their services. - Refraining from seconding teachers to public secondary schools, except in light of an urgent need for them, and having regard for the public interest. - Complying with the provisions of Law 442/2002, in respect of not transferring any new teacher before the expiry of the period prescribed for his transfer. - Complying with the provisions of Decree 4234/2000, in respect of completing the transfers of teachers before the beginning of each academic year, and seeking the opinion of each of the competent Educational Region and the Directorates of Primary and Secondary Education before conducting the transfers. - Examining the possibility of restoring the powers of conducting transfers of members of the teaching staff who are in the fourth category to the Director General of Education, pursuant to the provisions of the laws governing public service affairs. The observations set forth above show that the process of transfers is carried out in violation of the laws and regulations in force, and does not have regard for the public interest. As evidenced by the fact that those transferred are replaced by contracted secondary and primary teachers, which leads to an increase in expenditure without justification or need. Contracting conditions in public schools: The number of contractors in the secondary and basic education stages reached 13746 contractors, distributed as follows: 4873 contracted secondary teachers in secondary education and 8873 contracted teachers in the three stages of basic education. The number of contracted teachers in kindergartens and basic education schools, in the academic year 2002/2003, reached /8873/ teachers, distributed among the schools of the six governorates as follows: Beirut Governorate: 181 North Governorate: 3460 Bekaa Governorate: 2002 South Governorate: 1345 Mount Lebanon Governorate: 1166 Nabatieh Governorate: 719 That is, with an increase of /1259/ teachers over what the number of contractors was in the academic year 2001/2002.

The number of contracted professors in public secondary schools reached 4873 professors, that is, with a decrease of 472 professors from what the number was in the 2001/2002 academic year, and among the reasons for this is that the Ministry of Education and Higher Education proceeded to increase the teaching periods of professors assigned to tasks in counselling and guidance, at the expense of counselling periods; a matter which achieved a notable saving in favour of the Public Treasury; in addition to the appointment of a number of professors who are graduates of the Faculty of Pedagogy. Nevertheless, the total number of contracted staff remains large, and it exhausts the budgets of school funds, mutual funds and parents' councils; in addition to the damages resulting from the entry of these large numbers into the body of the teaching staff, without prior preparation or continuous qualification. Maintaining the level of public education requires taking a series of measures aimed at solving the historically recurring problem of contracted staff, namely: - By reconsidering the distribution of surplus teachers to needy schools. - Conducting transfers within the ranks of the members of the teaching staff in accordance with the provisions of Decree 4234/2000 - Applying the special law on preparing teachers at the Faculty of Pedagogy periodically, and not resorting to contracting except in cases of extreme necessity. Holding restricted competitive examinations to confirm successful contracted staff in permanent tenure, in accordance with Laws 441/2002 (for basic education) and 442/2002 (for secondary education), may not become a custom to which the State resorts whenever the problem of contracted staff swells and worsens, under the weight of pressures and strikes. The real solutions lie in the State charting the natural courses for preparing teachers, based on studies, statistics and anticipated needs. Persons Assigned Educational Tasks in Guidance and Counselling: Despite the repeated recommendations issued by the Central Inspection Board, the body assigned tasks in guidance and counselling remains in existence within the scope of the Directorate General of Education, along with the problematic issues that this raises at several levels, among which are: - The illegality of this body, in its present form, for its conflict with the provisions of the Law put into effect by Decree No. 3252 dated 17/5/ 1972 - The need of public secondary schools and schools for the secondary school teachers and teachers attached to this body, in order to benefit from their qualitative expertise, and to dispense with many contractual teaching hours, in avoidance of waste in public funds. - The duplication of guidance and counselling between this body and the Educational Inspectorate, in the absence of laws and regulations relating to putting technical guidance into execution, under the ceiling of what is stated in the Law put into effect by Decree No. 3252/72 And among the most important recommendations of the Educational Inspectorate to strengthen the conditions of the public school: - Providing the material conditions and securing specialised secondary school teachers and teachers to generalise the teaching of informatics in the basic and secondary education stages, and in all public schools of Lebanon. - Redistributing the numerical surplus of primary school teachers to the schools in need of their services. - Procuring the issuance of a law establishing mutual funds to legalise their status. - Not assigning any employee below the third category to conduct administrative investigations. - Returning the primary school teachers and secondary school teachers attached to the office of the Minister of Education and Higher Education and the offices of other ministries to their original duty stations, or redistributing them according to need. - Providing the material, human and technical capabilities to apply the education curricula in accordance with the educational objectives set for them. - Considering the possibility of procuring the issuance of a legal text to replace the first paragraph of Article Eight of Law 22/82, such that the employee forfeits a certain percentage of his salary, if his absence for health reasons exceeds a certain period in the academic year. - Redistributing kindergarten teachers to the schools that provide them with work within the scope of their specialisation. - Regularising the status of primary school teachers attached to public administrations, contrary to legal rules. - Reconsidering the quotas permitted for contracting, with respect to unifying them in accordance with Decree 44/64 - Amending the texts relating to the models of teaching licensing decisions, and adopting new models for the declaration of contractual teaching hours outside official working hours. Official Examinations: The Educational Inspectorate accompanied the official examinations for the Intermediate and General Secondary certificates, for the year 2003 and supervised the examination centres, and followed up the marking works and the announcement of results, and concluded with a number of important recommendations, among which we mention: Recommending to the Ministry of Education and Higher Education: - Working to avoid the absence of invigilators, by excluding those who annually submit medical reports when called upon for invigilation works. - Working to exclude certain buildings unfit to serve as centres for official examinations. - Emphasising the re-reading of examination paper questions and attempting to answer them by at least two persons prior to printing them, and distributing them - and in sufficient number - to the centres. - Regulating the process of participation in committees (question preparation and marking committees), through strictness in submitting the required and complete documents within their deadlines, and verifying their validity and conformity with the required conditions, prior to confirming the membership of their holders in the committees, while restricting the assignment of their rapporteurs to employees of the public teaching corps who are still in active service, to the exclusion of others. - Adhering to the content of assignment decisions and not exceeding them, with respect to entrusting tasks to persons other than their rightful holders, or adopting duplication of assignment. - Organising the process of setting marking criteria, through the prior announcement of their final and fixed dates, and imposing the obligation of attendance upon all those concerned therewith, and controlling this attendance through signing a special register, while giving sufficient time for discussion and agreement upon clear and final marking criteria. - Regulating the marking process through excluding incompetent markers on the one hand, and setting a ceiling for the number of examination papers that may be handed over to the marker or verifier daily depending on the subject, while adopting fairness in distributing them among the markers, on the other hand, alongside imposing the permanent presence of the committee rapporteur and his deputy, for the proper supervision of the work and the control of its details0. - Prior designation of the sorting and results announcement committees, proceeding from the content of the relevant decisions0 - Adhering to Decree No. 5697 dated 15/6/2001, with respect to the conditions for accepting candidacy applications and holding "supplementary" sessions. - Restricting the assignment of roving delegates to examination centres to employees of the third category and above, with a clear definition of their tasks and the centres required to be visited, and requesting the preparation of a report on the completion of the mission, a copy of which shall be communicated to the Educational Inspectorate. - Progress of work in vocational schools and institutes: As a result of following up on the progress of work in vocational and technical schools and institutes, during the 2002/2003 academic year, the Educational Inspection recorded observations, and sent the necessary recommendations regarding them to the Directorate General of Vocational and Technical Education, the most important of which are: - Delay in issuing amendments to the curricula until the beginning of the 2002/2003 academic year, without this being accompanied by any decision or circular in this regard, whereby the directorate of schools and institutes was notified of these amendments by telephone; a matter which caused confusion in the distribution of programmes, and the completion of the curricula. - Failure to train teachers on the amended curricula and advanced equipment. - Delay in auditing the budgets specific to technical schools and institutes. - Absence of studies for specialisations and the extent of their suitability to the surroundings, and adopting the same specialisations in adjacent schools. - Poor distribution of equipment specific to workshops, whether in terms of its not being based on need, or because it is incompatible with the required technical conditions. - Failure to adopt specific criteria for selecting teachers contracted to teach by the hour; which allowed contracting with holders of the Technical Baccalaureate, for example, instead of holders of higher degrees of whom the necessary number is available for this purpose. - Delay in issuing a decision to hold the extraordinary session examinations which were held after the beginning of the academic year. - Employment of a large number of servants, guards and gardeners at the expense of the funds of technical schools and institutes, in an unstudied manner, and in violation of the provisions of the decrees and regulations in force which determine the number of these persons, on the basis of specific data; a matter which caused a waste of public funds, and an exhaustion of the funds of these schools, and negatively affected the distribution of the budget in each school or institute across all expenditure chapters, particularly equipment. - Random employment in the schools and institutes of joint projects, especially within the framework of administrative tasks; despite the availability of vocational education teachers on the cadre in these institutions. - Carrying out of restoration and maintenance works by the Council for Development and Reconstruction in some schools and institutes, during the academic year. - Distribution of technical teachers across schools and institutes, in an unstudied manner; a matter which led to an excess in the number of these teachers in some of them, and a shortage in others, which was compensated for by resorting to contracting. - Assignment of some technical teachers to administrative tasks, in a manner contrary to the texts in force, and adopting contracting to compensate for the shortage in their number. Official examinations in the Directorate General of Vocational and Technical Education: Among the most important recommendations that were communicated to the Directorate General of Vocational and Technical Education: - Separating written examinations from practical work examinations. - Assigning the necessary number of invigilators and avoiding surplus, on the basis of objective studies. - Seeking clarification from the directorate of some schools regarding complaints by candidates concerning the setting of questions from outside the official curriculum. - Inviting the Lebanese Red Cross to secure volunteers in official examination centres. - Taking the necessary measures against candidates who were caught in attempts at cheating. - Imposing disciplinary penalties against employees who failed to participate in the official examinations without an excuse. - Avoiding the presence of candidates with their teachers in examination halls, and preparing a special form pursuant to which the teacher assigned to participate in the examinations undertakes, on his personal responsibility, not to participate in any practical or oral examination for candidates of the vocational schools and institutes in which he teaches. Restricting the mission of training, to the exclusion of preparation, to a portion of the Male and Female Teachers Training Colleges, and conducting training courses for teachers at limited times, and during the summer vacation, resulted in two issues of considerable importance: - Human Resources: The number of secondary school professors attached to the Colleges amounts to 122 professors, the number of teachers attached to these Colleges amounts to 77 teachers, the number of administrative employees from the cadre of the Center for Educational Research and Development amounts to 72 permanent and contractual employees, and the number of ushers, servants, and guards is 48, meaning that there are 319 employees who receive their salaries and wages from the State Treasury, and perform only a negligible fraction of the works entrusted to them, not for reasons attributable to them, but rather due to the conditions to which the Male and Female Teachers Training Colleges have come. In addition, the Center for Educational Research and Development delegates certain secondary school professors who are not attached to these Colleges to carry out the burdens of training. The modern concept of administration or Management considers that the provision of services must be based primarily on results, and that the administration must adhere to three principles, which are: relevance, effectiveness, and economy. In practice, this means sound management of public funds and the application of the laws and regulations in force. And whereas the mission of the Central Inspection is to supervise public administrations, public institutions and municipalities, and to work on improving the workflow therein, and in order for the Central Inspection to keep pace with this modern concept of administration, and assist it in abandoning bureaucracy in favor of a productive administration that has clear objectives, relies on standards of good performance, and clear and accurate indicators to measure its achievements, it carried out, during the year 2003, a field experiment in which it applied the measurement of institutional performance in the Ministries of Environment and Public Works and Transport, and relied in this measurement process on six principles governing administration, which are: - Results-based strategic management. - Citizen focus. - Strengthening administrative organization. - Human resources development. - Financial management. - Internal control, oversight and evaluation. And it established for each principle thereof ten /10/ indicators showing the extent to which the public administration in Lebanon performs its duty, and to what extent it approaches the modern concept of Management, and what its strengths or weaknesses are, and what it must do to improve its performance. To that end, the Central Inspection formed inspection teams from General Inspectorates of various specializations to carry out this mission. The reports - attached in the annex - show the first experiment of the Central Inspection in this process of institutional performance assessment. Second - Works of the Government Commissioner's Office before the Higher Disciplinary Board A - On Missions and Powers: Legislative Decree No. 112/59 provided in its fifty-seventh Article for the position of Government Commissioner before the General Disciplinary Council, which was entrusted to an Inspector General on the cadre of the Central Inspection, and Article 59 of the aforementioned Decree stipulated the powers of the Government Commissioner concisely. And Law No. 54/65 dated 2/10/65, which established a General Disciplinary Council for Civil Servants (which subsequently became the Higher Disciplinary Board), provided in Article 13 thereof - para. 6 - for the establishment and determination of the cadre of the Government Commissioner's Office pursuant to Schedule No. 2 attached to the aforementioned Law and amended by Decree No. 12662 dated 22/7/98. As for the powers of the Government Commissioner, mention thereof was made in Decree No. 7236/67 dated 8/5/67 (Regulations of the Higher Disciplinary Board) in Articles 11 - 12 - 13 - 31 - 32 thereof concisely, whereby certain points of his powers remained ambiguous and the possibility of clarifying them was left to case law. B - On the Works of the Government Commissioner's Office - On the reasons for the impossibility of establishing an annual program and the delay in preparing certain submissions The referral of an employee to the Higher Disciplinary Board takes place according to Article /58/ of Legislative Decree No. 112/59 by a decree or by a decision from the authority vested with the right of appointment, and he is also referred by a decision from the Central Inspection Board. And Article 3 of Decree No. 7236 dated 8/5/67 stipulates that referral to the Higher Disciplinary Board "takes place in accordance with the provisions of the laws and regulations applied in the administration to which the employee belongs". It is inferred from the texts mentioned above that the Government Commissioner cannot establish an annual program for the work of the Commissioner's Office following the example of the other General Inspectorates in the Central Inspection because his work depends solely on the volume of files referred to him by the Central Inspection or the concerned administrations. It was stated in Article 59 of Legislative Decree No. 112/59 that "the Government Commissioner studies the file of the case... then prepares a submission which he sends with the file to the Higher Disciplinary Board within a month from his receipt of the file". In practice, the administration frequently sends an incomplete file to the Higher Disciplinary Board or to the Government Commissioner containing only the referral decree and the violations attributed to the referred person, which obliges the Government Commissioner to request the administration to provide all the documents of the file provided for in Articles 4 and 5 of Decree No. 7236 /67 and to supply him with the administrative investigation supposed to be conducted in the administration to secure the elements of proof, and this despite the repeated circulars issued by the Presidency of the Council of Ministers regarding the necessity of complying with the legal texts and compiling a complete file for the referred person before sending it to the Commissioner's Office. And with the issuance of Law No. 227 dated 2/6/2000, the State Council became the appellate authority for all judgments issued by administrative courts, including the decisions of the Higher Disciplinary Board, which according to Article 13 of Law No. 54/65 dated 2/ 10/65 had not been subject to any avenue of recourse, including a request for annulment for excess of power or a request for compensation by way of full jurisdiction. And on 1/4/2003, the State Council issued Decision No. 74/2002 - 2003 quashing the decision of the Higher Disciplinary Board in the case of an employee in Electricité du Liban and returned the file to the Higher Board to examine the case in light of what was stated in the recitals of its decision, including that the Board had not relied on facts established before the criminal judiciary, which in this case had ruled to dismiss the public prosecution action against the petitioner due to the three-year statute of limitations and had not addressed the merits of the case. Therefore, the Government Commissioner became compelled to wait in preparing his submission on the merits until after the issuance of the decision of the competent criminal judiciary in the case when the employee is referred at the same time before the criminal judiciary and before the Higher Disciplinary Board, or until after the completion of the file, which postpones the commencement of the running of the one-month time limit for a long period due to the necessity of securing the elements of proof. Chapter Two The Central Inspection: Its Tasks and Capabilities First - Mission and Objective of the Central Inspection Second - Its Jurisdictions: a - With Respect to Administrations b - With Respect to Employees Third - Its Capabilities: a - Organizational Structure of the Central Inspection b - Rules and Procedures c - Human Resources The Central Inspection: Its Responsibilities and Capabilities The Central Inspection has been entrusted, pursuant to the texts that govern its affairs directly or that are related to it, in particular Article One of Legislative Decree No. 115/59 (Establishment of the Central Inspection), with jurisdictions and tasks which we detail as follows: First: Mission and Objective of the Central Inspection 1 - Oversight over Administrations and Employees: This is carried out through recording violations, investigating them, establishing responsibility, identifying those responsible therefor, and imposing disciplinary measures against them where necessary. 2 - Guidance: The Central Inspection undertakes the task of guiding administrations to address problems relating to the public service and the workflow therein, through studying the conditions therein, evaluating the work, and proposing organizational solutions. Second: Its Jurisdictions The jurisdictions of the Central Inspection include the following: With Respect to Administrations - All public administrations. - Public institutions (with the exception of the Council for Development and Reconstruction, the National Social Security Fund, the Banque du Liban, and the Public Institution for the Encouragement of Investments in Lebanon). - Municipalities (except for the deliberative and executive authorities therein). * In the financial field only: - The Judiciary. - The Army. - The Internal Security Forces. - General Security. - State Security. - Lebanese missions abroad. - The Lebanese University in all its branches and specializations. And indirectly - The Régie Libanaise des Tabacs et Tombacs of public utility. - The Agricultural, Industrial, and Real Estate Credit Bank. This is by way of oversight over the work of both the Government Commissioner and the Financial Controller for these administrations. With Respect to Employees: - All those who work in public administrations, public institutions, and municipalities in a permanent or temporary capacity, including civil servants, employees, wage earners, contractors, or collaborators, and everyone who draws a salary or wage from their funds, within the provisions of the texts to which they are subject. Furthermore, the Government may assign to the Central Inspection, on a permanent or emergency basis, new responsibilities by subjecting to its authority all other public institutions subject to the oversight of the Court of Accounts. Third: Capabilities a - Organizational Structure of the Central Inspection The Central Inspection consists of the following bodies: 1 - The Central Inspection Board: 2 - The Central Inspection Administration: - The Central Administration. - The General Administrative Inspectorate. - The General Engineering Inspectorate. - The General Educational Inspectorate. - The General Health, Social, and Agricultural Inspectorate. - The General Financial Inspectorate. - The Government Commissariat before the Higher Disciplinary Board. 3 - The Administration of Research and Guidance. 4 - The Administration of Tenders. Each administration and each general inspectorate is headed by a First Category employee, to whom are attached specialized inspectors or controllers belonging to either the Second or Third Category, and employees of the Second Category and below. The inspectors perform their tasks in the public administrations on the basis of special assignments and pursuant to annual programs approved by the Board, and as a result of their work they draw up reports which are submitted to the competent Inspector General to express his proposals, who in turn submits them to the President of the Central Inspection, who expresses his opinion thereon and presents them to the Board to decide upon them. Furthermore, the Administration of Research and Guidance seeks to improve the methods of administrative work, and exercises its tasks through what reaches it and what it reviews of the conditions of the administrations by means of its controllers, thus guiding the administrations to the means capable of raising the level of administrative work and increasing its effectiveness. As for the Administration of Tenders, it conducts the procurement transactions for supplies and works that reach it, by means of a special technical body. b - Rules and Procedures The Central Inspection is composed of two independent bodies: - The Investigation Body: It consists of inspectors who undertake the inspection of public administrations and the investigation of employees regarding committed disciplinary violations, and propose the measures that must be taken to regulate work and ensure its proper functioning.... - The Decision Body: It is composed of a special board that examines the reports and decides upon the penalties that must be imposed on offending employees, and issues the necessary recommendations. The inspectors review the matters that are the subject of inspection or investigation, audit the documents, registers, entries, and papers in the departments they undertake to inspect, study the replies of the employees to the faults attributed to them, record the facts and statements, and analyze them, and then as a result thereof draw up their final reports which the Inspectors General study and submit, accompanied by their proposals, to the President of the Central Inspection Board, who in turn draws up his opinion thereon. The Central Inspection Board examines the reports and issues in respect thereof either disciplinary decisions or recommendations of a guiding nature to improve work methods. c - Human Resources The following detailed table illustrates the current state of vacancy occurring in the various administrations of the Central Inspection. Conclusion This report contains a brief presentation of the reality of the administration. Like previous reports, it includes within its folds a number of guiding and organizational recommendations and solutions, and the difficulties that still impede the course of administrative work. The annual report for the year 2002 had public and private reactions, which resulted in the formation of a committee to study this report and propose the necessary solutions to overcome the difficulties arising from the problems mentioned in Chapter Three of the report. The committee drew up its report, highlighted these problems, and proposed the necessary solutions therefor without this being coupled with execution. These difficulties remained at the forefront of administrative concern, pushing the administration into further regression and decline, until the public administration became proverbial for favoritism, exploitation, deviation, indifference, backwardness, and maladministration. This is due to several considerations, as the vacancy in some Third Category posts remains as it is, added to it the vacancy of Second and First Category posts, especially First Category posts for some positions in the oversight bodies. In order to fill this shortage occurring in leadership establishments, some officials resort to circumventing the law by not filling the vacant posts and sufficing with resorting to cases of «acting assignment», which is a legal violation, in addition to being mostly a source of harm to the administration given the general lack of competence of the assigned person, his lack of influence over the employees subordinate to him, and his inability, by law, to take the decision necessary for the proper functioning of the public administration. Furthermore, no measure was taken to redress the injustice resulting from inequality in dealing with employees of the same status, which led to a feeling of frustration among employees, particularly those who bear heavier responsibilities and enjoy high competencies, and this reflected negatively on the proper functioning of administrative work. As for the parallel administration, complained of in some ministries and known as «advisors to the Minister», it remains as it is, and is indeed increasing, such that the advisor now has an advisor, exercising functional authority that does not belong to him, replacing the competent employee, and confusing and fragmenting administrative work, without accountability or oversight, because he is not subject to any oversight authority. The appointment of advisors is not limited to those from outside the administration; rather, some of them resort to attaching employees to themselves in violation of the law without these employees performing, in some cases, any task or work, and yet they collect their salaries in violation of the principle of «no pay without work». Add to that the non-completion of the restructuring of public administrations and the definition of the tasks of certain posts, and the shortening of the workflow of transactions in order to serve the citizen seriously and swiftly to spare hardship, and the weakness of administrative leaderships resulting from the poor selection of these leaderships and their lack of experience in the affairs of the public service, and the tendency among some of them to consider the public service a social prestige without seeking to carry out any work to develop the public administration and make it more suitable to serve the citizen. And 431/2003 Having reviewed the report of the Engineering Inspectors Messrs.: Elias Kosta, Amin Abdel Samad, and Younes Al-Rabih, and the Administrative Inspector: Mr. Rateb Al-Ayoubi dated 21/2/2003 and 29/4/2003, as a result of the investigation into the interruption of the electrical current in the areas of Beddawi, Minieh and into the cause of the explosion of the station transformer in the Deir Ammar area. Having reviewed the opinion of the Engineering Inspector General dated 14/5 /2003 Having reviewed the two opinions of the Administrative Inspector General dated 22/ 2/2003 and 17/5/2003 Having reviewed the opinion of the President of the Central Inspection dated 27 /5/2003 And whereas it appeared from the documents of the file that the Secretary General of the Council of Ministers requested from the Central Inspection, pursuant to his letter No. 193/9 dated 14/2/2002, and based upon the instructions of His Excellency the President of the Council of Ministers, to conduct a comprehensive and detailed investigation regarding the continuous interruption of the electrical current during the first half of the month of February of the year 2003 in certain areas of the North, in particular the areas of Deir Ammar, Beddawi and Minieh, and to set forth all the administrative, technical and technological reasons that led to that interruption and to determine the functional and personal responsibilities resulting therefrom, and that the Minister of Energy and Water requested on 7/2/2003, from the Central Inspection Administration to conduct an immediate technical and administrative investigation into the same subject and to propose what is appropriate as a result thereof, and the joint assignment No. 6/3/2003 and 2/4/2003 dated 14/2/2003 was issued to investigate the subject. And whereas it appeared from the investigation, that on 5/8/2002, a malfunction occurred in the main transformer that supplies the areas of Beddawi, Minieh and Deir Ammar with electrical current, and that the aforementioned malfunction could not have been forestalled by those concerned at the Electricité du Liban, and that the Establishment took the measures conducive to securing the repair of the transformer at the lowest possible cost, and also brought in a mobile station with a capacity of (20MVA) to secure the electrical current in the aforementioned areas, which in turn was subjected, at dawn on Saturday falling on 8/2/2003, to the burning of the internal coil of the transformer (Bobine) as a result of the occurrence of a short circuit therein (court Circuit) due to the climbing of a wild animal "mongoose" onto its three phases. And whereas it appeared from the mobile station that it was operating at its maximum load due to the continuous and heavy consumption of the electrical current resulting from the existence of numerous infringements on the network, when the "internal coil of the transformer" was subjected to burning, and that this method of operation leads to the loss by the transformer of some of its technical characteristics, and consequently to its breakdown upon the occurrence of any accidental incident or short circuit. And whereas it appeared from the Electricité du Liban that it brought in on 10/2 /2003 another mobile station following the breakdown of the first mobile station, and with the same capacity (20 MVA) which was transferred from Deir Nbouh under difficult conditions, and that this station exploded after its installation and its placement under the tension of 66KV before placing the load on it, and that the true causes of the explosion cannot be known except after dismantling the transformer, a matter which was impossible to carry out because the station is still connected to the network by way of (ByPASS).

Secretariat of the Board Session: 2/2003 Item: 9 Decision No. 24/2003 The Central Inspection Board, Having examined the file of the case registered under No. 16/4/2002 with all its contents. Having examined the report of the engineering inspectors Messrs: Georges Doumit, Issam Chabani, and Rola Abou Daher, dated 28/11/ 2002, following the investigation into the power outage across most of the Lebanese territory on 16/10/2002 Having examined the opinion of the Engineering Inspector General dated 27/ 12/2002 Having examined the opinion of the President of the Central Inspection 31/12/ 2002 Whereas it appears from the documents of the file that the Chairman of the Board of Directors and Director General of Electricité du Liban requested the Central Inspection, pursuant to his letter No. 9675 dated 17/10/2002, to conduct the necessary investigation into the power outage across most of the Lebanese territory on the morning of Wednesday, 16/ 10/2002, and that His Excellency the Minister of Energy and Water requested that investigations be conducted into the aforementioned outage, pursuant to his letter No. 4431 /W dated 21/10/2002, addressed to the Central Inspection in this regard, and Assignment Order No. 16/4/2002 was issued to investigate the matter. Whereas it appears from the investigation that a very strong lightning discharge occurred at dawn on Wednesday, 16/10/2002, on the /150/ kV transmission lines connecting the Jiyeh thermal power plant to the main transformer substation in Jamhour, which led to the power outage as a result of the aforementioned transmission lines being subjected to a sharp rise in voltage due to being struck by lightning. Whereas it appears that the insulators of the transmission line network, which was established more than thirty years ago, had lost their insulating capacity over the years, and leaked the current to the ground, which caused the protection relays to intervene to isolate the lines. Whereas it appears that the electricity network in general has doubled in size, and that the method currently followed to protect it is not commensurate with the emerging reality, which requires recommending the adoption of a scientific and organised protection method commensurate with the new realities arising on the network, and consequently requesting assistance from Electricité de France in its capacity as (the consultant) to Electricité du Liban, in order to establish temporary solutions to protect the network in its present state pending the completion of work on the new network. Whereas it appears that work on the high-voltage network (220K.V) has not been completed to date, and that this is due to the delay occurring in the issuance of certain corrections in the expropriation decrees pertaining thereto and the unavailability of the necessary appropriations, in addition to the occurrence of objections to the erection of electricity poles, as is happening in certain villages and towns (Kfarhaqel, Mansourieh...). Whereas it appears that it is impossible to execute protection works on the electrical network in a scientific and effective manner before completing the connection of all lines and substations in a final manner, which requires recommending the acceleration of the completion of the /220 kV/ network so that comprehensive protection of the electrical network may be executed in a final manner, and the strengthening of the connection between the /220/ and 150/ kV networks. Whereas it appears that coordination between the production plants, the substations, and the central administration is carried out by means of telephone communications due to the absence of a National Control Centre (Centre de Controle National), which requires recommending working towards the establishment of the aforementioned centre given its importance in monitoring the operations of energy production and distribution. Whereas it is necessary to close the case with respect to the liability of the employees, and to recommend to Electricité du Liban to conduct periodic maintenance of the protection and reading equipment in all electrical plants and substations. And after deliberation, and in light of the circumstances of the case. Decides 1 - To close the case with respect to liabilities. 2 - To recommend to Electricité du Liban to work on the following: - Cooperating with the experts of Electricité de France (E.D.F) in order to execute the protection operation for the Lebanese electrical network in a manner commensurate with its current reality and generalising this protection subsequently, once all elements of the network are stabilised. - Conducting periodic and regular maintenance of the transmission lines and the insulators pertaining thereto, and securing the necessary equipment for the production plants to enable them to operate in accordance with the applicable technical rules. - Removing the obstacles facing the /220/ kV network, and accelerating its completion so that comprehensive protection of the electrical network may be executed in a final manner and strengthening the connection between the / 220 kV and /150/ kV networks. - Establishing the automated National Control Centre (N.C.C). - Conducting periodic maintenance of the protection and reading equipment in all electrical plants and substations. A decision issued unanimously in Beirut on the fifteenth of January of the year two thousand and three. Signature The Inspector General Member of the Board Dr. Gerges Ghalmieh Director General of the Research and Guidance Administration Member of the Board Ali Fakih President of the Central Inspection President of the Board Fouad Haydamous To be notified to: - The Minister of Energy and Water (in reply to his letter No. 4431/W dated 21/10/2002). - Electricité du Liban. - The Civil Service Board. - The Engineering Inspectorate General. - The Bureau of the Central Inspection.

Following deliberation, and in light of the circumstances of the case. It was decided: 1 - To issue a written remark to each of Messrs.: the engineer......... and the engineering assistant........., and the specialist worker Mahmoud......... at Electricité du Liban for the reasons set forth in the body of this decision. 2 - To recommend to Electricité du Liban the following: a - To expedite the repair of the fault in the main transformer (70 MVA) in preparation for placing it into actual service, and to repair the fault existing in the transformer of the alternative station for use when necessary. b - To work on following up the matter of installing meters on the feeders of the camps in order to control energy consumption and protect the stations and networks, and to generalise this measure to include the feeders of villages, municipalities, and large neighbourhoods in all cities and regions. c - Not to place any of the equipment belonging to the Establishment back into service, in the event that it ceases operating for a certain period of time, except after subjecting it to tests and trials that guarantee the safety of placing it into service. d - To keep an external register of the equipment of the Establishment in which all maintenance, repair, and measurement operations carried out on each of them since their placement into service are recorded. 3 - To close the case with respect to the remaining points. A decision issued unanimously in Beirut on the eleventh of the month of June of the year two thousand and three. The Inspector General, Member of the Board, Dr. Gerges Ghalmieh; The Director General of the Administration of Research and Guidance, Member of the Board, Ali Faqih; The President of the Central Inspection, President of the Board, Fouad Haydamous. To be notified to - The Secretary General of the Council of Ministers (in reply to his letter No. 193/9 dated 14/2/2003). - The Minister of Energy and Water (in reply to his letter dated 17/2/ 2003). - Electricité du Liban. - The Civil Service Board. - The General Administrative Inspectorate. - The General Engineering Inspectorate. - The Bureau of the Central Inspection.

Whereas the explosion of the mobile substation brought from Deir Nbouh could have been avoided had the maintenance team tested the insulation resistance (MEGGER) prior to operating the substation and heated the engine oil to reduce the percentage of moisture therein, resulting from its not having been placed in service for a period of approximately one year and a half, prior to placing it under 66KV voltage, and whereas the failure to conduct all the necessary tests prior to operating the transformer entails disciplinary liability on the part of each of the Engineer........., the Assistant Engineer Mr.........., and the Specialist Worker Mr.........., for their negligence in performing the functional duties imposed by the provisions of the laws and regulations in force. Whereas it was established that the operation of installing and operating the said substation, which took place in the open air, during the holiday recess, under stormy weather conditions, and amidst a pressing protest movement by citizens demanding the restoration of electric current to the area, contributed to the haste of the competent employees in placing the substation under voltage without conducting the necessary tests in order to save time and with a view to securing the restoration of the electric current, a matter which mitigates the liability incurred by the employees whose names are mentioned above, without removing it, which requires taking the appropriate disciplinary measures against them, pursuant to Regulatory Order No. 5/69, in force at Electricité du Liban. Whereas the overload on the substations and networks is caused by the multitude of infringements committed thereon, and the failure to install meters for certain areas supplied by these substations, in addition to the fact that the Beddawi camp for Palestinian refugees is supplied with electric current from the substation located inside the Deir Ammar plant in an unregulated manner, and whereas the Board of Directors of Electricité du Liban had previously taken a decision to address the issue of supplying the Palestinian camps with electric current through installing meters at their feeders to control and monitor the process of consuming electric energy and billing it, which requires recommending working on following up the issue of installing meters at the feeders of the camps in order to control the process of energy consumption and protect the substations and networks, and extending this measure to include the feeders of villages, towns, and large neighbourhoods in all cities and regions. Whereas it is required to recommend that Electricité du Liban expedite the repair of the fault in the main transformer (2MVA) in preparation for placing it in actual service, and the repair of the fault existing in the transformer of the alternative substation for its use when necessary, and not place any of the equipment belonging to the Establishment back into service in the event that it has ceased operation for a certain period of time until after subjecting it to the tests and trials that guarantee the safety of placing it in service, and keep a special register for the equipment of the Establishment in which all maintenance, repair, and measurement operations carried out on each of them since their placement in service shall be recorded.
