3- The grade of the end-of-year examination shall be deemed the third third of the annual grade

4- The final result shall be determined by calculating a general average of these thirds

Second- 1- A pupil in the intermediate stage shall be deemed passing if he obtains an average of 10/20 or above in the total of his final grades and the average does not fall below 5/20 in each of the foreign language subjects and below 6/20 in the remaining subjects 2- A pupil shall be deemed passing in the first secondary year - Scientific Branch if he obtains an average of 10/20 or above in the total of his final grades and the average does not fall below 5/20 in the foreign language subject and below 8/20 in the remaining subjects

3- A pupil shall be deemed passing in the first secondary year - Literary Branch if he obtains an average of 10/20 or above in the total of his grades and the average does not fall below 6/20 in the subjects of the foreign language and its literature, and below 5/20 in mathematics and sciences, and below 8/20 in the remaining subjects

4- A pupil shall be deemed eligible for a make-up examination in the first secondary year and in both the Scientific and Literary branches if he obtains an average of 10/20 of the total of his final grades and the grade of any subject falls below the average required for passing and specified in paragraphs 2 and 3, and the pupil shall not be entitled to sit for a make-up examination in more than two subjects

5- Certain pupils excelling in conduct and effort shall benefit from catch-up grades decided by the class teachers if they do not obtain the final average of 10/20, provided that this average does not fall below 1/2

9/20 6- A pupil shall be deemed failing:

a- If the cases mentioned in paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4 above do not apply to his situation or if he does not obtain the required grades in the make-up examination b- If he is absent from two tests regardless of the reasons or if he is absent from the end-of-year examination without a legitimate excuse

Third- 1- Every pupil who is absent from any scheduled test for illegitimate reasons shall receive a zero therein, and if he is absent therefrom for a legitimate reason of which the administration is convinced, the scheduled test shall be repeated or the daily effort grade shall replace the test grade

2- If the pupil is absent from the end-of-year examination for a legitimate reason, he may repeat it on the date specified by the principal of the secondary school, whether during the first registration period or during the second registration period, and in the event of absence from this examination due to illness, the pupil shall prove this at the time by a medical report sent on the first day of the examination to the secondary school, and he must also report to the administration of the secondary school upon the expiry of the period of the report, and the principal of the secondary school may verify the validity of the submitted medical report

3- Every pupil caught cheating or attempting to cheat during tests and written recitations or the examination shall receive a zero in the subject that was the object of the cheating, in addition to the disciplinary penalties that the principal of the secondary school may impose, and if the pupil repeats the cheating or attempt to cheat more than twice, he shall receive a zero in all subjects of the test or examination in which the violation took place and shall be excluded from the remaining subjects of the test or examination

Conduct Certificate: The conduct certificate shall be granted to pupils in accordance with the following assessment: Conduct Mark Very Good 20-18 Good 17-16 Fair 15-13 Satisfactory 12-10 Unsatisfactory Below 10

1- The ushers, attendants and hired labourers of the secondary school shall work in accordance with the instructions of its Principal or the General Supervisor in all matters relating to the secondary school, and in particular ensuring its cleanliness, preserving its furniture and guarding the main gate of the secondary school, especially during the daily recess periods.

2- The General Supervisor shall organise the working hours of the attendants and hired labourers assigned to clean the secondary school in accordance with a schedule communicated to the persons concerned. 3- The attendant shall refer to the General Supervisor or the supervisor in charge in all matters relating to the pupils.

4- The attendant must clean the school building in accordance with the instructions issued in this regard.

5- In the event that the usher or hired labourer fails to perform his duties or commits an act detrimental to the secondary school, its staff body or the pupils, the Principal of the secondary school may impose upon him the disciplinary penalties provided for by the regulations in force, subject to the approval of the Director of Secondary Education.

Prohibitions: All employees of the secondary school shall be prohibited from:

1- Engaging in any ideological, political or partisan activity of whatever kind (Civil Servants Regulations

2- Disclosing official information of which he becomes aware by virtue of his office, in particular the deliberations taking place in the Teachers' Council, the Discipline and Guidance Council or the subject committees.

3- Smoking in the classroom.

4- Any corporal punishment of whatever kind and any reprimand incompatible with upbringing and personal dignity. 5- Conducting and selling lotteries, and selling books and school supplies of various kinds for their own benefit.

Rules of Correspondence: Employees of public secondary schools must observe the following in their official correspondence:

1- Following the rule of administrative hierarchy.

2- Stating the subject at the top of the letter on the left side.

3- Stating the name of the secondary school in which they work.

4- Stating the financial number.

5- Writing the name clearly beneath the signature.

6- Stating the date.

Physical Education Teachers: Members of the teaching staff who teach the subject of physical education in public secondary schools shall be subject to the provisions of this Decision in all matters that do not conflict with their special regulations, and they must attend to the maintenance of the sports equipment and apparatus; one of them may also be assigned to coordinate sports activity in the secondary school.

The School Fund:

1- A financial fund called "the School Fund" shall be established in every secondary school, from which expenditures shall be made in cases required by the interest of the secondary school and the interest of the pupils.

2- This fund shall be financed from the financial contribution of the pupils and from various other revenues.

3- This fund shall be supervised by a committee composed of the principal of the secondary school, the general supervisor therein, and one member of the teaching staff chosen by the teachers' council. The committee shall keep an account book in which the amounts collected and the purposes of their expenditure shall be recorded.

4- The disbursement of any amount exceeding two hundred Lebanese pounds must be accompanied by prior approval from the Directorate of Secondary Education.
Exceptional Suspension: School buildings may not be evacuated or suspended on working days except with prior permission from the Directorate of Secondary Education.

School Publications: Public secondary schools shall have the right to issue school magazines or periodic publications of a purely educational nature, provided that all their materials are submitted in advance to the principal of the secondary school or the person assigned to that matter and obtain his written approval.

School Celebrations: The secondary school is prohibited from holding public celebrations to which parents are invited except with prior permission from the Director of Secondary Education, with the exception of the celebration of Teacher's Day, Arbor Day, Independence Day, Martyrs' Day, sports events, and exhibitions of drawing and handicrafts belonging to the pupils. As for recreational parties for pupils to which parents are not invited, they shall be organized under the supervision of the school administration.

Leaving Lebanon: No staff member of the public secondary schools may leave Lebanese territory during holidays and leaves before obtaining written permission from the Director of Secondary Education, and he must: in this case submit an application in accordance with the rules prior to the date of travel, stating therein the places to which he intends to travel, the reasons calling for that, and the period he will spend abroad.

Commencement of Work:

1- A transferred staff member must be notified of his transfer decision through the principal of the secondary school from which he was transferred: and must lodge with the principal of the secondary school to which he is transferred a certificate from the principal of his former school showing the date of his cessation of work therein, and the principal must submit the said certificate to the competent authority with his remarks regarding the commencement of work by the transferred teacher.

2- The principal of the secondary school must notify the competent authority by a certificate of the date of commencement of work of the new staff member attached to the secondary school.

The male betrothed acquires the capacity to marry upon completing the eighteenth year of age, and the female betrothed upon completing the seventeenth year of age.

The Sheikh Akl or the denominational judge may grant permission to marry to a male adolescent who has completed the sixteenth year of his age and has not completed the eighteenth year if it is medically proven to him that his condition bears that, provided that the permission of either of the two Sheikhs Akl or the denominational judge is subject to the permission of the guardian of the male adolescent.

The Sheikh Akl or the denominational judge may grant permission to marry to a female adolescent who has completed the fifteenth year of age and has not completed the seventeenth year if it is medically proven to him that her condition bears that and her guardian permits.

If the Sheikh Akl or the denominational judge grants permission for the marriage of a male adolescent and a female adolescent without the permission of the guardian, each of the male adolescent and the female adolescent shall have the right to request the annulment of the marriage within a period of six months commencing from the date of attaining the age set forth in the first Article.

No person at all may give in marriage a minor boy who has not completed the sixteenth year or a minor girl who has not completed the fifteenth year.

Nor may an imbecile man or an imbecile woman, or a man or a woman afflicted with one of the contagious diseases that prevent marriage, are incurable, and subsequently cause harm to the children, be given in marriage.

The Sheikh Akl or the denominational judge shall, before granting permission to marry, verify the soundness of the spouses from imbecility and contagious diseases by requiring them to produce a health certificate from a physician affiliated with one of the two Orders of Physicians in Lebanon, after conducting the medical examinations required by the competent authorities; objection may be made to this certificate before the denominational judge, and his decision thereon shall be subject to the avenues of review.

If an adult woman whose age ranges between the seventeenth and the twenty-first year requests to marry a person, the Sheikh Akl or the denominational judge shall notify her guardian thereof, and if the guardian does not object within a period of fifteen days from the date of his notification, or objects and his objection is deemed misplaced, the Sheikh Akl or the denominational judge shall grant permission for their marriage.

The guardian in marriage is the agnate in his own right in order of priority, provided that he is legally competent; thus, a minor boy, an insane person, and an imbecile shall have no guardianship over anyone at all.

If the applicant for marriage has no guardian, or if his guardian does not possess legal capacity, guardianship shall be exercised by the Sheikh Akl or the denominational judge or whomever he deputizes for this purpose.
A contract of marriage with the wife of another or with a woman observing his waiting period ('iddah) is prohibited and void.
Polygamy is prohibited; a man may not have two wives at the same time, and if he does so, his marriage to the second is void.
No one may remarry his divorced wife.

The marriage of women within the prohibited degrees of uterine kinship to a man between whom and them there is blood kinship is prohibited and void. The aforesaid women are of four classes:

1 - The man's mother and his grandmothers.

2 - Daughters and granddaughters.

3 - Sisters, and the daughters of brothers and sisters unconditionally, and their granddaughters.

4 - Paternal aunts and maternal aunts unconditionally.

A man is likewise prohibited from marrying his wet nurse or his foster sister by suckling.

The marriage of women to a man between whom and them there is affinity by marriage is prohibited and void. The aforesaid women are of four classes: 1- The wives of sons and grandsons 2- The mothers of wives and their grandmothers unconditionally 3- The wives of fathers and grandfathers 4- The daughters of wives and their granddaughters

A contract of marriage is concluded by offer and acceptance by the two parties at the session of the contract in the presence of witnesses; the witnesses may be from among the ascendants and descendants of the suitor and the betrothed woman, provided that their number is not less than four, and the contract must be executed in writing and signed by the two spouses and their witnesses, and if one of the spouses is unable to attend the session of the contract, an authorised proxy may sign it on that spouse's behalf pursuant to a written power of attorney certified by the mukhtar or the person acting in his stead, provided that the amount of the dower (mahr) is stated in the power of attorney or its determination is left to the discretion of the proxy, and provided that this power of attorney is annexed to the contract.
Offer and acceptance in marriage shall be in express words, and likewise in betrothal, and the sign of a mute person shall take the place of the spoken expression.
A contract of marriage shall not be valid unless it is solemnised by the Sheikh Akl or the judge of the confession (qadi al-madhhab) or the person deputised by him to solemnise it.

(As amended by the Law of 2 July 1959) Either of the two Sheikhs Akl or the denominational judge shall appoint one or more marriage officiants (ma'dhun) to perform the marriage contract in each sub-district (nahiya) or town as required, and the marriage officiant may not perform the contract before obtaining a special written permission to do so from either of the two Sheikhs Akl or the denominational judge.

(As amended by the Law of 2 July 1959) After the marriage officiant draws up the contract, he shall send it to either of the two Sheikhs Akl or the denominational judge for its ratification and registration, and the effect of this contract shall run as from the date of its conclusion.

The Sheikh Akl or the denominational judge shall register these contracts in a special register, the pages of which are stamped by him and numbered consecutively. The contract shall be returned to its holder within one month at the most from the date of its deposit with the denominational court for its registration.

The wife's dower (mahr) and her maintenance (nafaqa) shall be binding upon the husband as from the performance of the valid contract, and the right of mutual inheritance shall be established between them.
The wife has no right to claim the deferred portion of the dower before the arrival of one of the two terms, divorce or death.

After receiving the prompt dower and the performance of the lawful marriage contract, the wife must reside in her husband's house if it is a lawful dwelling, and she must likewise go with him if he wishes to go to another town and there is no serious impediment. A lawful dwelling is a dwelling in which the likes of the spouses can reside.

However, if the wife refuses to join the lawful marital dwelling or to go with her husband to another town and there is no serious impediment, the deferred dower shall be forfeited by her.
The husband must treat his wife well and treat her as an equal to himself, and the wife must also obey her husband in lawful marital rights.

The dower (mahr) is the property that is due by virtue of marriage and accrues against the husband in favour of the wife by the mere conclusion of a valid contract with her, and it is in two parts: prompt and deferred. The prompt portion accrues against the husband in favour of the wife by the mere existence of a valid contract, whereas the deferred portion accrues upon the arrival of one of the two terms, divorce or death, and is subject to the provisions stipulated in this Law.

Its amount shall be specified in the marriage contract, and if the amount of the dower is not specified in the contract, the judge shall award the dower of an equal (mahr al-mithl).

When the dower specified in paper currency, or what remains thereof, falls due, the value of the amount due shall be assessed at the time of calculation by the number of ounces of gold on the date of the contract in accordance with the records of the Bank of Lebanon, and the amount due shall be paid in gold in kind or the equivalent of its value in the prevailing paper currency in circulation.

The provisions of this Article shall apply to dowers specified in the marriage contract in the paper currency in circulation prior to the promulgation of this Law, provided that five years or more have elapsed since the marriage contract.
The dower may be specified and deferred in whole or in part.

Either the male fiancé or the female fiancée may withdraw from the betrothal without incurring any liability. However, with regard to betrothal gifts, if the withdrawal is on the part of the male fiancé, he may not recover anything he has given to the female fiancée, whether or not it remains in existence at the time of his withdrawal. If the withdrawal is on the part of the female fiancée, she must return everything the male fiancé has given to her; if it is still in existence, she shall return it in kind, and if it has perished at the time of her withdrawal, she shall return its equivalent or its value, unless there is a stipulation between them, in which case it shall be acted upon.

However, jewellery of gold and precious stones given by the male fiancé to his fiancée to be recorded in the marriage contract as prompt dower must be returned to the male fiancé.

If either spouse dies after the conclusion of a valid contract, the entire dower, in both its parts, becomes binding in full.

However, if divorce occurs between the spouses after the conclusion of a valid contract, the provisions of Articles 48 and 49 of this Law shall apply to the dower.

Maintenance is what a person spends on his dependants and his wife, and it includes food, clothing, lodging, medical treatment, and domestic service for a wife of social standing, or who is disabled or ill, and its performance is obligatory by mutual consent of the two parties or by a judgment of the judge.
After maintenance has been assessed, it may be increased or decreased according to changes in prices or a change in the financial condition of the spouses as to prosperity or hardship.

If a present husband abstains from maintaining his wife and the wife claims maintenance, the judge shall assess the maintenance according to the condition of both parties as from the day of the claim, and he may order that she be given an advance for such period as he specifies.

If the husband is unable to maintain his wife and the wife claims maintenance, the judge shall assess the maintenance as from the day of the claim as a debt owed by the husband, and shall authorise the wife to borrow in his name.

If the husband leaves his wife without maintenance and disappears, or absents himself by going to a distant place, or goes missing, the judge shall assess the maintenance as from the day of the claim after proof is established of the marriage, the absence, and his being missing, and after administering the oath to the wife that the husband did not leave her maintenance and that she is not divorced, and he shall authorise the wife, in case of need, to borrow in the husband's name.

Where the judge authorises the indigent wife to borrow pursuant to the provisions of the preceding articles and she borrows from a relative who is obliged to provide for her maintenance, such relative shall have a right of recourse against the husband only. However, if she borrows from a stranger, the creditor shall have the option to claim against the husband or the wife.

Where the absent husband has property in the possession of a third party or owed by him, and the depositary or debtor acknowledges the property in his possession or owed by him, or denies it and the wife proves the same before the competent civil court, then, after the wife establishes proof of the marriage and swears an oath that the husband did not leave her maintenance and that she is not divorced, maintenance shall be assessed for her out of that property, or out of its proceeds, or out of its price, with effect from the date of the application.
The accumulated amount of maintenance assessed judicially or by mutual consent shall not lapse upon divorce or upon the death of either spouse.

If the wife leaves her husband's house without a lawful cause, or if she is in her own house and prevents her husband from entering it before requesting that he move her to another house, her maintenance shall lapse for the duration of the continuance of such marital disobedience.
A marriage contract shall not be dissolved by divorce except by a judgment of the confessional judge.
A man's divorced wife shall never be lawful to him after the issuance of the judge's judgment of separation between them.

If it appears to the wife who is free from defects preventing sexual intercourse, before or after marriage, that her husband is afflicted with an illness with which she cannot cohabit with him without harm, such as leprosy, vitiligo, syphilis, and the like, she may apply to the judge and request separation. If the illness is incurable, the judge shall adjudge separation forthwith; and if there is hope for the cessation of the illness, the judge shall postpone the separation for two years, provided that he decides forthwith upon temporary separation between the spouses; and if the illness does not cease during this period, and the husband does not consent to divorce, and the wife insists upon her request, the judge shall adjudge separation. However, infirmities such as blindness and lameness shall not constitute a ground for separation.
If the husband is afflicted with impotence, the wife may request separation once it is medically established that such impotence is incurable.

If the husband becomes insane after the conclusion of the marriage contract and the wife applies to the judge requesting judicial separation, the judge shall adjourn the consideration of the application for a period of one year, and if the insanity does not cease during this period and the wife insists, he shall rule for judicial separation.

The spouses may annul the marriage contract by mutual consent, and such annulment shall be effected by declaring it in the presence of two witnesses before the judge, who shall issue a judgment thereon.

If the husband is convicted of the offence of adultery, the wife may request judicial separation, and if the wife is convicted of the offence of adultery and her husband divorces her for this cause, the deferred dower shall lapse from him.

The judge shall have the right to order the husband or the wife convicted of the offence of adultery to pay damages.

If the husband is sentenced to a penalty of imprisonment for a period of ten years or more and serves five consecutive years thereof, the wife may request judicial separation at the end of this period.

If the husband disappears or is absent for a period of three years and it is impossible to collect maintenance from him, the judge shall rule for judicial separation upon the request of the wife. However, if it is possible to collect maintenance, her request shall not be granted unless five years have elapsed since the absence without interruption, and if the present husband is ordered to pay maintenance and it is impossible to collect it from him for a period of two years, the wife may also request judicial separation.

If a judgment is issued for the annulment of the marriage of a woman due to the absence of the husband and she marries another and then the first husband appears, his appearance shall not necessitate the annulment of the latter marriage.

If a dispute or discord arises between the spouses and either of them applies to the judge, the judge shall appoint an arbitrator from the family of the husband and an arbitrator from the family of the wife, and if there is no one among their families who possesses the qualifications of an arbitrator, the judge shall choose an arbitrator from outside their families.

The judge may appoint a social or psychological specialist of experience and competence in cases that so require to act in the place of the two arbitrators.

The specialist or the two arbitrators shall ascertain the causes of the discord between the spouses and endeavour to reconcile them, and if reconciliation between them is not possible and the fault and persistence are on the part of the husband, the judge shall separate them and award the wife the whole or part of the deferred dower, and if it is on the part of the wife, the judge shall rule to forfeit the deferred dower in whole or in part, and the judge may in both cases order the spouse who is in the wrong to pay the other the compensation for damages to which they are entitled.

If it appears to the judge that the divorce is not justified by a lawful reason, he shall award the wife compensation for damages in addition to the deferred dower, provided that moral and material damage are taken into consideration.

The waiting period is four months, commencing from the date of the divorce, judicial separation, or death of the husband, and the waiting period of a pregnant woman ends upon delivery or miscarriage of the foetus.
No waiting period is required if the divorce or annulment occurs prior to consummation and sexual intercourse.
The waiting period commences from the date of occurrence of the divorce, annulment, or death of the husband, even if the wife was not aware of the death.
Maintenance during the waiting period is due to a divorced woman from her husband, and is not due to a woman whose husband has died, whether she is pregnant or not pregnant.
The mother has the prior right to the custody and upbringing of the child during the subsistence of the marriage and after separation, if she possesses the required capacity.

It is required of the female custodian that she be of age, of sound mind, trustworthy, physically healthy, capable of raising the child with a proper upbringing and safeguarding him, that she preserve the image of the father and his family with the child in custody, that she enable the father to perform the duties of his guardianship, and that she not be married to a person who is not within the prohibited degrees of marriage to the child in custody, and there is no difference in that regard between the mother and other female custodians.

If the female custodian, whether a mother or someone other than a mother, marries a husband who is not within the prohibited degrees of marriage to the minor, her right to custody shall lapse and pass to the next in entitlement among the female custodians; if no entitled woman qualified for custody is found, the guardian of the minor may take him, and once the impediment ceases, the right of custody shall revert to the entitled female custodian.

The right of custody derives from the mother's side; thus, the nearest in degree after the nearest on her side shall be considered, and a relative connected through the mother shall take precedence over a relative connected through the father when they are of equal degree of proximity. If the mother dies, or marries a relative, or is not qualified for custody, her right shall pass to her mother; if she is not living or is not qualified for custody, it shall pass to the father's mother, howsoever high, upon the lack of qualification of the nearer female relative; then to the minor's sisters, with precedence given to the full sister, then the uterine sister, then the consanguine sister; then to the sisters' daughters, with precedence given to the daughter of a full sister, then of a uterine sister; then to the maternal aunts - of the minor, with precedence given to the full maternal aunts, then the uterine maternal aunt, then the consanguine, to the daughter of the consanguine sister; then to the brother's daughters in like manner; then to the minor's paternal aunts, with precedence given to the full paternal aunt, then the uterine, then the consanguine; then the mother's maternal aunts; then the father's maternal aunts; then the paternal aunts of the mothers and fathers, in this order.

If there are no women within the prohibited degrees of marriage, or if such women exist but are not qualified for custody, custody shall pass to the agnates according to the order of inheritance; thus, precedence shall be given to the father, then the grandfather, then the full brother, then the consanguine brother, then the sons of the full brother, then the sons of the consanguine brother, then the full paternal uncle, then the consanguine paternal uncle. If those entitled to custody are equal within the same degree, precedence shall be given to the most suitable among them, and then to the eldest of them in age.

If there is no agnate entitled to custody, or if one exists who is not qualified therefor, the female ward under custody shall not be delivered to him, but shall be given to a cognate within the prohibited degrees of marriage. Precedence shall be given to the maternal grandfather, then the uterine brother, then his son, then the uterine paternal uncle, then the full maternal uncle, then the consanguine maternal uncle, then the uterine maternal uncle. The daughters of the paternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, and maternal aunt shall have no right to the custody of males, whereas they shall have the right to the custody of females. The sons of the paternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, and maternal aunt shall have no right to the custody of females, but rather they shall have the custody of males. If the female ward under custody has only a paternal uncle's son, the judge may grant him her custody if he deems him fit; otherwise, he shall deliver her to a reliable and trustworthy woman.

The remuneration for custody is distinct from the maintenance allowance, and the entirety of both shall be incumbent upon the father if the minor has no property; if the minor has property, no part thereof shall be incumbent upon his father unless he donates it voluntarily.

If the child's mother is his custodian and she is divorced, or married to a person within the prohibited degrees of marriage to the minor, or observing the waiting period for the father, she shall be entitled to remuneration. If the female custodian has no dwelling in which to keep the indigent minor, his father shall be obliged to provide housing for both of them. If the ward under custody requires a servant and his father is solvent, the father shall be obliged to provide one. Female custodians other than the mother shall be entitled to remuneration.

If the mother of a child, whether male or female, refuses to exercise custody over the child gratuitously, and the child has no property, and his father is insolvent, and no female relative within the child's prohibited degrees of marriage volunteers to do so, the mother shall be compelled to exercise custody over him, and her remuneration shall constitute a debt owed by his father, and she may borrow with the permission of the judge if she is insolvent.

If there is a female volunteer qualified for custody among the relatives of the child within the prohibited degrees of marriage, and the father is solvent and the minor has no property, the mother, even if she requests remuneration, has a greater right than the volunteer; however, if the father is insolvent and the boy has property or has no property, the mother shall be given the choice between keeping him free of charge and handing him over to the volunteer, and if she does not choose to keep him free of charge, he shall be removed from her and delivered to the volunteer, and the mother shall have the right to see the child and attend to him; and if the father is solvent and the boy has property and the volunteer is a stranger, the boy shall not be handed over to her, but rather shall be delivered to his mother for a remuneration of equivalence, even if from the property of the minor.

A - The period of custody of a boy ends upon his completion of the twelfth year of age, and the period of custody of a girl ends upon her completion of the 14 fourteenth year.

The father must take the child if he is capable of raising the ward with a sound upbringing and preserving and caring for him by himself or through another.

If the child has neither a father nor a grandfather, the ward shall be left with the female custodian if his mother is qualified for his custody and accepts it. Otherwise, he shall be delivered to the nearest agnate relative if he is a boy. As for a girl, she shall not be delivered to anyone other than a relative within the prohibited degrees of marriage, and if there is no agnate relative, the ward shall be left with the female custodian unless the judge sees that someone else is more entitled to him than her.

If the period of custody ends and the ward is mentally ill or a person with special needs, the judge may keep him with the mother if she requests that and it becomes apparent to him that the interest of the ward requires that; thereupon, maintenance of the ward and remuneration for her care shall be due to the female custodian, and the assessment thereof shall be for the judge in accordance with the provisions of this Law.

The right of custody does not lapse by waiver thereof, but rather by religious and legal impediments, and it returns upon their cessation.

B - If the distant one is with one of the parents, he may not prevent the other from visiting him, and if the parents do not agree on fixing the times and place of visitation, the judge may fix the time and place of visitation while observing the gradation of its duration according to the circumstances in a manner that achieves the interest of the minor, provided that it is not less than once a week.

Visitation may not take place in police stations or gendarmerie posts, nor in a place where moral values are not observed. The provisions of this Article shall apply to lawsuits that are still pending before the confessional courts at first instance and on appeal, and to lawsuits relating to custody in which judgments have been issued and are still under execution due to the ward not having reached the age specified in the judgment.

The father is prohibited from taking the child out of the town of his mother without her consent so long as her custody subsists; if the divorced husband takes his child from her due to her marriage to a stranger and he has no custodian other than her, it shall be permissible for him to travel with him until the right of his mother, or of the person who stands in her stead in custody, returns.

A divorced mother may not travel with the child in her custody from his father's town to a distant town without his father's permission, and no female custodian other than the mother may in any case remove the child from the place of his custody except with his father's permission, or with the judge's permission if he has no father.
Maintenance of its three kinds is incumbent upon the father for his poor minor child, whether male or female, until the male reaches the age of earning and is able to earn, and the female marries.

The father is obliged to provide maintenance for his poor adult child who is incapable of earning due to an infirmity that prevents him from earning, and maintenance for the poor adult female unless she marries.

No one shares with the father in the maintenance of his child unless he is insolvent and incapable of earning, in which case he is treated as one who is dead, maintenance falls from him, and it then becomes incumbent upon the person on whom the maintenance of the son is incumbent in the absence of the father.

The mother is obliged before all other relatives to spend on her child in the event of his father's insolvency; and if both parents are insolvent and have children who are entitled to maintenance, the nearest relative, if solvent, shall be ordered and compelled to provide it, and the expenditure of the relative shall be a debt upon the insolvent father for which recourse may be had against him if he becomes solvent, whether the person spending is a mother, a grandfather, or another.

If the father of the poor minor is destitute and he has solvent relatives among his ascendants, then if some of them are heirs to him and some of them are non-heirs and they are equal in degree of kinship and lineal connection, the heir is preferred and is obliged to provide the maintenance of the minor; if they are not equal in degree of kinship and lineal connection, the nearest in lineal connection is considered and is obliged to provide maintenance; and if his ascendants are heirs, his maintenance is upon him in proportion to their entitlement in inheritance.

If the relatives of the poor child whose father is destitute are partly ascendants and partly collaterals, then if one of the two classes is an heir and the other is a non-heir, the ascendant, not the collateral, is considered and is obliged to provide maintenance, whether he is the heir or not; and if both the ascendants and the collaterals are heirs, inheritance is considered and maintenance is incumbent upon them in proportion to their shares in the inheritance.

If the father is absent and has children among those whose maintenance is incumbent upon him, and he has property in their possession, or property deposited with someone, or a debt owed by him, and the property is movable, the judge may rule that expenditure be made on them out of it; however, if the property of the absent person is immovable, nothing of it shall be sold for maintenance, but permission shall be given to borrow against it for the maintenance of the children.

The father shall not be obliged to provide maintenance for the wife of his poor minor son unless he has guaranteed it; however, he shall be ordered to expend upon her, and it shall be a debt due to him for which he shall have recourse against his son if he becomes solvent.
The solvent child, whether major or minor, male or female, shall be obliged to provide maintenance for his poor parents, grandfathers, and grandmothers.

The maintenance of an insolvent woman married to someone other than the father of the child shall be incumbent upon her husband, not upon her child; however, if her husband is insolvent or absent and her child by another is solvent, he shall be ordered to expend, and it shall be a debt due to him for which he shall have recourse against her husband if he becomes solvent or returns.

A poor son shall not be obliged to provide maintenance for his poor father unless the son is capable of earning and the father is incapable of earning, and a needy mother holds the status of a father incapable of earning; and if the poor son has dependents, he shall join his needy parents to his dependents and expend upon all of them, and he shall not be compelled to give them anything separately.

If the son is absent and has property deposited with someone or a debt owed by him, the judge may award maintenance therefrom for his two poor parents; and if the depositary expends the deposit or the debtor the debt upon the parents of the absent person without his permission or without the order of the judge, he shall be liable to the absent person for what he expended and shall have no recourse against his parents.

Inheritance shall not be taken into consideration in the obligation of maintenance incumbent upon children towards parents; rather, lineality and kinship shall be considered so as to give precedence to the nearest, then the next nearest.

Maintenance shall be due to every poor kinsman within the prohibited degrees of marriage from those of his solvent relatives who would inherit from him, even if a minor, in proportion to their share of inheritance from him.

The father, even if of modest means, shall have guardianship over his minor children and his major children who lack legal capacity, whether male or female, over the person and over property, even if the minors are in the custody of the mother and their relatives.

If the child attains majority in a state of imbecility or insanity, the guardianship of his father over his person and his property shall continue; and if he attains majority of sound mind and subsequently becomes imbecilic or insane, the guardianship of his father shall revert by judgment of the judge.

If the father is upright and of praiseworthy conduct, or of unblemished reputation and trustworthy in the preservation of property, he may dispose of and trade with the property of the minor in a customary and proper manner.

If a father possessing the qualifications mentioned in the preceding Article sells any of his child's movable or immovable property, or purchases anything for him, or leases out any of his property with gross lesion, the judge shall appoint a guardian to petition for the annulment of the contract of sale or lease, and the annulment shall not depend upon the lease after majority. And if the child attains maturity before the expiration of the term of the valid lease, he shall not be entitled to rescind it, whereas the contract of purchase shall be enforceable against the legal guardian and not against his child.

If the father is of corrupt judgment and ill management, or is partially sentenced to a penalty that prevents him for a long period from performing the duties of guardianship, it shall not be permissible for him to sell the property of the minor, even if there is a benefit therein for the minor, save by permission of the judge.

If the father is a spendthrift who wastes the property of his child and is not trustworthy in preserving it, the judge may appoint a guardian, remove the property from the hand of his father, and deliver it to the guardian to preserve it.

It shall not be permissible for the father to purchase the property of his child for himself, nor by selling his own property to his child, nor to pledge his own property to his child or take in pledge the property of his child for himself, nor to lend the property of his child or borrow it, unless the judge permits the same and appoints a guardian to conclude the contract; and it shall not be permissible for the father under any circumstances to donate anything from the property of the minor, even for consideration.

A guardian is a person whom another has placed in his stead to dispose of his estate after his death, or whom the judge has appointed where there is a need therefor; thus a guardian is of two kinds: a chosen guardian whom the testator appoints during his lifetime, and an appointed guardian whom the judge designates.

Whoever is appointed as guardian by testament and accepts the guardianship during the lifetime of the testator shall be bound thereby, and he shall not be entitled to withdraw therefrom after the death of the testator save for compelling reasons approved by the judge.

A person appointed as guardian without his knowledge shall have the option, after the death of the testator, to accept the guardianship if he so wishes or to reject it if he so wishes, and in the case of rejection, he must notify the judge thereof.

Guardianship may be conferred upon the wife, the mother, and other women, and upon one of the heirs or others. The mother or another person may be appointed as supervisor alongside the guardian. The mother shall have priority over all other guardians.

A chosen guardian must have completed eighteen years of age, and a court-appointed guardian must have completed twenty-one years of age, and a chosen guardian, like a court-appointed guardian, must be of sound mind, trustworthy, of good conduct in management, and in possession of all civil rights.
If the chosen guardian does not possess the qualifications mentioned in the preceding Article, the judge may remove him and replace him.

The judge may not remove the chosen guardian if he is of upright character and capable of carrying out the guardianship; if he is incapable, the judge shall join another person to him or replace him, and if he subsequently becomes capable, the judge shall reinstate him as guardian.
The judge may remove the guardian whenever his breach of trust is proven before him.
Any person who has not completed eighteen years of age, whether male or female, shall be deemed a minor, and a guardian shall be appointed for him if he has no natural guardian or chosen guardian.
Once the minor reaches the age mentioned in the preceding Article, the guardianship over him shall cease by operation of law and his property shall be handed over to him.

A guardian shall not be discharged of liability by delivering to the minor his property if, upon attaining majority, he was insane, an imbecile, afflicted with simple-mindedness, or a prodigal. Delivery in such cases shall only be valid when made to the guardian appointed by the judge.
The duties of the guardian are to preserve the property of the minor and to develop it as far as possible.
The guardian may dispose of all the movables of the minor, even if the minor has no need of their price, provided that he obtains the permission of the judge therefor.

The guardian may not sell the immovables from the property of the minor except for one of the following lawful justifications: 1- That the sale of the real property be for the benefit of the minor, by being sold for more than its equivalent value 2- That the deceased owe a debt which cannot be satisfied except from the price of the real property 3- That there be in the estate an unrestricted (absolute) bequest and there be no goods or cash therein from which to execute it, whereupon so much of the real property shall be sold as is necessary to execute the bequest. 4- That the minor be in need of maintenance and have neither cash nor goods. 5- That its expenses and the state taxes accruing thereon exceed its yields. 6- That the real property be on the verge of ruin and the minor have no cash enabling him to carry out repairs

The authorisation of the judge is required for the effectiveness of a contract of sale based on one of the lawful justifications mentioned in the preceding Article. The judge may not grant the authorisation except after conducting a thorough investigation proving the aforementioned lawful justifications.

The guardian, whether testamentary or court-appointed, must, prior to commencing the duties of guardianship, draw up, through the person delegated by the judge to inventory the estate, a statement of the minor's movable and immovable property and submit it, accompanied by the supporting documents, for the endorsement of the judge thereon.

The testamentary or court-appointed guardian must submit at the end of every year an account to the judge of the minor's income and expenditure, and if he abstains after being warned, he shall be deemed negligent and removed.
The guardian may not sell his own property to the minor, or purchase for himself, or sell to any of his ascendants or descendants, the property of the minor.
The guardian may not settle his own debt from the property of the minor, nor lend it or borrow it, nor pledge his own property with the minor, nor take the minor's property in pledge.

The guardian may not appoint another as agent for what he is permitted to do himself in respect of the minor's property except by leave of the judge, save for agency for litigation and pleading, and the guardian may dismiss the agent.

If the deceased appointed two guardians or the judge selected them, neither of them may act alone in disposing of property except in the following cases:

1- Preparing the deceased for burial

2- Litigating on behalf of the minor

3- Demanding debts, but not collecting them.

4- Paying debts owed by him that are established by a judgment or by an official instrument.

5- Executing a specific bequest for a specific poor person.

6- Purchasing indispensable necessities for the minor.

7 - Accepting a gift

8- Returning a loan for use and established deposits.

9- Returning what the deceased usurped after a judgment of usurpation

10- Selling crops feared to perish.
If the testator appointed two guardians and one of them accepted the guardianship and the other refused, the judge may join another to him.
The mother's guardian may not dispose of anything that the minor inherited from an estate other than his mother's estate.
The guardian may not release the debtor of the deceased from the debt nor remit any part of it except by leave of the judge.

The guardian may enter into a settlement regarding the debt owed to the deceased and the debt owed to the orphan if they have no evidence and the debtor is in denial, provided that the approval of the judge is obtained for that.
The guardian may enter into a settlement regarding a right claimed against the deceased or the orphan if such right is established by an official deed or by a judicial judgment.
An acknowledgment by a testamentary guardian of a debt, specific property, or a bequest against the deceased shall not be valid.

If the testamentary guardian discharges a debt against the deceased without proof derived from an official instrument, without a judgment of the judge, or without the ratification of the adult heirs in respect of their shares, he shall be liable to make it good.

When the minor comes of age, he shall be entitled to demand an accounting from the testamentary guardian, and the testamentary guardian shall be bound to provide a detailed account, and the burden of proof shall lie upon him if the expenditure was not authorised by the judge or accounted for with the testamentary guardian.

If the testamentary guardian dies leaving the property of the ward unidentified, the liability to make it good shall lie upon his estate, and it shall be recovered in specie if found therein, or as a privileged debt if it has been consumed, prior to the distribution of the estate.
The testamentary guardian must deliver to the ward his property under the supervision of the judge or of whomever he deputises on his behalf.

The judge shall place under interdiction a lunatic, an imbecile, a prodigal, and a person of simple mind, and shall appoint a guardian over him after verifying the same by testimony and medical reports, or by either of them as the case may require.
When the judge places any of the aforementioned persons under interdiction, he shall make public to the people the cause of the interdiction.
The presence before the judge of the person sought to be placed under interdiction shall be required, and if that is impracticable, the judge must proceed in person to hear him where necessary.
The dispositions of an insane person before and after interdiction shall not be valid; however, his dispositions before interdiction shall be valid if made during a state of lucidity.
The dispositions of a mentally defective person and of an unwary person before and after interdiction shall not be valid unless they are of pure benefit to them:

The dispositions of a prodigal before interdiction are permissible and effective, whereas his dispositions after interdiction and its announcement shall not be valid, with the exception of marriage, divorce, maintenance of those whom he is obliged to maintain, and a bequest for charitable purposes if he has no heir.

The property of an insane person, a mentally defective person, a prodigal, or an unwary person shall not be delivered to him after the cessation of interdiction except pursuant to a judgment of the judge establishing the cessation of such cause.
A missing person is an absent person whose whereabouts are unknown and who is not known to be alive or dead.

If the missing person left an agent prior to his absence to preserve his property and manage his affairs, his agent shall not be dismissed by reason of his being missing unless his breach of trust or negligence becomes apparent, and the heirs shall not take the property out of his hands; the agent may not repair the immovable properties of the missing person if they are in need of repair except with the permission of the judge.

If the missing person did not leave an agent, the judge shall appoint on his behalf therein to preserve his property, collect his yields and a quarter of his immovable properties, and receive his debts acknowledged by his debtors.
The appointment of a curator shall be subject to the same conditions as the appointment of a testamentary guardian.

The curator may sell, with the permission of the judge, such of the movable property of the missing person as is subject to rapid deterioration, and such of his immovable property as is falling into ruin if the absent person has no funds enabling its restoration. The curator shall keep the price under the supervision of the judge in order to deliver it to the missing person if he appears alive, or to such of his heirs as are entitled to it after judgment of his death is pronounced.
The curator may expend from the property of the missing person upon those whom the latter is bound to maintain and upon what is required for the preservation of the property of the missing person.
The judge may grant the curator permission to litigate on behalf of the missing person.

The curator shall submit at the end of every year an account to the judge of the income and expenditure of the missing person, and if he abstains after being served with notice, he shall be deemed in default and shall be dismissed.

The judge shall adjudge the death of a missing person who is most likely to have perished after the expiration of ten years from the date he went missing; whereas in cases where he is not most likely to have perished, the matter of the period after which the death of the missing person is adjudged shall be left to the judge, after inquiring about him by all means conducive to knowing whether the missing person is alive or dead, and this period may not be less than ten years.

After judgment is pronounced of the death of the missing person in the manner set forth in the preceding article, his estate shall be divided among his heirs existing at the time of the judgment, provided that they shall not be entitled to dispose of any part of the inheritance before the lapse of two years from the judgment of death becoming final and conclusive.

If the missing person returns or it is established that he is still alive after judgment of his death is pronounced, such of his property as remains in the hands of his heirs he shall recover in kind, and for such of it as has been expended he shall claim its value as of the date of its disposal.
The minimum period of gestation is one hundred and eighty days and the maximum thereof is three hundred days.

If a wife gives birth, during the subsistence of a valid marriage, to a child at the completion of one hundred and eighty days or more from the time of its conclusion, his parentage from the husband shall be established; and if she delivers him at less than one hundred and eighty days since he married her, his parentage from him shall not be established unless he acknowledges him expressly or impliedly.

If the husband disavows the child born at the completion of one hundred and eighty days from the marriage contract, he shall not be disavowed unless he disavows him within one month from the date of birth if he is present, and from the date of his knowledge of the birth if he is absent.

The parentage of the child shall not be negated in the following cases: 1- If the husband disavows him after the lapse of the time set forth in the preceding Article 2- If he disavows him after acknowledging him expressly or impliedly 3- If the child is delivered dead and he then disavows him 4- If he disavows him after a judgment establishing his parentage according to religious law

If a divorced woman or a woman whose husband has died gives birth to a child at less than three hundred days from the time of the divorce or death, the parentage of her child shall be established. However, if she delivers him at more than three hundred days, his parentage shall not be established.

If the wife claims to have given birth and the husband denies it or denies the identity of the child, the birth shall be established, just as the identity of the child shall be established, by the testimony of the midwife and such women as attended the birth.

The parentage of the child shall be established if he is born at less than three hundred days from the time of separation if the husband or the heirs have acknowledged the pregnancy or the pregnancy was manifest and not concealed.

In the event of denial, parentage shall not be established for the child of a wife between whom and her husband the absence of meeting has been established from the side of the contract, nor shall parentage be established for the child of a wife who delivered him after three hundred days from the husband's absence from her.
A bequest is a transfer of ownership deferred until after death by way of the donor.

For a bequest to be valid, it is required that the testator be of full age, of sound mind, acting of his own free will, and possessing the legal capacity to make a gratuitous disposition, and that the subject matter of the bequest be capable of being transferred in ownership after the death of the testator.
A bequest shall not be executed if the estate of the testator is exhausted by debt, unless the creditors release him or ratify the bequest.
A bequest of the whole estate or of part thereof shall be valid, whether made in favour of an heir or a non-heir.
A legatee shall be deprived of what was bequeathed to him if he commits the premeditated or intentional killing of the testator.
A bequest is permissible for all charitable purposes.
Difference of religion and denomination shall not prevent the validity of a bequest.

The legatee shall acquire ownership of the subject matter of the bequest upon the death of the testator who persisted in his bequest, unless the legatee rejects the bequest; if he rejects it, his share of the bequest shall be distributed in accordance with the statutory shares of inheritance.
The testator may revoke the bequest in whole or in part, and may introduce into it or alter therein whatever he wishes.

If the bequeathed property perishes in the possession of one of the heirs of the testator without transgression, he shall not be liable therefor; however, if he consumes it, he shall be liable therefor.

If one of the legatees dies before the testator and the testator does not amend his will before his death, then if the deceased legatee has an heir, his share shall revert to his heirs according to the statutory share, and if he has no heir, his share shall revert to the living heirs of the testator.

If the testator and the legatee die at the same time and it is not proven which of them died before the other, the bequest shall become the right of the heirs of the legatee; however, if the legatee has no heir, the bequest shall be distributed among the heirs of the testator according to the Sharia statutory share.

If the testator makes a bequest before marriage and then marries and is blessed with a child, or makes a bequest after marriage when he had no child and is then blessed with a child, this bequest of his shall become void and his estate shall be distributed according to the Sharia statutory share, subject to the provisions of Article 169 of this Law. However, if he is not blessed with a child, the bequest shall be executed after the husband or wife is given the Sharia statutory share of the estate.

The testator has the option during his lifetime to authenticate and register his will before the sectarian judge or one of the two Sheikhs Aql. A registered will is enforceable without a judgment from the judge. An unregistered will, however, shall not be executed except after the issuance of a judgment by the judge validating it.

The legatees or one of them must apply to the judge requesting a judgment validating the will within a period of two years from the date of the testator's death, and if he fails to do so, his right to claim the bequest shall lapse. The provisions of the aforementioned Article shall not apply against a minor, an absentee, or a mentally deficient person. The original will shall be kept with the judge, and the interested party shall be given a certified copy thereof.
The judge may delegate one of the religious men to draw up or authenticate the will, and the delegate must submit it to the judge for registration if the testator so requests.

If the testator is in a foreign country, he may authenticate his will before the competent official authority in that country. The will shall not be executed in Lebanon unless it is granted an enforcement formula by the sectarian judge in accordance with the procedures observed for the enforcement of foreign judgments in Lebanese territory.

The will shall be registered in the register of the judge, and the testator shall affix his signature in the register in the presence of the judge and the witnesses to the will, or at least two of them, and the witnesses shall affix their signatures in the register together with the testator; the judge shall then authenticate the transaction carried out before him, and the copy retained in the possession of the testator shall be endorsed with the authentication clause entered in the register.

If the testator is illiterate, his acknowledgement of his will before the judge shall be taken by affixing his thumbprint in the register after the judge has read out the contents of the will to him in the presence of its witnesses, or in the presence of at least two of them.

The will may be kept secret, in which case the testator shall place his will inside an envelope which he shall seal with red wax in the presence of the judge and with the seal of the court, and shall sign it together with the judge and four witnesses; the judge shall then draw up a record thereof, which shall be entered in the register of wills, and a certified copy thereof shall be given to the interested party, and the sealed envelope containing the will shall be kept with the judge.

After the death of the testator, the envelope shall be opened in the presence of the interested parties, and the will shall be read out in their presence, registered in the register of wills and kept with the judge, and the interested parties shall be given a certified copy thereof.

If the testator wishes to retrieve his secret will in order to revoke it or amend it, the judge shall draw up a record to that effect, which shall be signed by the judge, the testator and the instrumental witnesses.

If one of the interested parties applies for the issuance of a judgment of death and determination of heirs, the judge shall rule on the distribution of the estate in accordance with the will drawn up and authenticated in accordance with this Law, and in the absence of a will, the estate shall be distributed in accordance with the Sharia rules of succession.
In the event of death intestate, or in the event of the invalidity of the will, the estate shall be distributed in accordance with the Sharia rules of succession.

In matters of inheritance, reference shall be made to the rules of the Sharia fixed shares of succession, with the exception of the rules thereof relating to the following:

- In the event that the deceased has no male children, but has female children, one or more daughters shall in this case be deemed a residuary heir in her own right, excluding other heirs from the inheritance, and shall inherit the entire estate of her decedent after the sharers of fixed portions have taken their fixed portions. If there are several of them, the shares shall be distributed among them equally.

- Exclusion by deprivation among the descendants of the deceased: the descendants of a descendant who died before the death of his decedent shall stand in his place and take his share as if he were alive.

Recourse shall be had, regarding the governance of the endowment (waqf), its binding nature, its exchange, its exploitation, the guardianship over it, the designation of its beneficiaries, and the distribution of its revenue, to the deeds of the endowment or the practice prevailing since antiquity, and to the religious (Sharia) provisions and the laws in force.

In all matters falling within the jurisdiction of the denominational judge (Qadi al-Madhhab) and for which no special provision is made in this Law, the aforementioned judge shall apply the provisions of Islamic law (Sharia), the Hanafi school, and all legal texts that do not conflict with Islamic law (Sharia).

This Law shall be published in the Official Gazette and all laws regulations contrary to it and inconsistent with its content shall be repealed.
